(1.5.1.1) He wept; because he wept, that is the origin of Rudra’s name, "Rudra. (1.5.1.1–2) What flowed from his eye became silver-gold; therefore, silver-gold is not to be given as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), for it is born of tears.

(1.5.1.2) He who gives on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) will have weeping in his house before a year has passed; therefore, one should not give on the sacrificial grass. That Agni said, "Let me have a share, and then this [gift] shall be yours. They replied, "The re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) shall be yours alone. He said, "He indeed shall prosper who establishes an Agni having me as its deity.

Pūṣan established him; through him, Pūṣan prospered. Therefore, cattle are called *pauṣṇa* (belonging to Pūṣan). Tvaṣṭṛ established him; through him, Tvaṣṭṛ prospered. Therefore, cattle are called *tvāṣṭra* (belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ).
Manu established it; through it Manu prospered. Therefore, offspring are called "descendants of Manu" (*mānavya*).

Dhātṛ established it; through it Dhātṛ prospered. Dhātṛ is indeed the Year; therefore, offspring and cattle are born following the Year. He who thus knows the prosperity of the re-establishment of the fires [attains it].
He who knows its kinship in this way indeed prospers; he becomes possessed of kinsmen.
When the fire has been established, it seeks its own portion and rushes toward the progeny and cattle of the sacrificer.
He should remove it and establish it again; thus he causes it to prosper through its own portion, and furthermore, this is its pacification.

(1.5.1.4) One should establish [the fires] under the Punarvasus; for the Punarvasus are indeed the lunar mansion of the re-establishment of the fires. Having established them under their own deity, he becomes endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*).
(1.5.1.4) He establishes them with *darbha* grass for the sake of freshness.
(1.5.1.4) He establishes them with *darbha* grass; verily, having won them from the waters and the plants, he establishes them.
There is a sacrificial cake on five potsherds; for there are five seasons; verily from the seasons he wins it and bestows it.
(1.5.2.1) Verily, he who extinguishes the sacred fire casts away the sacrifice and the cattle.
(1.5.2.1) There is a sacrificial cake on five potsherds; the sacrifice is fivefold and cattle are fivefold; verily, he wins both the sacrifice and the cattle.
(1.5.2.1) He who extinguishes the sacred fire is indeed a slayer of the hero among the gods.
(1.5.2.1) No Brahmins devoted to the sacred law have ever eaten his food in the past.
(1.5.2.1) The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are in the *paṅkti* meter.
The sacrifice is fivefold; man is fivefold. Having offered a hero to the gods, he restores Agni once again.
There are one hundred syllables; man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers. He finds firm standing in life and in power.
Or, when the fire that has been established does not prosper, he desires a greater share; in that everything belongs to Agni, that itself is his prosperity.

Speech indeed becomes confounded in the house of him who extinguishes the fire; the sacrificer is liable to perish following that confounded speech. There are case-endings (*vibhaktayaḥ*) for the separation of speech and to prevent the sacrificer’s ruin. He performs the case-ending; he thereby makes the *brahman* itself. He sacrifices in a low voice (*upāṃśu*); just as one who has found desirable wealth hides it, so it is with that. He announces the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering to Agni; just as one who has found desirable wealth desires to go forth openly, so it is with that.
(1.5.2.3) Having uttered the case-ending, he pronounces the *vaṣaṭ* with the *prayāja*; thus he does not depart from his proper place.

(1.5.2.3–4) The sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is indeed the sacrificer, and these two oblations are cattle. In that he offers these two oblations on both sides of the sacrificial cake, he encloses the sacrificer himself on both sides with cattle.
(1.5.2.4) "The *yajus* has been performed; the materials have been gathered," they say. "The materials need not be gathered, nor need the *yajus* be performed."
(1.5.2.4) Moreover, the sacrificial materials must indeed be collected; the Yajus formula is to be performed for the success of the sacrifice.

(1.5.2.4) A chariot repaired again is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), as is a garment mended again, and an ox released again; this is for the success of the re-establishment of the sacred fires. (1.5.2.4) He offers the Agnihotra with the verse: "Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues..."
(1.5.2.4) From whichever place it has been deposited, from that very place he wins it back.

(1.5.2.5) He who extinguishes the fire is indeed a slayer of the heroes among the gods; Varuṇa is his creditor. Therefore, one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Varuṇa. Whomsoever he slays and whosoever is his creditor—both he satisfies with their respective portions. The sacrificer does not come to ruin.
The earth by its abundance, the sky by its width, and the mid-air by its greatness—within your lap, O Goddess Aditi, I place Agni, the eater of food, for the sake of obtaining food.
(1.5.3.1.b) This spotted bull has come; he has reached his mother again, and as he moves toward heaven, he reaches his father.
He shines across thirty realms; Speech has taken refuge in the winged one. Carry [the offering] toward him with the days.
From his out-breathing comes the in-breathing; moving within, he illumines the radiant spheres. The Mighty One has revealed the heavens.
Whatever you, O Agni, the enraged one, cast away through fury or through misfortune—that of yours we restore well-fashioned; we kindle you once again.
That which of yours, sown by wrath, was scattered across the earth—that the Ādityas, all the gods, and the Vasus gathered together.
(1.5.3.2.g) May the mind, as light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it join together this interrupted sacrifice. May Bṛhaspati extend this for us; may all the gods rejoice here.

Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues, seven the seers, and seven your beloved abodes. The seven officiating priests worship you in seven ways; fill the seven wombs with clarified butter.
(1.5.3.3.i) Return again with strength, O Agni, return with food and long life; protect us again from every side.
(1.5.3.3.k) Return with wealth, O Agni; overflow with a stream that nourishes all, from every side.

Leka, Saleka, Suleka—may those Ādityas, enjoying the clarified butter, partake of it. Keta, Saketa, Suketa—may those Ādityas, enjoying the clarified butter, partake of it. Vivasvant, Aditi, Devajūti—may those Ādityas, enjoying the clarified butter, partake of it.
"Earth by its breadth, heaven by its width," he says; verily, with this blessing he establishes him.
The serpents, as they were growing old, reflected; Kasarṇīra Kādraveya saw this mantra, and thereby they cast off their worn-out bodies.
He establishes the Gārhapatya fire with verses addressed to the Queen of Serpents; having made it new again and free from decay, he establishes it.
(1.5.4.1) Now, even though the earth was purified, food did not approach her; she saw this mantra. (1.5.4.2) Thereupon, food indeed approached her.
In that he establishes the *gārhapatya* fire with the verses of the Queen of Serpents (*sarparājñī*), it is for the attainment of food.
Moreover, he thus establishes it so that it is firmly established upon this very earth.
When he says, "What thou hast scattered while angry," he thereby takes away that [anger] from him. When he says, "We kindle thee again," he truly kindles him.
When he says, "That of thine which was scattered by wrath," he restores him by means of the deities.

The sacrifice of one who extinguishes the fire is indeed torn asunder. He approaches with a verse addressed to Bṛhaspati; for Bṛhaspati is the Brahman among the gods. By means of the Brahman, he thus joins together the sacrifice.
"May this [Brahman] join together this torn sacrifice," he says for the sake of continuity.
"May all the gods rejoice here," he says; by means of continuity alone, he assigns the sacrifice to the gods.
"Seven are thy kindling-sticks, O Agni, seven thy tongues," he says. There are indeed sevenfold seven dear bodies of Agni; verily, he wins them.
With the words, "Return with strength, together with wealth," he offers two oblations on both sides of the sacrificial cake; thus he encloses the sacrificer on both sides with strength and wealth.

The Ādityas went from this world to that world. They became thirsty in that world; having returned again to this world and established the sacred fires (*agni*), they offered these oblations (*homa*) and prospered. They went to the heavenly world.
He who establishes the fires after the *punarādheya* (re-establishment of the fires) should offer these oblations; he attains that very prosperity which the Ādityas attained.
(1.5.5.1.a) As we approach the sacrifice, let us utter a prayer to Agni, who hears us even from afar.
Following his ancient splendor, the bold ones have milked the bright milk from the seer who wins a thousandfold.
Agni is the head of heaven, the summit, the lord of this earth; he quickens the seeds of the waters.

(1.5.5.1ḍ) This one has been established here as the first by the establishers, the Hotṛ-priest, most skilled in sacrifice, to be praised at the rites—he whom Apnavāna and the Bhṛgus caused to shine forth, the wonderful, all-pervading one, for every clan within the woods.

(1.5.5.1.e) Both of you, Indra and Agni, I call upon to aid; both of you, together, I call to rejoice in the gift. Both of you are givers of food and riches; I invoke you both for the winning of strength.

(1.5.5.2.f) This is your seasonal birthplace, from which, once born, you shone forth. Knowing it, O Agni, ascend it, and then increase our wealth. (1.5.5.2.g) O Agni, you purify our lifespans; send us strength and nourishment. Drive misfortune far away.
(1.5.5.2) O Agni, purify yourself, you who are skillful in action; bestow upon us splendor and heroic strength. (1.5.5.3) Granting me nourishment and wealth.
O Agni, purifier, with your radiant and pleasant tongue, O god, bring the gods hither and worship them.
(1.5.5.3.k) O purifying, radiant Agni, bring the gods here to us, to our sacrifice and our oblation.
Agni, whose vows are most pure, is pure as a sage, pure as a seer; offered with oblations, he shines forth in purity.
(1.5.5.3ṃ) O Agni, your pure, bright, and radiant flames rise upward; your lights are your rays of fire.
(1.5.5.3ṇ) O Agni, you are the giver of life; give me life. (1.5.5.4) O Agni, you are the giver of splendor; give me splendor. O Agni, you are the protector of the body; protect my body.
(1.5.5.4.o) O Agni, whatever is deficient in my body, fill that up for me. (1.5.5.4.p) O Citrāvasu, may I reach your end in safety.

(1.5.5.4.q) Kindling thee for a hundred winters, may we kindle thee, radiant ones, full of vigor, O maker of vigor; glorious, O maker of glory; possessing noble heroes, O invincible one—O Agni, the subduer of rivals, upon the highest firmament.
(1.5.5.4.ṛ) O Agni, thou hast united with the splendor of Sūrya, with the praise of the seers, and with thy beloved abode.
(1.5.5.4.ṣ) Thou art, O Agni, possessed of the splendor of Sūrya; endow me with long life, with splendor, and with progeny.
(1.5.6.1.a) I behold all offspring, the human progeny of Iḍā; may they all abide in our home.

(1.5.6.1.b) You are the waters; may I partake of you. You are greatness; may I partake of you. You are power; may I partake of you. You are vigor; may I partake of you. (1.5.6.1.c) O wealthy ones, rejoice! In this world, in this fold, in this dwelling, in this womb—stay right here; do not depart. May you become many for me.
(1.5.6.2ḍ) You are the *saṃhitā*, possessing all forms; come to me with vigor, with abundance of cattle, and with the increase of wealth.
(1.5.6.2.e) May I nourish your thousandfold prosperity; may your riches rest within me.
(1.5.6.2.f) Day by day, O Agni, illuminator of the darkness, we approach you with prayer, bringing homage.
(1.5.6.2.g) The one who reigns over the sacrifices, the radiant guardian of the cosmic order, increasing in his own abode.
O Agni, be easy of access to us like a father; attend to us for our well-being.

O Agni, be our closest [friend]; be a protector, auspicious and providing a secure refuge. To you, O most radiant and shining one, we now pray for the welfare of our friends. Agni is the Vasu, renowned for wealth; come hither, most brilliant one, and grant us riches.
(1.5.6.3.k) With vigor I look upon you; with vigor look upon me. With the increase of wealth I look upon you; with the increase of wealth look upon me.
(1.5.6.3ḷ) You are the *iḍā*s, honey-makers; enter me, being pleasant and intoxicating. May I thrive through your thousandfold prosperity! (1.5.6.4) May your riches rest within me!
We meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he inspire our thoughts.
O Brahmaṇaspati, make Soma the one who brings forth praise, even as you did for Kakṣīvān, the son of Uśij.
(1.5.6.4.o) Never are you barren, O Indra; you never fail the donor. More and more, O Maghavan, does your gift as a god increase.
(1.5.6.4.p) O Agni, we place you around us as a fortress—you, the inspired sage, O powerful one—of bold appearance day by day, the breaker of the treacherous foe.

(1.5.6.4.q) O Agni, lord of the house, may I be a good lord of the house through you as lord of the house; may you be a good lord of the house through me as lord of the house. For a hundred winters, I invoke this blessing, full of light, for my progeny; I invoke this blessing, full of light, for so-and-so.

(1.5.7.1) That which is without *sāman* is indeed no sacrifice. When he says, "Approaching the sacrifice with *sāman*," he thereby yokes the *stoma* for him. When he says, "We have approached,"—for offspring and cattle are what approach this world—he thereby approaches offspring, cattle, and this world.
(1.5.7.1) When he says, "Following his ancient splendor,"—for the ancient [place] is the heavenly world—he thereby ascends to the heavenly world.
(1.5.7.1–2) When he says, "Agni is the head of heaven, the summit," he thereby makes him the head of his equals; furthermore, he establishes himself from the world of the gods in the world of men.
"This one was first established here by the establishers," he says; thus he makes him preeminent.
"Both of you, Indra and Agni, I invoke," he says; thus he wins vigor and strength.
"This is your seasonal womb," he says; wealth is indeed cattle; thus he wins cattle.

He worships with six [verses]. There are indeed six seasons; verily, he finds firm support in the seasons. He worships with the next six [verses]; they amount to twelve. Twelve months are a year; verily, he finds firm support in the year.

Just as a man, a horse, or a cow grows old, so does the fire, once established, grow old. After a year has passed, he worships with the *āgnipāvamānī* verses; verily, he makes it new again and ageless, and moreover, he purifies it.

(1.5.7.3) He approaches [the fire]; this is indeed his application (*yoga*) that approaches him. (1.5.7.4) This is indeed his self-restraint (*dama*) that approaches him; this is indeed his supplication (*yācñā*) that approaches him. It is just as when one who is inferior, having brought something to a superior, pays homage—that is exactly what it is like.

(1.5.7.4) "O Agni, you are the giver of life; give me life," he says, for he is indeed the giver of life. "O Agni, you are the giver of splendor (*varcas*); give me splendor," he says, for he is indeed the giver of splendor.

(1.5.7.4) "O Agni, you are the protector of the body; protect my body," he says. (1.5.7.5) For he is indeed the protector of the body. "O Agni, whatever is deficient in my body, fill that up for me," he says; "whatever is deficient in my progeny and cattle, fill that up for me"—this is what he truly says. (1.5.7.5) "O Citrāvasu, may I safely reach your further shore," he says. Citrāvasu is indeed the night. Formerly, the Brāhmaṇas were afraid of this night before its dawning; [by saying this] he wins the dawning itself.

"Kindling thee for a hundred winters," he says. Man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers; verily, he establishes himself in life and power. This is indeed a spear with a barb; with this, the gods used to strike down the hundredfold hosts of the Asuras. In that he places a kindling-stick with this [verse], the sacrificer hurls a hundred-slaying thunderbolt at his enemy to lay him low, so that there is no failure.

“O Agni, you have united with the splendor of the sun,” he says; this indeed means, “May I become that which you are. “You, O Agni, are possessed of the splendor of the sun,” he says; he thereby invokes this very blessing for himself.
(1.5.8.1.a) "I behold all creatures," he says; as many domestic animals as there are, those very ones he wins.
(1.5.8.1) "Ye are water; may I partake of your water."
"Thus he says, for these are waters (*ambhas*).
'Ye are greatness; may I partake of your greatness,' he says, for these are greatness."
(1.5.8.1) "You are power; may I share in your power," he says, for these [plants] are indeed power. (1.5.8.1) "You are strength; may I share in your strength."
(1.5.8.1) Thus. (1.5.8.2) "They have brought vigor, for these are vigor," he says.
(1.5.8.2) "O wealthy ones, rest here!
he says; for the wealthy ones (*revatī*) are indeed cattle; verily, he causes cattle to rest within himself.
"Stay right here; do not go away," he says;
thus he makes them firm and non-departing.
One fire is built with bricks, another is built with animals; you are the *saṃhitā* (the connected one), possessing all forms.
(1.5.8.2) With these words he touches the calf; he thus brings it close and makes him rich in cattle.
(1.5.8.3) He who stands in worship before the Āhavanīya fire falls away from this world. He stands in worship before the Gārhapatya fire; verily he finds firm support in this very world.
Moreover, he pays homage specifically to the Gārhapatya.
He worships with *gāyatrī* verses; the *gāyatrī* is indeed brilliance, and thus he places brilliance within himself.
Moreover, that he recites this triplet is for the sake of continuity.
Indeed, it is after the *gārhapatya* fire that two-footed heroes are born.
He who, knowing thus, worships the Gārhapatya fire with the verses consisting of two feet.
"A hero is born from his mouth.
"With vigor I look upon you; with vigor look upon me," he says;
thus he invokes this very blessing.
He says, "That desirable [splendor] of Savitṛ," for the sake of impulsion; "the Soma-presser, the one who makes sound."
Thus he says; verily he wins the drinking of Soma.
"Make [it], O Brahmaṇaspati," thus he says for the sake of impulsion.
(1.5.8.4) "The one who makes the Soma resound," he says; verily, he wins the drinking of Soma. (1.5.8.4) "O Brahmaṇaspati, make [it so]... he says.
Thus he says; verily he wins spiritual luster. "Never art thou barren," thus he says; he does not dwell in a barren night.
He who, knowing thus, worships Agni with the words, “O Agni, we [take] thee around as a fort” (RV 10.87.22), thereby places this very enclosure around him so that nothing may spill.
“O Agni, lord of the house,” he says; this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula. “A hundred winters.”
Thus he says:
"May I kindle thee for a hundred winters"—
this is indeed what he thereby says.
He utters his son’s name; verily, he makes him an eater of food.

He should say, "I invoke that blessing, full of light, for the sake of progeny. For one whose son has not yet been born, a son who is radiant and endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*) is born.
"I invoke this blessing, full of light, for such-and-such a person," he should say if a son has been born to him; thus he bestows splendor and sacred luster upon that child.
(1.5.9.1) He offers the Agnihotra.
Whatever indeed belongs to the sacrificer as his own property,
that he pours forth as seed into the organ of generation.
For Agni is indeed procreation; moreover,
he burns even the plants that have reached their end,
and from that they are born again in greater abundance.
When he offers the evening oblation, he indeed pours forth seed;
with the morning oblation, he brings that very seed to birth.
That seed, once poured forth, is not brought to birth unless it has been transformed by Tvaṣṭṛ.
(1.5.9.1) As long as Tvaṣṭṛ fashions the forms of the emitted seed, so long indeed does it come into being.
(1.5.9.2) He who sacrifices is indeed the divine Tvaṣṭṛ;
he approaches with many [verses].
(1.5.9.2) He indeed transforms the many forms of the emitted seed;
(1.5.9.2) he is truly born;
(1.5.9.2) he becomes greater day by day—he who, knowing thus, worships Agni.
Day belonged to the gods, night to the Asuras.
Those Asuras, together with whatever wealth and property of the gods was to be known, entered into the night. The gods, feeling themselves deprived, reflected [upon this].
They saw: "The night belongs to Agni; cattle belong to Agni. Let us praise this very Agni; being praised, he will give the cattle back to us.
They praised Agni. Being praised by them, he drove the cattle out from the night toward the day for them. Having recovered the cattle, those gods fulfilled their desires.
He who, knowing thus, pays homage to Agni becomes possessed of cattle.
(1.5.9.4) Aditya went from this world to that world.
Having gone to that world, he looked back again toward this world.
Having returned to this world, he was afraid of death.
"For this world is as if joined with death. He reflected:
"I shall praise this very Agni; once praised, he will cause me to go to the heavenly world."
He praised Agni. Being thus praised, he caused him to go to the heavenly world.
He who, knowing this, pays homage to Agni, goes indeed to the heavenly world.
He attains a full lifespan.
Indeed, he who pays homage to these two fires mounts upon them;
and just as one who has mounted upon a superior person acts according to his desire, so does he act.
(1.5.9.5) He worships at night, not in the morning;
for at night the vows are released together,
so that both the superior and the inferior sit down together.
Agni is indeed light, and the night is darkness.
In that he worships at night, he overcomes darkness by means of light itself.
"The fires are to be worshipped," they say; "they are not to be worshipped," they also say.

(1.5.9.6) "For indeed, when one brings [something] day after day as a human being and then asks for it, that person surely oppresses him. Who then would ask the gods day after day? Therefore, one should not wait upon them."
(1.5.9.6) Now, moreover, they say: "For what purpose does the sacrificer sacrifice? It is for the sake of a blessing.
(1.5.9.7) This, indeed, is the blessing of one who has established the sacred fires, namely that he worships the fire; therefore, it should be worshipped.
Prajāpati created cattle;
once created, they entered into day and night;
he recovered them by means of the meters.
(1.5.9.7) When he worships with the meters, he seeks after his own [self].
(1.5.9.7) "There is no repetition (*jāmi*) there," they say, "for him who worships day after day.
But he who worships the fire facing it directly, it burns him back.
He who goes away from his offspring and cattle, turning away and spreading out in all directions, should stand near as if turning aside;
thus it does not burn him back, nor does he go away from his offspring and cattle in all directions.
(1.5.10.1.a) O Jātavedas, that name which my father and mother first gave me at the beginning—bear that for me until I return; O Agni, I shall bear your name.

(1.5.10.1.b) O Jātavedas, we two who move about wearing our names like two garments—let us exchange them back again, so that you may live for your own life-span and we for ours, each according to his proper measure.
(1.5.10.1.c) Homage to Agni the Unpierced; homage to the Unassailable; homage to the Sovereign. Invincible is Agni—of great vigor, all-conquering, victorious, and the most excellent Gandharva.
(1.5.10.2ḍ) O Agni, your fathers are the gods; the oblations are yours, and the invocations are yours. Endow me with life and with lordship over cattle; establish me in well-being.
This Agni is the most excellent, this is the most blessed, this is the best winner of thousands; may there be great heroic power for him.
May the mind, as light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it join together this interrupted sacrifice. Those dawns and those sunsets that have been offered, these I unite with the oblation of ghee.
(1.5.10.2.g) The plants are full of milk; (1.5.10.3) the milk of the creepers is full of milk. With that milk which is the milk of the waters, O Indra, unite me.
(1.5.10.3) O Agni, Lord of Vows, I shall perform the vow; may I be able to do it, and may it be successful for me.
(1.5.10.3.i) I invoke here Agni the Hotṛ, whom we summon here among the gods worthy of sacrifice. May the gods come with benevolent minds; may the gods partake of this my oblation.
(1.5.10.3.k) Who yokes you? Let him yoke you.
Whatever potsherds the wise ones assemble for the Gharma, may Indra and Vāyu release them as well within the domain of Pūṣan.

(1.5.10.4) The Gharma-vessel is unbroken, the giver of life; from where it was taken, there it has returned again. The fuel, the altar, and all the enclosing-sticks follow along the life-span of the sacrifice.
The thirty-three threads which have been stretched out, those who sustain this sacrifice with their own inherent power—to them I restore what was severed; *svāhā*! Let the Gharma go unto the gods.
May Vaiśvānara come to us with his aid from afar, Agni, brought by our hymn as a vehicle.
We implore the righteous Vaiśvānara, the lord of the light of Truth, the imperishable heat.

(1.5.11.1.c) By his skillful work, the solitary sage has brought forth a great [song] from the wondrous deeds of Vaiśvānara. Exalting both parents, Agni was born from Heaven and Earth, who are rich in seed.
Sought in heaven, sought on earth, Agni has entered all plants; Agni Vaiśvānara, sought with power, may he protect us from harm by day and by night.
O Agni, when born you looked out upon the worlds like a watchful herdsman wandering around his cattle; O Vaiśvānara, find a path for our prayer. Do you all protect us always with blessings.
(1.5.11.2.f) O Agni, blazing with your flame at your birth, you filled the two worlds, heaven and earth; O Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, by your greatness, you released the gods from the curse.

(1.5.11.2.g) O Agni Vaiśvānara, maintain for us among the liberal patrons an unaging sovereignty and great heroic power; may we win booty by the hundreds and by the thousands through your protections, O Agni.
May we abide in the good-will of Vaiśvānara; for he is indeed the king, the glory of all beings. Born from here, he beholds this entire universe; Vaiśvānara vies with the Sun.
(1.5.11.3.i) We appease your wrath, O Varuṇa, with prostrations, with sacrifices, and with oblations. O wise Asura, O King, as you rule over us, loosen the sins we have committed.
O Varuṇa, loosen the uppermost bond from us, untie the lowest, and release the middle one. Then, O Āditya, may we be sinless before you and before Aditi within your sacred law.
I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan, the victorious, the spirited steed. May he make our mouths fragrant; may he prolong our lives.

(1.5.11.4) Dadhikrā, by his strength, has overspread the five peoples as the sun with its light overspreads the waters. May the prize-winning steed, winner of thousands and hundreds, unite these words with the bride.
Agni is the head of the world.
O Maruts, when we, seeking favor, call upon you from heaven, come hither unto us!

(1.5.11.5.q) Those protections which you have for the one who exerts himself, grant them in threefold measure to the donor! Extend those to us, O Maruts; bestow upon us wealth, O bulls, with excellent heroes.
(1.5.11.5ṛ) May Aditi protect us; may Aditi grant us shelter; may Aditi save us from distress.

Let us invoke for our protection the great Mother of those who observe sacred vows, the consort of *Ṛta*, the one of mighty dominion, the ageless, the far-reaching Aditi, the provider of excellent shelter and perfect guidance.
May we ascend for our well-being the divine ship—Sutrāman, the Earth, the faultless Heaven, Aditi who provides good shelter and excellent guidance—a ship with fair oars, sinless and leakless.
Mount this good ship, which has a hundred oars and a hundred paddles, which is leakless and carries one across.
(1.6.1.1.a) I sprinkle you with the sacrificial formula for progeny, long life, and wealth. Impelled by Bṛhaspati, may the sacrificer here meet with no harm.

(1.6.1.1.b) You are the clarified butter; you are truth; you are the overseer of truth; you are the oblation; you belong to Vaiśvānara and the All-gods; you are of purified vigor, possessing true power, and strength. You are the subduing one; you are the subduer. Subdue the enemies; subdue those who act as enemies; subdue the hostile armies; subdue those who attack us. You possess thousandfold heroism; quicken me! You are the clarified butter of the clarified butter; you are the truth of truth; you are the life of truth. You are the vigor of truth. With truth I sprinkle you. May I partake of that which is yours.

(1.6.1.2.c) I take you for the restraint and support of the five winds. (1.6.1.2ḍ) I take you for the restraint and support of the five seasons. (1.6.1.2.e) I take you for the restraint and support of the five directions.
(1.6.1.2.f) I take you for the restraint and support of the fivefold five peoples. (1.6.1.2.g) I take you for the restraint and support of the five-holed ladle.
(1.6.1.2.h) I take you for the splendor of the Brahman, for its restraint and support.

(1.6.1.2.i) "For the vigor and restraint of the ruling power (*kṣatra*), I take [thee]; (1.6.1.3.k) for the support, I take thee; (1.6.1.3.l) for the people, for their restraint and support, I take thee; (1.6.1.3.m) for great heroism, I take thee."
(1.6.1.3ṃ) I take you for the sake of good offspring; (1.6.1.3ṇ) I take you for the sake of the increase of wealth;
(1.6.1.3.o) I take you for the sake of spiritual luster.
(1.6.1.3.p) "Bhūḥ! Our oblation is for the gods; may the blessings belong to the sacrificer. I take you for the deities of the gods.
(1.6.1.3.q) "I take you for desire."

(1.6.2.1.a) You are firm; may I be firm among my kinsmen—wise, perceptive, and a finder of wealth. (1.6.2.1.b) You are fierce; may I be fierce among my kinsmen—fierce, perceptive, and a finder of wealth.
(1.6.2.1.c) You are a conqueror; may I be a conqueror among my kinsmen—a conqueror, perceptive, and a finder of wealth.

(1.6.2.1ḍ) I yoke you with the divine prayer (*brahman*) so that you, O Jātavedas, may carry this oblation. Kindling you, may we live long, possessing good offspring and brave sons, offering tribute to you.

(1.6.2.1.e) Whatever of this sacrifice of mine may be damaged, O Agni, or whatever of the clarified butter may be spilled, O Viṣṇu—with that I strike down my rival, the ill-fated one; I place him in the lap of Destruction.
(1.6.2.2.f) Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ.
(1.6.2.2.g) O Agni, be glowing for the sacrificer; be extinguishing for him who seeks to harm us.

(1.6.2.2.h) O Agni, kindled by the gods, kindled by the wise, with thy lovely tongue, O immortal Hotṛ, I sprinkle thee upon the head for the increase of wealth, for good progeny, and for heroic vigor.
(1.6.2.2.i) You are the mind, belonging to Prajāpati; enter me with the mind, with existence.
(1.6.2.2.k) You are speech, belonging to Indra, the destroyer of rivals; enter me with speech, with power.
(1.6.2.3) I gratify the spring among the seasons; may it, being gratified, gratify me.
(1.6.2.3ṃ) Of the seasons, I gratify the summer; may it, being gratified, gratify me.
(1.6.2.3ṇ) Of the seasons, I gratify the rainy season; may they, being gratified, gratify me.
(1.6.2.3.o) Of the seasons, I gratify the autumn; may it, being gratified, gratify me.
(1.6.2.3.p) Of the seasons, I gratify the two, Hemanta and Śiśira; may they, being gratified, gratify me. (1.6.2.3.q) Through the sacrifice to the gods Agni and Soma, may I become possessed of sight.
(1.6.2.3.ṛ) Through the sacrifice to the god Agni, may I become an eater of food.
(1.6.2.4ṣ) You are a deceiver; may I become undeceived; may I deceive so-and-so. (1.6.2.4ṭ) By the sacrifice to the gods Agni and Soma, may I become a slayer of Vṛtra.
(1.6.2.4.u) By the sacrifice to the gods Indra and Agni, may I become possessed of power and an eater of food.
(1.6.2.4.v) Through the sacrifice to the god Indra, may I become possessed of power. (1.6.2.4.w) Through the sacrifice to the god Mahendra, may I attain victory and greatness.
(1.6.2.4.x) Through the sacrifice to the god Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, may I, long-lived, attain a firm foundation through the sacrifice.

(1.6.3.1.a) May Agni protect me from ill-sacrificed rites; may Savitṛ protect me from the malevolent. (1.6.3.1.b) Whoever acts as an enemy toward me, whether near or far, him may I conquer by means of this.
(1.6.3.1.c) O you of beautiful form and rain-like luster, come hither! Come toward these auspicious dwellings, following my will.
(1.6.3.1ḍ) Truly, do you spare our heads!
(1.6.3.1.e) O Iḍā, come hither; O Aditi, come hither; O Sarasvatī, come hither!
(1.6.3.1.f) Thou art delight; thou art enjoyment; thou art prosperity.
(1.6.3.1.g) In what is pleasing, may I obtain your pleasure; in what is invited, may I obtain your invitation.
(1.6.3.2) May this be my true blessing of this sacrifice. (1.6.3.2.i) With an untroubled mind, may I be able to accomplish that.
(1.6.3.2.k) May the sacrifice ascend to heaven; may the sacrifice go to heaven.

(1.6.3.2ḷ) By that path which leads to the gods, may the sacrifice reach the gods. (1.6.3.2ṃ) May Indra bestow power upon us; may wealth and sacrifices attend us; may blessings be with us—may she be dear to us, victorious, and bountiful.
(1.6.3.2ṇ) You are delight; delight us! You are delighted by us; may I attain your delight.
(1.6.3.3.o) May the mind, the light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it join together this severed sacrifice. May Bṛhaspati extend this for us; may all the gods rejoice here.
(1.6.3.3.p) Swell with strength!
(1.6.3.3.q) May what I give not fail; may what I do not perish.
(1.6.3.3.r) You are the portion of Prajāpati, full of vigor, full of milk.
(1.6.3.3ṣ) Guard my out-breath and in-breath; guard my common breath and diffused breath; guard my upward breath and diffused breath.
(1.6.3.3ṭ) You are imperishable; for imperishability, I take you. May you not perish for me there, in yonder world.
(1.6.4.1.a) Through the sacrifice to the god Barhis, may I become possessed of offspring.
(1.6.4.1.b) Through the sacrifice to the god Narāśaṃsa, may I become possessed of cattle.
(1.6.4.1.c) Through the sacrifice to the god Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, may I be long-lived and, by means of this sacrifice, attain a firm foundation.
(1.6.4.1ḍ) Following the victory of Agni, may I conquer. (1.6.4.1.e) Following the victory of Soma, may I conquer. (1.6.4.1.f) Following the victory of Agni, may I conquer.

(1.6.4.1.g) May I win following the victory of Agni and Soma. (1.6.4.1.h) May I win following the victory of Indra and Agni. (1.6.4.1.i) May I win following the victory of Indra. (1.6.4.2) May I win following the victory of Indra.
(1.6.4.2.k) May I conquer following after the victory of Mahendra.
(1.6.4.2ḷ) May I conquer following after the victory of Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
(1.6.4.2ṃ) By the impulse of strength, with the upward-grasp, he has grasped me up; then Indra, by the downward-grasp, has made my rivals low.
The gods have increased the sacred word, both the uplifting and the grasping; then may Indra and Agni scatter my rivals in all directions.
(1.6.4.2.o) These prayers have come, desiring milk, accompanied by Indra. (1.6.4.3) May we win; may we milk forth offspring and nourishment.

(1.6.4.3.p) May Agni, the deity, cause you to go to the divine state by means of the ruddy horse; may Indra, the deity, cause you to go to the divine state by means of the two bay horses; may Sūrya, the deity, cause you to go to the divine state by means of Etaśa.

(1.6.4.3.q) I unloose your reins, I unloose the traces, I unloose the yokes and those things that bind you fast. Bestow upon us wealth and whatever is auspicious; announce us as sharers among the deities.
(1.6.4.3ṛ) By the sacrifice and the worship of the auspicious Viṣṇu, may I attain a firm foundation.
(1.6.4.3ṣ) By the sacrifice to the god Soma, may I, possessing good seed, deposit seed.
(1.6.4.4) By the sacrifice to the god Tvaṣṭṛ, may I nourish the form of cattle.
(1.6.4.4.u) The wives of the gods and Agni Gṛhapati are the couple of the sacrifice; by the sacrifice to these two gods, may I prosper through that couple.
(1.6.4.4.v) You are the Veda; you are acquisition; may I acquire. (1.6.4.4.w) You are action; you are the agent of action;
you are the performance. (1.6.4.4.x) You are gain; you are the winner; may I win.
May the Veda grant nourishment of wealth—abounding in ghee, nest-like, thousandfold, and powerful.

(1.6.5.1.a) May the *dhruvā* ladle swell with clarified butter for every sacrifice performed by those seeking the gods; may the earth, the udder of Sūryā and the lap of Aditi, yield her wide stream at this sacrifice.
(1.6.5.1.b) Prajāpati’s world is named Vibhān; in it I place you, together with the sacrificer.
(1.6.5.1.c) You are existence; may you become existence for me. You are all; may you become all for me. You are full; may you become full for me. You are imperishable; may you not perish for me.

(1.6.5.1ḍ) May the gods and the officiating priests purify me in the eastern quarter; may the months and the ancestors purify me in the southern quarter; may the houses and the cattle purify me in the western quarter; may the waters, the plants, and the trees purify me in the northern quarter; may the sacrifice, the year, and the lord of the sacrifice purify me in the upward quarter.
(1.6.5.2.e) Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of the adversary; with the Gāyatrī metre, I step across the earth. He whom we hate is excluded and cast out.

(1.6.5.2.f) You are Viṣṇu’s stride, the slayer of curses; with the Triṣṭubh metre, I stride across the intermediate region. Excluded is he whom we hate. (1.6.5.2.g) You are Viṣṇu’s stride, the slayer of the hostile; with the Jagatī metre, I stride across the sky. Excluded is he whom we hate. (1.6.5.2.h) You are Viṣṇu’s stride, the slayer of the enemy; with the Anuṣṭubh metre, I stride across the quarters. Excluded is he whom we hate.
(1.6.6.1.a) We have gone to heaven; we have gone to heaven.

(1.6.6.1.b) May I not be cut off from your sight; whatever heat is yours, may I not be deprived of that which is yours. (1.6.6.1.c) You are well-being, the best of rays; you are the giver of life, grant me life; you are the giver of splendor, grant me splendor.
(1.6.6.1ḍ) Here I exclude this rival from these quarters, from this heaven, from this atmosphere, from this earth, and from this food; excluded is he whom we hate.
(1.6.6.2.e) I have become united with light. (1.6.6.2.f) I turn according to the turning of Indra. (1.6.6.2.g) May I be united with progeny; may progeny be united with me.
(1.6.6.2: May I be united with the increase of wealth; may the increase of wealth be united with me.
(1.6.6.2.i: O Agni, being kindled, shine for me; O Agni, may I, as one who has kindled you, shine.
(1.6.6.2.k: May the sacrifice be rich in wealth; may I become more wealthy.
O Agni, you purify our lives; bring us strength and nourishment, and drive misfortune far away.
(1.6.6.2) O Agni, purify yourself with a beautiful form for us; bestow upon me splendor, heroic vigor, nourishment, and wealth. (1.6.6.3) Bestowing prosperity and riches upon me.

(1.6.6.3ṇ) O Agni, lord of the house, may I be a good lord of the house through you as lord of the house; may you be a good lord of the house through me as lord of the house for a hundred winters. I invoke this blessing, full of light, for my progeny; I invoke this blessing, full of light, for that person.
(1.6.6.3.o) Who yokes you? Let him unyoke you.

(1.6.6.3.p) O Agni, Lord of Vows, I have performed the vow; I was able to do it; it has been successful for me. (1.6.6.3.q) The sacrifice has come into being; it has come into existence; it has been born; it has grown. It has become the sovereign lord of the gods; may it make us sovereign lords; may we be masters of riches.

(1.6.6.4ṛ) O Agni, this sacrifice is rich in cattle, rich in sheep, rich in horses, accompanied by heroic friends, ever indestructible. It is full of nourishment, O Asura, rich in progeny, a long-lasting wealth, broad-based, and possessed of a noble assembly.
(1.6.7.1) Just as those who have pressed the *soma* together, so too are these two, the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), sacrifices whose rites are performed in common.
(1.6.7.1) To whom, indeed, do the gods come for the sacrifice, and from whom do they not?
Of many sacrificers, he who first secures the deities sacrifices to them on the following day.
(1.6.7.1) The Āhavanīya fire is indeed the abode of the gods; the space between the two fires is the abode of cattle;
the Gārhapatya fire is the abode of human beings.
The Anvāhāryapacana fire belongs to the ancestors;
he takes up the fire,
and thus he encompasses the deities within their own proper abode.
On the following day, he sacrifices them.
By means of the vow (*vrata*), Agni is pure; he is the Lord of the Vow (*vratapati*).
The Brāhmaṇa is the bearer of the vow.
(1.6.7.2) One who is about to enter upon a vow should say:
(1.6.7.2) "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall observe the vow.
(1.6.7.2) For Agni is indeed the lord of vows among the gods.
Having announced it to him, he undertakes the vow.
He enters upon the vow with sacrificial grass at the full moon, and with calves at the new moon;
for this is the abode of these two.
(1.6.7.2) "Both the eastern fire and the western fire are to be strewn with grass," they say.
(1.6.7.3) Humans indeed desire what has been strewn; how much more so the gods, for whom there is ever-new dwelling?
The deities dwell in that fire on which one who knows this strews grass, thinking, "Tomorrow I shall sacrifice here."
(1.6.7.3) "The sacrificer must acquire both domestic animals and wild animals," they say.
(1.6.7.3) In that he observes the fast with respect to the domestic animals, by that he acquires the domestic ones; in that he eats of the wild animal, by that he acquires the wild ones.
(1.6.7.3) If he were to fast without having eaten, it would belong to the Pitṛs as its deity. (1.6.7.3) He eats forest-grown food.
(1.6.7.4) Forest-grown food, indeed, is power (*indriya*).
(1.6.7.4) He bestows sensory power upon himself when he fasts without having eaten. (1.6.7.4) If he were to eat, Rudra would turn his mind against his cattle.
(1.6.7.4) He eats water. (1.6.7.4) That is neither eaten nor uneaten. (1.6.7.4) He does not become hungry.
Rudra does not turn his wrath against his cattle;
for the sacrifice is indeed the thunderbolt,
and hunger is truly the enemy of man.
In that he fasts without eating,
he strikes away hunger, his rival, directly with the thunderbolt itself.

(1.6.8.1) Verily, he who performs a sacrifice without having first taken hold of faith—people do not place their trust in his sacrifice. He pours forth the waters; for the waters are faith. Thus, by taking hold of faith, he performs the sacrifice with the sacrifice, and both gods and men place their trust in his sacrifice. Regarding this they say: "These [waters] flow over Vṛtra, or they flow beyond speech. But rather, it is the mind that does not flow over them. He pours them forth with the mind; for the mind is this [earth]. It is by means of this very earth that he pours them forth. He whose sacrificial offering is not spilt is he who knows thus.
(1.6.8.2) He collects the sacrificial implements. The sacrificial implements are indeed the sacrifice; thus he collects the sacrifice itself.
If he were to collect them one by one, they would belong to the ancestors; if he were to collect all of them together, they would belong to men.
He collects them two by two; he thereby creates the form of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, and also ensures a pairing.
(1.6.8.2) Verily, he who knows the ten sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*)—for him the sacrifice is prepared from the very beginning.

(1.6.8.3) The wooden sword (*sphya*), the potsherds (*kapāla*), the *agnihotra*-ladle, the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), the yoke-pin (*śamyā*), the mortar (*ulūkhalam*), the pestle (*musalam*), the lower grinding stone (*dṛṣad*), and the upper grinding stone (*upalā*)—these indeed are the ten sacrificial implements. For him who knows thus, the sacrifice is prepared from the very beginning. (1.6.8.3) Verily, he who sacrifices with the sacrifice after having announced it to the gods—the gods enjoy his oblation.
(1.6.8.3) He should address the oblation as it is being set down with the mantra: "I invoke here Agni, the Hotṛ."
Having announced it to the gods themselves, he performs the sacrifice with the sacrifice; the gods enjoy his oblation.
This indeed is the grasping of the sacrifice; having grasped it, he performs the sacrifice.
Having uttered that, he restrains his speech for the support of the sacrifice.
(1.6.8.4) Moreover, Prajāpati indeed extended the sacrifice by means of the mind; he extends the sacrifice by means of the mind alone, so that the Rākṣasas may have no access to it.
(1.6.8.4) "He who indeed yokes the sacrifice when the time for yoking has arrived, he yokes it among those who are yoking.
"Who yokes you? Let him yoke you," he says. Ka is indeed Prajāpati; verily, by means of Prajāpati he yokes it, he yokes it among those who are yoking.

Prajāpati created the sacrifices: the Agnihotra and the Agniṣṭoma, the Full-moon sacrifice and the Ukthya, the New-moon sacrifice and the Atirātra. He measured them out: as great as the Agnihotra was, so great was the Agniṣṭoma; as great as the Full-moon sacrifice was, so great was the Ukthya; as great as the New-moon sacrifice was, so great was the Atirātra.

(1.6.9.1) He who, knowing thus, performs the Agnihotra, obtains as much as one obtains by the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. (1.6.9.1) He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the full moon day, obtains as much as one obtains by the Ukthya sacrifice. (1.6.9.2) He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the new moon day, obtains as much as one obtains by the Atirātra sacrifice.
This sacrifice belonged to Parameṣṭhin in the beginning;
by means of it, he reached the highest point,
and by means of it, he caused Prajāpati to dwell out [from himself].
By means of it, Prajāpati reached the highest goal;
by means of it, he caused Indra to dwell apart [from his enemies];
by means of it, Indra reached the highest goal.
By that, he caused Agni and Soma to dwell apart;
by that, Agni and Soma reached the highest point.
He who, knowing thus, performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices, reaches the very highest point.
(1.6.9.3) He who performs the sacrifice with a sacrifice that has offspring is propagated with offspring, cattle, and pairs.
(1.6.9.3) Twelve months are a year; twelve are the pairs in the New and Full Moon sacrifices; they say these are to be accomplished.
(1.6.9.3) He lets down the calf and places the cooking-pot on the fire.
(1.6.9.3) He strikes down [the pestle] and beats together the two millstones; (1.6.9.3) he scatters [the grain] upon them and places the potsherds underneath;
(1.6.9.3–4) he places the sacrificial cake [upon the potsherds] and puts the clarified butter on the fire.
He carries away the *stambayajus* and takes hold of it;
he encloses the altar and girds the wife;
and he sets down the sprinkling waters and the clarified butter.
These indeed are the twelve pairs in the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
He who, having thus prepared them, performs the sacrifice, sacrifices with a procreative sacrifice; he is propagated with offspring, cattle, and pairs.

(1.6.10.1) "Thou art firm; may I be firm among my kinsmen," he says; verily, he makes them firm. (1.6.10.1) "Thou art fierce; may I be fierce among my kinsmen," he says; verily, he makes them non-resistant. (1.6.10.1) "Thou art a conqueror; may I be a conqueror among my kinsmen," he says; whoever seeks to rise up against him, him he overcomes.
(1.6.10.1) "I yoke thee with the divine prayer," he says; this indeed is the yoking of Agni, and by means of it he yokes him.

(1.6.10.2) By the success of the sacrifice, the gods went to the heavenly world; by the failure of the sacrifice, they brought the Asuras to ruin. "Whatever of this sacrifice of mine may be injured, O Agni," he says; thus, by the success of the sacrifice, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world, and by the failure of the sacrifice, he brings his rivals to ruin.

(1.6.10.2) One should set down the Agnihotra with these *vyāhṛtis*. The Agnihotra is indeed the mouth of the sacrifice, and these *vyāhṛtis* are the Brahman; thus he places the Brahman at the very mouth of the sacrifice. (1.6.10.3) When the year has come around, one should set it down with these same [syllables]; by means of the Brahman, he encloses the year on both sides.

One who performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices or the Four-Monthly sacrifices should set down the oblations with these *vyāhṛtis*. The New and Full Moon sacrifices and the Four-Monthly sacrifices are indeed the mouth of the sacrifice, and these *vyāhṛtis* are the Brahman. Thus, he places the Brahman at the very mouth of the sacrifice. When the year has come around, he should set them down with these same [formulas]; by means of the Brahman, he encompasses the year on both sides.

Whatever of the sacrifice is performed with a *sāman*, the blessing (*āśis*) of the sacrifice goes to the ruling power (*rāṣṭra*); whatever is performed with a *ṛc*, the blessing of the sacrifice goes to the people (*viś*). Thus, a Brahmin sacrifices with a sacrifice that lacks a blessing. When about to recite the *sāmidhenī* verses, he should place these *vyāhṛtis* at the beginning; he thereby makes the sacred word (*brahman*) his opening step. In this way, the Brahmin sacrifices with a sacrifice that possesses a blessing.

(1.6.10.4) If he should desire of a sacrificer, "May the blessing of this sacrifice go to his rival," he should place these *vyāhṛtis* in the *puro'nuvākyā*. For the *puro'nuvākyā* has the rival as its deity; thus the blessing of his sacrifice goes to the rival. (1.6.10.5)

(1.6.10.5) If he should desire of certain sacrificers, "May the blessing of the sacrifice reach them equally," he should place one of these *vyāhṛtis* at the half-verse of their *puro'nuvākyā*, one before the *yājyā*, and one at the half-verse of the *yājyā*. Thus the blessing of the sacrifice reaches them equally.
(1.6.10.5) Just as Parjanya rains down a good rain, so does the sacrifice rain for the sacrificer. As they dam up water on dry land, so the sacrificer dams up the sacrifice with its blessing.

(1.6.10.5) "Thou art the mind, belonging to Prajāpati. (1.6.10.6) "Enter me with the mind, with being," he says. The mind indeed belongs to Prajāpati, and the sacrifice belongs to Prajāpati; verily, he places the sacrifice within himself by means of the mind.

(1.6.10.6) "Thou art speech, belonging to Indra, the destroyer of rivals; enter me with speech, with power," he says. Speech indeed belongs to Indra; verily, he places the speech of Indra within himself.
(1.6.11.1) He who knows Prajāpati as the seventeenfold one who is inherent in the sacrifice stands firm through the sacrifice and does not fall away from the sacrifice.

(1.6.11.1) “Ā śrāvaya” consists of four syllables; “astu śrauṣaṭ” consists of four syllables; “yaj” consists of two syllables; “ye yajāmahe” consists of five syllables; and the *vaṣaṭ*-call consists of two syllables.
(1.6.11.1) This indeed is the seventeenfold Prajāpati who is inherent in the sacrifice.
(1.6.11.1) He who knows thus stands firm through the sacrifice; he does not fall away from the sacrifice.
(1.6.11.2) Verily, he who knows the beginning, the foundation, and the rising of the sacrifice reaches the completion with a sacrifice that is firmly established and uninjured.
"Ā śrāvaya," "Astu śrauṣaṭ," "Yaja," "Ye yajāmahe," and the *vaṣaṭ*-call—this indeed is the beginning of the sacrifice, this is its foundation, and this is its rising.
He who knows thus reaches the conclusion with a sacrifice that is firmly established and uninjured. He who knows the milking of Sūnṛtā indeed milks her.
Sacrifice, verily, is Sūnṛtā.
"Āśrāvaya!"—with these words he called out to her. "Astu śrauṣaṭ!"—with this he caused her to descend.
"Yaja!"—with this he led her upward.
With "ye yajāmahe," he approached;
with the *vaṣaṭ*-call, he milked.
This, indeed, is the milking of *sūnṛtā* (truthful speech).
(1.6.11.3) He who knows thus indeed milks her.
(1.6.11.3) The gods, indeed, performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*);
their quarters were scattered.

(1.6.11.3) They saw this moist *paṅkti* [verse]: with "Ā śrāvaya" they generated the east wind; with "Astu śrauṣaṭ" they caused the cloud to swell; with "Yaja" they generated the lightning. (1.6.11.4) With "Ye yajāmahe" they caused it to rain, and with the *vaṣaṭ*-call they made it thunder. Then indeed, the quarters swelled for them.
For one who knows thus, the quarters swell for him.
(1.6.11.4) You know Prajāpati; Prajāpati knows you.
(1.6.11.4) He whom Prajāpati knows becomes meritorious. (1.6.11.4) This indeed is the metrical Prajāpati: *ā śrāvaya*, *astu śrauṣaṭ*, *yaja*, *ye yajāmahe*, and the *vaṣaṭ* call.
He who knows thus becomes meritorious.
"I gratify the spring among the seasons," he says;
for the *prayāja* offerings are indeed the seasons.
Verily, he gratifies the seasons; they, being gratified, become favorable to him in due order. The seasons become favorable to him who knows thus.
"Through the sacrifice to the gods Agni and Soma, may I become possessed of sight," he says.
For the sacrifice is indeed possessed of sight through Agni and Soma; through them alone he bestows sight upon himself.
"By the sacrifice to Agni, may I become an eater of food," he says. For Agni is indeed the eater of food among the gods; by means of him, he bestows the eating of food upon himself.
"You are the deceiver; may I become undeceivable; may I deceive so-and-so," he says.
By means of this very deception, the gods indeed deceived the Asuras; by that same [means], he deceives his rival.
"By the sacrifice to the gods Agni and Soma, may I become a slayer of Vṛtra," he says.
For by means of Agni and Soma, Indra indeed slew Vṛtra; through them alone, he lays low his rival.

"Through the sacrifice to the gods Indra and Agni, may I become possessed of power and an eater of food," he says; verily he becomes possessed of power and an eater of food. "Through the sacrifice to the god Indra, may I become possessed of power," he says.
He indeed becomes possessed of the senses.
"By the sacrifice to the god Mahendra, may I attain victory and greatness," he says; verily, he attains victory and greatness.

"By the sacrifice to the god Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, may I, possessing long life, attain firm standing through the sacrifice," he says. Verily, he bestows long life upon himself and stands firm through the sacrifice.
(1.6.12.1.a) We invoke Indra for you from all sides, away from other people; may he be ours alone.

(1.6.12.1.b) Men invoke Indra in the contest for the prize, so that those prayers may be harnessed for the decisive moment. O Hero, desiring power in the battle for men, do thou grant us a share in the stall rich in cattle.
O Śatakratu, those powers of yours which exist among the five peoples—O Indra, I choose them for you.

To thee was granted for thy great Indra-power; all was entirely yielded to thee in the slaying of Vṛtra. To thee was granted dominion and to thee was granted might, O worshipful Indra, by the gods, in the overcoming of men.
In whom the seven Vasus stand as if firmly rooted—Ṛṣi Dīrghaśravastama is indeed Indra’s guest, the heated oblation.
Within the raw you have placed the cooked; you have caused the sun to ascend to heaven. Heat it like the *gharma* with hymns, with well-fashioned praises—pleasing songs for the lover of song.
(1.6.12.2.g) To Indra alone have the singers chanted loudly; to Indra, with hymns, the chanters; to Indra have the voices cried out.
(1.6.12.2) The singers of the *gāyatrī* sing to you; (1.6.12.3) the chanters of hymns praise the song. O Śatakratu, the *brahmans* have raised you up like a pole.

(1.6.12.3.i) Let us offer this prayer to the deliverer from distress, chanting a hymn of praise to the one who gives most readily. O Indra, accept this oblation; may the desires of the sacrificer come true.

(1.6.12.3.k) Since the inspired thought has entered me and given me birth, I shall praise Indra before the decisive day, so that he may carry us across from distress—just as those on both sides call upon one who is traveling like a ship.

(1.6.12.3ḷ) Forward [we call] the sovereign, the first of sacrifices, the deliverer from distress, the bull among those worthy of worship, the Son of the Waters, and the Aśvins who hasten [to him]. O heroes, bestow upon this man Indra’s power and vital strength.
(1.6.12.4ṃ) O Indra, strike down our adversaries; cast those who attack us low. Place him beneath our feet who seeks to harm us.
O Indra, you were born for sovereign power, for lovely might, as the bull of the peoples; you drove away the unfriendly folk and made wide space for the gods.

Like a fearsome wild beast, roaming and dwelling in the mountains, he has come from the farthest distance. Having sharpened your bolt and made your weapon keen, O Indra, strike down the enemies and drive away the adversaries.
Drive away the enemies, drive away the mockers; break apart the jaws of Vṛtra. O Indra, quell the fury of the wrathful adversary who assails us.
I invoke Indra the protector, Indra the helper, the hero Indra who is easily invoked at every call; I now invoke the mighty Indra, invoked by many. May the bounteous Indra bestow well-being upon us.
(1.6.12.5ṛ) O powerful one, lord of bay horses, let us not fall into misfortune through this surrounding distress; protect us with your safe defenses, and may we remain dear to you among the patrons.
The Anus fashioned a chariot for your horse; Tvaṣṭṛ, O much-invoked one, fashioned the radiant thunderbolt. The Brahmins, magnifying Indra with hymns, strengthened him for the slaying of the serpent.

When the strong ones sang their hymn for you, the Strong One, O Indra—the pressing-stones and Aditi in accord; when the wheel-rims, without horses or chariots, impelled by Indra, rolled against the Dasyus.

(1.7.1.1) Cattle attend upon the *pākayajña* of one who has established the sacred fires; for the *pākayajña* is indeed *iḍā*. This very *iḍā* is placed within the world of the sacrificer between the *prayāja* and *anūyāja* offerings. As she is being brought forward, he should address her with the mantra:
"O thou of beautiful form and excellent color, come! For *iḍā* is cattle; verily, he thus invokes cattle. The gods milked the sacrifice, and the sacrifice milked the *asuras*.

(1.7.1.1) Those Asuras, milked by the sacrifice, were defeated. He who, knowing the milking of the sacrifice, performs the sacrifice, milks even another sacrificer. "May this true blessing of mine from this sacrifice come to pass," he says; for this indeed is the milking of the sacrifice.

(1.7.1.2) By that very means he milks her. For a cow yields when she has been let loose; the *iḍā* has been let loose for the sacrificer, and thus she yields for him. These indeed are the teats of the *iḍā*: "The *iḍā* has been invoked"—this is Vāyu, and the calf is Vāyu. When the Hotṛ invokes the *iḍā*, then the sacrificer, looking at the Hotṛ, should meditate upon Vāyu with his mind. (1.7.1.3) He lets the calf go to its mother. By means of the entire sacrifice, the gods went to the heavenly world.

(1.7.1.3) By means of the *pākayajña*, Manu performed his labor; the *iḍā* returned to Manu. The gods and the asuras called out for her together. The gods called her toward themselves, the asuras called her away from themselves. She returned to the gods; thus the cattle chose the gods and abandoned the asuras. If one should desire of someone, "May he be without cattle," he should call the *iḍā* away from him; verily, he becomes without cattle.
(1.7.1.4) If one should desire of someone, "May he be rich in cattle," he should call the *iḍā* toward him; verily, he becomes rich in cattle. The exponents of the Veda say:

(1.7.1.4) He should invite the *iḍā*, thinking: "He who invites the *iḍā* should also invite himself into the *iḍā*. He says, "May she be dear to us, the victorious, the bountiful," and thus, having invited the *iḍā*, he invites himself into the *iḍā*. (1.7.1.5) That part of the sacrifice which is the *iḍā* is, as it were, disjointed when they eat of it prematurely and wipe their mouths prematurely. It was at this point that the sacrifice of the Asuras was cut off.

(1.7.1.5) "The gods have united with the *brahman*; may Bṛhaspati extend this for us," he says. Bṛhaspati is indeed the *brahman* of the gods; verily, by means of the *brahman*, he unites the sacrifice. "May he unite this severed sacrifice," he says for the sake of continuity. "May all the gods rejoice here," he says; thus, by means of continuity, he directs the sacrifice toward the gods. Whatever sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) one gives at the sacrifice, after that his cattle follow along.

(1.7.1.6) This very person who has sacrificed is liable to become one who lacks cattle; indeed, they say that this must be done by the sacrificer: "So that he may make what is given reach the gods and cause cattle to rest within himself. He says, "O Bradhna, swell! The sacrifice is indeed Bradhna; he thus magnifies the sacrifice itself. Furthermore, he makes what is given reach the gods and causes cattle to rest within himself. He says, "May it not fail for me as I give! He thus attains non-deprivation. He says, "May it not perish for me as I act! He thus attains abundance.

(1.7.2.1) Saṃśravas Sauvarcanasa said to Tumiñja Aupoditi: (1.7.2.1) "When you were the *hotṛ* priest for those performing a sacrificial session (*sattra*), what *iḍā* did you invoke? (1.7.2.1) He replied: "I invoked that [iḍā] which sustains the gods by means of the out-breath (*prāṇa*), humans by means of the diffused breath (*vyāna*), and the ancestors by means of the in-breath (*apāna*)."
"Does it cut, or does it not cut?
"It cuts," he said. "In truth, you have merely called it the body," he replied.
The cow, indeed, is her body. It was regarding the cow that those two spoke.

That which is given at the sacrifice, she sustains the gods with the out-breath (*prāṇa*); that by which humans live, she sustains humans with the diffused breath (*vyāna*); that which they slaughter for the ancestors, she sustains the ancestors with the in-breath (*apāna*).
He who knows thus becomes possessed of cattle.
Now, he said, "I have indeed invoked her," referring to her as "she who comes back to meet the offspring as they are being born.
"This is indeed food for her," he said, "that you have invoked her."
(1.7.2.3) Plants indeed are her food. (1.7.2.3) Plants, indeed, are the creatures that arise and return again. He who knows thus becomes an eater of food.
(1.7.2.3) "Now indeed, I have invoked her," he said, "she who favors the offspring that perish and receives back those that return.
(1.7.2.3) "Verily, you have invoked her foundation," he said.
(1.7.2.4) "For this earth is her foundation; this earth indeed favors the offspring that perish and receives back those that return."

He who knows thus stands firm. Then indeed, he said, "I invoke her, she at whose stepping forth living creatures drink the clarified butter. "Does she cut [the plants], or does she not cut them? he asked. "She cuts them," they replied. "No, she does not cut them," he said. "She cuts them, for she is the one who brings forth all this. "No, she does not cut them; she is the one who nourishes all this. "She both cuts them and does not cut them. "How so? "In that she brings forth all this, she cuts it; in that she nourishes all this, she does not cut it. "She is the one who brings forth all this and nourishes all this. "She is indeed the one who brings forth all this and nourishes all this. "Who is she? "The cow. "What is the cow? "Speech. "What is speech? "The Ṛg. "What is the Ṛg? "The Yajus. "What is the Yajus? "The Sāman. "What is the Sāman? "The Uktha. "What is the Uktha? "The Mahad Uktha. "What is the Mahad Uktha? "The person. "What is the person? "The sacrifice. "What is the sacrifice? "The year. "What is the year? "The day-and-night. "What is the day-and-night? "The food. "What is the food? "Water. "Therefore, one should meditate upon water as food, for food is water. "One who knows thus becomes possessed of food. "And how is it that water is food? "Because when it rains here, everything becomes fit for food. "Therefore, one should meditate upon water as food, for food is water. "One who knows thus becomes possessed of food. "And how is it that water is food? "Because when it rains here, everything becomes fit for food. "Therefore, one should meditate upon water as food, for food is water. "One who knows thus becomes possessed of food. "And how is it that water is food? "Because when it rains here, everything becomes fit for food. "Therefore, one should meditate upon water as food, for food is water. "One who knows thus becomes possessed of food. "And how is it that water is food? "Because when it rains here, everything becomes fit for food. "Therefore, one should meditate upon water as food, for food is water. "One who knows thus becomes possessed of food. "And how is it that water is food? "Because when it rains here, everything becomes fit for food. "Therefore, one should meditate upon water as food, for food is water. "One who knows thus becomes possessed of food. "And how is it that water is food? "Because when it rains here, everything becomes fit for food. "Therefore, one should meditate upon water as food, for food is water. "One who knows thus becomes possessed of food. "And how is it that water is food? "Because when it rains here, everything becomes fit for food. "Therefore, one should meditate upon water as food, for food is water. "One who knows thus becomes possessed of food. "And how is it that water is food? "Because when it rains here, everything becomes fit for food. "Therefore, one should meditate upon water as food, for food is water. "One who knows thus becomes possessed of food. "And how is it that water is food? "Because when it rains here, everything becomes fit for food. "Therefore, one should meditate upon water as food, for food is water. "One who knows thus becomes possessed of food. "And how is it that water is food? "Because when it rains here, everything becomes fit for food. "Therefore, one should meditate upon water as food, for food is water. "One who knows thus becomes possessed of food. "And how is it that water is food? "Because when it rains here, everything becomes fit for food. "Therefore, one should meditate upon water as food, for food is water. "One who knows thus becomes possessed of food. "It does not cut," he said, "but rather it brings forth.
"Verily, you have invoked the *iḍā*," he said;
for the *iḍā* is indeed rain.
(1.7.2.4) Indeed, at the place of descent for rain, creatures who are sustained by life drink the clarified butter. He who knows thus is procreated and becomes an eater of food.
(1.7.3.1) Some gods are worshipped invisibly, others visibly. When he sacrifices, he worships those very gods who are worshipped invisibly;
when he brings the *anvāhārya* rice, he gratifies those very gods who are visible, namely the Brahmins.
Moreover, this is his very sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*);
furthermore, he thereby mends whatever breach there is in the sacrifice.
Whatever in the sacrifice is cruel or whatever is injured, that he repairs by means of the *anvāhārya*.
(1.7.3.2) That is why the *anvāhārya* is called *anvāhārya*. (1.7.3.2) The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are indeed the messengers of the gods.
In that he brings the *anvāhārya*, he gratifies the messengers of the gods.
(1.7.3.2) Prajāpati assigned the sacrifices to the gods. (1.7.3.2) Feeling himself depleted, he reflected; (1.7.3.2) he saw this Anvāhārya rice as a means of providing sustenance.
He placed that within himself. This Anvāhārya rice-offering indeed belongs to Prajāpati.
For whomsoever, knowing thus, the Anvāhārya is brought, he directly prospers through Prajāpati.
(1.7.3.2) An unlimited [portion] is to be offered.
(1.7.3.2) Prajāpati is unlimited.
(1.7.3.3) [This is] for the attainment of Prajāpati.
Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did that as well.
The gods saw this Anvāhārya [rice-offering] belonging to Prajāpati; they brought it forth.
(1.7.3.3) Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
For one who knows this, when the *anvāhārya* rice is brought forward, he prospers in himself and his rival is defeated.
Through sacrifice one becomes successful by means of the offering; through cooked food, one becomes successful by means of the fulfillment.
(1.7.3.3) For whomsoever, knowing thus, the *anvāhārya* rice is brought, he indeed becomes one who has performed both sacrifice (*iṣṭā*) and pious works (*pūrta*).
(1.7.3.4) "Thou art the portion of Prajāpati," he says;
verily, he causes Prajāpati to prosper with his own share.
"Full of vigor, full of milk," he says;
verily, he bestows vigor and milk upon him.
"Protect my out-breath and in-breath; protect my middle-breath and diffused-breath," he says.
(1.7.3.4) He thus invokes this very blessing:
(1.7.3.4) "Thou art imperishable; for imperishability, I take thee. Mayest thou not perish for me in yonder world, in that world," he says.
(1.7.3.4) For food indeed perishes in yonder world.
"For from this world, indeed, creatures subsist upon what is given to that world.
In that he touches it thus, he causes it to go to imperishability; his food does not perish in that world."
"By the sacrifice to the gods with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), may I become possessed of offspring," he says.
For by means of the sacrificial grass, Prajāpati created offspring; verily, by that very means, he creates offspring.
"By the sacrifice to Narāśaṃsa, may I become possessed of cattle," he says.
For by means of Narāśaṃsa, Prajāpati created cattle; by that very means, he creates cattle.

(1.7.4.1) "By the sacrifice to the god Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, may I, possessing long life, attain firm standing through the sacrifice," he says. (1.7.4.1) Verily, he bestows life upon himself and stands firm through the sacrifice.
(1.7.4.2) Indeed, by means of the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the gods followed after victory and drove away the Asuras with the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
(1.7.4.2) "May I win following the victory of Agni," he says.

(1.7.4.2) Thus, in the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the sacrificer wins following the victory of the deities; by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, he drives away his rivals. He separates [the two portions] with the two verses containing the word *vāja*.
Food, indeed, is strength (*vāja*).
Verily, he wins food.
With two [verses], for the sake of stability.

(1.7.4.2) Verily, he who, knowing the two milkings of the sacrifice, performs the sacrifice, milks the sacrifice from both sides—from the front and from behind. (1.7.4.3) One milking of the sacrifice is indeed this [one], and the other is in the *iḍā*.
When the Hotṛ should utter the name of the sacrificer, then he should say:
"Hither have come these blessings, desiring to be milked."
(1.7.4.3) He milks the deities who have been praised together.
(1.7.4.3) Moreover, he milks the sacrifice from both sides—from the front and from behind.
(1.7.4.3) "May Agni cause thee to go to the deity by means of the ruddy one," he says.
(1.7.4.3) These, indeed, are the divine horses; the sacrificer is the *prastara* (grass-bundle).
(1.7.4.4) In that he casts the *prastara* with these [stalks], he causes the sacrificer to go to the heavenly world by means of the divine horses.
(1.7.4.4) "I unloose thy reins, I unloose thy traces," he says.
(1.7.4.4) This, indeed, is the release of Agni; by that very means he releases him.
"Through the sacrifice to the gods, through the sacrifice of Viṣṇu Śamyo, may I attain a firm foundation," he says.
(1.7.4.4) Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; verily, he establishes himself within the sacrifice.
(1.7.4.5) "By the sacrifice to the gods through Soma, may I, possessing good seed, (1.7.4.5) deposit seed," he says.
Soma is indeed the depositor of seed; by means of that very [Soma], he deposits seed within himself.
"By the sacrifice to the god Tvaṣṭṛ, may I nourish the form of cattle," he says.
Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the fashioner of the forms of cattle in their pairs;
by that very means, he takes the form of cattle for himself.
"The wives of the gods, Agni the lord of the house—this is the couple of the sacrifice. Through the sacrifice to these two deities, may I prosper by means of this couple," he says.
For from this very couple Prajāpati was born by means of a couple;
therefore, the sacrificer is born by means of a couple.
"You are the Veda; you are acquisition; may I acquire," he says.
By means of the Veda, indeed, the gods found the wealth of the Asuras that was to be found;
that is the reason for the Veda's name "Veda."
(1.7.4.6) Whatever of his rival he might covet, he should utter the name of that;
thus he seizes all of it from him.
"May the Veda grant us nourishment rich in ghee, full-housed, thousandfold, and vigorous," he says.
He who knows this obtains a thousand cattle; a vigorous son is born among his offspring.
When the *dhruvā* is being emptied, the sacrifice is emptied after it; the sacrificer is emptied after the sacrifice; and the offspring are emptied after the sacrificer.
When the *dhruvā* is being replenished, the sacrifice is replenished after it; the sacrificer is replenished after the sacrifice; and the offspring are replenished after the sacrificer.
"Let the *dhruvā* be replenished with ghee," he says.
(1.7.5.1) He causes the *dhruvā* ladle itself to swell.
As it swells, the sacrifice swells after it; after the sacrifice, the sacrificer; and after the sacrificer, the offspring.
(1.7.5.1–2) “The world named Vibhān belongs to Prajāpati; in that I place you, together with the sacrificer,” he says.
(1.7.5.2) This world of Prajāpati is indeed named Vibhān;
in that very world he places him together with the sacrificer.
Verily, that which one sacrifices is, as it were, emptied.
(1.7.5.2) In that he eats the sacrificer’s portion, he gratifies his very self.
(1.7.5.2) The sacrifice is indeed as large as the sacrificer’s portion;
the sacrifice is the sacrificer.
(1.7.5.2) In that he eats the sacrificer’s portion, he establishes the sacrifice within the sacrifice itself.
(1.7.5.2) This, indeed, is good pasture and water: namely, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and the waters.
(1.7.5.3) This, indeed, is the sacrificer’s abode: namely, the altar (*vedi*).
In that he pours out the full vessel within the altar, he provides good pasture and water in its own proper place.
"Thou art real; mayest thou become real for me," he says.
The sacrifice, indeed, is the waters.
The waters are immortality.
He places the sacrifice itself, which is immortality, within his own self. Indeed, all beings follow one who undertakes the vow.
"In the eastern direction, may the gods, the officiating priests, purify me," he says. This indeed is the *avabhṛtha* (concluding purificatory bath) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
(1.7.5.4) Those very beings that follow him as he enters upon the vow—along with them he goes down to the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
(1.7.5.4) The gods, having Viṣṇu as their head, conquered these worlds by means of the meters so as not to be defeated.
In that he strides the strides of Viṣṇu, the sacrificer becomes Viṣṇu himself.
(1.7.5.4) By means of the meters, he conquers these worlds so as not to be defeated.
(1.7.5.4) "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of the adversary," he says.
(1.7.5.4) The Gāyatrī is indeed the earth, the Triṣṭubh is the intermediate space, the Jagatī is the sky, and the Anuṣṭubh is the quarters.
By means of the meters, he thus conquers these worlds in their proper order.
"We have gone to heaven; we have gone to heaven," he says; verily, he goes to the world of heaven.
"May I not be cut off from thy sight; may I not be deprived of that heat of thine," he says;
this is according to the sacrificial formula itself.

(1.7.6.1) "Thou art well-being, the best of rays; thou art the giver of life, grant me life," he says. (1.7.6.1) Verily, he invokes this very blessing. He who strides the Viṣṇu-steps indeed departs from this world, for the Viṣṇu-steps are stridden for the sake of the heavenly world.
(1.7.6.2) The exponents of the Veda say:

(1.7.6.2) He indeed should step the Viṣṇu-strides who, having seized these worlds from his rival, would descend again to this world. (1.7.6.2) This is the descent back to this world: when he says, "Here I [drive] that rival away from these quarters, from this sky."
Having seized these very worlds from his rival, he descends again toward this world.
"I have become united with light," he says;
thus he establishes himself firmly in this very world.
"He turns following the turn of Indra," he says.
For yonder sun is indeed Indra; he thus turns following Indra’s very turn.
He turns toward the south; he thus turns following his own vigor. Therefore, the right side of the body is more vigorous; moreover, he turns following the turn of the sun itself.
(1.7.6.3) "May I be united with offspring; may offspring be united with me," he says.
(1.7.6.4) Thus he invokes this very blessing.
(1.7.6.4) "O Agni, being kindled, shine for me; may I, O Agni, kindling you, shine," he says.
(1.7.6.4) This is according to the sacrificial formula itself.
(1.7.6.4) "May the sacrifice be wealthy; may I become more prosperous," he says.
(1.7.6.4) He thus invokes this very blessing.

(1.7.6.4) Much indeed that is mixed is performed at the end of the *gārhapatya* rite; he worships the *gārhapatya* with two verses addressed to Agni-Pāvamāna. He thus purifies the fire and purifies himself; he does so with two verses for the sake of stability.

(1.7.6.5) "O Agni, lord of the house," he says. This is according to the sacrificial formula. "A hundred winters," he says; by this he means, "May I kindle thee for a hundred winters. He pronounces the name of his son; he thereby makes him an eater of food.

(1.7.6.5) He should say, "I invoke this blessing, full of light, for my lineage. For him whose son is yet unborn, a son endowed with splendor and sacred luster (*brahmavarcas*) is born. (1.7.6.6) He should say, "I invoke this blessing, full of light, for [him], [named] so-and-so. For him whose son is already born, he bestows upon him splendor and sacred luster.
Verily, he who, having set the sacrifice in motion, does not release it, becomes one who lacks a firm foundation.

"Who yokes you? Let him unyoke you," he says. Ka is indeed Prajāpati; verily by Prajāpati he yokes him, and by Prajāpati he unyokes him, for the sake of stability.
