The vow, when not formally released, is liable to burn [the sacrificer]. "O Agni, Lord of the Vow, I have performed the vow," he says; thus he releases the vow for the sake of peace and to prevent burning. The sacrifice indeed goes away and does not return again. But he who, knowing the re-seizing of the sacrifice, performs the sacrifice, toward him the sacrifice returns.

(1.7.6.7) “The sacrifice has come into being; it has truly come into being,” he says. This is indeed the re-seizing of the sacrifice; by means of this, he seizes it again. (1.7.6.7) The *virāj* of one who has established the sacred fires but lacks a *sabhā* (assembly hall) remains unattained. For cattle are indeed the *sabhā* of a Brāhmaṇa. Having sacrificed, he should step forward toward the east and say, “O Agni, may the sacrifice be rich in cattle, rich in sheep, and rich in horses. Thus he secures a *sabhā*; he obtains a thousand cattle, and a vigorous son is born among his offspring.

(1.7.7.1.a) O divine Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice; impel the lord of the sacrifice for his prosperity. The celestial Gandharva, the purifier of intentions, shall purify our intention; may the Lord of Speech make our speech sweet today.

(1.7.7.1.b) You are the thunderbolt of Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra; with you, may this man slay Vṛtra. (1.7.7.1.c) Now, at the impulse of strength, we celebrate with our speech the great Mother, named Aditi, in whom this entire world has entered; may the god Savitṛ impel the sacred law for us within her.
(1.7.7.1ḍ) Within the waters is immortality; within the waters is healing. And through the praises of the waters, O spirited ones, you become horses.
Either Vāyu has yoked you, or Manu, or the twenty-seven Gandharvas; they first harnessed the horse, and they placed speed within him.
(1.7.7.2.f) O Son of the Waters, swift-moving, whose wave is humped, impetuous, and most effective in winning the prize—with that, may this man win the prize.
(1.7.7.2.g) You are the stride of Viṣṇu; you are the step of Viṣṇu; you are the wide-stride of Viṣṇu.

(1.7.7.2.h) The two hooks, the two descending hooks on both sides of the chariot, which move along the darkness and the edge of the wind—the far-shooting, powerful, winged ones: may those fires carry us across.
(1.7.8.1.a) At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, may I, through Bṛhaspati the winner of the prize, win the prize.
(1.7.8.1.b) At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, may I, through Bṛhaspati the winner of the prize, ascend to the highest firmament.
(1.7.8.1.c) Speak the word to Indra; make Indra win the prize; Indra has won the prize.
(1.7.8.1ḍ) O horse-whip, O powerful one, O you who possess power in contests for booty, grant vigor to the horses in battles!
(1.7.8.1.e) You are a steed, you are a courser, you are a prize-winner.
(1.7.8.1.f) O prize-winners, run for the prize; conquer in the impulse of the Maruts; measure out the leagues, steady the paths, and reach the goal!
(1.7.8.2.g) O swift ones, protect us in every contest for booty; O wise, immortal, knowers of Truth! Drink of this honeyed draught, rejoice, and being satisfied, go by the paths traveled by the gods.

(1.7.8.2) May they, the swift coursers who hear our invocation, all the prize-winning steeds, hear our call. (1.7.8.2.i) They who run with measured pace, winners of thousands, eager for gain in the winning of the sacrifice; they who have displayed great joy in the battles—may those prize-winning steeds be auspicious to us at our invocations. (1.7.8.2.k) At the assembly of the gods, may the swift-paced, well-praising steeds, crushing the serpent, the wolf, and the demons, drive them entirely away from us, as well as all diseases. (1.7.8.3) [May they keep] all maladies far from us.
(1.7.8.3ḷ) This steed hastens toward the whip, bound by the neck, at the flanks, and in the mouth; Dadhikrā, exerting his strength in accordance with his will, springs along the curves of the paths.
And indeed, as he rushes forward, speeding like a bird eager for its prey, the wind blows after him; as Dadhikrāvan flies with his might, crossing over the curve of the earth like a swooping falcon.
May the impulse of strength come to me; may Heaven and Earth, who bring all-beneficence, come to me; may my two fathers and my two mothers come to me; may Soma come to me for the sake of immortality.
O prize-winning steeds, about to run for the prize and about to win the prize, smell the portion of Bṛhaspati.
(1.7.8.4.p) O ye steeds, winners of the prize, having run for the prize, having won the prize, take your rest in the portion of Bṛhaspati.
(1.7.8.4.q) This has become that true compact for you which you made with Indra.
(1.7.8.4ṛ) O trees, you have caused Indra to win; release the prize.

(1.7.9.1.a) You are the caul of the kṣatra; you are the womb of the kṣatra. (1.7.9.1.b) O wife, come! Let us two ascend to heaven; indeed, let us two ascend to heaven. I shall cause both of us to ascend to heaven.
(1.7.9.1.c) Vāja and Prasava and Āpija and Kratu and Suva and Mūrdhan and Vyaśniya and Antyāyana and Antya and Bhauvana and Bhuvana and Adhipati.

(1.7.9.1ḍ) May life be perfected through sacrifice; may breath be perfected through sacrifice; may out-breath (1.7.9.2) be perfected through sacrifice; may diffused breath be perfected through sacrifice; may sight be perfected through sacrifice; may hearing be perfected through sacrifice; may mind be perfected through sacrifice; may speech be perfected through sacrifice; may the self be perfected through sacrifice; may sacrifice itself be perfected through sacrifice.
(1.7.9.2.e) We have gone to the light of heaven; we have become immortal; we have become the offspring of Prajāpati.
(1.7.9.2.f) May I be united with offspring, and may offspring be united with me; may I be united with the increase of wealth, and may the increase of wealth be united with me.
(1.7.9.2.g) For food thee, for the eating of food thee, for strength thee, for the winning of strength thee!
(1.7.9.2.h) Thou art immortality; thou art nourishment; thou art procreation.
(1.7.10.1.a) This impulse of strength first brought forth King Soma in the plants and in the waters. May they be sweet for us; may we, acting as domestic priests, remain vigilant in the kingdom.
(1.7.10.1.b) This has come about through the impulse of strength, encompassing all these worlds on every side. He moves around the Virāj, knowing all, increasing offspring and prosperity for us.

(1.7.10.1.c) This impulsion of strength has taken its stand upon heaven and all these worlds, O Sovereign. May he, knowing all, cause us to give wealth even to one who would not give; and may he bestow upon us riches accompanied by all heroic sons.
O Agni, speak here to us; be well-disposed toward us. Bestow upon us, O Lord of the World, for you are the giver of wealth to us.
May Aryaman grant us [blessings]; may Bhaga, may Bṛhaspati, may the gods, and may Sūnṛtā grant them; may the goddess Vāc bestow them upon us.
(1.7.10.2.f) Urge Aryaman, Bṛhaspati, and Indra to bestow gifts; [urge] Vāc, Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, and the prize-winning Savitṛ.
(1.7.10.3.g) We take hold of King Soma, Varuṇa, and Agni; the Ādityas, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, and Bṛhaspati the Brahman.

(1.7.10.3.h) At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech—with the sovereignty of Agni, I consecrate you; with the sovereignty of Indra and Bṛhaspati, I consecrate you.
(1.7.11.1) Agni won speech by means of the one-syllable [meter];
the Aśvins won out-breathing and in-breathing by means of the two-syllable [meter];
Viṣṇu won the three worlds by means of the three-syllable [meter].
Soma won four-footed cattle with a four-syllable [meter]; Pūṣan won the *paṅkti* [meter] with a five-syllable [meter];
Dhātṛ won the six seasons with a six-syllable [meter].
(1.7.11.1) By means of the seven-syllable [meter], the Maruts won the *śakvarī* consisting of seven feet;
(1.7.11.1) Bṛhaspati, by means of the eight-syllable [meter], won the *gāyatrī*;
(1.7.11.1) Mitra, by means of the nine-syllable [meter], won the *trivṛt* stoma.
(1.7.11.2) Varuṇa won the Virāj with ten syllables;
Indra won the Triṣṭubh with eleven syllables;
the Viśve Devas won the Jagatī with twelve syllables.
(1.7.11.2) By means of thirteen syllables, the Vasus won the thirteenth *stoma*.
(1.7.11.2) By means of fourteen syllables, the Rudras won the fourteenth *stoma*.
(1.7.11.2) By means of fifteen syllables, the Ādityas won the fifteenth *stoma*.
Prajāpati won the seventeenfold Stoma by means of the seventeen-syllable [meter].
(1.7.12.1.a) You are taken with a support; I take you, who sit among men, who sit on the wood, who sit in the world, as one pleasing to Indra.

This is your resting place; for Indra, you! (1.7.12.1.b) You are taken with a support; I take you, who sit in the waters, who sit in the clarified butter, who sit in the sky, as one pleasing to Indra. This is your resting place; for Indra, you! (1.7.12.1.c) You are taken with a support; I take you, who sit on the earth, who sit in the intermediate space, who sit on the firmament, as one pleasing to Indra. This is your resting place; for Indra, you!

(1.7.12.1ḍ) Those cups belonging to the five peoples, whose highest-born are three—the divine cask is overturned. Of those with wide-open jaws, I have seized the food and the strength. This is your womb; for Indra, you! (1.7.12.2.e) The essence of the waters, swelling upward, gathered by the rays of the sun—that which is the essence of the essence of the waters, that most excellent one I take from you. This is your womb; for Indra, you!

(1.7.12.2.f) By this manifestation, generating mighty deeds, he indeed is the glowing one, the wide path for the choice. He has risen up as the supporter, the summit of the honey, when he extended his own body from his body.
(1.7.12.2.g) You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Prajāpati. This is your womb; for Prajāpati, you!
The months followed him, as did the forests, the plants, and the mountains; both worlds, yearning, and the waters followed Indra as he was being born.

(1.7.13.1.b) To you was granted for your great Indra-power all [the world] at once in the slaying of Vṛtra; to you, O worshipful Indra, were granted dominion and might in the overcoming of men by the gods. (1.7.13.1.c) Among these women, I have heard that Indrāṇī is the one with the excellent husband; for her husband shall never die, not even by old age.
(1.7.13.2ḍ) O Indrāṇī, I have no pleasure apart from my friend Vṛṣākapi, whose dear oblation, consisting of water, goes to the gods.
He who, as soon as born, was the first wise god, who by his power surpassed the gods; at whose breath the two worlds trembled through the greatness of his manly might—he, O people, is Indra.

(1.7.13.2.f) O Indra, your greatness, O fierce one, rises up when the armies, striving together with common intent, encounter one another. Let it fly like a bird from the arms of the hero; let not your mind wander away in every direction.

Do not neglect us; bring it, give that to us—abundant wealth which you have to bestow upon the worshipper. When this new gift has been proclaimed and this hymn of praise recited, we shall speak forth, O Indra, extolling you.
Bring it hither! Let no one hold this back from us, for we know you as the lord of riches. O Indra, Lord of Bay Steeds, bestow upon us that magnificent gift which is yours to give. Grant it forth!
We invoke Indra, the giver, with our oblation. Fill both your hands with wealth; bestow it from the right and from the left.

The giver, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the bull, the subduer of the swift, the impetuous king, the slayer of Vṛtra, the drinker of Soma—having sat down upon the sacrificial grass at this sacrifice, be now a source of well-being and prosperity for the sacrificer.

May Indra, the good protector, the possessor of wealth, through his aids, be most gracious, he who possesses all knowledge. May he drive away hostility and grant us fearlessness; may we become masters of heroic vigor.
May we abide in the favor of that one worthy of sacrifice, and in his auspicious goodwill. May that Indra, the good protector and possessor of wealth, drive far away from us all who hate us.
May there be for us, in the company of Indra, wealthy and abundant refreshments, through which we may rejoice, possessing food.

Sing forth this strengthening hymn for this Indra, whose chariot is foremost; he is the maker of space even in close combat, the slayer of Vṛtra in the clash of battles. Be our inspirer! May the bowstrings upon the bows of our enemies snap asunder!
(1.8.1.1) He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Anumati; a milch-cow is the sacrificial fee.
(1.8.1.1) Those [embers] which fall behind the yoke-pin, from them he prepares a cake on one potsherd for Nirṛti; a black garment with a black fringe is the sacrificial fee.
"Come! Svāhā! May you enjoy the oblation!"
(1.8.1.1) This is your portion, O Nirṛti; you are possessed of the oblation once it has been offered. Release this person from distress! Svāhā! Homage to him who has done this!
He offers a caru-oblation to Āditya; a choice gift is the sacrificial fee.
(1.8.1.1) An offering to Agni and Viṣṇu on eleven potsherds; a dwarf draft-ox is the sacrificial fee. (1.8.1.1–2) [An offering] to Agni and Soma on eleven potsherds; gold is the sacrificial fee.
(1.8.1.2) An offering to Indra on eleven potsherds; a draft-bull is the sacrificial fee.

(1.8.1.2) An offering on eight potsherds for Agni, curd for Indra; a draft-bull is the sacrificial fee. (1.8.1.2) An offering on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni, a pap for the Viśvedevas; a first-born calf is the sacrificial fee. (1.8.1.2) A pap of millet for Soma; a garment is the sacrificial fee. (1.8.1.2) A pap for Sarasvat; a pair of cattle is the sacrificial fee.

(1.8.2.1) He offers an oblation on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Sarasvatī, a pap for Pūṣan, a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts, curdled milk (āmikṣā) for the Viśve Devas, and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth.
(1.8.3.1.a) [One offers] a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and Agni, curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) for the Maruts, curd-mixture for Varuṇa, and a cake on one potsherd for Ka.

(1.8.3.1.b) We invoke the Praghāsya Maruts, the bearers of sacrifice, who are well-pleased with the groats (*karambha*). (1.8.3.1.c) O Indra, O God, do not leave us behind in battles; may you be our protection, O Mighty One, for great indeed is the bounty of this bounteous Lord. The song of the sacrificer praises the Maruts.

(1.8.3.1ḍ) Whatever sin we have committed in the village, whatever in the forest, whatever in the assembly hall, whatever in our sensory faculties, whatever toward a Śūdra, whatever toward an Ārya, whatever against the law of a single person—for that, you are the expiation; *svāhā*! (1.8.3.1.e) The performers of ritual action have performed their work together with the joy-bestowing voice. Having performed the work for the gods, go home, O bounteous ones!

(1.8.4.1.a) He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Anīkavat at the rising of the sun; at midday, he offers a pap to the Sāṃtapana Maruts; in the evening, he offers a pap cooked in the milk of all [the cows] to the Gṛhamedhin Maruts. (1.8.4.1.b) Full, O ladle, fly away; well-filled, fly back again! Like goods, let us barter for food and strength, O Śatakratu!
(1.8.4.1.c) Give to me; I give to you. Bestow upon me; I bestow upon you. Bring the offering to me; I bring the offering for you. (1.8.4.2) I bring the offering for you.

(1.8.4.2ḍ) He offers a cake on seven potsherds to the sporting Maruts at the time when the sun has risen. He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni; a pap to Soma; a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ; a pap to Sarasvatī; a pap to Pūṣan; a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra-Agni; a pap to Indra; and a cake on one potsherd to Viśvakarman.

(1.8.5.1.a) He offers a cake on six potsherds to Soma accompanied by the Fathers; parched grains to the Fathers seated on the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣad*); and a stirred drink (*mantha*) made with the milk of a cow that has calved for the first time to the Fathers consumed by fire (*agniṣvātta*).

(1.8.5.1.b) "This is for you, father, and for those who follow you; this is for you, grandfather and great-grandfather, and for those who follow you. Here, O Fathers, rejoice according to your respective portions. (1.8.5.1.c) "O Bounteous One, may we gladden thee, who art so fair to behold. Now, O thou whose chariot-seat is full, being praised, thou goest according to thy will. Yoke now, O Indra, thy two bay steeds!"

(1.8.5.2ḍ) They have eaten and they have rejoiced; the dear ones have shaken themselves free. The self-luminous sages have offered praise with a most recent hymn: "Now, O Indra, yoke thy two bay steeds!"
(1.8.5.2.e) The fathers have eaten; the fathers have rejoiced; the fathers have been satisfied; the fathers have cleansed themselves.
(1.8.5.2.f) Depart, O Soma-loving fathers, by the deep, ancient paths! Then come to the benevolent fathers who feast together with Yama in joy.

(1.8.5.2.g) We now summon the mind with the Nārāśaṃsa hymn, and with the prayers of the Fathers. (1.8.5.2.h) May our mind return to us for wisdom, for skill, and for life, so that we may long behold the sun.
(1.8.5.3.i) May the divine folk, our fathers, grant us back our mind; may we be united with the company of the living.

Whatever injury we have done to the atmosphere, the earth, or the sky, or to our mother or our father—may Agni Gārhapatya release me from that sin; may he free me from whatever misdeeds we have committed and make me sinless.
(1.8.6.1.a) He offers one cake on a single potsherd for each person, with one remaining.
(1.8.6.1.b) "As many as we are who belong to the household, for them I have made [this] pleasure.
(1.8.6.1.c) "Thou art the protection of cattle; thou art the protection of the sacrificer; grant me protection."
(1.8.6.1ḍ) Rudra is indeed one; he has no second standing alongside him.
(1.8.6.1.e) O Rudra, the mouse is your animal; accept it with favor.
(1.8.6.1.f) This, O Rudra, is your portion, together with your sister Ambikā; accept it with favor.

(1.8.6.1.g) A remedy for the cow, a remedy for the horse, a remedy for man, and for us as well—a most excellent remedy—so that there may be a good path for the ram and the ewe. O Mother, we have appeased Rudra; we have appeased the god Tryambaka, so that he may make us better, so that he may make us wealthier, so that he may make us possessors of cattle, and so that he may grant us firm resolve.
(1.8.6.2.i) We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity. Like a cucumber from its stem, may I be released from death, but not from immortality.
(1.8.6.2.k) This, O Rudra, is your portion; enjoy it. With that favor, pass beyond the Mūjavat mountains.
(1.8.6.2.l) With bow unstrung, Pināka in hand, clothed in a skin.

(1.8.7.1.a) A cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni, a pap for the Viśvedevas, a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra Śunāsīra, milk for Vāyu, and a cake on one potsherd for Sūrya; the sacrificial fee is a plough drawn by twelve oxen.

(1.8.7.1.b) He offers a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap of *gāvīdhuka* grain for Rudra, curds for Indra, and a pap of barley for Varuṇa; the sacrificial fee is a milch-cow with a calf that has not yet calved.

(1.8.7.1.c) Those gods who sit in the east, led by Agni; those who sit in the south, led by Yama; those who sit in the west, led by Savitṛ; those who sit in the north, led by Varuṇa; those who sit above, led by Bṛhaspati—the slayers of Rākṣasas—may they protect us, may they aid us; to them [be] homage! Svāhā! (1.8.7.2ḍ) The Rākṣasa is gathered up, the Rākṣasa is consumed. Here I utterly consume this Rākṣasa. (1.8.7.2.e) To Agni, the slayer of Rākṣasas, svāhā! To Yama, to Savitṛ, to Varuṇa, to Bṛhaspati, the worshipful slayer of Rākṣasas, svāhā!
(1.8.7.2.f) A chariot drawn by side-horses is the sacrificial fee.
(1.8.7.2.g) At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I offer the slayer of the Rakṣas; the Rakṣas is slain, we have struck down the Rakṣas.
(1.8.7.2.h) That which it wears is the sacrificial fee.
(1.8.8.1) He offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Dhātṛ; (1.8.8.1) a pap to Anumati;
(1.8.8.1) a pap to Rākā.
(1.8.8.1) A pap for Sinīvālī; (1.8.8.1) a pap for Kuhū;
(1.8.8.1) a pair of cattle as the sacrificial fee.
(1.8.8.1) He offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu;
(1.8.8.1) [a cake] on eleven potsherds to Indra and Viṣṇu;
(1.8.8.1) and [a cake] on three potsherds to Viṣṇu.
A dwarf is the vehicle;
a cow is the sacrificial fee. He offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma, and a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Soma.
A pap of cooked rice for Soma; a brown animal is the sacrificial fee;
he offers a pap of cooked rice for Soma and Pūṣan.
(1.8.8.1) A pap of cooked rice for Indra and Pūṣan; (1.8.8.1) a pap of cooked rice for Pūṣan.
(1.8.8.1) A dark-colored animal is the sacrificial fee.
He offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara;
the sacrificial fee is gold;
[and] a pap made of barley to Varuṇa.
A horse is the sacrificial fee.

(1.8.9.1) He offers a *caru* oblation to Bṛhaspati in the house of the Brahman; a white-backed bull is the sacrificial fee. (1.8.9.1) [He offers] a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra in the house of the Rājanya; a bull is the sacrificial fee. (1.8.9.1) [He offers] a *caru* oblation to Aditi in the house of the Mahiṣī; a milch-cow is the sacrificial fee.
(1.8.9.1) An oblation of cooked rice for Nirṛti is offered in the house of the woman who has been superseded; the sacrificial fee is black rice split by the fingernails and a black ewe.
(1.8.9.1) An offering on eight potsherds for Agni is offered in the house of the commander of the army; the sacrificial fee is gold.
(1.8.9.1) An offering on ten potsherds for Varuṇa is offered in the house of the charioteer; the sacrificial fee is a castrated bull.
(1.8.9.1) An offering to the Maruts on seven potsherds at the house of the *grāmaṇī*; a dappled cow (*pṛśni*) is the sacrificial fee.
(1.8.9.2) An offering to Savitṛ on twelve potsherds at the house of the *kṣattṛ*; a speckled bull (*upadhvasta*) is the sacrificial fee.
An offering to the Aśvins on two potsherds at the house of the *saṃgrahītṛ*; two calves born from the same mother (*savātyau*) are the sacrificial fee.
(1.8.9.2) In the house of the *bhāgadugha*, he offers a pap (*caru*) to Pūṣan; a dark-colored ox is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
(1.8.9.2) In the house of the *akṣāvāpa*, he offers a pap of *gāvīdhuka* seeds to Rudra; a brindled ox with a white back is the sacrificial fee.
(1.8.9.2) He prepares a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra Sutrāman and for Indra Aṃhomuc, [thinking]: "May this king, the slayer of Vṛtra, having become king, slay Vṛtra."

(1.8.9.2) There is an offering to Mitra and Bṛhaspati. It is performed with ghee that has been self-formed and self-churned from the milk of a white cow with a white calf, in a four-cornered vessel made of *aśvattha* wood. (1.8.9.3) From a branch that has fallen of its own accord, one should separate the rice grains into those with kernels and those without kernels. Those with kernels are for Bṛhaspati in the milk; those without kernels are for Mitra in the ghee.
The altar is self-made, the sacrificial grass is self-cut, and the fuel is self-prepared.
That very white cow with a white calf is the sacrificial fee.

(1.8.10.1.a) He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Gṛhapati from black rice; a pap of millet to Soma Vanaspati; a cake on twelve potsherds of fast-ripening rice to Savitṛ Satyaprasava; a pap of *gavidhuka* seeds to Rudra Paśupati; a pap of wild rice to Bṛhaspati Vācaspati; a cake on eleven potsherds of large rice to Indra Jyeṣṭha; a pap of *amba* grains to Mitra Satya; and a pap made of barley to Varuṇa Dharmapati.

(1.8.10.1.b) May Savitṛ impel you among those who impel; Agni among householders; Soma among the lords of the forest; Rudra among cattle. (1.8.10.2) Bṛhaspati among words; Indra among the eldest; Mitra among the truthful; Varuṇa among the lords of dharma.

(1.8.10.2.c) O gods who are the impellers of the gods, do you impel this man, the son of such-and-such a father, toward freedom from enemies, toward great sovereignty, toward great overlordship, and toward great rule over the people.
(1.8.10.2ḍ) This is your king, O Bharatas; Soma is the king of us Brāhmaṇas.

(1.8.10.2.e) That name and sovereignty have been restored; Varuṇa has clothed himself in his own body. We have become observers of the vows of the pure Mitra; we have meditated upon the name of the great *ṛta*. (1.8.10.2.f) All the hosts have become subject to Varuṇa; Mitra, through his deeds, has overcome hostility. The worshipful ones have prospered through *ṛta*; Trita has driven away our old age. (1.8.10.2.g) You are the stride of Viṣṇu; you are the step of Viṣṇu; you are the wide-stride of Viṣṇu.

(1.8.11.1.a) You are purposeful; you are the lord of the waters; you are the male; you are the wave with a male host; you dwell in the enclosure; you are the vigor of the Maruts; you possess the luster of the sun; you possess the skin of the sun; you are the refreshing ones; you are the lowing ones; you are the powerful ones; you are the sustainers of all; you are the sustainers of men; you are the essence of Agni’s brilliance; you are the sap of the waters and the plants. (1.8.11.1.b) They have taken up the divine, honey-sweet waters, full of strength, collected for the Rājasūya sacrifice—those waters with which they consecrated Mitra and Varuṇa, and with which they led Indra beyond his enemies.
(1.8.11.1.c) You are givers of kingship; grant us kingship, svāhā! You are givers of kingship; grant that [person] there kingship.
(1.8.12.1.a) O divine waters, rich in sweetness, mingle with those rich in sweetness, winning great splendor for the kṣatriya.
(1.8.12.1.b) Sit down, unassailable and full of vigor, bestowing great splendor upon the kṣatriya. (1.8.12.1.c) You are uncrushed, the kinsman of speech, born of heat; you are the gift of Soma.
(1.8.12.1ḍ) With the bright I purify your bright [waters], with the shining your shining, with the immortal your immortal—*svāhā*! You who are gathered for the *rājasūya*.

(1.8.12.1.e) These companions in revelry, radiant, full of vigor, unassailable, and active—clothing himself in them, Varuṇa has made his dwelling-place within the waters, like a child in the most motherly ones.

(1.8.12.2.f) You are the caul of the kṣatra; you are the womb of the kṣatra. (1.8.12.2.g) Agni, lord of the household, has been won over; Indra of far-reaching fame has been won over; Pūṣan, the all-knowing, has been won over; Mitra and Varuṇa, the increasers of cosmic order, have been won over; Heaven and Earth, whose vows are firm, have been won over; the goddess Aditi, of all forms, has been won over; this man, so-and-so, the son of such-a-one, has been won over for this people, for this kingdom, for great kṣatriya power, for great sovereignty, for great lordship over the people. (1.8.12.2.h) This, O Bharatas, is your king; Soma is the king of us Brāhmaṇas.
(1.8.12.2.i) You are Indra’s thunderbolt; you are the slayer of Vṛtra; may this man slay Vṛtra with you.
(1.8.12.3.k) You are the repellers of enemies.
(1.8.12.3ḷ) Protect me from behind; protect me from the side; protect me from the front; protect me from the quarters; protect me from all destructive powers.
O you two of golden hue, at the breaking forth of the dawns, O Varuṇa and Mitra, ascend the chariot-seat at the rising of the sun, which has pillars of bronze; from there, behold both Aditi and Diti.

(1.8.13.1.a) Ascend the *samidh*! May the *gāyatrī* among the meters protect you; the *trivṛt* hymn-form, the *rathantara* chant, and Agni as the deity—may these be your wealth of sacred power (*brahman*).

(1.8.13.1.b) Ascend the *ugrā*! May the *triṣṭubh* among the meters protect you; the *pañcadaśa* hymn-form, the *bṛhat* chant, and Indra as the deity—may these be your wealth of sovereign power (*kṣatra*). (1.8.13.1.c) Ascend the *virāj*! May the *jagatī* among the meters protect you; the *saptadaśa* hymn-form, the *vairūpa* chant, and the Maruts as the deity—may these be your wealth of the people (*viś*).

(1.8.13.1ḍ) Stand up toward the north; may the *anuṣṭubh* among the meters protect you, the twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*) hymn-form, the *vairāja* chant, and Mitra and Varuṇa as the deities—strength is the wealth. (1.8.13.2.e) Stand up erect; may the *paṅkti* among the meters protect you, the twenty-seven-fold and thirty-three-fold hymn-forms, the *śākvara* and *raivata* chants, and Bṛhaspati as the deity—splendor is the wealth.
(1.8.13.2.f) Such-like and other-like, this-like and counter-like, measured and well-measured, and the bringers of bounty.

(1.8.13.2.g) Śukrajyotis, Citrajyotis, Satyajyotis, Jyotiṣmant, Satya, and Ṛtapā; (1.8.13.3) Atyaṃhas. (1.8.13.3ḥ) Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to Savitṛ! Svāhā to Sarasvatī! Svāhā to Pūṣan! Svāhā to Bṛhaspati! Svāhā to Indra! Svāhā to Ghoṣa! Svāhā to Śloka! Svāhā to Aṃśa! Svāhā to Bhaga! Svāhā to Kṣetrasya pati! Svāhā!

(1.8.13.3.i) Svāhā to the earth! Svāhā to the atmosphere! Svāhā to the sky! Svāhā to the sun! Svāhā to the moon! Svāhā to the stars! Svāhā to the waters! Svāhā to the plants! Svāhā to the trees! Svāhā to moving and unmoving beings! Svāhā to those that float! Svāhā to those that crawl! Svāhā!
(1.8.14.1.a) You are the brilliance of Soma; may my brilliance be like yours. (1.8.14.1.b) You are immortality; protect me from death.
(1.8.14.1.c) Shining forth, protect me! (1.8.14.1ḍ) The biters have been driven away!
(1.8.14.1.e) The head of Namuci has been cast out!

(1.8.14.1.f) King Soma, Varuṇa, the gods, and those who are the impellers of dharma—may they inspire your speech; may they inspire your breath; may they inspire your sight; may they inspire your hearing. (1.8.14.1.g) With the splendor of Soma, with the brilliance of Agni, with the radiance of Sūrya, with the power of Indra, with the heroism of Mitra and Varuṇa, and with the might of the Maruts, I sprinkle you.
(1.8.14.2h) Among the rulers, you are the lord of the ruling power.
(1.8.14.2.i) Guard beyond the sky!
(1.8.14.2.k) They have turned back from below, flowing upward, moving along after the serpent of the deep; like ships on the back of the bull-like mountain, they move, self-pouring as they flow.
O Rudra, that which is your supreme name, the buyer, for that you are offered; you are the one sacrificed to by Yama.
(1.8.14.2ṃ) O Prajāpati, none other than you has encompassed all these created beings. Whatever desire we have as we offer this oblation to you, may that be ours; may we be masters of riches.
(1.8.15.1.a) You are Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra; with you may he slay Vṛtra.
(1.8.15.1.b) By the command of Mitra and Varuṇa, the two directors, I yoke you for the performance of the sacrifice.
(1.8.15.1.c) You are Viṣṇu’s stride, you are Viṣṇu’s step, you are Viṣṇu’s wide stride.
(1.8.15.1ḍ) May I conquer by the impulse of the Maruts; (1.8.15.1.e) the mind has been attained; (1.8.15.1.f) may I be united with sensory power and vigor.
(1.8.15.1.g) You are the fury of cattle; may my fury be like yours. (1.8.15.1ḥ) Homage to Mother Earth! May I not harm Mother Earth; may Mother Earth not harm me.
(1.8.15.2.i) Such is your life-span; bestow life-span upon me. You are vigor; bestow vigor upon me. You are a yoke; you are luster; bestow luster upon me.
(1.8.15.2.k) To Agni, the lord of the household, svāhā! To Soma, the lord of the forest, svāhā! To the strength of Indra, svāhā! To the vigor of the Maruts, svāhā!

(1.8.15.2ḷ) The swan dwelling in the light, the Vasu dwelling in the atmosphere, the priest dwelling at the altar, the guest dwelling in the house; dwelling among men, dwelling in the best places, dwelling in the Truth, dwelling in the sky; born of the waters, born of the kine, born of the Truth, born of the mountains—the Great Truth.
(1.8.16.1.a) You are Mitra; you are Varuṇa. (1.8.16.1.b) May I be united with all the gods.
(1.8.16.1.c) You are the navel of sovereignty; you are the womb of sovereignty.
Sit on the pleasant one; sit on the easy-to-sit-upon seat.
May it not harm you, and may you not harm it.
Varuṇa, of firm vows and wise intellect, has sat down in his dwellings for sovereign rule.

(1.8.16.1.g) O King, you are the Brahman; you are the Brahman. You are Savitṛ, whose impulse is true. O King, you are the Brahman; you are the Brahman. You are Indra, whose might is true. (1.8.16.2) O King, you are the Brahman; you are the Brahman. You are Mitra, who is most gracious. O King, you are the Brahman; you are the Brahman. You are Varuṇa, whose law is true.
(1.8.16.2ḥ) You are the thunderbolt of Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra; with it, make me successful. (1.8.16.2.i) This king has come toward the quarters. He has become the sovereign.

(1.8.16.2.k) To him of fair renown, of auspiciousness, whose kingship is truth! (1.8.16.2ḷ) Svāhā to the grandson of the waters! Svāhā to the grandson of vigor! Svāhā to Agni, the lord of the household!

(1.8.17.1) He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni; gold is the sacrificial fee. A pap to Sarasvatī; a heifer is the sacrificial fee. A cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ; a dusty bull is the sacrificial fee. A pap to Pūṣan; a dark-grey animal is the sacrificial fee. A pap to Bṛhaspati; a white-backed animal is the sacrificial fee. A cake on eleven potsherds to Indra; a bull is the sacrificial fee. A cake on ten potsherds to Varuṇa; a large castrated bull is the sacrificial fee. A pap to Soma; a brown animal is the sacrificial fee. A cake on eight potsherds to Tvaṣṭṛ; a hornless animal is the sacrificial fee. A cake on three potsherds to Viṣṇu; a dwarf animal is the sacrificial fee.
(1.8.18.1) They consecrate him on the same day; (1.8.18.1) they purchase the Soma on the same day;
(1.8.18.1) he presents a lotus-wreath.
He purchases the Soma with ten young bulls;
it is the Daśapeya sacrifice;
a hundred Brahmins drink [the Soma].
The stotra consists of seventeen verses.
He gives two luminous vessels to the Adhvaryu and a garland to the Udgātṛ.
(1.8.18.1) A gold ornament for the Hotṛ;
(1.8.18.1) a horse for the Prastotṛ and Pratihartṛ;
(1.8.18.1) twelve four-year-old mares for the Brahman.
A cow for the Maitrāvaruṇa; a bull for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin;
two garments for the Neṣṭṛ and Potṛ.
(1.8.18.1) A single-seated cart laden with barley is for the Achāvāka; (1.8.18.1) an ox is for the Agnīdh;
(1.8.18.1) the Hotṛ is a Bhārgava.
The Śrāyantīya is the Brahman’s chant; the Vāravantīya is the Agniṣṭoma chant.
He draws the waters of the Sarasvatī.
(1.8.19.1) He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni; the sacrificial fee is gold. (1.8.19.1) [He offers] a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra; the sacrificial fee is a bull.
(1.8.19.1) [He offers] a pap to the Viśve Devas; the sacrificial fee is a reddish-brown four-year-old cow.
(1.8.19.1) There is curdled milk (āmikṣā) for Mitra and Varuṇa; a barren cow is the sacrificial fee.
(1.8.19.1) There is a pap (caru) for Bṛhaspati; a white-backed bull is the sacrificial fee.
(1.8.19.1) He sacrifices a dewlap-bearing pregnant cow to Aditi.
He offers a spotted heifer of three years old to the Maruts;
a cake on twelve potsherds to the Aśvins and Pūṣan; a pap to Sarasvatī of true speech; and a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ of true impulsion.
A bow with three arrows and a dried skin-bag is the sacrificial fee.
He offers an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni, a pap to Soma,
and an oblation on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ.
An oblation of cooked rice for Bṛhaspati;
a cake on eight potsherds for Tvaṣṭṛ;
a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara.
The right horse that draws the chariot-stand is the sacrificial fee. He offers a pap to Sarasvatī;
he offers a pap to Pūṣan.
An oblation of cooked rice for Mitra; an oblation of cooked rice for Varuṇa;
an oblation of cooked rice for Kṣetrapati.
A pap of rice for Āditya;
a northern chariot-horse is the sacrificial fee.

(1.8.21.1.a) I mix you, the sweet, with the sweet; the sharp, with the sharp; the immortal, with the immortal—[I mix] you with Soma. You are Soma; be prepared for the Aśvins, be prepared for Sarasvatī, be prepared for Indra the Good Protector.
(1.8.21.1.b) May the daughter of the Sun purify your flowing Soma, with the eternal fleece as a filter.
Vāyu, purified by the filter, Soma has flowed forth westward, the worthy companion and friend of Indra.

(1.8.21.1ḍ) Surely, just as those possessing barley reap the barley in due order, separating it out, so do you provide food here for those who have not come to the trimming of the sacrificial grass with their homage.
(1.8.21.1.e) He offers a smoke-colored animal to the Aśvins, a ram to Sarasvatī, and a bull to Indra.
(1.8.21.1.f) He offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra, one on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ, and one on ten potsherds to Varuṇa.
(1.8.21.1.g) O Fathers who have Soma as your face, may you be satisfied.
(1.8.21.1) A mare is the sacrificial fee.
O Agni and Viṣṇu, great is that majesty of yours; enjoy the secret names of the clarified butter. Bestowing the seven treasures in every house, let your tongue move toward the clarified butter.

O Agni and Viṣṇu, you enjoy the great, beloved domain and the secret portions of the clarified butter with delight; increasing through our excellent praises in every house, let your tongue rise up toward the clarified butter.
May the divine Sarasvatī, rich in spoils, protect us with her strengths as the furtherer of our prayers.

From the great heaven, from the mountain, may Sarasvatī, the worshipful goddess, come to our sacrifice. May she, the butter-dripping one, rejoicing in our invocation, graciously hear our longing and effective speech.
O Bṛhaspati, who belongs to all the gods, graciously accept our oblations; bestow treasures upon the donor.

(1.8.22.2.f) Thus let us serve the Father, the possessor of all gods, the Bull, with sacrifices, with homage, and with oblations. O Bṛhaspati, may we, possessing good offspring and heroic sons, be masters of riches.
O Bṛhaspati, that which surpasses the worthy rival, which shines brilliantly and powerfully among the people, and which glows with might—bestow upon us that wonderful wealth born of the *ṛta*.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, you of excellent wisdom, sprinkle our pastures with clarified butter and the regions of space with honey.
Stretch forth your arms that we may live; sprinkle our pastures with ghee. O youthful ones, make us famous among the people; hear these my invocations, O Mitra and Varuṇa.
(1.8.22.3.k) With my song, I praise Agni, the ancient god among your treasures; serving him who is beloved by many, like Mitra, the one who establishes us in our fields.

(1.8.22.3ḷ) Swift is the chariot of the one who possesses the gods; or he is a hero in every battle whatsoever. He who, as a sacrificer, strives to win the minds of the gods—he shall surely prevail over those who do not sacrifice.

(1.8.22.4ṃ) O sacrificer, you shall not come to harm; neither shall the presser of soma nor the one devoted to the gods. Therein shall be great heroic power, and even that wealth consisting of horses. No one shall reach him by his ritual act, nor shall he be forsaken, nor shall he be separated from it.

The rivers flow toward him, bringing refreshment; like milch-cows, they approach the one who has sacrificed and the one who is about to sacrifice, the one who bestows gifts and the one who fulfills them. Seeking glory, the streams of clarified butter flow toward him from every side.
O Soma and Rudra, tear asunder in all directions the disease that has entered our home; drive far away Destruction, and release us from whatever sin we have committed.
O Soma and Rudra, bestow upon us all these remedies within our bodies. Untie and release from us whatever sin has been committed that is bound within our persons.

O Soma and Pūṣan, you two are the progenitors of riches, the progenitors of heaven, and the progenitors of earth; born as the guardians of the entire world, the gods have made you the navel of immortality.

(1.8.22.5ṛ) May these two gods, at their birth, take pleasure [in this]; may they conceal the hated darknesses. Through these two, Soma and Pūṣan, Indra produced the cooked [milk] within the raw cows.
(2.1.1.1) One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal dedicated to Vāyu.
(2.1.1.1) Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity; (2.1.1.1) he thus approaches Vāyu with his own share.
(2.1.1.1) That very deity leads him to prosperity; he indeed becomes prosperous. (2.1.1.1) "The deity is too swift," they say, "it is liable to burn him up."
(2.1.1.1) While he is in this very state, one should sacrifice a victim to Vāyu Niyutvat.
(2.1.1.1) For the *niyuts* are his means of support (*dhṛti*).
(2.1.1.1) Thus, being supported, he attains prosperity without being consumed by fire.
(2.1.1.1) It indeed comes to pass. (2.1.1.2) One who desires a village should sacrifice to Vāyu with his team of horses (*niyut*).
For Vāyu leads these creatures along as if they were tied to a nose-rope;
it is to Vāyu with his team that he has recourse with his own share.
(2.1.1.2) He indeed delivers to him offspring bound like a nose-rope;
he becomes truly domesticated;
it is for Niyutvat [that the verse] is used.
(2.1.1.2) He makes them firm for him and non-departing.
(2.1.1.2) One desiring offspring should sacrifice to Vāyu Niyutvat.
Vāyu is indeed the out-breath; the *niyuts* are the in-breath.

(2.1.1.2) Indeed, the out-breath and the in-breath depart from that person who, though being capable of procreation, does not obtain offspring. (2.1.1.3) He resorts to Vāyu, accompanied by his team, with his own share;
he (Vāyu) indeed causes him to procreate offspring through the out-breath and the in-breath.
(2.1.1.3) He obtains offspring.
(2.1.1.3) One who has been ill for a long time should sacrifice an animal to Vāyu Niyutvat;
for Vāyu is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*), and the *niyuts* are the in-breath (*apāna*).
(2.1.1.3) Indeed, the out-breath and in-breath depart from him who is long ill.
(2.1.1.3–4) He hastens to Vāyu, accompanied by his team, with his own portion; he alone bestows the out-breath and in-breath upon him.
(2.1.1.4) Or even if his life-breath has departed, he indeed continues to live.
(2.1.1.4) Prajāpati alone was this [universe] in the beginning. (2.1.1.4) He desired.
(2.1.1.4) "May I create offspring and cattle," he thought;
(2.1.1.4) he extracted the omentum from his own body and offered it into the fire.
(2.1.1.4) From that, a hornless goat came into being.
(2.1.1.4) He offered it to its own deity.
(2.1.1.4) Thereupon, indeed, he created offspring and cattle.
(2.1.1.4) He who desires offspring, (2.1.1.5) or who desires cattle, should sacrifice this hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati. (2.1.1.5) He thus approaches Prajāpati with his own share;
he himself procreates for him offspring and cattle.
That which has a beard is the form of men;
that which is hornless is the form of horses; that which has teeth on one side is the form of cattle.
That which is like the hooves of sheep belongs to sheep; that which is goat-like belongs to goats. These indeed are the domestic animals.
(2.1.1.5) By means of form itself, he wins them.
(2.1.1.6) One desiring cattle should sacrifice a three-year-old goat dedicated to Soma and Pūṣan.
For the she-goat has two teats.
Two are born separately for vigor and nourishment; the third is for both. He has recourse to Soma and Pūṣan with their own respective portions; they two indeed procreate cattle for him.
Soma is indeed the depositor of seed; Pūṣan is the progenitor of cattle. Soma deposits seed for him, and Pūṣan procreates cattle.
The sacrificial post is made of Udumbara wood.
The udumbara is indeed strength, and cattle are strength; by means of strength he wins for him strength and cattle.
(2.1.2.1) Prajāpati created offspring. (2.1.2.1) Once they were created, they moved away from him; (2.1.2.1) they went to Varuṇa.
(2.1.2.1) He went after them; (2.1.2.1) he begged for them back; (2.1.2.1) but he did not give them back to him.
He said,
"Choose a boon, and then give it back to me. He chose a boon from them.
(2.1.2.1) He became a black bull with one white foot.
(2.1.2.1) Whoever should be seized by Varuṇa should sacrifice this black bull with one white foot dedicated to Varuṇa.
(2.1.2.1) Thus he approaches Varuṇa with his own portion. (2.1.2.2) [He thus delivers him] from Varuṇa.
He alone releases him from the noose of Varuṇa. It is a black one-footed [animal] that is used,
for it belongs to Varuṇa by deity.
(2.1.2.2) For prosperity.
(2.1.2.2) Suvarbhānu, the son of Asura, pierced the sun with darkness.
The gods sought an expiation for him.
(2.1.2.2) That first darkness which they struck away became a black ewe;
that second became a *phalgunī*;
that third became a *bhalakṣī*.
(2.1.2.2) What he stood upon, they cut away; that became the ewe, the barren cow (*vaśā*).
(2.1.2.3) Those gods said, "This has indeed become a sacrificial animal for the gods; from whom shall we obtain this?"
(2.1.2.3) Now, at that time, the earth was small and the plants had not yet been born.
They offered that ewe, a barren cow, to the Ādityas for the sake of desire. Thereupon, indeed, the earth expanded and the plants were born.
(2.1.2.3) He who should desire, "May I expand with cattle; may I be propagated with offspring," he should offer this ewe, barren, to the Ādityas for the sake of his desire.
(2.1.2.4) Verily, he hastens to the Ādityas, the very desire, with their own portion.
(2.1.2.4) These very [bricks] extend him with cattle and cause him to be born forth with offspring.
(2.1.2.4) Yonder sun did not shine;
for it the gods sought an atonement.
(2.1.2.4) Therefore, they offered these dewlap-bearing animals: a black-necked one dedicated to Agni, a brindled one dedicated to Indra, and a white one dedicated to Bṛhaspati.
(2.1.2.4) By means of these very [offerings], they bestowed radiance upon him.

(2.1.2.5) Whoever should desire spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), for him he should offer these dewlap-bearing animals: a black-necked one dedicated to Agni, a brindled one dedicated to Indra, and a white one dedicated to Bṛhaspati.
(2.1.2.5) He approaches these very deities with their own respective portions; (2.1.2.5) they bestow spiritual luster upon him; (2.1.2.5) he indeed becomes endowed with spiritual luster.
(2.1.2.5) In spring, at dawn, he should sacrifice a black-necked cow to Agni; in summer, at midday, a brindled cow to Indra; in autumn, in the afternoon, a white cow to Bṛhaspati.
(2.1.2.5) There are indeed three splendors of the Sun: in spring at dawn, in summer at midday, and in autumn in the afternoon.
(2.1.2.6) As many splendors as there are, those very ones he secures for himself.
(2.1.2.6) They are sacrificed to throughout the year.
(2.1.2.6) The year, indeed, is the bestower of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*);
it is the year itself that bestows spiritual luster upon him.
(2.1.2.6) He indeed becomes endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*).
(2.1.2.6) They become pregnant.
(2.1.2.6) For the embryo is indeed sensory power (*indriya*).
(2.1.2.6) They bestow the very sense-organ upon him.
(2.1.2.6) One who is capable of speaking but does not speak should offer a ewe sacred to Sarasvatī.
Sarasvatī is indeed speech.
(2.1.2.6) He has recourse to Sarasvatī herself with her own portion; she alone bestows speech upon him, and he becomes a speaker of speech.
(2.1.2.7) She is one whose teeth have not yet fallen out;
therefore, human beings speak all forms of speech.
(2.1.2.7) One who has been ill for a long time should offer a black-necked animal to Agni and a brown one to Soma.
(2.1.2.7) Indeed, the body of one who is long ill goes to Agni, and his vital essence (*rasa*) goes to Soma.
(2.1.2.7) From Agni he thus ransoms his body, and from Soma his vital essence.
(2.1.2.7) Or even if his life-breath has departed, he indeed continues to live.

(2.1.2.7) One desiring offspring should sacrifice a brown animal dedicated to Soma and a black-necked one dedicated to Agni. (2.1.2.8) Soma, indeed, is the bestower of seed; Agni is the progenitor of offspring.
Soma indeed bestows seed upon him; Agni procreates offspring.
He obtains offspring.
A Brāhmaṇa who, having studied the Vedas, does not shine forth, should sacrifice a black-necked animal to Agni and a brown one to Soma.
(2.1.2.8) In that there is an offering to Agni, he thereby bestows brilliance upon him; in that there is one to Soma, he thereby bestows spiritual luster.
The black-necked one belongs to Agni; he thereby drives away darkness from him.
(2.1.2.8) It becomes white; (2.1.2.9) verily he bestows radiance upon him. (2.1.2.9) The brown one belongs to Soma; verily he bestows spiritual luster and brilliance upon him.
One who is contending for the office of domestic priest should offer a black-necked animal to Agni and a brown one to Soma, followed by a black-necked animal to Agni.
The Brāhmaṇa indeed belongs to Agni, and the Rājanya belongs to Soma. On both sides of the offering to Soma there are offerings to Agni;
thus, by means of brilliance itself, he encompasses the kingdom on both sides for the sake of the Brāhmaṇa.
(2.1.2.9) He gathers [them] together in a single way; they place him in front.
(2.1.3.1) The gods and the asuras contended for these worlds.
(2.1.3.1) Viṣṇu saw this dwarf;
he offered it as a sacrifice to his own deity.
(2.1.3.1) By means of that, he indeed conquered these worlds.
(2.1.3.1) One who is contending should offer a dwarf bull sacred to Viṣṇu.
(2.1.3.1) Having become Viṣṇu himself, he conquers these worlds.
(2.1.3.1) He should sacrifice with uneven [animals];
for these worlds are indeed uneven;
[this is] for the sake of prosperity.
(2.1.3.1) One should offer a spotted bull with forward-pointing horns to Indra Manyumat Manasvat in a battle when it has been joined.
(2.1.3.2) For by means of power (*indriya*), fury (*manyu*), and mind (*manas*), one conquers battle.
Verily, he has recourse to Indra himself, who is possessed of fury and mind, with his own portion.
He alone bestows sensory power, fury, and mental vigor upon him;
he conquers that battle.
One who desires a village should offer a *pṛśnisaktha* animal to Indra accompanied by the Maruts.
(2.1.3.2) He has recourse to Indra accompanied by the Maruts with his own share;
he (Indra) indeed bestows his kinsmen upon him,
and he becomes a village headman.
In that it is a bull, by that it belongs to Indra;
in that it is speckled, by that it belongs to the Maruts—
for the sake of prosperity.
(2.1.3.3) Behind it is one with speckled thighs;
(2.1.3.3) thus he makes for him a people that settles behind him.
One desiring food should offer a brown animal sacred to Soma.
Food belongs to Soma;
he thus approaches Soma with his own share,
and he alone bestows food upon him.
(2.1.3.3) He indeed becomes an eater of food; (2.1.3.3) he becomes tawny;
(2.1.3.3) for this is the form of food.
(2.1.3.3) For prosperity. (2.1.3.3) One who is capable [of ruling] but to whom sovereignty does not come should sacrifice a brown animal dedicated to Soma.
(2.1.3.4) Sovereignty indeed belongs to Soma.
(2.1.3.4) He has recourse to Soma with his own share;
he alone bestows sovereignty upon him.
Sovereignty bows down before him.
(2.1.3.4) He is tawny;
(2.1.3.4) for this is indeed the form of Soma;
(2.1.3.4) it is for the sake of prosperity.
(2.1.3.4) One who has lost his prosperity and desires a firm foundation should offer a spotted, forward-pointing horned animal to Indra, the Overcomer of Vṛtra.
Having indeed overcome the evil Vṛtra, he attains a firm foundation.
(2.1.3.4–5) He who is seized by evil should offer a spotted, forward-pointing horned animal to Indra, the Slayer of the Enemy.
(2.1.3.5) Evil, indeed, is the adversary.
(2.1.3.5) He has recourse to Indra, the slayer of the adversary, with his own share;
he [Indra] drives away evil and the adversary from him.
(2.1.3.5) One who, though being fit for kingship, does not attain the kingdom, should offer a spotted, forward-pointed horned animal to Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt.
He thus approaches Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, with his own share; he [Indra] bestows the thunderbolt upon him.
That thunderbolt kindles him for prosperity; sovereignty bows down before him; he becomes marked with a blaze on his forehead and possesses forward-pointing horns.
(2.1.3.5) This indeed is the form of the thunderbolt;
it is for the sake of prosperity.
(2.1.4.1) Yonder sun did not shine.
(2.1.4.1) The gods sought an atonement for it. For it, they immolated this victim consisting of ten bulls; by that very act, they bestowed radiance upon him.
(2.1.4.1) He who may desire spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice this [cow] with ten bulls.
(2.1.4.1) He thus approaches that very Sun with his own share; he (the Sun) bestows spiritual luster upon him.

(2.1.4.1) He indeed becomes endowed with the splendor of Brahman. (2.1.4.1) In the spring, at dawn, he should sacrifice three with red marks on their foreheads; in the summer, at midday, (2.1.4.2) three with white backs; in the autumn, in the afternoon, three with white tails.
(2.1.4.2) For there are three splendors of the sun: in the spring at dawn, in the summer at midday, and in the autumn in the afternoon.
As many as are the fires, so many indeed he wins.
Three are sacrificed at each time;
verily, he bestows brilliance upon him in successive order.
(2.1.4.2) They are sacrificed to throughout the year.
(2.1.4.2) The year, indeed, is the bestower of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). It is the year itself that bestows spiritual luster upon him.
(2.1.4.2) He indeed becomes endowed with the splendor of Brahman.
(2.1.4.2) After a year has passed, he should offer a spotted animal dedicated to Prajāpati.
(2.1.4.3) Prajāpati is all the deities.
(2.1.4.3) He finds firm support among the deities themselves.
(2.1.4.3) If he should fear,
"I shall become afflicted with skin disease," he should offer a dark-colored animal to Soma and Pūṣan.
Man is indeed related to Soma by deity, and cattle are related to Pūṣan.
By means of his own deity and by means of cattle, he provides him with skin;
he does not become afflicted with a skin disease.
(2.1.4.3) The gods and Yama indeed contended for this world.
(2.1.4.3) That Yama seized the sensory power and vigor of the gods. (2.1.4.3) That is the origin of Yama’s name. (2.1.4.4) It is his quality as Yama.
(2.1.4.4) Those gods reflected, "Yama has indeed become this which we once were. They ran to Prajāpati.
(2.1.4.4) Prajāpati fashioned these two from his own self, a bull and a cow.
(2.1.4.4) The gods offered a cow to Viṣṇu and Varuṇa and a bull to Indra.
Having caused him to be seized by Varuṇa, they drove him away by means of Viṣṇu, the sacrifice; and by means of Indra, they appropriated his power.
(2.1.4.4) He who has rivals, being in competition, should offer a barren cow to Viṣṇu and Varuṇa and a bull to Indra.

(2.1.4.5) Having caused his rival to be seized by Varuṇa, he drives him away by means of Viṣṇu, the sacrifice; by means of the [offering] to Indra, he appropriates his [rival’s] power. He prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated.
Indra slew Vṛtra.
Once Vṛtra was slain, he pierced him with sixteen coils.
From the head of that Vṛtra, the cows emerged.
They became Vaidehīs;
after them, a bull followed at their rear.
Indra perceived him.
He thought,
"Whoever should sacrifice this [animal] would be freed from this evil.
He sacrificed a black-necked animal to Agni and a bull to Indra.
(2.1.4.6) Agni himself, approached by his own portion, burnt away the sixteen coils of Vṛtra; by means of the [offering] to Indra, he placed power within himself.
(2.1.4.6) He who is seized by evil should offer a black-necked animal to Agni and a bull to Indra.
(2.1.4.7) Agni himself, approached by his own portion, burns away his evil; by means of the [offering] to Indra, he places power within himself.
(2.1.4.7) He is released from evil. (2.1.4.7) He indeed prospers. (2.1.4.7) One who has been long excluded from his kingdom should sacrifice a cow to Heaven and Earth.
For indeed, this one is unestablished between these two;
moreover, he who has long been excluded from power resorts to Heaven and Earth with their own respective portions,
and they two cause him to attain a firm foundation.

(2.1.4.7) He stands firm against [his enemies]; (2.1.4.7) he becomes one who has borne a child around [the womb]. For the kingdom of him who has been long exiled is, as it were, one that has borne a child around [the womb].
(2.1.4.7) For prosperity,
(2.1.4.7) he should offer a calf to Vāyu.
(2.1.4.8) Vāyu, indeed, is the calf of these two.
(2.1.4.8) Indeed, these worlds have become parched for him, and the people have become parched.
(2.1.4.8) Now, this one who has long been excluded from his realm resorts to Vāyu with his own share;
he (Vāyu) indeed causes him to bestow these worlds and the people upon him.
(2.1.4.8) These worlds flow toward him; the peasantry enjoys him and waits upon him.
Indra opened the cave of Vala.
He seized the animal that was at the very top by its back and pulled it out;
a thousand animals followed after it.
(2.1.5.1) It became elevated.
(2.1.5.1) He who desires cattle should offer this elevated victim dedicated to Indra.
(2.1.5.1) Thus he has recourse to Indra himself with his own portion.
(2.1.5.1) He indeed bestows cattle upon him; he becomes possessed of cattle.
(2.1.5.1–2) He becomes elevated.

(2.1.5.2) This high [altar] is indeed thousandfold fortune (*lakṣmī*). By means of this very fortune he wins cattle. When he should obtain a thousand cattle, then he should offer a dwarf animal dedicated to Viṣṇu.
(2.1.5.2) Indeed, he stood over that thousand. Therefore, this dwarf, when impelled, bestows a firm foundation upon the offspring of cattle. "Who is worthy to obtain a thousand cattle? they say.
Having accomplished a thousand days and nights, he obtains cattle;
or rather, the days and nights themselves are cattle.
Thus, he causes the cattle that have been born to reach a firm foundation.
(2.1.5.3) One desiring offspring should offer a barren cow to the plants.
(2.1.5.3) Indeed, the plants obstruct him from offspring who, though capable of having offspring, does not obtain offspring.
(2.1.5.3) Moreover, the plants indeed destroy the fetus of that which becomes a barren cow.
Verily, he has recourse to the plants with their own share;
they, for him, procreate offspring from their own womb;
he obtains offspring.
The waters, indeed, are the plants; the person was non-existent. The waters alone bestow existence upon him from that which is non-existent.
Therefore they say: "Both he who knows thus and he who does not."
(2.1.5.4) "May the waters, bestowing what is truly existent, clothe you.
(2.1.5.4) One who desires prosperity should sacrifice a barren cow to Indra.
He who, though capable of prosperity, does not attain it, is indeed as if unborn.
(2.1.5.4) Indeed, having given birth to Indra, this cow became barren.
(2.1.5.5) He has recourse to Indra himself with his own share; he (Indra) leads him to prosperity; he indeed becomes prosperous.
(2.1.5.5) He should sacrifice that very [cow] which, having calved, would become barren; it belongs to Indra. This indeed is that power of Indra;
verily, he directly obtains power.
(2.1.5.5) One who has not drunk Soma up to the third generation of his lineage should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Indra and Agni that has been set free again.
(2.1.5.5–6) For the Soma-drinking of that man is indeed severed who, though being a Brāhmaṇa, does not drink Soma up to the third generation of his lineage.
He approaches Indra and Agni with their own respective share.
Those two indeed bestow the Soma-draught upon him;
the Soma-draught inclines toward him.
In that it belongs to Indra—and the Soma-draught is indeed power—he wins both power and the Soma-draught.

(2.1.5.6) In that it belongs to Agni, and the Brāhmaṇa indeed belongs to Agni, he extends himself along his own deity. (2.1.5.6) It is one released again; for his Soma-draught is, as it were, released again. (2.1.5.7) His Soma-draught is, as it were, released again.
(2.1.5.7) For prosperity,
one practicing exorcism should sacrifice a hornless goat dedicated to Bṛhaspati;
he thus approaches Bṛhaspati with his own share.
(2.1.5.7) He cuts it off for him;
(2.1.5.7) he swiftly meets with calamity. (2.1.5.7) It is hornless.
(2.1.5.7) This hornless animal is indeed a mark with razor-sharp edges;
it serves for prosperity.
(2.1.5.7) The sacrificial post is made of *sphya*-wood; the *sphya* is indeed a thunderbolt; verily, he hurls the thunderbolt against him.
The sacrificial grass made of *śara* reeds shatters him; the fuel-stick made of *vaibhīdaka* wood splits him apart.
(2.1.6.1) One who desires a village, who should wish, "May I be the back [the preeminent one] among my equals," should sacrifice a white-backed animal dedicated to Bṛhaspati.
Verily, he has recourse to Bṛhaspati with his own share.
(2.1.6.1) He alone makes him the back among his equals;
(2.1.6.1) he becomes truly a village-dweller;
(2.1.6.1) he is white-backed.
For this [victim] belongs to Bṛhaspati by deity; for the sake of prosperity, one who desires food should offer a dark-colored victim to Pūṣan.
Pūṣan is indeed food. He approaches Pūṣan with his own share; he, verily, bestows food upon him.
(2.1.6.2) He becomes an eater of food; (2.1.6.2) he becomes dark-complexioned.
(2.1.6.2) For this indeed is the form of food.
(2.1.6.2) For prosperity,
one who desires food should offer a dappled animal to the Maruts. (2.1.6.2) The Maruts are indeed food.
(2.1.6.2) He has recourse to the Maruts with their own portion;
they alone bestow food upon him. He indeed becomes an eater of food.
(2.1.6.2) It is spotted;
(2.1.6.2) for this is indeed the form of food;
(2.1.6.2) it is for the sake of prosperity.
(2.1.6.2) One who desires sensory power should sacrifice a reddish-brown animal dedicated to Indra.
(2.1.6.3) He approaches Indra himself with his own portion; he (Indra) bestows sensory power upon him.
It indeed becomes possessed of the senses;
it becomes ruddy and full of luster;
for this, indeed, is the form of Indra.
(2.1.6.3) For prosperity,
one who desires gain should offer a spotted animal dedicated to Savitṛ;
for Savitṛ indeed is the lord of instigations.
He has recourse to Savitṛ with his own share;
he himself impels gain for him,
and his offspring become desirous of giving.
He becomes defiled;
for this [oblation] belongs to Sāvitrī by its deity,
for the sake of prosperity.
(2.1.6.4) One who desires food should sacrifice a multiform animal dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
(2.1.6.4) Food indeed belongs to the Viśvedevas. (2.1.6.4) He thus approaches the Viśvedevas with their own share.
(2.1.6.4) They themselves bestow food upon him;
(2.1.6.4) he becomes an eater of food; (2.1.6.4) he becomes multiform.
For food is multiform;
for the sake of prosperity,
one who desires a village should sacrifice a multiform animal dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
(2.1.6.4) The *sajātās* (kinsmen) belong to the *vaiśvadevas*.
(2.1.6.4) He approaches the All-Gods with their own respective share;
(2.1.6.5) they themselves bestow the *sajātās* upon him.
He indeed becomes domestic;
he becomes multiform,
for he has many deities.
(2.1.6.5) For prosperity:
one whose illness has been long-lasting but whose cause is unknown should sacrifice a hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati.
For man is indeed related to Prajāpati.
Prajāpati indeed knows that of which one is long ill as if it were unknown;
he has recourse to Prajāpati himself with his own share;
he alone releases him from that disease.
It is hornless;
for it belongs to Prajāpati by deity,
[and this serves] for prosperity.
(2.1.7.1) The *vaṣaṭ*-call indeed cut off the head of the Gāyatrī.
Its essence flew away; Bṛhaspati caught it, and it became a white-backed cow. (2.1.7.1) The second [essence] that flew away, Mitra and Varuṇa caught it, and it became a two-colored cow.
(2.1.7.1) That which fell for the third time, the Viśve Devās seized; it became a multi-colored cow.
(2.1.7.1) That which fell for the fourth time entered the earth; Bṛhaspati seized it, thinking, "Let this indeed be for my enjoyment," and it became a bull-cow.
(2.1.7.2) That which fell as blood, Rudra seized; she became the ruddy barren cow belonging to Rudra.
(2.1.7.2) One desiring spiritual luster should sacrifice a white-backed cow dedicated to Bṛhaspati. (2.1.7.2) He thus approaches Bṛhaspati with his own portion.
He alone bestows spiritual luster upon him; he indeed becomes possessed of spiritual luster.
The barren cow is indeed the essence of the meters.
(2.1.7.2) Spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) is indeed like sap.
(2.1.7.3) By means of the very sap of the meters, he secures the sap that is spiritual luster.
(2.1.7.3) One who desires rain should offer a two-colored cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.
The day belongs to Mitra and the night to Varuṇa;
indeed, it is through day and night that Parjanya rains. Verily, he approaches Mitra and Varuṇa with their own respective portions.
These two indeed cause Parjanya to rain for him by means of day and night. The cow is indeed the essence of the meters;
and rain, truly, is like that essence.
(2.1.7.3) By means of the very essence of the meters, (2.1.7.4) he secures the essence, which is rain.
(2.1.7.4) One desiring offspring should sacrifice a two-colored cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa;
for the day belongs to Mitra and the night belongs to Varuṇa.
(2.1.7.4) Verily, by means of day and night, creatures are born.
(2.1.7.4) He has recourse to Mitra and Varuṇa with their own respective portion; they two indeed cause him to procreate offspring by means of day and night.
The cow is indeed the essence of the meters;
for offspring are truly like an essence.
By means of the essence of the meters, he secures the essence, offspring.
(2.1.7.5) One desiring food should sacrifice a multiform animal dedicated to the Viśve Devas.
(2.1.7.5) Food indeed belongs to the Viśve Devas. (2.1.7.5) He thus approaches the Viśve Devas with their own share.
(2.1.7.5) They indeed bestow food upon him; (2.1.7.5) he becomes an eater of food.
(2.1.7.5) For the cow is the essence of the meters.
(2.1.7.5) Food is indeed like sap.
(2.1.7.5) By means of the very sap of the meters, he secures food as sap.
(2.1.7.5) One who desires a village should offer a multi-colored victim sacred to the Viśvedevas.
The *sajātāḥ* (kinsmen) belong to the Viśvedevas.
He approaches the Viśvedevas with their own portion;
they indeed bestow the *sajātāḥ* upon him.
He indeed becomes one of the village. The cow is indeed the essence of the meters; and kinsmen are truly like that essence.
(2.1.7.6) By means of the essence of the meters, he wins the essence of his kinsmen.
(2.1.7.6) One desiring spiritual luster should offer a bull and a cow to Bṛhaspati. He thus approaches Bṛhaspati with his own share.
He alone bestows spiritual luster upon him; he indeed becomes endowed with spiritual luster.
For the bull moves according to its own will.
(2.1.7.7) Spiritual luster is indeed like a *vaśá* cow.
By means of a *vaśá*, one secures spiritual luster as a *vaśá*.
One practicing exorcism should sacrifice a red cow to Rudra.
(2.1.7.7) He has recourse to Rudra with his own portion;
he cuts him off for that very reason;
he swiftly meets with ruin.
The sacrificial post is made of *rohiṇī* wood; for it belongs to Rudra by deity, [and this serves] for prosperity.
The wooden sword (*sphya*) becomes the sacrificial post; the wooden sword is indeed a thunderbolt; verily, he hurls the thunderbolt at him.
The sacrificial grass is made of *śara* reeds; verily, he shatters him.
The fuel-stick is made of vibhīdaka wood; it indeed splits him apart.
(2.1.8.1) Yonder sun did not shine.
(2.1.8.1) The gods sought an expiation for it.
By that very [means], they bestowed radiance upon it.

(2.1.8.1) He who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer this white cow dedicated to Sūrya. He thus approaches that very Sun with his own portion; he [the Sun] bestows spiritual luster upon him.
(2.1.8.1) He indeed becomes endowed with spiritual luster.
(2.1.8.1) The sacrificial post is made of Bilva wood.
(2.1.8.2) For from that place where yonder Āditya was born, from there the Bilva tree sprang up.
(2.1.8.2) Verily, from his own source he wins spiritual luster.
(2.1.8.2) One practicing exorcism should offer a cow with brown ears to Brāhmaṇaspati;
he should first offer a cake on ten potsherds to Varuṇa.
(2.1.8.2) Having caused his rival to be seized by Varuṇa himself, he lays him low with the Brahman.
(2.1.8.2) It has brown ears;
this indeed is the form of the Brahman.
(2.1.8.2) For prosperity, the wooden sword (*sphya*) becomes the sacrificial post (*yūpa*); the wooden sword is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*); verily, he hurls the thunderbolt at him.
(2.1.8.3) The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of *śara* reeds; he thus shatters him.
(2.1.8.3) The fuel-sticks should be of vibhīdaka wood; this indeed splits him open. He for whom the sacrifice does not come to pass should offer a dwarf animal dedicated to Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu, indeed, is the sacrifice.
Verily, he has recourse to Viṣṇu with his own share.
He alone bestows the sacrifice upon him;
the sacrifice bows down to him;
he becomes small in stature.
For he belongs to Viṣṇu by deity;
[it is] for prosperity.
One desiring cattle should sacrifice a barren she-mule to Tvaṣṭṛ.
Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the progenitor of animals that are in pairs.
He approaches Tvaṣṭṛ with his own share;
he, verily, procreates paired animals for him.
For indeed, offspring and cattle have entered into this [horse].
Now, being a male yet a stallion, he directly wins for himself offspring and cattle.
One who desires a covenant should offer a white animal to Mitra when a battle has been joined.
(2.1.8.4) He has recourse to Mitra himself with his own portion; he (Mitra) leads him into union with Mitra.
It becomes broad;
it indeed causes him to exert himself.
One who desires rain should sacrifice a black animal dedicated to Prajāpati.
Prajāpati indeed rules over rain;
he approaches Prajāpati himself with his own share;
he, for his part, causes the rain-god Parjanya to send rain for him.
It becomes black;
this, indeed, is the form of rain.
By means of that very form, he wins rain.
(2.1.8.5) It becomes brindled; having produced lightning for him, it causes rain.
(2.1.8.5) It has downward-pointing horns.
(2.1.8.5) He bestows rain upon him.
(2.1.9.1) When Varuṇa had performed the consecration, food did not approach him. He beheld this black cow dedicated to Varuṇa;
he offered her to its own deity, and then indeed food approached him.
(2.1.9.1) If one who is capable of obtaining food should find that food does not come to him, he should offer this black cow to Varuṇa.
(2.1.9.1) He thus has recourse to Varuṇa with his own share; he indeed bestows food upon him, and he becomes an eater of food. (2.1.9.2) It is black. It is black.
For this [victim] belongs to Varuṇa by deity;
[it is for] prosperity.
One who desires food should sacrifice a white victim to Mitra and a black one to Varuṇa at the junction of the waters and the plants.
The plants belong to Mitra, and the waters belong to Varuṇa.
Indeed, we live upon the essence of both the waters and the plants.
He thus approaches Mitra and Varuṇa with their own respective portions.
Those two indeed bestow food upon him; he becomes an eater of food.
(2.1.9.3) He should sacrifice at the junction of the waters and the plants for the attainment of both.
(2.1.9.3) One who has been long ill should sacrifice a white animal to Mitra and a black one to Varuṇa.
In that it belongs to Mitra, he pacifies Varuṇa for him by means of Mitra himself.
Since it belongs to Varuṇa, he releases him directly from the noose of Varuṇa;
even if his life-breath has departed, he yet lives.
Indeed, the gods could not find prosperity.
(2.1.9.4) They saw her in the form of a pair; (2.1.9.4) they could not succeed with her. Then those two Aśvins said:
"This belongs to us two; do not speak ill of her," they said, and so she became the property of the Aśvins.
He who desires prosperity should sacrifice this barren cow dedicated to the Aśvins.
Verily, he has recourse to the Aśvins with their own share;
they two bestow nourishment upon him; he prospers with offspring and cattle.
(2.1.10.1) One who is a "bad Brāhmaṇa" and desires to drink Soma should sacrifice a smoke-colored horse with a mark on its forehead to the Aśvins.
(2.1.10.1) For the Aśvins were indeed among the gods those who did not drink Soma; they subsequently obtained the right to drink Soma.
The Aśvins are the deities of him who, being a bad Brahmin, desires to drink Soma.
He has recourse to the Aśvins with their own share;
they indeed grant him the drinking of Soma, and the drinking of Soma comes to him.
In that he is smoke-colored, he drives away the very state of smokiness from him.
He is marked with a white spot on his forehead; thus he places brilliance upon his face.
One should offer a wild ox to Vāyu for one whom they may accuse, even though he has not committed a murder.
(2.1.10.2) Speech indeed reaches one who is impure when they falsely accuse someone who has not killed [an animal].
(2.1.10.2) That which is the *gomṛga* is neither a domestic animal nor a wild animal.
(2.1.10.2) He whom they falsely accuse of having killed is neither in the village nor in the forest.
Vāyu is indeed the purifier of the gods. He has recourse to Vāyu himself with his own share; he, verily, purifies him.
The dawn indeed rises for him turned away from it; he enters into darkness and evil, for whom the sun does not become visible while the *Aśvina* hymn is being recited.
He should offer a multi-colored animal to Sūrya.
Verily, he has recourse to that very Āditya with his own portion.
That very [light] drives away from him the darkness, the evil; as it dawns facing him, it shines forth, and it strikes away the darkness, the evil.
(2.1.11.1.a) Indra for you from every side; (2.1.11.1.b) Indra, the men; (2.1.11.1.c) O Maruts, when indeed from heaven...

(2.1.11.1ḍ) That shelter which is yours—(2.1.11.1.e) in battles we invoke Indra, who is easy to call upon, the deliverer from distress, the well-doing divine folk; Agni, Mitra, Varuṇa, Bhaga for our gain, Heaven and Earth, and the Maruts for our well-being.

(2.1.11.1.f) May Parijman, the slayer of the dawn-demons, exhilarate us; may Vāta, the bull of the waters, exhilarate us. O Indra and Parvata, sharpen our [senses] for us! May all the gods grant us this wide space. (2.1.11.1.g) I invoke the dear names of you, the swift ones, so that the Maruts, longing [for us], may be satisfied.

(2.1.11.2) For the sake of glory, they have mingled themselves with splendors; they, with their rays, with the chanters, are well-armed. Armed with axes, impetuous, and fearless, they have found the beloved domain of the Maruts.

May Agni, the first, protect us along with the Vasus; may Soma guard us by his own self together with the Rudras. May Indra, in accordance with the seasons, act with the Maruts, and may Varuṇa, together with the Ādityas, sharpen us.

May the divine Agni with the Vasus be united with us; may Soma with his Rudra-like powers be united with us; may Indra with the worshipful Maruts be united with us; may Varuṇa with the Ādityas cause us to be known.
(2.1.11.3ḷ) Just as the Ādityas were united with the Vasus, and the Rudras came together with the Maruts, so may all the gods, free from malice, be of one mind toward us, O eater of the triple food.
(2.1.11.3ṃ) Wherever his assembly is held, men rejoice in the seat of heroes; even those who are worthy, he kindles, and living beings bring him to birth.
When we gather together the offerings and the oblations of men, then from the splendor of his power he grasps the rein of Cosmic Order.
The sacrifice goes forth toward the favor of the gods; O Ādityas, be gracious. May your benevolent thought turn hitherward, which finds wider space even from distress.

Pure, with good pastures, undeceived, and possessing brave sons, he dwells among the waters, having reached old age; no one slays him, neither from near nor from afar, who abides under the guidance of the Ādityas.

(2.1.11.4.q) Supporting that which moves and that which stands, the Ādityas are gods, the guardians of the entire world; far-sighted, they protect the divine power, being observers of Truth and exactors of debts.

(2.1.11.5ṛ) Sustaining the three earths and the three heavens, they maintain the three ordinances within their assembly. By the Eternal Law, O Ādityas, your greatness is mighty; that, O Aryaman, Varuṇa, and Mitra, is beautiful.
Now we pray for protection to those Kṣatriyas, the Ādityas, the most merciful ones, for our assistance.

(2.1.11.5ṭ) Neither the right nor the left is distinguished, neither the eastward direction, O Ādityas, nor the westward; whether through simplicity or through wisdom, O Vasus—(2.1.11.6) led by you, may I attain the light that is free from fear.

Through the newest protection of the Ādityas, may we prevail with their most auspicious shelter; may the swift ones, listening to us, establish this sacrifice in sinlessness and in the state of Aditi.
O Varuṇa, hear this my invocation; be gracious to me today as well. Seeking your protection, I yearn for you.
This I ask of you, honoring you with sacred prayer; this the sacrificer seeks from you with oblations. O Varuṇa, be present here without anger; O you of wide renown, do not steal away our life.
(2.2.1.1) Prajāpati created offspring.
(2.2.1.1) Once they were created, Indra and Agni hid them away.
(2.2.1.1) Prajāpati perceived this.
(2.2.1.1) "Indra and Agni have indeed driven away my offspring," he thought.
(2.2.1.1) He saw this cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and Agni;
he offered it.
(2.2.1.1) Those two provided offspring for him. (2.2.1.1) Indeed, Indra and Agni conceal the offspring of one who, though being capable of having offspring, does not obtain offspring.
(2.2.1.1) One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni.
(2.2.1.1) Indra and Agni—(2.2.1.2) he indeed approaches them with their own respective portions; (2.2.1.2) those two alone bring forth offspring for him;
he obtains offspring.
(2.2.1.2) One who is contending for land or among his kinsmen should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni.
(2.2.1.2) He approaches Indra and Agni with their own share;
through them, he wrests away power and vigor from his rival.
(2.2.1.2) He conquers evil and the rival.
(2.2.1.2) Indeed, power and vigor depart from him who goes forth to battle.
(2.2.1.2–3) One who is about to go forth to battle should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni.

(2.2.1.3) He has recourse to Indra and Agni with their own respective portions; they two bestow sensory power and vigor upon him. Endowed with that sensory power and vigor, he advances and conquers that battle.
(2.2.1.3) He who wins a battle is indeed deprived of his sensory power and vigor.
Having won a battle, he should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni.
Verily, he thus approaches Indra and Agni with their own respective portions.
(2.2.1.3) Those two alone bestow upon him sensory power and vigor; he is not deprived of sensory power or vigor.
(2.2.1.4) Indeed, sensory power and vigor depart from him who goes to a public assembly.
