One who is about to go to a public assembly should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni.
(2.2.1.4) He has recourse to Indra and Agni with their own respective portions; they two bestow sensory power and vigor upon him,
and he goes forth among the people endowed with sensory power and vigor.
(2.2.1.4) One should offer a pap of cooked rice to Pūṣan.
(2.2.1.4) Pūṣan is indeed the bestower of power and vigor. (2.2.1.4) It is to Pūṣan alone that one has recourse by means of his own portion. (2.2.1.5) He approaches him with his own share.

(2.2.1.5) He alone bestows upon him sensory power and vigor. (2.2.1.5) Having arrived at a settlement, one should offer a *caru* oblation to Kṣetrapati. (2.2.1.5) For this earth is indeed the mistress of the field.
(2.2.1.5) He finds firm support in this very [earth].
(2.2.1.5) One should subsequently offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni.
(2.2.1.5) By means of this very support, he places power and vigor within himself subsequently.
(2.2.2.1) One who, being a regular performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, should omit either the New Moon day or the Full Moon day, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt.
(2.2.2.1) He who, being a regular performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, omits either the New Moon day or the Full Moon day, indeed goes from the path by way of a non-path.
He resorts to Agni Pathikṛt with his own share.
He indeed leads him from the wrong path to the right path;
an ox is the sacrificial fee, for it is a carrier,
for the sake of success.

(2.2.2.1) To Agni, Lord of Vows. (2.2.2.2) He who, having established the sacred fires, should act as if violating his vows, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, Lord of Vows. He thus approaches Agni, Lord of Vows, with his own portion; he (Agni) causes him to take up the vow again.
(2.2.2.2) He becomes one under a vow.
(2.2.2.2) He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, the slayer of demons, for whomsoever the demons may pursue.
(2.2.2.2) Verily, he has recourse to Agni, the slayer of demons, with his own share.
(2.2.2.2) That very [offering] drives away the *rakṣas* from him;
(2.2.2.2) he should offer it when the night has grown sharp.
For when the night has become sharp, the *rakṣases* stir up;
he strikes them down precisely as they are thus stirred up.
He should perform the sacrifice within an enclosed space (*pariśrita*) so that the *rakṣases* do not penetrate it.
(2.2.2.3) The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are those that destroy demons (*rakṣoghnī*), for the purpose of striking down the demons.
(2.2.2.3) One practicing exorcism (*abhicaran*) should offer a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) to Agni accompanied by Rudra (*rudravat*).
(2.2.2.3) For Rudra is his terrible form.
(2.2.2.3) He cuts him down for that very reason;
he swiftly meets with ruin.
(2.2.2.3–4) One whose cattle or men have died, or who is afraid, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Surabhimat.
(2.2.2.4) This indeed is his healing body, namely that which is fragrant.
With that very [body] he provides a remedy for him.
It becomes fragrant for the removal of foul odor.
(2.2.2.4) When a battle has been joined, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat.
(2.2.2.4) Having appeased him with his own portion, he directs [his power] against the enemies.
He whom they pierce among those on their own side lives.
(2.2.2.4) He who dies before others conquers that battle. (2.2.2.5) Indeed, he overcomes those whose ancestors die one after another in succession,
for the human oblation is his most beloved.
(2.2.2.5) He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat. (2.2.2.5) By means of his own portion, he pacifies him;
none of these shall die before their full span of life.
(2.2.2.5) He indeed cries out against the house of him whose house he burns.
(2.2.2.5) One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat. (2.2.2.5) Thus, by means of his own portion, one pacifies him.
(2.2.2.5) No other fire burns his house.
(2.2.3.1) He for whom a desire does not come to pass should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kāma.
(2.2.3.1) Verily, he has recourse to Agni Kāma with his own share; (2.2.3.1) he, indeed, fulfills him with that very desire.
Desire bows down to him.
One who is contending for land or among his kinsmen should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Yaviṣṭha.
Verily, he has recourse to Agni Yaviṣṭha with his own share.
(2.2.3.1) By that very means, he deprives his rival of his sensory power and vigor. (2.2.3.2) He is separated from evil and conquers his rival.
One who is being subjected to malevolent magic should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Yaviṣṭha.
(2.2.3.2) He has recourse to Agni Yaviṣṭha with his own share;
he (Agni) alone drives away the *rakṣases* from him. One who practices sorcery against him does not strike him down.
(2.2.3.2) He who desires, "May I attain a full lifespan," should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Āyuṣmat.
He thus approaches Agni Āyuṣmat with his own share.
He alone bestows life upon him; he attains a full lifespan.
One who desires prosperity should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jātavedas.
(2.2.3.3) He has recourse to Agni Jātavedas with his own portion; he (Agni) leads him to prosperity; he indeed becomes prosperous.
(2.2.3.3) One who desires radiance should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Rukmat.
(2.2.3.3) Verily, he has recourse to Agni Rukmat with his own portion; he (Agni) bestows radiance upon him.
(2.2.3.3) It is indeed pleasing. (2.2.3.3–4) One desiring splendor should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tejasvat.
Verily, he has recourse to Agni Tejasvat with his own share.
He alone bestows brilliance upon him;
he indeed becomes brilliant.
One who desires to overcome others should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Sāhantya.
(2.2.3.4) He has recourse to Agni, the conqueror, with his own share; by that very means he conquers whomever he desires to overcome.
(2.2.4.1) He who desires, "May I be possessed of food," should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Annavat.
(2.2.4.1) Verily, he has recourse to Agni Annavat with his own share; he [Agni] makes him possessed of food, and he indeed becomes possessed of food.
(2.2.4.1) He who desires, "May I be an eater of food," should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, the Eater of Food.
(2.2.4.1) Verily, he has recourse to Agni, the Eater of Food, with his own share.
(2.2.4.1) He [Agni] makes him an eater of food; indeed, he becomes an eater of food. (2.2.4.2) Thus it is.
(2.2.4.2) He who desires, "May I become a lord of food," should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, the Lord of Food.
(2.2.4.2) Verily, he has recourse to Agni, the Lord of Food, with his own portion; he (Agni) makes him a lord of food, and he indeed becomes a lord of food.
(2.2.4.2) One who has been ill for a long time should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pavamāna, to Agni Pāvaka, and to Agni Śuci.
In that he offers to Agni Pavamāna,
he thereby bestows vital breath upon him.
(2.2.4.2) That which [is offered] to Agni; (2.2.4.3) to Pāvaka—by that he places speech within him;
(2.2.4.3) that which [is offered] to Agni Śuci.
(2.2.4.3) By this [offering], he bestows life-span upon him; even if his life has departed, he indeed lives.
(2.2.4.3) One who desires sight should offer this very [oblation]; in that he offers to Agni Pavamāna, he thereby bestows vital breath upon him.
(2.2.4.3) In that [he offers] to Agni Pāvaka, (2.2.4.3) by that he places speech in him; (2.2.4.3) in that [he offers] to Agni Śuci...
(2.2.4.3) By means of that [offering], he bestows sight upon him. (2.2.4.4) Even if he is blind, he indeed sees.
(2.2.4.4) One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Putravat;
[and] a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Putrin.
Agni alone begets offspring for him;
Indra bestows it when it has grown.
He who desires, "May I be full of essence," should offer a pap of cooked rice in goat's milk to Agni Rasavat.

(2.2.4.4) He has recourse to Agni himself, the possessor of essence, with his own share; he (Agni) makes him a possessor of essence. (2.2.4.5) He indeed becomes a possessor of essence. It is performed with goat's milk, for the goat belongs to Agni.
(2.2.4.5) He directly obtains the essence.
(2.2.4.5) He who desires, "May I be possessed of wealth," should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vasumat.
He thus approaches Agni Vasumat with his own share.
(2.2.4.5) He indeed makes him possessed of wealth; he himself becomes wealthy.
(2.2.4.5) One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vājasṛt when a battle is joined.
(2.2.4.6) He who desires to win a battle seeks to win booty.
Agni, indeed, is the winner of the prize among the gods; he approaches Agni, the winner of the prize, with his own share.
He speeds toward the prize, slays Vṛtra, and conquers that battle.
Moreover, he becomes as unassailable as Agni himself.

(2.2.4.6) One whose fire they should carry out from the fire [of another] should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni-with-fire. (2.2.4.6–7) Of these two, one has its portion assigned and the other has its portion unassigned; when these two come together, they overwhelm the sacrificer. He is liable to meet with misfortune. In that he offers to Agni-with-fire, [he avoids this].
(2.2.4.7) By means of their respective portions, he pacifies these two;
the sacrificer does not come to ruin.

(2.2.4.7) One for whom the fire, having been taken out, should go out before the Agnihotra has been offered, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat. They say, "One should take another fire from a neighboring house and re-establish it"—but that should not be done. Since the former fire was taken out for its own portion, why should another be brought? Having placed those very same embers together, one should churn [the fire].

(2.2.4.8) "From here Agni was first born, Jātavedas from his own womb; may he, knowing, carry the oblation to the gods by means of the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Jagatī. (2.2.4.8) Verily, by means of the meters he causes him to be born from his own womb. "This indeed is that Agni," they say, "but his light has flown away. When he offers to Agni Jyotiṣmat, he wins back whatever light of his had flown away.
One who is being accused should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara, a pap to Varuṇa, and a pap to Dadhikrāvan.

In that there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara—Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year—it is through the year that he makes him palatable and strikes away his evil color. By means of the offering to Varuṇa, he releases him from the noose of Varuṇa; by means of the offering to Dadhikrāvan, he purifies him.
Gold is the sacrificial fee; gold is indeed a means of purification; it purifies him, and his food becomes fit to be eaten.

(2.2.5.1) One desiring offspring should offer this very [oblation]. (2.2.5.1–2) The year, indeed, being unappeased, burns up the womb for his offspring and cattle—he who, though capable of having offspring, does not obtain offspring.

(2.2.5.2) In that there is an offering to Vaiśvānara on twelve potsherds—Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year—he pacifies the year itself with its own portion. Thus pacified, he produces offspring for him from his own womb. By means of the offering to Varuṇa, he releases him from the noose of Varuṇa; by means of the offering to Dadhikrāvan, he purifies him.
(2.2.5.2) Gold is the sacrificial fee; gold is indeed a means of purification; verily, he purifies him. (2.2.5.3) He obtains offspring.
One should offer an oblation to Vaiśvānara on twelve potsherds when a son is born.

(2.2.5.3) In that it is on eight potsherds, he purifies him with the *gāyatrī* and with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). In that it is on nine potsherds, he bestows brilliance (*tejas*) upon him by means of the *trivṛt*. In that it is on ten potsherds, he bestows food-eating power (*annādya*) upon him by means of the *virāj*. In that it is on eleven potsherds, he bestows sensory power (*indriya*) upon him by means of the *triṣṭubh*. In that it is on twelve potsherds, he bestows cattle (*paśu*) upon him by means of the *jagatī*. (2.2.5.3–4) He for whom, when born, one performs this sacrifice, becomes purified, brilliant, an eater of food, possessed of sensory power, and rich in cattle.

(2.2.5.4) He who, being a performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, lets either the new moon or the full moon pass by, is indeed cut off from the heavenly world; for it is for the sake of the heavenly world that the New and Full Moon sacrifices are offered.
(2.2.5.4) Having let the new moon or the full moon pass by, he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara.
Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; verily he gratifies the year, and moreover, he bestows the year upon him for the attainment of the heavenly world.
(2.2.5.5) Moreover, by taking hold of the deities themselves, he goes to the heavenly world.
(2.2.5.5) He who extinguishes the sacred fire is indeed a slayer of the heroes among the gods; truly, the Brāhmaṇas who seek the Truth have not eaten his food in the past.
(2.2.5.5) He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni.
(2.2.5.5) When one is about to extinguish the fire, [he offers] a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara.

(2.2.5.5) In that it is on eight potsherds—the Gāyatrī has eight syllables and Agni is of the Gāyatra nature—he thereby performs hospitality for Agni as he truly is. (2.2.5.5) Moreover, it is just as when one provides provisions for a person who is traveling; such indeed is this. (2.2.5.6) It is exactly like that.
The cake for Vaiśvānara is on twelve potsherds;
there are twelve months in a year, and the year is indeed the womb of Agni. Thus he causes him to go to his own womb.
His food becomes edible.
One desiring a village should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara and a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts.
He places the offering for Vaiśvānara on the Āhavanīya fire and that for the Maruts on the Gārhapatya fire, for the sake of separating the better from the worse.
The offering to Vaiśvānara consists of twelve potsherds; the year has twelve months; verily, by means of the year, he causes his kinsmen to fall away [from him].
(2.2.5.6) There is an offering to the Maruts. (2.2.5.7) The Maruts are indeed the clans (*viś*) of the gods; by means of the divine clan, he thereby wins for himself the human clan.
(2.2.5.7) It consists of seven potsherds; the Maruts are indeed divided into seven groups; by means of the group-by-group division, he wins for himself his kinsmen.
(2.2.5.7) He deposits [the oblation] while the invitatory verse is being recited.
He thus makes the people themselves follow after him.
(2.2.6.1) One who is about to go forth to battle should offer a *caru* oblation to Āditya.
(2.2.6.1) This earth, indeed, is Aditi.
(2.2.6.1) It is upon this very [earth] that those who come before find their firm footing.
(2.2.6.1) Having gone to his place, he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara.
(2.2.6.1) Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year;
the year, verily, is the abode of the gods.
(2.2.6.1) From this very abode, indeed, the gods conquered the Asuras.
(2.2.6.1) In that he offers the cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara,
he strives for the very abode of the gods.

(2.2.6.1) He conquers that battle; (2.2.6.1) for it is in this [battle] that these two wipe themselves clean. (2.2.6.2) He who eats the food of two people who are at enmity—one who has eaten the food of two people who are at enmity—should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara.
Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; he eats only what has been made savory by the year;
they do not wipe away [the impurity] upon him.
(2.2.6.2) These two who enter into a compact together are indeed joined for a year.

Of these two, Varuṇa seizes him who first commits an offense against the other. Having committed an offense against one with whom he has entered a compact, he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara.
Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year.
Having attained the year itself, he goes beyond Varuṇa; Varuṇa does not seize him.
He who accepts a sheep as a gift accepts his own impurity.

(2.2.6.3) One who has accepted a sheep as a gift should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. (2.2.6.3) Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; thus, he accepts [the gift] as one already tasted by the year.
(2.2.6.3) He does not accept a boat.
(2.2.6.3) Verily, he who accepts anything with two rows of teeth—whether a horse or a human—attains his own measure of destruction.
(2.2.6.3–4) Having accepted anything with two rows of teeth, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara.
Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; he thus receives what has been made savory by the year, and does not exceed his own measure.
(2.2.6.4) One who is about to go seeking wealth should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara.
(2.2.6.4) Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year.
For when one moves about among the people for a full year, then he becomes worthy of wealth.
In that he offers the cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara, he indeed moves forward toward the gain won by the year.
His offspring become desirous of giving to him.
Verily, he who, having yoked the year, does not release it, becomes without a firm foundation.
(2.2.6.5) Having returned, one should indeed offer this same Vaiśvānara sacrifice.
Whatever [deity] one employs, that one he releases by means of its share, for the sake of firm establishment.
With the same rope with which one would drive away the best cow, that one should send forth to the rival.
Verily, he sends Destruction away from him.
(2.2.7.1) One desiring cattle should offer a *caru* oblation to Indra.
(2.2.7.1) Cattle indeed belong to Indra. (2.2.7.1) He thus approaches Indra with his own share.
(2.2.7.1) He indeed bestows cattle upon him; he becomes possessed of cattle. (2.2.7.1) There is a sacrificial pap.
(2.2.7.1) From its own womb he produces cattle for him.
(2.2.7.1) One desiring cattle should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra, the possessor of power.
(2.2.7.1) Cattle are indeed power.
(2.2.7.1) He has recourse to Indra, the possessor of power, with his own portion.
(2.2.7.2) He, indeed, bestows power and cattle upon him; he becomes possessed of cattle.
(2.2.7.2) One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra accompanied by the Gharma. (2.2.7.2) The Gharma is indeed spiritual luster.
(2.2.7.2) He thus approaches Indra, who is accompanied by the Gharma, with his own portion.
He alone bestows spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) upon him; he indeed becomes possessed of spiritual luster.
One who desires food should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra accompanied by the *arka* hymn.
The *arka* is indeed the food of the gods.
Verily, he approaches Indra, who possesses the *arka*, with his own portion;
he, in turn, bestows food upon him.
He indeed becomes an eater of food.
One who desires prosperity should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Gharma-vat, to Indra Indriyāvat, and to Indra Arkavat.
In that he offers to Indra Gharma-vat, he thereby forms his head.
(2.2.7.3) In that [he offers] to Indra the powerful, he thereby makes his very self powerful.
(2.2.7.3) In that [he offers] to Indra the radiant, he finds firm footing in existence and in the eating of food; he indeed prospers.
(2.2.7.4) He who is seized by evil should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the deliverer from distress.
(2.2.7.4) Evil, indeed, is distress.
(2.2.7.4) He has recourse to Indra, the deliverer from distress, with his own portion; he (Indra) alone delivers him from evil and distress.
(2.2.7.4) One for whom enemies tremble or against whom rival kingdoms have risen should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Vaimṛdha.
(2.2.7.4) He has recourse to Indra Vaimṛdha with his own share; he (Indra) indeed strikes away the enemies from him. (2.2.7.5) He strikes them away.
(2.2.7.5) One who is bound or besieged should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Protector.
(2.2.7.5) He resorts to Indra the Protector with his own share;
he indeed protects him.
(2.2.7.5) One whose great sacrifice does not succeed should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra, accompanied by the *arka* and the *aśvamedha*.
(2.2.7.5) For the *arka* and the *aśvamedha* are indeed the two final forms of the great sacrifice.
(2.2.7.5) He thus approaches Indra, who possesses the *arka* and the *aśvamedha*, with his own share.
(2.2.7.5) It is he who ultimately causes the great sacrifice to fail for him;
(2.2.7.5) the great sacrifice inclines toward him.
(2.2.8.1) One who desires a village should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Anvṛju.
(2.2.8.1) He thus approaches Indra Anvṛju with his own share;
he (Indra) makes his kinsmen favorable to him.
(2.2.8.1) He indeed becomes a village-dweller. (2.2.8.1) One whose army is as if not yet sharpened should offer a pap to Indrāṇī.
(2.2.8.1) Indrāṇī, indeed, is the deity of the army.
(2.2.8.1) He has recourse to Indrāṇī with her own portion;
she alone sharpens his army—even the *balbaja* grass. (2.2.8.2) He should bind even *balbaja* grass into the fuel-bundle.
(2.2.8.2) Where a cow has wallowed and urinated, from there the *balbaja* grasses sprang up. (2.2.8.2) Having led him into the very path of the cows, he makes him find the cows.
(2.2.8.2) When a battle is joined, one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra, the wrathful and the mindful.

(2.2.8.2) By means of power (*indriya*), fury (*manyu*), and mind (*manas*), one conquers battle. (2.2.8.2) He has recourse to Indra himself, who possesses fury and possesses mind, with his own portion; he (Indra) bestows upon him power, fury, and mind.
(2.2.8.2) He conquers that battle.
(2.2.8.3) One who is dejected in mind, as if he were himself at fault, should offer this very [oblation].
For these [breaths] have indeed departed from him.

(2.2.8.3) Now, this one who is dejected in mind and himself a sinner resorts to Indra, the wrathful and the wise, with his own portion. He (Indra) bestows upon him power, wrath, and wisdom; thus he does not remain dejected in mind or himself a sinner.
(2.2.8.3) He who desires, "May my offspring be inclined toward giving," should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Giver.
(2.2.8.4) Thus, he has recourse to Indra the Giver with his own share.
(2.2.8.4) He indeed makes offspring desirous of giving to him; (2.2.8.4) offspring become desirous of giving to him.
(2.2.8.4) One for whom what was intended to be given has not been given should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Pradātṛ.
(2.2.8.4) He has recourse to Indra the Bestower with his own share;
he alone causes [wealth] to be bestowed upon him.
(2.2.8.4–5) One who has been expelled, or one who is being expelled, should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Good Protector (*sutrāman*).
(2.2.8.5) He has recourse to Indra Sutrāman with his own portion;
he indeed protects him.
He becomes one who cannot be driven away.
Indra was indeed equal to the other deities; he did not attain distinction. He ran to Prajāpati for refuge.
For him he offered this cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Indra;
by that very means he bestowed power (*indriya*) upon him.
He made the *śakvarī* verses the invitatory and offering prayers.
The Śakvarī is indeed a thunderbolt;
that thunderbolt kindled him for prosperity.
He became that;
he was afraid,
thinking, "The existent will consume me."
(2.2.8.6) He ran back again to Prajāpati.
(2.2.8.6) Prajāpati fashioned the Revatī verse from the Śakvarī for the sake of peace and to prevent burning.
For one who is capable of prosperity but remains on equal footing with his peers, he should offer this cake on eleven potsherds to Indra.
(2.2.8.6) He has recourse to Indra himself with his own portion; he (Indra) bestows power upon him.
The *revatī* verse serves as the invitatory formula (*puro'nuvākyā*) for the sake of peace and to prevent burning.
(2.2.8.6) The *śakvarī* is the offering verse.
(2.2.8.6) The *śakvarī* is indeed a thunderbolt;
that thunderbolt kindles him for prosperity.
It indeed comes to be.
(2.2.9.1) One practicing sorcery should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu; Sarasvatī should have a portion of clarified butter, and there should be a pap for Bṛhaspati.

(2.2.9.1) In that there is a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu—Agni is all the deities and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice—he thus practices sorcery against him both by means of the deities and by means of the sacrifice.
Sarasvatī has a share of the clarified butter; Sarasvatī is indeed speech; verily by means of speech he assails him.
There is a pap for Bṛhaspati; Bṛhaspati is the sacred power (*brahman*) among the gods; verily by means of the sacred power he assails him.
(2.2.9.2) They indeed counter-magic against one who practices magic from beyond.

One should employ two *puro’nuvākyā*s for each [verse] to ensure non-overstepping. He who is being subjected to magic should sacrifice with this very [offering]; by means of the deities he counters the deities, by means of the sacrifice the sacrifice, by means of speech the speech, and by means of the sacred formulation (*brahman*) the sacred formulation. He thus slips between the deities and the sacrifice; for him there is no affliction from any quarter whatsoever.
(2.2.9.2) One who practices sorcery does not strike him down.
(2.2.9.2–3) He whose sacrifice does not succeed should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu.

Agni is all the deities, and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; he thus approaches both Agni and Viṣṇu with their own respective portions. Those two then bestow the sacrifice upon him, and the sacrifice comes to him.
(2.2.9.3) One desiring sight should offer a pap of cooked rice in clarified butter to Agni and Viṣṇu.

(2.2.9.3) For by the eye of Agni, human beings see; by the eye of the sacrifice, the gods [see]. He has recourse to both Agni and Viṣṇu with their own respective portions. (2.2.9.4) Those two bestow sight upon him; he indeed becomes possessed of sight.
Clarified butter is indeed the seed of the cow, and rice grains are the seed of the ox; verily, from this pair he produces sight for him. It is in clarified butter;
clarified butter is brilliance, and sight is brilliance; by means of brilliance he wins for him both brilliance and sight.

The rival snatches away the power and vigor of the sacrificer who does not sacrifice. If the rival is sacrificing, one should offer the *adhvarakalpā* oblation; thus his power and vigor are not snatched away.

(2.2.9.5) Before speech is uttered, he should offer [the oblation]; by doing so, he seizes that very speech of his rival which has not yet been spoken. As that speech of his begins to be uttered, other speeches follow it; these [offerings] bestow power and vigor upon the sacrificer. (2.2.9.5) At the time of the morning pressing, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu; Sarasvatī should have a portion of clarified butter, and there should be a pap for Bṛhaspati.

(2.2.9.5) In that it is an offering on eight potsherds—the Gāyatrī has eight syllables and the morning pressing belongs to the Gāyatrī—he thereby obtains the morning pressing itself. (2.2.9.6) He should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu at the time of the midday pressing; Sarasvatī should have a portion of clarified butter, and there should be a pap for Bṛhaspati.
In that it is an offering on eleven potsherds—the Triṣṭubh has eleven syllables and the midday pressing belongs to the Triṣṭubh—he thereby obtains the midday pressing itself.

(2.2.9.6) One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu at the time of the third pressing; Sarasvatī should have a portion of clarified butter, and there should be a pap for Bṛhaspati.
In that it is on twelve potsherds—the Jagatī meter has twelve syllables and the third pressing belongs to the Jagatī—thereby he obtains the third pressing itself.

(2.2.9.7) By means of the deities he approaches the deities; by means of the sacrifice he approaches the sacrifice; by means of speech he approaches speech; by means of the sacred formulation (*brahman*) he approaches the sacred formulation. By means of the potsherds he obtains the meters; by means of the sacrificial cakes he obtains the pressings.
(2.2.9.7) At the time of the barren cow, he should offer a cake on one potsherd to Mitra and Varuṇa.
That very barren cow which is the *anūbandhyā* of his rival becomes this single-potsherd offering for him; for one cannot obtain a sacrificial animal by means of potsherds.
(2.2.10.1) That sun did not shine. The gods sought an atonement for it; they offered this *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra, and thereby they bestowed radiance upon it.

He who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer this *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra. He approaches both Soma and Rudra with their own respective portions; those two bestow spiritual luster upon him, and he indeed becomes possessed of spiritual luster.

(2.2.10.1) One should offer [the oblation] on the full moon day of the Tiṣya constellation; for Tiṣya is indeed Rudra, and the full moon is Soma. Thus he directly wins spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
(2.2.10.2) He causes the sacrifice to be performed in an enclosed space for the sake of securing spiritual luster.

The clarified butter consists of the churned milk of a white cow with a white calf; the sprinkling is done with clarified butter, and they purify themselves with clarified butter. Whatever constitutes spiritual luster, he makes all that. "Spiritual luster is produced in abundance," they say.

(2.2.10.2) "He is liable to become afflicted with skin disease"—in this case, one should insert two *ṛc* verses addressed to Manu as *dhāyyā*s. Whatever Manu has spoken is indeed a remedy. (2.2.10.3) Thus he provides a remedy for him.

If one should fear, "I shall become afflicted with skin disease," one should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Pūṣan. For man belongs to Soma by deity, and cattle belong to Pūṣan; thus, by means of his own deity and by means of cattle, he provides him with skin. He does not become afflicted with skin disease.

(2.2.10.3) One desiring offspring should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra. Soma, indeed, is the placer of seed; Agni is the progenitor of offspring. Soma bestows seed upon him, and Agni procreates offspring for him; he obtains offspring.

(2.2.10.4) One practicing exorcism should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra. Man belongs to Soma by deity; this Agni is Rudra. Having ransomed him from his own deity, he delivers him over to Rudra; he swiftly meets with ruin.

(2.2.10.4) One who has been long ill should offer an oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) to Soma and Rudra. Indeed, the vital essence (*rasa*) of one who is long ill goes to Soma, while his body goes to Agni. [By this offering] he redeems his essence from Soma and his body from Agni. Moreover, even if his life-force has departed, he shall live. For Soma and Rudra have seized him; the Hotṛ priest extracts him from their grasp. He is liable to suffer misfortune. An ox should be given as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the Hotṛ. The ox is a carrier (*vahni*), and the Hotṛ is a carrier. By means of a carrier, he rescues himself, the carrier.

(2.2.10.5) He who desires, "May I produce a rival for him in his own abode," should offer a pap to Soma and Rudra. Having enclosed the altar, he should dig up half of it but not the other half; he should spread half of the sacrificial grass but not the other half; he should place half of the fuel on the fire but not the other half. Thus, he produces a rival for him in his own abode.
(2.2.11.1) One who desires a village should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Indra and one on seven potsherds to the Maruts.
(2.2.11.1) He thus approaches both Indra and the Maruts with their own respective portions;
they themselves bestow his kinsmen upon him.
He remains in the village itself.
He places the oblation for Indra over the Āhavanīya fire and that for the Maruts over the Gārhapatya fire, for the sake of preventing the confusion of better and worse.
The offering to the Maruts consists of seven potsherds;
for the Maruts consist of seven groups.
Verily, by means of the groups, he wins his kinsmen for himself.
(2.2.11.1) While [the verse] is being recited, he deposits [the oblation];
(2.2.11.1) thus he makes the *viś* (the people) follow after him.
(2.2.11.2) He who desires this very thing should offer this [oblation].
(2.2.11.2) "May I cause strife between the nobility and the commoners," [thinking thus], he should say while cutting portions from the oblation for Indra.
(2.2.11.2) Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* with "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra," he should say: "Recite the offering verse for Indra."
(2.2.11.2) "Sacrifice to the Maruts," he should say while cutting portions of the offering for the Maruts;
having called for the formal announcement, he should say, "Recite the invitatory verse for the Maruts."
"Offer to Indra!"— thus he creates discord among them regarding their own respective shares; they remain standing, being torn asunder.
(2.2.11.2) He who desires, "May they be in harmony," should offer this very same [oblation].
(2.2.11.3) Having cut the portions according to the respective deities, he should sacrifice according to the respective deities.
(2.2.11.3) By means of their respective portions, he establishes them each in its proper place; thus they indeed become established.
(2.2.11.3) One who desires a village should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and a cake on twelve potsherds to the Viśve Devas.
He has recourse to Indra and all the gods with their own respective portions;
they indeed bestow his kinsmen upon him,
and he becomes a possessor of a village.
(2.2.11.3) Having taken a portion for Indra, he should take a portion for the Viśve Devas, and then again for Indra. (2.2.11.4) [He takes it] from above.
By means of his own power (*indriya*), he thus encompasses his kinsmen on both sides.
A garment preceded by a teacher’s fee (*upādhāyya*) is the sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) for the securing of kinsmen.
(2.2.11.4) One desiring a village should offer a pap of *priyaṅgu* grains cooked in the milk of a spotted cow to the Maruts.
For the Maruts were born from the milk of a spotted cow, and *priyaṅgu* grains belong to the spotted cow.
Indeed, those who are born together share the same deity, which is the Maruts.
(2.2.11.4) He has recourse to the Maruts with their own share;
they indeed bestow his kinsmen upon him,
and he becomes a leader of the village.
The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses contain the word "dear" (*priya*). Verily, he makes him dear among his peers.
The *puro'nuvākyā* consists of two-footed verses; verily, he wins bipeds.
The *yājyā* consists of four-footed verses; verily, he wins quadrupeds.
(2.2.11.5) The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict.

(2.2.11.5) Those gods were at variance with one another. (2.2.11.5) Not yielding to one another for the sake of preeminence, they divided themselves into four groups: Agni with the Vasus, Soma with the Rudras, Indra with the Maruts, and Varuṇa with the Ādityas.
That Indra ran to Prajāpati.
He caused him to sacrifice with this *saṃjñānī* [offering]:

he offered a cake on eight potsherds to Agni accompanied by the Vasus; a pap to Soma accompanied by the Rudras; a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra accompanied by the Maruts; and a pap to Varuṇa accompanied by the Ādityas.
(2.2.11.6) Therefore, indeed, the gods agreed upon Indra for preeminence.
(2.2.11.6) If one should be at variance with his peers, one should cause him to sacrifice with this *saṃjñānī* [rite].

He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni accompanied by the Vasus, a pap to Soma accompanied by the Rudras, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra accompanied by the Maruts, and a pap to Varuṇa accompanied by the Ādityas.
His peers recognize him as Indra himself for the sake of preeminence;
he becomes the most excellent among his equals.
(2.2.12.1.a) Hiranyagarbha; (2.2.12.1.b) Āpo ha yat; (2.2.12.1.c) Prajāpate.

He knows the father, he knows the mother; he becomes the son, he becomes the one who bestows wealth again. He has covered the sky, the mid-air, and the heavens; he has become all worlds, he has come into being.

(2.2.12.1.e) Upward [he has risen] toward that [light]. (2.2.12.1.f) The bright one. (2.2.12.1.g) As of old, with a newer splendor, O Agni, joined together, thou hast spread far and wide with thy lofty radiance.
(2.2.12.1) He bestows poetic wisdoms upon every worshipper, holding in his hand many manly deeds. Agni has become the lord of riches, having truly accomplished all immortal works.
(2.2.12.2.i) I invoke Savitṛ, the golden-handed, for aid; he, the god, knows the place.

(2.2.12.2.k) O Savitṛ, grant us what is desirable today, and what is desirable tomorrow; day by day, grant us what is desirable. For you, O God, are the master of abundant desirable wealth; through this prayer, may we be partakers of that which is desirable.
(2.2.12.2ḷ) Indeed, O Earth, you bear the weight that crushes the mountains; you, O vast one, who possess sloping paths, quicken all things by your greatness. (2.2.12.3) O Mighty One!
(2.2.12.3ṃ) O you who wander far, the hymns of praise resound toward you through the nights—you who, O radiant one, hurl forth the impeller like a neighing prize of victory.

May I be united with my friend Ṛdūdaras, who, when drunk, shall not harm me, O Lord of the Tawny Steeds. This Soma which has been deposited within us—I go toward Indra for the sake of that, so that he may grant me long life.

(2.2.12.3.o) Soma, whose wrath is all-pervading, who possesses swift-moving weapons, the shaker, the vigorous, the wielder of the spear, the consumer of the dregs—he has overcome all forests and thorns. No counter-measures have been able to deceive Indra from his side.

(2.2.12.3.p) Pressed out, Soma, seeking the *ṛta*, has become manifest; Jamadagni has offered prayer and sung praise to Indra. You are the bull, the controller of impetuous power; bestow it within, and grant firm support to the one who praises you. (2.2.12.4) Pressed out, Soma, seeking the *ṛta*, has become manifest; Jamadagni has offered prayer and sung praise to Indra. You are the bull, the controller of impetuous power; bestow it within, and grant firm support to the one who praises you.

(2.2.12.4.q) Men who offer prayer, performing their sacred rites, honor your overpowering exhilaration and your vigorous strength, whether it be the hymn that prevails or the sight of Soma; therein Indra bestows many spoils, and may we overcome [the enemy].

(2.2.12.4ṛ) O Viṣṇu, I offer the *vaṣaṭ* call to you from my mouth; O Śipiviṣṭa, may you graciously accept this oblation of mine. (2.2.12.5) May my well-spoken praises and songs increase you; and do you all protect us always with your blessings.
(2.2.12.5ṣ) Today, O Śipiviṣṭa, I, an Ārya who knows the sacred ways, proclaim that name of yours. Being myself weak, I praise you, the powerful one, who dwells in the far distance beyond this world.
(2.2.12.5ṭ) What was there to be hidden from you, O Viṣṇu, when you proclaimed, "I am Śipiviṣṭa"? Do not conceal this form from us, since you appeared in another form in the assembly.
O Agni, grant wealth consisting of heroic sons and abundance to the donor; sharpen us so that we may possess many sons.

Give us, O Agni, hundreds, give us thousands! Open up for us the doors to strength as if with fame. Make Heaven and Earth favorable through our sacred prayer; let the Dawns shine forth like the bright light of the sun.
May Agni grant wealth adorned with heroes; may Agni grant a seer who wins thousands. Agni has stretched the oblation to heaven; the domains of Agni are distributed in many places.

(2.2.12.6.x) Do not neglect us! (2.2.12.7.y) Bring it hither! (2.2.12.7.z) Like purified ghee, like a stainless body, like bright gold—so does that [glory] of yours shine, O self-dependent one, like a golden ornament.
O you of beautiful radiance, you cook both ladles of clarified butter in your mouth; therefore, O Lord of Might, fill us up during our hymns and bring nourishment to those who praise you.
O Vāyu, harness a hundred bay steeds that bring nourishment; or let your chariot, drawn by a thousand, come hither with its full splendor.

With those teams by which you go toward the donor for the sacrifice in his home, O Vāyu—bestow upon us here wealth that provides excellent enjoyment, and grant us a gift consisting of heroes, cattle, and horses.
May there be for us, in Indra's company, wealthy and abundant refreshments, through which we, possessing food, may rejoice.
O wealthy one, may the praiser of a bountiful patron like you indeed be prosperous; O Lord of the Bay Horses, let him be renowned.
(2.3.1.1) One desiring prosperity should offer a *caru* oblation to the Adityas who are "becoming" (*bhuvad-vat*).
Indeed, the Adityas push away from prosperity that man who, though capable of prosperity, does not attain it.
He approaches the very Adityas who are "becoming" with their own share.
(2.3.1.1) These very [deities] lead him to prosperity; he indeed prospers.
(2.3.1.1) One who has been expelled or is being expelled should offer a *caru* oblation to the Ādityas who uphold [the world].
The Ādityas are indeed the repellers; the Ādityas are the ones who cause [the enemy] to depart.
To the very Ādityas, the possessors of *dhārayadvat*, he has recourse with their own portion. They, verily, establish him firmly in the clan.
(2.3.1.2) He becomes one who cannot be driven away.
(2.3.1.2) While being driven away, he should place his foot upon [the earth] while saying, "O Aditi, grant permission.
For this earth is indeed Aditi.
"This very [earth] grants her approval for his sovereignty. "May my blessing be true," he says; thus he makes his blessing come true.

(2.3.1.2) Here he says, "The mind. (2.3.1.2) He thereby makes the subjects of one mind with him. (2.3.1.3) "Come hither, O Maruts, bounteous givers, together with this lord of the people, toward that king," he says.
The Maruts are indeed the people (*viś*),
and the eldest is the lord of the people (*viśpati*). By means of the people, he causes him to prosper with the kingdom.
(2.3.1.3) From the house of one who speaks vulgarly about another, he should fetch rice grains;
he should separate the white ones from the black ones.
Of those that are white, he should offer a *caru* oblation to Āditya.
The *viś* (the people) indeed has the Ādityas as its deity; verily, he goes down to the *viś*.
(2.3.1.4) "His *viṭ* is understood, but his *rāṣṭra* is not understood," they say.
(2.3.1.4) He should offer a *caru* oblation to Varuṇa consisting of those [grains] that are black.
(2.3.1.4) For the *rāṣṭra* belongs to Varuṇa.
(2.3.1.4) He indeed attains both the people and the royal power.
(2.3.1.4) If he should not attain them, he should offer this oblation, saying: "I set aside this portion for the Ādityas, so that [the people] from such-and-such a clan may come to me.
(2.3.1.4–5) The Ādityas themselves, seeking their own share, cause him to attain the people.
(2.3.1.5) If he should not obtain [them], he should strike seven shoots of the *aśvattha* tree onto the middle shaft with the formula:
"Here I bind the Ādityas from so-and-so for the sake of so-and-so, so that they may enter the clan.
(2.3.1.5) Thus the Ādityas, their heroes bound, cause him to enter the clan.
(2.3.1.5) If he should not attain [the goal], he should offer this very *caru* oblation to Āditya. (2.3.1.5) He should also bind the *mayūkha* pegs to the sacrificial fuel (*idhma*).
(2.3.1.5) Thus, he attains it without being obstructed.
(2.3.1.5) They are made of *aśvattha* wood;
for the *aśvattha* is indeed the vigor of the Maruts. By means of that very vigor, he enters among the people.
There are seven;
for the Maruts consist of seven groups. It is by means of the groups that he enters among the people.
(2.3.2.1) The gods were indeed afraid of death. (2.3.2.1) They ran to Prajāpati for help.
(2.3.2.1) For them, he offered this oblation of a hundred kṛṣṇalas dedicated to Prajāpati.
(2.3.2.1) By means of that very [offering], he placed immortality into these [worlds].
(2.3.2.1) For one who fears death, he should offer this oblation of a hundred *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces dedicated to Prajāpati.
(2.3.2.1) He thus approaches Prajāpati himself with his own share.
(2.3.2.1) He alone bestows life-span upon him; (2.3.2.1) he attains a full lifespan; (2.3.2.1) it consists of one hundred kṛṣṇala-weights.
A man has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundred faculties; he finds firm standing in both life and the faculties. It is in ghee.
Clarified butter is indeed life;
gold is immortality.
Thus, he bestows both life and immortality upon him in a unified manner.
(2.3.2.2) He cuts off four *kṛṣṇala* seeds each, for the attainment of the fourfold portion. (2.3.2.2) He presents them to the Brahman priest all at once.
(2.3.2.2) Thus, all at once, he bestows long life upon the sacrificer.
(2.3.2.2) Yonder sun did not shine.
(2.3.2.2) The gods sought an expiation for it.
(2.3.2.2) For it, they offered this oblation of cooked rice dedicated to Sūrya.
(2.3.2.2) By that very means they bestowed radiance upon him.
(2.3.2.3) For one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he should offer this oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) to Sūrya. Verily, he approaches yonder sun with his own share.
(2.3.2.3) He alone bestows spiritual luster upon him; (2.3.2.3) he indeed becomes possessed of spiritual luster.
(2.3.2.3) There are gold plates on both sides.
(2.3.2.3) He bestows radiance upon him from both sides.
(2.3.2.3) At each fore-offering he offers a kṛṣṇala;
verily, from the quarters he wins for him spiritual luster.
(2.3.2.3) One who desires, "May I find gold; may gold come to me," should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ, and a pap to Bhūmi.
(2.3.2.4) In that there is an offering to Agni—since gold belongs to Agni—he finds that very gold through him to whom gold belongs.
(2.3.2.4) It belongs to Savitṛ; impelled by Savitṛ, he indeed finds it.
(2.3.2.4) There is a pap for the Earth; on this very earth he finds it. Gold inclines toward him.
(2.3.2.4) He who finds gold is indeed deprived of power and vigor.
(2.3.2.5) Having found gold, he should offer this very [oblation];
thus he is not deprived of power and vigor.
(2.3.2.5) One should offer this very same [oblation] for whom gold might be lost.
(2.3.2.5) Since it belongs to Agni, and gold indeed belongs to Agni, he recovers that very gold by means of him to whom it belongs. It belongs to Savitṛ; verily, impelled by Savitṛ, he recovers it.
(2.3.2.5) There is a pap for Earth; for whatever is lost here on earth, it is indeed found again upon this very earth.
(2.3.2.6) Indra forcibly drank Tvaṣṭṛ’s Soma; he (Tvaṣṭṛ) fell apart in every direction.
(2.3.2.6) He was deprived of his sensory power and the drinking of Soma.
(2.3.2.6) That which he vomited upwards became the Śyāmāka grains.
(2.3.2.6) He ran to Prajāpati for refuge.
Therefore, he offered for him this *śyāmāka* pap dedicated to Soma-Indra; by that very act, he bestowed upon him power (*indriya*) and the drinking of Soma.
He who vomits Soma is indeed deprived of power and the drinking of Soma.
For one who is a vomiter of Soma, one should offer this *śyāmāka* pap dedicated to Soma-Indra.
He approaches both Soma and Indra with their own respective portions;
they two bestow upon him sensory power and the drinking of Soma.
He is not deprived of sensory power or the drinking of Soma.
(2.3.2.7) In that it belongs to Soma, he wins the drinking of Soma;
(2.3.2.7) in that it belongs to Indra—the drinking of Soma being indeed power—he wins power, the very drinking of Soma.
It is made of *śyāmāka* grain.

(2.3.2.7) This, indeed, is that Soma. (2.3.2.8) Verily, he directly obtains the drinking of Soma. One desiring cattle should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni the Giver, and a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Bestower.
Agni himself procreates cattle for him, and Indra bestows them once they have grown.
(2.3.2.8) There are curds, honey, ghee, water, and parched grains.
(2.3.2.8) This, indeed, is the form of cattle. (2.3.2.8) By means of this very form, he wins cattle.
(2.3.2.8) It consists of five portions, for cattle are fivefold. (2.3.2.8) It is multiform.
(2.3.2.8) For cattle are many-formed. (2.3.2.9) [The offering] is for prosperity. (2.3.2.9) It belongs to Prajāpati; for cattle indeed belong to Prajāpati.
Prajāpati himself procreates cattle for him.
Honey is indeed the self of man;
when he offers honey into the fire, the sacrificer thereby places his very self into the fire.
The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses consist of *paṅkti* meters.
Man is fivefold (*pāṅkta*), and cattle are fivefold.
Having ransomed himself from death, he thereby wins cattle.
(2.3.3.1) The gods, desiring glory, performed a sacrificial session of measured success.
Glory came to them in King Soma;
he went up to the mountain.
(2.3.3.1) Agni followed after him.
(2.3.3.1) Those two, Agni and Soma, became united.
(2.3.3.1) Indra, having been excluded from the sacrifice, followed after them.
He said to them, "Sacrifice for me. So they performed this sacrifice for him.
(2.3.3.1) An offering on eight potsherds for Agni, an offering on eleven potsherds for Indra, and a pap for Soma.
(2.3.3.1) By means of this very [offering], they bestowed upon him brilliance, sensory power, and Vedic luster.
(2.3.3.2) For one who has failed in a sacrifice, one should offer this sacrifice.
(2.3.3.2) An offering on eight potsherds for Agni, an offering on eleven potsherds for Indra, and a pap for Soma.
(2.3.3.2) In that there is an offering for Agni, he thereby bestows brilliance upon him;
in that there is an offering for Indra, he thereby bestows sensory power upon him.

(2.3.3.2) In that it belongs to Soma, it is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); therefore, one should join together the [cake] for Agni and the [milk] for Soma in the [oblation] for Indra. (2.3.3.2) Thus, he bestows both brilliance and spiritual luster upon him in a unified manner. (2.3.3.3) He places them together.
(2.3.3.3) One whose desire does not come to fruition should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma.
(2.3.3.3) For the Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni; he drinks the Soma.
(2.3.3.3) He has recourse to his own deity with its own portion; that very deity fulfills him according to his desire.
His desire comes to him.
(2.3.3.3) One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and Soma.
(2.3.3.3) Verily, he approaches Agni and Soma with their own portion; they two bestow spiritual luster upon him.
(2.3.3.3) He indeed becomes endowed with spiritual luster.
(2.3.3.4) In that it is offered on eight potsherds, it belongs to Agni;
in that it consists of *śyāmāka* grain, it belongs to Soma.
(2.3.3.4) For prosperity: he who fears impotence should offer a *śyāmāka* rice-oblation to Soma Vājin.
For it is from him that vital seed (*vājina*) departs, and thus he fears impotence.
(2.3.3.4) He has recourse to Soma, the prize-winner, with his own share; he (Soma) bestows upon him seed that is a prize-winner; he does not become impotent.
One who desires a village should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Bṛhaspati.
(2.3.3.5) He has recourse to Brahmaṇaspati with his own share;
he (Brahmaṇaspati) bestows his kinsmen upon him,
and he indeed becomes the lord of a village.
(2.3.3.5) The invitatory and offering verses contain the word "gaṇa" (host).
(2.3.3.5) Thus he makes him possessed of a host by means of his kinsmen.
(2.3.3.5) He who desires this very thing should offer this [oblation].
(2.3.3.5) "O Brahmin, may I destroy the people," with these words he should employ the invitatory and offering verses addressed to the Maruts;
thus, he indeed destroys the people through the Brahmin alone.
(2.3.4.1) One who desires heaven should offer a pap to Aryaman.
(2.3.4.1) Yonder sun, indeed, is Aryaman. (2.3.4.1) He thus has recourse to Aryaman with his own share.
(2.3.4.1) He indeed causes him to go to the heavenly world.
(2.3.4.1) One who desires, "May my offspring be inclined toward giving," should offer a *caru* oblation to Aryaman.
(2.3.4.1) Yonder sun, indeed, is Aryaman; he who truly gives is Aryaman.
One thus approaches Aryaman himself with his own share.
(2.3.4.1) He indeed is [the one]. (2.3.4.2) He makes offspring desirous of giving to him; offspring become desirous of giving to him.
(2.3.4.2) He who should desire [this] should offer a *caru* oblation to Aryaman.
"May this [person] go safely to the people.
Now, Aryaman is indeed that sun;
verily, he has recourse to Aryaman with his own share.
(2.3.4.2) He indeed leads him to that place where he desires to go. (2.3.4.2) Indra was once the youngest among the gods; he ran to Prajāpati for refuge.
For him, he offered this cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Indra Anuṣūk. By that very means, he led him to the forefront among the gods.
He made the invitatory and offering verses contain the words "foundation" (*budhna*) and "forefront" (*agra*); verily, from the foundation he led him to the forefront.
For a Rājanya who is inferior in rank, one should offer this cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Indra Anuṣūk.
(2.3.4.3) He has recourse to Indra himself with his own share; he, verily, leads him to the forefront among his equals.
(2.3.4.3) The invitatory and offering verses contain the words "foundation" (*budhna*) and "forefront" (*agra*); from the foundation itself, he leads him to the forefront.
(2.3.4.4) It is made of *ānuṣūka* grass, for this is the deity of him who is born after another.
(2.3.4.4) For prosperity:
for a Brāhmaṇa who is younger than his peers, he should offer this *ānuṣūka* oblation of cooked rice to Bṛhaspati.
He thus approaches Bṛhaspati with his own share; he [Bṛhaspati] leads him to the forefront among his equals.
The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses contain the words "foundation" (*budhna*) and "summit" (*agra*). Verily, from the foundation he leads him to the summit.
It belongs to one who is born after his elder brother (*ānuṣūka*), for such a person has that as his deity;
it serves for prosperity.
(2.3.5.1) Prajāpati had thirty-three daughters.
(2.3.5.1) He gave them to Soma, the King. (2.3.5.1) Of them, he approached Rohiṇī.
(2.3.5.1) They, being envious, went back again. (2.3.5.1) He followed after them.
(2.3.5.1) He asked for them back again.
(2.3.5.1) He did not give them back to him.
(2.3.5.1) "Strike truthfully; I will approach you on equal terms, and then I will give them back to you."
(2.3.5.1) He ate the *ṛta*.
(2.3.5.1) She gave them back to him.
(2.3.5.1–2) Of those, he approached only the Rohiṇī.
Consumption (yakṣma) seized him.

Because it seized the king, that is the origin of *rājayakṣma* (kingly consumption). Because he became worse off, that is the origin of *pāpayakṣma* (evil consumption). Because he found [the disease] among his wives, that is the origin of *jāyenya* (consumption from wives). He who thus knows the origin of these consumptions—these consumptions do not seize him.
(2.3.5.2) He ran toward them, paying homage.
(2.3.5.2) They said: "Let us choose a boon: let him approach us all equally."
For him they offered this oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) to Āditya;
by that very means they freed him from the wasting disease (*srāma*).
Whoever should be seized by the evil *yakṣma* disease, for him one should offer this oblation of cooked rice to Āditya.

Verily, he causes him to swell following after that very one as it swells. "New, ever new, he becomes as he is born"—this is the invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākyā*); by means of it, he bestows life-span upon him.
"The stalk which the Ādityas cause to swell"—by this sacrificial offering verse (*yājyā*), he indeed causes him to swell.
(2.3.6.1) Prajāpati assigned food to the gods.
"That which shall exceed these worlds..."
"This has become mine," he thought;
thus it overflowed beyond these worlds: Indra the King, Indra the Overlord, and Indra the Self-Ruler.
From that, indeed, he milked these worlds threefold.

(2.3.6.1) That is the threefold nature of the threefold world. (2.3.6.1) If he should desire of someone, "May he be an eater of food," for him he should offer this threefold oblation: a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the King; (2.3.6.2) [and cakes] to Indra the Overlord and to Indra the Self-Ruler.
(2.3.6.2) This king here is indeed Indra; this overlord is Indra; yonder sovereign is Indra.
He approaches these very worlds with their own respective portions;
they, in turn, bestow food upon him.
(2.3.6.2) He indeed becomes an eater of food.
(2.3.6.2) Just as one milks a cow that has been made to yield by means of its calf, even so he milks these worlds—which have been made to yield—according to his desire for food and nourishment.
(2.3.6.2) He places [the oblation] upon the potsherds which are turned face upwards.
(2.3.6.2) For the sake of freshness, there are three sacrificial cakes;
these worlds are three.
(2.3.6.2) For the attainment of these worlds.
(2.3.6.2) Each subsequent one becomes greater;
for indeed, these worlds are thus arranged.
(2.3.6.2) For the sake of prosperity,
he cuts off [the portions] while causing all [the deities] to partake; thus,
there is no failure.
(2.3.6.2) He recites [the verses] in reverse order; (2.3.6.2) this is for the sake of non-consumption by fire.
(2.3.7.1) The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict.
(2.3.7.1) The Asuras defeated those gods.
(2.3.7.1) Having been defeated, those gods entered into the service of the Asuras.
(2.3.7.1) Vital power and strength departed from them. (2.3.7.1) Indra perceived that; he followed after it as it departed.
(2.3.7.1) It could not hold itself;
it moved away from him.
It ran to Prajāpati for refuge.
(2.3.7.1) He caused him to sacrifice with this *sarvapṛṣṭhā* [offering].
By means of that very [offering], he bestowed sensory power and vigor upon him.
(2.3.7.1) Whoever should desire sensory power or vigor, for him one should cause to sacrifice with this *sarvapṛṣṭhā*.
(2.3.7.2) He approaches these very deities with their own respective portions;
they bestow sensory power and vigor upon him. In that he offers to Indra associated with the *rathaṃtara*, he wins that very brilliance which belongs to Agni.
(2.3.7.2) In that [he offers] for Indra of the Bṛhat-sāman, he wins whatever brilliance belongs to Indra.
(2.3.7.2) In that [he offers] for Indra of the Vairūpa-sāman, he wins whatever brilliance belongs to Savitṛ.
(2.3.7.3) In that [he offers] for Indra of the Vairāja-sāman, he wins whatever brilliance belongs to Dhātṛ.
(2.3.7.3) In that [he offers] for Indra Śākvara, he wins whatever brilliance belongs to the Maruts;
(2.3.7.3) in that [he offers] for Indra Raivata, he wins whatever brilliance belongs to Bṛhaspati.
He places [the oblation] upon the potsherds while they are turned face upwards.
The cake on twelve potsherds is offered for the sake of its being unwearied,
and for the sake of its belonging to the Viśvedevas.
He cuts off [the portions] all around;
verily, he bestows the senses and vigor upon the sacrificer all around. He recites the verses in alternating order.
(2.3.7.4) For one who cannot be consumed by fire;
(2.3.7.4) with this very [offering] should one who is being falsely accused sacrifice.
(2.3.7.4) If these deities indeed eat his food, then men will surely eat it as well.
Rājana Kauṇeya went to Kratujit Jānaki for the sake of the *cakṣurvanya* rite. For him, he performed this sacrifice:
a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Bhrājasvat, a pap for Sūrya, and a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Bhrājasvat.
(2.3.8.1) By means of that very [offering], he placed sight in him.
(2.3.8.1) For one who should desire sight, he should offer this sacrifice:
a cake on eight potsherds for Agni the Radiant, a pap for Sūrya, and a cake on eight potsherds for Agni the Radiant.
(2.3.8.1) By the eye of Agni indeed do humans see; by the eye of Sūrya, the gods.
(2.3.8.2) He approaches both Agni and Sūrya with their own respective portions; they two bestow sight upon him, and he becomes possessed of sight.
In that there are two offerings to Agni, he thereby bestows the two eyes upon him;
in that there is one to Sūrya, he thereby [bestows] the nose.
The two offerings to Agni are on both sides of the one to Sūrya.
(2.3.8.2) Therefore, the two eyes are on both sides of the nose;
(2.3.8.2) therefore, the two eyes are held apart by the nose;
(2.3.8.2) the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are identical.
For the eye is common for the sake of prosperity.
"Upwards that Jātavedas...
"Seven bay horses are in your chariot."
With the verse, "The brilliant face of the gods has risen," he offers the rice-balls;
verily, he bestows sight upon him—
whatever that [sight] of his is.
(2.3.9.1.a) You are firm; may I be firm among my kinsmen, wise, perceptive, and a finder of wealth.

(2.3.9.1.a) You are firm; may I be firm among my kinsmen, fierce, perceptive, and a finder of wealth. (2.3.9.1.a) You are firm; may I be firm among my kinsmen, a conqueror, perceptive, and a finder of wealth.

(2.3.9.1.b) You are the consenter; of those who are consenting, O gods, those kinsmen, the youths who are of one mind—them I desire with my heart. May they desire me with their hearts. Make them of one mind with me, Svāhā! (2.3.9.1.b) You are the consenter. (2.3.9.2) Of those who are consenting, O gods, those women who are of one mind—I desire them with my heart. May they desire me with their hearts. Make them of one mind with me, Svāhā!
One desiring a village should offer the *sāṃgrahaṇī* oblation dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
Kinsmen indeed belong to all the gods.
He approaches all the gods with their own respective portions;
they, in turn, bestow kinsmen upon him.
He indeed becomes a village-dweller;
it is the Sāṃgrahaṇī [offering]; for the Sāṃgrahaṇī is the grasping of the mind.
(2.3.9.2) "The mind alone seizes [the power] over his kinsmen.
(2.3.9.3) With the words, "Thou art firm; may I be firm among my kinsmen," he places the enclosing-sticks around.
By this, he indeed invokes this very blessing.
(2.3.9.3) Moreover, all this indeed comes under the control of those kinsmen for whom these enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) are laid down by one who knows thus.
(2.3.9.3) He offers three oblations with the verse: "Thou art the seat of the seat-loving gods.
(2.3.9.3) So many indeed are the kinsmen—those who are great, those who are small, and those who are women.
He wins those very things;
once won, they wait upon him.

(2.3.10.1.a) That which moved newly became fresh butter (*navanīta*); that which crept became clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*); that which was solidified became ghee (*ghṛta*). (2.3.10.1.b) You are the breath of the Aśvins; may they two grant it to you, whose breath you are—*svāhā*! You are the breath of Indra; may he grant it to you, whose breath you are—*svāhā*! You are the breath of Mitra and Varuṇa; may they two grant it to you, whose breath you are—*svāhā*! You are the breath of the All-gods (*viśve devāḥ*); may they grant it to you, whose breath you are—*svāhā*!
The stream of clarified butter, the path of immortality, bestowed by Indra and extended forth by the Maruts—Viṣṇu beheld that for you; Iḍā, rich in cattle, urged it toward you.

(2.3.10.2ḍ) By means of the *pāvamāna* hymn, by the path of the *gāyatrī*, by the power of the *upāṃśu* cup—may the god Savitṛ release you for life, for the sake of living! By means of the hymn of the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara*, by the path of the *triṣṭubh*, by the power of the *śukra* cup—may the god Savitṛ release you for life, for the sake of living! By means of the measure of Agni, by the path of the *jagatī*, by the power of the *āgrayaṇa* cup—may the god Savitṛ release you for life, for the sake of living!

(2.3.10.3.e) O Agni, make this [child] fit for long life and splendor; O Varuṇa, O King Soma, make him dear as seed. O Aditi, grant him protection like a mother, so that he may reach old age, O All-Gods!

(2.3.10.3.f) Agni is long-lived; he is long-lived through the trees. With that life-span, I make you long-lived. Soma is long-lived; he is long-lived through the plants. The sacrifice is long-lived; it is long-lived through the sacrificial fees. The Brahman is long-lived; it is long-lived through the Brahmins. The gods are long-lived; they are long-lived through the nectar of immortality. The ancestors are long-lived; they are long-lived through the *svadhā* offering. With that life-span, I make you long-lived.

(2.3.11.1) The body of such a person goes to Agni, the vital sap to Soma, Varuṇa seizes him with his noose, Sarasvatī takes away his speech, and Agni-Viṣṇu take away his self—he for whom there is long-lasting illness. For one who is long ill, or for one who should desire, "May I reach a full span of life," he should offer this sacrifice: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on ten potsherds for Varuṇa, a pap for Sarasvatī, and a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Viṣṇu.

(2.3.11.1) By means of Agni alone he ransoms his body; by means of Soma, his vital essence. (2.3.11.2) By means of Varuna alone he releases him from Varuna’s noose; by means of Sarasvatī, he bestows speech upon him.

Agni is all the deities, and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; thus, by means of both the deities and the sacrifice, he heals him, so that even if his life-breath has departed, he indeed lives. Looking at the clarified butter with the words, "That which came forth as new became fresh butter," he proclaims its very form and its greatness.

(2.3.11.2) "Thou art the breath of the Aśvins," he says; for the Aśvins are indeed the physicians of the gods. Through them, he provides healing for this [person]. (2.3.11.3) "Thou art the breath of Indra," he says; by this, he bestows sensory power upon him.
"Thou art the breath of Mitra and Varuṇa," he says;
by this, he bestows out-breath and in-breath upon him.
"Thou art the breath of the All-gods," he says; by this, he bestows vigor upon him.
"Of the stream of ghee, the path of immortality," he says;
this is according to the sacrificial formula itself.
"With the purifying hymn," he says.
By this [verse], he bestows vital breath (*prāṇa*) upon him.
"With the *stoma* of the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*"—he says this;
by this, he bestows vigor (*ojas*) upon him. "With the measure of Agni"—he says this; by this, he bestows the self (*ātman*) upon him.
The officiating priests chant around him; as many as there are officiating priests, they heal him.
Grasping the hand of the Brahman priest, they chant around him; thus, in a single way, they bestow life upon the sacrificer—whatever that [life] of his may be.

(2.3.11.4) From gold [he draws] ghee. Ghee is indeed life, and gold is immortality; verily from immortality he drinks up life. (2.3.11.5) It is one hundred mānas in weight; man has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundredfold power; he finds firm support in both life and power. Moreover, it should be of such a measure as he thinks he will live; this is for the sake of prosperity.

"O Agni, make this [child] for long life and luster," he says; verily, he bestows life and luster upon him. "May all the gods [grant that] he may reach old age," he says; verily, he makes him one who reaches old age. "Agni is long-lived," with these words he takes his hand.
These indeed are the long-lived gods; they bestow long life upon him, and he attains a full lifespan.
(2.3.12.1) Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa.
(2.3.12.1) He reached his own deity; (2.3.12.1) he was rent asunder.
He saw this oblation to Varuṇa on four potsherds;
he offered it,
and thereby he was indeed released from the noose of Varuṇa.
(2.3.12.1) Verily, Varuṇa seizes him who accepts a horse.
(2.3.12.1) As many horses as he may accept, so many four-potherd offerings to Varuṇa should he present.
(2.3.12.1) Thus he has recourse to Varuṇa himself with his own share.
He alone releases him from the noose of Varuṇa.
They consist of four potsherds;
for the horse has four feet, [and this serves] for prosperity.
(2.3.12.2) He should offer one additional oblation for whichever person he has accepted a gift from, or whom he does not study with;
by that very act, he is released from Varuṇa’s noose.
(2.3.12.2) If he should become a recipient of further gifts, he should subsequently offer a cake on one potsherd to Sūrya.
(2.3.12.2) He makes that very sun his high-pitch.
(2.3.12.2) He goes down to the waters for the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
(2.3.12.2) Varuṇa is indeed in the waters.
(2.3.12.2) He sacrifices directly to Varuṇa himself.
(2.3.12.2) Having returned, he should offer a pap for Aponapāt.
(2.3.12.2) For the horse has its origin in the waters.
He causes him to go to his very own womb;
he, being pacified, stands near him.
(2.3.13.1) O Indra and Varuṇa, that body of yours which is to be restrained, with that release this man from distress.

(2.3.13.1) O Indra and Varuṇa, that body of yours which is powerful, protective, and brilliant, with that release this man from distress. (2.3.13.1) O Indra and Varuṇa, whatever offense of yours is in the fire, that I appease for you with this [offering].

(2.3.13.1) O Indra and Varuṇa, whatever wasting disease (*srāma*) is in you among bipeds, among quadrupeds, in the cow-pen, in the houses, in the waters, in the plants, or in the trees—that I appease for you with this offering.
(2.3.13.2) Indeed, Indra departs from him with his power (*indriya*), and Varuṇa seizes him with the noose of Varuṇa, he who is seized by evil.

For one who has been seized by evil, one should offer this curd-mixture (*payasyā*) dedicated to Indra and Varuṇa. Thus, Indra bestows power upon him, and Varuṇa releases him from the noose of Varuṇa.

There is a dish of curdled milk (*payasyā*), for indeed, milk has departed from him; and he who is seized by evil is this [sacrificer]. Since there is a dish of curdled milk, it is with that [dish] that he bestows milk upon him.

Upon the dish of curdled milk, he places a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*); thus he makes him possessed of a body, and also possessed of a foundation. He divides [the cake] into four parts; verily, he establishes himself in the quarters.
(2.3.13.3) He gathers [the soil] together again; verily, he prepares a remedy for him from all the quarters.
Having gathered it, he cuts it off; as one cuts out what has been pierced, so is this.
"O Indra and Varuṇa, whatever flaw is in you within the fire, that do I expiate for you with this," he says; verily, he protects him from a defective sacrifice.

"O Indra and Varuṇa, whatever disease there is among your two-footed animals, that I appease for you with this," he says. For so many indeed are the waters, the plants, the trees, the progeny, and the cattle that provide sustenance; these very things he thereby releases from the noose of Varuṇa for him.
(2.3.14.1.a) He, like the ancients;
(2.3.14.1.b) down with his poetic insights;
(2.3.14.1.c) Indra for you from every side.
(2.3.14.1ḍ) Indra, [for] the men...
(2.3.14.1.e) O Soma, King, protect us from all sides against the one who intends evil; no one shall harm one such as you.

(2.3.14.1.f) Those abodes of yours which are in heaven, those on earth, and those upon the mountains, in the plants, and in the waters—with all of them, being well-disposed and free from anger, O Soma, as you reign, accept our offerings.
O Agni and Soma, you who possess common wealth and are invoked together, accept our songs; you have both become present among the gods.
(2.3.14.1–2) O Agni and Soma, you two of one mind have placed these luminous realms in heaven. O Agni and Soma, you released the rivers from the curse and from reproach when they were seized.
O Agni and Soma, you two bulls, graciously hear this my invocation; accept these hymns with favor and be a source of joy to the donor.
Mātariśvan brought one from heaven; the falcon churned the other from the rock. O Agni and Soma, having grown strong through the sacred word (*brahman*), you have made wide space for the sacrifice.
O Agni and Soma, partake of the presented oblation; accept it, O bulls, and enjoy it. Since you are providers of good protection and good aid, bestow well-being and prosperity upon the sacrificer.
(2.3.14.3ṃ) Swell up; (2.3.14.3ṇ) may [it] be united with thee.
We invoke you, the Lord of hosts, the sage among sages, possessed of most exalted fame, the supreme king of sacred prayers, O Brahmaṇaspati; hearing us, sit upon your seat with your aids.

He, with his people, with his clan, with his kin, with his sons, and with his men, wins booty and wealth—he who strives to win over the Father of the gods with an offering made with a mind full of faith, [offering] to Brahmaṇaspati.
With his well-praising, chanting host and with his roar, Bṛhaspati shattered Vala and Phaliga; he drove forth the lowing cows that provide the oblation, bellowing aloud.
(2.3.14.4ṛ) O Maruts, that which [you have] from heaven... (2.3.14.4ṣ) ...those shelters of yours.

Aryaman goes forth, the bull, the mighty, the giver of riches, invoked by many, the worthy one. May the thousand-eyed god, the breaker of enclosures with the thunderbolt in his arm, bestow wealth upon us.

(2.3.14.4.u) O Aryaman, those many paths of yours that lead to the gods, O King, which traverse the sky—by means of them, O God, grant us great protection; be a source of well-being for our bipeds and well-being for our quadrupeds.

Praised by the Aṅgirases, he drove from the base to the summit; Indra shattered the firm foundations of the mountain. He broke down their artificial embankments—those deeds Indra performed in the intoxication of Soma.

From the depths he measured out with measures from the summit; with his thunderbolt he pierced the channels of the rivers. He released them to flow freely along paths for long journeys—those deeds Indra performed in the exhilaration of Soma.
He who was born knowing his kinship—the god who proclaims all births—has brought forth the sacred word from the sacred word; from the midst, from below, he has risen upward by his own inherent power.
Great, having been born, he propped apart the two great worlds—the sky and the earthly realm. By his very birth, Bṛhaspati, the sovereign lord of the gods, reached from the foundation to the summit.

He who from the base rises toward the summit by his might—him, Bṛhaspati, the gods seek to win over. He cleaves Vala; he shatters the fortresses; bellowing aloud, he has won the light of heaven and the waters.
The gods, humans, and fathers were on one side; the asuras, rakṣases, and piśācas were on the other.
Of those gods, whatever small amount of blood they shed, the rakṣases struck it down with nights. When they had been struck down and dead, he (the Sun) shone forth upon them.
(2.4.1.1) Those gods knew:
"Whosoever among us dies here, it is surely the *rakṣases* who slay him. They invited the *rakṣases*, and they said to them:
(2.4.1.1) "Let us choose a boon: that we may conquer the Asuras; let that be ours in common.
(2.4.1.2) Thereupon, the gods indeed conquered the Asuras. Having conquered the Asuras, they drove away the Rakṣases.
(2.4.1.2) Those *rakṣas* entered upon the gods on all sides, thinking, "They have committed an untruth.
(2.4.1.2) Those gods sought refuge in Agni.
(2.4.1.2) They offered a cake on eight potsherds to Agni the Forward-moving, to Agni the Dispeller, and to Agni the Facing-one.
(2.4.1.2) In that they offered to Agni the Forward-moving, whatever *rakṣas* were in front, those they drove away by that act;
(2.4.1.3) in that [they offered] to Agni the Dispeller, whatever *rakṣas* were all around, those they dispelled by that act.
(2.4.1.3) By means of the offering to Agni Pratīkāvat, they drove away those very Rakṣases that were in the rear.
(2.4.1.3) Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
(2.4.1.3) He who has rivals should, while contending with them, sacrifice with this iṣṭi.
(2.4.1.3) One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pravata and to Agni Vibādhavat. (2.4.1.4) [And] to Agni Pratīkavat.
In that he offers to Agni Pravata, he thereby drives away from himself whatever rival is superior;
in that he offers to Agni Vibādhavat, he thereby repels whoever is his equal.
(2.4.1.4) When [he offers] to Agni Pratīkāvat, he thereby drives away whoever is more wicked than himself; "he drives away his rival who is superior," so it is said.
He surpasses one who is his equal, and the more wicked one does not reach him—provided that he, knowing this, performs this sacrifice with this offering.
(2.4.2.1) The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict.
(2.4.2.1) Those gods said: "Let us join ourselves to whichever among us is the most powerful."
(2.4.2.1) They said to Indra:
(2.4.2.1) "You indeed are the most powerful among us; let us take hold of you.
He replied:
(2.4.2.1) "These three bodies of mine are full of vigor; satisfy them, and then you shall overcome the Asuras.
(2.4.2.1) "Tell us what they are," they said.
(2.4.2.1–2) "This one is the dispeller of distress, this one is the crusher, and this one is endowed with power," he replied.
(2.4.2.2) They offered a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Aṃhomuc, to Indra Vaimṛdha, and to Indra Indriyāvat.
(2.4.2.2) In that they offered to Indra Aṃhomuc, they were thereby released from distress;
in that [they offered] to Indra Vaimṛdha, they thereby struck away their enemies.
(2.4.2.2) In that they offered [the oblation] for Indra, the possessor of power, they thereby placed power within themselves.
(2.4.2.2) They prepared a sacrificial cake on thirty-three potsherds;
for there are thirty-three deities, and Indra caused them to take hold of himself for the sake of prosperity.

(2.4.2.3) By means of that very victory, the gods indeed conquered the highest victory over the Asuras. He who has a rival and is contending with him should sacrifice with this offering. He should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Aṃhomuc, to Indra Vaimṛdha, and to Indra Indriyāvat. For he from whom a superior rival arises is seized by distress.

(2.4.2.3) In that he offers [an oblation] to Indra Aṃhomuc, by that very act he is released from distress. (2.4.2.3) He who is surpassed among his equals by another who is more excellent is indeed beset by *mṛdh*. (2.4.2.4) But he for whom there is no rival is not beset. In that he offers [an oblation] to Indra Vaimṛdha, by that very act he strikes away the *mṛdh*.
(2.4.2.4) "In that [he offers] to Indra, the possessor of power, he thereby bestows power upon himself.
(2.4.2.4) He prepares a sacrificial cake on thirty-three potsherds;
for there are indeed thirty-three deities.
(2.4.2.4) The sacrificer causes those very [oblations] to proceed within himself for the sake of prosperity. (2.4.2.4) This sacrifice is indeed named "Victory" (*vijiti*).
He who, knowing thus, performs this sacrifice, conquers the highest victory over his rival.
(2.4.3.1) The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict.
(2.4.3.1) Gāyatrī, having gathered their vigor, strength, sensory power, heroism, offspring, and cattle, took them away and stood apart.
(2.4.3.1) They reflected:
"Whichever side she turns toward, they shall become this world," they thought.
They called out to her: the gods said, "O Viśvakarman! and the Asuras said, "O Dābhi!
But she did not turn toward either of them.
(2.4.3.1) Those gods saw this sacrificial formula:
