(2.4.3.1) "Thou art vigor; thou art might; thou art strength; (2.4.3.2) thou art splendor; thou art the abode of the gods by name; thou art the All; thou art all-life; thou art the Whole; thou art whole-life; thou art the overcomer.
(2.4.3.2) Thus indeed did the gods wrest from the Asuras their vigor, strength, sensory power, heroism, progeny, and cattle.
Because Gāyatrī stood apart when she departed, therefore they call this the Gāyatrī sacrifice;
for Gāyatrī is indeed the year,
and it was the year that stood apart when it departed.

(2.4.3.2) Because by means of this [offering], the gods seized the vigor, strength, sensory power, and heroism of the Asuras, as well as their offspring and cattle, therefore they call this sacrifice the "Seizer" (*saṃvarga*). (2.4.3.3) He who has rivals should, while contending with them, perform this sacrifice.
He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Saṃvarga.
When that [milk] has been cooked and set down, he should touch it with this sacrificial formula:
"He appropriates the vigor, strength, sensory power, heroism, offspring, and cattle of his rival; he prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated."
Prajāpati created offspring. Once they were created, they moved away from him.
Wherever they settled, from that place a mound (*gramut*) arose.
Bṛhaspati and [Agni] followed after them.
Bṛhaspati said:
"With this [earth], I shall establish you; then the creatures will turn back to you."
He established it.
Thereupon, indeed, creatures turned toward Prajāpati.
He who should desire offspring should offer for himself this *gārmuta* oblation of cooked rice dedicated to Prajāpati.
(2.4.4.1) He approaches Prajāpati himself with his own portion;
(2.4.4.2) he, verily, procreates offspring for him.
Prajāpati created cattle; once created, they went away from him.
(2.4.4.2) Wherever they settled, from there the *garmut* plant sprang up.
(2.4.4.2) Pūṣan and [another] followed after them. (2.4.4.2) Then Pūṣan said:
"By means of this [plant], establish yourself; then the cattle will turn toward you," [said Soma].
"Establish yourself in me," Soma replied. "In me, indeed, is that which ripens without being ploughed. "I shall establish myself in both of you," he said.
(2.4.4.3) Those two departed.
(2.4.4.3) Thereupon, indeed, the cattle turned toward Prajāpati.
He who should desire cattle—for him he should offer this *gārmuta* pap dedicated to Soma and Pūṣan.
(2.4.4.3) He has recourse to Soma and Pūṣan with their own respective portions;
they two indeed procreate cattle for him. Soma, verily, is the depositor of seed.
Pūṣan is the progenitor of cattle;
Soma indeed bestows seed upon him, and Pūṣan procreates the cattle.
O Agni, come to us with cattle; O Soma, enjoy us with prosperity; may Indra be the sustainer within our homes.
May Savitṛ, who possesses a thousandfold power, take delight in our homes; may Pūṣan come hither with wealth.
(2.4.5.1.c) May Dhātṛ, the lord and master of the moving world, grant us wealth; may he favor us with abundance.
May Tvaṣṭṛ, who is the bull, the mighty one, delight in our homes with a thousand and ten thousandfold.
(2.4.5.1.e) By which the gods sent forth immortality and long-lasting fame in heaven; as such, do thou bestow upon us increase of wealth, a herd of cattle, and bring us life.
(2.4.5.2.f) Agni, lord of the house; Soma, winner of all; Savitṛ, the wise—Svāhā!

(2.4.5.2.g) O Agni, lord of the house, with that portion of thine which consists of ghee, bestow strength upon me as I advance. May I not stray from the path of excellence; may I become the head—Svāhā!
(2.4.6.1) One who desires cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā.
(2.4.6.1) This earth is indeed the Citrā;
for upon her all that has come into being is produced, and therefore she is called Citrā.
(2.4.6.1) He who, knowing thus, performs the Citrā sacrifice desiring cattle, is propagated with offspring, cattle, and pairs.
(2.4.6.1) By means of the offering to Agni, he causes [the seed] to be sown;
by means of the offering to the Maruts, he places the seed.

(2.4.6.1) Tvaṣṭṛ indeed fashions forms from the seed that has been deposited. (2.4.6.1) There are two offerings to Sarasvatī; for this is a divine pair. Verily, he places a divine pair in the middle for him, for nourishment and procreation.
(2.4.6.2) There is a pap for Sinīvālī; Sinīvālī is indeed speech, and speech is truly nourishment. Verily, he attains nourishment and speech.
The last oblation belongs to Indra; by that very means it forms a pair.
There are these seven oblations:
there are seven domestic animals, seven wild animals, and seven meters.
For the attainment of both.
Then he offers these oblations;
for these gods are indeed the lords of prosperity.
(2.4.6.2) They alone bestow nourishment upon him; he prospers with offspring and cattle.
(2.4.6.2) They alone bestow nourishment upon him.
He prospers with offspring and cattle;
furthermore, he offers these oblations for the sake of firm establishment.
(2.4.7.1.a) You belong to the Maruts; you are the vigor of the Maruts. Break the stream of the waters!

(2.4.7.1.b) O Maruts, cause the falcon to rest—the swift one, fleet as thought, the bull, the well-fashioned one—by which the fierce host goes forth when released. O Aśvins, provide for that with well-being!

(2.4.7.1.c) The east wind raining, the invigorating turn—*svāhā*. The wind-ridden rain, the fierce turn—*svāhā*. Thundersome rain, the terrifying turn—*svāhā*. Without lightning, with thundering, the flashing bolt raining, the brilliant turn—*svāhā*. Raining for three nights, the fulfilling turn—*svāhā*. (2.4.7.2) "He has rained much today," the famous turn—*svāhā*. Rain falling while shining, the sovereign turn—*svāhā*. Thundering, the flashing bolt raining, the existing turn—*svāhā*.

(2.4.7.2ḍ) The gladdening, lowing, purifying, swift ones; the luminous, darkening, moistening, well-foaming ones; the supporters of Mitra, the supporters of Kṣatra, the fair realms—here do you protect me.
(2.4.7.2.e) You are the tethering-rope of the potent horse; for the sake of rain, I bind you up.

(2.4.8.1.a) O gods who possess wealth, Agni, Soma, and Sūrya; O gods who provide refuge, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman; O gods who drink together, O Son of the Waters, O swift impeller—give us water! Break open the reservoirs! From Parjanya of heaven, from the intermediate space, and from the earth, favor us with rain from there.
(2.4.8.1.b) Even by day they create darkness with Parjanya, the bearer of waters, when they drench the earth.

(2.4.8.1.c) The men of liberal gifts have shaken down from heaven the treasure-chest for the one who offers oblations. The rain-clouds release their showers across the two worlds; the rains flow over the desert wastes. (2.4.8.2) The rains flow.

(2.4.8.2ḍ) O Maruts, you raise [the rain] from the ocean; you, rich in moisture, cause the rain to fall. Your milch-cows, O wonder-workers, never fail; as they go forth in splendor, their chariots have rolled along.
Release the rain from heaven; fill the ocean with waters. You are born of the waters, the first-born; you are the strength of the ocean.
Do not cause the earth to tremble; cleave open this celestial firmament. Grant us of the celestial waters; O Lord, release the leather bag.

(2.4.8.2.g) Those gods who have their portion in heaven, those whose portion is in the intermediate space, and those whose portion is on earth—may they protect this sacrifice; may they enter this field; may they settle throughout this field.
(2.4.9.1) "Thou art of the Maruts, the vigor of the Maruts," with these words he puts on a black garment with a black fringe. This, indeed, is the form of rain;
having become like it, he causes Parjanya to rain.
"Delight the Maruts, the swift-flying hawk," he says; he thus drives back the west wind and generates the east wind for the attainment of rain. He offers oblations with the names of the winds;
Vāyu indeed rules over rain.
(2.4.9.1) He has recourse to Vāyu himself with his own share; he (Vāyu) indeed causes Parjanya to rain for him.
(2.4.9.1–2) He offers eight oblations.
There are indeed four quarters and four intermediate quarters;
verily, from the quarters he causes rain to flow forth together.
He mixes [the flour] on a black antelope skin.
(2.4.9.2) He has indeed made it the oblation; (2.4.9.2) he mixes [the flour] within the altar for the sake of attainment.
As the ascetics were being devoured, their heads fell away; they became date-palms (*kharjūra*),
and their sap flowed upward.
(2.4.9.2) They became those *karīra* fruits.
*Karīra* fruits indeed belong to Soma;
for an oblation belonging to Soma truly causes rain to fall from heaven.
(2.4.9.2) That there are *karīra* fruits.
By the very oblation to Soma, he wins rain from heaven;
he mixes it with honey. Honey, indeed, is the essence of the waters and of the plants.
(2.4.9.3) It rains from the waters themselves and from the plants.
(2.4.9.3) Moreover, he brings down rain from the waters themselves and from the plants.
(2.4.9.3) With the words, "The gentle ones, the lowing ones," he mixes [the water].
He approaches them by their very names;
moreover, just as one might say,
"So-and-so, come here!"— in this very way he causes them to move forward by means of their names.
"You are the tethering-rope of the stallion; for rain I bind you," he says.
For the horse is indeed a stallion, and Parjanya is a stallion.
Having indeed become like blackness, it rains; verily,
by means of its own form, he causes it to prosper,
for the attainment of rain.
"The gods who possess wealth;
the gods who grant protection;
the gods who share in the drinking"—with these words he ties [the rope], and thus by means of the deities he seeks rain day after day.
(2.4.10.1) If it should rain, one should offer the oblation for that very duration.
(2.4.10.1) If it should not rain, one should prepare the sacrificial offering on the following day.
For Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed day and night.
(2.4.10.1) Indeed, Parjanya rains by means of day and night;
for he rains either by night or by day. It is to Mitra and Varuṇa alone that one has recourse with their own respective share.
(2.4.10.1) Those two indeed cause Parjanya to rain for him through day and night.
(2.4.10.2) He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Dhāmachad, a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts, and a cake on one potsherd to Sūrya.
(2.4.10.2) For it is Agni who from here sends forth the rain.
(2.4.10.2) "The Maruts lead [the rain] when it has been released.
Indeed, when that sun turns downward with his rays, then he rains; for having become, as it were, a coverer of the abodes, he rains.
These deities indeed have mastery over the rain; he approaches them with their own respective portions.
(2.4.10.2) These very [waters] cause Parjanya to rain for him.
(2.4.10.3) Even if he is not about to rain, he certainly rains.
(2.4.10.3) "Release the rain from heaven; fill the ocean with waters," he says.
He unites these waters with those waters; thus, by means of these very waters, he reaches those.
"Thou art born of the waters, thou art the first-born, thou art the strength of the ocean," he says.
(2.4.10.3) This is according to the sacrificial formula itself.
(2.4.10.3) With the words, "O rain-cloud, cause the earth to swell," he offers the Varṣāhva oblation.
(2.4.10.3) For this [oblation] is the rain-bringer among plants.
By that very [formula], he causes rain to fall.
With the words, "O gods who have your portion in heaven," he shakes the black antelope skin.
These very worlds become for him gratified and propitiated.
(2.4.11.1) "All the meters are to be recited in this sacrifice," they say.

(2.4.11.1) The *kakubh* is indeed the vigor of the *triṣṭubh*, and the *uṣṇih* is that of the *jagatī*. In that he recites both the *uṣṇih* and the *kakubh*, by that very means he wins all the meters.
(2.4.11.1) This *uṣṇih* is indeed a *gāyatrī*.
Those four syllables which are added [to it] are the four-footed cattle themselves.
Just as there is sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) upon a sacrificial cake, even so are those syllables added to the *ṛc*.
If he were to conclude with a *jagatī*, he would bring the sacrifice to its end.
He concludes with a *triṣṭubh*;
for the *triṣṭubh* is indeed power and vigor.
(2.4.11.2) He establishes the sacrifice in the very senses and vigor; he does not let it reach its end.
(2.4.11.2) With the verse containing the word "three," "O Agni, three are thy strengths, three thy abodes," he encloses it for the sake of uniformity.
(2.4.11.2) This Traidhātavīya sacrifice is indeed the whole sacrifice; it is employed for every single desire,
for the sacrifice is employed for all desires.
One who practices sorcery should sacrifice with the Traidhātavīya.
This Traidhātavīya is indeed the whole sacrifice;
thus, he practices sorcery against him with the entire sacrifice.
(2.4.11.3) He indeed overthrows him.
(2.4.11.3) One who is being subjected to malevolent magic should sacrifice with this very [offering].
(2.4.11.3) This Traidhātavīya is indeed the whole sacrifice.
(2.4.11.3) He sacrifices with the entire sacrifice;
no one practicing sorcery against him can strike him down.
(2.4.11.3) One who intends to sacrifice with a thousand [cattle] should sacrifice with this very [rite].
(2.4.11.3) He thus bestows it as already born.

(2.4.11.3) One who has sacrificed with a thousand should sacrifice with this very [offering]. (2.4.11.3) He who sacrifices with a thousand indeed reaches the end of cattle. (2.4.11.4) He who sacrifices with a thousand reaches the end of cattle.
Prajāpati indeed created cattle;
he created them by means of the Traidhātavīya sacrifice itself.
He who, knowing this, performs the Traidhātavīya sacrifice desiring cattle, creates them from that very womb from which Prajāpati created cattle; a further thousand cattle come to him.
(2.4.11.4) He who, having said "I shall sacrifice," does not sacrifice, is indeed cut off from the deities. (2.4.11.4) He should sacrifice with the Traidhātavīya.
(2.4.11.5) For this Traidhātavīya is the entirety of the sacrifice.
He sacrifices with the entire sacrifice;
he is not cut off from the deities.
There is a cake on twelve potsherds.
Those three cakes on four potsherds each are for the sake of threefold prosperity; there are thus three sacrificial cakes.
(2.4.11.5) These are the three worlds. (2.4.11.5) For the attainment of these worlds,
each subsequent one becomes greater than the preceding.
For these worlds are indeed thus:
the middle one is made of barley;
this, verily, is the form of the intermediate region.
For the sake of prosperity,
he cuts [the portions] while causing all [the gods] to partake together;
thus there is no failure.
He gives gold;
verily he wins brilliance.
He gives a garment of silk-cotton; [verily he wins splendor].
Verily, he wins cattle;
he gives a milch-cow;
verily, he wins blessings.
Gold is indeed the color of the Sāmans;
linen cloth is that of the Yajus formulas; and a cow is that of the Ukthas and Āmadas.
(2.4.11.6) He wins all these social classes.
(2.4.12.1) Tvaṣṭṛ, whose son had been slain, brought Soma that excluded Indra. (2.4.12.1) Indra sought an invitation to it, but he did not invite him.
"You have killed my son! he cried. Having caused a disturbance in the sacrifice, he forcibly drank the Soma.
What remained of it, Tvaṣṭṛ cast into the Āhavanīya fire.
"O Indra’s enemy, grow!"—
at whatever distance he threw it upward, at that very point it came to rest by itself, whether on a slope of such extent or at such a height above the fire.
(2.4.12.2) As he was coming into being, he came together with Agni and Soma.
(2.4.12.2) He grew to the size of an arrow’s length on all sides;
he encompassed these worlds.
Because he enclosed these worlds, that is the "vṛtra-ness" of Vṛtra. Therefore Indra was afraid,
as was Tvaṣṭṛ.
For him, Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned the thunderbolt.
That thunderbolt was indeed ascetic fervor (*tapas*);
he was unable to lift it up.
(2.4.12.2) Now at that time Viṣṇu was indeed another deity.
"Viṣṇu, come here! We two shall carry away this [sacrifice] by means of which he [the sacrificer] will obtain this world."

(2.4.12.3) That Viṣṇu distributed himself threefold: one third on the earth, one third in the intermediate space, and one third in the sky. (2.4.12.3) For he was afraid of being encompassed. (2.4.12.3) With that third part which was on the earth, Indra raised his thunderbolt, supported by Viṣṇu.
He said, "Do not strike me; there is indeed this vigor within me. I shall give that to you.
He gave it to him.
He accepted it, saying, "Yes, for me. He offered it to Viṣṇu, saying, "This for Viṣṇu. Viṣṇu accepted it.
"May Indra bestow power upon us," [he said].
That which was the third [portion] in the intermediate space, with that Indra, supported by Viṣṇu, raised up the thunderbolt.
He said:
"Do not strike me; for I possess this vigor within me. I shall give that to you.
He gave it to him, and he accepted it.
"Twice, O Mādhū," he said; "To Viṣṇu," he offered it.
Viṣṇu accepted it, saying:
"May Indra bestow power upon us."
(2.4.12.5) That which was in the third heaven, with that Indra, supported by Viṣṇu, raised up his thunderbolt.
(2.4.12.5) "Do not strike me! [With] that which I am here, (2.4.12.6) I shall give it to you."
"Indeed, I have spoken thus," he said.
"But let us make a compact; enter into me alone. "If you were to enter me, what would you consume of me? he asked.
"I would kindle you alone for my enjoyment; may I enter into you," he said.
Vṛtra entered him;
for Vṛtra is indeed the belly.
Hunger, indeed, is the enemy of man.
He who knows thus destroys his enemy, hunger.
It [the food] he gave to him.

He accepted it, saying, "Three times you have placed [it] in me. He offered it to Viṣṇu with the words, "This for Viṣṇu. Viṣṇu accepted it, saying, "May Indra bestow sensory power (*indriya*) upon us."
Because he offered three times and accepted three times, that is the reason for the *tridhātu* (three-layered) nature of the *tridhātu*.
Because Viṣṇu stood by him, he offered [the oblation] saying "to Viṣṇu"; therefore, the sacrificial offering (*havis*) belongs to Indra and Viṣṇu.
Whatever exists here, all that he offered to him: the *ṛc*s, the *sāmans*, and the *yajus* formulas.
He indeed gave him a thousand;
therefore, it has a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
The gods were indeed afraid of the *rājanya* as he was being born.
While he was still within [the womb], they bound him with a cord.
It is for this reason that this *rājanya* is born already bound.
If this [sacrificer] were to be born unassailable and should move about slaying his enemies—
[if one should desire] of a Rājanya:
"May he be born unassailable and move about slaying his enemies"— for him one should offer this oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) dedicated to Indra and Bṛhaspati.
The Rājanya indeed belongs to Indra, and Bṛhaspati is the Brahman.
By means of the Brahman, he releases him from the bond and the fetter.
A golden bond is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Verily, he releases him directly from the bond and from the obstruction of water.
Ever new he becomes as he is born; the banner of the days, he goes at the forefront of the dawns. Coming, he distributes his portion to the gods; the moon extends long life.
That stalk which the Ādityas cause to swell, which the imperishable ones drink as the imperishable—by that may King Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati, and the guardians of the world cause us to swell.

(2.4.14.1.c) In the eastern quarter, O Indra, you are king; and in the northern, O slayer of Vṛtra, you are the slayer of Vṛtra. Where the rivers flow, there is your victory. Be a bull from the south, worthy of being invoked.

(2.4.14.2ḍ) May Indra conquer, may he not be conquered; may he rule as supreme king among kings. For let him be superior to all hostile armies, so that he may be one to whom men resort for help and who is worthy of worship.

(2.4.14.2.e) His greatness indeed exceeds that of heaven, earth, and the intermediate space. Self-ruling Indra, praised by all, the self-resplendent and mighty one, has grown strong for the battle within his own home.
(2.4.14.2.f) O Hero, we cry out to you like unmilked cows, to you who rule over this moving world, O Indra, who look upon the light of heaven, and who rule over all that stands still.
(2.4.14.3.g) For we poets indeed invoke you alone for the winning of booty; O Indra, lords of the good, men invoke you in battles against the Vṛtras, and you in the races of the steed.

(2.4.14.3) Even if there were a hundred heavens, O Indra, and a hundred earths, not even a thousand suns could equal you, O wielder of the thunderbolt; nor could the two worlds encompass you at your birth.
(2.4.14.3.i) Drink the Soma, O Indra; let that which the stone has pressed for you exhilarate you, like a well-guided steed urged by the arms of the presser.
(2.4.14.4.k) May there be for us, in the company of Indra, wealthy and abundant refreshments, through which we, possessing food, may rejoice.
(2.4.14.4ḷ) Upward, O Agni, [shine] thy pure [flames];
(2.4.14.4ṃ) [spread] with light; (2.4.14.4ṇ) Up, that Jātavedas!
(2.4.14.4.o) O divine Sūrya, seven bay horses carry you in your chariot—you whose hair is flame, O far-seeing one.
The brilliant face of the gods has risen, the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni. Sūrya has filled heaven, earth, and the mid-air; he is the soul of all that moves and stands.
May all the gods, who increase the cosmic order and hear our invocation according to the seasons, enjoy the appropriate milk.

(2.4.14.5ṛ) O All-Gods, hear this my invocation—you who are in the intermediate space, you who dwell in heaven, you whose tongue is Agni, or you who are worthy of sacrifice—having seated yourselves upon this sacred grass, rejoice!

(2.5.1.1) Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, was indeed the domestic priest of the gods and the sister’s son of the Asuras. He had three heads: one for drinking Soma, one for drinking Surā, and one for eating food.
He assigned the sacrificial portion to the gods openly, but to the Asuras secretly. For they assign the portion openly to everyone; the portion of him to whom they speak secretly is truly declared.
(2.5.1.1) Therefore Indra was afraid, thinking, "One such as this will surely overturn the kingdom.

(2.5.1.1–2) Taking his thunderbolt, he cut off his heads: that which was the soma-drinking became a *kapiñjala* partridge; that which was the liquor-drinking became a *kalaviṅka* sparrow; that which was the food-eating became a *tittiri* partridge.
(2.5.1.2) He took the guilt of Brahmin-slaughter (*brahmahatyā*) in his joined palms and bore it for a year. All beings reviled him, crying out, "O slayer of a Brahmin!"
He approached the Earth,
saying, "Accept a third part of this Brahman-murder.
She replied:
(2.5.1.2) "I choose a boon: I think I shall perish from this pit; may I not perish because of it.
(2.5.1.2) "Before a year passes," he said, "it shall grow back for you. Therefore, before a year has passed, what is dug out of the earth grows back again, for that was the boon she chose.

(2.5.1.3) A third part of the murder of a Brahmin she accepted; that became the self-made saline wasteland (*svakṛta iriṇa*). Therefore, one who has established the sacred fires and is devoted to faith should not sit upon a self-made saline wasteland, for that is the color of the murder of a Brahmin. He then approached the trees.
"Take a third part of this Brahman-murder," [they said].
They replied, "We shall choose a boon; we think we are about to perish from being cut down, so let us not perish because of that."
(2.5.1.4) "More shall arise from you than from what is cut off," he said; therefore, more trees arise from what is cut off, for that was their chosen boon.

(2.5.1.4) They accepted a third part of the Brahman-slaying; it became resinous sap. Therefore, one should not eat resinous sap, for it has the color of Brahman-slaying. Moreover, indeed, that which is red and exudes from where it is cut off—of that one may eat, but not of anything else at will. He approached the place of the women's assembly.

"Take back a third of this Brahman-murder," they said. They replied, "We choose a boon: let us obtain offspring at the proper time, and let us unite according to our desire until childbirth. Therefore, women obtain offspring at the proper time and unite according to their desire until childbirth, for that was the boon they chose.

(2.5.1.5) They accepted a third part of the guilt of murdering a Brahmin; she became a woman with soiled garments. Therefore, one should not converse with a woman with soiled garments, nor sit with her, nor eat her food, for she remains there having assumed the form of the guilt of murdering a Brahmin.
(2.5.1.6) Now, moreover, they say:

(2.5.1.6) Ointment is indeed the food of a woman; ointment alone should not be accepted [as a gift], though anything else may be accepted at will. The son born from one who has intercourse while wearing soiled clothes is "accursed" (*abhiśasta*); the son of one who has intercourse in the forest is a thief; the son of one who has intercourse with her face turned away is "shame-faced" and timid; the son of one who bathes is a water-demon (*māruka*); the son of one who anoints herself is skin-deficient; the son of one who scrapes herself is bald and leprous; the son of one who applies collyrium is one-eyed; the son of one who [cleans] her teeth...

A dark-toothed man runs away from her who cuts her nails; a man with deformed nails from her who pares them; a eunuch from her who spins thread; a hanger-on from her who makes a rope; one prone to madness from her who drinks from a leaf-cup; and a dwarf from her who drinks from a broken vessel. For three nights she should observe a vow, drinking either from her cupped hands or from an unbroken vessel, for the protection of her offspring.
(2.5.2.1) Tvaṣṭṛ, whose son had been slain, brought the Soma that excluded Indra. (2.5.2.1) Indra sought an invitation to it, but he did not invite him.
"You have killed my son! he cried. Having caused a disturbance in the sacrifice, he forcibly drank the Soma.
Of that [Soma], what remained over, Tvaṣṭṛ poured into the Āhavanīya fire.
(2.5.2.1) "Svāhā! O enemy of Indra, grow strong!
(2.5.2.1) Because he turned [him] back, that is the "vṛtra-ness" of Vṛtra.
(2.5.2.1) Because he spoke thus...
(2.5.2.1) "Svāhā! O enemy of Indra, grow!"—therefore, Indra became his enemy.
(2.5.2.2) As he was coming into being, he grew toward Agni and Soma;
he grew in every direction, increasing by the measure of an arrow's length at a time.
(2.5.2.2) He enclosed these worlds.
Because he enclosed these worlds, that is the "vṛtra-nature" (*vṛtratva*) of Vṛtra.
Therefore, Indra was afraid.
(2.5.2.2) He ran to Prajāpati, saying,
"An enemy has been born to me!
(2.5.2.2) Having infused the thunderbolt with [the essence of] semen, he gave it to him.
"Kill with this! With that [formula] he drew it near. Agni and Soma said:
"Do not strike us; we are within [your own] property."
"You two indeed belong to me," he said; "come to me. They sought their own portion, and he presented to them this cake for Agni and Soma on eleven potsherds at the full moon sacrifice.
The two of them said, "We are indeed bitten; we are not able to go. Then Indra produced from himself the two Śītarūvas.
(2.5.2.3) That is the birth of Cold and Roughness.
(2.5.2.3) He who thus knows the birth of Cold and Roughness—(2.5.2.4) Cold and Roughness do not strike him; he leads him away from those two.
From him, as he was yawning, Agni and Soma departed;
indeed, it was his out-breath and in-breath that left him.
For skill is the out-breath, and resolve is the in-breath.
Therefore, while yawning, he should say:
"May skill and insight be in me. Thus he places the out-breath and the in-breath within himself.
(2.5.2.4) He attains a full lifespan.
(2.5.2.4) Having driven away the Vṛtras from the deities, he offered the oblation for the slaying of Vṛtra at the full moon.
(2.5.2.4) They indeed slay him at the full moon; (2.5.2.5) they cause him to swell at the new moon.
(2.5.2.5) Therefore, the two *vārtraghnī* verses are recited at the full moon sacrifice, and the two *vṛdhanvatī* verses at the new moon sacrifice.
(2.5.2.5) Having completed that *vārtraghna* oblation and taken up the thunderbolt, he advanced once more.
Then Heaven and Earth spoke:
"Do not strike; we two have indeed taken refuge here," they said.
"Let us choose a boon," they both replied. "May I be established among the constellations," said that one (the moon); "May I be established among the stars," said this one (the sun).
Therefore, that [sacrifice] is prescribed by the stars, while this one is prescribed by the multicolored [earth].
He who thus knows the excellence (*vara*) of heaven and earth—the excellence approaches him;
impelled by these two very worlds, Indra slew Vṛtra.
(2.5.2.6) Those gods, having slain Vṛtra, said to Agni and Soma:
(2.5.2.6) "Carry our oblation!
(2.5.2.6) They both replied:
"Those two were indeed devoid of splendor; Vṛtra was their splendor," they said. They asked, "Who will go for this?"
(2.5.2.6) They said, "The cow! Indeed, the cow is the friend of all.
(2.5.2.7) She said: "I shall choose a boon: let me enjoy both [the milk] while remaining right here.
(2.5.2.7) Then the cow brought that about.
Therefore, they enjoy both [products] from the cow.
Indeed, clarified butter is the brilliance of Agni;
milk is that of Soma.
(2.5.2.7) He who thus knows the splendor of Agni and Soma becomes truly splendid. (2.5.2.7) The exponents of the Veda say:
"To which deity does the Full Moon sacrifice belong?"
"One should say it belongs to Prajāpati," he said. "By means of that, he caused his eldest son Indra to dwell apart.
Therefore, they cause the eldest son to dwell apart by means of wealth.

(2.5.3.1) When Indra had slain Vṛtra, the adversaries trembled against him. He beheld this offering to Vaimṛdha to be offered subsequently at the full moon; he offered it, and by means of it, he struck away the adversaries. In that there is an offering to Vaimṛdha to be offered subsequently at the full moon, the sacrificer strikes away the adversaries by means of it.

(2.5.3.1) Having slain Vṛtra, Indra was deprived of his divine powers and his vital energy (*indriya*). He beheld this cake on eight potsherds for Agni at the new moon, and curd for Indra. (2.5.3.2) He offered it; by that, indeed, he regained both the divine powers and his vital energy.
In that there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni at the new moon and curd for Indra, the sacrificer thereby regains both the divine powers and his vital energy.
When Indra had slain Vṛtra, his vital power and heroic strength (*indriya-vīrya*) spread across the earth; it became the herbs and the plants.
He ran to Prajāpati, saying:
"When I had slain Vṛtra, my vital power and heroic strength spread across the earth and became the herbs and the plants."

(2.5.3.3) The animals brought that [milk] from the plants into themselves; they milked it back again. That which they brought together is the reason for the *sāṃnāyya* being called *sāṃnāyya*; that which they milked back again is the reason for the *pratidhuk* being called *pratidhuk*.

(2.5.3.4) "They have brought it together and milked it back, but it does not settle within me," he said. "Prepare this for him so that it is cooked (*śṛta*)," he said. They prepared it for him so that it was cooked. Verily, power and vigor settled within him; that is the reason for the *śṛta* being called *śṛta*.

(2.5.3.4) "They have mixed [the curds] together; they have milked back; they have made it cooked," he said. "But this does not satisfy me," he said. "Make this for him into curds," he said. They made that for him into curds; that satisfied him. That is the essence of the curd (*dadhi*).

(2.5.3.4) The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "One should cut off a portion of the previous [substance], namely the curds. (2.5.3.5) Disregarding the fact that curds are indeed made first, one should rather cut off a portion of the cooked [milk] first. Having thus infused power and vigor into it, one satisfies it with curds from above. Thus one proceeds according to the proper sequence.

(2.5.3.5) That which one should curdle with *pūtīka* plants or with bark-shavings is for Soma; that which with *kvala* fruits is for the Rākṣasas; that which with rice-grains is for the Viśvedevas; that which by means of the curdling agent is for Manuṣa; and that which with curds is for Indra. He curdles it with curds for the sake of its being accompanied by Indra.
(2.5.3.6) He curdles it over the remains of the Agnihotra for the continuity of the sacrifice.

(2.5.3.6) Having slain Vṛtra, Indra went to the farthest distance, thinking, "I have committed a transgression. The deities sought him out. Prajāpati said, "Whosoever finds him first, his shall be the first portion. The ancestors found him; therefore, the rite is performed for the ancestors on the preceding day. (2.5.3.6) He returned on the new moon night (*amāvāsyā*). The gods gathered around him, saying, "Truly, he dwells (*vasati*) with us today as our wealth (*vasu*). For Indra is the wealth of the gods; that is the etymological basis for the name *amāvāsyā*.

(2.5.3.7) The exponents of the Veda ask: "To which deity does the *sāṃnāyya* belong? One should say, "It belongs to the Viśvedevas," for all the gods gathered there to receive their share. However, one should rather say, "It belongs to Indra," for they gathered there to heal Indra.
(2.5.4.1) The exponents of Brahman say:
"He indeed should perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices who performs them as accompanied by Indra.

At the Full Moon sacrifice, there is an additional offering of the Vaimṛdha cake; thereby the Full Moon sacrifice is accompanied by Indra. At the New Moon sacrifice, there is curds for Indra; thereby the New Moon sacrifice is accompanied by Indra. He who, knowing thus, performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices, performs them as truly accompanied by Indra. Day after day it becomes more prosperous for him who has sacrificed.
Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did likewise. Those gods saw this offering:

a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu, a pap for Sarasvatī, and a pap for Sarasvant. Having completed the Full Moon sacrifice, they offered these subsequently. Thereupon the gods prospered, and the Asuras were defeated.

(2.5.4.2) He who has rivals should, having completed the Full-moon sacrifice, perform this offering. By means of the Full-moon sacrifice itself, he hurls the thunderbolt at his rival; with the offering to Agni and Viṣṇu, he appropriates both the deities and the sacrifice of his rival.
(2.5.4.2) With the two offerings to Sarasvatī, he appropriates the paired cattle—whatever he possesses, all that he appropriates.
(2.5.4.3) One who has rivals should sacrifice only at the Full moon, not at the New moon; having struck down the rival at the Full moon, he does not let him swell again.
One who desires cattle should sacrifice with the *sākamprasthāyīya*.

For one to whom they bring only a small amount does not satisfy himself, nor does he give to another; but for one to whom they bring much, he satisfies himself and gives to another. It should be offered full with a large quantity. Thus Indra, being satisfied, satisfies him with offspring and cattle.
(2.5.4.3) He offers with a wooden vessel, for what is made of clay does not receive the oblation.
(2.5.4.4) It is made of Udumbara wood; the Udumbara is indeed strength (*ūrj*), and cattle are strength. By means of strength, he wins for himself strength and cattle.
(2.5.4.4) One who has not attained prosperity should sacrifice to Mahendra.

There are indeed three who have attained prosperity: the learned man, the village headman, and the nobleman; for them, Mahendra is the deity. He who sacrifices beyond his own deity falls away from his own deity, does not reach the higher one, and becomes worse off.
He should sacrifice to Indra for a year, for he does not overstep the vow for a year. Thus, his own deity, being sacrificed to, kindles him with prosperity, and he becomes more wealthy.
After a year has passed, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati.
By means of Agni Vratapati, he causes him who has slain Vrtra to regain his vow after a year;
thereafter, he may sacrifice according to his desire.
One who has not sacrificed with Soma should not perform the *saṃnayya* offering; for him who has not sacrificed with Soma, the milk is as if it has not yet arrived.
If one who has not sacrificed with Soma were to perform the *saṃnayya*, that would be mere plunder and he commits a falsehood;
moreover, it is poured away in vain.
(2.5.5.1) Only one who has performed the Soma sacrifice should perform the *sāṃnāyya* offering; for Soma is indeed milk, and the *sāṃnāyya* is milk. By means of milk, he places milk within himself.
(2.5.5.1) He causes him to be deprived of offspring and cattle, and he increases his rival’s prosperity, for whom the moon rises after the sacrificial oblation has already been set out.
(2.5.5.2) He should divide the rice grains into three portions.

(2.5.5.2) Those [grains] which are of medium size, from them he should prepare a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Dātṛ; (2.5.5.2) those which are the largest, from them a pap of curdled milk for Indra Pradātṛ;
(2.5.5.2) those which are the smallest, from them a pap of boiled milk for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.
Agni alone generates offspring for him; Indra bestows them when they have grown.
Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice, and Śipi is cattle; thus he establishes himself in the sacrifice through cattle.
One should not sacrifice twice.

If one were to sacrifice with the first [verse] at the present time, he would perform the *chambaṭ* (futile) rite with the second; if he were to sacrifice with the second at the present time, he would perform the *chambaṭ* rite with the first. In that case, there is neither the *iṣṭi* nor the sacrifice; consequently, one is born timid and lacking in confidence.
One should sacrifice with only one [verse]; thus, his son is born confident.
(2.5.5.3) Disregarding that, he should sacrifice with only two [offerings].

By the first, he seizes the very mouth of the sacrifice; by the second, he sacrifices. By the first, he wins the deities; by the second, he wins power (*indriya*). By the first, he conquers the world of the gods; by the second, the world of men.
(2.5.5.4) He approaches more numerous sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*).
(2.5.5.4) This sacrifice is indeed named Sumanas. For him who sacrifices today and the moon rises behind him, there will be prosperity for him in this very world.
(2.5.5.4) One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Dākṣāyaṇayajña.
He should perform the *saṃnayana* at the full moon and sacrifice with the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa at the new moon.
At the full moon, the Soma of the gods is pressed; for them, this half-month is the [period when it is] pressed forward.
For them, on the new moon day, there is a barren cow for Mitra and Varuṇa as the *anūbandhyā* sacrifice. When he sacrifices on the previous day, he thereby prepares the altar;
when he drives away the calves, he thereby erects the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds.
(2.5.5.5) In that he sacrifices, he brings the Soma-pressing into union with the gods; for half a month he drinks Soma in communal revelry with the gods.

(2.5.5.5) In that he sacrifices on the new moon day with the curdled milk offering (*āmikṣā*) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa, that very cow which is the barren *anūbandhyā* of the gods becomes his own.
(2.5.5.5) Truly, he who undertakes their sacrifice mounts directly upon the gods. (2.5.5.6) Just as one who has mounted higher desires according to his superior status, so does he act.

(2.5.5.6) If he pierces [the mark], he becomes worse off; if he does not pierce it, he remains equal [to his rival]. One who desires distinction should sacrifice with this sacrifice, for this sacrifice has a razor-edge; either he quickly becomes meritorious or he perishes. (2.5.5.6) His vow is this:
he shall not speak untruth, he shall not eat meat, he shall not approach a woman, and they shall not wash his garment with lye. For the gods do none of these things.
(2.5.6.1) The New and Full Moon sacrifices are indeed the chariot of the gods.
He who, having performed the New and Full Moon sacrifices, performs the Soma sacrifice, settles at the end of his journey upon the excellent seat of the gods, as if on a chariot already prepared.
These New and Full Moon sacrifices are indeed the joints and limbs of the year.
He who, knowing thus, performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices, restores the very limbs and joints of the year.
These two, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, are indeed the eyes of the year.
He who, knowing thus, performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices, beholds the world of heaven by means of those two.
(2.5.6.2) These two, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, are indeed the stride of the gods.
He who, knowing this, performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices, strides along after the very stride of the gods.
(2.5.6.2) These two, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, are indeed the path traveled by the gods.
He who, knowing thus, performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices, ascends that very path which leads to the gods.
These two, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, are indeed the two bay horses (*harī*) of the gods.
He who, knowing thus, performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices, by means of those very two bay horses of the gods, carries the oblation to them.
(2.5.6.3) The New and Full Moon sacrifices are indeed the mouth of the gods.
He who, knowing this, performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices, offers directly into the mouth of the gods.
He who performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices is indeed the possessor of the oblation-holder.
(2.5.6.3) He offers the Agnihotra in the evening and morning; he performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices; every day there is the pressed [Soma] for those who possess the Havirdhāna sheds.

(2.5.6.3) For one who, knowing thus, performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices with the thought, "I am the possessor of the Havirdhāna," everything belonging to the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) becomes given to him.
(2.5.6.4) The gods, indeed, did not find the day fit for sacrifice; they purified the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
(2.5.6.4) These two, indeed, are pure and fit for sacrifice, namely the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
He who, knowing this, performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices, performs them with these two as being truly pure and fit for sacrifice.
On the day of the new moon and on the day of the full moon, he should not approach a woman.
(2.5.6.4) If he were to approach her, he would become devoid of virility.
(2.5.6.4) The nights of the half-month were indeed the wives of King Soma;
of them, he did not approach either the new moon night or the full moon night.
(2.5.6.5) They both embraced him.
(2.5.6.5) Consumption seized him. (2.5.6.5) "Consumption has seized the king," they said; that is the origin of *rājayakṣma*.
That which was when he became more wretched, that belongs to Pāpayakṣman;
that which he obtained from his two wives, that belongs to Jāyenya.
He who thus knows the origin of these diseases—these diseases do not find him.
(2.5.6.5) He ran toward them, paying homage.
(2.5.6.5) They said:
(2.5.6.5) "Let us choose a boon: let us two be the portions of the gods."
(2.5.6.6) "The gods have been invoked for the sacrifice," so it is said.
Therefore, among similar nights, the gods are sacrificed to on both the new moon day and the full moon day;
for these two are the portions of the gods.
(2.5.6.6) Men become sharers with him who knows thus.
(2.5.6.6) Beings struck down hunger: humans immediately, the gods after half a month, the ancestors after a month, and the trees after a year.
Therefore, day by day humans desire food; every half-month the gods are sacrificed to; every month offerings are made for the ancestors; and every year the trees bear fruit.
He who knows thus destroys his rival, hunger.
(2.5.7.1) The gods, indeed, did not find support in the Ṛc nor in the Yajus;
they found support in the Sāman alone.
He utters "hiṃ"; he thereby produced the Sāman itself.
He utters *hiṃ*; from that very place where the gods took refuge, he thus impels them forward.
He utters *hiṃ*; this is the harnessing of speech itself. He utters *hiṃ*; thereby the sacrificer creates offspring.

He recites the first verse three times and the last verse three times; this is indeed the binding of the sacrificial stake, to prevent it from slipping. He recites them continuously for the continuity of the vital breaths and of food.
(2.5.7.2) Moreover, for the sake of driving away the Rākṣasas,
he recites the first verse addressed to the Rathantara;
for this world is indeed related to the Rathantara.
He conquers this very world;
he draws [the water] three times,
for these worlds are three.
He conquers these very worlds.
He recites the final verse in the Bṛhatī meter; for that world above is indeed of the Bṛhatī nature.
He conquers that very world.
He recites the unexpressed verse addressed to Prajāpati, beginning with "pra vaḥ vājāḥ.
Prajāpati is indeed the sacrifice.
(2.5.7.3) He indeed takes hold of the sacrifice, Prajāpati.
(2.5.7.3) He recites, "Forward, O strengths!
(2.5.7.3) Strength (*vāja*) is indeed food.
Verily, he wins food.
He recites the verse, "Forward, O strengths," and therefore seed is deposited facing the east.
"O Agni, come for the feast," he says;
therefore offspring are born facing backward.
"Forward, O strengths!"—thus he recites after [the first verse].
The *vāja*s are indeed the months; the *abhidyava*s are the half-months. "The gods rich in oblation, the cow dripping with ghee—the sacrifice goes to the gods, the sacrificer seeking favor.
By saying, "This art thou! This art thou! he wins the beloved abode of the sacrifice.
Whomever he may desire—

Thinking, "May he attain a full lifespan," one should recite *pra vo vājāḥ*; then, immediately following that, one should take hold of the second half-verse of *agna ā yāhi vītaye*, which is the subsequent [verse] of the *saṃtata* (connected) sequence.
(2.5.7.5) By means of the out-breath (*prāṇa*), he indeed sustains the in-breath (*apāna*); he attains a full lifespan.
(2.5.7.5) Whosoever knows the "cubit" (*aratni*) of the *sāmidhenī* verses, he makes his rival a mere cubit away.
He joins together two half-verses.
(2.5.7.5) This, indeed, is the cubit of the *sāmidhenī* verses.
He who knows thus makes his rival [as small as] a cubit.
These *sāmidhenīs* were indeed fashioned by each and every seer.
If they were unconnected, they would drift apart from the progeny and cattle of the sacrificer.
He joins two half-verses together;
thus he truly connects them.
These, being joined and secured for him, milk out every blessing.
(2.5.8.1) That which is without the *sāman* is indeed no sacrifice. "O Agni, come for the feast," he says; this is the color of the *rathaṃtara*.
"Thee, O Aṅgiras, with fuel-sticks," he says; this is the color of the *vāmadevya*.
(2.5.8.1) "Great, O Agni, is thy heroic power," he says; for this is the color of the Great One. In that he recites this triplet, he thereby makes the sacrifice possessed of the *sāman*.
Agni was in yonder world, and Āditya was in this one.
These two worlds were then unpeaceful.
The gods said,
"Let us transpose these two."
With the verse, "O Agni, come for the feast," they established Agni in this world; with the verse, "Great is Agni’s heroic power," they established Āditya in yonder world.
From that, these two worlds became tranquil.
In that he recites thus, it is for the pacification of these two worlds.
These two worlds become tranquil for him who knows thus. He recites fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses;
there are indeed fifteen nights in a half-month.
The year is obtained by half-months;
there are three hundred and sixty syllables of those [verses],
and there are as many nights in the year.
(2.5.8.3) Thus, syllable by syllable, he attains the year.
(2.5.8.3) Nṛmedha and Parucchepa engaged in a theological debate, saying:
"Let us both produce fire within this moist piece of wood; whichever of us two is more learned in the Veda shall win."
Nṛmedha spoke; he generated smoke.
Parucchepa spoke; he generated fire.
"O Seer," he said, "since we both know the same thing, how is it that you have generated fire and not I?"
"I know the color of the *sāmidhenī* verses," he said.
"That which is recited as a verse containing the word 'clarified butter' (*ghṛta*) is their color.
When he says, "Thee, O Aṅgiras, with fuel-sticks," he thereby generates light within the *sāmidhenī* verses themselves.
(2.5.8.4) Therefore the *ṛc*s are female; therefore the *gāyatrī* meters are female; therefore the *sāmidhenī* verses are female.
(2.5.8.5) He recites [the verse] containing the word "bull" (*vṛṣan*); thereby they become male, thereby they possess Indra, and thereby they become a pair.
Agni was the messenger of the gods, and Uśanas Kāvya was the messenger of the Asuras.
(2.5.8.5) Those two went to Prajāpati with a question.
(2.5.8.5) That Prajāpati turned toward [the mantra] "We choose Agni as our messenger," and then the gods prospered while the Asuras were defeated.
For one who, knowing thus, recites, "We choose Agni as our messenger," he prospers in himself and his rival is defeated.
He recites the verse containing the word *adhvara*;
by this very verse, he strikes down his rival.
"O you with flaming hair, we implore him," he says; this is indeed a means of purification. By this [verse], he purifies the sacrificer.
"Kindled, O Agni, with an oblation," he says;
by this he indeed lays around this enclosing-stick so that nothing may be spilled.
If he were to place [fuel] beyond this point, it would be just as if something were to spill outside the enclosing-sticks.
(2.5.8.6) There are indeed three fires: Havyavāhana, the carrier of oblations for the gods; Kavyavāhana, the carrier of offerings for the ancestors; and Saharakṣas, belonging to the Asuras.
(2.5.8.6) They now vie with one another, each thinking, "He will choose me! He will choose me! (2.5.8.7) Thus it is said.
"Choose the bearer of oblations," he says;
thus he chooses him who belongs to the gods. He chooses one who is of a seer's lineage.
(2.5.8.7) It does not depart from the kinsman;
(2.5.8.7) moreover, it is for the sake of continuity that he chooses [the fires] from the further side toward himself.
Therefore, from beyond, the ancestors descend after the humans.
"O Agni, you are great," he says, for this Agni is indeed great.
"O Brahmin," he says, for he is indeed a Brahmin. "O Bhārata," he says, for he bears the oblation to the gods.
"Kindled by the gods," he says, for the gods indeed kindled him.
"Kindled by Manu," he says, for Manu, who is higher than the gods, indeed kindled him. "Praised by the seers," he says, for the seers indeed praised him.
"Rejoiced by the sages," he says; for those who have heard [the sacred tradition] are indeed sages.
"Praised by the seers," he says; for those who have heard [the sacred tradition] are indeed seers.
"Sharpened by the *brahman*," he says; for this [sacrifice] is indeed sharpened by the *brahman*.
"O you for whom the oblation is clarified butter," he says, for the oblation of clarified butter is indeed his most beloved.
"The leader of sacrifices," he says, for he is indeed the leader of sacrifices. "The charioteer of rites," he says, for he is the divine chariot.
"An invincible Hotṛ," he says, for no one whatsoever overcomes him. "The swift carrier of oblations," he says,
for he crosses over everything.
(2.5.9.3) “The vessel of the gods is the offering-spoon,” he says, for this is indeed the offering-spoon of the gods.
(2.5.9.3) “The cup is the drink of the gods,” he says, for this is indeed the cup from which the gods drink.
(2.5.9.3) “Like spokes, O Agni, you are the felly surrounding the gods,” he says, for this indeed surrounds the gods.

If he were to say, "Bring the gods for the god-loving sacrificer," he would produce a rival for him. He says, "Bring the gods for the sacrificer"; by this, he causes the sacrificer himself to prosper.
(2.5.9.4) "O Agni, bring hither Agni; bring hither Soma," he says; thus he invokes the deities in their proper order.
(2.5.9.4) "And, O Agni Jātavedas, bring the gods hither and sacrifice with a good sacrifice," he says;
thereby he sharpens Agni himself.
(2.5.9.4) "Thus sharpened, he carries the oblation to the gods;
(2.5.9.4) Agni is the Hotṛ," he says.
For Agni indeed is the Hotṛ of the gods.
(2.5.9.5) He chooses him who is the Hotṛ of the gods.
(2.5.9.5) "We are [here]," he says; thus he causes himself to attain existence.
(2.5.9.5) "O sacrificer, the deity is well-disposed toward you," he says; thus he invokes this very blessing.
If he were to say,
"He who has chosen Agni as the Hotṛ," one would enclose the sacrificer on both sides with fire, and he would be liable to die.
The *juhū* ladle has the sacrificer as its deity, while the *upabhṛt* ladle has the rival as its deity.
(2.5.9.6) If he were to speak as if there were two [verses], he would produce a rival for him.
(2.5.9.6) "O Adhvaryu, bring forward the ladle full of ghee," he says; by this, he causes the sacrificer himself to prosper.
(2.5.9.6) "Favoring the gods," he says, for she indeed favors the gods.
"O you who possess all boons," he says, for she protects everything.
"We shall praise the gods worthy of praise; we shall bow before those worthy of praise—the fathers worthy of praise, the gods worthy of sacrifice.
Thus he sacrifices to the deities according to their respective portions.
(2.5.10.1) One should recite three triplets for a Rājanya;
for there are three other types of men besides the Rājanya—the Brāhmaṇa, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra—and he thus makes them subject to him. One should recite fifteen [verses] for a Rājanya.
The Rājanya is indeed connected with the fifteenfold hymn-form; thus he establishes him in his own stomas.
He should conclude [the rite] with a Triṣṭubh verse.
The *triṣṭubh* is indeed power (*indriya*). Now, the Rājanya sacrifices desiring power;
by means of the *triṣṭubh*, he secures power for him.
(2.5.10.1) If he should desire, "May there be spiritual luster," he should enclose [the fire] with a *gāyatrī* verse.
(2.5.10.2) The *gāyatrī* is indeed spiritual luster; thus, he comes to possess spiritual luster.
One should recite seventeen verses for a Vaiśya;
the Vaiśya is indeed seventeenfold;
thus he establishes him in his own Stoma.
One should enclose it with a *jagatī* verse;
for cattle are indeed connected to the *jagatī*,
and the Vaiśya who sacrifices is indeed one who desires cattle.
By means of the Jagatī metre, he secures cattle for him.
He should recite twenty-one verses for one who desires a firm foundation;
the Ekaviṃśa is the foundation of the Stomas.
For the sake of stability. One should recite twenty-four verses for one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*);
the *gāyatrī* consists of twenty-four syllables, and the *gāyatrī* is spiritual luster.
By means of the *gāyatrī* itself, he wins for him spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
He should recite thirty [verses] for one who desires food;
the *virāj* consists of thirty syllables.
Food is the *virāj*;
by means of the *virāj*, he wins for himself the eating of food. He should recite thirty-two [verses] for one who desires a firm foundation.
The *anuṣṭubh* consists of thirty-two syllables;
the *anuṣṭubh* is the foundation of the meters,
for the sake of firm establishment.
One should recite thirty-six verses for one who desires cattle;
the *bṛhatī* consists of thirty-six syllables, and cattle are associated with the *bṛhatī*.
(2.5.10.3) By means of the *bṛhatī* meter, he wins cattle for him.
(2.5.10.4) He should recite forty-four verses for one who desires sensory power;
the *triṣṭubh* consists of forty-four syllables.
The *indriya* is the *triṣṭubh*; by means of the *triṣṭubh*, he secures *indriya* for him.
He should recite forty-eight [verses] for one who desires cattle.
The Jagatī has forty-eight syllables;
cattle are connected with the Jagatī. By means of the Jagatī, he wins cattle for him.
(2.5.10.4) One should recite all the meters for one who performs many sacrifices.
(2.5.10.4) Indeed, all the meters are won by him who performs many sacrifices.
(2.5.10.4) He should recite an unlimited number.
For the attainment of the immeasurable.
(2.5.11.1) The *nivīta* is for humans; (2.5.11.1) the *prācīnāvīta* is for the ancestors;
(2.5.11.1) the *upavīta* is for the gods.
He approaches;
verily, he thereby makes it the mark of the gods;
standing, he recites after [the verses].
For standing, one speaks more audibly; standing, one recites after [the response];
this is for the conquest of the heavenly world.
(2.5.11.1) He sacrifices while seated;
(2.5.11.1) thus he finds firm support in this very world.
(2.5.11.1) That which he recites in the *krauñca* manner belongs to the Asuras.
That which is low is human;
that which is between is divine;
it should be recited between the two.
(2.5.11.1) For the sake of being with the gods.
(2.5.11.2) In ancient times, the *hotṛ* priests were indeed knowers;
therefore, the paths became separated, and the ways did not converge.
One foot is within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*), the other is outside the altar (*bahirvedi*).
Then he recites:
"For the separation of roads, for the non-overlapping of paths."
Moreover, he wins both the past and the future;
moreover, he wins both the limited and the unlimited;
moreover, he wins both domestic animals and wild animals.
(2.5.11.2) Moreover, he conquers both the world of the gods and the world of men.
(2.5.11.3) Having recited the *sāmidhenī* verses, the gods did not perceive the sacrifice.
Prajāpati then poured the *āghāra* libation silently.
(2.5.11.3) Thereupon the gods indeed beheld the sacrifice.
In that he pours the silent *āghāra* libation, it is for the illumination of the sacrifice;
furthermore, he thereby anoints the *sāmidhenī* verses themselves.
He who knows this becomes free from harshness;
moreover, he truly satisfies them. He who knows this is satisfied with offspring and cattle.
If he were to pour with one [verse], he would gratify only one;
if with two, he would gratify two;
if with three, he would cause that [sacrifice] to overflow.
(2.5.11.4) He pours with the mind, for by the mind that which is unattained is attained.
(2.5.11.4) He pours across transversely, so as not to cause a failure.
Speech and mind would have suffered injury.
"I shall carry the oblation to the gods," Speech said; "I [shall carry it] to the gods," Mind said.
The two of them went to Prajāpati with this question. Prajāpati said:
(2.5.11.5) "You are indeed the female messenger of the mind, for whatever one conceives with the mind, that one speaks with speech.
(2.5.11.5) He said, "Indeed, you should not offer to her with speech. Therefore, they offer to Prajāpati with the mind.
For Prajāpati is like the mind;
he wipes the enclosing-sticks together for the attainment of Prajāpati.
He indeed purifies them.
He sprinkles three times on the middle [part]; for there are three vital breaths. He conquers these very worlds.
He sprinkles three times on the northern part; for there are three paths leading to the gods; he conquers those very paths.
He urges [the horse] three times; there are indeed three worlds of the gods; verily, he conquers the worlds of the gods.
They amount to twelve; the year has twelve months;
verily, he gratifies the year.
(2.5.11.6) Moreover, he bestows the year upon him for the attainment of the heavenly world. (2.5.11.6) He pours the libation.
(2.5.11.6) The world of heaven is, as it were, across. (2.5.11.7) Verily, he makes the world of heaven shine forth for him.
He pours [the ghee] straight; for the breath is, as it were, straight.
He pours [the ghee] continuously for the continuity of the vital breaths and of food;
furthermore, it is for the smiting away of the Rākṣasas.
Regarding whomsoever he may desire—
(2.5.11.7) "He would be liable to die," [thinking thus], one should pour [the liquid] crookedly for him;
(2.5.11.7) verily, one leads his breath away crookedly; (2.5.11.7) he dies quickly.
The *āghāra* libation is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the *dhruvā* spoon is its body. Having poured the *āghāra*, he anoints the *dhruvā*.
Thus, he restores the head to the very body of the sacrifice.
Agni was the messenger of the gods, while the divine one was the messenger of the Asuras.
(2.5.11.8) Those two went to Prajāpati with a question.
(2.5.11.8) That Prajāpati said to a Brāhmaṇa: (2.5.11.8) "Explain this to them."
When he causes the announcement to be made with the words, "O gods, hear this," he has indeed said, "Agni, the god, is the Hotṛ. He chose him who is the Hotṛ of the gods;
thereafter the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
(2.5.11.9) For one who knows thus, when they choose him as the *pravara*, he prospers in himself and his rival is defeated.
(2.5.11.9) If a Brahmin and a non-Brahmin should come to a dispute, one should speak in favor of the Brahmin;
for if one speaks in favor of the Brahmin, one speaks in favor of oneself.
In that he rejects the Brāhmaṇa, he rejects his own self;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa must not be rejected.
(2.5.12.1.a) May there be life for you.
(2.5.12.1.b) O Agni, giver of life. (2.5.12.1.c) Swell up.
(2.5.12.1ḍ) May [the waters] unite with thee.
(2.5.12.1.e) Away from us thy wrath.
(2.5.12.1.f) Upward the highest [knot].
(2.5.12.1.g) May the Goddess [Sarasvatī] come forward for us. (2.5.12.1.h) From heaven may she come to us.
(2.5.12.1.i) O Agni and Viṣṇu!
(2.5.12.1.k) O Agni and Viṣṇu;
(2.5.12.1ḷ) hear this my [call], O Varuṇa; (2.5.12.1ṃ) for that I entreat you.

(2.5.12.1ṇ) Upward that one; (2.5.12.1.o) the brilliant one. (2.5.12.1.p) For the Son of the Waters has mounted the lap of the prostrate ones, standing erect and clothed in lightning. Carrying his supreme majesty, the swift, golden-hued rivers flow around him.
Some flow together, others approach; the rivers fill the common ocean. To him, the pure and shining Son of the Waters, the pure waters have gathered all around.

The smiling young women, the waters, go around him, the youth, as they cleanse themselves; that Agni, with his bright and skillful [flame], has shone forth richly—unfed by wood, clothed in ghee, within the waters.
I choose for myself the protection of Indra and Varuṇa, the sovereign kings; may they be gracious to us in such a state.

(2.5.12.2ṭ) O Indra and Varuṇa, grant great protection to our sacrifice, to our people, and to our subjects! May we conquer in battles the evil-minded ones who seek to overcome us, even those who persist in long-enmity.
(2.5.12.3.u) O Mitra and Varuṇa, come to us! (2.5.12.3.v) Stretch forth your arms!

(2.5.12.3.w) O Agni, you who are wise, may you ward off from us the offense against the god Varuṇa; being the best of sacrificers, the most excellent bearer of oblations, and blazing brightly, release us from all hostilities.

(2.5.12.3.x) As such, O Agni, be our protector; be our closest friend at the breaking of this dawn. Appease Varuṇa for us, being gracious; grant us mercy; be easy for us to invoke. (2.5.12.4.y) This Agni of Bharata is far-famed, he who shines forth with great light like the sun. He who has stood against the Pūru in battles, the divine guest, has shone auspiciously for us.

(2.5.12.4.z) I sacrifice for you; I send forth this prayer to you, so that you may become worthy of our praise in our invocations. O Agni, ancient King, you are like a watering-place in the desert for the Pūru who desires to worship.
With your brilliance, with your light— O Agni, you who shine among the wide dwellings, burn against the sorceresses with your countenance.

May we, the ignorant, serve him who is fair of face, beautiful to behold, swift-moving, and more wise than the wise. May he, Agni, knowing all ways, perform the sacrifice and proclaim our oblation among the immortals.
(2.5.12.5.ee) To the one who releases from distress;
(2.5.12.5.ff) when he has entered me; (2.5.12.5.gg) O Indra, may you unbind for us.
(2.5.12.5ḥh) O Indra, the dominion; (2.5.12.5.ī) the powers of sense, O Śatakratu; (2.5.12.5.kk) it has been granted to you accordingly.
(2.6.1.1) He offers to the *samidhs*; verily he wins the spring among the seasons. (2.6.1.1) He offers to *tanūnapāt*; verily he wins the summer.
(2.6.1.1) He offers to the *iḍas*; verily he wins the rainy season.
(2.6.1.1) He offers to *barhis*; verily he wins the autumn.

(2.6.1.1) He offers with the exclamation *svāhā*; verily he wins the winter; therefore, in winter, animals settle down when the *svāhā* has been uttered. (2.6.1.1) He offers to the *samidhs*; verily he wins the deities of the dawn.
He sacrifices to Tanūnapāt; verily, he wins the sacrifice itself.
(2.6.1.2) He offers the *iḍā*; verily he wins cattle. (2.6.1.2) He offers the *barhis*; verily he wins progeny.
He pours together [the butter] from the *upabhṛt* [ladle].
Clarified butter is indeed splendor, and the sacrificial grass is offspring; verily, he bestows splendor upon offspring.
He offers with the utterance of "Svāhā."
Verily, he wins speech;
they amount to ten;
the *virāj* consists of ten syllables.
By means of the Virāj [verse], he wins food.
He offers the *samidh* oblations; verily, he finds firm footing in this very world.
He offers the *tanūnapāt* oblation.
(2.6.1.3) In the sacrifice itself he finds firm footing in the intermediate space;

(2.6.1.3) he offers the *iḍā* oblation and thereby finds firm footing among the cattle; (2.6.1.3) he offers the *barhis* grass and thereby finds firm footing upon those very paths that lead to the gods.
He offers with the *svāhā*-utterance; verily, he finds firm support in the world of heaven.
So many indeed are the worlds of the gods; in them he finds support according to their respective order.
The gods and the Asuras contended for these worlds.
(2.6.1.3) Those gods drove the Asuras away from these worlds by means of the *prayāja* offerings.
(2.6.1.4) That is the reason for the name of the *prayājas*.
For one who knows this and for whom the *prayājas* are performed, he drives his rivals away from these worlds.
(2.6.1.4) He offers while stepping forward;
(2.6.1.4) for the sake of victory.
(2.6.1.4) Verily, he who knows the pairing of the *prayāja* offerings is procreated with offspring, cattle, and pairs.
(2.6.1.4) He offers many kindling-sticks (*samidh*) as it were,
and Tanūnapāt as it were as one; that constitutes a pair.
(2.6.1.4) He offers many *iḍas*, as it were, and the *barhis* as one; that is a pairing.
This indeed is the pairing of the *prayājas*.
(2.6.1.4) He who knows thus is procreated with offspring, cattle, and pairs.
(2.6.1.5) Of old, the deities were not sacrificed to;
then the Asuras sought to destroy the sacrifice.
(2.6.1.5) Those gods split apart the *gāyatrī*.
Five syllables were directed forward and three were directed backward.
From that, it became armor for the sacrifice and armor for the sacrificer.

(2.6.1.5) When the *prayāja* and *anūyāja* offerings are performed, a coat of mail is thereby made for the sacrifice and a coat of mail for the sacrificer, for the sake of overcoming his rival. (2.6.1.5) Therefore, a protective enclosure is broader in front and narrower behind.
(2.6.1.6) The gods, indeed, perceived that the sacrifice was to be completed with the utterance of *svāhā* during the *prayāja* offerings so as to protect it from the *rakṣases*.
(2.6.1.6) They established it with the *svāhā* utterance during the *prayāja* offerings.
(2.6.1.6) "They indeed cut the sacrifice asunder when they conclude it with the *svāhā* utterance during the *prayāja* offerings.
Having performed the *prayāja* offerings, he pours clarified butter over the oblations for the continuity of the sacrifice.
(2.6.1.6) Now, he has indeed made the oblation; (2.6.1.6) now, he approaches in the proper order. The fore-offerings are indeed the father, and the after-offerings are the offspring.
(2.6.1.6) When, having performed the *prayāja* offerings, he sprinkles the sacrificial oblations with clarified butter, he thereby makes it common to both father and son.
(2.6.1.7) Therefore they say: "Whether one knows this or not, how can it be said that [the offering] belongs exclusively to the son, while [this] belongs in common to the father?"
That which spills when the fore-offerings have been offered is indeed not spilled;
by that, the Gāyatrī conceives a fetus,
and she brings forth offspring and cattle for the sacrificer.
(2.6.2.1) These two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) are indeed the eyes of the sacrifice.
In that he offers the two butter-portions, he thereby restores the eyes of the sacrifice. He offers in the eastern half.
Therefore, he offers the two eyes in the front part; he offers them side by side,
therefore the two eyes are side by side.
(2.6.2.1) By means of the fire, the sacrificer beholds the world of the gods; by means of the soma, the world of the fathers.
(2.6.2.1) He offers to Agni on the northern half [of the altar] and to Soma on the southern half.
(2.6.2.1) For these two worlds are thus [arranged]; it is for the sake of manifesting these two worlds.
(2.6.2.1) These two are indeed the kings among the deities.
(2.6.2.2) As for Agni and Soma: (2.6.2.2) these two deities are sacrificed to between [the other] deities for the sake of the separation of the deities;
therefore, by the king, men are held apart.
(2.6.2.2) The exponents of the Veda say:
"What does the sacrificer perform at the sacrifice by which he supports both the animals with teeth on one side and those with teeth on both sides?
Having recited the *ṛc* verse, he offers the *ājyabhāga* oblation with the word *juṣāṇa*; by this, he supports the animals with teeth on one side.
(2.6.2.2) Having recited a verse, he offers the oblation with a verse; thereby he supports [the sacrifice] on both sides.
The invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākyā*) contains the word "head" (*mūrdhan*); verily, he makes him the head of his equals.
(2.6.2.3) He sacrifices with the *niyutvatī* verse; he thus draws away the cattle of his rival.
Keśin Sātyakāmi said to Keśin Dārbhya:

"Tomorrow at your sacrifice, you shall employ for me the seven-footed *śakvarī* verse, by whose power one drives away born rivals and holds back those yet to be born; by whose power one establishes light in both worlds; and by whose power the ox enjoys the front half [of the offering] and the cow the hind half."
The *puro’nuvākyā* has its mark at the beginning; verily, he drives away his rivals who have already been born. The *yājyā* has its mark at the end; verily, he repels those who are yet to be born.
The *puro’nuvākyā* has its mark at the beginning; verily, he bestows light upon this very world.
The *yājyā* has its mark above; he thereby places light in that world.
Both these worlds become luminous for him who knows thus.
The *puro’nuvākyā* has its mark in front; therefore, the ox draws with the fore-part of his body.
The offering verse (*yājyā*) has its mark above; therefore, the cow is [milked] from the hind part.
He who knows thus—these two consume him.
The clarified butter (*ājya*) is a thunderbolt, the two *ājyabhāga* portions are thunderbolts, and the *vaṣaṭ*-call is a thunderbolt.
(2.6.2.5) Having prepared the threefold thunderbolt, he hurls it at his rival so that it does not miss its mark.
(2.6.2.5) Having brandished it, he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call for the sake of striking him down.
The *puro’nuvākyā* is a *gāyatrī*, and the *yājyā* is a *triṣṭubh*.
(2.6.2.5) He causes the ruling power (*kṣatra*) to take hold of the sacred word (*brahman*);
therefore, the Brāhmaṇa is the preeminent one.
He who knows thus becomes preeminent.
(2.6.2.5) He indeed impels him with the invitatory verse (puro’nuvākyā), leads him forward with the offering verse (yājyā), and causes him to go with the vaṣaṭ-call.
(2.6.2.5) He gives him over with the *puro'nuvākyā*;
(2.6.2.5) he hands him over with the *yājyā*;
(2.6.2.5–6) with the *vaṣaṭ*-call, he establishes him.
(2.6.2.6) The invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākyā*) consists of three feet;
(2.6.2.6) these worlds are three;
(2.6.2.6) verily, he finds firm support in these very worlds.
The *yājyā* consists of four feet;
verily, he wins four-footed cattle.
The *vaṣaṭ*-call has two syllables, and the sacrificer has two feet; verily, he finds firm support among the cattle at the end.
(2.6.2.6) The *puro'nuvākyā* is in the *gāyatrī* metre, and the *yājyā* is in the *triṣṭubh* metre.
(2.6.2.6) This indeed is the seven-footed *śakvarī*; whatever the gods sought to accomplish by means of this, they were able to accomplish.
He who knows thus is indeed able to accomplish whatever he learns.

(2.6.3.1) Prajāpati assigned the sacrifices to the gods; he placed the clarified butter within himself. The gods said to him, "This indeed is the sacrifice, namely the clarified butter; let there also be a share for us here. He replied, "I shall sacrifice for you; [therefore] you shall spread the under-layer and pour the [butter] over it. Therefore, they sacrifice with the two portions of clarified butter, spreading the under-layer and pouring [the butter] over it.

(2.6.3.1) The exponents of Brahman say: "On what basis is it that other oblations become stale (*yātayāma*), while clarified butter (*ājya*) remains unfading (*ayātayāma*)? (2.6.3.2) He should reply: "Because Prajāpati is unfading for the gods."

(2.6.3.2) The meters departed from the gods, saying, "We will not carry your oblation unless we receive a share. For them, they established this fourfold portion: for the invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākyā*), for the offering verse (*yājyā*), for the deity, and for the *vaṣaṭ*-call. In that he offers the fourfold portion, he thereby gratifies the meters; these meters, being gratified, carry his oblation to the gods.

(2.6.3.2) The Aṅgirases, indeed, were the first to go from here to the heavenly world. Then the seers came to the sacrificial site. They saw a sacrificial cake that had become a tortoise crawling about. They said to it, "Stand firm for Indra! Stand firm for Bṛhaspati! Stand firm for the All-gods! It did not stand firm. They said to it, "Stand firm for Agni! It stood firm for Agni. That the cake for Agni is never absent on the new-moon and full-moon days is for the conquest of the heavenly world.

(2.6.3.3) They said to him, "How did you remain? He replied, "I was anointed without being smeared," just as an axle is anointed without being smeared. (2.6.3.4) "It reaches down"—saying this, he smears [the butter] from above and anoints from below for the attainment of the heavenly world.
He spreads over all the potsherds; by that many sacrificial cakes he conquers in yonder world.

That which is burnt belongs to Nirṛti, that which is uncooked belongs to Rudra, and that which is cooked belongs to the gods. Therefore, one should cook it without burning it, for the sake of its belonging to the gods.

(2.6.3.4) He covers it with ashes; therefore the bone is covered by flesh. He covers it with the Veda-grass-bundle; therefore (2.6.3.5) the head is covered with hair. That oblation which has been cooked but not yet sprinkled [with ghee] has indeed departed from this world but has not yet reached the world of the gods. By sprinkling it and then covering it, he causes it to go to the gods.

(2.6.3.5) If one potsherd should be lost, one month of the year would remain unattained, and then the sacrificer might perish; if two should be lost, two months of the year would remain unattained, and then the sacrificer might perish. He sets them out after counting them, for the protection of the sacrificer. (2.6.3.6) If [a potsherd] should be lost, he should offer a cake on two potsherds to the Aśvins and a cake on one potsherd to Heaven and Earth. The Aśvins are indeed the physicians among the gods; through them, he provides medicine for him.
There is a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth; for whatever is lost is lost to these two, and he finds it again from these two alone, for the sake of stability.
(2.6.4.1) "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," with these words he takes up the wooden sword (sphyá), for the sake of impulsion.
"With the arms of the Aśvins," he says, for the Aśvins were the two Adhvaryu priests among the gods. "With the hands of Pūṣan," he says, for the sake of restraint.
(2.6.4.1) "Thou art hundred-edged, made of wood, the slayer of the hater," he says; verily, he thus sharpens the thunderbolt as he is about to strike his rival.
He carries away the *stambayajus*; for as great as this earth is, so great is the altar; from just that much of it, he excludes the rival.
Therefore, they do not allot a share to Nābhāga.
He takes [the portions] three times; these worlds are three; verily, from these worlds he excludes him.
He takes a fourth time silently; verily, from the unlimited he excludes him.
He digs up; he thereby drives away whatever in it is impure.
He digs up, therefore plants spring forth.
He cuts the root; he thus cuts the root of his rival.
(2.6.4.2) He digs it to the depth prescribed for the ancestors and the gods, commensurate with Prajāpati and the mouth of the sacrifice.
(2.6.4.3) He digs it as far as its foundation; verily, he causes the sacrificer to reach a firm foundation.
He makes it higher on the south; thus he has produced the form of the sacrificial ground.
He makes it possessed of loose soil (*purīṣavat*). Loose soil is indeed offspring and cattle; verily, he makes him possessed of offspring and cattle by means of loose soil.
He performs the second tracing of the altar. As great as this earth is—namely, as great as the altar—he thereby excludes his rival from just so much of it and performs the second tracing for himself.
For he does something harsh indeed when he prepares the altar.

(2.6.4.4) "Thou art *dhā*, thou art *svadhā*," with these words he polishes it for the sake of pacification. He sets down the sprinkling waters; for water is indeed a slayer of demons, [used] for the striking away of the *rakṣases*.
He sets them down in the track of the wooden sword (*sphya*) for the continuity of the sacrifice.
Whomever he may hate, let him meditate upon that person; verily, he strikes him with affliction.
(2.6.5.1) The exponents of Brahman say: "With water you sprinkled the oblations; with what [did you sprinkle] the waters? One should reply: "With the *brahman*."
(2.6.5.1) For it is with water that he sprinkles the oblations, and the waters are by means of the sacred word (*brahman*).
(2.6.5.1) He sprinkles the fuel and the sacrificial grass; verily, he thereby makes them pure for sacrifice.
(2.6.5.1) He sprinkles the altar.
(2.6.5.1) For this altar is indeed toothless, hairless, and impure;
he thus makes it pure.
(2.6.5.1) Having placed the sacrificial grass with the words, "For heaven thee! For the intermediate space thee! For earth thee!", he sprinkles it.
(2.6.5.2) Thus he sprinkles it for these very worlds. Indeed, he does something harsh when he digs.
He pours down water for the sake of pacification.
He takes the *prastara* from the front; he thereby makes it the principal one.
He takes it to this extent, commensurate with Prajāpati, the mouth of the sacrifice.
(2.6.5.2) He spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
(2.6.5.2) The sacrificial grass is indeed offspring; the altar is the earth.
Thus, he establishes offspring upon the earth.
He spreads [the grass] so that it is not too visible;
verily, by means of progeny and cattle, he makes him not too visible.
