(2.6.5.3) He places the *prastara* bundle to the north of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
(2.6.5.3) The *barhis* represents offspring, and the *prastara* represents the sacrificer.
(2.6.5.3) Thus, he makes the sacrificer superior to the non-sacrificer.
Therefore the sacrificer is superior to the non-sacrificer. He places [the offering] between for the sake of distinction.
He anoints it; verily he causes this oblation-maker to go to the world of heaven.
He anoints it three times.
(2.6.5.3) These are the three worlds.
(2.6.5.3) He thus anoints him for these very worlds;
he does not cause him to shrink back.
If he were to strike it down, the sacrificer would not attain a higher state;
therefore, he strikes it as if upward.
For the world of heaven is, as it were, above;
he restrains it;
verily, he bestows rain upon him.
(2.6.5.4) One should not throw [the grass] too far forward.
For if one were to throw it too far forward, the Adhvaryu’s wife would be prone to excessive wandering and would be liable to perish. (2.6.5.4) Nor should one cast it back toward the front.
If he were to throw it back toward the east, he would push the sacrificer away from the heavenly world. He throws it forward;
thus he causes the sacrificer himself to go to the heavenly world.
One should not separate [the fires] in different directions.
If one were to separate them in different directions, a female child would be born to him.
He separates them upwards.
For from a man, indeed, a man is born upwards;

if he should smooth [the ground] with either the wooden sword (*sphya*) or the fire-stirring stick (*upaveṣa*), that would be his destruction. He smoothes it with his hand for the protection of the sacrificer.
(2.6.5.5) The exponents of sacred knowledge say: "What is the sacrificer of the sacrifice?
"The *prastara* [grass-bundle]," they reply.
"Where is his world of heaven? "One should say: 'In the Āhavanīya fire.
For when he throws the *prastara* grass-bundle into the Āhavanīya, he causes the sacrificer himself to go to the world of heaven."
(2.6.5.6) Verily, the sacrificer is torn asunder when they smooth out the *prastara* [grass-bundle].
He throws the *barhis* after it for the sake of pacification.
At this time, the *adhvaryu* is, as it were, without support.
(2.6.5.6) He is liable to tremble.
(2.6.5.6) He touches this [earth] with the words, "Thou art firm.
(2.6.5.6) For this [earth] is indeed firm.
He finds firm support in this very [earth]; he does not tremble.
"The Agnīdh has come," he says.
If he were to say, "Agni has gone," he would cause Agni to go into the fire and would exclude the sacrificer from the world of heaven.
He should simply say, "He has gone"; thus he causes the sacrificer himself to go to the world of heaven.
(2.6.6.1) Agni had three elder brothers. While carrying the oblation to the gods, they perished.
(2.6.6.1) Agni was afraid, thinking, "In this very way, he too will meet with ruin.
He hid himself; he entered the waters. The deities sought him out.
The fish told him this; he cursed it, saying, "May they slay you with every thought who have revealed me! Therefore, people slay the fish with every thought, for it was cursed.
They found him; they said to him, "Turn toward us; carry our oblation."

He said, "I shall choose a boon: whatever of that which has been taken up but not yet offered should fall outside the enclosing-sticks, let that be the share of my brothers. Therefore, whatever of that which has been taken up but not yet offered falls outside the enclosing-sticks, that is their share; he gratifies them with that.
He lays down the enclosing-sticks for the smiting away of the Rākṣasas.
He makes them touch one another so that the Rākṣasas cannot pass between them.
(2.6.6.3) He does not place [the enclosing sticks] in front, for the sun, rising in the east, drives away the demons from the front.
(2.6.6.3) He places two fuel-sticks upright; thus he drives away the demons from above.
(2.6.6.3) One with a sacrificial formula and the other silently, for the sake of pairing.
He places two [bricks]; the sacrificer has two feet, for the sake of stability. The exponents of sacred knowledge say:
"Only he should sacrifice who would desire to prosper despite the failure of his sacrifice."
(2.6.6.3) "To the Lord of the Earth, Svāhā! To the Lord of the World, Svāhā! To the Lord of Beings, Svāhā!"—with these words he should consecrate what has been spilled.
(2.6.6.4) Through that very distress of the sacrifice, the sacrificer becomes more prosperous, for he gratifies many deities.
(2.6.6.4) Indeed, a repetition is committed in the sacrifice when two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are offered one after the other.
He performs the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice between [the two offerings] to avoid sameness and also for the sake of pairing.
Agni was in yonder world, and Yama was in this one.
Those gods said, "Let us transpose these two."
(2.6.6.4) With food the gods invited Agni; with sovereignty the fathers invited Yama. Therefore Agni is the eater of food among the gods, and Yama is the king of the fathers.
(2.6.6.5) He who knows thus attains sovereignty and the eating of food. To him they gave this as his portion: that which they cut off for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
(2.6.6.5) When he cuts off a portion for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, he thereby gratifies Rudra with his own share. He cuts off only once; for Rudra is, as it were, single.
He cuts off from the northern half; for this is the quarter of Rudra. Thus, he expiates for Rudra in his own quarter.
(2.6.6.6) He pours [the butter] over it twice for the attainment of the fourfold portion.
(2.6.6.6) The former oblations are indeed cattle;
this Agni is Rudra.
If he were to offer over the previous oblations, he would deliver the cattle to Rudra;
the sacrificer would be left without cattle.
He offers passing over the previous oblations for the protection of the cattle.
(2.6.7.1) Manu sought what was worthy of sacrifice on the earth.
(2.6.7.1) He found ghee that had been poured out.
(2.6.7.1) "Who is the lord over this [cow] even for the performer of the sacrifice?
(2.6.7.1) They both replied, "Mitra and Varuṇa; we two are indeed the lords over the cow for the performer. (2.6.7.1) "It belongs to us," they said.
(2.6.7.1) From there, the two of them caused the cow to move forward.
(2.6.7.1) Wherever she set her foot down, from that place clarified butter was pressed out;
therefore, she is called *ghṛtapadī*.
(2.6.7.1) That is his birth.
(2.6.7.1) "The Rathantara has been invoked together with the earth," he says.
"This [earth] indeed is the Rathantara;
he thus invokes this very earth together with food.
'The Vāmadevya has been invoked together with the intermediate space,' he says."
The Vāmadevya is indeed cattle;
verily, he invokes cattle together with the intermediate space.
"Invoked is the Bṛhat together with heaven," he says.
The Bṛhat is indeed *irā* (refreshment).
He thus invokes *irā* together with heaven.
"The cow has been invoked together with the bull," he says.
He invokes the pair itself.
"The food has been invoked; O friend! he says; thus he invokes the drinking of Soma itself.
"Upahūtā3ṁ ho! he says. He thus invokes himself;
for the self is the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*) among those who have been invoked.
(2.6.7.3) He invokes the *iḍā*.
(2.6.7.3) The *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
verily, he invokes cattle.
He invokes four times,
for cattle are four-footed. "Mānavī," he says, for Manu first saw her.
"O thou whose foot is dripping with ghee," he says; because ghee was squeezed from her foot, therefore he speaks thus.
"Belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa," he says; for Mitra and Varuṇa set her in motion.
"The prayer made by the gods is invited," he says.
He invokes the Brahman itself.
He says, "The divine Adhvaryus are invoked; the human [Adhvaryus] are invoked. Thus he invokes both gods and men.
"Those who have protected this sacrifice and those who shall increase the lord of the sacrifice," he says.
He pronounces a blessing for both the sacrifice and the sacrificer.
"Heaven and Earth are invoked," he says;
thus he invokes Heaven and Earth themselves.
"Born of old, observers of the cosmic order," he says, for these two are indeed born of old and are observers of the cosmic order.
"The goddesses, mothers of the gods," he says, for these two are indeed goddesses and mothers of the gods.
"This sacrificer is invited," he says.
He invokes the sacrificer himself:

"Invoked to the subsequent sacrifice to the gods; invoked to the greater preparation of the oblation; invoked to the celestial abode. He says this because the subsequent sacrifice to the gods is indeed offspring, the greater preparation of the oblation is cattle, and the celestial abode is the world of heaven.
"This art thou, this art thou"—thus he invokes the dear abode of the sacrifice.
"All that is dear to him has been invoked," he says;
thus he invokes without failure.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle; he takes it for himself by his own will, for no one else bestows the desired portion of cattle upon him.
"I eat thee, offered to Vācaspati," he says; verily, he gratifies Speech with its own share. "I eat thee, offered to Sadasaspati," he says, for the sake of making it *svagā*.
It consists of four portions; the oblation (*havis*) is fourfold, and cattle are fourfold.

(2.6.8.1) If the Hotṛ were to eat it himself, he would meet with ruin. (2.6.8.2) If he were to offer it into the fire, he would deliver the cattle to Rudra, and the sacrificer would become destitute of cattle.
(2.6.8.2) He says, "I eat thee, offered to Vācaspati"; thus he offers it out of sight. (2.6.8.2) He says, "I eat thee, offered to Sadasaspati," for the sake of making it *svagā*.
They eat at the proper place; they eat at the very ford. He gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); he gives the sacrificial fee at the very ford.
(2.6.8.2) They indeed tear asunder this sacrifice when they eat from the middle and purify themselves with water. Water is all the deities; verily, by means of the deities, they extend the sacrifice.
(2.6.8.3) The gods excluded Rudra from the sacrifice. He pierced the sacrifice. The gods gathered around it, saying, "May this of ours be made fit!
They said, "This shall indeed be well-sacrificed for us if we gratify him. That is the origin of the name *sviṣṭakṛt* ("well-sacrificing") of the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering.

(2.6.8.3) Its [the sacrificial post's] unperforated part is the *niṣka*. (2.6.8.4) They cut it to the measure of a barleycorn; therefore, one should cut off [the portion] the size of a barleycorn. If one were to cut off more than that, he would cause the sacrifice to fester. If one were both to spread [the butter] underneath and pour [it] over, he would make it swell on both sides. (2.6.8.4) Having cut off [the portion], he pours [butter] over it; thus it becomes twofold, for the sacrificer is two-footed, for the sake of stability.
If he were to carry it across transversely, he would pierce the unpierced [part] of the sacrifice.
He carries it around by the front; he carries it around by the very path [of the officiants].
When they carried it around for Pūṣan, (2.6.8.4) Pūṣan, having eaten it, knocked out his teeth. Therefore Pūṣan has ground food as his portion, for he is toothless.
The gods said to him: (2.6.8.5) [“Why have you done this?”]
"This man has indeed failed; he has become unworthy of the *prāśitra*," they said.
They then offered it to Bṛhaspati.
Bṛhaspati was afraid, thinking, "In this very way, he will surely bring ruin upon me."

(2.6.8.5) He saw this mantra and said, "I behold you with the eye of Sūrya. For nothing harms the eye of Sūrya. (2.6.8.6) He was afraid, thinking, "It might harm me as I receive it. He said, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I receive you. Thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he received it with the sacred word (*brahman*) and with the deities.
He was afraid, thinking, "It will injure me as I eat.
He said, "I eat thee with the mouth of Agni," for nothing injures anything within the mouth of Agni. He was still afraid, thinking, "It will injure me once it has been eaten."
"By the belly of the Brāhmaṇa," he said, "for nothing injures the belly of a Brāhmaṇa; by the sacred knowledge (*brahman*) of Bṛhaspati, for he is the most perfect in sacred knowledge.
Indeed, the vital breaths depart from him who eats the *prāśitra* portion. Having cleansed himself with water, he touches his vital breaths.
The vital breaths are indeed immortality, and the waters are immortality; he thus invokes the vital breaths back to their respective places.
He places [the kindling-stick] in the *agnīdh*’s fire; verily he gratifies the seasons, whose mouth is Agni.
He places a kindling-stick on the fire for the support of the subsequent oblations; moreover, he offers in a manner accompanied by fuel.
He wipes the enclosing-sticks; verily he purifies them. He wipes each one once, for at this stage the sacrifice is, as it were, turned away.

It becomes fourfold; cattle are four-footed; verily he wins cattle. "O Brahman, we shall set forth," he says; for at this moment the sacrifice is supported here where the Brahman is. From wherever the sacrifice is supported, from there he takes hold of it. If he were to support it with his hand, he would become trembling; if with his head, he would suffer a headache; if he were to remain silent, the sacrifice would be uncompleted.
"Establish it," he should say;
for the sacrifice is indeed supported by speech. From wherever the sacrifice is supported, from there he hands it over.
"O God Savitṛ, this we have proclaimed to you," he says for the sake of impulsion.
"Bṛhaspati is the Brahman," he says, for he is the most proficient in sacred knowledge (*brahmiṣṭha*). "Protect the sacrifice, protect the lord of the sacrifice, protect me," he says;
thus he invokes a blessing for the sacrifice, for the sacrificer, and for himself, so that there may be no misfortune.
Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Sacrifice to the gods.
Those who discourse on the Brahman say: "The deities have been sacrificed to; now, who are these gods? One should reply: "The meters—the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Jagatī."
Moreover, they indeed say:
"The *brāhmaṇas* are the meters";
it is them that he thus sacrifices to.
(2.6.9.4) The deities of the gods had already been sacrificed to, yet Agni did not blaze up. The gods found him through the *anūyāja* offerings.
(2.6.9.4) In that he performs the *anūyāja* offerings, he thereby kindles Agni himself.
There was indeed an Asura named Etadu.
He appropriated for himself the blessing of the sacrifice at this point.
If one were to say, "O Heaven and Earth, it has become auspicious," he would cause that very Asura Etadu to obtain the blessing of the sacrifice.
(2.6.9.5) “This has become auspicious for heaven and earth,” he should say; thus he causes the sacrificer to attain the blessing of the sacrifice.
(2.6.9.5) “We have attained the *sūktavāka* and the *namovāka*,” he says; by this he means, “We have succeeded.
(2.6.9.5) “I have resorted to heaven and earth,” he says, for the sacrifice is indeed supported upon heaven and earth.
"O Sacrificer, may Heaven and Earth be full of protection for you at this sacrifice," he says; thus he invokes this very blessing.
If he were to say, "May they be easy to settle upon and pleasant to dwell in," the sacrificer would be likely to die;
for when one dies, he then settles down upon this earth.
"One should say, 'easy of access and good for dwelling upon'; thus one prays for him a wider pasture, and he does not become liable to die prematurely.
(2.6.9.6) "Regarding those two, [the Hotṛ] says: 'Agni has accepted this oblation with knowledge. By this he means: 'Those deities whom we have sacrificed to, may we satisfy them.
If he were not to specify [them], the blessing of the sacrifice would go to a neighbor. (2.6.9.7)
"He invokes for this sacrificer, so-and-so," he says; by thus pointing him out, he causes him to go to the heavenly world.
"He invokes long life; he invokes abundance of offspring," he says; he thus invokes this very blessing.
"He invokes companionship with his kinsmen," he says; the kinsmen are indeed the vital breaths; verily, he does not exclude the vital breaths.
(2.6.9.8) “Then Agni, the god, wins for the gods; we [win] from Agni, O men,” he says. This indeed means: “Agni wins for the gods; we [win] from men.

(2.6.9.8) “Here is the attainment of what is desirable, and this homage to the gods,” he says. Thus he pays homage to both those deities whom he sacrifices to and those whom he does not, for his own safety.
(2.6.10.1) The gods, indeed, could not find anyone to perform the *svagā* for the sacrifice.
They said to Śamyu Bārhaspatya,
"Make this sacrifice of ours *svagā*."
He said, "I shall choose a boon: let that which belongs to me be the blessing of the sacrifice when one who is not addressed by a Brāhmaṇa and lacks faith performs a sacrifice.
Therefore, when one who is not addressed by a Brāhmaṇa and lacks faith performs a sacrifice, the blessing of the sacrifice goes only to Śamyu Bārhaspatya.
"This is mine," he said. "What shall I do with my offspring? [The other replied:
"He who threatens you, let him be punished with a hundred;
he who strikes you down, let him be punished with a thousand."
(2.6.10.2) "Whoever sheds blood shall not recognize the world of the ancestors for as many years as the number of grains of dust he gathers after the spilling.
(2.6.10.2) Therefore, one should not strike a Brāhmaṇa, nor should one kill him, nor should one cause him to bleed;
for by doing so, one incurs such sin.
"May we choose that which is auspicious," he says; thereby he makes the sacrifice itself go to its own place. "May we choose that which is auspicious," he says.
(2.6.10.3) He causes Śamyu Bārhaspatya himself to prosper with his own portion.
(2.6.10.3) "A way for the sacrifice, a way for the lord of the sacrifice," he says;
thus he invokes this very blessing.
He sacrifices to Soma; verily, he thereby bestows seed. He sacrifices to Tvaṣṭṛ; verily, Tvaṣṭṛ fashions forms for the seed that has been bestowed.
He sacrifices to the wives of the gods; this is for the sake of pairing.
He sacrifices to Agni Gṛhapati for the sake of stability;
for a repetition of the sacrifice is thereby committed.
(2.6.10.4) Since the *prayāja* offerings are performed with clarified butter and the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings [are likewise] with clarified butter,
he recites a verse for the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings and sacrifices with a verse; this is to avoid sameness and also to establish a pairing.
The sacrifice indeed begins with the *paṅkti* and ends with the *paṅkti*. Five *prayāja* offerings are performed;
there are four *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, and the *samiṣṭayajus* is the fifth.
Verily, they follow the *paṅkti* [meter]; they go along with the *paṅkti*.
(2.6.11.1.a) Harness, O Agni, like a charioteer, your steeds that best invoke the gods; sit down as the ancient Hotṛ-priest.
And so, O God, as one who knows best, speak for us to the gods; grant us full confidence in all desirable things.
For you, O youngest one, son of strength, when invoked with oblations, have become the observer of cosmic order (*ṛta*) and worthy of sacrifice.
This Agni is the lord of thousandfold and hundredfold strength; he is the sage, the head of riches.
(2.6.11.1.e) Bow down to him with joint invocations, as the *Ṛbhus* bend the felly; O *Aṅgiras*, come closer to the sacrifice! (2.6.11.2)
(2.6.11.2.f) Therefore, O Virūpa, now urge forth with an eternal voice a beautiful hymn of praise for that bull who shines toward heaven.
(2.6.11.2.g) With the host of this Agni, who looks back upon us, whom indeed shall we strike down as a Paṇi among the cattle?
(2.6.11.2) O cows, may the clans of the gods not abandon us, as if they were dappled mares plunging into water; may they not leave us emaciated, O inviolable ones.
May no calamity from any malevolent hater strike us down, as a wave strikes a ship.
(2.6.11.2.k) O God Agni, the people sing homage to you for your might; with your weapons, crush the enemy.
(2.6.11.3ḷ) Will you not, O Agni, truly bestow wealth upon us for the quest for cattle? O maker of wide space, make wide space for us!
(2.6.11.3ṃ) Do not abandon us in this great contest for wealth, like one who carries a burden; win the gathered prize, win the riches!
(2.6.11.3ṇ) May this distress, O Agni, pursue another than us out of fear; increase our impetuous might.
Whose reverent act or sacrifice the [gods] have accepted, him indeed Agni will favor with growth.
From the higher enclosure, cross over toward the lower ones; protect those where I am.
(2.6.11.4.q) For we have known you of old, O Agni, as one who provides aid like a father; therefore, we now seek your favor.
(2.6.11.4.ṛ) Like a fierce archer, or like a bull with sharpened horns, O Agni, you have shattered the fortresses.
O friends, bring together for Agni—a prayer and a hymn of praise—that is directed toward you, for him who is the highest of the dwellings, the offspring of vigor, the possessor of power.
(2.6.11.4ṭ) O bull Agni, you gather together all the wealth of the noble foe; you are kindled at the place of libation; as such, bring us riches.
(2.6.11.4.u) O Prajāpati! (2.6.11.4.v) He knows! (2.6.11.4.w) O Soma and Pūṣan!
(2.6.11.4.x) These two gods.
(2.6.12.1.a) Desiring you, we invoke you; desiring you, we kindle you. Desiring them, bring the desiring Fathers here to eat the oblation.
(2.6.12.1.b) O Soma, you are preeminent in wisdom; you lead us along the straightest path. Under your guidance, O Indu, our wise fathers obtained their share of treasure among the gods.

(2.6.12.1.c) For by you, O Soma, our ancient fathers performed their sacred rites, O Pavamāna, they who were wise. Winning [the prize], unassailed, open up the enclosures; become a bountiful lord for us with heroes and horses! (2.6.12.2) [Be so] for us!
O Soma, you, in harmony with the Fathers, have extended yourself across heaven and earth. To you, O Indu, we pay worship with this oblation; may we be masters of riches.

(2.6.12.2.e) O Agniṣvātta fathers, come hither; sit each upon his seat, O excellent leaders. Eat the oblations presented upon the sacrificial grass, and then bestow upon us wealth consisting of all heroic sons.

(2.6.12.2.f) O Fathers who sit upon the sacrificial grass, come hither with your aid; we have prepared these offerings for you—enjoy them! Come to us with most auspicious protection, and then bestow upon us well-being, health, and freedom from harm. (2.6.12.3) O Fathers who sit upon the sacrificial grass, come hither with your aid; we have prepared these offerings for you—enjoy them! Come to us with most auspicious protection, and then bestow upon us well-being, health, and freedom from harm.

(2.6.12.3.g) I have found the benevolent fathers, and the descendant, and the wide stride of Viṣṇu. Those who sit upon the sacrificial grass and partake of the pressed food with their own portion—may they come most readily here.
(2.6.12.3) Invited are the Soma-loving Fathers to their dear offerings upon the sacrificial grass; may they come hither, may they listen here, may they speak for us, and may they protect us.

(2.6.12.3.i) May the lower, the higher, and the middle ancestors, who are worthy of Soma, arise! Those who have gone to the life-breath (*asu*), who are harmless and knowers of the *ṛta*—may those ancestors protect us in our invocations.

(2.6.12.4.k) Let this homage be offered today to the fathers—those who departed in former times and those who went later; those who have settled in the earthly realm, or those who are now among the well-fortified clans.
And so, O Agni, as our ancient fathers of old, aspiring toward *ṛta*, went toward pure vision while reciting hymns; cleaving the earth, they disclosed the ruddy dawns.

(2.6.12.4) When you, O Agni, carrier of the *kavya*, shall sacrifice to the ancestors who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*), you shall carry forth the oblations both to the gods and to the ancestors. (2.6.12.5) When you, O Agni, carrier of the *kavya*, shall sacrifice to the ancestors who increase the cosmic order, you shall carry forth the oblations both to the gods and to the ancestors.

(2.6.12.5ṇ) O Agni Jātavedas, you who have been praised, having made the oblations fragrant, you have carried them away; you have given them to the ancestors, and they have eaten them with the *svadhā* call. O God, eat these presented offerings yourself.

Mātali is magnified by the Kavyas, Yama by the Aṅgirases, and Bṛhaspati by the Ṛkvans; those whom the gods have magnified and those who [magnify] the gods—some rejoice with the cry of *svāhā*, others with the cry of *svadhā*.
(2.6.12.6.p) Come, O Yama, sit upon this sacrificial grass, in harmony with the Aṅgiras fathers; let the mantras recited by the seers bring you here; O King, rejoice in this oblation.

Come with the Angirases, the ones worthy of sacrifice; O Yama, rejoice here with the Vairūpas! I invoke Vivasvat, who is your father, that he may sit down upon the sacrificial grass at this sacrifice.

The Aṅgirases are our fathers, the Navagvas, the Atharvans, and the Bhṛgus, who are worthy of Soma; may we abide in the good-will of those worthy of sacrifice, and likewise in their auspicious benevolence.
(3.1.1.1) Prajāpati desired, "May I create offspring.
(3.1.1.1) He performed austerity; he created serpents. (3.1.1.1) He desired, "May I create offspring."
(3.1.1.1) He heated himself a second time; he created birds. (3.1.1.1) He desired, "May I create offspring.
(3.1.1.1) He heated himself a third time; he saw this speech of the consecrated one (*dīkṣitavāda*); he spoke it, and from that indeed he created offspring.
(3.1.1.1) When, having performed austerity, he utters the words of the consecrated (*dīkṣita*), the sacrificer thereby creates offspring.
(3.1.1.2) For if one who is consecrated sees anything impure, the consecration departs from him; his luster becomes dark and fades away.
"Unbound is my mind, poor is my sight; the Sun is the best of lights. O Consecration, do not abandon me!"
Thus he says:
"The consecration does not depart from him; neither his dark-blue nor his tawny [complexion] fades away.
For when rain falls upon one who is consecrated, the divine waters—being unappeased—strike down his vigor, strength, consecration, and ascetic fervor.
"O flowing waters, bestow strength; bestow vigor; bestow strength! Do not destroy my consecration, do not destroy my ascetic heat!"—thus he says.
In this very way, he places all of this within himself.
(3.1.1.3) His vigor, strength, consecration, and ascetic fervor are not destroyed.

(3.1.1.3) Agni is indeed the deity of the consecrated one; he [Agni] now stands apart from him when he goes forth. At that time, the Rakṣases are capable of striking him down. (3.1.1.4) "From good, go toward what is better; let Bṛhaspati be your forerunner," he says. Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman among the gods; he [the sacrificer] takes hold of him, and he carries him safely across.
"We have come to this place of sacrifice on earth," he says;
for he who sacrifices comes to a place of sacrifice on earth.

"All the gods who of old took pleasure [in it]," he says; for all the gods take pleasure in this when the Brahmins cross over by means of the *Ṛc*, the *Sāman*, and the *Yajus*. "They crossed over with the *Ṛc*, the *Sāman*, and the *Yajus*," he says.

"For he who sacrifices crosses over by means of the *ṛc*, the *sāman*, and the *yajus*. "May we rejoice together with the increase of wealth and with nourishment," he says; thus he invokes this very blessing.
(3.1.2.1) "Tell Soma for me: 'This is your Gāyatra portion. (3.1.2.1) Tell Soma for me: 'This is your Triṣṭubh and Jāgata portion.
(3.1.2.1) Tell Soma for me: 'Go to the sovereignty of the Chandomas.'"

(3.1.2.1) Verily, he who purchases King Soma after having caused him to go to the world of sovereignty attains the sovereignty of his own people; for the meters are indeed the world of sovereignty of King Soma. (3.1.2.1) Before the purchase of Soma, one should address him thus: (3.1.2.2) "Having caused him to go to this very world of sovereignty, he purchases him; he attains the sovereignty of his own people."
(3.1.2.2) He who knows the foundation of the *tānūnaptra* indeed stands firm. (3.1.2.2) The exponents of the Veda say:
"They do not consume it, nor do they offer it as an oblation; where, then, does the *tānūnaptra* find its foundation? One should reply: "In Prajāpati, in the mind."
(3.1.2.2) He should smell [it] three times, saying:
(3.1.2.2) "I offer you into Prajāpati, into the mind.
This indeed is the foundation of the *tānūnaptra* rite; he who knows thus stands firm.
(3.1.2.2) Or, O Adhvaryu, he who knows the firm foundation of the Adhvaryu stands firmly established.
(3.1.2.3) From whatever place he may think, "I shall offer without stepping forward," standing there, he should cause the announcement to be made.
This indeed is the firm foundation of the Adhvaryu; he who knows thus stands firmly established.
(3.1.2.3) If he were to offer while stepping forward, he would depart from his firm foundation; therefore, the offering should be made by one standing in the same place, for the sake of stability.

(3.1.2.3) Whoever knows the property of the Adhvaryu becomes possessed of property. The *sruk* is his property, the *vāyavya* cup is his property, (3.1.2.4) the *camasa* ladle is his property. If he were to call for the *āśrāvaṇa* without grasping either the *vāyavya* or the *camasa*, he would depart from his property; therefore, he should call for the *āśrāvaṇa* while grasping [the vessel], so that he does not depart from his own property.

(3.1.2.4) Verily, he who begins the chant (*stotra*) without having established the *soma* becomes unestablished; the *soma* becomes unestablished, the hymn (*stoma*) becomes unestablished, the recitations (*ukthāni*) become unestablished, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) becomes unestablished, and the Adhvaryu priest becomes unestablished. The wind (*vāyu*) is indeed the support of the *soma*; the cup (*camasa*) is its support; the *soma* is the support of the hymn; and the hymn is the support of the recitations. Having either drawn a cup (*graha*) or filled the cup, one should begin the chant.

(3.1.2.4) He establishes the Soma for himself; he establishes the Stomas for himself; he establishes the Ukthas for himself; the sacrificer stands firm for himself, and the Adhvaryu stands firm for himself.
(3.1.3.1) Indeed, they gather together the sacrifice when [they take] the footprint of the Soma-purchase cow.
(3.1.3.1) The mouth of the sacrifice is the two Havirdhāna sheds.
(3.1.3.1) When they move the two Havirdhāna sheds forward, then he should smear that axle with it.
(3.1.3.1) He thus extends the sacrifice along the very mouth of the sacrifice.

(3.1.3.1) They carry the fire forward; they lead the wife upward; they move the carts after them. (3.1.3.1) Now, this hearth-altar (*dhiṣṇiya*) of his is left behind; it broods over him, and becoming Rudra, it is capable of destroying the progeny and cattle of the sacrificer. (3.1.3.2) [Therefore, one should perform the *anvāhāryapacana* rite.]
(3.1.3.2) When they lead the consecrated animal northward, he should then take away its fire for cooking the meat; by that very act, he makes it a sharer in the sacrifice.
(3.1.3.2) The Āhavanīya fire is indeed the sacrificer.
(3.1.3.2) Verily, when they carry the fire for cooking the animal from the Āhavanīya, they tear the sacrificer asunder.
(3.1.3.2) That [fire] itself should be used, or he should produce fire by friction, for the sake of the sacrificer’s integrity.
(3.1.3.2) If a portion of the animal should be lost, he should cut off a substitute from the clarified butter;
that indeed is the expiation for it.
(3.1.3.2) If those who would tear apart the sacrificial animal should be someone whom [the sacrificer] desires, thinking,
"May they meet with misfortune," he should offer an oblation in the Āgnīdhra fire with the verse containing the word "namovṛkti" and beginning with "kuvid aṅga.
He thereby appropriates their very act of humiliation (*namovṛkti*), and they immediately meet with misfortune.
To Prajāpati, announce these offspring being born and those already born; may he, the wise one, grant his approval.

(3.1.4.1.b) O Lord of Cattle, O Agni, I bind this animal for you today in the midst of the well-performed rite. Grant your approval; let us sacrifice with a successful offering. May this oblation be pleasing to the gods.

(3.1.4.1.c) Perceiving him, the ancestors receive the vital breath as it moves away from the limbs. Go to heaven by the paths traveled by the gods; establish yourself among the plants with your bodily parts.

(3.1.4.1ḍ) Of whom Paśupati is the lord—of the four-footed beasts and also of the two-footed—may this [victim], being redeemed, go to its sacrificial portion; may there be increases of wealth for the sacrificer.
(3.1.4.2.e) Those who, being bound, looked upon the one being bound with their mind and their eye—may the god Agni release them first, Prajāpati, in harmony with his offspring.

(3.1.4.2.f) Those wild animals which are multiform, though being diverse in shape, yet are of one form in many ways—may the god Vāyu release them first, together with Prajāpati, in harmony with progeny.

(3.1.4.2.g) Releasing the seed of the world, O gods, grant a path for the sacrificer. What has been brought near and offered by the one who toils, let that which is living go unto the domain of the gods. (3.1.4.3) Releasing the seed of the world, O gods, grant a path for the sacrificer. What has been brought near and offered by the one who toils, let that which is living go unto the domain of the gods.

(3.1.4.3) May the breath of the sacrificer be distinct from that of the animal; may the sacrifice, traveling by the path of the gods, go together with the gods. May the living soul of the gods reach their domain; may the desires of the sacrificer come true.
If the animal has uttered a cry or has struck its chest with its feet, may Agni release me from that sin and from all distress.
(3.1.4.3.k) O immolators, approach the sacrifice, which has been invited by the gods! Release the animal from the noose, and the lord of the sacrifice from his bond.
(3.1.4.4ḷ) May Aditi release this bond. I offer homage to the cattle and to the Lord of Cattle. I cast down the one who acts as an enemy; upon him whom we hate, I fasten the bond.

(3.1.4.4ṃ) Thee indeed they have established as the bearer of oblations, the preparer of the cooked offering, and the one worthy of sacrifice. O Agni, having become truly capable and possessed of true body, do thou, O Jātavedas, graciously accept the offerings.
O Jātavedas, go to the gods with the omentum, for you have become the first Hotṛ. Increase their bodies with clarified butter; may the gods eat the oblation consecrated with Svāhā.
Svāhā to the gods; to the gods, svāhā!
(3.1.5.1) Animals indeed belong to Prajāpati; Rudra is their overlord.
(3.1.5.1) In that he dedicates them with these two [verses], he sacrifices them after having announced it to those two, so that there may be no injury to himself.
(3.1.5.1) He dedicates them with two [verses].
The sacrificer has two feet for the sake of stability;
having performed the introductory rite, he offers five oblations.
(3.1.5.1) Cattle are fivefold;
(3.1.5.1) verily he wins cattle. (3.1.5.1) That which is an animal is led forth unto death.
If he were to touch it, the sacrificer would be liable to die.
"The breath of the sacrificer [is] separate from that of the animal," he says, for the sake of distinction.
He offers with the words, "Since the animal has uttered a cry," for the sake of pacification. He says, "O immolators,
come hither!"— this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula.
When the omentum is being brought forward, the essence of Agni departs.
He offers an oblation over the omentum with the verse, "Thee indeed they have established as the bearer of oblations.
Thus, he secures the very essence of Agni for himself.

(3.1.5.2) Moreover, for the sake of cooking [the omentum], he offers on both sides of the omentum with the formula, "Svāhā to the gods! Svāhā to the gods!"—for some gods have their *svāhā*-utterances first, while others have their *svāhā*-utterances later.
(3.1.5.2) He offers on both sides of the omentum with the words, "Svāhā to the gods! To the gods, svāhā!"
(3.1.5.2) He thus gratifies both of them.

(3.1.6.1.a) Whoever performs a sacrifice not according to its deities is cut off from the deities and becomes worse off; he who performs it according to the deities is not cut off from the deities and becomes more prosperous. (3.1.6.1) He should touch the *āgnīdhra* shed with a verse addressed to Agni, the *havirdhāna* shed with one addressed to Viṣṇu, the ladles with one addressed to Agni, the *vāyavya* cups with one addressed to Vāyu, and the *sadas* with one addressed to Indra. Thus he performs the sacrifice according to its deities; he is not cut off from the deities and becomes more prosperous.

(3.1.6.1.b) I yoke for you the earth together with light; I yoke Vāyu for you together with the intermediate space. (3.1.6.2) I yoke speech for you together with the sun; I yoke for you the three divisions of the sun.

(3.1.6.2.c) Agni is the deity, the Gāyatrī the metre; you are the vessel for the Upāṃśu cup. Soma is the deity, the Triṣṭubh the metre; you are the vessel for the Antaryāma cup. Indra is the deity, the Jagatī the metre; you are the vessel for Indra and Vāyu. Bṛhaspati is the deity, the Anuṣṭubh the metre; you are the vessel for Mitra and Varuṇa. The Aśvins are the deity, the Paṅkti the metre; you are the vessel for the Aśvins. Sūrya is the deity, the Bṛhatī the metre; you are the vessel for the Śukra cup. Candramas is the deity.

Satobṛhatī is the metre; thou art the vessel of the Manthin cup; the Viśve Devas are the deity. Uṣṇih is the metre; thou art the vessel of the Āgrayaṇa cup; Indra is the deity. Kakubh is the metre; thou art the vessel of the Ukthas; Pṛthivī is the deity. Virāj is the metre; thou art the vessel of the Dhruva cup.
(3.1.7.1) The Adhvaryu is indeed the one who incurs the loss of what is sacrificed for the sacrificer; for it is the one who sacrifices first who suffers the loss.
(3.1.7.1) "Protect me from the mantra of the mouth, from every curse!
(3.1.7.1) Thus he should offer an oblation before the Prātaranuvāka; thereby the Adhvaryu binds protection upon himself beforehand, so that there may be no injury.
(3.1.7.1) For lying down, for sitting down, for the overcoming of the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Jagatī—svāhā!

(3.1.7.1) O out-breath and in-breath, protect me from death; O out-breath and in-breath, do not abandon me among the deities. Indeed, those for whom the Soma comes into conflict struggle against one another regarding these two, out-breath and in-breath. (3.1.7.2) For lying down, for sitting down, for you—svāhā!

Thus he says: "The meters are indeed the reclining and the sitting; by means of the meters, he appropriates his meters. The *ājya* stotras contain the word "forward" (*pra*) for the sake of conquest; the opening verses (*pratipad*) contain the word "Maruts" for the sake of victory.
Both the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara* [sāmans] are employed.

(3.1.7.2) This [earth] indeed is the *rathaṃtara*, yonder [sky] is the *bṛhat*; verily by means of these two he passes him between. (3.1.7.2) Today indeed is the *rathaṃtara*, tomorrow is the *bṛhat*; verily from today and tomorrow he passes him between. (3.1.7.2) The past indeed is the *rathaṃtara*, the future is the *bṛhat*; verily from both the past and the future he passes him between. (3.1.7.3) The past indeed is the *rathaṃtara*, the future is the *bṛhat*; verily from both the past and the future he passes him between.
(3.1.7.3) The *rathantara* is indeed limited, while the *bṛhat* is unlimited; he thus enters him from both the limited and the unlimited.

(3.1.7.3) Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni contended with Vasiṣṭha. Jamadagni saw this *vihavya* hymn; by it, he indeed appropriated the power and vigor of Vasiṣṭha. When the *vihavya* is recited, the sacrificer thereby appropriates the power and vigor of his rival.
(3.1.7.3) "He whose sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) are more numerous," they say, (3.1.7.3) "he appropriates the deities.

(3.1.7.3) If the *soma* sacrifice beyond this point should be an *agniṣṭoma*, he should perform an *ukthya*; if it should be an *ukthya*, he should perform an *atirātra*. By means of the sacrificial rites themselves, he appropriates his deities; he becomes more prosperous.

(3.1.8.1.a) You are the Nigrābhyās, heard by the gods. Satisfy my life; satisfy my out-breath; satisfy my in-breath; satisfy my diffused breath; satisfy my eye; satisfy my ear; satisfy my mind; satisfy my speech; satisfy my self; satisfy my limbs; satisfy my offspring; satisfy my cattle; satisfy my house; satisfy my groups; satisfy me with all my groups; satisfy me! (3.1.8.2) May my groups not thirst.
(3.1.8.2.b) The plants are indeed the subjects (*viś*) of Soma; and the subjects, indeed, have the power to bestow [their lord] upon a king. Soma belongs to Indra.

(3.1.8.2) "I have magnified you with my mind, O well-born ones, born of *ṛta*; may we be yours for fortune. May the divine plants, in agreement with Indra, consent to the pressing of the Soma," he says.
Thus, having formally assigned him to the plants, to his own subjects, and to his own deity, he presses him.

(3.1.8.2.c) Indeed, whichever first shoot of the Soma being pressed falls out, it is capable of destroying the sensory power, vigor, offspring, and cattle of the sacrificer. He should address it with this mantra:
(3.1.8.3) "May it fall back to me along with offspring and along with the increase of wealth; do not destroy my sensory power and vigor!
Thus he invokes this very blessing for the non-destruction of sensory power, vigor, offspring, and cattle.

(3.1.8.3ḍ) The drop has fallen upon the earth and the sky, upon this womb and that which was before; following it as it moves through the third womb, I offer the drop according to the seven priestly offices.
(3.1.9.1.a) He who endows the gods with the glory of the gods and men with the glory of men becomes possessed of the glory of the gods among the gods and possessed of the glory of men among men.

(3.1.9.1) Those cups which he should draw prior to the Āgrayaṇa, he should draw them silently; those which are subsequent, he should draw them with a sound. Thus he endows the gods with the glory of the gods and men with the glory of men; he becomes possessed of the glory of the gods among the gods and possessed of the glory of men among men.

(3.1.9.1.b) May Agni protect us at the morning pressing—Vaiśvānara, by his greatness, the benefactor of all. May he, the purifier, bestow wealth upon us. (3.1.9.2) May we be long-lived, sharing in the draught together.
(3.1.9.2.c) May the All-Gods, the Maruts, and Indra not abandon us at this second libation. Endowed with long life and speaking what is pleasing to them, may we abide in the good favor of the gods.

(3.1.9.2ḍ) This is the third pressing of the seers, those who by means of the *ṛta* set the chalice in motion. May those sons of Sudhanvan, having attained the heavenly light, lead our well-performed sacrifice toward greater prosperity.
(3.1.9.2.e) Some oblations are offered with a foundation, while others are without a foundation.

(3.1.9.2) Those that have the *āghāra* libation are those with a foundation; those that belong to Soma are those without a foundation. Having taken the cup for Indra and Vāyu, he should pour the *āghāra* libation, [saying]:

(3.1.9.3) "O Gods, let this sacrifice be a peaceful *adhvara* for the plants, for our cattle, for our people, and for every living being; you are the peaceful *adhvara*. Swell, O divine Soma, rich in ghee! (3.1.9.3) *adhvaro yajño 'yam astu devā oṣadhībhyaḥ paśave no janāya viśvasmai bhūtāyādhvaro 'si sa pinvasva ghṛtavat*.
Thus, he makes those oblations pertaining to Soma possess a firm foundation; he who knows this becomes possessed of a firm foundation. Moreover, he moistens heaven and earth with clarified butter.
(3.1.9.3) These two [sacrificial spoons] are those upon which one lives; they are the means of living. He who knows thus becomes one who lives [well].
(3.1.9.4.f) "This, O Rudra, is your portion, that which you have requested; enjoy it! May you find cattle-herdship, the increase of wealth, heroic vigor, and well-being for a year.
(3.1.9.4.g) Manu divided his inheritance among his sons; he excluded Nābhānediṣṭha, who was living as a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*). He returned, and [Manu] spoke.

(3.1.9.4) "Why have you excluded me? he asked. "I have not excluded you," he replied. "These most excellent Aṅgirases are sitting here; they do not know the way to the heavenly world. Speak this Brāhmaṇa to them. As they go to the heavenly world, they will give you whatever cattle they possess.
(3.1.9.5) He spoke that to them, and as they were going to the heavenly world, they gave him the cattle they had.

(3.1.9.5) While he was moving about with the sacrificial animals on the sacrificial ground, Rudra approached him. He said, "These animals belong to me! [The gods] replied, "We have indeed given them to you. He said, "They do not truly belong to him; they belong to me, for whatever is left on the sacrificial ground is mine. Therefore, one should not step upon the sacrificial ground. (3.1.9.6) He said, "Grant me a share in the sacrifice, and then you shall no longer think ill of my animals.
For him, they offered the residue of the *manthin* cup. Then indeed Rudra no longer thought ill of his animals.
Where one who knows this thus offers the residue of the *manthin* cup, there Rudra does not direct his wrath against the cattle.
(3.1.10.1.a) May I be beloved of speech, beloved of the Lord of Speech, O Goddess Vāk! Place me in that which is the sweetness of speech; Svāhā to Sarasvatī!
With the *ṛc*, perfect the *stoma*; with the *gāyatra* chant, [perfect] the *rathaṃtara*; [and perfect] the *bṛhat* which follows the path of the *gāyatra*.

(3.1.10.1.c) That drop of yours which spills, that stalk of yours which has fallen from the arms or from the lap of the two pressing-boards, or that which [falls] from the purifier of the Adhvaryu—this, consecrated with Svāhā, I offer to Indra.

(3.1.10.1ḍ) That drop, the stalk which has fallen upon the earth—from the *parivāpa*, from the *puroḍāśa*, from the *karambha*, from the parched grains (*dhānā*), from the *soma*, from the *manthin*, from the *śukra*—that which is consecrated with *svāhā*, he offers that to Indra for Indra.

(3.1.10.2.e) That drop of thine which is honeyed and full of power, consecrated with Svāhā, returns again to the gods; from heaven, from earth, and from the intermediate space, I offer it to Indra, consecrated with Svāhā.
(3.1.10.2.f) "The Adhvaryu is indeed the first of the officiating priests to be joined; by him the *stoma* should be yoked," so they say.
(3.1.10.2.g) "May Speech go at the head, going straight forward to the gods, bestowing glory upon me, vital breaths upon the cattle, and offspring upon me and the sacrificer."
Thus he says; thereby he yokes speech itself at the mouth of the sacrifice.
Now, this is indeed made a dwelling-place for the sacrifice when, having drawn the cups, they proceed to the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant.

For they go away from here, and they chant with verses directed away. Having returned, he stands worshipping with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu; Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; thus he has made the sacrifice [his own].
"O Viṣṇu, you who are our closest, grant us protection, O Conqueror! Your streams, dripping with honey, milk out an inexhaustible spring," he says.
Whatever of him dries up while he lies there, that very part he causes to swell again by this [verse].
(3.1.11.1.a) Through Agni, may one obtain wealth and nourishment day by day—wealth that is glorious and most abundant in heroic sons.

(3.1.11.1.b) O Agni, this sacrifice has cattle, sheep, and horses; it has heroic companions and is ever unassailable. It is rich in *iḍā*, O Asura, and full of progeny; it is long-lasting wealth, broad-based, and fit for the assembly hall.
(3.1.11.1.c) "Swell up" (3.1.11.1ḍ) "May [the waters] unite with thee."
(3.1.11.1.e) Here I invoke Tvaṣṭṛ, the foremost, who possesses all forms; may he belong to us alone.

O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, being gracious, release for us that generative seed which is nourishing, from which is born a hero—skilled in action, highly dexterous, one who sets the pressing-stones in motion, and a lover of the gods.
(3.1.11.2.g) O auspicious Tvaṣṭṛ, come here; as a pervasive nourisher, come by your own self. Aid us in every sacrifice.
Tawny-hued, well-nourished, bestowing vital strength, a hero is born through obedience, one who loves the gods. May Tvaṣṭṛ open up the navel of progeny for us; then may he go to the path of the gods.
(3.1.11.2.i) May the goddess [Sarasvatī] come forward for us. (3.1.11.2.k) From heaven, may she come to us.
May we milk from Sarasvatī’s swelling breast—she who is visible to all—the offspring and nourishment.
O Sarasvatī, those waves of yours which are honeyed and dripping with ghee—of those we seek your favor.
He whose vow all cattle follow, whose vow the waters attend, in whose vow the Lord of Prosperity is established—him, Sarasvant, we invoke for protection.
We invoke for our protection that Sarasvant, the divine, well-winged bird of great size, the embryo of the waters, the bull of the plants, who satisfies all sides with rain.
O Sinīvālī of the broad tresses, you who are the sister of the gods, accept this offered oblation; O goddess, grant us progeny.
(3.1.11.4.q) To her who has beautiful hands, beautiful fingers, who is prolific and bears many children—to that Sinīvālī, the mistress of the people, offer the oblation.
(3.1.11.4ṛ) Indra for you from every side;
(3.1.11.4ṣ) Indra, the men.
The dark-colored, tawny-winged birds, clothing themselves in mist, fly up to heaven; having made their dwellings, they have returned, and because of them the earth is sprinkled with clarified butter.
Golden-haired in the expanse of the atmosphere, the serpent is a roaring one, swift-gliding like the wind; he is the brightly shining one of the dawns, mindful, glorious, active, and true.

(3.1.11.5.v) Your well-guided [horses] have hastened here with their impulses; the black bull has bellowed when this occurred. He has come with auspicious, smiling [waters]; the raindrops fall, the clouds thunder.
Like a lowing cow, the lightning bellows; it follows its calf like a mother, when their rain has been released.
Even the mountain, though greatly grown, was afraid; even the ridge of heaven trembled at your roar. When you play, O Maruts, armed with spears, you rush together like waters.
Roar out! Thunder! Place the embryo [within the cloud]. Fly around with your water-bearing chariot. Draw forth the loosened leather bag downward; let the heights and the lowlands become level.
(3.1.11.6.z) O Agni, you [devour] even those things that are immovable, like a beast in a pasture; for when your powers, O undecaying one, hew down the trees, you are skillful.

O Agni Jātavedas, O self-dependent god, many are your abodes of immortality. And all those manifold powers of the masters of illusion, O all-enlivener, you have gathered within yourself, O you whose kinship is sought.
O Maruts, grant us rain from heaven; cause the streams of the stallion to swell. Come hither with this thundering, pouring down the waters, O Asura, our father.

The Maruts, the bounteous givers, swell the waters; they are present at the sacrifices with milk mixed with clarified butter. Like a swift steed for the sake of rain, they lead forth the prize-winning horse; they milk the thundering, inexhaustible spring.

O Maruts, you who move through the waters, send forth that rain which all the Maruts impel! The thunderbolt roars like a maiden pierced by love, striking the swelling cloud as a wife strikes her husband.
Sprinkle heaven and earth with ghee and honey; make the waters and the plants full of milk. Cause nourishment and favor to swell there where you, O Maruts, pour forth the honey for the men.
(3.1.11.8.ff) Upward that one; (3.1.11.8.gg) the wondrous one.
Like Aurva and Bhṛgu, like Apnavāna, I invoke the pure Agni, whose garment is the ocean.
I call upon Agni, who is clothed in the ocean, for instigation like that of Savitṛ and for enjoyment like that of Bhaga.
I invoke the sage who sounds like the wind, the force that roars like Parjanya, Agni whose garment is the ocean.
(3.2.1.1) He who, knowing the ascents of the *pavamāna* [stotras], performs the sacrifice, ascends after the *pavamānas* and is not cut off from the *pavamānas*.
(3.2.1.1) "You are the falcon, having the *gāyatrī* metre; I take hold of you—convey me safely across! You are the eagle, having the *triṣṭubh* metre; I take hold of you—convey me safely across!"
(3.2.1.1) "Thou art a leader, of the *jagatī* metre; I take hold of thee; lead me safely across," he says.
(3.2.1.1) These, indeed, are the ascents after the *pavamāna* chants. (3.2.1.2) These, indeed, are the ascents after the *pavamāna* chants.
(3.2.1.2) He who, knowing thus, performs the sacrifice, ascends after the *pavamāna* chants; he is not cut off from the *pavamāna* chants.
(3.2.1.2) Verily, he who knows the continuity of the *pavamāna* reaches a full lifespan; he does not die before his time; he becomes possessed of cattle and obtains offspring.
(3.2.1.2) The cups for the *pavamāna* are drawn.

(3.2.1.2) Or rather, these [vessels] of his—the *droṇakalaśa*, the *ādhavanīya*, and the *pūtabhṛt*—are not yet drawn. If he were to proceed with the ritual without having drawn them, he would cut across the *pavamāna* [laud]. As that [laud] is being cut across, the breath of the *adhvaryu* would follow after it and be cut across.
(3.2.1.3) "Thou art taken with a support; for Prajāpati, thee!"—with these words, he should touch the *droṇakalaśa*.
(3.2.1.3) "For Indra thee!"—with these words [he pours] into the *ādhavanīya* vessel.
(3.2.1.3) "For all the gods thee! [he pours].
Thus, he extends the *pavamāna* chant over the *pūtabhṛt* vessel; he attains a full lifespan, does not die before his time, becomes possessed of cattle, and obtains offspring.

(3.2.2.1) There are indeed three pressings. Now, they omit the third pressing by not including the *aṃśu* cup. Having offered the *upāṃśu* cup, he places the *aṃśu* stalk into the *upāṃśu* vessel; having mixed it into the third pressing, he should press it. In that he causes it to swell, thereby it possesses the *aṃśu*; in that he presses it, thereby it is with the dregs (*arjīṣin*). Thus he makes all the pressings possess the *aṃśu*, possess the pure juice (*śukra*), and equal in strength.
(3.2.2.1) Two oceans, vast and undecaying, revolve like feet within the belly. Beholding one of them, they pass beyond; not beholding the other, (3.2.2.2) they pass beyond it by means of a bridge.
Two firm, continuous garments he wears; the one with long hair, knowing all beings, goes forth veiling himself in black, yet takes up the bright [garment] for his aged wife.
(3.2.2.2) Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did that too.
(3.2.2.2) Those gods saw this Great Sacrifice; they performed it.
(3.2.2.2) They performed the Agnihotra as their vow;
therefore, one should observe two vows,
for they offer the Agnihotra twice.
They made the Full Moon sacrifice the animal sacrifice for Agni and Soma;
they made the New Moon sacrifice the animal sacrifice for Agni;
they made the Vaiśvadeva the morning pressing.

(3.2.2.3) They made the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings the midday pressing, the Sākamedha offerings the Pitṛyajña, and the Tryambaka offerings the third pressing. (3.2.2.3) The Asuras sought to follow after this sacrifice of theirs, but they could not follow it. They said, "These gods have indeed become inviolable."
That is the reason why the *adhvara* is called *adhvara*. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
He who, knowing this, sacrifices with Soma, prospers in himself; his rival is defeated.

(3.2.3.1.a) Encompassing Agni, encompassing Indra, encompassing all the gods, encompass me with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). Flow pure for us, bringing peace to our cattle, peace to our people, peace to our horses, and peace, O King, to the plants. May we be givers of undiminished wealth, O Lord of Riches, of heroic power, and of the increase of prosperity. Grant me of that; may I partake of that which is yours; of that of yours, I wipe this [portion] clean.
(3.2.3.1.b) For my out-breath, you who grant splendor, purify yourself for splendor! (3.2.3.1.c) For my in-breath; (3.2.3.1ḍ) for my diffused breath.
(3.2.3.1.e) To Speech.
(3.2.3.2.f) For skill and will. (3.2.3.2.g) O you two who bestow splendor upon my eyes, purify yourselves for splendor.
(3.2.3.2.h) For hearing.
(3.2.3.2.i) For the self;
(3.2.3.2.k) for the limbs;
(3.2.3.2ḷ) for long life.
(3.2.3.2ṃ) For valor; (3.2.3.2ṇ) of Viṣṇu; (3.2.3.2.o) of Indra.
(3.2.3.2.p) You are the belly of the Viśve Devas; as the giver of splendor, purify yourself for my splendor.

(3.2.3.2.q) Who are you? What is your name? For whom are you? To whom are you? You whom I have satiated with Soma, you whom I have exhilarated with Soma—may I be rich in offspring through offspring, rich in heroes through heroes, rich in splendor through splendor, and rich in nourishment through nourishments. (3.2.3.2ṛ) As the giver of splendor for all my forms, purify yourself for splendor; grant that to me; may I partake of that of yours; this of yours I wipe away. (3.2.3.3) As the giver of splendor for all my forms, purify yourself for splendor; grant that to me; may I partake of that of yours; this of yours I wipe away.

(3.2.3.3) One who desires to prosper should look [at the Soma]; for this sacrificial vessel is Prajāpati, the sacrifice is Prajāpati. He gratifies him; he, being gratified, purifies him with prosperity. (3.2.3.3) One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should look [at the Soma]; for this sacrificial vessel is Prajāpati, the sacrifice is Prajāpati. He gratifies him; he, being gratified, purifies him with spiritual luster. (3.2.3.4) One who is afflicted by illness should look [at the Soma]; for this sacrificial vessel is Prajāpati, the sacrifice is Prajāpati. He gratifies him; he, being gratified, purifies him with long life.

(3.2.3.4) One practicing exorcism should look [at it], for this is indeed Prajāpati in the form of the sacrificial vessel; he is Prajāpati, the sacrifice. He thus gratifies him. Being gratified, he (Prajāpati) departs from him [the practitioner] by means of his out-breath and in-breath, his speech, his skill and resolve, his two eyes, his two ears, his limbs, and his life-force. Swiftly he perishes.

(3.2.4.1.a) The wooden sword is well-being, the mallet is well-being; the sacrificial post, the altar, and the axe are well-being for us. You are worthy of sacrifice and performers of the sacrifice; do you invite me to this sacrifice. (3.2.4.1.b) May Heaven and Earth invite me; may the place of praise, the pitcher, Soma, and Agni invite me; may the gods and the sacrifice invite me; may the invocations invite me to the invitation.
(3.2.4.1.c) Homage to Agni, the slayer of Makha; may the glory of Makha come to me.

(3.2.4.1) Thus he worships the Āhavanīya fire: "The sacrifice is indeed Makha. (3.2.4.2) On that day, he has indeed slain the sacrifice; having paid homage to him, he proceeds to the Sadas for his own safety.
(3.2.4.2ḍ) "Homage to Rudra, the slayer of Makha! Having paid homage, protect me!
(3.2.4.2) Thus [he says] regarding the Āgnīdhra fire; having paid homage to him, he proceeds to the Sadas for his own safety.
(3.2.4.2.e) "Homage to Indra, the slayer of Makha! Do not strike away from me my *indriya* and my vigor!
(3.2.4.2) Thus he pronounces this blessing at the Hotṛ’s station, so that his *indriya* and vigor may not be destroyed.
(3.2.4.2.f) Whatever deities bring affliction upon one in the *sadas*, if he, knowing them, moves forward, he does not meet with affliction in the *sadas*. Homage to Agni, the slayer of Makha!
Thus he says: "These deities indeed are in the assembly; he incurs misfortune. "You two are firm, you two are relaxed, you two are united; protect me from distress!
May the god Sūrya protect me from celestial distress, Vāyu from the intermediate space! "Agni [protects] from the earth, Yama from the fathers, Sarasvatī from men."
(3.2.4.4.i) O divine doors, do not burn me!
(3.2.4.4.k) Homage to the assembly, homage to the lord of the assembly, homage to the eye of friends who go before; homage to heaven, homage to earth!
(3.2.4.4.l) O son of a remarried woman, stand aside; sit on the seat of another, he who is more foolish than we!
(3.2.4.4m) May I go down into the hollows and up the heights.
(3.2.4.4n) O Heaven and Earth, protect me this day.

(3.2.4.4.o) The ancestors indeed follow after him as he creeps toward the *sadas* hall; they are capable of harming him. Having crept toward the *sadas*, he should look back toward the southern half [of the hall].
"Come, O fathers; may I be possessed of fathers through you, and may you be possessed of good offspring through me.
Having thus paid homage to them, he creeps forward to the *sadas* for his own safety.
(3.2.5.1.a) Consume me; enter me for long life, for health, for the increase of wealth, for splendor, and for good progeny. Come, O Vasu, O Purovasu; you are dear to my heart.
(3.2.5.1.b) May I grasp you with the arms of the Aśvins.
(3.2.5.1.c) O divine Soma, may I, being of good sight, look down upon you, who have the gaze of a hero.

(3.2.5.1ḍ) May Vāc, the delightful, the overcomer, the banner of sacrifices, rejoicing, be satisfied with the Soma; may the delightful, heaven-resounding Aditi, whose head is unassailable, Vāc rejoicing, be satisfied with the Soma.

(3.2.5.1.e) Come, O you who move among all people! (3.2.5.2) Be auspicious, be a source of joy, bring well-being to me; O golden-hued one, proceed for the sake of wisdom, for skill, for the increase of wealth, and for heroic progeny.
(3.2.5.2.f) Do not terrify me, O King; do not strike my heart with your brilliance—for the sake of virility, strength, long life, and splendor.

(3.2.5.2.g) O God Soma, belonging to the troop of the Vasus, who art possessed of wisdom, of the morning pressing, having the *gāyatrī* metre, drunk by Indra, drunk by Narāśaṃsa, drunk by the Fathers, full of sweetness—being invited, I partake of thee who art invited. (3.2.5.2.h) O God Soma, belonging to the troop of the Rudras, who art possessed of wisdom, of the midday pressing, having the *triṣṭubh* metre, drunk by Indra, drunk by Narāśaṃsa, drunk by the Fathers, full of sweetness—being invited, I partake of thee who art invited. (3.2.5.3) O God Soma, belonging to the troop of the Vasus, who art possessed of wisdom, of the third pressing, having the *jagatī* metre, drunk by Indra, drunk by Narāśaṃsa, drunk by the Fathers, full of sweetness—being invited, I partake of thee who art invited.

(3.2.5.3.i) O God Soma, belonging to the troop accompanied by Āditya, who art finder of thought, of the third libation, having the *jagatī* metre, drunk by Indra, drunk by Narāśaṃsa, drunk by the Fathers, full of sweetness—being invited, I partake of thee who art invited.
(3.2.5.3.k) Swell up; let virility come to you from every side, O Soma; be present at the gathering of strength.
(3.2.5.3ḷ) Stir my limbs, O Lord of the Bay Steeds; do not let my troops thirst. Be auspicious toward my seven seers; do not pass over my navel. (3.2.5.4) Do not go beyond!
(3.2.5.4ṃ) We have drunk the Soma; we have become immortal. We have seen the light; we have found the gods. What can hostility do to us? And what, O Immortal One, can the malice of a mortal do?
Whatever injury has occurred to my self, Agni Jātavedas, the all-seeing, has brought that back again.
Agni has given sight back; Indra and Bṛhaspati have given it back. O Aśvins, you two have restored sight to my eyes once more.

(3.2.5.4.o) Of thee, O divine Soma, whose sacrificial formulas have been offered, whose hymns of praise have been chanted, (3.2.5.5) whose recitations have been performed, who art accompanied by the bay steeds, drunk by Indra, full of sweetness, and invited—I, being invited, partake.
(3.2.5.5.p) You are to be filled; fill me with offspring and with wealth.
(3.2.5.5.q) This for you, father, and for those who follow you; this for you, grandfather, and for those who follow you; this for you, great-grandfather, and for those who follow you.

(3.2.5.5ṛ) Here, O fathers, rejoice according to your respective portions. (3.2.5.5ṣ) Homage to you, O fathers, for your essence; homage to you, O fathers, for your vigor; homage to you, O fathers, for your life; homage to you, O fathers, for your *svadhā*! Homage to you, O fathers, for your wrath; homage to you, O fathers, for your terrible power; O fathers, homage to you!

(3.2.5.6ṭ) Those who are in this world, let them follow you; those who are in this world, let them follow me. (3.2.5.6.u) You who are in this world, may you be the most excellent among them; I who am in this world, may I be the most excellent among them.
(3.2.5.6.v) O Prajāpati, none other than you has encompassed all these created beings. (3.2.5.7) Whatever desire we have as we offer this to you, let that be ours; may we be masters of riches!
(3.2.5.7.w) You are the expiation for sin committed against the gods; you are the expiation for sin committed against men; you are the expiation for sin committed against the ancestors.

(3.2.5.7.x) O divine Soma, of you who have been washed in the waters, pressed by the men, whose sacrifice has been performed, whose *stoma* has been praised, and whose *uktha* has been recited—of that portion of yours which wins horses and which wins cattle, of that portion of yours prepared as food by the ancestors, being invited, I, invited, partake.

(3.2.6.1.a) You are the milk of the great ones; you are the body of all the gods. May I succeed today in drawing the cup of the speckled ones; you are the cup of the speckled ones. You are the heart of Viṣṇu. One step Viṣṇu strode across you for food. May prosperity increase through curds and ghee. May the wealth of that which is sacrificed and consumed come to me. You are the light belonging to Vaiśvānara; you are the milk of the speckled cow.
(3.2.6.1.b) As great as heaven and earth are in their magnitude, and as far as the seven rivers extend—so great, O Indra, do I draw this cup for you, together with strength, invincible. (3.2.6.2)

(3.2.6.2) If a black bird should touch the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), his Śūdras would be liable to die; if a dog should touch it, his four-footed livestock would be liable to die; if it should spill, the sacrificer would be liable to die. Speckled butter is indeed cattle; the cattle of one whose speckled butter spills away are lost. In that he takes up the speckled butter again, he recovers his cattle for himself.

The speckled butter is indeed the vital breath; the vital breath indeed spills away for him whose speckled butter spills. When he takes up the speckled butter again, he thereby takes up the vital breath again for him.

He takes it up after placing gold within; gold is indeed immortality, and the speckled butter is the vital breath; thus he places immortality in his vital breath. It is of a hundred measures; man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers; he thus finds firm support in life and in power.
(3.2.6.3) He causes the horse to smell [the offering]. The horse belongs to Prajāpati; breath belongs to Prajāpati. Verily, from its own womb he fashions breath for him.

(3.2.6.3) The sacrifice of him whose *pṛṣadājya* spills is indeed torn asunder. He takes it up again with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu. Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; verily, by means of the sacrifice he joins the sacrifice together.
(3.2.7.1.a) O God Savitṛ, he has declared this to you; impel it and perform the sacrifice.
(3.2.7.1.b) Bṛhaspati is the Brahman priest.
(3.2.7.1.c) May you not depart from the long-lived Ṛc nor from the body-protecting Sāman.
(3.2.7.1ḍ) May your blessings be true; may your intentions be true.
(3.2.7.1.e) Speak *ṛta* and truth.
(3.2.7.1.f) Praise at the impulse of the god Savitṛ.

(3.2.7.1.g) Of the hymn, the hymn is yours; may the hymn yield me strength; may the hymn of the hymn come to me. (3.2.7.1.h) Of the recitation, the recitation is yours; may the recitation yield me strength; may the recitation of the recitation come to me.
(3.2.7.2.i) Endowed with power, we win; may we milk forth offspring and nourishment.
(3.2.7.2.k) May this my true blessing be realized among the gods. (3.2.7.2ḷ) May spiritual splendor come to me.
(3.2.7.2ṃ) The sacrifice came into being; it has come into existence; it was born; it grew. It became the sovereign lord of the gods. May it make us sovereign lords; may we be masters of riches.
(3.2.7.2) Indeed, the sacrifice either milks the lord of the sacrifice, or the lord of the sacrifice milks the sacrifice.

(3.2.7.3) He who performs the sacrifice without knowing the milking of the *stotra* and the *śastra* is milked by the sacrifice; having sacrificed, he becomes worse off. He who performs the sacrifice knowing their milking milks the sacrifice; having sacrificed, he becomes more prosperous.

(3.2.7.3) "The *stotra* of the *stotra* art thou; may the *stotra* yield me strength; may the *stotra* of the *stotra* come to me! The *śastra* of the *śastra* art thou; may the *śastra* yield me strength; may the *śastra* of the *śastra* come to me!"—so he says. This indeed is the milking of the *stotra* and the *śastra*. He who, knowing thus, performs the sacrifice, truly milks the sacrifice; having sacrificed, he becomes more prosperous.

(3.2.8.1.a) To the eagle that flies, Svāhā! Vaṭ! Adoration to him who has willed himself forth! To the support of the cosmic order, Svāhā! Vaṭ! Adoration to him who has willed himself forth! To the enclosure that spreads out the people, Svāhā! Vaṭ! Adoration to him who has willed himself forth! To the vigor of the oblations, Svāhā! Vaṭ! Adoration to him who has willed himself forth! To the milk of the oblations, Svāhā! Vaṭ! Adoration to him who has willed himself forth! To Prajāpati Manu, Svāhā! Vaṭ! Adoration to him who has willed himself forth! To the Truth, O guardian of Truth, the seeker of heaven, Svāhā! Vaṭ! Adoration to him who has willed himself forth! To him, adoration!
(3.2.8.1.b) May the invocations be satiated with the honeyed ghee.

(3.2.8.1.c) The seers have said that the lord of the sacrifice was afflicted by sin; his offspring were excluded and were consumed by remorse. He failed to offer those two honeyed drops. May Viśvakarman unite us with them.
(3.2.8.2ḍ) Terrible are the seers; let there be homage to them! At the junction of their eye and mind, to Bṛhaspati, the great, the glorious, be homage! Homage to Viśvakarman; may he protect us.

(3.2.8.2.e) Thinking of no others as Soma-drinkers, the wise man who knows the breath is not bound by sin in the conflict; though he has committed a great transgression against them, O Viśvakarman, release him for his well-being!

(3.2.8.3.f) Those who, while consuming, did not bestow riches, whom the fires of the hearths (dhiṣṇiya) consumed with heat—for their ill-offered sacrifice, let this be the expiation; may Viśvakarman make that our sacrifice well-performed.

(3.2.8.3.g) Homage to the fathers who have looked upon us, the performers of sacrifice, the lovers of sacrifice, the good gods! We have not brought you a sacrificial fee out of desire; do not cause us to suffer for that sin.

(3.2.8.3.h) As many as are the members of the assembly (*sadasya*), they are all worthy of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇya*). He who would not bring a sacrificial fee to them would be cut off from them. In that he offers the oblations to Viśvakarman, he thereby gratifies the members of the assembly.

(3.2.8.4.i) O Gods, take heed of us for our glory, so that the husband and wife may obtain the desirable wealth through the *āśir* mixture. A male son is born; he acquires riches, and then the entire household prospers, free from affliction.

(3.2.8.4.k) May the husband and wife, receiving the blessing, obtain what is desirable; may they, unharmed, possess wealth together with their dwelling. May he who poured out the milk along with the jar, at the sacrifice, abandon his lack of insight through his desired goal.

(3.2.8.4ḷ) One with a neck like clarified butter; (3.2.8.5) his wife is stout, his sons are stout and not emaciated—he who, together with his kin, desiring the sacrifice, has offered the *āśira* mixture for Indra along with the jar.
(3.2.8.5) May the *āśis* bestow upon me strength, good progeny, nourishment, and resplendent wealth. May Indra, conquering lands by his might, subjugate my other rivals.
(3.2.8.5ṇ) You are the existent; place me in existence. You are the face; may I become the face.
(3.2.8.5.o) I enclose you from heaven and earth.
(3.2.8.5.p) May all the gods, common to all men, cause you to move forward.
(3.2.8.6.q) In heaven, establish the gods; in the intermediate space, the birds; on earth, the earthly beings.
(3.2.8.6ṛ) With this firm oblation, we lead Soma hither, so that our entire living world may be free from disease and well-disposed.
(3.2.8.6ṣ) Just as Indra shall make all these subjects entirely ours and of one mind, so that all the quarters of space shall be exclusively ours.
(3.2.9.1) When the Hotṛ calls out to the Adhvaryu, he hurls a thunderbolt at him.

(3.2.9.1) Having responded to the morning pressing with "O reciter of the hymn" (*ukthaśas*), there are these three syllables; the Gāyatrī has three feet, and the morning pressing belongs to the Gāyatrī. Thus, by means of the Gāyatrī itself, he places the thunderbolt within the morning pressing.

"Ukthaṃ vāci," he says, having responded to the midday pressing. These are four syllables; the *triṣṭubh* has four feet, and the midday pressing belongs to the *triṣṭubh*. By means of the *triṣṭubh*, he thus places the thunderbolt within the midday pressing.

(3.2.9.2) “The hymn is for Indra in speech,” he says, having responded at the third pressing. These are seven syllables; the *śakvarī* consists of seven feet. The *vajra* is *śākvara*. By means of the *vajra*, he thus places the *vajra* within himself at the third pressing.
(3.2.9.2) The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say:

“That one indeed should be the *adhvaryu* who, in the response according to each pressing, would bring the meters into correspondence—he should place brilliance in himself at the morning pressing, sensory power at the midday pressing, and cattle at the third pressing.”

(3.2.9.2) Having responded to the morning pressing, he says, "The reciter of hymns" (*ukthaśas*). These are three syllables. (3.2.9.3) The *gāyatrī* consists of three feet; the morning pressing belongs to the *gāyatrī*. Thus, in the response at the morning pressing, he brings the meters together.
Moreover, the *gāyatrī* is indeed splendor, and the morning pressing is splendor; verily, he bestows splendor upon himself at the morning pressing.

(3.2.9.3) Having responded to the midday pressing, he says, "The hymn is in speech. These are four syllables; the *triṣṭubh* has four feet, and the midday pressing belongs to the *triṣṭubh*. Thus, at the response during the midday pressing, he causes the meters to attain completion. (3.2.9.4) Moreover, the *triṣṭubh* is indeed power, and the midday pressing is power. Verily, he places power within himself at the midday pressing.

"‘The hymn is in the voice for Indra,’ he says, having responded at the third pressing. These [syllables] are seven; the *śakvarī* consists of seven feet, cattle are connected with the *śakvarī*, and the third pressing belongs to the *jagatī*. Thus, by responding at the third pressing, he unites the meters with the third pressing itself.
Moreover, the *jagatī* is indeed cattle, and the third pressing is cattle; verily, he bestows cattle upon himself at the third pressing."
(3.2.9.4) When the Hotṛ calls out toward the Adhvaryu, he places a ram in him; if he were not to drive that away, his household would surely fall into distress before the year is out.
(3.2.9.5) He responds with "Śoṃsā modīva," and by that very means he drives it away.
Just as one awaits a person approaching, so does the Adhvaryu await the response.
(3.2.9.5) If one were to respond prematurely, it would be just as if one were to collide with a moving chariot.
(3.2.9.5) If [the response] were to be omitted from the half-verse, it would be just as if one were left behind by those who are running.

(3.2.9.5) Indeed, the *udgītha* of the officiating priests is simultaneous; the *udgītha* itself belongs to the *udgātṛ*s. (3.2.9.6) The *praṇava* belongs to the *ṛc* verses; the *pratigara* belongs to the chanters of the *uktha*s and to the *adhvaryu*s.
He who, knowing thus, responds [with the *pratigara*] becomes an eater of food; a vigorous son is born among his offspring.
This earth, indeed, is the *hotṛ*, and yonder sky is the *adhvaryu*.
When he recites while seated, the *hotṛ* thereby does not depart from this earth—for she, as it were, sits; moreover, by that means the sacrificer milks her.

(3.2.9.6) When he responds while standing, the Adhvaryu does not depart from that very world beyond. (3.2.9.7) For yonder world stands, as it were; moreover, by this means the sacrificer milks yonder world.

Because he recites while sitting, the gods subsist on offerings from here; because he responds while standing, men subsist on offerings from there. Because he recites facing east while sitting and responds facing west while standing, therefore seed is deposited facing forward and offspring are born facing backward.
When the Hotṛ calls out to the Adhvaryu, he hurls a thunderbolt at him; the Adhvaryu turns away, and thus he strikes down that very thunderbolt.
(3.2.10.1.a) You are taken with a support; you are the sitter in speech. I take you for the two guardians of speech, the two guardians of the ritual will, the two supervisors of this firm sacrifice.
(3.2.10.1.b) You are taken with a support; you are the sitter in truth. I take you for the two guardians of sight, the two guardians of the ritual will, the two supervisors of this firm sacrifice.

(3.2.10.1.c) You are taken with a support; you are the sitter in what is heard. I take you for the two guardians of hearing, the two guardians of the ritual will, the two supervisors of this firm sacrifice.
For the gods thee;
for the Viśvedevas thee;
for all the gods thee.
(3.2.10.1.g) O Viṣṇu of the wide stride, this Soma is yours; protect it! (3.2.10.2) Let not the evil-eyed one look upon it for you.
(3.2.10.2.i) In me is the Vasu, the Purovasu; O protector of speech, protect my speech! In me is the Vasu, the Vidadvasu; O protector of sight, protect my sight!
(3.2.10.2.k) In me is the Vasu, the gatherer of wealth; O protector of hearing, protect my hearing.
(3.2.10.2ḷ) Thou art the Bhū, the best of rays; O protector of breath, protect my breath. (3.2.10.2ṃ) Thou art the Dhū, the best of rays; O protector of out-breath, protect my out-breath.
(3.2.10.2ṇ) He who assails us, O Indra and Vāyu;
(3.2.10.2.o) he who assails us, O Mitra and Varuṇa;
(3.2.10.2.p) he who assails us, O Aśvins—he who is our rival, who swells with power, O Lords of Splendor—here I cast him down beneath my feet, so that I may be supreme, O Indra, and discern clearly.
