(3.2.11.1.a) O Agni, he whom you have protected through friendship overcomes [all] with your aids that bring heroic sons and deeds of victory.
(3.2.11.1.b) Bring forth a lofty, ancient word for the Hotṛ, for Agni—the ordainer who bears the lights of inspired songs.

O Agni, three are your strengths, three your abodes, and three are your ancient tongues, O you who are born of Truth. Three also are your bodies beloved by the gods; with these, protect our hymns without fail.

(3.2.11.1ḍ) Together with your ritual act and together with nourishment, I impel you both, O Indra and Viṣṇu, at the completion of this work. May you enjoy the sacrifice and bestow wealth upon us, carrying us across by paths that are free from harm.
(3.2.11.2.e) You both have conquered; you are not defeated; neither of you has been defeated. O Indra and Viṣṇu, when you two strove together, you divided the thousandfold [booty] into three parts.

(3.2.11.2.f) Three are your lifespans, O Jātavedas; three are your births from the dawns, O Agni. With these, as the one who knows, sacrifice for the protection of the gods, and then become the source of peace and well-being for the sacrificer.

(3.2.11.3.g) Agni, the sage, dwells in the three triadic domains of the sacrifice; may he, the wise and consecrated messenger, worship and satisfy the thirty-three gods here for us. May all others perish!
O Indra and Viṣṇu, you shattered the ninety-nine strong fortresses of Śambara; together you struck down a hundred and a thousand of the Asura Varcin’s heroes without resistance.
(3.2.11.3.i) And the Mother gave her approval to the buffalo: "O son, these gods are abandoning you. Then Indra, about to slay Vṛtra, said: "O friend Viṣṇu, stride out even further!"

(3.3.1.1.a) O Agni, full of splendor, may you be full of splendor among the gods; make me full of splendor, long-lived, and radiant among men. I offer you for the sake of consecration (*dīkṣā*) and for the splendor of ascetic heat (*tapas*).
(3.3.1.1.b) You are the knower of splendor; may splendor not forsake me, may I not forsake splendor, and may splendor not forsake me.

(3.3.1.1.c) O Indra, full of vigor (*ojas*), may you be full of vigor among the gods; make me full of vigor, long-lived, and radiant among men. I offer you for the vigor of the spiritual power (*brahman*) and the ruling power (*kṣatra*).
(3.3.1.2ḍ) You are the possessor of vigor; may vigor not desert me; may I not desert vigor; may vigor not desert me.

(3.3.1.2.e) O radiant Sūrya, may you be radiant among the gods; make me radiant, long-lived, and glorious among men; I offer you the radiance of Vāyu and of the waters. (3.3.1.2.f) You are the finder of heaven; may heaven not desert me; may I not desert heaven; may heaven not desert me.

(3.3.1.2.g) May Agni bestow wisdom upon me, offspring upon me, and splendor upon me; may Indra bestow wisdom upon me, offspring upon me, and virility upon me; may Sūrya bestow wisdom upon me, offspring upon me, and radiance upon me.

(3.3.2.1.a) Vāyu is the *hiṃ*-singer, Agni the *prastotṛ*, Prajāpati the *sāman*, Bṛhaspati the *udgātṛ*, the Viśve Devas the *upagātṛ*s, the Maruts the *pratihartṛ*s, and Indra the *nidhana*. May those gods, the Prāṇabhṛts, bestow vital breath upon me.

(3.3.2.1.b) Indeed, when the Adhvaryu initiates [the sacrifice], he initiates it for the sake of the Udgātṛs. "May those gods, the Prāṇabhṛts, bestow vital breath upon me," he says; thus he places all this within himself.
(3.3.2.1.c) Iḍā is the caller of the gods; Manu is the leader of the sacrifice.
(3.3.2.1ḍ) Bṛhaspati shall recite the hymns and songs of praise. (3.3.2.1.e) May all the gods be speakers of well-spoken words.
(3.3.2.2.f) O Earth, Mother, do not harm me!
(3.3.2.2.g) I shall conceive honey; I shall be born from honey; I shall speak honey; I shall utter honey. May I raise up speech full of honey for the gods, and worthy of being heard by men.
(3.3.2.2ḥ) May the gods protect me for the sake of splendor; may the ancestors rejoice after me.
(3.3.3.1.a) May the Vasus lift you up with the Gāyatrī metre; go to the beloved domain of Agni.
(3.3.3.1.b) May the Rudras lift you up with the Triṣṭubh metre; go to the beloved domain of Indra.
(3.3.3.1.c) May the Ādityas lift you up with the Jagatī metre; go to the beloved domain of all the gods.
(3.3.3.1ḍ) In the *māndā* [verses], O bright one, I shake your bright [essence] for you;
(3.3.3.1.e) in the *bhandanā* [verses]; (3.3.3.1.f) in the *kotanā* [verses].
(3.3.3.1.g) in the new (3.3.3.1ḥ) ewes (3.3.3.1.i) and in the rams.
(3.3.3.1.k) among the axes,
(3.3.3.1ḷ) among the all-sustaining ones,
(3.3.3.1ṃ) among the honeyed ones.
(3.3.3.1ṇ) In the Kakubhas; (3.3.3.1.o) in the Śakvarīs.
(3.3.3.2.p) O bright one, from the bright [waters], I shake forth thy brightness. (3.3.3.2.q) With the bright, I take thy brightness, with the form of the day, with the rays of the sun.
(3.3.3.2ṛ) Into this [cup] the fierce ones have poured the streams from heaven; they flow unceasingly.
(3.3.3.2ṣ) The lofty form of the bull shines forth; Soma is the precursor of Soma, the bright one is the precursor of the bright one.
(3.3.3.2ṭ) O Soma, that invincible and wakeful name of yours—unto that name of yours, O Soma, to Soma, *svāhā*!
(3.3.3.2.u) You, O divine Soma, are a seeker (*uśij*); with the *gāyatrī* metre, go along the beloved path of Agni. (3.3.3.3) Go along the beloved path.
(3.3.3.3.v) O divine Soma, you are the controller; with the Triṣṭubh metre, enter the beloved abode of Indra.
(3.3.3.3.w) O divine Soma, you are our friend; with the Jagatī metre, enter the beloved abode of all the gods.
(3.3.3.3.x) May breath come to us from afar, from the intermediate space, and from heaven; may life come from the earth. You are immortality; for breath, I take you.
May Indra and Agni bestow luster upon me; may Soma and Bṛhaspati bestow luster; may all the gods bestow luster upon me; O Aśvins, bestow luster upon me!
Whether he has run forth or has recited the sacred hymns (*brahmāṇi*) after them—that is his own. He has encompassed all poetic insights (*kāvyā*) as the felly encompasses the wheel.
(3.3.4.1) This indeed is the secret name of the waters, namely, "the rushing ones" (*ādhāva*).
(3.3.4.1) "O bright one, I shake the bright [Soma] into the *māndā* waters," he says.
(3.3.4.1) By means of this secret name of the waters, he wins the rain from heaven.
(3.3.4.1) "I take your bright [portion] with the bright," he says.
(3.3.4.1) For the night is indeed the form of this day;
the rays of the sun rule over the rain.

By means of the very form of the day, he causes the rain from heaven to fall through the rays of the sun. "Into this one the fierce ones have caused [the rain] to flow," he says; this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula.
"The preeminent form of the bull shines forth greatly," he says. This, indeed, is his preeminent form: rain.
By means of that very form, he secures rain.
"When you say, 'O Soma, that which is your invincible name, O watchful one,' he who,
having drawn the *adābhya* cup, offers it to Soma, truly sacrifices an oblation with an oblation. However,
the life-span and the vital breath of him who draws the *aṃśu* cup depart."
"May breath come to us from afar," he says; thus he places life-breath and vitality within himself. "Thou art immortality; for breath, thee! with these words, he breathes over the gold.
Gold is indeed immortality, and breath is life.
By means of immortality, he bestows life upon himself.
It is one hundred mānas in weight.
A man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers; he thus establishes himself in life and power. He touches water.
Water is indeed medicine;
he thus makes it medicine.
(3.3.5.1.a) You are Vāyu, named Prāṇa; under the overlordship of Savitṛ, grant me apāna. (3.3.5.1.b) You are the eye, named Śrotra; under the overlordship of Dhātṛ, grant me life.
(3.3.5.1.c) You are form, named Varṇa; under the overlordship of Bṛhaspati, grant me progeny.
(3.3.5.1ḍ) You are the *ṛta*, whose name is Truth; under the sovereignty of Indra, may you bestow the ruling power (*kṣatra*) upon me.
(3.3.5.1.e) You are the past, whose name is the future; under the sovereignty of the Fathers, may you hold the embryo of the waters and the plants.
(3.3.5.1.f) For the expanse of the *ṛta*, I take you.
(3.3.5.1.g) For the pervasiveness of *ṛta*, thee!
(3.3.5.2ḥ) For the support of *ṛta*, thee! (3.3.5.2.i) For the truth of *ṛta*, thee!

(3.3.5.2.k) "For the light of *ṛta*, thee! Prajāpati beheld the Virāj; with it he created both what has been and what is to be. He concealed it from the seers. Jamadagni beheld it through austerity; with it he indeed created manifold desires (*pṛśni*). That is the reason for the "manifold" nature of the *pṛśni* [cups]. When the *pṛśni* cups are drawn, the sacrificer wins manifold desires by means of them.

(3.3.5.2) "You are Vāyu, you are Prāṇa," he says; verily, he wins for himself out-breathing and in-breathing. (3.3.5.3) "You are sight, you are hearing, you are Name," he says; verily, he wins for himself life.
(3.3.5.3) "You are form, you are color, you are Name," he says; verily, he wins for himself progeny.
(3.3.5.3) "Thou art the *ṛta*, thy name is Truth," he says; verily, he wins sovereignty (*kṣatra*).

(3.3.5.3) "Thou art the past, thy name is the future," he says; cattle indeed are the embryo of the waters and the plants; verily, he wins cattle. (3.3.5.4) So much, indeed, surrounds the person; verily, he wins that very thing.
(3.3.5.4) “Thee for the expanse of Truth,” he says; this earth indeed is the expanse of Truth; verily, he conquers this earth.

(3.3.5.4) “Thee for the wide space of Truth,” he says; the intermediate region indeed is the wide space of Truth; verily, he conquers the intermediate region. (3.3.5.4) “Thee for the support of Truth,” he says; the sky indeed is the support of Truth; verily, he conquers the sky.
(3.3.5.4) “For the sake of *ṛta* (Cosmic Order), for the sake of truth, thee! he says. The quarters are indeed the truth of *ṛta*; verily, he conquers the quarters.
(3.3.5.5) “For the sake of the light of *ṛta*, thee! he says. The heavenly world is indeed the light of *ṛta*; verily, he conquers the heavenly world.
So many indeed are the worlds of the gods; verily, he conquers them.
They amount to ten; the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is food; verily, he finds firm support in the Virāj, in the eating of food.
(3.3.6.1) Whatever the gods did not obtain through the sacrifice, that they obtained by means of the *parā* cups.
That is the reason for the name of the *parā* cups.
When the *parā* cups are drawn, it is for the attainment of whatever one has not obtained through the sacrifice.
By that which he draws first, he conquers this very world;
by that which he draws second, the intermediate space;
by that which he draws third, he conquers yonder world.

(3.3.6.1) That these [cups] are drawn is for the conquest of these worlds. (3.3.6.2) On the subsequent days, they are drawn from there towards this side; having conquered these worlds, they descend again toward this world.
Because on the preceding days they are drawn from here towards that side, therefore these worlds extend from here towards that side.
Because on the subsequent days they are drawn from that world toward this one, therefore these worlds are directed from that world toward this one;
therefore, people subsist upon these worlds which have not lost their vitality. Thus say the exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*).

(3.3.6.2) On what basis do plants arise from the waters? (3.3.6.3) "Plants are the food of human beings; offspring are born after Prajāpati"—to this one should reply, "after the ancestors. This is what he takes up.
"In thee I take from the waters, from the plants," he says; therefore, from the waters the plants arise.
When he takes [the water], [he says]:
"In thee I take from the plants, for offspring"; therefore, plants are the food of human beings.
When he takes [the cup] with the words, "I take thee for offspring, for Prajāpati," therefore offspring are born after the likeness of Prajāpati.
Prajāpati created the gods and the Asuras.
Following that, the sacrifice was created, and from the sacrifice, the meters were created. They went forth in all directions.
(3.3.7.1) The sacrifice departed after the Asuras, as did the meters.
(3.3.7.1) Those gods reflected: (3.3.7.1) "Those [Asuras] have indeed become what we once were."
(3.3.7.1) They ran to Prajāpati. (3.3.7.1) Prajāpati said:
"Having taken the vigor of the meters, I shall bestow it upon you."
Having taken the vigor of the meters, he gave it to them.
Following that, the meters departed; the meters are the sacrifice. Thereupon, the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
He who thus knows the vigor of the meters becomes the *āśrāvaya*, the *astu śrauṣaṭ*, the *yaja*, and the *ye yajāmahe*; the *vaṣaṭ*-call becomes his very self, and his rival is defeated.
The exponents of the Brahman say:
"For what purpose does the Adhvaryu call for the *āśrāvaṇa*?"
(3.3.7.2) He should say, "For the vigor of the meters.
(3.3.7.3) This indeed is the vigor of the meters: *ā śrāvaya*, *astu śrauṣaṭ*, *yaja*, *ye yajāmahe*, and the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
(3.3.7.3) He who knows thus worships with the meters that possess vigor; whatever he worships, it is with those very meters endowed with vigor.

(3.3.7.3) When Indra slew Vṛtra, that was impure; when he cast away the Yatis, that was impure. Yet they ask: "Why then is the sacrifice dedicated to Indra until its completion? (3.3.7.3) This sacrifice is indeed Indra’s sacrificial body; it is that very body which they worship.
He who knows thus, the sacrifice inclines toward him.

(3.3.8.1.a) O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation, be one whose path is broadened by ghee and whose source is ghee! Having drunk the ghee and the sweet, pleasant [milk] of the cow, protect this [sacrificer] as a father protects his son.
(3.3.8.1) The sacrificer is indeed severed from the two fires when, having prepared the cooked offering for them, he goes elsewhere for the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
When about to go to the purificatory bath, he should offer with the verse, "O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation. By this offering, he pacifies those two;
the sacrificer does not meet with misfortune.
(3.3.8.1.b) Whatever debt remains unpaid by me, through which I move about as a tribute-bearer for Yama—being right here, I discharge that very thing; thus, O Agni, I become free from debt.

(3.3.8.2.c) O Viśvalopa, I offer you a portion of the all-consuming [fire]. One is for what has been eaten, one for what has not been offered, and one for what has been gathered together. May they provide us with healing, a dwelling, strength, and that which is most excellent.
(3.3.8.2ḍ) May this one, swelling with moisture, protect us from the front; so that our houses may not be destroyed, may we have many houses.
(3.3.8.2.e) As such, O Lord of the Sky, bestow strength upon us with auspiciousness. Restore to us what we have lost; restore to us our wealth.
(3.3.8.3.f) O God, Increaser, you are the master of thousandfold nourishment. Grant us vigor, the increase of riches, and heroic offspring, as well as well-being for the coming year.
Agni, indeed, is Yama; this earth is Yamī.
The sacrificer takes up this debt of Yama when he strews the altar with plants.
If he were to depart without having paid it back, they would lead him away in the other world with his neck bound.
(3.3.8.4) "Whatever debt remains unpaid by me"—by offering thus, even while remaining here, he pays off that debt to Yama and, free from debt, goes to the heavenly world.
(3.3.8.4) If he should act as if mixed [with falsehood], he should offer groats with his cupped hands into a forest fire.
(3.3.8.4) For this forest fire is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara; it is he who makes it palatable for him.
(3.3.8.4) On the Ekāṣṭakā day, which is the divider of the days, one should bake a cake of four śarāva-measures and, early in the morning, burn the brushwood with it.
(3.3.8.5) If it burns, it is equal to merit; if it does not burn, it is equal to evil. By means of this very sign of knowledge, the seers of old used to enter upon long sacrificial sessions.
He who, knowing the overseer, the listener, and the announcer, performs sacrifice, attains in that world the merit of his sacrifices and good works.
Agni is indeed the overseer, Vāyu is the listener, and Āditya is the announcer.
He who, knowing them thus, performs sacrifice, attains in that world the merit of his sacrifices and good works.
"This one before us with the sky," he says; for Agni is indeed "this one before us with the sky"—it is to Agni that he thereby speaks.
"Guard this for me," [he says];
"O lord of the sky, protect us," he says.
"Vāyu, indeed, is the lord of the sky; it is to Vāyu that he says this:
'Guard this for me.
'O God Saṃsphāna,' he says."
(3.3.8.6) "Yonder sun is indeed the god Saṃsphāna; it is to the sun that he thereby says: 'Guard this for me. (3.3.8.6) "Etan me gopāya" ("Guard this for me").
(3.3.9.1.a) This youth I entrust to you; sport with him, your beloved. O fortunate ones, do not curse us by birth; may we rejoice in the increase of wealth and in nourishment.

(3.3.9.1.b) Homage to your greatness and to your eye, O father of the Maruts! That I proclaim; grant your approval, and let us sacrifice with a well-performed rite. May this oblation be acceptable to the gods.
(3.3.9.1.c) This was the secret storehouse of the gods, the germ of the waters deposited within the plants; Pūṣan chose the drop of Soma. (3.3.9.2) A great rock became that of them.

He is the father of the calves, the lord of the inviolable cows; he is also the father of the great jars. He is the calf, the afterbirth, the fresh milk, the first milk, the curd, the whey, and the clarified butter—this is his seed.
The cattle chose you for sovereignty; the Maruts, who sing beautiful hymns, call upon you. Resting upon the height, at the peak of dominion, from there, O fierce one, distribute wealth among us.
(3.3.9.2) He who does not perform these rites sacrifices with an unsuccessful animal; but he indeed sacrifices with a successful one for whom these are performed.
May the god Sūrya for those dwelling in heaven, Dhātṛ for sovereign power, and Vāyu for progeny—may Bṛhaspati offer you, full of light, unto Prajāpati.
(3.3.10.1.b) Her whose embryo is tawny and whose womb is golden, her whose limbs are unimpaired—her I have united with the gods.
O Returner, cause him to return; O Non-returner, cause him to return, O Indra Nardabuda! From the four quarters of the earth, by means of them, cause him to return again.

(3.3.10.1ḍ) I split open your womb, I split open the birth-channels, I split open the two sides of the belly; I split open both mother and son, and the embryo and the afterbirth. (3.3.10.2.e) May your hair be outside!
(3.3.10.2.f) The wide-drop, multiform Indu, the purifying sage, has anointed the embryo.
(3.3.10.2.g) One-footed, two-footed, three-footed, four-footed, five-footed, six-footed, seven-footed, eight-footed—may she spread through the worlds, svāhā!
(3.3.10.2.h) May the great Heaven and Earth sprinkle this sacrifice for us; may they fill us with nourishments.
(3.3.11.1.a) This dear oblation is placed in your mouths, O Indra and Bṛhaspati; the hymn and the exhilarating draught are recited.
(3.3.11.1.b) This Soma is poured out for you both, O Indra and Bṛhaspati—delightful for exhilaration and for drinking.
O Indra and Bṛhaspati, bestow upon us wealth consisting of hundreds, abounding in horses, and reaching into the thousands.
May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind, and from above, and from below, from the one who intends evil; may Indra from the front and from the middle grant wide space to us, his friends, as a friend.

(3.3.11.1.e) O Agni, thy pure, brilliant flames, impelled by the wind, spread forth in every direction. Mighty-crushing, divine, and ever-new, they boldly strike down the forests, breaking them asunder.

(3.3.11.2.f) O Agni, the human tribes praise you—the knower of the *hotṛ*-office, the discerning one, the greatest bestower of jewels; you who, though dwelling in secret, are blessed, visible to all, possessed of mighty spirit, worthy of fair sacrifice, and radiant with ghee.
May Dhātṛ, the lord and master of the moving world, grant us wealth; may he favor us with his full bounty.
Dhātṛ rules over progeny and wealth; Dhātṛ has generated this entire world. Dhātṛ shall give a son to the sacrificer; to him we shall offer an oblation rich in ghee.
May Dhātṛ grant us wealth and an unending, forward-reaching life; may we obtain the favor of the god whose bounty is true.

(3.3.11.3.k) May Dhātṛ grant riches to the donor who desires offspring within his home, O bounteous one! May all the immortal gods, and Aditi in harmony with them, bestow their protection upon him. May all the gods, in unison, grant their favor.
May Anumati favor our sacrifice today among the gods; and may Agni, the bearer of oblations, be a source of joy for the donor.
(3.3.11.3ṃ) O Anumati, do thou indeed grant us thy approval; bestow welfare upon us. Impel us toward wisdom and skill, and prolong our lives.

May she grant her consent, she who is well-disposed, [granting] undecaying wealth accompanied by progeny. May we not incur her displeasure; may that goddess, who is easy to invoke, extend protection to us.
In whatever direction this world shines, toward whom the living beings turn in adoration; she whose lap is the wide mid-air—may that goddess, easy to invoke, grant us protection.

I invoke Rākā, who is easily summoned, with a beautiful hymn; may the fortunate one hear us and take note of us herself. May she sew together our works with a needle that does not break, and may she grant us a praiseworthy hero who bestows a hundredfold.

(3.3.11.5.q) O Rākā, those benevolent thoughts of yours which are well-formed, by which you bestow riches upon the donor—with those, come to us today with a gracious mind, O fortunate one, granting us thousandfold prosperity.
(3.3.11.5ṛ) O Sinīvālī, she who has beautiful hands!

(3.3.11.5ṣ) I repeatedly invoke with loud calls at this sacrifice Kuhū, the fortunate one, whose works are known; may she grant us the renown of the ancestors. To you, O Goddess, we pay homage with this oblation.

Kuhū, the goddess and consort of the gods and of immortality, may she take heed of this our oblation. May she bestow abundant wealth upon the donor; may she grant increase of riches to the one who knows.
(3.4.1.1) The sacrifice of one whose oblation is left over indeed fails.
(3.4.1.1) He says, "The god Sūrya for those who dwell in heaven.
(3.4.1.1) Thus, by means of Bṛhaspati and Prajāpati, he heals whatever has failed in his sacrifice.
The Rakṣases indeed cling to that animal when, having been dedicated to a single deity, it becomes larger.
He says, "O thou whose embryo is yellow," whereby he causes it to go to the gods for the purpose of driving away the Rakṣases.
"O bringer back, bring them back," he says.
(3.4.1.2) By means of the *brahman* he causes him to turn back. (3.4.1.2) "I split open thy palate," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula (*yathāyajus*).
"Of wide drops, multiform, the drop," he says. The drop is indeed offspring and cattle; verily, by means of offspring and cattle, he causes him to prosper.
(3.4.1.2) Indeed, that part of the sacrifice which is deficient goes to heaven, while that which is redundant goes to the earth.
(3.4.1.2) If one were not to appease that [redundancy], the sacrificer would meet with ruin.
"May the great Heaven and Earth be favorable to us," he says.
By means of Heaven and Earth, he pacifies whatever in the sacrifice has been deficient or redundant; the sacrificer does not come to ruin.
He covers it with ashes for the sake of making it acceptable (*svagākṛti*).

(3.4.1.3) Moreover, he is indeed the embryo of these two; verily, he places him within these two. (3.4.1.3) If he were to cut off [the portion], he would cause it to overflow; if he were not to cut off [it], he would not cut off from the animal that has been immolated.
(3.4.1.3) One should cut one portion from in front of the navel and another from behind it.
(3.4.1.4) For in front of the navel is the out-breath (*prāṇa*), and behind it is the in-breath (*apāna*).
He cuts from as much of the animal as there is [of the body].
(3.4.1.4) He offers to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.
Whatever is redundant in the sacrifice, whatever is the abundance of the animal, whatever is its prosperity—that is Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.
Thus he places the redundant upon the redundant for the pacification of the redundant.
(3.4.1.4) Gold weighing eight *pr̥ṣṭha*s is the sacrificial fee;
for this [earth] has eight feet,
and the self is the ninth.
(3.4.1.4) For the attainment of the victim:
it is wrapped with a turban inside the sheath;
for such indeed is the victim—like the fetal membrane, like the skin, like the flesh, and like the bone.
(3.4.1.4) To whatever extent the animal extends, having reached it, he wins it;
for him for whom this expiation is performed at the sacrifice, having sacrificed, he becomes more prosperous.
O Vāyu, drinker of the pure, come to us; a thousand are your teams, O possessor of all boons. To you this exhilarating juice is offered, of which, O God, you have the first draught.

(3.4.2.1.b) For intention thee, for desire thee, for prosperity thee! *Kikkiṭā*! Thy mind to Prajāpati, svāhā! *Kikkiṭā*! Thy breath to Vāyu, svāhā! *Kikkiṭā*! Thy eye to Sūrya, svāhā! *Kikkiṭā*! Thy hearing to Heaven and Earth, svāhā! *Kikkiṭā*! Thy speech to Sarasvatī, svāhā!

(3.4.2.2.c) You are the fourth, the controller, the mistress; when once the embryo entered you with the mind, you went as a mistress, a controller, to the gods. May the desires of the sacrificer come true!
(3.4.2.2ḍ) You are an unborn one, established in wealth; sit upon the earth. Stand upright, reaching toward the intermediate space; in heaven is your great light.
(3.4.2.2.e) Spinning out the thread, follow the radiance of the region. Guard the luminous paths fashioned by wisdom.
(3.4.2.2.f) Weave it without flaw, O active ones; become Manu and bring forth the divine race.
(3.4.2.2.g) You are the oblation of the mind, the color of Prajāpati; may we become sharers in your limbs.
(3.4.3.1) These two were indeed together.
(3.4.3.1) Vāyu blew them apart; (3.4.3.1) they conceived an embryo.
Soma generated him; Agni swallowed him. Prajāpati saw this cake on eight potsherds for Agni;
he offered it.
By that very means he ransomed her from Agni.
Therefore, even when one is sacrificing an animal dedicated to another deity, he should first offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni.
Having thus ransomed her from Agni, he sacrifices her.
(3.4.3.1) Because Vāyu blew apart [the world], therefore it belongs to Vāyu; (3.4.3.2) because these two [Heaven and Earth] placed the embryo therein, therefore it belongs to Heaven and Earth;
(3.4.3.2) because Soma generated it and Agni swallowed it, therefore it belongs to Agni and Soma.
Because Vāc spoke when these two were separated, she belongs to Sarasvatī;
because Prajāpati ransomed her from Agni, she belongs to Prajāpati;
indeed, this barren goat belongs to all the deities.
(3.4.3.2) One who desires prosperity should sacrifice an animal to Vāyu.
(3.4.3.2) Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity; (3.4.3.2–3.4.3.3) he approaches Vāyu himself with his own share.
He indeed leads him to prosperity.
One who is plowing and desires a firm foundation should offer an animal to Heaven and Earth.
For him, Parjanya rains from heaven, plants sprout upon this earth, and his crop becomes abundant.
(3.4.3.3) One who desires, "May I be possessed of food and be an eater of food," should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma.
(3.4.3.3) By means of Agni he wins food, and by means of Soma he wins the enjoyment of food.
(3.4.3.3) He indeed becomes possessed of food and an eater of food. (3.4.3.3) He who, though being capable of speaking, does not speak—let him offer a victim to Sarasvatī.
(3.4.3.4) Sarasvatī is indeed speech.
(3.4.3.4) He has recourse to Sarasvatī herself with her own share;
she alone bestows speech upon him.
(3.4.3.4) He who desires [something] should offer an animal to Prajāpati.
Thinking, "May I conquer what has not been conquered," he dedicates it with a verse addressed to Vāyu;
thus, having secured it from Vāyu itself, he obtains it.
"For intention thee, for desire thee," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula (*yajus*). He offers with the sound *kikkiṭā*.
(3.4.3.5) By means of the *kikkiṭākāra* cry, domestic animals delight, while wild animals flee.
(3.4.3.5) In that he offers with the *kikkiṭākāra*, it is for the support of domestic animals. He offers while the fire is being carried around [the victim].
(3.4.3.5) He causes her to go to the heavenly world while she is still living.
(3.4.3.5) "Thou art the fourth, the controller, the ruling one," he says;
thus he causes her to go among the gods.
"May the desires of the sacrificer come true," he says.
This indeed is the desire of the sacrificer: that he reaches the conclusion without being afflicted;
therefore he speaks thus.
(3.4.3.6) "Thou art unborn, abiding in wealth," he says.
(3.4.3.6) He thus establishes her firmly in these very worlds.
(3.4.3.6) "In heaven be thy great light," he says.

(3.4.3.6) "Verily, he bestows light upon him in the heavenly world. (3.4.3.6) "Stretching the thread, follow the radiance of the region," he says. (3.4.3.6) Thus, he makes these worlds luminous for him.
(3.4.3.6) "Weave it without flaw, O singers, with your song," he says.
(3.4.3.7) Whatever in the sacrifice is done in excess, this [verse] is the pacification of that very thing.
"Become Manu, beget the divine race," he says.
(3.4.3.7) Human beings indeed are offspring; he thus makes them his own today.
(3.4.3.7) "Thou art the oblation of the mind," he says, for the sake of making it *svagā*.
"May we be sharers of your limbs," he says;
verily, he invokes this very blessing.
Of this [sacrifice], there is indeed one thing that is not a place of sacrifice for the gods: when she has been seized, if a cloud arises.
(3.4.3.8) If it should rain after she has been seized, he should either cast her into the waters or consume her entirely.
(3.4.3.8) If he were to cast her into the waters, he would cause a disturbance of the sacrifice;
therefore, he should consume her entirely, for thus he bestows sensory power within himself.

(3.4.3.8) This [offering], indeed, is appropriated only by three kinds of people: those who sit for the year-long sacrifice (*saṃvatsarasad*), those who perform the thousand-fold sacrifice (*sahasrayājin*), and householders (*gṛhamedhin*).
Only they should sacrifice with this;
for them alone is it obtained.
(3.4.4.1.a) Mind and thinking, intention and purpose, the known and knowledge, the mind and the *śakvarī* verses, the new moon and the full moon, the *bṛhat* and the *rathaṃtara*.

(3.4.4.1.b) Prajāpati gave these victories to Indra, the bull, the fierce one in the battles; to him all the people bowed down, for he became fierce and worthy of invocation. (3.4.4.1) The gods and the asuras were arrayed for battle; Indra ran to Prajāpati, and he gave these victories to him; he offered them as oblations.
(3.4.4.1) From that, indeed, the gods conquered the Asuras. Because they conquered (*ajayan*), that is the reason for the name "conquests" (*jayānām*).
These [oblations] should be offered by one who is contending; he surely conquers that host.

Agni is the overlord of beings; may he protect me. Indra [is the overlord] of the eldest; Yama [of the earth]; Vāyu of the atmosphere; Sūrya of the sky; Candramas of the stars; Bṛhaspati of sacred knowledge (*brahman*); Mitra of truths; Varuṇa of the waters; the ocean of rivers; food of sovereignties—may that overlord protect me. Soma of plants; Savitṛ of instigations; Rudra of cattle; Tvaṣṭṛ of forms; Viṣṇu of mountains; the Maruts, the overlords of hosts—may they protect me.
(3.4.5.1.b) O fathers, grandfathers, further ancestors, and nearer ones, our forefathers and great-forefathers, protect me here!

(3.4.5.1.c) In this sacred knowledge (*brahman*), in this sovereignty (*kṣatra*), in this blessing (*āśis*), in this office of domestic priest (*purodhā*), in this rite (*karman*), and in this invocation of the gods (*devahūti*).
Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did that too.
The gods perceived these *abhyātāna* formulas;
they performed them.
That which was the ritual act of the gods succeeded;
that of the Asuras did not succeed.
Therefore, one should offer oblations in whatever ritual act one desires to accomplish.
(3.4.6.1) One indeed prospers by that rite.

Because the All-gods (viśve devāḥ) brought them together, they are called the Abhyātānas and belong to the All-gods. Because Prajāpati bestowed the Jayas, they are called the Jayas and belong to Prajāpati.
(3.4.6.2) Because they took possession of the kingdom by means of the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*, that is the reason for the *rāṣṭrabhṛts* being called *rāṣṭrabhṛts*.
(3.4.6.2) Those gods enveloped the Asuras with the *abhyātānas*, conquered them with the *jayas*, and took possession of the kingdom with the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*.
(3.4.6.2) Because the gods enveloped the Asuras with the *abhyātānas*, that is the reason for the *abhyātānas* being called *abhyātānas*.

Because they conquered by means of the *jayas*, that is the reason for the *jayas*' name "conquerors. Because they took possession of the kingdom by means of the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*, that is the reason for the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*' name "kingdom-sustainers. Thereupon, the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
(3.4.6.2) He who has rivals should offer these oblations.

By means of the *abhyātāna* formulas, he stretches out against his rivals; by means of the *jaya* formulas, he conquers; by means of the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* formulas, he takes possession of the kingdom. He prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated.

(3.4.7.1.a) Agni, the upholder of *ṛta*, whose abode is *ṛta*, is the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the plants, named Ūrjas. May he protect this spiritual power (*brahman*) and this ruling power (*kṣatra*); may they protect this spiritual power and this ruling power. To him, *svāhā*! To them, *svāhā*!

(3.4.7.1.b) Saṃhita, the possessor of all melodies, Sūrya is the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the rays, the Āyus. (3.4.7.1.c) Suṣumna, the sun-rayed one, Candramas is the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the stars, the Bekurīs.
(3.4.7.1ḍ) Bhujyu Suparṇa, the sacrifice, is the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the Dakṣiṇās, called Stavās.
(3.4.7.1.e) Prajāpati Viśvakarman, the mind, is the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the Ṛks and Sāmans, called Vahnīs.
(3.4.7.2.f) Iṣira Viśvavyacas, the wind, is the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the waters, called Mudās.

(3.4.7.2.g) O Lord of the world, you whose dwellings are above and here on earth—grant us prosperity, the increase of wealth, heroic strength, and well-being for the year. (3.4.7.2.h) Parameṣṭhin is the overlord; Mṛtyu is the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the Viśvas, the Bhuvās, the Sukṣitis, the Subhūtis, the Bhadrakṛts, and the Suvarvats. (3.4.7.2.i) Parjanya is the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the lightnings, the Rucs.
(3.4.7.2.k) Dūreheti, the merciless one; (3.4.7.3) Mṛtyu is the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the Bhīruvas.

Cāru, the wretched-looking one; Kāma is the Gandharva; his Apsarases are named Śocayantīs (the Sorrows). May he protect this priesthood and nobility; may they protect this priesthood and nobility. To him, svāhā! To them, svāhā!
(3.4.7.3.m) O Lord of the world, you whose dwellings are above and here on earth—for this priesthood and this nobility, grant wide and great protection.

(3.4.8.1) They should be offered for one who desires a kingdom; for the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings are indeed the kingdom. By means of the kingdom itself, he wins the kingdom for him; he becomes the very kingdom. (3.4.8.1) They should be offered for oneself; for the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings are the kingdom, offspring are the kingdom, cattle are the kingdom, and that which makes one the best is the kingdom. By means of the kingdom itself, he wins the kingdom; he becomes the most excellent among his peers.

(3.4.8.1) They should be offered for one who desires a village. The *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings are indeed the kingdom, and kinsmen are the kingdom. By means of the kingdom, he wins for himself the kingdom and his kinsmen; he thus becomes a possessor of a village. (3.4.8.2) He offers on the gambling-ground. On the gambling-ground itself he wins his kinsmen for him; once won, they wait upon him. (3.4.8.2) They should be offered at the front of the chariot for one who desires vigor. The *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings are indeed vigor, and the chariot is vigor. By means of vigor, he wins vigor for himself; he thus becomes vigorous.

(3.4.8.2) For one who has been expelled from his kingdom, the oblations should be offered for him; he should say to as many chariots as he possesses, "Yoke them!"—verily, he thus yokes the kingdom for him.

(3.4.8.3) The oblations of one whose kingdom is not in order are indeed unprepared. Having loosened the right wheel of his own chariot, he should offer [the oblation] over the axle-rod; thus he prepares his oblations, and as they become prepared, his kingdom follows in being prepared.

(3.4.8.3) When battle is joined, these [oblations] are to be offered. The *rāṣṭrabhṛt* (kingdom-sustainers) are indeed the kingdom; for those who engage in battle are indeed contending for the kingdom. He for whom they offer first becomes the victor and wins that battle. The fuel consists of *māndhūka* wood. (3.4.8.4) As the embers roll back, they envelop the army of his enemies.

(3.4.8.4) For one who is going mad, these [oblations] should be offered. It is the Gandharvas and Apsarases who drive him mad; for these *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings are indeed the Gandharvas and Apsarases. He offers with the words, "To him svāhā! To them svāhā!"—by this very means he pacifies them.

(3.4.8.4) The fuel consists of wood from the *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *plakṣa* trees; for these are the dwellings of the Gandharvas and Apsarases. Thus, he pacifies them in their own abode. (3.4.8.5)
(3.4.8.5) By one practicing exorcism, they are to be offered in reverse order; thus he repels his vital breaths from behind, and thereby he lays him low with whatever means he chooses.

He offers in a self-made hollow or in a cleft; for this is seized by Nirṛti, and so he causes Nirṛti herself to seize him. With that which is cruel in speech he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call; he cuts him down with the very cruelty of speech, and he swiftly meets with ruin.

(3.4.8.5) For whomsoever he should desire, "May I take away his food," he should lie down on his back in that person's assembly hall and gather blades of grass while reciting, "O Lord of the World. Prajāpati is indeed the Lord of the World; verily, through Prajāpati, he takes away that person's food. He says, "Here I take away the food of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so"; thus he truly takes away his food. He gathers it with six [verses]; for there are six seasons. Having taken away the food through Prajāpati, the seasons hand it over to him.

(3.4.8.7) If one's eldest kinsman should be deprived of his position, one should settle him on dry ground, cook a *brahmaudana* of four *śarāva*-measures, and offer it to him. For the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings are the height (*varṣman*), and dry ground is the height; verily by means of the height he causes him to attain the height among his equals. It consists of four *śarāva*-measures; verily he finds firm support in the quarters. It is prepared with milk; verily he bestows luster upon him. He draws it up for the sake of its being cooked. It contains clarified butter for the sake of its being fit for sacrifice. Four *ārṣeya* priests consume it; verily he offers in the light of the quarters.

(3.4.9.1) One desiring offspring should offer the Devikā oblations. The Devikās are indeed the *chandas* meters; and offspring are indeed like the *chandas* meters. By means of the *chandas* meters, he procreates offspring for him. He makes Dhātṛ the first [deity]; by that, he creates a pair. Anumati gives her consent after it; Rākā bestows [the gift]; Sinīvālī procreates. When the offspring have been born, Kuhū establishes speech among them.

(3.4.9.1) One who desires cattle should offer these very oblations; for the Devikās are the meters, and cattle are indeed like the meters. By means of the meters, he procreates cattle for him. He makes Dhātṛ the first; by that, he causes [the seed] to be sown. Anumati gives her approval for him; Rākā grants [the gift]; Sinīvālī brings forth the cattle; and by means of Kuhū, he establishes the cattle once they have been born.

One who desires a village should offer these very same [oblations]. The Devikās are indeed the meters; a village is, as it were, the meters. By means of the meters, he wins a village for him. He places Dhātṛ in the middle; verily, he establishes him in the middle of the village.

(3.4.9.3) One who has been long ill should offer these very oblations. The Devikās are indeed the metres; and the metres, verily, take pity upon him who is long ill. By means of the metres he makes him free from disease. He places Dhātṛ in the middle; for that which is disordered in the middle of one who is long ill, he thereby sets right by placing [Dhātṛ] in the middle.

(3.4.9.3) These same [oblations] he should offer for one whom the sacrifice does not approach. The Devikās are indeed the meters; truly, the meters do not incline toward him whom the sacrifice does not approach. He makes Dhātṛ the first; thus he places the meters at the very beginning for him, and the sacrifice inclines toward him.

One who has already sacrificed should offer these very same [oblations]. The minor deities (*devikā*) are indeed the *chandas* meters; for the *chandas* of one who has sacrificed have, as it were, become exhausted. By making Dhātṛ the last [deity], he secures for himself the *chandas* meters which are no longer exhausted from above, and the subsequent sacrifice inclines toward him.

One for whom wisdom does not come should offer these very same oblations. The Devikās are indeed the meters; truly, the meters do not incline toward him for whom wisdom does not incline. He makes Dhātṛ the first [deity]; thus he places the meters at the very beginning for him, and wisdom inclines toward him.

(3.4.9.5) One should offer these very [oblations]. (3.4.9.6) He who desires luster should offer them; for the Devikās are the meters, and luster is indeed like the meters. Verily, by means of the meters he bestows luster upon him. They are prepared with milk; verily, they bestow luster upon him. He places Dhātṛ in the middle; verily, he bestows luster upon him from the middle.

(3.4.9.6) Anumati is the Gāyatrī, Rākā is the Triṣṭubh, Sinīvālī is the Jagatī, Kuhū is the Anuṣṭubh, and Dhātṛ is the Vaṣaṭ-call. Rākā is the bright fortnight, Kuhū is the dark fortnight, Sinīvālī is the new moon, Anumati is the full moon, and Dhātṛ is the moon.

(3.4.9.6) Eight. (3.4.9.7) The Vasus are eight; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables. The Rudras are eleven; the Triṣṭubh has eleven syllables. The Ādityas are twelve; the Jagatī has twelve syllables. Prajāpati is the Anuṣṭubh; Dhātṛ is the Vaṣaṭ-call.

(3.4.9.7) These Devikās indeed are all the metres, all the deities, and the *vaṣaṭ*-call. If he were to offer them all together, they would be liable to burn him up. Having offered two first, he should offer the third to Dhātṛ; likewise he should offer the remaining two. Thus they do not burn him, and moreover, he attains through them whatever desire for which they are offered.

(3.4.10.1.a) O Lord of the Dwelling, acknowledge us! Be a gracious refuge for us and free from disease. Whatever we implore of you, accept that favorably; be a source of well-being for our bipeds and well-being for our quadrupeds.
O Vāstoṣpati, may we be united with your auspicious, delightful, and path-providing assembly. Grant us the best [fortune] in rest and in exertion. Do you all protect us always with blessings.

(3.4.10.1) In that he performs the Agnihotra offering morning and evening, those oblations are indeed the bricks he lays down. (3.4.10.2) For the sacrificer who has established the sacred fires, the days and nights are his bricks; in that he offers morning and evening, having obtained the days and nights, he makes them into bricks and lays them down.
He offers ten times at one place; the Virāj consists of ten syllables; having obtained the Virāj, he makes it into a brick and lays it down.

(3.4.10.2) Moreover, he attains the sacrifice through the *virāj* itself; his fire-altar becomes both piled and unpiled. Therefore, when he departs after staying for ten nights, that is the sacrificial site (*yajñavāstu*); anything prior to that is not a sacrificial site. (3.4.10.3) Rudra, indeed, is Vāstoṣpati. If he were to depart without having offered the oblation to Vāstoṣpati, Agni, becoming Rudra, would rise up after him and slay him. He offers the oblation to Vāstoṣpati; verily, by means of his own portion, he pacifies him, and the sacrificer does not come to ruin.

(3.4.10.3) If he were to offer while [the horse] is yoked, it would be just as if one were to offer an oblation at a dwelling where [the owner] has already departed; if he were to offer while it is unyoked, it would be just as if one were to offer an oblation while at rest. In that case, his offering to Vāstoṣpati would be as if unoffered. (3.4.10.4) The right [horse] is yoked and the left is unyoked. Then he offers the oblation to Vāstoṣpati; thus he performs both and pacifies it entirely without omission. If he were to offer with only one [verse], he would perform a *darvihoma*; rather, having recited the *puro'nuvākyā*, he offers with the *yājyā* for the sake of its being accompanied by the gods.

(3.4.10.4) If he were to place [the fire] on what has been burnt, he would cause Rudra to ascend after his house; if he were to depart without having thoroughly cleansed the embers, that would be just like a sacrificial ruin or a conflagration. (3.4.10.4) With the words, "This is thy womb, fit for the season," he causes [the fire] to ascend into the two kindling woods. (3.4.10.5) This indeed is the womb of Agni; verily, he causes him to ascend into his own womb. Now, moreover, they say: "If [the fire], having ascended into the two kindling woods, should be lost, his fire would perish; it would have to be established again."
"O Agni, with that body of yours which is worthy of sacrifice, come and ascend here"—with these words, he causes [the fire] to ascend into himself.
For the sacrificer is indeed the womb of Agni; thus he causes him to ascend into his own womb.
(3.4.11.1.a) O Agni, you, the sage, the young master of the house, bestow great vital strength upon the donor, O God.

Agni, the bearer of oblations, our ageless father, is pervasive, radiant, and beautiful to behold for us. With your excellent household-fire, shine forth upon us nourishments; measure out for us glorious renown according to our desire.
And you, O Soma, being our will, let us not die, but live on—you who are the beloved singer of praise, the Lord of the Forest.

Brahman among the gods, the pathfinder of the poets, the seer among the wise, the buffalo among wild beasts, the falcon among vultures, the axe among the forests—Soma flows over the filter, singing aloud.
Today we choose with hymns Savitṛ, the lord of the good, who belongs to all the gods, whose impulse is true.
(3.4.11.2.f) Moving through the true realm, establishing both the immortal and the mortal, the god Savitṛ comes on his golden chariot, beholding all beings.
(3.4.11.2.g) As Aditi may grant us Rudra’s favor for our cattle, for our men, for our kine, and for our offspring.

(3.4.11.2) Do not harm us in our children or grandchildren, nor in our life; do not harm us in our cattle, nor in our horses. O Rudra, do not slay our heroes in your anger. Bearing oblations, we shall worship you with homage. (3.4.11.3) Do not harm us in our children or grandchildren, nor in our life; do not harm us in our cattle, nor in our horses. O Rudra, do not slay our heroes in your anger. Bearing oblations, we shall worship you with homage.
Like water-dwelling birds guarding their young, like the thundering roars of a rain-cloud, like waves breaking from the mountains, the hymns have resounded toward Bṛhaspati with joy.
Like swans, with his shouting companions, Bṛhaspati cast off his stone-made bonds; he bellowed toward the cows, and being wise, he both praised them aloud and sang for them.
O Indra, bring us wealth that is winning, victorious, ever-conquering, and most excellent, for our protection.

(3.4.11.4ṃ) O you who are invoked by many, you have utterly subdued your enemies; let your supreme strength be here, and let your bounty be present. O Indra, become [the giver] with your right hand; you are the lord of the wealthy rivers.
O Indra of noble wisdom, you were born instantly grown great for the drinking of the pressed juice, for the sake of supreme sovereignty.

(3.4.11.4.o) O Indra, through the sacred word (*brahman*) you have become great; you have become worthy of sacrifice at all libations (*savana*). You have become the shaker of men in every battle, and the most excellent counsel. (3.4.11.5) O you who belong to all people!
The glory of the god Mitra, the sustainer of the people, is winning, true, and most wonderful in renown.
Mitra, knowing all, impels men; Mitra has supported both the earth and the sky. Mitra gazes unblinking upon the people. Let us offer an oblation rich in ghee to the Truthful One.

(3.4.11.5ṛ) May that mortal, O Mitra, be foremost who bestows offerings upon you, O Āditya, according to your law. Protected by you, he is neither slain nor conquered; no distress reaches him, neither from near nor from afar.
For even as we, O God Varuṇa, measure out thy law day by day, just as subjects [follow] their king.
Whatever offense we humans commit against the divine host, O Varuṇa, whether through lack of awareness or by violating your laws—O God, do not harm us because of that sin.
Whatever wrongs the gamblers have committed in play, whether they be true or whether we do not know them—loose all those like loosened bonds, O God; then, O Varuṇa, may we be dear to you.
Full behind and full before, the Paurṇamāsī has triumphed from the midst as well. Upon her, the gods dwelling together shall rejoice here on the highest firmament.

(3.5.1.1.b) That portion which the gods, dwelling together in greatness, assigned to you at the new moon—O you who possess all boons, fulfill our sacrifice with that; O fortunate one, bestow upon us wealth accompanied by heroic sons.

(3.5.1.1.c) She who brings us home, who gathers together all treasures, causing all forms and riches to enter [us]; may she, the fortunate one, bestowing thousandfold prosperity, come to us with splendor, in harmony [with us].

(3.5.1.2ḍ) O Agni and Soma, foremost in heroic power, quicken here the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas! Delight in the midday full-moon sacrifice, you who have grown great through sacred prayer and the attainment of good deeds; then bestow upon us wealth together with heroic sons.
(3.5.1.2) The Ādityas and the Aṅgirases established the sacred fires; they desired to obtain the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

(3.5.1.2) Of those Aṅgirases, the oblation had already been set aside, but then the Ādityas saw these two offerings and offered them. Thereupon, indeed, they obtained the New and Full Moon sacrifices first.
(3.5.1.3) One who is about to perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices should offer these two offerings beforehand; thus he obtains the New and Full Moon sacrifices directly.
(3.5.1.3) The exponents of the Veda say:
"Only he should perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices who knows both their forward order and their reverse order.
(3.5.1.3) That which follows after the New Moon is the forward order; that which precedes the Full Moon is the reverse order.
(3.5.1.3) If one were to sacrifice the Full Moon [offering] first, he would be sacrificing them in reverse order; following that waning moon, he himself would waste away.

(3.5.1.4) He should offer two oblations to Sarasvatī beforehand. The New Moon is indeed Sarasvatī; thus he sacrifices them in the proper order, and following that waxing moon, he himself prospers. (3.5.1.4) Beforehand, he should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a cake on twelve potsherds to Sarasvant.
(3.5.1.4) In that it belongs to Agni—Agni, indeed, is the mouth of the sacrifice—he places prosperity at the very beginning of the sacrifice.

(3.5.1.4) In that it belongs to Viṣṇu—Viṣṇu, indeed, is the sacrifice—he extends the sacrifice after having grasped it. There is a pap for Sarasvatī and a cake on twelve potsherds for Sarasvant; the new moon is Sarasvatī and the full moon is Sarasvant; he thus directly grasps those two and prospers through them.
The offering to Sarasvatī consists of twelve potsherds for the sake of pairing and procreation;
a pair of cattle is the sacrificial fee for the sake of prosperity.
(3.5.2.1) The seers did not see Indra face to face. Vasiṣṭha saw him face to face.
He said, "I shall tell you the Brāhmaṇa, so that with you as their domestic priest, offspring will be propagated; but do not speak of me to the other seers."
He spoke these *stomabhāga* formulas to him;
from that, creatures with Vasiṣṭha as their domestic priest were born. Therefore, a descendant of Vasiṣṭha should be made the *brahman* priest; thus he is indeed propagated.
(3.5.2.1) "Thou art a ray; for habitation thee, quicken the habitation," he says. The gods are indeed the habitation; verily, he announces the sacrifice to the gods. (3.5.2.2) "Thou art an impulse;

for dharma thee, quicken dharma," he says. Men are indeed dharma; verily, he announces the sacrifice to men. "Thou art a following; for the sky thee, quicken the sky," he says; verily, he announces the sacrifice to these worlds.
(3.5.2.2) "Thou art a support; for rain thee, quicken the rain," he says; verily, he secures rain. (3.5.2.3) He secures rain.
"Flowing on, flow around," he says for the sake of pairing.

"Thou art the eager one; for the Vasus, thee! Quicken the Vasus! he says. There are eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, and twelve Ādityas—so many indeed are the gods; it is to them that he announces the sacrifice. "Thou art vigor; for the Pitṛs, thee! Quicken the Pitṛs! he says; thus he extends the sacrifice in accordance with the divine Pitṛs.

(3.5.2.3) “You are a thread; for offspring, you, the thread, quicken offspring,” he says. Thus, he extends the offspring along after the ancestors. (3.5.2.4) “You are a conqueror of armies; for cattle, you, the conqueror, quicken cattle,” he says. Thus, he extends the cattle along after the offspring. (3.5.2.4) “You are wealthy; for plants, you, the wealthy one, quicken plants,” he says. Thus, he establishes the cattle within the plants.
(3.5.2.4) "Thou art the victorious one, with the yoked stones; for Indra thee! Quicken Indra! he says, for the sake of victory. "Thou art the overlord; for breath thee! Quicken breath! he says;

verily, he places breaths in the offspring. (3.5.2.5) "Thou art the threefold; thou art the increasing," he says, for the sake of pairing. "Thou art the ascending; thou art the descending," he says, for the sake of procreation.
"You are Vasu-ka, you are Veṣa-śrī, you are Vasyaṣṭi," he says for the sake of firm establishment.

(3.5.3.1.a) With Agni as my god, I conquer the hostile armies; with the Gāyatrī metre, the Trivṛt hymn-form, the Rathantara chant, and the *vaṣaṭ*-call as my thunderbolt, I cast down my previously born rivals, I press them low, I drive them away. In this dwelling, in this world of earth, him who hates us and whom we hate, I step over them with the stride of Viṣṇu.
(3.5.3.1.b) With the god Indra, I conquer the hostile armies with the *triṣṭubh* metre, the fifteenfold *stoma*, the *bṛhat* *sāman*, and the *vaṣaṭ*-call as my thunderbolt.

(3.5.3.2.c) With all the gods, I conquer the hostile armies with the *jagatī* metre, the seventeenfold *stoma*, the *vāmadevya* *sāman*, and the *vaṣaṭ*-call as my thunderbolt—[conquering] those born later.
(3.5.3.2ḍ) United with Indra, may we overcome those who attack us, slaying the resistless enemies.

(3.5.3.2.e) O Agni, that which is your brilliance, through that may I become brilliant; that which is your luster, through that may I become lustrous; that which is your heat, through that may I become hot.

(3.5.4.1.a) Those gods who are destroyers of the sacrifice and stealers of the sacrifice, who dwell upon the earth—may Agni protect me from them; may we go to the world of those who have performed good deeds.

(3.5.4.1.b) We have come, O Mitra and Varuṇa, to you who are worthy of choice; yours is the portion of the nights that exists. Grasping the firmament in the world of the well-done, upon the third back, in the luminous realm of heaven.

(3.5.4.1.c) Those gods who are destroyers of the sacrifice and stealers of the sacrifice, who dwell in the intermediate space—may Vāyu protect me from them; may we go to those who have performed good deeds.

(3.5.4.1ḍ) O Savitṛ, those nights of yours which travel between heaven and earth along the paths of the gods—may we, ascending to the light of heaven with all our households and progeny, cross over the regions.
(3.5.4.2.e) Those gods who are slayers of the sacrifice and stealers of the sacrifice who dwell in heaven—may Sūrya protect me from them; may we, the doers of good deeds, go [to the world of light].

(3.5.4.2.f) O Jātavedas, with that supreme oblation wherewith you brought forth the waters for Indra—with that, O Agni, do thou cause this man to prosper; bestow upon him preeminence among his kinsmen.

(3.5.4.2) There are indeed gods who destroy the sacrifice and those who steal the sacrifice. (3.5.4.3) They dwell in these worlds, seizing and plundering the property of whoever gives and whoever sacrifices. "Those gods who, as destroyers of the sacrifice, dwell upon the earth, those in the intermediate space, and those in heaven"—by saying this, he passes beyond these very worlds and goes to the heavenly world together with his household and his cattle.

(3.5.4.3) Indeed, from one who has sacrificed with Soma, both the deities and the sacrifice depart. He should offer a cake on five potsherds to Agni as a concluding oblation (*udavasānīya*). Agni is all the deities; (3.5.4.4) the sacrifice is fivefold. Thus he wins back both the deities and the sacrifice. (3.5.4.4) Agni is connected to the *gāyatrī*, and his metre is the *gāyatrī*. If he makes it a cake on five potsherds, he deprives him of his metre. It should be made on eight potsherds. The *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables; Agni is connected to the *gāyatrī*, and his metre is the *gāyatrī*. Thus he unites him with his own metre.
The invitatory and offering verses are in the *paṅkti* metre; the sacrifice is fivefold; thus he does not depart from the sacrifice.

(3.5.5.1.a) May the god Sūrya protect me from the gods; may Vāyu protect me from the intermediate space; may Agni, the sacrificer, protect my eyes. O impetuous one, O strength, O Savitṛ, you who belong to all people—O Soma, with these names we shall worship you; with these names, O Soma, we shall worship you. (3.5.5.1.b) I am above, I am below; by means of light, I have dispelled the darkness. That which is the intermediate space—that has become my father. I have beheld the sun on both sides. May I become the highest among my equals.

(3.5.5.2.c) From the ocean and from the intermediate space, may Prajāpati cause the reservoir to flow; may Indra pour it forth, and may the Maruts cause it to rain. (3.5.5.2ḍ) Make the earth swell; burst open this celestial cloud. Grant us of the celestial water; O Lord, release the leather bag.

(3.5.5.2.e) These Ādityas are indeed cattle, and this Agni is Rudra. By casting the plants into the fire and offering the Āditya oblation, he interposes the cattle from Rudra; moreover, he establishes the cattle within the plants themselves.

(3.5.5.3.f) The sage extends the path of the sacrifice upon the back of the firmament, in the luminous realm of heaven—by which path you carry the oblation as you go as a messenger from here, wise and more bountiful than the one there.

(3.5.5.3.g) O Agni, those kindling-sticks of thine which exist on the earth, upon the sacrificial grass, and in the sun—let them go to this oblation of clarified butter, providing protection for the god-seeking sacrificer.
(3.5.5.3) Desiring heroic strength, the increase of wealth, and possession of good horses—being greeted with a welcome by Bṛhaspati and by wealth, stand firm for me, the sacrificer!
(3.5.6.1.a) I bind you together with milk and ghee; I bind you together with the waters and the plants. I bind you together today with progeny; as one consecrated, may you win strength for us.
(3.5.6.1.b) Let the wife of Brahmaṇaspati go forward; let her sit upon the altar with splendor.
(3.5.6.1.c) Then may I, following my desire, enter here into my own world.
(3.5.6.1ḍ) With good offspring and as excellent wives, we have approached you, O Agni—the subduer of rivals—who are yourself inviolable and cannot be deceived.
(3.5.6.1.e) I loosen this bond of Varuṇa which the kindly one has bound upon me. In the womb of Dhātṛ, in the world of good deeds, I make it pleasant for me together with my husband.

(3.5.6.2.f) Go forth! Come out! Follow the lovely ones of *ṛta*. May Agni lead you at the front; may Aditi grant you the middle. You are released by Rudra; your name is Youthful (*yuvan*); do not harm me!
(3.5.6.2.g) For the Vasus, for the Rudras, for the Ādityas—for all you gods—I take the foot-washing waters. (3.5.6.2.h) For the sacrifice, I set down for you the foot-washing waters.
(3.5.6.2.i) Of you, the all-encompassing, the possessor of all, the possessor of virility— (3.5.6.3) O Agni, may I, under your auspicious gaze, place within me all generative powers.

(3.5.6.3.k) The sacrifice has gone to the gods; the goddesses have bestowed blessings upon the gods for this sacrifice. For this pressing sacrificer, may there be blessings consecrated with *svāhā*. Standing in the ocean, take your place after the Gandharva; in the flight of the wind, may you, the *iḍ*s, be praised.

The *vaṣaṭ*-call indeed severed the head of the Gāyatrī; its sap flew away and entered the earth, and it became the *khadira* tree. He whose offering-spoon (*sruva*) is made of *khadira* cuts [the portion] with the very sap of the meters; thus his oblations become full of sap.

(3.5.7.1) In the third heaven from here, Soma was. Gāyatrī fetched him; his leaf (*parṇa*) was torn off, and that became the *parṇa* tree. That is the reason for the name of the *parṇa* tree. For whomsoever the *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*, (3.5.7.2) his oblations become related to Soma; the gods relish his oblations. The gods, indeed, were discussing the *brahman*; the *parṇa* tree overheard it. It is truly "Well-heard" (*suśravas*) by name for whomsoever the *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*; he does not hear an evil report.

The *parṇa* tree is indeed the *brahman*, and the *maruts* are the *viś*. The *aśvattha* tree is food, and the *māruta* is food. When one has a *juhū* ladle made of *parṇa* wood and an *upabhṛt* ladle made of *aśvattha* wood, one wins food through the *brahman* itself; moreover, one places the *brahman* upon the *viś*.

The *parṇa* tree is the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*), and the *aśvattha* is the people (*viś*). In that the *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood and the *upabhṛt* ladle is made of *aśvattha* wood, he places the kingdom upon the people.

Prajāpati indeed offered oblations. Wherever that oblation found its firm foundation, from there the *vikaṅkata* tree arose; from there he created offspring. For him whose *dhruvā* ladle is made of *vikaṅkata*, his oblations find their firm foundation, and moreover, he himself is procreated.
This is indeed the form of the *sruva* ladles; for him whose offering-ladles (*sruc*) have this form, all the forms of cattle attend upon him, and no formless thing is born within his self.

(3.5.8.1.a) You are taken with a support; for Prajāpati, the luminous, I take you, the luminous; for Dakṣa, the increaser of skill, [I take you] offered to the gods whose tongue is Agni, who live by the Truth, who have Indra as their eldest, Varuṇa as their king, Vātāpi as their breath, and Parjanya as their soul; for heaven you, for the atmosphere you, for the earth you!
(3.5.8.1.b) O Indra, strike away the mind of the one who hates us, strike away the one who seeks to overcome us; strike away whoever acts as our enemy, strike him down!

For out-breathing thee, for in-breathing thee, for diffused-breathing thee; for what exists thee, for what does not exist thee; for the waters thee, for the plants thee; for all beings thee. From whom offspring were born unimpaired—to that Prajāpati, the all-encompassing, the luminous, I offer thee, the luminous one.
Whatever deity the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer have bypassed, from that they are cut off.
They should draw the *dadhigraha* cup for Prajāpati;
Prajāpati is all the deities.
(3.5.9.1) They indeed conceal [the offering] from the deities.
(3.5.9.1) This is the eldest of the cups;
he for whom it is drawn attains preeminence.
(3.5.9.1) This cup is indeed the form of all the deities.
For whomsoever this is drawn, all the forms of cattle attend upon him. (3.5.9.2) "Thou art taken with a support; for Prajāpati, the luminous, I take thee, the luminous," he says.
(3.5.9.2) He thus makes him the light among his equals.
(3.5.9.2) "To those whose tongue is Agni, who live by the Ṛta," he says.
(3.5.9.2) For so many indeed are the deities.
He draws it from all of them;
he says, "O Indra, [drive] away the mind of the hater," for the purpose of driving away the rival.
"Into out-breath for thee, into in-breath for thee," he says;
verily, he places the vital breaths in the sacrificer. "To him, Prajāpati, the wide-giving, the luminous, I offer thee, the luminous," he says.
Prajāpati is all the deities;
he offers him to all the deities indeed.
One should take a portion of clarified butter for one who desires splendor.
Clarified butter is indeed brilliance;
he becomes brilliant indeed.
One desiring spiritual luster should draw the Soma-cup.
Soma is indeed spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); he who performs [this rite] becomes possessed of spiritual luster.
One who desires cattle should draw the *dadhi-graha* cup.
Curd is indeed strength;
cattle are strength. By means of strength, he wins for him strength and cattle.
(3.5.10.1.a) All turn their will toward you, when these helpers become twice or thrice [in number]. Mix the sweeter with the sweet; then, indeed, contend well with honey against honey.
(3.5.10.1.b) "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Prajāpati. This is thy womb; for Prajāpati, thee!

(3.5.10.1) He draws the Prāṇagrahas (the breath-cups). Of such extent indeed is all that exists as these cups, the Stomas, the metres, the Pṛṣṭhas, and the directions—as much as there is, that he secures.

(3.5.10.2) In former times, the eldest Brāhmaṇas, knowing this, performed these [rites]; therefore, all the directions became conquered by them. For whomsoever these are drawn, he attains pre-eminence and conquers the directions.

Five are taken; there are five directions; thus they prosper in all directions. Nine each are taken; there are indeed nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person; verily, they bestow vital breaths upon the sacrificers. They are taken at the introductory (*prāyaṇīya*) and the concluding (*udayanīya*) rites; for the *prāṇagraha* cups are indeed the vital breaths. By means of the vital breaths they set forth, and by means of the vital breaths they rise up.

On the tenth day, the Prāṇagrahas are drawn. The Prāṇagrahas are indeed the vital breaths. Truly, offspring depart from the vital breaths when the Vāmadevya departs from its womb; for on the tenth day, the Vāmadevya departs from its womb. When they are drawn on the tenth day, offspring do not depart from the vital breaths.
(3.5.11.1.a) Bring forth the god Jātavedas with divine thought; may he carry our oblations to him in due order.
(3.5.11.1.b) And this very one, seeking the gods, is led forth as the Hotṛ for the sacrifice; like a well-guarded chariot, he, glowing with heat, takes heed by himself.
(3.5.11.1.c) This Agni protects [us] as if from an immortal birth; a god more powerful than even power itself, he has been made for the sake of life.
In the place of Iḍā, upon the navel of the earth, we establish you, O Jātavedas Agni, so that you may carry the oblation.

(3.5.11.2.e) O Agni of beautiful countenance, together with all the gods, sit down first upon this wool-lined seat; lead the sacrifice, nest-like and rich in ghee, successfully to Savitṛ for the sacrificer.

(3.5.11.2.f) Sit down, O Hotṛ, in your own place; being wise, establish the sacrifice in the womb of good action. As one who pleases the gods, worship the gods with the oblation; O Agni, bestow great vitality upon the sacrificer.

The Hotṛ, knowing his place, has sat down upon the seat of the Hotṛ—resplendent, shining, most skillful, the protector of infallible vows, the most excellent Agni with a pure tongue, the bringer of a thousandfold wealth.

(3.5.11.2) You are the messenger; you indeed are our protector from afar. O Bull, you are the leader to better fortune. O Agni, for the extension of our offspring and our bodies, be a watchful, shining guardian. (3.5.11.3) You are the messenger; you indeed are our protector from afar. O Bull, you are the leader to better fortune. O Agni, for the extension of our offspring and our bodies, be a watchful, shining guardian.
(3.5.11.3.i) O God Savitṛ, sovereign lord of all desirable things, we ever seek a portion from you, O bounteous one.
May the great Heaven and Earth bedew this sacrifice for us; may they nourish us with their sustenances.
(3.5.11.3ḷ) From the lotus, O Agni, Atharvan churned you forth from the head of the entire universe, he the priest.

(3.5.11.3) And him, the slayer of Vṛtra, the shatterer of forts, did the seer Dadhyañc, the son of Atharvan, kindle. (3.5.11.4) And him, the slayer of Vṛtra, the shatterer of forts, did the seer Dadhyañc, the son of Atharvan, kindle.
The Pāthya Vṛṣan has kindled you, the greatest slayer of Dasyus, the winner of wealth in every battle.
(3.5.11.4.o) And let the people say: "Agni has arisen as the slayer of Vṛtra, the winner of wealth in every battle."
Him whom they bear like a child just born, or like a ring in the hand—Agni, who performs the sacrifice well for the people.
Bring forth the god, the best finder of wealth, for the feast of the gods; let him sit down in his own place.
Sharpen the beloved guest who has been born within Jātavedas; [sharpen] the master of the house upon his pleasant seat.
By Agni is Agni kindled—the seer, the lord of the house, the youth, the bearer of oblations, whose mouth is the sacrificial ladle.
For you, O Agni, are kindled by fire, by the sage through the sage, by the being through the being, and by the friend through the friend.
They groom him, the one of pure wisdom, the leader in battles, the prize-winner in his own dwellings.
With sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; those were the first ordinances. Those great ones attained the firmament where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide.
Harnessing his mind first, Savitṛ, having realized the intentions for the sake of truth, and having perceived Agni as the light, brought him forth from the earth.
Having yoked the gods with his mind, as they go toward the sun through the sky with their thought, Savitṛ impels those who are about to produce the great light.
(4.1.1.1.c) With a concentrated mind, we [act] at the impulse of the god Savitṛ, for the sake of the power that leads to the heavenly world.

(4.1.1.1ḍ) The inspired poets yoke their minds and yoke their thoughts for the sake of the great, inspired, wise one; he alone, the knower of all ways, ordains the priestly functions. (4.1.1.2) Great is the praise of the divine Savitṛ!

(4.1.1.2.e) I yoke for you both an ancient prayer with prostrations; the hymns go forth like suns upon their paths. All the sons of immortality listen, they who have taken up their stations in the celestial realms.

(4.1.1.2.f) Others have followed after his departure, as the gods sang the praise of the greatness of the god; he who has measured out the earthly realms, that god Savitṛ, the steed Etaśa, by his majesty.

(4.1.1.2.g) O divine Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice; impel the lord of the sacrifice for his good fortune. May the celestial Gandharva, the purifier of intentions, purify our intention. May the Lord of Speech make our speech sweet today.
O divine Savitṛ, impel this sacrifice of ours toward the gods—[a sacrifice] that finds friends, wins all, conquers wealth, and wins the light of heaven.
(4.1.1.3.i) Accomplish the hymn with the *ṛc*; [accomplish] the *rathantara* with the *gāyatra*, and the *bṛhat* whose path is the *gāyatra*.

(4.1.1.3.k) At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take you with the Gāyatrī metre, in the manner of the Aṅgirases. (4.1.1.3ḷ) You are a spade; you are a woman. From the seat of the earth, bring forth Agni Purīṣya in the manner of the Aṅgirases. I take you with the Triṣṭubh metre, in the manner of the Aṅgirases. (4.1.1.4ṃ) You are a carrier; you are a woman. Through you, may we be able to dig for Agni Purīṣya in his dwelling place. I take you with the Jagatī metre, in the manner of the Aṅgirases.

(4.1.1.4ṇ) Having taken it in his hand, Savitṛ, bearing a golden spade, dug up Agni with that [spade] for eternal light; having dug him up, bring him to us. With the *anuṣṭubh* metre I take you, as did Aṅgiras.

(4.1.2.1.a) The seers grasped this rein of Cosmic Order in the ancient times during the sacrificial assemblies. By means of it, the gods attained the pressed [Soma]; it is the flowing stream of the navel of Cosmic Order.
(4.1.2.1.b) O vigorous steed, run forward swiftly along the widest expanse! Your highest birth is in heaven, your navel in the intermediate space, and your womb upon the earth.
(4.1.2.1.c) "Harness the donkey, O you two of abundant wealth, for this journey, as it carries Agni who is well-disposed toward us."
(4.1.2.1ḍ) In every endeavor, in every contest, we, as friends, invoke the most powerful Indra for our protection.

(4.1.2.1.e) Overcoming [the obstacles], come! Treading down the curses, come as one who brings bliss from the followers of Rudra, the Lord of Ganas! Traverse the wide mid-air, creating security, a pasture for cattle, and freedom from fear.
(4.1.2.2.f) Together with Pūṣan as your companion, go from the dwelling-place of the earth for Agni Purīṣya, in the manner of the Aṅgirases.
(4.1.2.2.g) We approach Agni Purīṣya in the manner of the Aṅgirases.
(4.1.2.2.h) We shall carry Agni Purīṣya in the manner of the Aṅgirases.
(4.1.2.2.i) We bear Agni of the soil, in the manner of Aṅgiras.
(4.1.2.2.k) Agni Jātavedas, the first, has looked along the forefront of the dawns, along the days; he has extended his rays in many places along the sun, and along heaven and earth.
Having come from the paths, the prize-winner shakes off all adversaries; he seeks to perceive Agni with his eye in the great assembly-place.
(4.1.2.3ṃ) Having stepped upon the earth, O steed, seek Agni with your luster; having found him, tell us so that we may dig him up from there.
Heaven is your back, the earth your seat, the intermediate space your soul, and the ocean your womb. Having looked out with your eye, do you trample upon those who attack us.
(4.1.2.4.o) Step forth for great good fortune from this place, O bestower of wealth, O vigorous one! May we abide in the favor of the Earth while we dig for Agni in her lap.

The wealth-giver, the prize-winning steed, has stepped forth toward this world, the well-fashioned realm of the earth. Thence let us dig up Agni of the beautiful countenance, as we ascend to the highest firmament of heaven.
(4.1.2.4.q) O divine Waters, release the honey-sweet waters for the health of all creatures; from their place let the plants rise up, bearing goodly fruit.

(4.1.2.4ṛ) I sprinkle Agni with my mind and with clarified butter—him who looks toward all beings, broad and vast with transverse vigor, most extensive, impetuous, and the finder of food. (4.1.2.5) I sprinkle Agni with my mind and with clarified butter.
I sprinkle you with speech and with ghee; accept that with a mind free from demons. Agni, possessing the beauty of a youth and a desirable hue, exulting in his own body, cannot be touched.
(4.1.2.5ṭ) Agni, the sage and lord of booty, has stepped around the oblations, bestowing treasures upon the donor.
(4.1.2.5.u) O Agni, O powerful one, we place you around us as a fortress—you, the inspired sage, of bold appearance day by day, the breaker of the treacherous foe.
(4.1.2.5.v) O Agni, you are born from the days; you, the one eager to blaze, are born from the waters, from the stone, from the forests, and from the plants; O Lord of men, you are born pure.
(4.1.3.1.a) At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I dig for Agni Purīṣya in the dwelling-place of the Earth, in the manner of the Aṅgirases.

(4.1.3.1.b) O Agni, you who are full of light, of beautiful countenance, shining with undecaying radiance—auspicious to all creatures and non-injurious—I dig you, the Agni of the soil, out of the dwelling-place of the earth, in the manner of Aṅgiras.
(4.1.3.1.c) You are the back of the waters, wide-spreading and broad, destined to bear Agni, never to be overturned. Growing great, O lotus-leaf, expand with the measure and the expanse of heaven.
(4.1.3.1ḍ) You two are a shelter; (4.1.3.2) you two are a shield, both of you unbroken and wide. Being spacious, clothe yourselves together and bear Agni Purīṣya.
May you two, finders of heaven, dwell together in harmony, with your chests and your very selves turned toward each other, bearing within yourselves Agni, the luminous and imperishable.
(4.1.3.2.f) You are the filler of the soil, the sustainer of all; Atharvan was the first to churn you forth, O Agni.
(4.1.3.2.g) From the lotus, O Agni, Atharvan churned you forth from the head of the entire world, he the priest.
(4.1.3.2) And him, indeed, the seer Dadhyañc, the son of Atharvan, kindled—(4.1.3.3) the slayer of Vṛtra, the shatterer of forts.
(4.1.3.3.i) And Pāthya Vṛṣan has kindled you, the greatest slayer of Dasyus, the winner of wealth in every battle.

(4.1.3.3.k) Sit down, O Hotṛ, in your own place; being wise, establish the sacrifice in the womb of good action. As one who pleases the gods, worship the gods with the oblation; O Agni, bestow great vitality upon the sacrificer.

(4.1.3.3ḷ) The Hotṛ priest, knowing his place, has sat down upon the seat of the Hotṛ—resplendent, shining, most skillful; Agni, whose wisdom protects his unfailing vows, the most excellent, the bringer of thousands, with his pure tongue.

(4.1.3.3) Sit down together; you are great. Shine forth, (4.1.3.4) you who are most beloved by the gods! O Agni, worthy of the sacrificial food, O praised one, emit your ruddy smoke, beautiful to behold.
