(4.7.15.3.i) I have invoked for my protection the two best of charioteers, who travel most splendidly with well-governed horses; O two Gods, whose power among the gods is unyielding, may you both release us from sin.

Since you two came as the bridal procession for Sūryā with your three-wheeled chariot, seeking a place of assembly—I praise the divine Aśvins, I call upon them in my need—may they two release us from sin.
I call to mind the Maruts; may they speak for us, and may all of them protect this entire speech. I invoke the swift ones who are easy to guide for our aid; may they release us from sin.

(4.7.15.4) Sharp is their weapon, firm and powerful; they are the divine host, (4.7.15.5) victorious in battles. I praise the gods, the Maruts; seeking protection, I call upon them repeatedly: may they release us from sin.
I call to mind the gods; may they speak for us, and may all of them protect this entire speech. I invoke the swift ones, easy to control, for our aid; may they deliver us from sin.
Whatever distress afflicts me here, whether caused by men or by the gods—I, seeking protection, call upon all the gods with my voice; may they deliver us from sin.
(4.7.15.5.p) May Anumati favor us today; (4.7.15.5.q) may she indeed favor us now, O Anumati;
(4.7.15.6ṛ) may Vaiśvānara come to our aid.

(4.7.15.6ṣ) Praised in heaven; (4.7.15.6ṭ) those two who spread themselves out with immeasurable powers, who became the foundations of all treasures—I praise Heaven and Earth, I call upon them in my need; may you two deliver us from distress.
O wide Heaven and Earth, create space for us; as the two wives of the field, speak in our favor. I praise Heaven and Earth; seeking protection, I call upon you repeatedly. Deliver us from distress.
Whatever offense we have committed against you among men, O youngest one, through ignorance—whatever it may be—make us sinless before Aditi; loosen our transgressions on every side, O Agni.
Just as you, O Vasus, worthy of worship, released even the Gaurī cow that was bound by the foot, so do thou release from us this distress; O Agni, prolong our life further.
(5.1.1.1) He offers oblations with verses addressed to Savitṛ for the sake of impulsion;
he offers with [the ladle] taken four times.
(5.1.1.1) Cattle have four feet; (5.1.1.1) verily he wins cattle;
(5.1.1.1) there are four quarters.
(5.1.1.1) He finds firm support in the very quarters. (5.1.1.1) The meters departed from the gods,
saying, "We will not carry the oblation for you if we receive no share."
(5.1.1.1) For them they held out this fourfold-drawn portion: for the invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākyā*), for the offering verse (*yājyā*), for the deity, and for the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
(5.1.1.1) In that he offers what has been fourfold-drawn, he thereby gratifies the meters (*chandāṃsi*).
(5.1.1.1) These, being pleased, carry his oblation to the gods for whomever he may desire.
(5.1.1.1) Whomever he may desire.
(5.1.1.2) "May he become worse," [thinking thus], one should offer for him one by one.
By means of the oblations, one indeed drives him away; he becomes worse.
[This applies to] whomsoever one should desire.
(5.1.1.2) Thinking, "May he become more prosperous," one should recite all [the formulas] for him and offer them.
By means of the oblation itself, one causes him to advance; he becomes more prosperous.
Moreover, this is the advancement of the sacrifice itself.
(5.1.1.2) He indeed departs from the prosperity of the beginning of the sacrifice who departs from Agni as the deity.
(5.1.1.2) These Savitṛ-verses are eight;
the Gāyatrī has eight syllables.

(5.1.1.2) It belongs to the Gāyatrī. (5.1.1.3) Agni—by means of that very [metre], through prosperity from the mouth of the sacrifice, he does not depart from the deity Agni. (5.1.1.3) There are eight verses addressed to Savitṛ; the ninth is the oblation.
(5.1.1.3) He thus spreads out the threefold sacrifice at its opening.
(5.1.1.3) If he should desire, "May I endow the meters with the glory of the sacrifice," he should make the *ṛc* the final one.
(5.1.1.3) He thus endows the meters themselves with the glory of the sacrifice.
(5.1.1.3) If he should desire,
"May I endow the sacrificer with the glory of the sacrifice," he should make the *yajus* the final element.
(5.1.1.3) He thus endows the sacrificer himself with the glory of the sacrifice. (5.1.1.3–4) "Complete the hymn with a verse," he says— for the sake of prosperity.
(5.1.1.4) He takes up the spade with four [verses]. (5.1.1.4) There are four meters; [he does so] by means of the meters themselves.
(5.1.1.4) "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he says, for the sake of impulsion.
(5.1.1.4) Agni hid himself from the gods.
He entered the bamboo.
He moved along this protection which is the hollow of the bamboo. Therefore, the spade has a hollow; it is for the sake of common origin.
(5.1.1.4) Wherever he dwelt, that became black;
it becomes speckled for the sake of the perfection of form.
It is sharp on both sides.
(5.1.1.4) And for this reason, as well as for that, it is of the measure of a fathom, for the attainment of the sun;
(5.1.1.4) for indeed, such is the vigor in a man.
It is commensurate with vigor;
it is unlimited,
for the sake of attaining the unlimited.
(5.1.1.4) That among trees which bears fruit is full of vigor for them; (5.1.1.4) the bamboo indeed bears fruit.
(5.1.1.4) It is made of bamboo for the attainment of vigor.
(5.1.2.1) That which is performed in the sacrifice without a sacrificial formula is indeed unsuccessful.
(5.1.2.1) With the words, "They have grasped this rein of Order," he takes up the horse's halter for the sake of providing a sacrificial formula and for the success of the sacrifice.
(5.1.2.1) "O courser, run forward!"—with these words he addresses the horse; thus he proclaims its form and its greatness.
(5.1.2.1) "Yoke the donkey, you two"—with these words [he addresses] the donkey.
(5.1.2.1) He establishes the donkey upon that which is non-existent;
therefore, the donkey is less substantial than the horse.
(5.1.2.1) He says, "In every yoking, the more powerful one."
"In every yoga, he indeed yokes him.
"In every contest for booty we invoke," he says;
for booty (*vāja*) is indeed food.
Verily, he wins food.
"O friends, Indra for our aid," he says;
verily, he wins power.
Agni hid himself from the gods;
Prajāpati found him.
The horse belongs to Prajāpati.
(5.1.2.2) He gathers [the materials] with a horse for the sake of attainment.
(5.1.2.2) Indeed, a state of inverted order is created when those who are superior and those who are inferior perform the same work together;
for (5.1.2.3) the donkey is inferior to the horse.
(5.1.2.3) They lead the horse in front to ward off misfortune;
therefore, the inferior follows behind the superior.
For one who prospers has many rivals.
(5.1.2.3) Indeed, he who piles the fire-altar becomes, as it were, a thunderbolt; the horse is a thunderbolt.
"Come forward, overmastering, trampling down the curses," he says.
(5.1.2.3) By means of the thunderbolt itself, he strikes down his evil rival.
(5.1.2.3) "From the lordship of Rudra," he says; for cattle indeed belong to Rudra—from Rudra himself [he obtains them]. (5.1.2.4) Having requested the cattle, he performs the ritual act for himself.
"With Pūṣan as his companion," he says;
for Pūṣan is the leader of roads; [he says this] for the sake of complete attainment.
(5.1.2.4) This Agni indeed has the loose soil as his abode.
(5.1.2.4) The Aṅgirases first gathered him together among the deities.
"From the seat of the earth, come to Agni Purīṣya like an Aṅgiras," he says.
(5.1.2.4) He thus provides him with a foundation by means of the deities.
(5.1.2.4) "We approach Agni Purīṣya in the manner of the Aṅgirases," he says;
(5.1.2.5) by that which he thereby unites with, he appropriates his strength.
(5.1.2.5) "Having announced it to Prajāpati, Agni is to be prepared," so they say.
(5.1.2.5) This earth, indeed, is Prajāpati;
and that which is the anthill is its ear.
(5.1.2.5) "We shall carry Agni Purīṣya in the manner of the Aṅgirases," with these words he approaches the ant-hill.
(5.1.2.5) Having thus directly announced [his intention] to Prajāpati, he collects the fire.
(5.1.2.5) "We carry Agni Purīṣya in the manner of the Aṅgirases," he says.
(5.1.2.5) With that by which he comes together with the prize, he appropriates his very prize.
(5.1.2.6) "Agni has looked upon the forefront of the dawns," he says;
for the sake of looking after [them].
"Having come, O steed, from the path; having stepped upon the earth, O racer," he says.
By the first [verse] he desires him; by the second he finds him. With two [verses] he causes him to step forward.
For the sake of stability;
with two verses that have the same meter;
therefore, animals are born in accordance with their kind.
"May heaven be your back, earth your seat," he says.
For Prajāpati indeed fashioned this [sacrificial animal] from these worlds;
thus he proclaims its form and its greatness.
(5.1.2.6) This horse is indeed a thunderbolt.
It has more teeth on one side than those with teeth on both sides, and more hair than those with teeth on both sides.
He whom he hates, he should meditate upon as being beneath his feet.
(5.1.2.6) By means of the thunderbolt itself, he strikes him down.
With the two verses, "He has stepped forth" and "He has stepped out," he causes him to step out for the sake of firm establishment;
they are used as a pair of corresponding verses.
(5.1.3.1) Therefore, animals are born according to their kind. (5.1.3.1) He pours water down; for wherever the waters go, there the plants take root.
(5.1.3.1) As the plants take root, the animals take root after them;
(5.1.3.1) after the animals, the sacrifice;
(5.1.3.1) after the sacrifice, the sacrificer.
(5.1.3.1) Progeny [follows] the sacrificer;
therefore he pours out water for the sake of stability.
(5.1.3.1) If the Adhvaryu were to offer an oblation in that which is not fire, the Adhvaryu would become blind, and the Rakṣases would destroy the sacrifice.
(5.1.3.2) Having placed gold [in the fire], he offers;
thus he offers in that which possesses fire.
(5.1.3.2) The Adhvaryu does not become blind, nor do the Rakṣases destroy the sacrifice.
(5.1.3.2) "I sprinkle Agni with mind and with ghee," he says;
for by means of the mind a person approaches the sacrifice.
"He says, 'Looking toward all beings,' for he indeed dwells facing everything;
'Broad, vast, with transverse age,' he says."
"For this one, though born small, becomes great. "Most extensive food, impetuous and piercing," he says;
verily, he makes food palatable for him.
"Everything is palatable to him who knows thus.
(5.1.3.3) "I sprinkle you with speech and with ghee," he says; therefore, whatever a person conceives in his mind, that he speaks with his voice.
"Free from Rakṣases," he says,
for the sake of driving away the Rakṣases; "Agni, whose splendor is mortal and whose color is desirable," he says.
(5.1.3.3) He bestows honor upon him;
(5.1.3.3) he who knows thus becomes possessed of honor.
(5.1.3.4) But he is indeed able to attain that [honor] which the Adhvaryu offers as an oblation in what is not fire, by means of the mind.
(5.1.3.4) He offers with two verses containing the word *manas*.
(5.1.3.4) This is for the attainment of two oblations;
(5.1.3.4) by means of two [verses].
(5.1.3.4) For the sake of stability.
(5.1.3.4) Indeed, at every opening of the sacrifice, as it is being performed, the Rakṣases seek to destroy the sacrifice.
Now, this indeed is the opening of the sacrifice when the oblation reaches it.
He draws a line around for the smiting away of the Rakṣases;
he draws it around with three [verses].
Agni is indeed threefold;
as great as Agni is, by that much he drives away the Rakṣases.
(5.1.3.5) He encloses it with the Gāyatrī.
(5.1.3.5) The Gāyatrī is indeed splendor;
verily, by means of splendor he encompasses it.
(5.1.3.5) He traces around with a *triṣṭubh* verse.
(5.1.3.5) The *triṣṭubh* is indeed power;
verily, by means of power he encloses him.
(5.1.3.5) He draws around with an *anuṣṭubh* verse.
(5.1.3.5) The *anuṣṭubh* encompasses all meters; it serves for complete attainment.
(5.1.3.5) He does so from the middle with an *anuṣṭubh*.
Speech, indeed, is the *anuṣṭubh*;
therefore, we speak with speech from the middle.
He draws the line first with the *gāyatrī*, then with the *anuṣṭubh*, and then with the *triṣṭubh*.
The Gāyatrī is indeed brilliance, the Anuṣṭubh is the sacrifice, and the Triṣṭubh is power.
By means of both brilliance and power, he encompasses the sacrifice on both sides.

(5.1.4.1) "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," with these words he digs for the sake of impulsion; moreover, by this he generates smoke. (5.1.4.1) "Thee, O Agni, full of light, with a fair countenance," he says; by this he generates light.
That Agni, once born, afflicted creatures with heat; the gods appeased him with a half-verse.
(5.1.4.1) "Auspicious, not harming the offspring," he says; verily, he pacifies it for the sake of the offspring.
(5.1.4.1) He digs with two [verses] for stability.
(5.1.4.2) "Thou art the back of the waters," [with these words] he brings a lotus leaf; for this lotus leaf is indeed the back of the waters; verily, he brings it by its own form.

(5.1.4.2) He gathers [the materials] with a lotus leaf; the lotus leaf is indeed the womb of Agni; verily, he gathers Agni together with his own womb. (5.1.4.2) He gathers with a black antelope skin; the black antelope skin is the sacrifice; verily, by means of the sacrifice he gathers the sacrifice.

(5.1.4.2) If he were to gather with the skin of domestic animals, he would afflict the domestic animals with pain; he gathers with a black antelope skin; verily, he afflicts only the wild animals with pain. (5.1.4.3) He afflicts them with pain.

(5.1.4.3) Therefore, among animals that are born in equal numbers, the wild animals are fewer, for they have been struck by grief. (5.1.4.3) He collects [the hair] from the hairy side, for it is from that side that his [body] is pure.

(5.1.4.3) He spreads out both a black antelope skin and a lotus leaf; this earth is indeed the black antelope skin and yonder sky is the lotus leaf; verily, by means of these two, he encloses him on both sides.
(5.1.4.3) Agni hid himself from the gods; Atharvan perceived him.

(5.1.4.3–4) "Atharvan was the first to churn you forth, O Agni," he says; by means of him who perceived him, he thus gathers him together. (5.1.4.4) "From the lotus, O Agni," he says, for he found him resting upon the lotus leaf.
(5.1.4.4) "The seer Dadhyañc [knew] you," he says; for Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa was indeed full of splendor; verily, he bestows splendor upon him.
(5.1.4.4) "The Pāthya bull [knew] you," he says; what was previously uttered, he extols further with the latter [verse].
(5.1.4.5) He gathers with four [verses]; there are four meters; thus it is by means of the meters.
(5.1.4.5) With *gāyatrī* verses for a Brāhmaṇa, for the Brāhmaṇa is connected to the *gāyatrī*; with *triṣṭubh* verses for a Rājanya, for the Rājanya is connected to the *triṣṭubh*.

(5.1.4.5) For whomsoever he should desire, "May he become more prosperous," he should collect [the materials] for him with both kinds [of verses]. Thus he bestows upon him brilliance and sensory power in harmony.
(5.1.4.5) He collects with eight [verses]; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and Agni is of the Gāyatrī nature; as great as Agni is, so much of him he collects.
(5.1.4.5) "Sit down, O Hotṛ! he says; thus he establishes the deities for him.

"Sit down as a Hotṛ among men," he says; "sit together with the birds," he says; "be born, O conqueror, at the beginning of days," he says. Thus he causes gods and men who have sat together to be born for him.
(5.1.5.1) For when he digs, he does something harsh to her; he pours water down upon it. Water, indeed, is peaceful.
(5.1.5.1) By means of these very peaceful [verses], he pacifies her distress.
(5.1.5.1) "May Vāyu Mātariśvan bestow [life] upon you," he says.
(5.1.5.1) Vāyu is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
(5.1.5.1) By means of breath alone he joins her breath together.
(5.1.5.1) "May Vāyu join you," he says;
therefore rain, driven by Vāyu, moves forth from heaven.
(5.1.5.1) And for him, O Goddess, let there be *vaṣaṭ*! (5.1.5.2) "To you," he says;
(5.1.5.2) for there are six seasons. Verily, he bestows rain upon the seasons.
Therefore, it rains during all the seasons.
If he were to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call, the Rakṣasas would destroy the sacrifice.
He says, "Vaṭ! instead.
(5.1.5.2) He utters the *vaṣaṭ* call in a hidden manner; his *vaṣaṭ* call does not become exhausted, nor do the *rakṣases* strike down the sacrifice.
(5.1.5.2) With the verse, "Well-born together with light," he ties [the horse] up using an *anuṣṭubh*.
(5.1.5.2) The Anuṣṭubh. (5.1.5.3) All the meters; for the meters are indeed Agni’s beloved body.
Verily, he encloses him with his own beloved body.
He who knows thus becomes a finder of clothing; for Agni, when bound, belongs to Varuṇa.
With two verses addressed to Savitṛ—"Arise, O performer of fair sacrifice! and "Upward indeed for our aids!"—he rises up.
Thus impelled by Savitṛ, he releases the upward-pointing wrath of Varuṇa from him.
With two [verses],
for the sake of stability:
"Once born, you are the embryo of the two worlds," he says.
"These two, indeed, are heaven and earth; Agni is their embryo;
therefore he speaks thus."
"O Agni, thou art beautiful, distributed among the plants," he says;
for when they carry him [the fire] about, he then becomes more beautiful.
"He goes forth bellowing from his mothers," he says.
"The plants, indeed, are his mothers";
it is from them that he causes him to move forth.
With the words, "Be firm, O you of strong limbs," he places [the brick] upon the donkey.
With this [verse] he girds him for stability;
he gathers [the materials] with a donkey;
therefore the donkey is the best bearer of burdens among animals.
(5.1.5.5) He gathers [the materials] with a donkey;
therefore, even though the donkey is a source of distress (*anāleśa*), it becomes fatter than other animals.
For with it they gather food and light (*arka*).
(5.1.5.5) He gathers [the materials] with a donkey;
therefore, although the donkey has double seed, it is born as the smallest among animals,
for fire burns up its womb.
(5.1.5.5) At this time, he has indeed mounted upon the offspring.
(5.1.5.6) That Lord would have consumed the creatures with his heat;
(5.1.5.6) "Be auspicious to the creatures," he says;
(5.1.5.6) thus he pacifies him for the sake of the creatures.
"O Aṅgiras, [protect] you from human women," he says,
for offspring are of human origin.
"Do not burn against heaven and earth, nor the intermediate space, nor the trees," he says.
(5.1.5.6) He pacifies him for these very worlds. (5.1.5.6) "Let the prize-winner go forth, neighing," he says; for this [horse] is indeed a prize-winner.
"Neighing, the ass has flown," he says;
for the seers called this one "the ass.
"Bearing Agni Purīṣya," he says.
"For he indeed bears Agni;
'May you not fall before your full span of life,' he says. Thus, he bestows life upon him."
(5.1.5.7) Therefore, the donkey reaches its full lifespan;
therefore, people are afraid when a donkey dies before its time.
He says, "Bearing the bull Agni, the bull."
"For he is indeed a bull; Agni is a bull.
"The embryo of the waters, belonging to the ocean," he says.
For this Agni is the embryo of the waters.
With the words, "O Agni, come hither for the feast," these two worlds went apart; thus, when he says, "O Agni, come hither for the feast."
(5.1.5.8) For the separation from these two worlds.
(5.1.5.8) He has indeed fallen away from his abode and has not yet reached a firm foundation.
(5.1.5.8) At this moment, he meditates upon both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer.
(5.1.5.8) “*Ṛtam*, *satyam*,” he says.
(5.1.5.8–9) *Ṛta* is indeed this [earth], and *satya* is that [heaven].
(5.1.5.9) Verily, he establishes him upon these two; neither the *adhvaryu* nor the sacrificer comes to ruin.
(5.1.5.9) This Agni, when bound [with grass], approaches the sacrificer like Varuṇa. "O plants, receive this Agni," he says,
for the sake of pacification.
"Driving away all ignorance and hostilities," he says,
for the purpose of striking down the *rakṣases*.
"Sitting down, may he strike away evil thought from us," he says.
"For the sake of stability.
"O plants, rejoice in him! he says.
For plants are indeed the portion of Agni.
(5.1.5.10) By means of those very [verses] he causes him to prosper.
(5.1.5.10) "Blooming, with good fruit," he says; therefore the plants bear fruit.
"This germ of yours, timely, has sat down in the ancient dwelling-place," he says;
by those [deities] from whom he causes him to move forth, in them he establishes him.
He brings him down with two verses.
For the sake of stability.
Agni, when bound, belongs to Varuṇa.
With the words, "With his power," he loosens him; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he releases Varuṇa’s wrath from him in all directions.
(5.1.6.1) He pours water down. (5.1.6.1) Water, indeed, is peaceful; with that which is peaceful, he pacifies his impurity.
(5.1.6.1) He pours it out with three verses.
(5.1.6.1) For Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, he thus pacifies his heat.
"Mitra, having united the earth," he says. Mitra is indeed the auspicious one among the gods;
by him alone he unites this [earth].
(5.1.6.2) For the sake of pacification:
(5.1.6.2) if he were to mix [the clay] with the potsherds of domestic vessels, he would afflict the domestic vessels with impurity. He mixes it with the potsherds of a deserted dwelling.
(5.1.6.2) These, indeed, are things not to be lived upon; (5.1.6.2) he delivers them over to distress; (5.1.6.2) he mixes them with pebbles.
(5.1.6.2) For support; (5.1.6.2) and also for peace.
(5.1.6.2) He mixes it with goat’s wool.
The goat, indeed, is the beloved body of Agni;
verily, he unites him with his own beloved body, and also with splendor.
He unites [the horse] with the hair of the black antelope skin.
The black antelope skin is indeed the sacrifice.
By means of the sacrifice itself, he unites the sacrifice.
"The Rudras, having gathered the earth," he says.
(5.1.6.3) These deities indeed first brought him together;
with those very [deities] he now brings him together.
"Thou art the head of Makha," he says.
The sacrifice is indeed Makha;
this fire-pan is its head;
therefore he speaks thus.
"Ye two are the feet of the sacrifice," he says; for these two are indeed the feet of the sacrifice,
and also for the sake of stability.
With some he restrains [the breath], with others he converses;
this is for the sake of pairing.
He makes it threefold in height; these worlds are three, and it is for the attainment of these worlds.
(5.1.6.4) He performs it with the meters.
(5.1.6.4) The meters are indeed vigor;
(5.1.6.4) thus he constructs it by means of vigor itself.
He fashions the cavity with a *yajus* formula for the sake of distinction;
he fashions it to this extent.
(5.1.6.4) He makes it two-breasted, measured by Prajāpati, the mouth of the sacrifice,
for the milking of heaven and earth.
He makes it four-teat for the milking of cattle;
he makes it eight-teat.
(5.1.6.4) For the milking of the meters,
(5.1.6.4) one who practices sorcery should fashion [the sacrificial post] with nine edges.
Having thus prepared the threefold thunderbolt, he hurls it at his rival.
Having made it for the sake of spreading, he deposits it with the words, "Having fashioned the great fire-pan.
He thus establishes it among the deities.
(5.1.7.1) He fumigates with seven [kinds of incense].
(5.1.7.1) There are indeed seven vital breaths in the head.
(5.1.7.1) This fire-pan (*ukhā*) is the head of the sacrifice.
(5.1.7.1) Verily, he places the vital breaths in the head of the sacrifice; therefore there are seven vital breaths in the head.
(5.1.7.1) He fumigates it with horse-dung.
The horse belongs to Prajāpati, for the sake of common origin.
"Aditi [be] yours," he says.
(5.1.7.1) This earth, indeed, is Aditi.
(5.1.7.1) By means of Aditi he digs into the earth, so that he does not cause injury to her;
for one does not harm oneself.
"May the wives of the gods [accept] thee," he says;
for the wives of the gods fashioned her first;
with them indeed he establishes her.
"By the *dhiṣaṇās*," he says.
The *dhiṣaṇās* are indeed the sciences (*vidyā*). By means of the sciences, he kindles it.
"O wives," he says; the wives are indeed the meters. Verily, by means of the meters, he cooks it.
"By the protectors," he says. The *hotṛ*-priests are indeed the protectors;
by means of the *hotṛ*-priests, he cooks it.
"Obeisance to the progenitors," he says;
for the wives of the gods are indeed the progenitors.
With them, he cooks it.
(5.1.7.3) He cooks with six [pots].
(5.1.7.3) There are indeed six seasons.
(5.1.7.3) Verily, by means of the seasons he cooks it.
"Let them cook twice," he says;
therefore, the crop ripens twice in the year.
The cauldron, kindled by Varuṇa, has been heated.
He approaches with friendliness for the sake of peace;
"May the god Savitṛ dig thee up," he says.
"Impelled by Savitṛ, he raises her up with the sacred word and with the deities.
"May the earth, not falling away, fill the regions and the quarters," he says;
therefore Agni shines throughout all the quarters.
"Arise, become great; stand upright, you who are firm," he says for the sake of stability.
The vessel belonging to the Asuras is uncovered.
(5.1.7.4) He mixes it, making it for the gods; (5.1.7.4) he mixes it with goat’s milk;
(5.1.7.4) for goat’s milk is indeed the highest form of milk.
(5.1.7.4) He moistens it with the highest milk;
(5.1.7.4) [he does so] with a *yajus* formula for the sake of distinction.
(5.1.7.4) He covers it with the meters;
for it is indeed made with the meters. Thus, by means of the meters, he covers the meters themselves.
(5.1.8.1) He buys the human head with twenty-one beans.
(5.1.8.1) Beans are indeed impure, and the human head is impure. By means of these impure things, he removes its impurity; having made it pure, he carries it away.
There are twenty-one;
for man indeed consists of twenty-one parts,
[and this is] for the attainment of man.
(5.1.8.1) This human head is indeed deprived of the vital breaths and is impure.
(5.1.8.1) He places it upon an anthill that has been split into seven parts;
for there are seven vital breaths in the head.
Verily, he causes it to prosper through the vital breaths;
for the sake of its sacrificial purity.
As many as are the kinsmen of death, over them Yama has attained lordship.
He chants around it with the verses of Yama; verily, he appropriates it from Yama. He chants around it with three verses.
(5.1.8.2) These are the three worlds. (5.1.8.2) He excludes him from these very worlds; therefore, one should not give [the Sāman] to one who sings it.
(5.1.8.2) For the Gāthā takes that away. (5.1.8.2) He offers animals to the Agnis;
for the Agnis are indeed desires.
(5.1.8.2) Verily, he wins desires.

(5.1.8.2) If he were not to sacrifice the animals, his cattle would remain unobtained. (5.1.8.3) If he were to release them after they have been carried around the fire, he would cause a disturbance of the sacrifice.
(5.1.8.3) If he were to complete [the sacrifice], the heads would become exhausted;

(5.1.8.3) in that he immolates the animals, by that very act he wins the animals; (5.1.8.3) in that he releases them after they have been carried around the fire, it is for the sake of ensuring that the heads do not become exhausted.
He concludes with the *prājāpatya* [offering]. Prajāpati is indeed the sacrifice; verily, he establishes the sacrifice within the sacrifice itself.
Prajāpati created living beings;
having become emptied, he reflected.
He saw these Āprī verses.
With them, he indeed gratified his own self from the front.
That these Āprīs exist is for this reason.
The sacrifice is indeed Prajāpati.
By means of these [verses], he gratifies the sacrifice itself from the very beginning.
They consist of an unlimited number of meters.
Prajāpati is unlimited;
[this is] for the attainment of Prajāpati.
The deficient and the redundant are a pair.
(5.1.8.4) For the sake of procreation; this metre is indeed named Lomaśa, belonging to Prajāpati;
cattle are hairy.
Verily, he wins cattle;
for all these are forms,
and all forms are employed in the piling of the fire-altar.
Therefore, these [verses] belong to the piled fire-altar.
He recites twenty-one *sāmidhenī* verses; the twenty-first is indeed splendor (*ruk*); verily, he attains splendor.
(5.1.8.5) Moreover, it is indeed a foundation, for the twenty-one-fold [stoma] is a foundation.
(5.1.8.5) He recites twenty-four [verses];
there are twenty-four half-months in a year.
The year is Agni Vaiśvānara;
verily, he directly obtains Vaiśvānara;
he recites [the verses] in forward order.
"For the world of heaven is, as it were, turned away.
"May the seasons, O Agni, strengthen thee with the years," he says;
verily, by means of the years, he strengthens Agni.
(5.1.8.6) "With the seasons, [he wins] the year.
(5.1.8.6) "Illumine all the quarters of the earth," he says;
(5.1.8.6) therefore Agni shines forth across all the quarters.
"The Aśvins have driven death away from him," he says;
verily, he drives death away from him. "We have risen up out of the darkness," he says.
Darkness is indeed evil; he thus strikes away evil from him. "We have gone to the highest light," he says.
(5.1.8.6) Yonder sun, indeed, is the highest light.
(5.1.8.6) He attains union with the sun itself.
(5.1.8.6) The year does not stand still for him, nor does his prosperity stand still, for whom these [rites] are performed.
He recites the final verse containing the word "light. He thereby places light above him for the purpose of illuminating the world of heaven.
(5.1.9.1) He consecrates him with six [verses].
(5.1.9.1) There are indeed six seasons;
(5.1.9.1) verily, by means of the seasons, he consecrates him.
(5.1.9.1) He consecrates him with seven [verses]. (5.1.9.1) There are seven meters. (5.1.9.1) Verily, by means of the meters, he consecrates him.
(5.1.9.1) With the final verse, "Of every god who leads," he offers an *anuṣṭubh* [verse].
(5.1.9.1) The *anuṣṭubh* is indeed speech; therefore, among the vital breaths, speech is the highest.
(5.1.9.1) From a single syllable, the first foot is incomplete.
(5.1.9.1) Therefore, men subsist upon that which is incomplete in speech;
he offers with a full [ladle].
For Prajāpati is indeed like one who is full.
(5.1.9.2) For the attainment of Prajāpati,
(5.1.9.2) he offers with a deficient [verse];
for from what was deficient, Prajāpati created offspring.
For the sake of the creation of offspring:
if he were to pour [the ghee] onto the flame, he would obtain what has already come into being; if onto the embers, what is yet to be.
He scatters it upon the embers;
thus he wins what is yet to be,
for what is yet to be is more than what has already come to be.
He unites [the fire] with two verses;
the sacrificer has two feet,
for the sake of stability.
This fire-pan is indeed prepared with the *brahman* and the *yajus*; if it were to break, it would bring about ruin.
(5.1.9.3) The sacrificer would be struck down; his sacrifice would perish.
(5.1.9.3) "O Mitra, heat this fire-pan," he says. (5.1.9.3) Mitra is indeed the Brahman.
He establishes it in the Brahman itself;
the sacrificer does not come to ruin, nor is his sacrifice destroyed.
If [the vessel] should break, he should join it together with those very same potsherds.
That itself is the expiation for that case.
For one whose prosperity has departed, he should place [the fire] after churning it;
for he has indeed become [like] a living being.
He who desires prosperity approaches his own deity. He who would be produced from the fire-pan (*ukhā*)— that very deity shall be his,
for it is from that [deity] that he is produced.
He indeed becomes the one named Svayambhū (the Self-Existent), whomever he may desire.
(5.1.9.4) "I shall produce a rival for him," thinking thus, he should bring [the earth] from elsewhere and place it down;
verily, he produces a rival for him directly.
(5.1.9.4) For one who desires food, he should place [the earth] taken from a frying pan.
In the frying pan (ambarīṣa), food is carried;
thus he wins food from its very source. He places muñja grass therein.
(5.1.9.5) Muñja grass is indeed strength; verily, he bestows strength upon him.
(5.1.9.5) Agni hid himself away from the gods.
He entered the *krumuka* tree;
he places a *krumuka* [branch] down; whatever of his was deposited there, that very thing he thereby secures.
(5.1.9.5) He mixes it with clarified butter. (5.1.9.5) Clarified butter, indeed, is the dear abode of Agni;
verily, he causes him to prosper through his own dear abode, and also through splendor. (5.1.9.6) He places a splinter of Vikankata wood upon it.
Verily he wins radiance;
he places a fuel-stick of *śamī* wood for the sake of peace.
With the three verses beginning, "Sit down upon the lap of this mother," he pays homage to the newborn.
These are the three worlds;
verily, he attains knowledge within these very worlds.
Moreover, he thereby places the vital breaths within himself.

(5.1.10.1) Formerly, indeed, Agni would not burn what had been cut down by anything other than an axe. Then the seer Prayoga made it palatable for him when he places a fuel-stick with the words, "O Agni, whatever [pieces] there may be."
He makes it palatable for him even though it has not been cut by an axe; everything becomes palatable for him who knows thus.
He places a post made of Udumbara wood.
The udumbara is indeed vigor;
verily, he bestows vigor upon him. Prajāpati created Agni.
(5.1.10.1) When he had been created, the *rakṣases* sought to destroy him.
(5.1.10.2) He saw this *rakṣoghna* [verse]; with it, indeed, he struck away the *rakṣases*.
In that there is a verse destructive of demons (*rākṣoghna*), by means of it he strikes away the demons from Agni as soon as he has been born.
He places a piece of *aśvattha* wood [on the fire].
The *aśvattha* is indeed the most powerful subduer of rivals among trees; it serves for victory.
He places a fuel-stick of *vaikaṅkata* wood;
verily, he wins light.
He places a fuel-stick made of *śamī* wood.
(5.1.10.2) For the sake of peace:

(5.1.10.2) "Sharpened is my sacred power; I have extended their arms"—with these words, he makes [the sacrificer] recite over the two last *audumbara* posts. (5.1.10.3) He causes him to recite: "By means of the *brahman* alone he sharpens the *kṣatra*, and by means of the *kṣatra* the *brahman*."
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa who possesses a Rājanya surpasses another Brāhmaṇa; therefore, a Rājanya who possesses a Brāhmaṇa surpasses another Rājanya. This Agni is indeed death;
gold is immortality.
He fastens a gold plate inside;
verily he places immortality between himself and death. It has twenty-one knobs.
(5.1.10.3) There are indeed twenty-one worlds of the gods: twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun as the twenty-first. (5.1.10.4) So many indeed are the worlds of the gods;
from them he excludes his rival.
With the *nirbādhas* (pressing-out bricks), the gods pressed the Asuras out and excluded them.
(5.1.10.4) That is the reason for the "Nirbādhas" being called Nirbādhas.
(5.1.10.4) He becomes possessed of Nirbādhas; (5.1.10.4) he indeed casts his rivals into the Nirbādhas.
He fastens it with the Sāvitrī verse for the sake of impulsion; he uses the next verse, "Night and Dawn," [for the same purpose].
(5.1.10.4) By means of day and night alone he raises him up.
(5.1.10.4) "The gods, the givers of wealth, supported Agni," he says.
(5.1.10.4) The gods who give wealth are indeed the vital breaths.
Having raised him up by means of day and night, he supports him with the vital breaths.
Sitting, he fastens [the cord];
therefore, offspring are born sitting.
The black antelope skin is on top.
Gold is indeed brilliance, and the black antelope skin is the Brahman.
Thus, he encloses him on both sides with both brilliance and the Brahman.
The sling has six supports;
for there are six seasons.
Verily, by means of the seasons, he raises it up.
That which has twelve supports is [attained] through the year itself.
It is made of *muñja* grass; for *muñja* grass is indeed strength.
Verily, by means of strength he causes him to prosper.
"Thou art Suparṇa, Garutman," with these words he gazes;
verily, he thus proclaims his form and his greatness.
"Go to heaven, fly to the light," he says;
verily, he causes him to go to the world of heaven.
(5.1.11.1.a) Kindled and anointing the vessel of our hymns, O Agni, swelling with honeyed ghee—bearing strength, O Jātavedas, bring the prize-winning steed to the beloved assembly-place of the gods.

Anointing with ghee the paths that lead to the gods, may the steed, knowing them, go toward the deities. O courser, let the quarters attend upon you; bestow self-sustaining power upon this sacrificer.

(5.1.11.1.c) You are worthy of praise and worthy of adoration, O vigorous steed; you are swift and fit for sacrifice, O courser. May Agni Jātavedas, in harmony with the gods and the Vasus, carry you—the beloved bearer—forward.
The sacrificial grass is strewn, well-spread; may Aditi, rejoicing with the gods, making it a pleasant seat as it spreads wide and broad upon the earth, bestow it for our prosperity.
(5.1.11.2.e) May these blessed, all-formed divine doors—being opened wide with their wings and uplifted, lofty yet resonant, and being beautified—be easy of access for you.
Moving between Mitra and Varuṇa, being in agreement regarding the face of the sacrifices—O Dawn and Night, you who possess fine gold and beautiful forms, I seat you here in the womb of Cosmic Order.

(5.1.11.3.g) O two gods, golden-hued, traveling together on one chariot, beholding all beings—first of you both, measuring out your impulses, as Hotars, you point out the light by means of the quarters of space.

May Bhāratī with the Ādityas desire our sacrifice; may Sarasvatī together with the Rudras protect us. Invoked along with the Vasus, may the goddesses Iḷā, being in harmony, place our sacrifice among the immortals.
Tvaṣṭṛ begot the hero who loves the gods; from Tvaṣṭṛ was born the swift, fleet horse. Tvaṣṭṛ begot this entire world; O Hotṛ, worship here the maker of much.

(5.1.11.4.k) Anointed by itself with clarified butter, let the horse go to the gods according to the seasons; may the Lord of the Forest, knowing the world of the gods, carry the offerings made savory by Agni.

(5.1.11.4ḷ) Increasing through the ascetic fervor of Prajāpati, as soon as you were born, O Agni, you took possession of the sacrifice. As the leader, come with the oblation consecrated by *svāhā*; let the Sādhyas, the gods, eat the offering.

(5.2.1.1) The gods, with Viṣṇu at their head, conquered these worlds by means of the meters so as to be invincible. In that he strides the strides of Viṣṇu, the sacrificer, having become Viṣṇu himself, conquers these worlds by means of the meters so as to be invincible.
"Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu; drive away the adversary," he says.
The Gāyatrī is indeed the earth; the Triṣṭubh is the intermediate space;
the Jagatī is the sky.
(5.2.1.1) The quarters are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter. (5.2.1.1) By means of the meters, he thus conquers these worlds in their proper order.
(5.2.1.1) Prajāpati created Agni.
(5.2.1.1) Once created from him, (5.2.1.2) he went away turned back; (5.2.1.2) she followed him with this [verse]: "He cried out."
(5.2.1.2) By that [verse], indeed, he won the dear abode of Agni; in that he recites this [verse], he wins the dear abode of Agni by means of it.
(5.2.1.2) He who strides the Viṣṇu-strides is liable to burn away from himself.
(5.2.1.2) It proceeds with four [verses]; (5.2.1.2) there are four meters; (5.2.1.2) for the meters are indeed Agni’s beloved body.
He turns toward his own dear body; he turns toward the south;
he turns according to his own heroic power.
Therefore, the right side of the self is more powerful.
Moreover, he turns around following the course of the sun.
Varuṇa seized Śunaḥśepa, the son of Ajīgarta.
(5.2.1.3) He saw this [verse] addressed to Varuṇa. (5.2.1.3) By means of it, he indeed released himself from the noose of Varuṇa.
(5.2.1.3) Varuṇa indeed seizes him who puts on the fire-pan (ukhā).
(5.2.1.3) "Loosen the highest bond from us, O Varuṇa," he says. By this [verse], he releases himself from the bonds of Varuṇa.
(5.2.1.4) "I have brought you hither," he says.
"For he indeed carries him away. "Stand firm, unshakable," he says for the sake of stability.
"May all the subjects desire you," he says; verily, by means of the subjects, he causes him to prosper. "In this man let the kingdom be established," he says.
(5.2.1.4) He has thus made the kingdom stable for him.
(5.2.1.4) With regard to whomsoever he should desire, "May he possess the kingdom," he should meditate upon that person with his mind.
He indeed becomes the kingdom itself.
"Great at the head, he has risen erect above the dawns," he says;
verily, he makes him the foremost among his equals.
"He has emerged from the darkness," he says.
"It drives away darkness from him," he says; "He has come with light," he says; verily, he bestows light upon him.
He settles it with four [verses]; there are four meters; thus, by means of the meters themselves.
(5.2.1.5) With the *atichandas* as the last [verse].
(5.2.1.5) The *atichandas* is indeed the summit among the meters;
verily, he makes him the summit among his equals.
(5.2.1.5) It is accompanied by the word "being" (sat). (5.2.1.6) It causes him to attain being itself.
He worships with the Vātsapra hymn.
By this, Vatsaprī Bhālandana indeed obtained the dear abode of Agni.
By this, one obtains the dear abode of Agni.
It consists of eleven [verses].
(5.2.1.6) Verily, he bestows vigor upon the sacrificer in a single way.
(5.2.1.6) By means of the *stoma*, the gods prospered in this world; by means of the *chandas* meters, they prospered in yonder world. Indeed, the Vātsapra is the very form of the *stoma*.
(5.2.1.6) Or rather, that he worships with the Vātsapra hymn.
(5.2.1.7) By that, he conquers this very world;
in that he strides the Viṣṇu-strides, he conquers yonder world by them.
He strides forward on the previous day and worships on the following day.
(5.2.1.7) Therefore, the mind of some other creatures is directed toward acquisition (*yoga*), while that of others is directed toward security (*kṣema*).
(5.2.1.7) Therefore, the wanderer (*yāyāvara*) has mastery over security; (5.2.1.7) therefore, the wanderer settles in a place of security.
(5.2.1.7) He clenches his fists; (5.2.1.7) he restrains his speech, for the support of the sacrifice.
"O Lord of food, give us food," he says.
Agni, indeed, is the Lord of food;
he himself bestows food upon him.
"Of the one free from disease, the vigorous," he says; by this he means "of the one free from consumption. "Further the giver; bestow strength upon us, bipeds and quadrupeds," he says.
(5.2.2.1) Verily, he invokes this very blessing.
(5.2.2.1) "May all the gods lift thee up," he says.
(5.2.2.2) The All-Gods are indeed the vital breaths; verily, by means of the vital breaths, he raises him up.
"O Agni, may they bear [thee] with their thoughts," he says; by that very thought for which he raises him up, he causes him to prosper. He sets him down with four verses.
(5.2.2.2) There are four meters; (5.2.2.2) by means of the meters themselves,
(5.2.2.2) with the *ati-chandas* as the last.
The *aticchandas* is indeed the pre-eminence among the meters;
verily, he makes him the pre-eminence among his equals.
It contains the word "sitting" (*sad*).
(5.2.2.2) It leads him to being itself.
(5.2.2.2) "Go forward, O Agni, full of light! (5.2.2.3)—thus he says; verily, he bestows light upon him. For he whom he injures, he injures by means of his own body.
"Do not harm the offspring with your body," he says;
thus he pacifies it for the sake of the offspring.
Indeed, the *rakṣas* demons attend the sacrifice whenever one lets out a cry during the *ana*.
(5.2.2.3) He recites, "He cried out," for the purpose of driving away the Rakṣases.
(5.2.2.3) They carry [the horse] with a cart.
(5.2.2.3) Verily, he bestows honor upon him; (5.2.2.3) therefore, the owner of a wagon and the owner of a chariot are the two most honored among guests.
(5.2.2.4) He becomes one who receives honor who knows thus. (5.2.2.4) With the words, "Honor Agni with fuel," he places a fuel-stick smeared with ghee upon the fire when it has been extinguished.
Just as hospitality accompanied by clarified butter is prepared for a guest who has arrived, even so is that.

(5.2.2.4) With a *gāyatrī* verse he [should perform the rite] for a Brāhmaṇa, for the Brāhmaṇa is of the *gāyatra* nature; (5.2.2.4) with a *triṣṭubh* verse for a Rājanya, for the Rājanya is of the *traiṣṭubha* nature. He causes the ashes to enter into the waters.
(5.2.2.4) Agni indeed has his origin in the waters; (5.2.2.4) he thus causes him to go to his own womb;
(5.2.2.4) he causes him to enter with three verses.
Agni is indeed threefold. He causes Agni, in his full extent, to attain a firm foundation. Verily, he who casts the ashes into the waters scatters Agni.
(5.2.2.5) He places [the two stones] with two verses containing the word "light";
verily he bestows light upon him;
with two [verses], for the sake of stability.
(5.2.2.5) He who casts ashes into the waters indeed scatters away his offspring and cattle.
With the words, "Return with vigor and with wealth," he rises up again;
thus he places offspring and cattle within himself.
(5.2.2.5) "May the Ādityas [kindle you] again! (5.2.2.6) "May the Rudras and Vasus kindle you together," he says. For these deities indeed kindled him at the beginning;
with them alone he now kindles him.
(5.2.2.6) He approaches with the words, "For the sake of awakening, thou art awakening. (5.2.2.6) Verily, he awakens him. (5.2.2.6) Therefore, after sleeping, living beings awaken.
(5.2.2.6) It stands by according to its place;
therefore, cattle, having returned from wherever their place was, stand by [their owners].

(5.2.3.1) As great as the earth is, over it Yama has attained sovereignty. (5.2.3.1) Verily, he who piles the fire-altar on this earth without having asked Yama for the place of sacrifice piles it for Yama. (5.2.3.1) He causes [the site] to be settled with the words, "Depart!"
(5.2.3.1) Having requested Yama himself as the sacrificial ground for her, he piles the fire-altar for himself.
(5.2.3.1) Desiring immortality for her, they did not find it even with the tip of an arrow;
those gods then perceived this sacrificial formula.
(5.2.3.1) "It has departed" (apeta)—
by this [term], one determines [the absence of the breath].
(5.2.3.2) He piles the fire-altar while it is indeed immortal.
(5.2.3.2) He digs up [the ground]; whatever impurity there is in this earth, that he drives away.
(5.2.3.2) He sprinkles water for the sake of pacification; (5.2.3.2) he scatters sand.
(5.2.3.2) This, indeed, is the form of Agni Vaiśvānara. (5.2.3.2) By means of this very form, he wins Vaiśvānara. (5.2.3.2) He scatters saline soil.
(5.2.3.2) Prosperity indeed is this, and procreation is salt-earth;
verily in prosperity and in procreation he piles the fire-altar. Moreover, it is for the sake of recognition.
(5.2.3.2) For this saline soil (*ūṣas*) is indeed the consciousness of cattle.
(5.2.3.3) Heaven and Earth were together;
as they were separating, they spoke.
"Let that which is fit for sacrifice be common to us both," he said.
That which was fit for sacrifice in her, he placed in this [earth], and it became the saline soil (*ūṣāḥ*).
That which was fit for sacrifice in this [earth], he placed in her; that is the black spot in the moon.
(5.2.3.3) While scattering saline soil, he should meditate on that [world]; thus he piles the fire upon the sacrificial ground of heaven and earth.
(5.2.3.3–4) "This is that Agni"—this hymn of Viśvāmitra is used.
By means of this, Viśvāmitra indeed won the beloved abode of Agni.
By this, he wins the beloved abode of Agni. By means of the meters, the gods indeed went to the heavenly world.
He places four bricks facing eastward.
(5.2.3.4) There are four meters. (5.2.3.4) By means of the meters, the sacrificer thus goes to the heavenly world.
(5.2.3.4) As they were departing for the heavenly world, the quarters collapsed.
(5.2.3.4) They placed two bricks facing each other in the east and two facing each other in the west.
(5.2.3.5) By means of them, they indeed made firm the quarters; for when he places two facing each other in the east and two facing each other in the west.
For the support of the quarters.
Moreover, the meters are indeed cattle;
verily, he bestows cattle upon him in a forward direction.
He places eight bricks.
The Gāyatrī has eight syllables; Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī. Thus he builds Agni in his full extent.
(5.2.3.5) He places eight [bricks].
(5.2.3.5) The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables; (5.2.3.5) the Gāyatrī knows the heavenly world directly.
(5.2.3.5) For the sake of perceiving the world of heaven,
(5.2.3.6) he places thirteen *lokampṛṇā* bricks;
they amount to twenty-one.
The twenty-one-fold [stoma] is indeed a foundation, and the Gārhapatya fire is a foundation.
By following the foundation that is the Gārhapatya of the twenty-one-fold, he finds firm standing;
he who knows thus stands firm, having piled the fire-altar.
One who is building for the first time should pile [the altar] with five layers; the sacrifice is fivefold, and cattle are fivefold.
Verily, he wins both the sacrifice and cattle. One who builds for a second time should build with three layers;
these worlds are three.
(5.2.3.6) In these very worlds they find firm support.
(5.2.3.7) One who is building the third layer should build it as a single layer;
for the world of heaven is indeed one-fold.
(5.2.3.7) By means of that which has a single covering, he goes to the heavenly world; (5.2.3.7) he covers it with loose soil; therefore, the bone is covered with flesh.
He who knows thus does not become afflicted with skin disease. There are five layers;
he covers them over with five fillings of earth.
They amount to ten; the *virāj* consists of ten syllables,
and the *virāj* is food.
Verily, he finds firm support in the Virāj and in the eating of food.
(5.2.4.1) These two indeed hate each other: the fire that was formerly [the original fire] and the one that is in the fire-pan.
(5.2.4.1) With the four verses beginning "Be united," he pours them together; [there are] four meters.
(5.2.4.1) The meters are indeed the dear body of Agni; (5.2.4.1) with that very dear body he consecrates these two. "Be united," he says.
Therefore, the *kṣatra* comes together with the *brahman*, in that he spreads [the fires] after having piled them up; therefore, the *kṣatra* departs from the *brahman*.
(5.2.4.1) They consecrate him by means of the seasons;
(5.2.4.2) he is released by means of the seasons alone.
(5.2.4.2) "Like a mother her son, the earth [bears] the one who is of the soil," he says.

(5.2.4.2) Verily, he consecrates him by means of the seasons and releases him by means of the seasons. (5.2.4.2) With a verse addressed to Vaiśvānara, he takes up the sling; verily, he thereby makes it palatable.
There are three black *nairṛta* cakes baked on husks. The husks are indeed the portion for Nirṛti, and black is the form of Nirṛti. By means of her very form, he makes expiation to Nirṛti.
They go toward this direction.
This, indeed, is the direction of Nirṛti;
thus he propitiates Nirṛti in her own direction.
(5.2.4.3) He places it on a self-made mound or in a cleft.
(5.2.4.3) This, indeed, is the abode of Nirṛti.
(5.2.4.3) In her very own abode he appeases Nirṛti.
(5.2.4.3) He places the sling over it.
(5.2.4.3) The noose belongs to Nirṛti;
verily, he releases him directly from the noose of Nirṛti.
He places three [bricks]. Man is indeed divided into three parts;
as great as man is, from him he thus expiates misfortune.
He places them facing away; verily, he drives Nirṛti away from him facing away.
They go without looking back.
(5.2.4.4) For concealment from Nirṛti; (5.2.4.4) having sprinkled themselves with water, they stand near for the sake of purity.
(5.2.4.4) They stand by the *gārhapatya* fire. Having wandered in the world of *nirṛti*, purified, they turn toward the world of the gods.
(5.2.4.4) They stand by it with one [verse].
(5.2.4.4) They bestow vigor upon the sacrificer in a single way.
(5.2.4.4) "The dwelling-place, the gatherer of riches," he says.
(5.2.4.4) Offspring indeed are cattle; cattle are riches.
Verily, they cause him to prosper with offspring and cattle.
(5.2.5.1) He measures it with a man's length. (5.2.5.1) For the man is commensurate with the sacrifice;
he thus measures it by means of the joints of the sacrifice.
(5.2.5.1) As tall as a man with his arms raised is he;
(5.2.5.1) for such is the strength in a man. (5.2.5.1) By means of that very strength, he measures him out.
(5.2.5.1) He becomes a bird; for one without wings is not fit to fly.
(5.2.5.1) By means of a cubit, the two wings become longer.
(5.2.5.1) Therefore, birds have wings that extend to the side; its two wings and its tail are each a fathom in length.
(5.2.5.1) For this much indeed is the vigor in a man; it is commensurate with his vigor.
(5.2.5.2) He measures with a bamboo reed; (5.2.5.2) for the bamboo reed belongs to Agni, [and this serves] for the sake of common origin.
(5.2.5.2) He yokes with a *yajus*;
(5.2.5.2) he plows with a *yajus*,
for the sake of distinction.
(5.2.5.2) He ploughs with a team of six oxen.
(5.2.5.2) There are indeed six seasons; (5.2.5.2) thus he ploughs it by means of the seasons.
(5.2.5.2) Because of the twelve-ox [ploughing] performed for a year, this very earth was afraid of being over-burnt by Agni.
(5.2.5.2) She saw this twofold [state]: the ploughed and the unploughed. (5.2.5.2) Thereupon, he did not burn her beyond measure.
That which is both ploughed and unploughed exists for this earth so that it may not be over-burnt;
they say, "A double [layer] is required to bear the fire," because there is both the ploughed and the unploughed.
(5.2.5.3) For the rising of Agni.
(5.2.5.3) Indeed, animals are of these two kinds: those with two feet and those with four feet.
(5.2.5.3) If he were to let them loose toward the east, he would deliver them over to Rudra.
If he were to set it down toward the south, it would be for the ancestors; if toward the west, the *rakṣases* would slay him. He releases it toward the north.
(5.2.5.3) This indeed is the peaceful quarter of gods and men. (5.2.5.4) He releases them following that very [quarter]. Moreover, he releases this [other] quarter; for yonder sun is the breath.
(5.2.5.4) He releases them following after the vital breath itself. (5.2.5.4) They turn back toward the south; they turn back following after their own vigor.
Therefore, the right side of the body is more vigorous.
Moreover, they turn around following the course of the sun;
therefore, animals stand facing away [from the center] and return facing toward it.
(5.2.5.4) Three furrows each; (5.2.5.5) he ploughs them. He thus extends the threefold sacrifice at its opening.
He sows the plants.
Through the *brahman*, he wins food.
On the *arka* [altar], the *arka* is piled;
with fourteen [verses] he sows.
There are seven cultivated plants and seven wild ones;
for the acquisition of both,
he sows of every kind of food.
(5.2.5.5) For the attainment of every kind of food,
he sows in ploughed ground;
for in ploughed ground plants find their firm foundation.
He sows along the furrows for the sake of procreation;
he sows in twelve furrows.
Twelve months are a year;
by means of the year itself, he cooks food for him who builds the fire-altar. If he were to eat what has not been secured, he would be deprived of what has been secured.
(5.2.5.6) Those fruits of the trees that are gathered, he should sprinkle them on the fuel as well,
for the sake of securing what has not yet been secured.
(5.2.5.6) He throws clods of earth together from the various directions.
Having secured the vigor of the quarters, he piles the fire-altar in the vigor of the quarters.
If he should hate someone, he should bring a clod of earth from the direction in which that person is located, saying:
"I take from here food and strength. Thus, he secures the food and strength of that very direction.
(5.2.5.6) He becomes hungry, for he is in that direction.
(5.2.5.6) He scatters [the earth] upon the high altar (*uttaravedi*).
(5.2.5.6) For it is upon the high altar that the fire is piled.
Moreover, the high altar is indeed cattle;
verily he wins cattle.
Moreover, it is for the sake of not interrupting the joints of the sacrifice.
(5.2.6.1) "O Agni, yours is fame and vigor"—with these words he scatters sand. This, indeed, is the hymn (*sūkta*) of Agni Vaiśvānara;
by means of this very hymn, he wins Vaiśvānara.
(5.2.6.1) He scatters with six [verses].
(5.2.6.1) For the year consists of six seasons;
(5.2.6.1) and Agni Vaiśvānara is the year.
Verily, he directly wins Vaiśvānara. This metre is indeed named "The Ocean" (*samudra*);
after the ocean, offspring are born.
(5.2.6.1) That he scatters what has been moistened with this [mixture] is for the procreation of offspring.
(5.2.6.1–2) Indra hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra.
(5.2.6.2) He divided himself threefold: one third became the wooden sword (*sphyá*), one third the chariot, and one third the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
(5.2.6.2) Those internal reeds that were shattered became gravel stones (*śarkarā*);
that is the origin of the name "gravel" (*śarkarā*).
Gravel is indeed a thunderbolt, and Agni is an animal.
In that he measures out the fire with gravel, he encloses the animals for him by means of the thunderbolt itself.
Therefore, cattle are encompassed by the thunderbolt;
therefore, one who is more stable does not yield to one who is less stable.
One should measure out [the altar] with twenty-one [bricks] for one who desires cattle.
There are indeed seven vital breaths in the head;
cattle are the vital breaths;
verily, by means of the vital breaths, he wins cattle for him.
(5.2.6.3) For one who has rivals, [the sacrifice] is performed with the Triṇava [stomas]. Having prepared a threefold weapon, he hurls it at his rival for the purpose of striking him down.
(5.2.6.3) One should measure [the altar] with an unlimited number [of bricks], for the attainment of the unlimited.
(5.2.6.3) If he should desire of someone, "May he be without cattle," one should scatter pebbles and sand over his [altar] without measuring them.
Thus, his seed, being unrestrained, is poured out in all directions.
He indeed becomes one who possesses no cattle.
(5.2.6.4) If he should desire of someone, "May he be rich in cattle," having measured it out, he should scatter pebbles and pour [the liquid] over them.
(5.2.6.4) Thus, for him, he pours forth the seed in a concentrated manner once it has been enclosed.
He indeed becomes possessed of cattle; he separates [the layers] with those belonging to Soma; for Soma is the bestower of seed.
(5.2.6.4) Thus he bestows seed.
(5.2.6.4) With a *gāyatrī* verse for a Brāhmaṇa, for the Brāhmaṇa is connected to the *gāyatrī*; (5.2.6.4) with a *triṣṭubh* verse for a Rājanya, for the Rājanya is connected to the *triṣṭubh*.
(5.2.6.4) Śamyu Bārhaspatya did not accept the sacrificial food; he entered into Agni.
(5.2.6.5) He, having assumed the form of a black antelope, went forth from Agni; (5.2.6.5) he entered the horse;
(5.2.6.5) he became the intermediate hoof of the horse.
(5.2.6.5) In that he makes the horse step forward, he wins back that very essence which entered the horse.
(5.2.6.5) "Agni is to be piled by Prajāpati," they say;
the horse belongs to Prajāpati.
(5.2.6.5) In that he makes the horse step upon [the altar], he piles the fire-altar by means of Prajāpati himself.
(5.2.6.5) He places a lotus leaf [upon it];
for the lotus leaf is indeed the womb of Agni.
(5.2.6.5) He piles the fire upon its own womb.
(5.2.6.5) He places [the brick] with the words, "Thou art the back of the waters.
For that which is the lotus leaf is indeed the back of the waters.
Verily, he lays it down with its own form.
(5.2.7.1) With the words, "The Brahman was born," he places the gold plate.
(5.2.7.1) Prajāpati indeed created creatures with the Brahman as their mouth;
thus, the sacrificer creates the creatures with the Brahman as their mouth.
"He says, 'The Brahman was born first,'" [therefore] the Brāhmaṇa is preeminent.
He who knows thus becomes preeminent.
(5.2.7.1) The exponents of Brahman say:
"The fire-altar is not to be built on earth, nor in the intermediate space, nor in heaven.
(5.2.7.1) If one were to build it on earth, he would afflict the earth with pain.
Neither herbs nor trees would be able to propagate if he were to pile [the altar] in the intermediate space; he would afflict the intermediate space with pain,
and birds would not be able to propagate.
If he were to pile [the fire-altar] in the sky, he would afflict the sky with pain;
Parjanya would not rain. He places a gold plate.
Gold is indeed immortality;
he piles the fire in immortality for the sake of procreation.
He places a golden man for the support of the sacrificer’s world.
If he were to place it upon the perforation of the brick, he would obstruct the breath of both the cattle and the sacrificer.
(5.2.7.2) To the south, (5.2.7.3) he places it facing eastward.
(5.2.7.3) He supports the world of the sacrificer;
he does not obstruct the vital breath of either the cattle or the sacrificer.
(5.2.7.3) Now, moreover, he places [the butter] upon the perforation of the brick (5.2.7.3) for the release of the vital breaths (5.2.7.3);
he touches it with the words, "The drop has fallen."
(5.2.7.3) He establishes him in the very *hotṛ*-functions.
(5.2.7.3) He places two offering-spoons (*sruk*):
one made of *kārṣmarya* wood, filled with clarified butter; the other made of *udumbara* wood, filled with curds.
(5.2.7.3) This one, indeed, is made of *kārṣmarya* wood; that one is made of *udumbara* wood.
(5.2.7.3) He thus places these two very [bricks];
he places them silently.
For he ought not to obtain these two sacrificial posts with a single *yajus* formula— the southern one made of *kārṣmarya* wood and the northern one made of *udumbara* wood.
Therefore, this [northern post] is higher than that [southern one].
(5.2.7.3) A ladle full of clarified butter made of *kārṣmarya* wood.
(5.2.7.3) Clarified butter is indeed a thunderbolt, and the *kārṣmarya* tree is a thunderbolt.
(5.2.7.3) By means of the thunderbolt, he strikes away the Rakṣases from the south of the sacrifice.
(5.2.7.3) A vessel of Udumbara wood filled with curds;
for curds are cattle and the Udumbara is vigor; verily he bestows vigor upon cattle.
He places [the bricks] on a full [altar];
verily, he establishes him in that world which is full.
"The fire-altar is to be piled in the Virāj," they say.
The offering-ladle (*sruc*) is indeed the *virāj*.
In that he places two offering-ladles, he piles the fire-altar in the *virāj* itself.
At every opening of the sacrifice, when it is being performed, the Rakṣases seek to destroy the sacrifice.
The gold plate is the mouth of the sacrifice.
In that he sprinkles [clarified butter] over the gold plate, he strikes away the *rakṣas* from the very mouth of the sacrifice.
He sprinkles it with five [verses].
The sacrifice is fivefold;
as great as the sacrifice is, from that he drives away the Rakṣases.
He sprinkles transversely.
Therefore, animals move their limbs crosswise for the sake of stability.
(5.2.8.1) He places the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.
(5.2.8.1) This earth, indeed, is the *svayamātṛṇṇā*;
it is this very [earth] that he thus places.
(5.2.8.1) He causes the horse to smell [the earth]; verily, he bestows breath upon her.
Moreover, the horse belongs to Prajāpati.
(5.2.8.1) By means of Prajāpati himself, he piles the fire-altar.
(5.2.8.1) The first brick, as it is being laid down, bestows vital breath upon both the sacrificial animals and the sacrificer.
(5.2.8.1) It is a naturally perforated (*svayamātṛṇṇā*) stone.
(5.2.8.1) For the emission of the vital breaths and for the illumination of the heavenly world.
(5.2.8.1) "Fire is to be piled upon fire," they say.
(5.2.8.2) This Brahmin is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara.
(5.2.8.2) To him he should hand over the first brick prepared with a *yajus* formula; (5.2.8.2) both the [sacrificer] and the Brāhmaṇa should lay it down.
Thus, he piles fire upon fire.
(5.2.8.2) He who, being ignorant, lays down a brick is indeed liable to suffer misfortune.
(5.2.8.2) One should grant three boons; for there are indeed three vital breaths.
For the sake of securing the vital breaths,
two [cows] indeed should be given,
for there are two vital breaths.
(5.2.8.2) Only one [animal] is to be given. (5.2.8.2) For the vital breath is indeed one. (5.2.8.2–3) This Agni is indeed an animal.
(5.2.8.3) Indeed, cattle do not delight in mere grass.
He places a dūrvā-brick for the support of cattle;
with two verses, for stability.
"Growing up from joint to joint," he says; for by means of every single joint this [durvā grass] establishes itself.
"Thus, O durvā, extend us with a thousand and a hundred," he says.
Prajāpati is thousandfold;
[it serves] for the attainment of Prajāpati.
The three-lined [brick] is indeed the mark of the gods.
(5.2.8.3) The gods placed that one with the mark above, and the Asuras [placed] the one with the mark below.
(5.2.8.4) Whomever one should desire, thinking, "May he become more prosperous," for him one should place [the brick] with the mark above.
(5.2.8.4) He indeed becomes more prosperous.
(5.2.8.4) If one should desire of someone,
"May he become worse off," one should place for him [a brick] marked with downward signs.
He causes him to follow after the womb of the Asuras;
he becomes worse off. It is marked with three lines.
(5.2.8.4) These worlds indeed are the three-lined [brick].
(5.2.8.4) From these very worlds he excludes his rival.
(5.2.8.4) When the Aṅgirases were going to the world of heaven, the sacrificial cake, having become a tortoise, crawled after them.
(5.2.8.5) In that he places the tortoise, just as one who knows the terrain leads straight to his destination, even so does the tortoise lead him straight to the heavenly world.
(5.2.8.5) The tortoise is indeed the vital essence (*medhas*) of animals.
In that he places the tortoise, the animals attend upon it, beholding their own vital essence.
(5.2.8.5) Indeed, this is being made into a cemetery when the heads of dead animals are placed down.
(5.2.8.5) In that he places a living tortoise, by that it is not piled as a cemetery. (5.2.8.6) For this tortoise is indeed a dweller in the homestead.
(5.2.8.6) With the verse, "The winds are honey for the one who follows the cosmic order," he anoints it with curds mixed with honey.
(5.2.8.6) Thus he makes it palatable. For curds are food of the village, while honey is food of the wild.
(5.2.8.6) That he anoints [the horse] with curds mixed with honey is for the attainment of both.
(5.2.8.6) He says, "May the great heaven and earth [protect] us.
(5.2.8.6) Verily, by means of these two, he encloses him on both sides.
(5.2.8.6) He places it facing eastward.
(5.2.8.7) Therefore, from the front, animals approach the sacrificial offering facing westward.
For whoever piles the fire-altar without a navel, it enters into the navel of the sacrificer.
(5.2.8.7) He is liable to injure him. (5.2.8.7) He places the mortar down; (5.2.8.7) for this indeed is the navel of Agni.
(5.2.8.7) He piles the fire with its own navel for the sake of non-injury.
(5.2.8.7) It is made of Udumbara wood. (5.2.8.7) The Udumbara is indeed vigor.
Verily, he wins strength;
he places it in the middle;
verily, he bestows strength upon him in the middle.
Therefore, they consume strength from the middle. It is of this size; it is commensurate with Prajāpati, the mouth of the sacrifice.
He strikes down;
he has indeed made food.
He places [it] down with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice;
the trees belong to Viṣṇu.
Thus, he establishes the sacrifice within the sacrifice itself.
(5.2.9.1) This fire-pan (*ukhā*) is indeed the light gathered for these worlds.
In that he places the fire-pan, he wins light from these very worlds. He places it in the middle.
(5.2.9.1) He thus bestows light upon him from the very middle;
(5.2.9.1) therefore we worship the light from the middle.
(5.2.9.1) He fills [the pit] with sand.
(5.2.9.1) This, indeed, is the form of Agni Vaiśvānara. (5.2.9.1) By means of this very form, he wins Vaiśvānara. (5.2.9.1) Whomever he may desire—
(5.2.9.1) "He should be hungry," [thinking thus], one should add a deficient [verse] for him;
(5.2.9.2) he indeed becomes hungry— [this applies to] whomsoever one should desire.

(5.2.9.2) "He shall eat food that does not fail him"—for this purpose, one should place a full [vessel] for him. (5.2.9.2) Thus he eats food that indeed does not fail him. (5.2.9.2) For a man bestows a thousand cattle; a thousand are the other cattle.
(5.2.9.2) He places the human head in the middle for the sake of possessing vigor;
he places it within the fire-pan.
(5.2.9.2) He thus causes it to reach a firm foundation.
(5.2.9.2) This human head is indeed deprived of the vital breaths and is impure; however, the vital breaths are truly immortal, and gold is immortal. (5.2.9.3) Gold is immortal.
(5.2.9.3) He throws pieces of gold into the vital breaths; having thus caused it to reach a firm foundation, he unites it with the vital breaths. He fills [the vessels] with curds mixed with honey.
"May I be sweet," [he says];
by means of the boiled *ātaṅkya* he attains purity.
For curd is village food, while honey is forest food.
In that he fills [the vessels] with curds mixed with honey, it is for the attainment of both;
he places the heads of animals [on the altar],
for the heads of animals are indeed cattle.
(5.2.9.3) Verily, he wins cattle.
(5.2.9.3) Regarding whomsoever one might desire:
"May he be without cattle. (5.2.9.3) [For him, one should perform this rite.]
(5.2.9.3) He should place them facing in different directions;
thus he places cattle facing in different directions away from him, and he becomes indeed destitute of cattle.
(5.2.9.3) If he should desire of someone,
"May he be possessed of cattle," he should place those bricks for him with their faces turned toward one another; verily, he bestows cattle upon him in a unified manner.
He indeed becomes possessed of cattle.
He places the horse's brick facing westward in the front, and the bull's brick facing eastward in the back.
For other than cows and horses, animals are indeed not true cattle.
(5.2.9.3) He thus provides him with cattle and horses facing toward him.
(5.2.9.3) So many indeed are the animals—both bipeds and quadrupeds.
(5.2.9.4) It is these that he places into the fire when he lays down the heads of the sacrificial animals.
(5.2.9.4) "I assign that one for you to the forest," he says. (5.2.9.4) Thus he releases distress upon the wild animals from the domestic animals.
Therefore, among animals that are born in equal numbers, the wild animals are fewer.
For they are impelled by grief;
he places a serpent’s head [on the altar]; whatever brilliance is in the serpent, that he thereby wins.

If he were to place [the bricks] together with the animal heads facing toward each other, the domestic animals would be liable to be bitten; if [he places them] facing away from each other, the wild animals [would be so].
Therefore, he should simply recite the *yajus* formula.
(5.2.9.5) He secures that brilliance which is in the serpent;
(5.2.9.5) he harms neither domestic animals nor wild animals; (5.2.9.5) nevertheless, it should indeed be placed.
In that he lays them down, he thereby wins that brilliance which is in the serpent; in that he recites the sacrificial formula (*yajus*), it is thereby pacified.
This Agni is indeed an animal.
Now, that sacrificial formula (*yajus*) which is performed prior to the bricks is the womb from which the animal is fashioned; the *apasyā* bricks are the seed.
He places the *apasyā* bricks;
verily he deposits seed in the womb;
he places five.
(5.2.10.1) Cattle are fivefold;
(5.2.10.1) verily he procreates cattle for him.
Five [are placed] to the south.
The Apasyā bricks are indeed the thunderbolt.
By means of the thunderbolt, he strikes away the Rakṣases from the south of the sacrifice.
He places five [bricks] behind, facing eastward.
(5.2.10.2) Indeed, seed is deposited from behind toward the front;
verily, he deposits seed for him from behind toward the front.
He places five bricks facing west in front, and five facing east behind.
Therefore, semen is deposited facing eastward, yet offspring are born facing westward. There are five *chandasyā* bricks on the north;
for the *chandasyās* are indeed cattle.
Verily, he carries the procreated cattle back to their own abode.
Indeed, this [earth] was afraid of Agni’s excessive burning;
she beheld these *apasyā* bricks.
He laid them down;
then indeed he did not burn this [earth] excessively.
In that he lays down the *apasyā* bricks, it is for the sake of preventing the excessive burning of this [earth].
He said, "It has been given; he shall eat the food of Brahman, he for whom these are laid down, and he who knows them thus. He lays down the Prāṇabhṛt bricks.
Verily, he places the vital breaths in the *retas*;
therefore, an animal is born capable of speaking, breathing, seeing, and hearing.
He places [the brick] in front with the words, "This one before, Bhuvas."
By these [verses], he indeed supports the vital breath.
"This one on the south, Viśvakarman," [he says] on the south;
by these [verses], he indeed supports the mind.
"This one behind is all-pervading"—thus [he places one] behind.
By these [formulas], he has indeed supported the eye.
"This one above is heaven"—thus [he places one] from the north.
By these [verses], he indeed sustains the ear.
With the words, "This thought is above," he [places them] above.
By these [verses], he indeed sustains speech.
He places them ten by ten for the sake of possessing strength.
He places them crosswise;
therefore, animals move their limbs crosswise.
For the sake of stability:
by those [lines] which run eastward Vasiṣṭha prospered; by those which run southward Bharadvāja prospered.
(5.2.10.5) With those that face westward, Viśvāmitra; with those that face northward, Jamadagni;
with those that face upward, Viśvakarman.
(5.2.10.5) He who thus knows their prosperity indeed prospers;
(5.2.10.5) he who thus knows their kinship becomes possessed of kin;
(5.2.10.5) he who thus knows their arrangement finds success. (5.2.10.6) Success comes to him.
(5.2.10.6) He who knows their abode in this way becomes possessed of an abode;
(5.2.10.6) he who knows their foundation in this way stands firm indeed. Having laid down the breath-holders, he lays down the restrainers.
Having placed the vital breaths within him, he unites them with the *saṃyats*. That is the essence of the *saṃyats*.
Moreover, he places the out-breath (*apāna*) within the in-breath (*prāṇa*).
Therefore, the out-breath and the in-breath move together.
He lays them down facing in different directions;
therefore, the out-breath and the in-breath move in different directions.
Whatever of Agni is unrestrained, that part of his is not conducive to heaven; Agni is indeed conducive to heaven.
In that he lays down [the bricks] restrained, he restrains him completely and makes him conducive to heaven.
(5.2.10.7) "The three-year-old is the vigor of the Ayas," he says; (5.2.10.7) by means of the birds he wins the Ayas, and by means of the Ayas he wins the birds.
(5.2.10.7) On all sides they contain the word "wind" (vāyu); therefore, this [wind] blows from every direction.
May the Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, Anuṣṭubh, along with the Paṅkti, Bṛhatī, Uṣṇihā, and Kakubh, pierce you with needles.
Whether they be two-footed, four-footed, three-footed, or six-footed; whether they have regular meters or irregular meters—may they pierce you with needles.
May the Mahānāmnīs, the Revatīs, all the quarters that bring forth, the clouds, the lightnings, and the voices—with their needles—stitch you together.
Silver, golden, and leaden—these yokes are joined for the rites; let them fasten you with needles upon the skin of the vigorous horse.
(5.2.11.1.e) O women! (5.2.11.2) May those wives comb out the hair with their wisdom; may the wives of the gods, the quarters of space, stitch you together with needles.

(5.2.11.1.f) Surely, just as those who possess barley reap the grain in due order, separating it out, so do you prepare food here for those who have not come to the trimming of the sacred grass with their homage.
(5.2.12.1.a) Who flays you? Who dissects you? Who carves your limbs? And who is your wise immolator?
(5.2.12.1.b) May the seasons, as your immolators, dissect your joint according to the seasons; may they prepare you with the nourishment of the year and with their skillful acts.
(5.2.12.1.c) May the divine Adhvaryus cut you and direct you; may they, performing their work, fashion your limbs joint by joint.
May the half-months and the months, healing you, set your joints right; may the Maruts heal whatever is injured in you through days and nights.
(5.2.12.1.e) May the earth together with the intermediate space and Vāyu heal your wound; may the sky together with the constellations fashion your form perfectly.
May there be well-being for your upper limbs, may there be well-being for your lower limbs; may there be well-being for your bones and marrow, and may there be well-being for your body.
(5.3.1.1) This Agni is indeed a sacrifice that has been destroyed.
(5.3.1.1) What is performed for him, and what is not?
Whatever part of the sacrifice is omitted while it is being performed, that part of his becomes putrid.
(5.3.1.1) He places the *āśvinī* bricks.
(5.3.1.1) The Aśvins are indeed the physicians of the gods; through them he provides medicine for him.
He offers five; the sacrifice is fivefold;
as great as the sacrifice is, for that he provides a remedy.
(5.3.1.1) He places the seasonal bricks; for the proper ordering of the seasons.
(5.3.1.2) He offers five;
for there are five seasons— just as many as the seasons are.
(5.3.1.2) He arranges them;
(5.3.1.2) they have the same beginning and the same end,
therefore the seasons are the same.
(5.3.1.2) By means of a single foot they turn away;
(5.3.1.2) therefore the seasons turn away.
He places the Prāṇabhṛts.
Verily, he places the vital breaths within the seasons; therefore, although the seasons are alike, they do not decay.
Moreover, he causes them to procreate.
(5.3.1.2) This indeed is Vāyu, which is the vital breath. (5.3.1.2) When, having laid down the seasonal bricks, one lays down the breath-supporting bricks.
He lays them down; therefore, Vāyu revolves through all the seasons.
He lays down the rain-winning bricks;
verily, he wins rain. If he were to lay them down in one place, it would rain for only one season.
He sets them down in a continuous circuit; therefore it rains during all the seasons.
In that, having placed the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks, he places the rain-winning (*vṛṣṭisani*) bricks, therefore the rain, impelled by the wind, flows down from heaven.
The *vayasyā* bricks are indeed cattle.
(5.3.1.3) Animals indeed have diverse minds and diverse vows; they are, however, unanimous with respect to water alone.
(5.3.1.4) If he should desire of someone,
