"May he be without cattle," he should place the vayasyā bricks after laying down the apasyā bricks for him; thus he brings about a lack of harmony with cattle for him,
and he indeed becomes without cattle.

(5.3.1.4) If he should desire of someone, "May he be rich in cattle," he should place the *apasyā* bricks for him and then place the *vayasyā* bricks; verily, he brings about recognition for him through cattle, and he indeed becomes rich in cattle.
(5.3.1.4) He places four in front;
therefore there are four forms of the eye: two white and two black.
They consist of verses containing the word "head" (*mūrdhan*);
therefore, the head is in front.
He places five bricks on the southern hip and five on the northern; therefore, the animal is broader behind and slopes forward.
(5.3.1.5) With the words, "The ram is our strength," he places [a brick] on the right shoulder; with the words, "The bull is our strength," on the left.
Thus he restores the two shoulders.
(5.3.1.5) With the words, "The tiger is our strength," he places [a brick] on the right wing; with the words, "The lion is our strength," on the left.
Verily, he bestows vigor upon the two wings; "Man is the strength," he says in the middle; therefore, man is the lord of animals.
(5.3.2.1) "O Indra and Agni, [you two who are] unshakable," with these words he places the *svayamātṛṇṇā* (self-perforated brick).
(5.3.2.1) Indeed, these two worlds are held apart by Indra and Agni;
[he does this] for the sake of holding these two worlds apart.
(5.3.2.1) This middle layer is, as it were, unsupported;
(5.3.2.1) it is, as it were, the intermediate space.
"O Indra and Agni," he says.
Indra and Agni are indeed the upholders of vigor among the gods. By means of vigor itself, he piles her in the intermediate space for the sake of support.
(5.3.2.1) He places the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.
(5.3.2.1) The *svayamātṛṇṇā* is indeed the intermediate space.
(5.3.2.1) Thus he places the intermediate space itself.
(5.3.2.1) He causes the horse to smell [the earth].
(5.3.2.2) Thus he bestows breath upon her;
moreover, the horse belongs to Prajāpati.
(5.3.2.2) Verily, by means of Prajāpati he piles the fire-altar.
(5.3.2.2) There is a naturally perforated brick for the emission of the vital breaths.
(5.3.2.2) Moreover, it is for the illumination of the world of heaven.
(5.3.2.2) When the gods were proceeding to the world of heaven, the quarters collapsed; they saw these [bricks] belonging to the quarters.
They laid them down;
by means of them, they indeed made firm the quarters.
In that he lays down the bricks pertaining to the quarters, [it is for this purpose].
For the support of the quarters,
he places ten life-sustainers in front;
there are indeed nine vital breaths in a person, and the navel is the tenth.
(5.3.2.3) Verily, he places the vital breaths in the front; therefore the vital breaths are in the front.
(5.3.2.3) He places the last brick as the luminous one.
Therefore, among the vital breaths, speech is the highest light. He places ten [bricks] down;
the *virāj* consists of ten syllables.
The Virāj is the light among the meters.
He places light in front;
therefore, we worship light from the front.
(5.3.2.3) The meters ran a race for the cattle;
the Bṛhatī won them. Therefore, cattle are said to belong to the Bṛhatī. (5.3.2.4) Therefore, cattle are called *bārhatāḥ*.
(5.3.2.4) "Mā is the metre," he places [the brick] on the south; therefore beans turn toward the right.
(5.3.2.4) "Pṛthivī is the metre," [he places it] on the west for stability.
(5.3.2.4) "Agni is the deity," [he places it] on the north; Agni is indeed vigor; verily he bestows vigor on the north; therefore one who advances toward the north conquers.
They amount to thirty-six;
the *bṛhatī* consists of thirty-six syllables, and cattle are connected with the *bṛhatī*.
By means of the Bṛhatī itself, he wins cattle for him.
The Bṛhatī attained sovereignty among the meters;
for whomsoever these [bricks] are laid down, he attains sovereignty.
(5.3.2.5) He places seven *vālakhilyā* bricks in front and seven behind.
(5.3.2.5) There are indeed seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in the head and two downward breaths; [this is done] for the sake of providing the vital breaths with strength.
(5.3.2.5) With the words, "Thou art the head, the sovereign," he places one in front; with the words, "The controller, the sovereign," he places one behind.
Verily, he bestows the vital breaths upon him in their proper order.
Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did that as well.
Those gods saw these Akṣṇayāstomīya [hymns]; they recited them in one way and performed them in another.
The Asuras did not follow that;
therefore the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
In that he lays down the Akṣṇayāstomīya bricks differently from how they are recited, it is for the sake of overcoming his rival.
(5.3.3.1) He prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated.
(5.3.3.1) "The swift Trivṛt"—with these words he places it in front;
for the Trivṛt is indeed the mouth of the sacrifice.
(5.3.3.2) He extends the very mouth of the sacrifice in front;
(5.3.3.2) "The sky, the seventeenfold," he says on the south.
The sky is indeed food.
Food is seventeenfold.
He places food on the right;
therefore, food is eaten with the right hand.
(5.3.3.2) "The support, the twenty-onefold"—the twenty-onefold is indeed a foundation;
(5.3.3.2) [it serves] for stability.
(5.3.3.2) "The shining, the fifteenfold"—[this is] from the north.
(5.3.3.2) Power indeed is the *bhānta* [chant];
(5.3.3.2) power is the fifteenfold [stoma];
(5.3.3.2) verily, he bestows power upon the north.
(5.3.3.2) Therefore, he who advances from the north conquers.
(5.3.3.2) With the words, "The onset, eighteenfold," he places [the bricks] in the east.
(5.3.3.3) He places two *trivṛt* [bricks] one after the other at the beginning of the sacrifice, thereby causing them to extend.
(5.3.3.3) "The Abhivarta with twenty [verses]" is on the south side. (5.3.3.3) Food, indeed, is the Abhivarta;
food is that which has twenty.
(5.3.3.3) He places food on the right side;
therefore food is eaten with the right hand.
(5.3.3.3) "Splendor, the twenty-second," [he says] behind.
In that there are twenty, and two of them, by that they are two *virāj*s;
in that there are two, they are a support.
Thus, he establishes himself successively in the food-eating power of the two *virāj*s.
(5.3.3.3) "Austerity is nineteenfold," [he says] on the north;
therefore the left [hand] is more ascetic of the two hands.
(5.3.3.4) "The womb is twenty-fourfold," he places [the brick] in front.
The Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables;
the Gāyatrī is the mouth of the sacrifice.
Verily, he extends the mouth of the sacrifice from the front.
(5.3.3.4) "The embryos are the twenty-fivefold [stoma]," [he says] on the south side. (5.3.3.4) Embryos are indeed food;
(5.3.3.4) the twenty-fivefold [stoma] is food.
(5.3.3.4) He places food on the right;
therefore food is eaten with the right hand.
(5.3.3.4) "The twenty-sevenfold is vigor," [he says] behind.
(5.3.3.4) These worlds indeed are the twenty-sevenfold [stoma].
(5.3.3.4) He finds firm support in these very worlds.
(5.3.3.4) "The twenty-threefold is the gathering," (5.3.3.5) [he says] from the north.
(5.3.3.5) Therefore, between the two hands, the left hand is more to be honored.
(5.3.3.5) "The sacrifice is the thirty-onefold"—with these words he places [the brick] in front; for the sacrifice is indeed speech.
Speech is indeed the mouth of the sacrifice;
thus he extends the very mouth of the sacrifice from the front.
"The summit of the ruddy one, the thirty-fourfold [stoma]"—thus on the south.
(5.3.3.5) Yonder sun, indeed, is the summit of the firmament;
(5.3.3.5) verily he bestows spiritual luster upon the right side;
(5.3.3.5) therefore the right half is more endowed with spiritual luster.
"The thirty-threefold is the foundation," [he says] toward the west,
for the sake of stability;
"the vault is the thirty-sixfold," [he says] toward the north.
The world of heaven is indeed the firmament;
[this is] for the attainment of the world of heaven.
(5.3.4.1) With the words, "Thou art the portion of Agni," he places [a brick] in front.
(5.3.4.1) For Agni is the mouth of the sacrifice;
the consecration (*dīkṣā*) is the mouth of the sacrifice.
(5.3.4.1) Brahman is the mouth of the sacrifice;
(5.3.4.1) the *trivṛt* is the mouth of the sacrifice.
(5.3.4.1) Thus, he extends the very mouth of the sacrifice at the beginning.
(5.3.4.1) "Thou art the portion of the Nṛcakṣases," [he says] on the south.
(5.3.4.1) The Nṛcakṣases are indeed those who have heard [the Veda];
the Dhātṛ is food.
(5.3.4.1) He indeed bestows food upon him as soon as he is born;
therefore, once born, he eats food.
"The birthplace is protected, the seventeenfold hymn-form," he says.
(5.3.4.1) Food, indeed, is the place of birth.
Food is seventeenfold.
He places food on the right side;
therefore, food is eaten with the right hand.
(5.3.4.2) "Thou art the portion of Mitra," [he says] at the back;
(5.3.4.2) Mitra is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*), Varuṇa is the in-breath (*apāna*); verily, he bestows both out-breath and in-breath upon him.
"Rain from heaven, winds won over, the twenty-onefold hymn-form," he says;
for the twenty-onefold is a firm foundation,
[and thus it serves] for stability.
(5.3.4.2) "Thou art the portion of Indra," [he says] to the north. (5.3.4.2) Indra is vigor;
Viṣṇu is vigor.
(5.3.4.2) Vital power is the ruling power;
(5.3.4.2) vital power is the fifteenfold [stoma].
Verily, he bestows vigor from the north;
therefore, one who advances toward the north conquers.
With the words, "Thou art the portion of the Vasus," he places [the brick] in the east.
The Vasus are indeed the mouth of the sacrifice;
the Rudras are the mouth of the sacrifice;
the Caturviṃśa is the mouth of the sacrifice.
(5.3.4.3) He extends the very mouth of the sacrifice in the east.
(5.3.4.3) "Thou art the portion of the Ādityas," [he says] on the south;
for the Ādityas are indeed food.
(5.3.4.3) Food is the Maruts;
(5.3.4.3) food is the embryos;
(5.3.4.3) food is the twenty-fivefold [stoma].
(5.3.4.3) He places food on the right side;
therefore food is eaten with the right hand.
(5.3.4.4) "Thou art the portion of Aditi," [he says] behind.
Aditi is indeed a firm foundation; Pūṣan is a firm foundation;
the Triṇava is a firm foundation.
(5.3.4.4) For the sake of stability.
(5.3.4.4) "Thou art the portion of the god Savitṛ," [he says] on the north side.
The god Savitṛ is indeed Brahman.
Brahman is Bṛhaspati;
the Catuṣṭoma is Brahman.
Verily, he bestows spiritual luster from the north.
Therefore, the northern half is more endowed with spiritual luster;
it contains the Sāvitrī verse for the sake of impulsion.
(5.3.4.4) Therefore, the gain of the Brāhmaṇas is directed toward the north.
(5.3.4.4) He places [the brick] in front with the words, "The Dhartra is the Catuṣṭoma";
for the Dhartra is indeed the mouth of the sacrifice.
The Catuṣṭoma is the mouth of the sacrifice;
verily he extends the mouth of the sacrifice at the beginning with the words,
"Thou art the portion of the Yavas."
(5.3.4.5) To the south.
(5.3.4.5) The *yāva*s are indeed the months and the *ayāva*s are the half-months; therefore, the months turn toward the south.
(5.3.4.5) Food indeed is the barley-grass; (5.3.4.5) food is offspring;
(5.3.4.5) verily, he places food on the right side.
Therefore, food is eaten with the right hand. With the words, "Thou art the portion of the Ṛbhus," he places it behind for the sake of stability.
(5.3.4.5) "The *vivarta* is the forty-eighth," [he says] from the north.
(5.3.4.5) For the sake of the vigor of these two worlds, (5.3.4.5) therefore these two worlds are equal in vigor.
(5.3.4.6) He for whom the *mukhyavatī* bricks are laid down in the east becomes preeminent;
(5.3.4.6) a preeminent son is born to him.
(5.3.4.6) He for whom the *annavatī* bricks are [laid] on the south eats food.
One who has [the bricks] on the east becomes an eater of food;
one for whom they are established on the west is firmly established;
and one for whom they are vigorous on the north becomes truly vigorous.
(5.3.4.6) He is born vigorous of mouth.
(5.3.4.6) This Agni is indeed the *arka*; this is his very *stotra* and this is his *śastra*.
(5.3.4.6) In that this *vidhā* is so arranged—(5.3.4.7) the *arka* is indeed arranged according to that *arkya*.
(5.3.4.7) He eats food; he becomes an eater of food, for whomsoever this *vidhā* is so arranged, and who knows it thus.
(5.3.4.7) He lays down the *sṛṣṭi*-bricks.
(5.3.4.7) He obtains it exactly as it was created.
(5.3.4.7) "Verily, this [world] was neither day nor night; it was undifferentiated. (5.3.4.7) Those gods saw these *vyuṣṭi*-offerings.
They laid them down;
from that, indeed, this world shone forth.
For whomsoever these are laid down, for him it shines forth.
Moreover, he indeed drives away the darkness.
(5.3.5.1) "O Agni, drive away our born enemies," with these words he places [the brick] in the east;
thus he drives away his born rivals.
"Those born by force," [with these words] he places it in the west.
(5.3.5.1) He repels those very ones who are about to be born.
(5.3.5.1) "The forty-fourfold hymn-form," he says on the south side.
The forty-fourfold hymn-form is indeed spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Verily, he bestows spiritual luster on the right side;
therefore the right half is more endowed with spiritual luster.
"The sixteenfold hymn-form," [he says] on the left side.
The sixteenth [stotra] is indeed vigor. He places vigor on the north side; therefore, one who advances toward the north conquers.
The forty-fourfold [stoma] is indeed a thunderbolt, and the sixteenfold is a thunderbolt.
In that he lays down these two bricks, having driven away both his born and his yet-to-be-born rivals, he hurls the thunderbolt after them for their destruction.
He places [the brick] containing loose earth in the middle;
the middle indeed is the internal substance of the self;
thus he piles the fire-altar as one possessed of its own body.
He who knows this becomes possessed of a self in that world.
These indeed are the bricks named Asapatnā;
he for whom these are laid down [becomes so].
(5.3.5.3) He has no rival.
(5.3.5.3) This Agni is indeed an animal;
he places it upon the last layer of the Virāj.
He places the Virāj itself as the highest among the cattle;
therefore, one who possesses cattle speaks the highest speech.
He lays them down ten by ten for the sake of possessing strength.
He places them crosswise;
therefore animals move their limbs crosswise, for the sake of stability.
Those meters which were conducive to heaven, by means of them the gods went to the heavenly world.
(5.3.5.3) By means of that, the seers (ṛṣis) (5.3.5.4) exerted themselves; (5.3.5.4) they practiced austerity;
(5.3.5.4) through austerity, they perceived those [Vedas].
For them, he fashioned these bricks:
"The *evaś* metre, the *varivas* metre"—
thus they laid them down.

(5.3.5.4) By means of them, indeed, they went to the heavenly world. (5.3.5.4) In that he lays down these bricks, (5.3.5.4) by those very meters which lead to heaven, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world.

(5.3.5.4) By means of the sacrifice, Prajāpati indeed created offspring; (5.3.5.4) he created them by means of the Stomabhāgas. (5.3.5.5) In that he lays down the Stomabhāgas, the sacrificer thereby creates offspring.
(5.3.5.5) Bṛhaspati indeed gathered together this brilliance of the sacrifice, which is the Stomabhāgas. In that he lays down the Stomabhāgas, he piles the fire-altar with its very brilliance.
Bṛhaspati indeed perceived this foundation of the sacrifice, which is the Stomabhāgas.
(5.3.5.5) In that he lays down the *stomabhāgā* bricks, it is for the stability of the sacrifice.
(5.3.5.5) He lays them down seven by seven for the sake of possessing strength; three in the middle for the sake of stability.
With "the ray," he created the sun; with "the advance," he created dharma; with "the following," he created the sky.
The junction is the intermediate space;
the support is the earth;
the pillar is the rain.
"Prava" follows the day;
"anuvā" follows the night;
"uśij" [belongs] to the Vasus.
(5.3.6.1) With "Praketa," [he addresses] the Rudras;
(5.3.6.1) with "Sudīti," the Ādityas; (5.3.6.1) with "Ojas," the Pitṛs.
"Thread" refers to offspring; "conqueror of armies" refers to cattle; "wealthy" refers to plants.
(5.3.6.1) "Thou art the victorious one, with the pressing-stones yoked. (5.3.6.2) Saying, "For Indra thee! Quicken Indra!", he thus brandished the thunderbolt from the south for the sake of victory.
(5.3.6.2) He created those creatures without vital breath; saying, "Thou art the overlord," he thus bestowed vital breath upon them.
"Yanta" is the out-breath;
"Saṃsarpa" is the eye;
"Vayodhā" is the ear.
Those creatures, though breathing out and breathing in, seeing and hearing, did not become paired.
Into them he placed the pair by means of [the formula] "Thou art the threefold.
Those creatures, even while becoming paired, did not procreate.
With the words, "Thou art growth; thou art non-decay," he brought them forth.
Those creatures, once born, did not find firm support.
With the words, "Thou art Vasuk, thou art Veṣaśri, thou art Vasyaṣṭi," he established them firmly in these worlds.
When he says,
"Thou art Vasuku, thou art Veṣaśrī, thou art Vasyaṣṭi," he establishes the very progeny born in these worlds;
with his self, he ascends the intermediate region.
Possessing vital breath, he becomes established in yonder world;
he does not fail in his out-breath and in-breath, who knows thus.
(5.3.7.1) By means of the *nākasads*, the gods indeed went to the heavenly world; that is why they have the character of *nākasads*.
When he lays down the *nākasads*, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world by means of those very *nākasads*.
The world of heaven is indeed the *nāka*.
For him for whom these [bricks] are laid down, there is no suffering (*aka*).
The *nākasad* is indeed the station of the sacrificer.
(5.3.7.1) In that he lays down the *nākasad* bricks, the sacrificer thereby creates a firm foundation for himself.
(5.3.7.1) The *nākasad* bricks are indeed the concentrated splendor of the *pṛṣṭha* stotras.
(5.3.7.2) In that he lays down the *nākasad* bricks, he wins for himself the very splendor of the *pṛṣṭha* stotras.
(5.3.7.2) He places down five with fringes.
These, having become Apsarases, lie down beside him in yonder world. Moreover, these are indeed protectors of the body for the sacrificer.
While laying down [a brick], he should meditate upon whomsoever he hates.
He cuts him off from these very deities;
he swiftly meets with ruin.
(5.3.7.2) He places the subsequent [bricks] upon the *nākasad* bricks;
it is just as when one brings home a wife and seats her in the house. (5.3.7.2) It is exactly like that.
(5.3.7.3) He places the last brick facing eastward from behind; therefore the wife sits behind, facing eastward.
(5.3.7.3) He places the *svayamātṛṇṇā* and the *vikarṇī* as the two uppermost bricks.
The *svayamātṛṇṇā* is indeed breath, and the *vikarṇī* is life.
He bestows both breath and life, the two highest among the vital breaths;
therefore, breath and life are the two highest among the vital breaths.
He should not place any other brick above them.
If he were to place another brick above it, he would obstruct the breath and the life-span of both the cattle and the sacrificer;
therefore, no other brick should be placed above it.
He places the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.
(5.3.7.4) He places that very naturally perforated brick;
he causes the horse to smell it, thereby bestowing vital breath upon it.
Moreover, the horse belongs to Prajāpati; thus, by means of Prajāpati himself, he piles the fire-altar.
The naturally perforated brick is used for the release of the vital breaths and also for the illumination of the world of heaven.
This Vikarṇī brick is indeed the stride of the gods; in that he lays down the Vikarṇī, he strides along after the very stride of the gods.
He places it to the north;
therefore, the fire has its ritual service from the north.
It contains the word "Vāyu."
For the sake of kindling.
He places the meters;
the meters are indeed cattle;
verily, he wins cattle.
The meters are indeed the desirable wealth of the gods, and cattle are desirable wealth. Verily, he wins for himself both desirable wealth and cattle.
Yajñasena Caitriyāyaṇa, it is said, discovered this very layer.
(5.3.8.1) By means of it, he indeed won cattle;
(5.3.8.1) in that he lays down this [brick], he wins cattle.
He lays down the Gāyatrī verses in front.
The Gāyatrī is indeed splendor; verily, he places splendor at the very beginning. They consist of verses containing the word "head."
(5.3.8.2) He thus makes him the head of his equals.
(5.3.8.2) He places *triṣṭubh* verses;
the *triṣṭubh* is indeed power (*indriya*).
(5.3.8.2) Verily, he places the sense-organ in the middle;
(5.3.8.2) he lays down the *jagatī* verses; for cattle are indeed connected with the *jagatī*.
Verily, he wins cattle.
He places [bricks] of the *anuṣṭubh* metre;
for the *anuṣṭubh* is indeed the vital breaths.
For the release of the vital breaths, he lays down bricks with various meters: *bṛhatīs*, *uṣṇihās*, *paṅktis*, and *akṣarapaṅktis*;
for cattle are indeed of diverse forms.
(5.3.8.2) Cattle. (5.3.8.3) The meters.
Verily, he wins cattle of diverse forms;
diverse forms are seen in the house of him for whom these [bricks] are laid down, and also for him who knows them thus.
He places a brick with an *aticchandas* verse.
The *aticchandas* indeed contains all the meters;
thus, he builds it up with all the meters.
The *aticchandas* is indeed the summit among the meters.
In that he lays down an *aticchandas*, he makes him the summit among his equals.
He lays down [bricks] in the *dvipadā* meter.
The sacrificer has two feet;
[this is] for the sake of stability.

(5.3.9.1) Indeed, Agni is piled for all the deities. (5.3.9.1) If he were not to lay down the *sayuj* bricks, the deities would exclude him from the fire-altar. In that he lays down the *sayuj* bricks, he piles it with its own self as a companion; thus he is not deprived of the fire-altar.
(5.3.9.1) Moreover, just as a man is held together by his sinews, even so is Agni held together by these [bricks].
(5.3.9.1) By means of Agni, the gods went to the heavenly world; they became those Kṛttikās.

For one for whom these are laid down, he goes to and reaches the heavenly world; he becomes manifest and resplendent. (5.3.9.2) He indeed attains and enters the heavenly world; he becomes truly brilliant.
(5.3.9.2) He lays down the mandala-bricks.
(5.3.9.2) These worlds, indeed, are the mandala-bricks. (5.3.9.2) These worlds, moreover, are the fortresses of the gods.
(5.3.9.2) He who has piled the fire enters the very citadels of the gods and does not come to ruin.
(5.3.9.2) He places the Viśvajyotis bricks.
(5.3.9.2) By means of these, he makes these worlds possessed of light.
Moreover, these [deities] sustain the vital breaths of the sacrificer.
These deities indeed lead to heaven; by taking hold of them, he goes to the heavenly world.
He places the rain-winning bricks;
verily he wins rain. If he were to place them all at once, it would rain for only one season.
He sets them down while moving around them; therefore it rains during all the seasons.
"Thou art the precursor of the east wind," he says.
This, indeed, is the form of rain.
By means of form alone, he wins rain.
By means of the *saṃyānī* verses, indeed, the gods went together to these worlds; that is why they have the name *saṃyānī*.

(5.3.10.1) In that he lays down the *saṃyānī* bricks, it is just as one travels across the waters by means of a boat; in this very way, by means of these bricks, the sacrificer traverses these worlds. (5.3.10.2) Indeed, these *saṃyānī* bricks are a raft for Agni. In that he lays down the *saṃyānī* bricks, he provides this very raft for Agni.
Moreover, when these [bricks] have been laid down, even if the waters carry away his fire, his fire is indeed not carried away.
He lays down the Āditya bricks.
Verily, the Ādityas push back from prosperity that man who, though capable of prosperity, does not attain it.
The Ādityas indeed cause him to attain prosperity.
Yonder sun, indeed, takes away the luster of one who, having piled the fire-altar, does not shine.
In that he lays down the Āditya bricks, yonder sun bestows luster upon him.
Just as he is pleasing to the gods, even so is he pleasing to human beings;
he places the ghee-bricks.
Ghee, indeed, is the beloved abode of Agni.
Verily, he causes him to prosper with his own dear abode; moreover, with splendor.
He sets it down while moving around it; verily, he bestows splendor upon him without leaving any part excluded.
Prajāpati piled the fire-altar; he was deprived of glory. He saw these [bricks] that bestow glory.
He laid them down;
with them, he indeed placed glory within himself. In that he lays down these "glory-bestowing" bricks, the sacrificer places glory within himself by means of them.
He offers five; man is fivefold.
As great as man is, in him he bestows glory.
(5.3.11.1) The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict.
(5.3.11.1) The gods were fewer, while the Asuras were more numerous.
(5.3.11.1) Those gods saw these bricks.
They laid them down with [the formulas]: "Thou art the maker of more," and thus they became more abundant through trees and plants;
"Thou art the maker of room," and thus they conquered this earth.
(5.3.11.1) "Thou art the eastern," with these words they conquered the eastern quarter; (5.3.11.1) "Thou art the upward," with these words they conquered yonder [sky];
(5.3.11.1) "Thou art seated in the intermediate space, sit in the intermediate space," with these words they conquered the intermediate space.
(5.3.11.1) Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. (5.3.11.2) For whomsoever these [bricks] are laid down, he indeed becomes superior; he conquers these worlds.
(5.3.11.2) He prospers in his own person, while his rival perishes.
(5.3.11.2) "Thou art seated in the waters; thou art seated in the falcon," he says.
(5.3.11.2) For this indeed is the form of Agni.
By means of form itself, he wins Agni.
"I set thee in the wealth of the earth," he says;
by these [verses], he makes these very worlds possessed of wealth.
He places the life-bestowing bricks.
Verily, he bestows life upon him.
"O Agni, that which is thy highest heart-name," he says.
“This indeed is Agni’s beloved abode; he thus attains his beloved abode.
“Come, let us two grasp hands,” he says.
Verily, he encloses him with this.
"Be thou also among the five peoples, O Agni," he says;
for that fire which consists of five layers is indeed the fire of the five peoples.
Therefore he says this:
"He places the seasonal bricks.
For these seasonal bricks are indeed the dear abode of the seasons.
Verily, he wins the beloved abode of the seasons. "Well-established," he says; for the well-established is indeed the year.
He attains the beloved abode of the year itself.
The eye of Prajāpati swelled;
it fell away,
and it became a horse.
That which swelled became the horse-nature (*aśvatva*) of the horse. The gods restored that [loss] by means of the Aśvamedha itself.
Verily, he who sacrifices with the Aśvamedha makes Prajāpati whole.
(5.3.12.1) He indeed becomes everything;
(5.3.12.1) for this is the expiation for everything and the remedy for everything.
(5.3.12.1) By means of this, the gods crossed over all evil.

(5.3.12.1) Or rather, by means of this [sacrifice], they crossed over the murder of a Brahmin; (5.3.12.1) he crosses over every evil. (5.3.12.2) He who sacrifices with the Aśvamedha and he who knows it thus cross over the murder of a Brahmin.
(5.3.12.2) That upper eye of Prajāpati indeed swelled.
Therefore, they cut portions from the horse on the left side, whereas for other animals it is from the right side. There is a mat made of reeds; for the horse has its origin in the waters.
The reed grows in the waters;
he thus establishes it in its own womb.
The Catuṣṭoma becomes the Stoma.
(5.3.12.2) Saraḍ Ḍha indeed tore out the thigh of the horse.
(5.3.12.2) The gods restored it by means of the Catuṣṭoma itself.
(5.3.12.2) That the Catuṣṭoma stoma is employed is for the sake of the completeness of the horse.
(5.4.1.1) The gods and the asuras were engaged in conflict; (5.4.1.1) they could not overcome one another.
Then Indra beheld these bodily forms.
He deposited those [bricks];
with them, he indeed placed within himself his body, sensory power, and vigor.
Thereupon, the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
(5.4.1.1) In that he lays down the *indratanū* bricks, the sacrificer thereby bestows upon himself body, sensory power, and vigor.
(5.4.1.1) Moreover, he piles the fire-altar together with Indra and with a body; (5.4.1.1) he prospers in his own person, and his rival is defeated. (5.4.1.2) He prospers.
(5.4.1.2) The sacrifice departed from the gods.
(5.4.1.2) They were unable to capture it.
(5.4.1.2) They saw these bodies of the sacrifice.
They laid them down;
by means of them, they indeed secured the sacrifice.
In that he lays down the bodies of the sacrifice, the sacrificer secures the sacrifice itself by means of them.
He places thirty-three [bricks]. There are indeed thirty-three deities; verily, he wins the deities.
(5.4.1.2) Moreover, he thus piles the fire-altar together with its own self and its body.
(5.4.1.2–3) He who knows this becomes possessed of his own self in yonder world.
(5.4.1.3) He lays down the light-bricks.
Verily, he bestows light upon him.
For by these [verses] Agni, when piled, blazes; with those very ones he kindles him.
Light belongs to him in both worlds.
He places the star-bricks;
these, indeed, are the lights of heaven.
Verily, he wins those very things; for the constellations are the lights of the doers of good deeds; verily, he attains them.
(5.4.1.3) Moreover, these indeed provide a reflection. (5.4.1.4) He creates lights for the purpose of illuminating the world of heaven.
If he were to lay them down touching one another, he would block out the space for rain; Parjanya would fail to rain.
He lays them down without touching one another; thus he makes room for rain, and Parjanya becomes a rain-giver.
(5.4.1.4) He places some bricks facing west in the east, and others facing east in the west;
therefore the constellations revolve both eastward and westward.
(5.4.2.1) He places the seasonal bricks; (5.4.2.1) for the proper ordering of the seasons.
(5.4.2.1) He places them in pairs.
(5.4.2.1) Therefore, the seasons are in pairs.
(5.4.2.1) For this middle layer is, as it were, unsupported;
it is, as it were, the intermediate space.
(5.4.2.1) He places the pairs in the other layers, four in the middle for the sake of stability.
These seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*) are indeed the internal cement of the layers;
in that he places the seasonal bricks, it is for the separation of the layers.
(5.4.2.1) He places *avakā* grass along [the layers].
(5.4.2.1) This, indeed, is the womb of Agni; (5.4.2.2) thus he piles the fire in its own womb.
Viśvāmitra said:

"He indeed bestows food through the sacred word (*brahman*)—he for whom these [bricks] are laid down, and he who knows them thus. Verily, the year drives away from his foundation him who, having piled the fire-altar, does not find a firm standing.
There are five preceding layers; then he piles the sixth layer. There are six seasons in the year;
verily, he finds firm support in the seasons, in the year.
(5.4.2.2) These indeed are the bricks named Adhipatnīs.
(5.4.2.3) He for whom these are laid down becomes the sovereign lord of his equals. While laying them down, he should meditate upon him whom he hates.
(5.4.2.3) He cuts him away from these very deities;
he meets with ruin.
(5.4.2.3) When the Aṅgirases were going to the heavenly world, they pushed back that which was the restoration of the sacrifice to the seers.
That became gold.
In that he sprinkles with chips of gold, it is for the restoration of the sacrifice;
moreover, he thereby provides a remedy for it.
(5.4.2.4) Moreover, he thus endows it with form;
(5.4.2.4) moreover, by means of golden light, he goes to the heavenly world;
(5.4.2.4) he sprinkles it with [water] accompanied by a thousandfold [mantra].
"Prajāpati is thousandfold;
[it serves] for the attainment of Prajāpati.
"May these bricks of mine, O Agni, be milch-cows," he says.
Verily, he makes them into milch-cows;
they, as milkers of desires, attend upon him in yonder world.
(5.4.3.1) This Agni is indeed Rudra. He is born at this time when he has been completely piled up. Just as a newborn calf seeks the udder, even so does he at this time seek his portion.
(5.4.3.1) If one were not to offer an oblation to him, he would consume both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer.
(5.4.3.1) He offers the Śatarudrīya;
verily, by means of his own portion, he pacifies him.

(5.4.3.1) Neither the Adhvaryu nor the sacrificer comes to ruin. (5.4.3.1) If he were to offer with the milk of domestic animals, he would afflict the domestic animals with pain; if [he offers] with that of wild animals, [he would afflict] the wild animals.
(5.4.3.2) One should offer either a gruel of wild sesamum or a gruel of *gavīdhuka* millet;
(5.4.3.2) thus one does not harm domestic animals nor wild animals.
Furthermore, they say:
(5.4.3.2) "Sesamum seeds from wild plants and gavīdhuka seeds are indeed not a proper oblation.
(5.4.3.2) He offers with goat's milk.
(5.4.3.2) For the goat is related to Agni.
(5.4.3.2) He offers with the very oblation;
he harms neither domestic animals nor wild animals.
(5.4.3.3) When the Aṅgirases were going to the heavenly world, they poured the Gharma into a she-goat.
Grieving, she cast off a leaf;
that became the *arka* tree.
That is the essence of the *arka*'s name.
(5.4.3.3) He offers with an Arka leaf for the sake of providing a common origin.
(5.4.3.3) He offers while standing facing north;
this is indeed the quarter of Rudra.
(5.4.3.3) He propitiates Rudra in his own quarter;
he offers the oblation on the final brick. (5.4.3.3) Thus, at the very end, he propitiates Rudra.
He offers it divided into three parts;
these worlds are three.
Thus he makes these very worlds equal in power.
At first he offers at this much; then at this much, then at this much. These are the three worlds;
it is from these very worlds that he pacifies him.
(5.4.3.4) He offers three subsequent oblations;
they amount to six.
There are indeed six seasons.
(5.4.3.4) By means of the seasons, he indeed pacifies him.
(5.4.3.4) If he were to offer oblations while moving around [the fire] in sequence, he would make Rudra one who moves within [the sacrifice].
Furthermore, they say:
"In which direction, then, is Rudra, and in which? "The oblation should be offered while walking around [the fire] in succession; thus he pacifies him completely, leaving nothing out."
(5.4.3.5) These deities who are last are indeed those that lead to heaven.
(5.4.3.5) He makes the sacrificer recite for them;
by means of them alone he causes him to go to the heavenly world.
(5.4.3.5) One whom he hates, against him he should cast [the bone] at the gathering of cattle;
whichever animal stands first [upon it] meets with misfortune.
With the words, "O stone, [bestow] strength," he sprinkles around;
he thus purifies it,
and furthermore, he truly gratifies it.
(5.4.4.1) Satisfied, not hungering, and not grieving, he approaches that world.
(5.4.4.1) He who knows this is satisfied with offspring and cattle. "O Maruts, being well-disposed, bestow upon us that food and strength," he says.
Food indeed is vigor;
the Maruts are food;
verily, he wins food.
"May hunger seize your flesh; may fever seize that one whom we hate," he says.
Verily, he afflicts with both hunger and fever him whom he hates.
(5.4.4.2) He goes around sprinkling three times.
(5.4.4.2) Agni is indeed threefold; as great as Agni is, he thus pacifies his heat.
He goes around three times again;
thus they amount to six.
There are indeed six seasons.
(5.4.4.2) Verily, by means of the seasons he pacifies his sorrow.
(5.4.4.2) The cane is indeed the flower of the waters; the reed and the avakā plant are [also] of the waters. (5.4.4.3) [He places them] for the sake of the waters.
He draws it apart with a branch of cane and with avakā plants.
Water is indeed peaceful; by means of these peaceful things, he pacifies his affliction.
(5.4.4.3) Or, whichever animal first steps upon the piled fire-altar, it is liable to burn him with its heat.
(5.4.4.3) He draws [the furrow] with a frog;
for this is the one among animals that cannot be lived upon.
(5.4.4.3) This [plough] is not fixed upon either domestic animals or wild animals;
(5.4.4.3) he afflicts it with pain.
(5.4.4.3) He ploughs with eight [oxen].
The Gāyatrī has eight syllables;
Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī.
As great as Agni is, he thus pacifies his heat.
(5.4.4.4) With verses containing the word *pāvaka*.
(5.4.4.4) Food, indeed, is *pāvaka*.
(5.4.4.4) By means of food itself, he pacifies his impurity.
(5.4.4.4) This fire, indeed, is death. (5.4.4.4) The black antelope skin is the form of Brahman. (5.4.4.4) He puts on shoes made of black antelope skin.
By means of the *brahman* alone he places a barrier against death;
he places a barrier against death. "He places a barrier against food," they say.
(5.4.4.4) He fastens one [kindling stick] and not another within; (5.4.4.5) thus he places himself beyond death and secures food.
(5.4.4.5) "Homage to thy flame, to thy heat," he says;
for having paid homage, people attend upon one who is more excellent.
"May your missiles burn others than us," he says; he thus inflicts pain upon him whom he hates. "Be purifying and auspicious for us," he says.
Food indeed is the purifier;
verily, he wins food.
He strides across with two verses for the sake of firm support.
(5.4.4.5) With two verses containing the word "water," for the sake of peace.
(5.4.5.1) With the words, "To the one seated among men, vaṭ! he sprinkles [the clarified butter].
(5.4.5.1) By means of an oblation in the *pañkti* meter, he takes hold of the mouth of the sacrifice.
(5.4.5.1) He sprinkles it crosswise.
(5.4.5.1) Therefore, animals move their limbs crosswise for the sake of stability.
(5.4.5.1) If he were to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call, his *vaṣaṭ* call would become exhausted;
if he were not to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call, the *rakṣases* would destroy the sacrifice.
(5.4.5.1) He says "vaṭ"; thus he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call in a secret manner.
His *vaṣaṭ* call does not become exhausted, and the Rakṣases do not strike down his sacrifice.
For some gods are indeed eaters of the oblation.
(5.4.5.2) Others are not eaters of oblations;
(5.4.5.2) the builder of the fire-altar alone gratifies both of them.
(5.4.5.2) With the mantra, "O gods who are among the gods," he sprinkles [the altar] with curd mixed with honey.
The sacrificer gratifies both the gods who eat the oblation and those who do not eat the oblation;
they in turn gratify the sacrificer.
He gratifies those who eat the oblation with curds, and those who do not eat the oblation with honey.
(5.4.5.2) This curd is indeed domestic food, while honey is wild.
When he sprinkles with curd mixed with honey, it is for the attainment of both. He sprinkles with a handful of grass.
(5.4.5.2) The handful of grass belongs to Prajāpati; (5.4.5.3) it serves for the sake of having a common origin.
(5.4.5.3) With two [verses] it is for the sake of stability. He sprinkles water around it in a continuous circle.
(5.4.5.3) He thus gratifies them completely.
(5.4.5.3) He who, while piling the fire-altar, steps over it, is indeed deprived of his vital breaths, his offspring, and his cattle.
"O givers of breath! O givers of out-breath! he says.
Verily, he bestows the vital breaths upon himself.
"Bestower of luster, bestower of wide space," he says; for offspring is indeed luster, and cattle are wide space.
Verily, he bestows offspring and cattle upon himself.
Indra slew Vṛtra;
once slain, Vṛtra bound him with sixteen coils.
He saw this oblation for Agni Anīkavat;
he offered it. Agni Anīkavat, gratified by his own portion, burned away the sixteen coils of Vṛtra.
By means of [the offering] to Viśvakarman, he was released from evil.
When he offers an oblation to Agni Anīkavat, Agni Anīkavat himself, being gratified by his own share, burns away his evil;
by means of [the offering] to Viśvakarman, he is released from evil.
(5.4.5.4) If he should desire of someone, "May he be released from evil for a long time," (5.4.5.5) he should offer one oblation for each [of those verses] on his behalf;
thus he is indeed released from evil for a long time.
(5.4.5.5) If he should desire of someone,
"May he be quickly released from evil," he should offer all [the oblations] for him while reciting them in succession;
he is indeed quickly released from evil.
Moreover, he indeed offers with two different hymns;
he bestows the vigor of the two hymns separately.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of stability.
(5.4.6.1) "Lead him upward," with these words he places the fuel-sticks.
(5.4.6.1) Just as one provides assistance to a person who is traveling, so too is this;
he places three [sticks].
Agni is indeed threefold. To Agni, in his full extent, he thus provides his portion. They are made of Udumbara wood.
The udumbara is indeed strength;
verily, he bestows strength upon him. "Upward thee all the gods," he says.
The All-Gods are indeed the vital breaths;
verily, by means of the vital breaths he raises him up.
"May they bear [him] with their thoughts, O Agni," he says.
With whatever intention he raises him up, with that very intention he causes him to prosper.
"May the five divine quarters, the goddesses, protect the sacrifice," he says;
for he moves along these very quarters.
"Driving away lack of wisdom and evil thought," he says, for the purpose of driving away the Rākṣasas.
"Bestowing upon the lord of the sacrifice a share in the increase of wealth," he says;
for the increase of wealth is indeed cattle.
Verily, he wins cattle;
he carries with six verses,
for there are six seasons.
(5.4.6.3) Verily, he carries him [the fire] by means of the seasons.
(5.4.6.3) There are two verses containing the word "parigṛhya" (having grasped), for the purpose of driving away the Rakṣases.
(5.4.6.3) He says: "The sun-rayed, golden-haired one in the east..."
"For the sake of procreation," he says; "therefore may the purifying ones accept our prayers.
Food, indeed, is the purifying one.
(5.4.6.3) Verily, he wins food.
(5.4.6.3) The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. Those gods perceived this Apratiratha [hymn].
By that very means, they, being irresistible, conquered the Asuras;
that is the reason for the *apratiratha* (the "unopposable") hymn's name.
When the second Hotṛ recites the *apratiratha*, the sacrificer likewise conquers his rivals by becoming irresistible.
Moreover, he conquers even what has not been conquered.
It consists of ten verses;
the *virāj* has ten syllables.
These two worlds are supported by the *virāj*.
For the support of these two worlds;
moreover, the *virāj* consists of ten syllables.
Food is the *virāj*;
verily, he finds firm support in the *virāj*, in the eating of food.
The intermediate space, indeed, is as if non-existent.
The Āgnīdhra shed is like the intermediate space;
in the Āgnīdhra shed he deposits a stone for the sake of strength.
With two [verses],
for the sake of stability,
he says: "This measurer of the sky sits in the midst."
(5.4.6.5) By means of this [verse], he measures it out completely.
(5.4.6.5) "The speckled stone is placed in the midst of heaven," he says. (5.4.6.5) The speckled one, indeed, is food.
Verily, he wins food;
with four [verses] he goes as far as the tail; there are four meters.
(5.4.6.5) By means of the meters indeed;
(5.4.6.5) "All have made Indra grow," he says; (5.4.6.5) thus he turns toward growth itself.
"The lord of the lords of strength" (vājānām satpatiṃ patiṃ), he says. "Strength" (vāja) is indeed food;
verily, he wins food for himself.
"May the sacrifice, the bringer of favor, bring the gods hither," he says.
Offspring indeed is favor; verily, he bestows offspring and cattle upon himself.
"May Agni the god sacrifice to the gods and bring them hither," he says for the sake of making the *svāhā* offering.
"By the impulse of strength, with the upward-grasping, he has grasped me," he says.
Yonder sun, indeed, when rising, is the lifting-up; he, when setting, is the pressing-down.
By means of the *brahman* he lifts himself up; by means of the *brahman* he presses down his rival.
"Go forward along the eastern quarter, O wise one," he says; by this [verse], he indeed turns toward the world of the gods. "Step forth with Agni to the firmament," he says.
(5.4.7.1) By means of this [verse], he strides across these very worlds.
(5.4.7.1) "From the earth I have ascended to the mid-region," he says;
by means of this, he indeed ascends to these very worlds.
“They do not look back when going to heaven,” he says; by this [verse], he indeed goes to the heavenly world. “O Agni, go forward as the first of those seeking the gods,” he says.
By this [verse], he bestows sight upon both gods and men;
he strides across with five [steps]; the sacrifice is fivefold.

(5.4.7.2) To the very extent that the sacrifice is, with that he goes to the heavenly world. (5.4.7.2) He recites the invitatory verse beginning with "Night and Dawn" for the sake of obtaining [the result].
"O Agni, thousand-eyed," he says;
Prajāpati is thousandfold;
[it is] for the attainment of Prajāpati.
"To that strength of yours we pay homage, Svāhā! he says.
Strength is indeed food;
verily, he secures food for himself.
(5.4.7.3) He offers a vessel full of curds made of Udumbara wood upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick. (5.4.7.3) Curds are indeed strength; the Udumbara is strength.
(5.4.7.3) That [brick] is the naturally perforated one (*svayamātṛṇṇā*).
(5.4.7.3) He places vigor (*ūrj*) in that very [brick]; therefore, from there, we live upon vigor directed hitherward.
He settles it with three [verses]. Agni is indeed threefold; he thus causes Agni, in his full extent, to reach a firm foundation.
(5.4.7.3) “O Agni, blazing forth, shine before us!”—with these words he places a branch of *udumbara* wood. This is indeed a glowing iron tube with perforations.
By means of this, the gods used to crush the hundredfold hosts of the Asuras.

(5.4.7.4) In that he places a kindling-stick with this [verse], the sacrificer hurls a hundred-slaying thunderbolt at his rival for the sake of striking him down. (5.4.7.4) It is so that there may be no failure.
(5.4.7.4) "We would worship thee in thy highest birth, O Agni"—with these words he places a stick of *vaikaṅkata* wood.
Verily, he wins radiance. With the verse, "That wondrous [gift] of Savitṛ, the desirable," he offers a fuel-stick made of *śamī* wood for the sake of peace.
Indeed, either the fire milks the one who has piled the fire-altar, or the one who has piled the fire-altar milks the fire.
(5.4.7.4) Regarding that [verse], he says: (5.4.7.5) "Of Savitṛ, the most excellent, the wonderful...
(5.4.7.5) This, indeed, is the milking of Agni;
Kaṇva Śrāyasa alone knew it.
(5.4.7.5) By means of that, he indeed milks him completely. (5.4.7.5) In that he places a kindling-stick with this [verse], the piler of the fire thereby milks the fire.
"Seven are thy kindling-sticks, O Agni, seven thy tongues," he says.
(5.4.7.5) He gratifies his seven sets of seven.
(5.4.7.5) He offers with a full [ladle];
for Prajāpati is, as it were, full.
(5.4.7.5) Of Prajāpati. (5.4.7.6) For the sake of attainment, he offers with a deficient [verse]; for from what was deficient, Prajāpati created offspring.
For the creation of offspring.
Agni hid himself from the gods;
he entered into the quarters.
While offering, he should meditate on the quarters with his mind;
thus he wins them from the very quarters.
He offers curds first and ghee afterwards.
He bestows upon him brilliance and sensory power together.
The cake for Vaiśvānara is offered on twelve potsherds;
the year consists of twelve months.
The year is Agni Vaiśvānara;
[it is] directly [so]. Verily, he obtains Vaiśvānara.
If one were to perform the *prayāja* and *anūyāja* offerings, that would be a dismemberment of the sacrifice.
(5.4.7.7) He performs the *darvihoma* for the firm establishment of the sacrifice.
(5.4.7.7) Vaiśvānara is indeed the kingdom, and the Maruts are the people (*viś*).
Having offered to Vaiśvānara, he offers to the Maruts.
(5.4.7.7) He thus binds the people to the kingdom itself.
(5.4.7.7) He causes the announcement for Vaiśvānara to be heard aloud, but he offers the oblations to the Maruts in a low voice;
therefore, the kingdom speaks over the people.
The [stotras] belong to the Maruts;
for the Maruts are the subjects (*viś*) of the gods.
By means of the divine subjects, he thereby secures for himself the human subjects.
There are seven;
for the Maruts consist of seven groups.
Verily, by means of the groups, he wins over the people.
He offers, following one group after another;
verily, he makes the people follow his path.
He offers the stream of wealth (*vasor dhārā*).
Indeed, this is offered with the thought, "May there be for me a stream of wealth.
Or rather, this stream of clarified butter stands by him in yonder world, swelling.
(5.4.8.1) He offers with clarified butter.
(5.4.8.1) Clarified butter is indeed splendor; the stream of wealth is splendor.
By means of splendor, he wins splendor for him.
(5.4.8.1) Now, the streams of wealth are indeed desires;
(5.4.8.1) he verily obtains his desires.
(5.4.8.1) Whomever he may desire—
(5.4.8.1) "May I cut off his vital breaths and his food," [thinking thus], he should offer the oblation with a pause.
(5.4.8.2) Verily, he cuts off his vital breaths and his food.
Whomever he may desire—
(5.4.8.2) "May I extend his vital breaths and his food," [thinking thus], he should offer them continuously;
verily, he extends his vital breaths and his food.
He offers twelve by twelves; twelve months are a year.
By means of the year itself, he wins food for him. "Food for me and freedom from hunger for me," he says.
This, indeed, is the form of food.
(5.4.8.3) By means of form itself, he wins food.
(5.4.8.3) "May Agni and me, and may the waters and me," he says.
(5.4.8.3) This, indeed, is the womb of food.
Verily, from its own source he wins food;
he offers oblations to Ardhendras;
verily, he wins the deities.

Since Indra takes half of all [the portions], therefore Indra is the deity that receives the largest share among the gods. He pronounces Indra as the final one; verily, he bestows power upon him from above.
He offers the sacrificial implements.
The sacrificial implements are indeed the sacrifice;
verily, he wins the sacrifice itself.
(5.4.8.4) Now, this indeed is the form of the sacrifice.
(5.4.8.4) By means of its very form, he wins the sacrifice.
(5.4.8.4) "The purificatory bath for me, and the cry of 'svagā' for me," he says.
"For the sake of making [the offering] one's own.
"Agni and my Gharma," he says;
for this is indeed the form of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
By means of form (*rūpa*) alone, he wins spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
"May the *ṛc* be mine and the *sāman* be mine," he says. This, indeed, is the form of the meters (*chandas*).
By means of form alone, he wins the meters.
"May my embryos and my calves," he says.
This, indeed, is the form of cattle;
by means of that very form, he wins cattle.
He offers the *kalpa* oblations for the successful arrangement of what has not been arranged;
he offers them in pairs and singly.
For the sake of pairing;
they are possessed of the higher;
for the sake of advancing.
"May one and may three for me," he says;
for one and three indeed constitute the meter of the gods.
(5.4.8.6) Four and eight [verses] have the meter of men; (5.4.8.6) thus he wins both the meters of the gods and the meters of men.
(5.4.8.6) He offers up to thirty-three [verses].
There are indeed thirty-three deities;
verily, he wins the deities themselves.
He offers forty-eight oblations.
The Jagatī consists of forty-eight syllables;
cattle are of the nature of the Jagatī. By means of the Jagatī, he wins cattle for him.
He offers the twelfth oblation with the words, "Vāja and Prasava.
There are twelve months in a year;
verily, he finds firm support in the year itself.
Agni departed from the gods, seeking his own portion.
The gods said to him:
“Turn back to us; carry our oblation.”
He said, "I shall choose a boon: let me alone offer the *vājaprasavīya* oblation.
Therefore, they offer the *vājaprasavīya* to Agni.
In that he offers the *vājaprasavīya* oblations, he thereby gratifies Agni with his own share;
moreover, this is his consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
He offers with fourteen [verses].
(5.4.9.1) There are seven cultivated plants and seven wild ones. (5.4.9.2) [He offers] for the acquisition of both; he offers of every kind of food.
(5.4.9.2) For the attainment of every kind of food,
he offers with a ladle made of Udumbara wood;
for the Udumbara is strength, and food is strength.
(5.4.9.2) By means of vigor, he wins for himself vigor and food.
(5.4.9.2) Agni is indeed the consecrated one among the gods; the builder of the fire-altar (*agnicit*) is [the consecrated one] among men.
Therefore, when it rains, the builder of the fire-altar should not run.
For his food has been secured. Rain, indeed, is like food.
If he were to run, he would run away from his food.
He should turn toward it;
he turns toward food itself.
With the words, "Night and Dawn," he offers an oblation of milk from a black cow that has a white calf.

By means of the day he causes him to obtain the night, and by means of the night the day; day and night, thus bestowed upon him, milk for him his desire and food. He offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations.
Verily, he wins the kingdom;
he offers with six [verses]; for there are six seasons.
(5.4.9.3) He finds firm support in the very seasons. (5.4.9.3) With the words, "O Lord of the World," he offers five oblations at the front of the chariot.
(5.4.9.3) The chariot is indeed a thunderbolt.
(5.4.9.3) By means of the thunderbolt itself, he conquers the quarters.
(5.4.9.4) Indeed, in yonder world, the wind blows over the one who has piled the fire-altar;
therefore, he offers oblations with names of the wind.
(5.4.9.4) Verily, the wind blows toward him in yonder world.
(5.4.9.4) He offers three oblations;
these worlds are three.
(5.4.9.4) From these very worlds he wins the wind.
(5.4.9.4) "Thou art the ocean, full of mist," he says.
This indeed is the form of the wind.
By means of form alone he wins over Vāta.
He offers with joined palms,
for in no other way can an oblation to these be properly prepared.

(5.4.10.1) Indeed, the divine chariot is yoked for the sake of the heavenly world, whereas the human chariot is yoked for whatever purpose one intends. This Agni, indeed, is the divine chariot. "I yoke Agni with power and with ghee," he says; thus he truly yokes him. Yoked, he carries him toward the heavenly world.

(5.4.10.1) If he were to yoke with all five [verses], Agni would be yoked for him but would be displaced; the oblations would be unstable, the *stomas* unstable, and the *ukthas* unstable. At the morning pressing, he touches it with three verses; Agni is indeed threefold (*trivṛt*). As much as Agni is, so much of him he yokes. Just as when a load is placed upon a yoked cart, even so do the oblations find support, the *stomas* find support, and the *ukthas* find support.

(5.4.10.2) At the *yajñāyajñiya* chant, he touches [the altar] with two verses. "The sacrifice is indeed as great as the *agniṣṭoma*; a further abundance of it is performed beyond this point. Thus, he ascends at the end to the very extent of the sacrifice. He does so with two verses for the sake of stability; one remains unchanted, and then he touches it. The subsequent sacrifice inclines toward him, and furthermore, it is for the sake of continuity.

(5.4.10.3) He who piles the fire-altar indeed falls away from this world. For him, no oblation offered without a brick is properly established. Whatever oblation he offers without a brick, it flows away; and as that [oblation] flows away, the sacrifice perishes, and with the sacrifice, the sacrificer perishes. When he piles the *punar-citi* (re-piling), it is for the firm establishment of the oblations; thus the oblations become firmly established. (5.4.10.4) Neither the sacrifice nor the sacrificer perishes.

He lays down eight bricks. The Gāyatrī has eight syllables; verily, by means of the Gāyatrī metre he piles him. When there are eleven, it is by means of the Triṣṭubh; when twelve, it is by means of the Jagatī; verily, by means of the metres he piles him.
This fire which is the *punar-citi* (re-piling) is indeed named "the Son. He who, knowing thus, performs the *punar-citi*, eats food as far as the third generation of men.

(5.4.10.4) Just as the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) is, so is the re-piling of the altar (*punaścit*). He who does not prosper through the establishment of the fires establishes the fires again; he who, having piled the fire-altar, does not prosper, piles it again. In that he piles it again, it is for the sake of prosperity. (5.4.10.5) Now, however, they say: "It should not be piled. Agni is indeed Rudra; it is just as if one were to awaken a sleeping tiger—such is that act. Now, however, they say: "It should be piled. It is just as if one awakens a more powerful person by means of a sacrificial portion—such is that act.
Manu piled the fire-altar; he did not prosper by it. He saw this *punaściti* (re-piling); he piled it, and by it he indeed prospered. In that one piles the *punaściti*, it is for prosperity.
(5.4.11.1) One who desires cattle should pile the Chandaściti; for the meters are indeed cattle, and he becomes possessed of cattle.

(5.4.11.1) One who desires the heavenly world should pile the Śyenaciti; for the hawk is the swiftest of birds, and having become a hawk, he flies to the heavenly world. (5.4.11.1) He who desires, "May I be possessed of a head in yonder world," should pile the Kaṅkaciti; he indeed becomes possessed of a head in yonder world.

(5.4.11.1) One who desires stability should pile the *alaja-citi* in four furrows; there are four directions, and thus he finds firm standing in the very quarters. (5.4.11.1–2) One who has rivals should pile the *prauga-citi*; he thus drives away his rivals. He who desires, "May I drive away those rivals already born and those yet to be born," should pile the *ubhayataḥ-prauga-citi*; he thus drives away the rivals already born and repels those yet to be born.

(5.4.11.2) One who has rivals should pile the fire-altar in the shape of a chariot-wheel; the chariot is indeed a thunderbolt, and thus he hurls the thunderbolt at his rivals. (5.4.11.2) One who desires food should pile it in the shape of a trough (*droṇa*); for food is borne in a trough, and thus he secures food from its very source. (5.4.11.2) One who desires cattle should pile it by gathering [the earth] together; he becomes possessed of cattle.
(5.4.11.3) One who desires a village should pile the *paricāyya* altar; he indeed becomes possessed of a village.

(5.4.11.3) He who desires, "May I prosper in the world of the fathers," should pile the *śmaśānacit* altar; he indeed prospers in the world of the fathers. Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni contended with Vasiṣṭha. Jamadagni saw these *vihavyā* bricks and laid them down. By means of them, he appropriated the sensory power and vigor of Vasiṣṭha. In that he lays down the *vihavyā* bricks, the sacrificer appropriates the sensory power and vigor of his rival by means of them.

He places [the bricks] on the *dhiṣṇya* of the Hotṛ; for the Hotṛ is indeed the station of the sacrificer. Thus, in his own station, he secures for himself power and vigor. He places twelve [bricks]; the *jagatī* consists of twelve syllables, and cattle are of the nature of the *jagatī*. By means of the *jagatī*, he secures cattle for him. On the other *dhiṣṇyas*, he places eight [bricks] each; cattle have eight hooves; thus, he secures cattle.
Six [bricks] on the Mārjālīya altar; for there are six seasons, and the seasons are indeed the divine ancestors. Verily, he gratifies the seasons, the gods, and the ancestors.
(5.4.12.1) "Flow for the winning of booty"—this *anuṣṭubh* verse serves as the opening.
(5.4.12.1) There are three *anuṣṭubh*s and four *gāyatrī*s.
(5.4.12.1) Because there are three *anuṣṭubh*s, therefore the horse stands supported by three [legs].
Because there are four *gāyatrī*s, he escapes while restoring all four feet. This *anuṣṭubh* is indeed the highest of the meters; the *catuṣṭoma* is the highest of the *stomas*.
The three-night sacrifice is the highest of sacrifices; the horse is the highest of animals. By means of the highest, he causes him to reach the highest state.
The twenty-first day occurs on which the horse is sacrificed.
There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun as the twenty-first; he is Prajāpati, for the horse belongs to Prajāpati.
He prospers directly with that very [sāman].
The Śakvarī verses constitute the *pṛṣṭha* chant;
each is a different metre.
(5.4.12.2) These animals that are sacrificed are various; they are as if domestic, and as if wild.
(5.4.12.2) In that the Śakvarī verses become the *pṛṣṭha* chant, it is for the sake of the horse’s wholeness.
(5.4.12.2) The *Pārthuraśma* becomes the *brahmasāman*.
(5.4.12.2) By means of the rein, indeed, the horse is guided.
(5.4.12.3) For the horse is liable to go to the furthest distance, unguided and without support.
In that the *pārthuraśma* becomes the *brahmasāman*, it is for the guidance and the firm support of the horse.
(5.4.12.3) The *achāvāka*sāman is performed after the *saṃkṛt* [laud].
(5.4.12.3) "The Aśvamedha is indeed a sacrifice that has fallen into ruin," they say; "who knows whether it is performed in its entirety or not?"

In that the *achāvāka-sāman* is performed with the *saṃkṛtī* verses, it serves for the wholeness of the horse, for its completion, and for its lack of interruption. The final day is an *atirātra* sacrifice consisting of all the *stomas*, for the attainment of everything and for the conquest of everything.
By means of this, one attains everything and conquers everything.
(5.5.1.1) That he completes [the sacrifice] with one [offering] is for the continuity and non-interruption of the sacrifice.
(5.5.1.1) The animals that are males belong to Indra.
(5.5.1.1) Since they, being dedicated to Indra, are offered to the fires, he creates strife among the deities.
(5.5.1.1) One should employ *ṛc*s in the *triṣṭubh* metre as the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyānuvākyā*). (5.5.1.1) Insofar as they are addressed to Agni, they belong to Agni;
insofar as they are *triṣṭubh*s, they belong to Indra.
(5.5.1.1) For prosperity; (5.5.1.1) he does not create discord among the deities.
He sacrifices a hornless goat to Vāyu Niyutvat; Vāyu is the brilliance of Agni.
(5.5.1.1) This [fire] is obtained from heat;
therefore, in whatever direction the wind blows, in that very direction the fire burns. It follows its own heat.
(5.5.1.2) If it were not for the one accompanied by the *niyuts*, the sacrificer would become deranged.
(5.5.1.2) It is offered to the one accompanied by the *niyuts* to prevent the sacrificer from becoming deranged.
(5.5.1.2) The invitatory and offering verses contain the words "Vāyu" and "white" (*śveta*).
(5.5.1.2) For the sake of brilliance,
he pours the *āghāra* libation with the verse, "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning," for Hiraṇyagarbha is indeed Prajāpati.
(5.5.1.2) For the sake of conformity with Prajāpati,
(5.5.1.2) he indeed obtains all the forms of cattle;
that which is the beard is (5.5.1.3) the form of men.
That which has no testicles belongs to the horses;
that which has teeth on one side belongs to the cows;
that whose hooves are like those of sheep belongs to the sheep.
(5.5.1.3) That which is unborn belongs to the goats.
(5.5.1.3) Vāyu is indeed the dear abode of cattle; since it is dedicated to Vāyu, the cattle, recognizing him, attend upon it.
(5.5.1.3) "Should it be offered to Vāyu or to Prajāpati? they ask.
(5.5.1.3) If one were to offer it to Vāyu, one would depart from Prajāpati;
if one were to offer it to Prajāpati, one would depart from Vāyu. (5.5.1.4) [Therefore...]

In that the animal victim belongs to Vāyu, by that he does not depart from Vāyu; in that there is a cake for Prajāpati, by that he does not depart from Prajāpati; in that it is on twelve potsherds, by that he does not depart from Vaiśvānara.
(5.5.1.4) He who is about to be consecrated offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu.
(5.5.1.4) Agni is all the deities, and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice. (5.5.1.4) Thus he takes hold of both the deities and the sacrifice.
Agni is the lowest of the deities, Viṣṇu the highest.
When he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu, the sacrificer, having grasped the deities on both sides, wins them.
By means of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), the gods prospered in yonder world; by means of the cooked rice oblation (*caru*), in this world.
(5.5.1.5) He who should desire,
"May I prosper in yonder world," he should prepare a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). In yonder world itself, he prospers.
In that it is on eight potsherds, it belongs to Agni;
in that it is on three potsherds, it belongs to Viṣṇu—
for the sake of prosperity.
(5.5.1.5) He who should desire,
"May I prosper in this world," he should prepare a *caru* offering:
clarified butter for Agni, rice grains for Viṣṇu.
Therefore, a *caru* offering should be prepared.
In this very world he prospers;
he becomes like Āditya.
(5.5.1.6) This earth, indeed, is Aditi.
He finds firm support in her; moreover, he extends the sacrifice upon her.
Verily, for him who piles the fire-altar without having carried the fire in the pan for a year, it is just as if a fetus were to fall prematurely.
(5.5.1.6) He would meet with misfortune.
(5.5.1.6) One should first offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year.
(5.5.1.6) Just as one who has reached the full year is born when the time arrives, even so, having reached the full year, he piles the fire-altar when the time arrives; he does not come to ruin.
(5.5.1.7) Vaiśvānara is indeed the dear body of Agni.
Verily, he wins his dear body;
there are these three oblations,
for these worlds are three.
For the ascent to these worlds.
(5.5.2.1) Prajāpati, having created the creatures, entered into them with his vital breath. (5.5.2.1) He was unable to come forth from them again;
he said:
"He would have prospered, he who would have rebuilt for me from this [ruin]," they said.
The gods rebuilt him;
then indeed they prospered.

(5.5.2.1) Because he piled [it] together (*sam-acinvan*), that is the reason for the piled nature (*cityatva*) of the fire-altar (*agni*). (5.5.2.1) He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar, truly prospers.
(5.5.2.1) "For what purpose is the fire-altar piled? they ask.
(5.5.2.1) "May I possess fire. It is for this reason that the fire-altar is built. (5.5.2.2) Thus, he indeed becomes possessed of fire.
(5.5.2.2) "For what purpose is the fire-altar built? they ask.
"Agni is piled so that the gods may know him," they say; "the gods already know him.
"For what purpose is Agni piled? they ask.
"Agni is piled with the thought, 'May I be a householder';
indeed, he becomes a householder.
For what purpose, and for whom, is Agni piled? they ask.

"Agni is piled with the thought, 'May I be possessed of cattle'; he indeed becomes possessed of cattle. For what purpose, they ask, is Agni piled? (5.5.2.3) They say: "For whom is Agni piled? (5.5.2.3) He is piled with the thought, "May I be possessed of cattle"; he indeed becomes possessed of cattle. (5.5.2.3) For what purpose, they ask, is Agni piled? (5.5.2.3) [He is piled] for the sake of one who desires cattle. (5.5.2.3) He indeed becomes possessed of cattle. (5.5.2.3) For what purpose, they ask, is Agni piled? (5.5.2.4) "I will act in such a way that it will not burn you excessively," he said.
He then touched this [earth]:
"May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras."
(5.5.2.4) Thus it is said:
"Having made this very [earth] into a brick, he places it down so that there shall be no excessive burning.
(5.5.2.4) "Whatever [altar] one should pile facing the fire, one should touch that."
(5.5.2.4) "May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras!
(5.5.2.5) Having thus made this very iṣṭakā, he places it down so that there shall be no excessive burning.
(5.5.2.5) Prajāpati desired.
(5.5.2.5) "May I be propagated," he thought;
(5.5.2.5) he saw this fire-pan (ukhya),
and he carried it for a year.
(5.5.2.5) From that, indeed, he was born.
(5.5.2.5) Therefore, one should wait for a year; [only then] is one truly born.
The Vasus said to him:
(5.5.2.5) "Thou hast been born; may we be born," he said.
(5.5.2.5) He gave him to the Vasus. They carried him for three days.
(5.5.2.5) By means of that, (5.5.2.6) they created three hundred and thirty-three [deities]. Therefore, one should observe the Tryaha; thus he is indeed born again. Those Rudras said:
(5.5.2.6) "May you be born forth; may we be born forth," they said.
(5.5.2.6) They presented him to the Rudras;
they carried him for six days.
(5.5.2.6) By means of that, they created three hundred and thirty-three [deities].
(5.5.2.6) Therefore, one should perform the six-day rite; thus he is indeed procreated.
(5.5.2.6) The Ādityas said to them:
(5.5.2.6) "You have been born forth; we too shall be born forth," they said.
(5.5.2.7) They presented him to the Ādityas, and they carried him for twelve days.
(5.5.2.7) By means of that, they created three hundred and thirty-three;
therefore, the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) should be performed, for one is indeed born through it.
By that very same [rite], they created a thousand, with the fire-pan (*ukhā*) as the thousandth.
He who thus knows the thousandfold fire-altar belonging to the fire-pan (ukhya) obtains a thousand cattle.
(5.5.3.1) This fire-pan is prepared with a *yajus*, cooked with a *yajus*, and released with a *yajus*.
"It is now exhausted," they say, "it is not to be used again.
[To counter this] he offers an oblation into the fire-pan with the verses: "O Agni, yoke those [steeds] that are yours; yoke those who best invite the gods."
(5.5.3.1) By that very means he joins her again; by that she becomes untiring.
(5.5.3.1) Whoever yokes the fire when the time for yoking has arrived, he yokes it among those who are yoking.
(5.5.3.1–2) "O Agni, yoke indeed those [horses] which are yours; yoke indeed those who best invoke the gods," he says.

(5.5.3.2) This indeed is the harnessing of Agni; with that very [harnessing] he harnesses him; he harnesses him among those who are harnessing. The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say:
(5.5.3.2) "Should the fire-altar be built face-downward or face-upward?
(5.5.3.2) This fire-altar is indeed built as a likeness of birds.
If one were to build it face-downward, the oblations would strike it from behind.
(5.5.3.2) If it were laid face upwards, it would not be able to fall, and he would not attain the heavenly world.

(5.5.3.2) [He lays it] facing eastward, with the face upwards. (5.5.3.3) He places the human head; thus the oblations reach him from the very mouth. He does not pile it face upwards; he thereby attains the heavenly world.
He offers with a verse addressed to Sūrya; he thereby bestows sight upon him.
(5.5.3.3) He offers twice, for there are two eyes. (5.5.3.3) He offers with the same [verse] for both, for the eye is common to both; this is for the sake of prosperity.
(5.5.3.3) The gods and the asuras were engaged in conflict.
They deposited that desirable wealth together; the gods appropriated it through the Vāmabhṛt [offering];
that is why the Vāmabhṛt has its name "Vāmabhṛt" (the bearer of the desirable).
In that he places the *vāmabhṛt* brick, the sacrificer thereby appropriates the desirable wealth of his rival.
It has a golden head;
for gold is light, and light is the desirable.
By means of light itself, he appropriates the desirable light of this [sacrificer].
There are two *yajus* formulas for the sake of stability.

The waters were the wives of Varuṇa; Agni lusted after them and united with them. His seed fell away, and that became this [earth]; what second seed fell away, that became yonder [sky]. This [earth] is indeed Virāj, and yonder [sky] is Svarāj.
In that he lays down two Virāj bricks, he thus lays down these two.

(5.5.4.1) Or rather, that seed which he sheds settles in this earth; it grows forth, and these become plants and creepers. (5.5.4.2) Agni eats them—he who knows thus is indeed propagated and becomes an eater of food. If one should be possessed of seed, he should place both bricks in the first layer of piling for him; verily, these two worlds, facing each other, pour seed for him. If one should have already shed his seed, he should place one brick in the first layer of piling and the other in the last; verily, by means of these two, he encloses the seed he has shed on both sides.
(5.5.4.2) For a year one should not descend toward anyone at all; for these two do not descend toward anyone at all—this is their vow.
(5.5.4.3) Verily, he who piles the fire-altar without a head becomes headless in yonder world; he who piles it with a head becomes possessed of a head in yonder world.

(5.5.4.3) "I offer consciousness with mind and ghee, so that the gods, who increase the cosmic order and enjoy the oblation, may come here. In the path of the ocean, the means of knowledge, I offer an immortal oblation for Viśvakarman every day. Having laid down the naturally perforated brick (*svayamātṛṇṇā*), he makes this offering.
(5.5.4.4) This, indeed, is the head of Agni; he who knows thus piles the fire with its head, and he becomes possessed of a head in yonder world.
(5.5.4.4) This fire is piled for the sake of the heavenly world; whatever is done for it out of order is not conducive to the heavenly world for him, for the fire is intended for the heavenly world.
Having laid down a layer, he should touch it.

(5.5.4.4) "May he, the wise one, discern thought and thoughtlessness; may he separate mortals as straight and crooked are the backs [of a chariot]. O God, grant us wealth and good offspring; grant us *Diti* and ward off *Aditi*. Thus he places it as before. He builds it facing eastward; it becomes conducive to heaven for him.

(5.5.5.1) Viśvakarman, lord of the quarters: may he protect our cattle; may he protect us; homage to him! (5.5.5.1) Prajāpati, Rudra, Varuṇa, Agni, lord of the quarters: may he protect our cattle; may he protect us; homage to him!
(5.5.5.1) These indeed are the deities, the lords of these cattle.
(5.5.5.1) Indeed, he who piles up the heads of the sacrificial animals is cut off from those very deities.
(5.5.5.1) He piles up gold bricks;
thus he pays homage to those very deities.
(5.5.5.1) The exponents of the Veda (brahmavādinaḥ) say:
(5.5.5.2) "He consigns the domestic animals to Agni and subjects the wild animals to his heat; what does he leave remaining from that?
(5.5.5.2) In that he lays down bricks of gold—gold being indeed immortality—he thereby provides a remedy for the domestic animals by means of immortality; he does not injure them.
The first naturally perforated brick is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the second is the diffused breath (*vyāna*), and the third is the in-breath (*apāna*).
Having laid down the first naturally perforated brick, he should breathe out;
thus, by means of the out-breath itself, he brings the out-breath into harmony.
(5.5.5.2) He should breathe out. (5.5.5.3) Having laid down the second [brick], he unites the diffusive breath (*vyāna*) with the diffusive breath itself.
(5.5.5.3) Having laid down the third, he should breathe in.
By means of the out-breath (*apāna*) alone, he unites the out-breath;
furthermore, by means of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), he kindles him.
With the words "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar," they place the naturally perforated bricks (*svayamātṛṇṇā*).
(5.5.5.3) These worlds, indeed, are the naturally perforated bricks (*svayamātṛṇṇā*).
By means of these very *vyāhṛti*s, Prajāpati was born.
In that he lays down the naturally perforated bricks with these *vyāhṛti*s, having laid down these very worlds, he is born upon these worlds. (5.5.5.4) Thus he is procreated within these worlds.
(5.5.5.4) For out-breath, for diffused breath, for in-breath; for speech thee, for sight thee! By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm.
(5.5.5.4) By means of Agni, indeed, the gods desired to go to the heavenly world; with him they were unable to fly.
(5.5.5.4) They saw these four naturally perforated bricks; (5.5.5.4) they placed them in the quarters;
(5.5.5.4) by means of that [which is] all-seeing, they went to the heavenly world.
In that he places four naturally perforated bricks in the quarters, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world by means of Agni, who has eyes on all sides.
(5.5.6.1.a) "O Agni, come for the feast!"— with these words he indeed summons him. (5.5.6.1.b) "We choose Agni as our messenger."
(5.5.6.1) Thus he says; having offered the oblation, he chooses him. (5.5.6.1.c) "By fire is fire kindled," (5.5.6.1) thus he says; he truly kindles him.
(5.5.6.1ḍ) "May Agni strike down the Vṛtras," he says; thus, while he is kindled, he bestows sensory power upon him.
(5.5.6.1.e) "O Agni, we meditate upon the hymn."
"Thus he says; verily, he thinks of him. These indeed are the forms of the days. Day by day he piles him up;
verily, he wins the forms of the days."

(5.5.6.2) The exponents of Brahman say: "On what basis is it that other bricks are exhausted (*yātayāmnī*), while the *lokampṛṇā* brick is not exhausted? One should reply: "Because [it belongs] to Indra-Agni and Bṛhaspati.
For among the gods, Indra, Agni, and Bṛhaspati are those who are not exhausted.
It has an after-offering; this is to avoid sameness. He performs the after-offering with an *anuṣṭubh* verse.
(5.5.6.2) The *lokampṛṇā* is indeed the self (*ātman*), and the *anuṣṭubh* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Therefore, the vital breath moves through all the limbs.
(5.5.6.2) "These [bricks] of his yield milk," he says.
(5.5.6.3) Therefore, there is sap in every joint.
“They mix Soma with speckled [milk],” he says. Speckled [milk] is indeed food; verily, he wins food.
Agni is indeed the Arka; the Arka is food; verily, he wins food.
"O gods, at the birth of the clans, in the three bright realms of heaven," he says.
Verily, he makes these worlds luminous for him.
He who knows the foundation of the bricks stands firm.
"By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm," he says.
This indeed is the foundation of the bricks; he who knows thus stands firm.
This Agni is indeed built for the sake of the heavenly world. The set of eleven [stakes] is a thunderbolt.
If one were to erect the set of eleven in the fire-altar, he would exclude it from the heavenly world by means of the thunderbolt.
If he were not to set up the sacrificial posts, he would deprive the animals of their vital breaths. He sets up a single post;
thus he does not exclude him from the heavenly world by means of the thunderbolt, nor does he deprive the animals of their vital breaths by means of the sacrificial posts.
