(5.5.7.1) He who, while piling the fire-altar, steps upon it, is deprived of his sensory power and vigor. (5.5.7.2) One should place an *iṣṭakā* brick while reciting a verse addressed to Indra as he steps upon it;
thus, he is not deprived of his sensory power and vigor.
Agni, indeed, is Rudra;
he has three arrows: one directed backward, one directed crosswise, and one directed forward.
He who piles the fire-altar is cut down by these [arrows].
Having piled the fire-altar, one should give a bow with three arrows, unasked for, to a Brahmin.
Thus he pays homage to them;
moreover, he thereby ransoms himself from them.
(5.5.7.2) That bow which you hold, O Rudra, in front—let the wind blow after it for you. To that [bow] of yours, O Rudra, I pay homage with the year.
(5.5.7.3) That bow which you hold, O Rudra, on the right—let the wind blow after it for you.
To you, O Rudra, I pay homage with the Parivatsara year.
That bow of yours, O Rudra, which is behind, may the wind blow after it. To you, O Rudra, I pay homage with the Idāvatsara year.
O Rudra, may the wind blow along with that bow of yours which is above;
to that bow of yours, O Rudra, I pay homage for a year. O Rudra, may the wind blow along with that bow of yours which is overhead.
(5.5.7.4) To you, O Rudra, I pay homage with the year.
(5.5.7.4) This Agni is indeed Rudra;
he stands there now like an enraged tiger.
He worships the piled [fire] with these [verses]. By means of salutations, he indeed pacifies it.
"The fires that have entered the earth, which are associated with the soil... (5.5.7.5)
Of these you are the highest; impel us toward life.
(5.5.7.5) I have attained you, O Agni, with the mind. (5.5.7.5) I have attained you, O Agni, with fervor. (5.5.7.5) I have attained you, O Agni, with consecration.
(5.5.7.5) O Agni, may I attain you with the *upasad* rites; (5.5.7.5) O Agni, may I attain you with the *sutyā* sacrifice;
(5.5.7.5) O Agni, may I attain you with the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
"O Agni, may I attain you with the *avabhṛtha* bath;
O Agni, may I attain you with the *vaśā* cow;
O Agni, may I attain you with the utterance of *svagā*," he says.
This indeed is the attainment of Agni; by it he attains him.
(5.5.8.1) With the Gāyatra he worships from the front; verily, he bestows breath upon him.
(5.5.8.1) With the Bṛhat and Rathantara he worships the two wings; verily, he bestows vigor upon him.
(5.5.8.1) With the Yajñāyajñīya, established in the seasons, he worships the tail; verily, he finds firm support in the seasons.
He worships with the *pṛṣṭha* chants.
The *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed splendor;
verily, he bestows splendor upon him.
Prajāpati created Agni. Once created, he went away from him. He restrained him with the Vāravantīya [Sāman]; that is why the Vāravantīya has its name "Vāravantīya."
With the Śyaita [sāman], he made the two white ones; that is the reason for the name of the Śyaita.
In that he worships with the Vāravantīya, he indeed restrains him;
with the Śyaita, he makes him white;
with the Heart of Prajāpati, he worships him limb by limb.
He indeed attains love for him. "With the eastern quarter I settle thee; with the Gāyatrī metre, with Agni as the deity; with the head of Agni, I place the head of Agni.
"With the southern quarter I settle thee; with the Triṣṭubh metre, with Indra as the deity; with the wing of Agni, I place the wing of Agni."
(5.5.8.2) "I settle you with the western quarter; with the Jagatī metre, with Savitṛ as the deity, I place the tail of Agni upon the tail of Agni.
(5.5.8.3) "I settle you with the northern quarter; with the Anuṣṭubh metre, with Mitra and Varuṇa as the deity, I place the wing of Agni upon the wing of Agni.
(5.5.8.3) "I settle you with the upward quarter; with the Paṅkti metre, with Bṛhaspati as the deity, I place the back of Agni upon the back of Agni."
(5.5.8.3) He who piles the fire-altar without its self becomes selfless in yonder world;
he who piles it with its self becomes possessed of a self in yonder world.
He places the *ātman*-bricks.
This indeed is the self of Agni; he who knows this piles Agni with his own self, and he becomes possessed of his own self in yonder world.
(5.5.9.1.a) O Agni, from the ocean, with that arrow of yours named *yuvan*, be gracious to us! Homage to it! May we live subsisting upon it!
(5.5.9.1.b) O Agni, the fierce one! (5.5.9.1.c) The secret one!
O Kiṃśila, O Vanya, with that arrow of yours named Yuvan, be gracious to us! Homage to it! May we live depending upon it.

(5.5.9.1.f) There are indeed five fires which are the layers: the first is named Udadhi, the second Dudhra, the third Gahya, the fourth Kiṃśila, and the fifth Vanya. If one were not to offer oblations to them, they would consume both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer. In that he offers these oblations, he pacifies them with their own portion; neither the Adhvaryu nor the sacrificer comes to ruin.

(5.5.9.2.g) May speech be in my mouth, breath in my nostrils, sight in my eyes, hearing in my ears, strength in my arms, vigor in my thighs; may all my limbs and my body be unharmed. (5.5.9.3) Through this body, together with me, let there be homage to you; do not harm me.

(5.5.9.3ḥ) The vital breaths indeed depart from him who, while piling the fire-altar, steps over it. "May speech be in my mouth, breath in my nostrils," he says; thus he places the vital breaths within himself.

(5.5.9.3.i) "To that Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants—to that Rudra who has entered all beings, let there be homage. (5.5.9.3.k) "Some Rudras indeed have the *āhuti* as their portion, others have the *havis* as their portion. (5.5.9.4) Having offered the *Śatarudrīya*, one should place a *gavīdhuka* pap on the final brick with this *yajus*. By means of its own portion, he pacifies him. They say, "The *Śatarudrīya* has been truly offered for him by whom this is performed in the fire."

(5.5.9.4ḷ) May the Vasus with the Rudras protect you from the east; may the Fathers, whose king is Yama, protect you from the south with the Pitṛs; may the Ādityas with all the gods protect you from the west; may Dyutāna Māruta protect you from the north with the Maruts. (5.5.9.4.5) May the gods, whose chief is Indra and whose king is Varuṇa, protect you from below and from above.

(5.5.9.5ṃ) Indeed, it is neither purified, nor fit for sacrifice, nor sprinkled if one sprinkles it prior to this point; but in that he sprinkles the piled altar with clarified butter, by that it becomes purified, by that it becomes fit for sacrifice, and by that it becomes sprinkled.
(5.5.10.1.a) You are named Samīcī, the eastern direction (5.5.10.1). Of you, Agni is the overlord and Asita is the protector.
To him who is the overlord and him who is the guardian, homage! May they both be gracious to us.
Him whom we hate and him who hates us, I place within your jaws.
You are the southern quarter, named Ojasvinī;
Indra is its overlord, and the viper is its guardian.
(5.5.10.1) You are named Prācī, the eastern direction. (5.5.10.2) Of you, Soma is the overlord; Svaja is your [name].
(5.5.10.2) You are named Avasthāvān, the northern direction.
Of that [quarter] of yours, Varuṇa is the overlord; the cross-lined snake is its guardian.
You are the overmistress, the great quarter named Bṛhatī.
Of that [quarter] of yours, Bṛhaspati is the overlord; the white snake is its guardian.
This quarter is named Vaśinī;
Yama is its overlord, and Kalmāṣagrīva is its protector.
To him who is the overlord and him who is the protector, homage! May they both be gracious to us.
(5.5.10.2) "Him whom we hate and him who hates us—him I place within your jaws.
(5.5.10.3.b) These deities indeed protect the piled fire-altar; if one were not to offer oblations to them, they would consume both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer.
(5.5.10.3) In that he offers these oblations, he pacifies them with their own portion;
neither the Adhvaryu nor the sacrificer comes to ruin. (5.5.10.3.c) "You are the darts by name."
(5.5.10.3) Your dwellings are in front; (5.5.10.3) Agni is your arrows, the water is your [weapon].
(5.5.10.3–4) You are the ones named Nilmipas.
Your sacrificial fee is houses;
O Fathers, your arrows are the ocean; you are named the Thunderbolt-bearers.
(5.5.10.4) Your houses are behind you; (5.5.10.4) sleep is your arrows, and the abyss is your home.
(5.5.10.4) You are named "Those Who Remain Behind."
(5.5.10.4) Your homes are in the north;
(5.5.10.4) the waters are your arrows, the ocean your [home]; (5.5.10.4) you are named the Overlords.
(5.5.10.4) Your dwelling-places are above them;
(5.5.10.4) rain is your arrows, O unclad ones! (5.5.10.4) You are named the flesh-eaters, you who belong to the earth.
(5.5.10.4) Your homes are here. (5.5.10.5) Food is your arrow; the winking of eyes is your name. (5.5.10.5) Homage to you! Be gracious to us.
(5.5.10.5) "Him whom we hate and him who hates us—him I place within your jaws.
(5.5.10.5ḍ) Some gods are eaters of oblations, others are non-eaters of oblations;
the builder of the fire-altar (agnicit) alone gratifies both of them.
(5.5.10.5) He offers these oblations with curds mixed with honey;
(5.5.10.5) verily, he gratifies them with their own portion.
(5.5.10.5) Now, moreover, they say:
"The bricks, indeed, are the gods who eat what is not offered."
He offers while moving around [the fire]. Thus he gratifies them completely, leaving none out.
"Suck this milk-yielding breast, rich in nourishment, swollen with water, O Agni, in the midst of the flood."
Delight in the honeyed spring; enter the oceanic expanse as your dwelling place.

(5.5.10.6.f) He who, having yoked the fire, does not release it—just as a horse that is yoked but not released perishes from hunger, even so his fire perishes. (5.5.10.6) As that fire perishes, the sacrificer perishes after it. (5.5.10.7) Having piled the fire, he becomes emaciated.
(5.5.10.7) With the words, "Suck this breast, full of vigor, of the waters," he offers a ladle full of clarified butter.
(5.5.10.7) This, indeed, is the unyoking of Agni. Having unyoked him, he bestows food upon him.
Therefore they say: "Whether one knows thus or not, the swift horse, being well-fed, indeed bestows prosperity.
Agni, verily, is the swift horse.
He thus gratifies him; he, being gratified, gratifies him in return, and he becomes more prosperous.
(5.5.11.1) For King Indra, a boar; (5.5.11.1) for King Varuṇa, a black antelope; (5.5.11.1) for King Yama, a porcupine.
To the bull-king, a gayal; to the tiger-king, a gaur;
to the king of men, a monkey.
The quail belongs to Kṣipraśyena;
the blue-footed antelope belongs to Nīlagu; the kuluṅga gazelle belongs to King Soma.
(5.5.11.1) From the ocean comes the porpoise; (5.5.11.1) from the Himalayas comes the elephant.
The mayu belongs to Prajāpati;
the ūla, the halīkṣṇa, and the vṛṣadaṃśa belong to Dhātṛ; for Sarasvatī, the white śāri that speaks like a man.
To Sarasvatī, a white parrot that speaks like a human; to Pūṣan, a wild goat, a mongoose, and a śaka-bird;
to Vāc, a curlew.
To the grandson of the waters, Jaṣa! To the crocodile, the makara, and the kulikaya—these belong to Akūpāra.
To Vāc, Paiṅgarāja!
(5.5.13.1) For Bhaga, the *kuṣītaka*; (5.5.13.1) the *ātīvāha* and the *darvī*—these are for Vāyu; (5.5.13.1) for the quarters, the *cakravāka*.
(5.5.14.1) For strength, the python;
(5.5.14.1) the mouse, the *sṛjaya*, and the *śayaṇḍaka*—these are for Mitra;
(5.5.14.1) the black snake is for Death.
(5.5.14.1) To Manyu, the self-born;
(5.5.14.1) the Kumbhīnasas, the Puṣkarasādas, and the Lohitāhis—these are the offspring of Tvaṣṭṛ;
(5.5.14.1) the Vāhasas, for the sake of the echo.
(5.5.15.1) The male deer for the Moon;
(5.5.15.1) the iguana, the kālakā bird, and the woodpecker—these for the Trees; (5.5.15.1) the female antelope for the Day, the black one for the Night.
The cuckoo, the screech-owl, and the blue-headed one—these are for Aryaman;
the katkaṭa bird is for Dhātṛ.
The crane belongs to Sūrya;
the antelope, the peacock, and the hawk belong to the Gandharvas;
the francolin partridge belongs to the Vasus.
The partridge belongs to the Rudras;
the red *kuṇḍṛṇācī* and the *golattikā* belong to the Apsarases;
the *sṛmara* belongs to the Forest.
The spotted antelope belongs to the Viśvedevas;
the nyanku belongs to Pitṛvan; the kaśa belongs to Anumati;
the anyavāpa belongs to the half-months.
(5.5.17.1) Kaśyapa for the months; (5.5.17.1) kvayi, kuṭaru, and dātyauha for Sinīvālī;
the śitpuṭa for Bṛhaspati.
Śakā Bhaumī, Pāṅktra Kaśa, and Mānthīlava belong to the ancestors; Jahakā belongs to the seasons.
(5.5.18.1) For the year, a female lizard; (5.5.18.1) the dove, the owl, and the hare—these belong to Nirṛti; (5.5.18.1) the cock belongs to Savitṛ.
The ruru deer belongs to Rudra;
the chameleon, the bird, and the pippakā—these belong to the arrow-point; the hariṇa deer belongs to the Maruts.
To Brahmán, a śārga;
to Tarakṣu, a black dog; to the Itarajanas, a four-eyed donkey;
to Agni, a dhūṅkṣṇā.
The *alaja* is of the intermediate space;
the *udra*, the *madgu*, and the *plava* are of the waters;
the *haṃsasāci* is for Aditi.
For Indrāṇī, the kīrśa; the vulture and the white-breasted vārdhrāṇasa—these are yours, O celestial ones;
for Heaven and Earth, the porcupine.
The *suparṇa* belongs to Parjanya;
the *haṃsa*, the *vṛka*, and the *vṛṣadaṃśa* belong to Indra;
the *udra* belongs to the Waters.
For Aryaman, the lopāśa;
for Mahendra, the lion, the mongoose, and the tiger;
for Kāma, the parasvān.
(5.5.22.1) A black-necked animal for Agni; (5.5.22.1) a ewe for Sarasvatī;
(5.5.22.1) a brown one for Soma.
A dark-grey animal is for Pūṣan;
one with a white back is for Bṛhaspati;
a craftsman is for the Viśvedevas.
(5.5.22.1) The reddish-brown one is for Indra;
(5.5.22.1) the speckled one is for the Maruts;
(5.5.22.1) the piebald one is for Indra and Agni.
A goat with white markings on its lower parts is for Savitṛ; a ram is for Varuṇa.
The horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal—these belong to Prajāpati.
Two black-necked goats belong to Agni;
two with hairy thighs belong to Tvaṣṭṛ.
(5.5.23.1) Two with white backs for Bṛhaspati;
(5.5.23.1) one with a speckled belly for Dhātṛ;
(5.5.23.1) a white ram for Sūrya.
(5.5.24.1) For Agni Anīkavat, a red-marked ox; (5.5.24.1) two with dark spots on their chests for Savitṛ; (5.5.24.1) two with silver navels for Pūṣan.
(5.5.24.1) Two reddish-brown hornless goats for the Viśvedevas;
(5.5.24.1) one speckled goat for the Maruts; (5.5.24.1) a black goat for Agni.
A ewe for Sarasvatī;
a black ram with one white foot for Varuṇa.

Golden-hued, pure, and purifying—those waters in which Kaśyapa was born and in which Indra [was born], who, being of diverse forms, bore Agni as their embryo—may those waters be auspicious and pleasant to us.
(5.6.1.1.b) Those in whose midst King Varuṇa moves, beholding the truth and falsehood of men—those waters that drip with sweetness, pure and purifying—may they be auspicious and pleasant to us.

(5.6.1.1.c) Those whose portion the gods make in heaven, those who exist manifoldly in the intermediate space, those who moisten the earth with their milk—may those pure waters be auspicious and pleasant for us.
(5.6.1.2ḍ) Behold me with a gracious eye, O Waters; touch my skin with your gracious bodies. I invoke you, all the Agnis who dwell in the waters; bestow upon me luster, strength, and vigor.
Because you roared there as you were being led forth when the dragon was slain, therefore you are called "Nadyas" (Rivers); those are your names, O Sindhus.
When, impelled by Varuṇa, you rushed together swiftly, Indra reached you as you were going; therefore, O Waters, you follow after him.
Flowing away at will, you have opened wide the roar; O goddesses, Indra with his powers has driven you forth. Therefore, the name "Vārs" is well-bestowed upon you.
(5.6.1.3) "A single god stood over the flowing [waters], according to his will; 'The great ones have risen up,' they said; therefore it is called water (*udaka*)."

(5.6.1.3.i) The waters are auspicious; the waters were indeed clarified butter. Those waters support Agni and Soma. They possess a potent juice, rich in sweetness. (5.6.1.4) Come readily to me, together with breath and splendor!
(5.6.1.4.k) Then indeed I see, or else I hear; the sound of them comes to me, their voice has reached me. I think that I have partaken of immortality when I was sated by you, O golden-hued ones.
(5.6.1.4ḷ) O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss; grant us strength for great joy and for the sake of vision.
(5.6.1.4ṃ) Whatever most auspicious essence you possess, grant us a share of it here, like longing mothers.
To him for whose abode you quicken us, to him may we go readily; O Waters, give us also life.
(5.6.1.4.o) Rest in heaven; strive in the intermediate space; be united with the earth. You are spiritual luster; for the sake of spiritual luster, I take you.
(5.6.2.1) He draws the cups of water.
(5.6.2.1) These cups are indeed the Rājasūya; the Sava is Agni.
(5.6.2.1) The Varuṇasava is the Rājasūya, and the Agnisava is the piling of the altar.
By means of these two alone he is consecrated.
Moreover, he conquers both worlds: that which belongs to one who has sacrificed with the Rājasūya and that which belongs to one who has piled the fire-altar.
There are waters.
(5.6.2.1) Water, indeed, is the rival of fire.
(5.6.2.1) In that he places the waters below the fire, it is for the sake of overcoming his rival; he prospers in himself and his rival is defeated.
(5.6.2.1) Water is indeed immortality.
(5.6.2.2) Therefore, they sprinkle one who is exhausted with water;
he does not meet with misfortune, but reaches a full lifespan, for whom these [bricks] are laid down and who knows them thus.
Water is indeed food;
water is cattle;
food is cattle.
He becomes an eater of food and possessed of cattle, for whom these [bricks] are laid down and who knows them thus.
There are twelve;
the year consists of twelve months.
By means of the year itself, he wins food for him.
There are vessels;
indeed, food is eaten from a vessel.
Verily, from his own source he wins food.
He eats food for twelve generations of men, and moreover, he is not severed from his vessel, for whom these [bricks] are laid down and who knows them thus.
The *kumbha* and *kumbhī* bricks form pairs.
(5.6.2.3) For the procreation of the pair;
he is propagated with offspring, cattle, and pairs, for whom these [bricks] are laid down, and who knows them thus.
(5.6.2.4) Agni is indeed pain.
(5.6.2.4) It [the fire] afflicts the Adhvaryu, the sacrificer, and the offspring with pain.
(5.6.2.4) In that he lays down the waters, he pacifies his very pain.
Neither the Adhvaryu nor the sacrificer comes to ruin; the offspring find peace where these [bricks] are laid down.
(5.6.2.4) These waters are indeed the hearts of the waters.

(5.6.2.4) In that he lays down these waters, he unites them with the celestial waters; Parjanya becomes a bringer of rain. (5.6.2.5) Whoever knows their abode and their arrangement becomes possessed of an abode; for him, everything is arranged.
He places it along the furrow.
This indeed is their abode, this is their proper arrangement.
He who knows thus becomes possessed of an abode; for him, everything is properly arranged.
(5.6.2.5) He places the others in pairs, four in the middle for the sake of support.
(5.6.2.5) The bricks are indeed food;
this oblation-pot (caru), verily, is food manifest.
In that he places this rice-pap offering, he directly secures food for him. He places it in the middle;
verily, he bestows food upon him in the very center.
Therefore, food is eaten from the middle.
It belongs to Bṛhaspati;
for Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman among the gods.
"By means of the *brahman* alone, he wins food for him.

"Thou art spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); for spiritual luster, thee!"—so he says. He becomes radiant and endowed with spiritual luster for whom this [brick] is laid down, and also for whoever knows it thus.
(5.6.3.1) He lays down the *bhūteṣṭakā* bricks.
(5.6.3.1) For here indeed death is born;
wherever death is born, from that very place he sacrifices him away.
(5.6.3.1) Therefore, the builder of the fire-altar attains a full lifespan, for all deaths have been warded off by him.
(5.6.3.1) Therefore, one who builds the fire-altar must not practice sorcery; the sorcery recoils upon him and strikes him down.
He who builds the fire-altar is indeed consecrated.
(5.6.3.1) These are the oblations of the Devasū.
(5.6.3.1) For so many indeed are the pressings (sava) of the gods;
(5.6.3.2) they themselves bestow those pressings upon him.
(5.6.3.2) They impel him.
(5.6.3.2) Agni is the *sava*, Varuṇa is the *sava*, the Rājasūya is the *sava*, and the piled altar is the *brahmasava*.
"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he says.
Impelled by Savitṛ, he consecrates him with the sacred word and with the deities.
He consecrates him with every kind of food,
for the attainment of every kind of food.
He sprinkles him from the front while facing westward;
for food is eaten from the front while facing westward. He sprinkles him from the head.
(5.6.3.2) For food is eaten from the head;
(5.6.3.2) he causes it to flow down along the mouth.
(5.6.3.3) Verily, he bestows upon him food from the very mouth.
(5.6.3.3) "With the sovereignty of Agni, I consecrate you," he says.
(5.6.3.3) This, indeed, is the self-sovereignty of Agni.
With that very [substance] he consecrates him.
"O Bṛhaspati, I consecrate you with sovereignty," he says.
Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman among the gods.
(5.6.3.3) He consecrates him with the Brahman itself.
(5.6.3.3) "I consecrate you with the sovereignty of Indra," he says. (5.6.3.3) Thus he bestows power upon him from above.
(5.6.3.3) This indeed is the form of the Rājasūya.
(5.6.3.4) He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar, conquers both worlds: that of one who has performed the Rājasūya and that of one who has piled the fire-altar.
(5.6.3.4) When Indra had pressed the Soma, his power and vigor fell away in ten directions.
(5.6.3.4) The gods gathered that [essence] together by means of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
(5.6.3.4) Indeed, he who piles the fire-altar is consecrated.
(5.6.3.4) Having piled the fire-altar, he should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī; thus, having gathered sensory power and vigor, he places them within himself.
In harmony with the year and its months;
in harmony with the dawn and its ruddy beams;
in harmony with the sun and his coursers.
(5.6.4.1) May the Aśvins, in joyful accord with their wondrous deeds,
(5.6.4.1) may Agni Vaiśvānara, in accord with the *iḍā*-invocations, (5.6.4.1) [be pleased] with clarified butter; *svāhā*!
The year, indeed, is the cloud;
the months are the rain-showers;
the dawn is the ruddy one.
Sūrya is Etaśa;
these two are the Aśvins;
the year is Agni Vaiśvānara.
The *iḍā* is cattle;
ghee is cattle.
Cattle are born after the pattern of the year.
By means of the year itself, he causes cattle to be born for him.
He offers the oblation upon a clump of *darbha* grass;
for whatever is the immortality and whatever is the vigor of this [earth], that is the *darbha* grass.
(5.6.4.2) He offers into that; he is indeed born and becomes an eater of food for whom they offer in this manner.
(5.6.4.2) These deities are indeed the portions of Agni that precede him.
(5.6.4.2) He thus gratifies them;
furthermore, he places the eye of Agni in front.
He who knows this becomes free from blindness.
(5.6.4.2) In the beginning, this world was indeed water, a vast expanse.
That Prajāpati, having become the wind, moved restlessly upon the leaf of a lotus. He found no firm support. (5.6.4.3) He [found] no support.
(5.6.4.3) He saw this nest of the waters;
(5.6.4.3) upon it he piled the fire-altar;
(5.6.4.3) that became this earth.

(5.6.4.3) Thereupon he indeed stood firm. That which he placed in front became his head; that was the eastern direction. That which he placed on the south became his right wing; that was the southern direction.
That which she placed in the west became the tail; she is the western direction (*pratīcī dig*).
That which she placed in the north became the northern wing; she is the northern direction (*udīcī dig*). That which she placed above became the back; she is the upward direction (*ūrdhvā dig*).
(5.6.4.4) This earth, indeed, is Agni consisting of five bricks. Therefore, whatever they dig into it, they pierce a brick; whatever they crush, they pierce a pebble.
Indeed, this [earth] shines at night for all birds to see.
Therefore, birds do not sit upon this earth at night.
He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar, stands firm and conquers the quarters.
Indeed, the Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni.
Therefore, for a Brāhmaṇa, there is failure in all directions; he follows his own direction alone. For fire is the nest of the waters.
Therefore, the waters seek Agni;
they thus enter their own source.

(5.6.5.1) Having carried the fire in the *ukhā* for one year, in the second year he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra, a cake on twelve potsherds to the Viśvedevas, a pap to Bṛhaspati, and a cake on three potsherds to Viṣṇu.
(5.6.5.1) In the third year, he should sacrifice with the *Abhijit*.
In that there is a cake on eight potsherds—the Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and the morning pressing belongs to Agni and is of the Gāyatra nature.
By this, he supports the morning pressing and the *gāyatrī* metre.
In that there is a cake on eleven potsherds— the *triṣṭubh* has eleven syllables, and the midday pressing belongs to Indra and the *triṣṭubh*—
by this he supports the midday pressing and the *triṣṭubh* metre.
In that there is an offering on twelve potsherds— the Jagatī has twelve syllables and the third pressing belongs to the Viśvedevas—
he thereby supports the third pressing and the Jagatī metre. In that there is a pap for Bṛhaspati— Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman among the gods.
By that very act, he has supported the Brahman; for in that there is a cake on three potsherds for Viṣṇu— Viṣṇu being the sacrifice—
he has thereby supported the sacrifice itself.
In that he sacrifices with the Abhijit in the third year, it is for the sake of conquest.
In that he carries the fire-pan (*ukhya*) for a year, he thereby wins this very world. In that he piles the fire-altar in the second year, he thereby wins the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
In that he sacrifices in the third year, he thereby wins that very world.
Para Āṭṇāra, Kakṣīvat Auśija, Vītahavya Śrāyasa, Trasadasyu Paurukutsya—they, desiring offspring, built this [fire-altar].
Thereby they indeed obtained a thousand sons each.
He prospers with offspring and cattle; he attains that same measure which those who knew thus attained when they piled the fire. Therefore, one who knows this should pile the fire.
Prajāpati piled the fire-altar;
having become one whose edge was like a razor, he stood there.
The gods, being afraid, did not approach him.
Having covered themselves with the meters, they approached;
that is the "meter-ness" of the meters.
The meters are indeed Brahman.
The black antelope skin is the form of Brahman.
He puts on shoes made of black antelope skin;
having thus covered himself with the meters, he approaches the fire for his own protection from harm.

(5.6.6.1) This Agni is indeed deposited as a treasure for the gods. (5.6.6.2) For others find a treasure that is not guarded, or one does not recognize it. He steps upon the fire-pan; he thus makes himself his own guardian for protection.
Moreover, they say:
(5.6.6.2) "One should not step upon it.
(5.6.6.2) The fire-pan belongs to Nirṛti; if one were to step upon it, one would deliver oneself to Nirṛti. Therefore, one should not step upon it.
He places the human head [on the altar] for protection.
Moreover, it is just as if one were to say, "Guard this for me"; such indeed is that.
Prajāpati is indeed Atharvan;
Agni himself is Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa;
his bricks are his bones.
(5.6.6.3) Regarding this, the seer indeed spoke thus:
"With the bones of Dadhyañc, Indra... (5.6.6.3).
When he piles the fire-altar with bricks, he piles the fire-altar as one possessed of its own body.
(5.6.6.3) He who knows this becomes possessed of a self in that world.
(5.6.6.3) This altar which is built up is indeed the body of Agni; Vaiśvānara is the self.
(5.6.6.3) When one offers to Vaiśvānara upon the built-up altar, having consecrated the very body, (5.6.6.4) he ascends [to it].

(5.6.6.4) Indeed, when the sacrificer piles the fire-altar, he constructs this very body. When he offers the Vaiśvānara oblation over the piled altar, having prepared his body, he ascends into it with his own self.
Therefore, they do not cut off portions from him; while still alive, he goes even unto the gods.
(5.6.6.4) He places the loose soil with a verse addressed to Vaiśvānara.
(5.6.6.4) This earth, indeed, is Agni Vaiśvānara; this layer of loose soil is his altar.
(5.6.6.4) He piles Agni Vaiśvānara himself. (5.6.6.4) Vaiśvānara is indeed this dear body of Agni;
verily, he wins his dear body.
(5.6.7.1) By means of the consecration of Agni, the gods attained the Virāj.
(5.6.7.1) One should remain consecrated for three nights;
the Virāj consists of three feet.
He attains the Virāj.
He should remain consecrated for six nights;
for the year consists of six seasons.
The year is the Virāj; he attains the Virāj.
He should remain consecrated for ten nights.
The *virāj* consists of ten syllables; he attains the *virāj*.
He should remain consecrated for twelve nights.
Twelve months are a year;
the year is the *virāj*; he attains the *virāj*.
(5.6.7.1) One should be consecrated for thirteen nights.
(5.6.7.1) Thirteen (5.6.7.2) months are a year;
the year is the *virāj*.
(5.6.7.2) He should remain consecrated for fifteen nights.
(5.6.7.2) For there are fifteen nights in a half-month;
by [consecration] for half-months, the year is attained.
The year is the Virāj; he attains the Virāj.
He should remain consecrated for seventeen nights.
Twelve months and five seasons—that is the year. The year is the Virāj; he attains the Virāj.
One should remain consecrated for twenty-four nights.
There are twenty-four half-months in a year;
the year is the *virāj*.
He attains the *virāj*.
One should remain consecrated for thirty nights; the *virāj* consists of thirty syllables;
he attains the *virāj*.
(5.6.7.3) He should remain consecrated for a month.
(5.6.7.3) That which is a month is the year;
(5.6.7.3) the year is the Virāj.
(5.6.7.3) He attains the Virāj.
(5.6.7.3) He should remain consecrated for four months.
For it was during these four months that the Vasus bore him; they conquered the earth and the Gāyatrī metre.
(5.6.7.3) The eight Rudras won the intermediate region; the Gāyatrī metre [was their share].
(5.6.7.3) The eight Rudras won the intermediate region; the Triṣṭubh metre [was their share]. (5.6.7.3) The twelve Ādityas won the sky; the Jagatī metre [was their share].
(5.6.7.3) Thereupon they indeed attained distinction and preeminence among the gods.
(5.6.7.3) Therefore, having supported [the fires] for twelve months, one should pile the fire-altar;
for twelve months constitute a year.
The year is the fire-altar to be piled;
its bricks are the days and nights.
He piles it with bricks that have been obtained; thus he attains distinction and preeminence among his equals.
(5.6.8.1.a) This Agni is indeed built for the sake of the heavenly world;
if one were not to follow him [in ascending], the sacrificer would be excluded from the heavenly world.
"I have stepped upon the earth; may my vital breath not forsake me."
"I have stepped upon the intermediate space; may my offspring not forsake me.
I have stepped upon the sky; we have gone to the light of heaven," he says.
(5.6.8.1) This indeed is the mounting after Agni; by means of it he mounts after him for the attainment of the heavenly world.
(5.6.8.1.b) If he were to measure it equal to the wings, he would enter upon a lesser sacrificial rite; his offspring would become more wretched.
(5.6.8.2) He measures it equal to the altar;
thus he enters upon a greater sacrificial rite.
(5.6.8.2) His offspring does not become more wicked than he.
(5.6.8.2.c) One who is building for the first time should pile [the fire-altar] consisting of a thousand [bricks];
for this world is measured by a thousand.
He conquers this very world.
One who builds for a second time should pile a double-thousand-fold altar;
for the intermediate space is indeed double-thousand-fold.
Verily, he conquers the intermediate space;
one building the third layer should pile it as a three-thousandfold altar.
(5.6.8.3) This world above is indeed three-thousandfold; verily, he conquers that very world.
(5.6.8.3ḍ) One who is building for the first time should pile [the altar] knee-deep;
by means of the Gāyatrī metre, he ascends this world.
One building a second altar should not build it reaching up to the navel;
by means of the Triṣṭubh meter he ascends to the intermediate space.
One building a third altar should build it reaching up to the neck.
By means of the *jagatī* metre, he ascends to that world.
Having piled the fire-altar, he should not approach a beautiful woman, thinking, "I shall deposit my seed in what is not a womb.
Having piled it a second time, he should not approach the wife of another.

(5.6.8.4) Having piled the third [altar], he should not approach any woman. (5.6.8.4) For when he piles the fire-altar, he deposits semen; if he were to approach a woman, he would be deprived of his semen.
(5.6.8.4) Now, moreover, they say:
"That would be childless if one were not to approach [the fires].
(5.6.8.4) In that he lays down the two *retaḥsic* bricks, those two indeed sustain the seed of the sacrificer.
Therefore, one should approach [his wife] so that the seed does not spill;
for there are indeed three seeds: the father, the son, and the grandson.
If he were to lay down only two semen-shedders (*retaḥsic*), he would cut off the semen.

He lays down three for the continuity of the semen. This first semen-shedder is indeed this [earth]; this [earth] is speech. Therefore, when they see her, they see her as seeing; when she speaks, they see her as speaking.
The intermediate space is the second; the breath indeed is the intermediate space, therefore they do not see the intermediate space, nor do they see the breath.
That [heaven] is the third; the eye indeed is that [heaven], therefore they see it—that is, they see the eye.
With a *yajus*-formula he lays down this [earth] and that [heaven]; with his mind, the middle one.
"For the arrangement of these worlds;
and also for the vital breaths.
"The sacrifice has been offered by the Bhṛgus, the bestower of blessings by the Vasus; may I here partake of the wealth of that sacrifice which has been offered and enjoyed," he says.

(5.6.8.6) By this [verse], he milks out both the *stotra* and the *śastra*: "Father Mātariśvan has established flawless steps; the eager ones have fashioned flawless steps after them. May Soma, the all-knowing leader, lead us; may Bṛhaspati recite the hymns and songs of praise (*ukthāmadāni*)," so he says.
This, indeed, is the hymn (*uktha*) of Agni.
With that very [verse], he recites after it.
(5.6.9.1.a) He who is carried in the fire-pan is indeed consecrated among the fires.
(5.6.9.1) If he were to set it down below, the embryos would be born prematurely;
moreover, it would be just as when one descends from a chariot.
(5.6.9.1) He sets down the stool for the support of the embryos so that they do not fall. (5.6.9.1) Moreover, he thereby makes it a productive impulse (*sava*).
(5.6.9.1b) For this fire in the pan is indeed an embryo, and the sling is the womb.
(5.6.9.1) If one were to take the fire-pan down from the sling, one would strike the embryo out of the womb.
(5.6.9.1) The sling has six supports;
for man is indeed constituted in six parts: the self, the head, and the four limbs. (5.6.9.2) Thus it is.
(5.6.9.2) He indeed bears him within his own self.
(5.6.9.2.c) This Agni is Prajāpati; his fire-pan and mortar are his two breasts.
(5.6.9.2) His offspring live upon those two;
in that he lays down both the fire-pan and the mortar, by means of them the sacrificer milks Agni in yonder world.
(5.6.9.2ḍ) This Agni is indeed the year.
(5.6.9.2) Of that [fire-altar], there are bricks arranged in three groups: those belonging to Prajāpati, those belonging to Viṣṇu, and those belonging to Viśvakarman.
(5.6.9.3) The days and nights are indeed its [bricks] belonging to Prajāpati;
when he carries the fire in the pan (*ukhya*), he thus lays down the bricks belonging to Prajāpati.
(5.6.9.3) In that he places the fuel-sticks— trees indeed belong to Viṣṇu—
he thus lays down what belongs to Viṣṇu.
(5.6.9.3) In that he piles the fire with bricks, this earth is indeed Viśvakarman.
Thus he lays down those bricks belonging to Viśvakarman;
therefore they say,
"Agni is threefold."
(5.6.9.3.e) Indeed, the sacrificer himself should pile this [altar].

If someone other than he were to pile it, and if he were not to satisfy that person with sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*), he would deprive him of his fire. Therefore, whoever piles his fire, he should satisfy that person with sacrificial gifts.
(5.6.9.3) By this, he indeed strengthens Agni.
Prajāpati built the fire-altar by means of the seasons during the year. By means of spring, he built its eastern half; by means of summer, the right wing.
(5.6.10.1) The tail with the rainy season;
(5.6.10.1) the right wing with autumn;
(5.6.10.1) the middle with winter.
(5.6.10.1) By means of the *brahman* he piled its eastern half;
(5.6.10.1) by means of the *kṣatra*, the right wing; (5.6.10.1) by means of the cattle, the tail.
The wing consists of one hundred and one bricks;
the middle [brick] is placed with the expectation [of the future].
He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar, piles it indeed by means of the seasons.
Moreover, he thus secures all this;
they hear him as he has piled the fire-altar, and he eats food.
It is pleasing.
This first layer is indeed this [earth]; the plants and trees are the filler (purīṣa). The second layer is the intermediate space; the birds are the filler.
(5.6.10.2) That [third layer] is the stars, and the loose soil is the filling; (5.6.10.2) the sacrifice is the fourth, and the sacrificial fee is the loose soil;
(5.6.10.2) the sacrificer is the fifth, and the offspring is the loose soil.
If one were to pile it with three layers, he would exclude the sacrifice, the sacrificial fee, himself, and his offspring;
therefore, it should be piled with five layers.
In this way, he secures all of this.
(5.6.10.2) That there are three layers.
For Agni is threefold.
Since there are two [bricks], it is for the support of the sacrificer, who is two-footed; there are five layers.
Man is fivefold;
he thus preserves his very self.
There are five layers.
He piles on with five layers of loose soil;
they amount to ten.
The person indeed consists of ten syllables.
He wins the man in his full extent;
moreover, the *virāj* consists of ten syllables,
and the *virāj* is food.
Verily, he finds firm support in the Virāj and in the eating of food. The sixth layer is indeed the year;
the loose soil is the seasons.
There are six layers and six fillings;
they amount to twelve. Twelve months are a year.
Verily, he finds firm support in the year itself.
The red, the smoke-red, and the jujube-red—these belong to Prajāpati.
The brown, the ruddy-brown, and the parrot-brown—these belong to Rudra.
The white, the white-eyed, and the white-necked—these have the Pitṛs as their deity.
(5.6.11.1) Three black barren cows are for Varuṇa;
three white barren cows are for Sūrya;
and hornless, smoke-colored bulls with white spots on their foreheads are for Mitra and Bṛhaspati.
The speckled, the cross-speckled, and the upward-speckled—these belong to the Maruts.
The pale, the red-wooled, and the white-eyed—these belong to Sarasvatī.
The spotted, the large-spotted, and the small-spotted—these belong to the Viśvedevas.
(5.6.12.1) Three black barren cows are for Pūṣan;
(5.6.12.1) three ruddy barren cows are for Mitra;
(5.6.12.1) those with reddish marks on their foreheads and hornless are for Indra and Bṛhaspati.
(5.6.13.1) Those with white forelegs—whether white on one side or white all over—are for Indra and Vāyu.
(5.6.13.1) Those with white nostrils—whether white on one side or white all over—are for Mitra and Varuṇa.
(5.6.13.1) Those with white tails—whether entirely white-tailed or having a jewel-like tail—are for the Aśvins.
(5.6.13.1) Three brindled cows for the Viśvedevas;
(5.6.13.1) three white-eyed ewes for Parameṣṭhin; hornless rams with black spots on their foreheads for Soma and Pūṣan.
(5.6.14.1) The humped bull and the dwarf—these are for Indra and Varuṇa.
(5.6.14.1) The white-kneed, the white-backed, and the white-rumped—these are for Indra and Bṛhaspati.
(5.6.14.1) The white-footed, the white-lipped, and the white-browed—these are for Indra and Viṣṇu.
(5.6.14.1) Three speckled barren cows are for Viśvakarman;
three spotted ones are for Dhātṛ; and three white-spotted hornless rams are for Indra and Pūṣan.
Three black-eared ones are for Yama;
three white-spotted ones are for Soma; three mongooses are for Agni Yaviṣṭha;
three red cows are for the Tryavis; these belong to the Vasus.
Three reddish-brown oxen for driving are for the Rudras;
those with brown marks on their foreheads and hornless are for Soma and Indra.
(5.6.16.1) Three with prominent teeth are for Viṣṇu;
(5.6.16.1) three with long ears are for Viṣṇu Urukrama;
(5.6.16.1) three with pendulous dewlaps are for Viṣṇu Urugāya.
Twenty-five three-year-old speckled cows are for the Ādityas;
three three-year-old reddish-brown cows are for the Aṅgirases; and hornless white-spotted bulls are for Indra and Viṣṇu.
(5.6.17.1) Three white-backed [bulls] for Indra the King;
(5.6.17.1) three white-humped [bulls] for Indra the Overlord;
(5.6.17.1) three white-rumped [bulls] for Indra the Self-Ruler.
(5.6.17.1) Three four-year-old cows are for the Sādhyas;
(5.6.17.1) three six-year-old cows are for the Viśvedevas;
(5.6.17.1) those dedicated to Agni and Indra are hornless bulls with black spots on their foreheads.
(5.6.18.1) Three reddish-brown ones for Aditi;
(5.6.18.1) three black-spotted ones for Indrāṇī; (5.6.18.1) three ruddy ones for Kuhū.
(5.6.18.1) Three milch-cows for Rākā; (5.6.18.1) three oxen for Sinīvālī;
(5.6.18.1) hornless bulls with red spots on their foreheads for Agni and Viṣṇu.
Three tawny ones for Soma;
three dappled ones for King Soma;
those with the appearance of the sky for Parjanya.
Three hornless, long-tailed goats for Indrāṇī; three ewes for the Ādityas;
two hornless, long-tailed rams for Heaven and Earth.
Three black-spotted animals for Varuṇa;
three red-spotted animals for Varuṇa the King;
three ruddy-spotted animals for Varuṇa the Destroyer of Enemies.
Three of the *śilpa* type are dedicated to the Viśvedevas;
three *pṛśni* ones are dedicated to all the gods;
and hornless ones with white spots on their foreheads are dedicated to Indra and Sūrya.
(5.6.21.1) To Soma, the self-ruling king, two oxen that draw the cart;
(5.6.21.1) to Indra and Agni, the givers of vigor, two camels;
(5.6.21.1) to Indra and Agni, the givers of strength, two sheep that draw the plow.
Two milch-cows for the earth;
a mare for the quarters;
two milch-cows for the earth.
Two Vairājī cows for Puruṣa; two milch-cows for Bhūmi;
two oxen that carry the mounting-steps for Vāyu.
The two black female sheep belong to Varuṇa; the two divine bulls, Arāḍyas, are for Parimara.
(5.6.22.1) Eleven bovine animals are offered in the morning; a spotted goat, a *kikidīvi* bird, and a *vidīgaya*—these belong to Tvaṣṭṛ.
(5.6.22.1) Nine white barren cows are the *anūbandhya* victims for Sūrya.
(5.6.22.1) Those belonging to Agni, Indra-Agni, and the Aśvins are offered at the *viśāla-yūpa*.
(5.6.23.1) Three tawny ones for the spring; (5.6.23.1) three dappled ones for the summer;
(5.6.23.1) three speckled ones for the rainy season.
Three *pṛśni* (spotted) are for the autumn;
three *pṛśnisaktha* (spotted-thighed) are for the winter; three *avalipta* (smeared) are for the cool season.
(5.6.23.1) For the sake of the year, those with broad chests.
(5.7.1.1) He who piles the fire-altar not according to its deities is cut off from the deities and becomes worse off;
he who piles it according to the deities is not cut off from the deities and becomes more prosperous.

(5.7.1.1) He should touch the first layer with a *gāyatrī* verse addressed to Agni, the second with a *triṣṭubh*, the third with a *jagatī*, the fourth with an *anuṣṭubh*, and the fifth with a *paṅkti*.
(5.7.1.1) He piles the fire-altar according to the respective deities; he is not cut off from the deities and becomes more prosperous. (5.7.1.1) This is indeed a division of *iḍā*;
cattle are *iḍā*.
(5.7.1.1) He piles it with cattle.
(5.7.1.2) Verily, he who piles the fire after having announced it to Prajāpati does not meet with ruin.
Two horses should stand on either side: a black one to the north and a white one to the south.
Having touched those two, he should place the bricks.
This, indeed, is the form of Prajāpati;
the horse belongs to Prajāpati.
(5.7.1.2) Having announced it directly to Prajāpati, he piles the fire-altar; he does not come to ruin.
(5.7.1.2) This indeed is the form of the day: that the horse is white; [this is] for the night, that it is black.
(5.7.1.2–3) This is the form of the day: that the bricks are [white]; for the night, the loose earth (*purīṣa*).
(5.7.1.3) When about to lay down the bricks, he should touch a white horse; when about to lay down the loose earth, a black one.
(5.7.1.3) Thus, by means of day and night, he piles it.
He gives a golden vessel filled with honey.
"May I be worthy of honey," [he says];
he gazes at two sun-deities verses containing the word "wonderful" (*citra*) at midday; thus, it indeed becomes wonderful at midday.
(5.7.1.3) He causes the horse to smell [the offering].
(5.7.1.3) Yonder sun is indeed Indra; he is Prajāpati, and the horse belongs to Prajāpati.
(5.7.1.3) He prospers directly through that alone.

(5.7.2.1.a) O Agni, I have come to you, the bull, the one who is observant, generating you again as a youth. May our household duties not be deficient; sharpen us with your keen sacred word (*brahman*).
(5.7.2.1) These bricks are indeed cattle. In each layer he places a bull; he thus creates a pair for his sacrifice for the sake of procreation. Therefore, in every herd there is a bull.
(5.7.2.1.b) O Night, you whom they worship as the image of the year—having made [us] rich in offspring and heroes, may we attain a full span of life.
(5.7.2.1) He places this brick pertaining to Prajāpati. (5.7.2.2) This Ekāṣṭakā is indeed this earth; whatever food is prepared on the Ekāṣṭakā, that he wins by means of this [brick].

This is indeed Prajāpati’s wish-fulfilling cow; by her the sacrificer milks Agni in yonder world. (5.7.2.2.c) By which the gods went upward with light, by which the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Rudras, by which the Aṅgirases attained greatness—by that may the sacrificer go in safety.
(5.7.2.2) This Agni is indeed built for the sake of the heavenly world.
(5.7.2.3) With the words, "By whom the gods rose upward with light," he kindles the fire in the pan; he thus lays down these very bricks made of wood for the attainment of the heavenly world.
(5.7.2.3d) "To him who has a hundred weapons, a hundred powers, a hundred aids, the overcomer of enemies—he, Indra, may lead us across all difficulties, unvanquished through a hundred autumns."

(5.7.2.3.e) Those four paths leading to the gods which extend between heaven and earth—of these, may he who brings us freedom from injury and victory; to him, O gods, (5.7.2.4) do you all grant protection here.
May summer, winter, and spring, autumn and the rainy season be auspicious for us. In the shelter of these seasons, throughout a hundred autumns, may we abide in safety.

(5.7.2.4.g) To the *iduvatsara*, to the *parivatsara*, and to the *saṃvatsara*, offer great homage! May we, in the benevolent favor of those worthy of sacrifice, remain for a long time undefeated and unslain.

(5.7.2.4) O gods, you have led us from good to better; through you as our protection, may we attain you. As one who brings bliss, O food, enter into us—be auspicious for our offspring and pleasant for our bodies. (5.7.2.5)
(5.7.2.5) He places these "unfailing" bricks. These indeed are the unconquered deities; he enters into them and is never conquered.
(5.7.2.5) The exponents of sacred knowledge say:
"Since the half-months, months, seasons, and the year cause the plants to ripen, why then is the *Āgrayaṇa* offering set aside for other deities?"
For these deities indeed won that [victory] when one might offer [the oblations] to the seasons; he would thereby create discord among the deities.
Having offered the Āgrayaṇa, he offers these oblations.
Thus he gratifies the half-months, the months, the seasons, and the year, and does not create discord among the deities.
"O gods, you have led us from good to better," he says for the sake of the sacrificer’s eating of the oblation and to prevent his defeat.

(5.7.3.1.a) You are Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra, our body-protector, our scout. Whoever, seeking to harm us, assails us from the east, from the south, from the west, or from the north—let him strike this stone.
(5.7.3.1) The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. (5.7.3.1) Those Asuras assailed them from all directions. The gods drove them away with both arrows and the thunderbolt.
In that he lays down the *vajriṇī* bricks, the sacrificer thereby drives away his rivals with both the *iṣu* and the *vajra*. He lays them down in the quarters;
verily, he surrounds himself with these divine fortresses which protect the body.
(5.7.3.2.b) O Agni and Viṣṇu, being of one accord, may these songs increase you both; come hither with splendors and with strengths.
(5.7.3.2) The exponents of Brahman say: "Since they do not offer it to a deity, then to which deity does the *vasordhārā* belong?
Fire is the *vasu*; this stream belongs to him.
Viṣṇu is the Vasu; this is his stream.
With a verse addressed to Agni and Viṣṇu, he offers the Vasordhārā. By means of their respective portions, he thus brings them into harmony.
(5.7.3.2) Now, he makes this very oblation possessed of a proper abode.
(5.7.3.3) Whatever desire he has when he offers it, that very thing he attains. For this Agni is indeed Rudra.
(5.7.3.3) These two are his bodies: one is terrible, the other is auspicious.
When he offers the Śatarudrīya, he pacifies with it that body of his which is terrible;
when he offers the Vasordhārā, he gratifies with it that body of his which is auspicious.
(5.7.3.3) He who knows the support of the stream of wealth (vasoḥ dhārayai) indeed finds firm standing.
(5.7.3.4) Whatever clarified butter (ājya) may remain, one should cook a brahmin's rice-mess (brahmaudana) in it. Four Brahmins should consume it.
(5.7.3.4) This Brāhmaṇa is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara;
this Vaiśvānara is truly the beloved body of Agni. He thus establishes him upon his own beloved body.
(5.7.3.4) He should give four milch cows;
by means of them alone, the sacrificer milks Agni in that world.
"I offer thought with mind and ghee," he says. This oblation to Viśvakarman is indeed called "the invincible."
(5.7.4.1) An adversary does not harm him who has piled this [fire-altar].
(5.7.4.1) Moreover, he wins the very deities.
(5.7.4.1b) O Agni, him today...
(5.7.4.1) Thus he offers with a *paṅkti* verse; by means of the *paṅkti* oblation, he commences the mouth of the sacrifice.
(5.7.4.1.c) "Seven, O Agni, are your fuel-sticks, seven your tongues."
Thus he says;
verily, he wins the offices of the Hotṛ-priests. Agni departed from the gods, seeking his own portion.
To him they gave this as his portion;
for this indeed is Agni’s Agnihotra.
Truly, he is born at this very moment when he has been completely piled.
Verily, he bestows food upon him as soon as he is born;
being pleased, he makes him pleased, and he becomes more prosperous.

(5.7.4.2ḍ) The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "Since this Gārhapatya fire is piled up, then where is its Āhavanīya? One should reply: "That [sun] in the sky. For it is into that [sun] that they offer oblations for all the deities.

(5.7.4.3) He who, knowing thus, piles the fire, directly prospers through the deities. (5.7.4.3.e) O glorious Agni, endow this man with glory; bring hither the honor associated with Indra. May he be the supreme head, full of splendor, and the one of highest renown among his peers.

Beholding what is auspicious, the seers who have found the light of heaven sat down in the beginning, performing austerity and consecration; from that, sovereignty, strength, and vigor were born—may the gods bow down before this man.

(5.7.4.3) Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and the Supreme One; (5.7.4.4) furthermore, Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, and Virāj; the Stomas, the Metres, and the Nivids—they have declared this to me: "We bow down together toward this sovereignty."
(5.7.4.4) Turn back toward us; come together to us! May this one be your ruler and teacher. Adhere to his wisdom; all of you, live following after him.
(5.7.4.4) He places these Rāṣṭrabhṛt bricks.
(5.7.4.4) This indeed is the Rāṣṭrabhṛt piling of Agni; by means of it, he bestows royal power upon him.
He indeed becomes the kingdom;
the kingdom does not fall away from him.

(5.7.5.1.a) Just as a son who has been born dies, so indeed does he die whose *ukhya* fire goes out. (5.7.5.1) If he were to produce it by friction, he would cut [the continuity] and generate a rival for himself. That very same fire must be carried around again.
(5.7.5.1) He generates him from his own womb; he does not generate a rival for him.
Indeed, darkness seizes him whose *ukhya* fire goes out.
Death is darkness;
a black garment and a black cow are the sacrificial fee.
By means of darkness itself, one strikes away death, which is darkness.
(5.7.5.2) He gives gold.
(5.7.5.2) Gold, indeed, is light. By means of light itself, he strikes away the darkness.
(5.7.5.2) Now, gold is indeed brilliance; he thus places brilliance within himself. (5.7.5.2.b) As the sun is to the heat, so be it, svāhā!
(5.7.5.2.b) *Suvar* like the sun, *svāhā*!
(5.7.5.2.b) *Suvar* like the bright [light], *svāhā*!
(5.7.5.2.b) *Suvar* like the light, *svāhā*!
(5.7.5.2.b) "Like the sun in the sky, svāhā!
(5.7.5.2) This Agni is indeed the *arka*, and yonder Āditya is the *aśvamedha*.
(5.7.5.3) In that he offers these oblations, he unites the lights of both the *arka* and the *aśvamedha*.
(5.7.5.3) This indeed is the *arkāśvamedha* for whom this is performed in the fire.
(5.7.5.3.c) In the beginning, this world was the waters, the ocean. Prajāpati beheld this first layer; he laid it down, and it became this earth.
Viśvakarman said to him: "I will come to you. He replied:
"There is no world here."
He saw this second layer; he laid it down, and it became the intermediate space.
That Sacrifice said to Prajāpati: "I will come to you."
"There is no world here," he said;
he spoke to Viśvakarman:
"I shall come to you."
"With what will you approach me? he asked.
"With the quarters," he replied.
He approached him with the quarters.
He deposited them;
they became the quarters.
That Parameṣṭhin spoke to Prajāpati.
"I will come to you," he said;
"There is no world here," he replied.
He then spoke to Viśvakarman and to the sacrifice.
"I will come to you," he said;
"There is no world here," they replied.
He then beheld this third layer.
He placed it down;
that became yonder [heaven]; he became the Āditya. He said to Prajāpati:
"I will come to you," he said;
"There is no world here," he replied. He spoke to Viśvakarman and the Sacrifice.
"I shall come unto you," he said; "There is no world here," they replied.
He then spoke to Parameṣṭhin.
"I will come to you," he said. "With what will you approach me? he asked.
"With the *lokampṛṇā* [bricks]," he replied.
He approached it with a *lokampṛṇā* brick;
therefore, the *lokampṛṇā* is of unexhausted vigour (*ayātayāman*),
for yonder sun is indeed of unexhausted vigour.
The seers said to them: "We will approach you. [They asked:
"By what means will you approach us?"
(5.7.5.7) "By means of abundance," they said.
(5.7.5.7) They approached them with two layers;
thus it became five-layered.
He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar becomes greater indeed; he conquers these worlds, and the gods know him.
Moreover, he attains union with these very deities.
(5.7.6.1.a) Agni is indeed vital breath; if one who has built the fire-altar should eat the flesh of birds, he would be eating that very Agni and would meet with misfortune.
(5.7.6.1) He should observe the vow for a year, for the vow does not exceed a year.
This Agni is indeed an animal.
Now, an animal does indeed injure him who approaches it from the front while facing westward.
Therefore, one should approach it from behind while facing eastward, for the sake of one's own non-injury.

(5.7.6.1.c) "Thou art brilliance; grant me brilliance; sustain the earth! (5.7.6.2) "Protect me from the earth! Thou art light; grant me light; sustain the intermediate space; protect me from the intermediate space! Thou art heaven; grant me heaven; sustain the sky; protect me from the sky!
Thus he says, for by these [bricks] indeed these worlds are held apart.
In that he lays them down, it is for the support of these worlds.
Having laid down the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks, he lays down the gold bricks. These worlds are indeed the *svayamātṛṇṇā*s; gold is light.

In that he lays down the gold bricks after laying down the *svayamātṛṇṇā*s, he makes these worlds possessed of light by means of them; moreover, through these very bricks, these worlds shine forth for him.
"O Agni, those splendors of yours which, when the sun has risen, spread across the sky with its rays—by all of those, grant splendor to our people."
O gods, whatever splendors are yours in the sun, whatever splendors are in the cows and in the horses—with all those splendors, O Indra and Agni, and you, Bṛhaspati, bestow splendor upon us.

(5.7.6.3) Bestow radiance upon us! (5.7.6.4) Grant us radiance among the Brāhmaṇas; grant us radiance among the Kṣatriyas; grant us radiance among the Vaiśyas and the Śūdras; bestow radiance upon me with radiance.

(5.7.6.4) The glory and power of one who has piled the fire-altar go in two directions: either to the fire that has been piled or to the sacrificer who has performed the sacrifice. (5.7.6.4) When he offers these oblations, he places glory and power within his very self.
He who, while piling the fire-altar, steps over it, is liable to meet with misfortune.
He should offer an oblation with the verse addressed to Varuṇa: "This I implore of thee, adoring thee with a sacred prayer. This is indeed a pacification of the fire and a protection for oneself.
(5.7.6.5.f) He who piles the fire-altar is indeed the preparer of the oblation.

Just as an oblation spills, so does he spill who, having piled the fire-altar, approaches a woman. He should sacrifice with curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa; thus he attains the state of Mitra and Varuṇa for the sake of not spilling from himself.
(5.7.6.5.g) He who knows the fire-altar as established in the seasons—season after season comes to him in due order, and he stands firm.

Agni is indeed the year. The seasons are his constituent parts: spring is his head, summer his right wing, the rainy season his tail, autumn his left wing, and winter his middle. The bright fortnights are the layers (*citayaḥ*), the dark fortnights the loose soil (*purīṣam*), and the days and nights the bricks. This Agni, who stands in the seasons, belongs to him who knows thus; for him, every season proceeds in its proper order. He who knows this stands firm. Prajāpati, desiring preeminence, established this [altar].
(5.7.6.6) From that, indeed, he attained preeminence.
He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar, attains preeminence.

Whatever has flowed forth from intention, or what has been gathered from the heart or from the mind, or from the eye—follow after that toward the world of the well-done, where the seers are, those who were first-born and ancient.
(5.7.7.1.b) This common dwelling-place I entrust to you, which Jātavedas has brought as a treasure-store. The lord of the sacrifice shall come here to you; recognize him there in the highest heaven.

(5.7.7.1.c) Let him recognize him in the highest heaven; O gods, you who share his dwelling place, know his form! When he has arrived (5.7.7.2) by the paths traveled by the gods, let him make manifest for him the merit of his sacrifices and pious works.
(5.7.7.2ḍ) Move forward together; follow along, proceed! O Agni, prepare the paths that lead to the gods. In this highest gathering-place, may all the gods and the sacrificer sit down together.

With the sacrificial grass-bundle, the enclosing sticks, the offering-ladle, the altar, and the sacred grass—by means of this *ṛc*, carry this sacrifice of ours to the gods so that it may go to the heavenly world.
Whatever has been sacrificed, whatever has been given away, whatever has been bestowed, and whatever sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)—may Agni Vaiśvakarman place all that for us among the gods in heaven.
(5.7.7.3.g) O Agni, with that [power] by which you carry a thousand, by which you carry all-wealth, with that carry this sacrifice of ours to go to the light among the gods.

O Agni, with that [power] by which the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) are joined and the officiating priests carry the sacrifice, with that, carry this sacrifice of ours so that it may go to the light among the gods.
O Agni, by that well-trodden path upon which the streams of honey have flowed, convey this sacrifice of ours to the gods so that it may go to the light of heaven.
Where the streams of honey and of ghee do not fail, there may Agni Vaiśvakarman bestow upon us the heavenly light among the gods.
(5.7.8.1.a) O Agni, those logs of thine, those abodes, those tongues, O Jātavedas, that flame; those ladles of thine, O Agni, those drops—with these do thou, knowing [the way], build up thyself.

(5.7.8.1) This Agni is indeed a sacrifice that has been destroyed. What is done for him, and what is not? Whatever the Adhvaryu passes between while piling the fire, he passes between his own self. (5.7.8.2) "Those logs of thine, O Agni, those abodes," he says; this is indeed Agni’s self-piling. Thus it is Agni himself who piles Agni, and the Adhvaryu does not pass between his own self.

(5.7.8.2) Let the four quarters proceed; may Agni, knowing this, lead our sacrifice. Causing the imperishable ghee to swell for the sake of heroic strength, the sacred word becomes the fuel for the oblations.

(5.7.8.2) This tortoise is indeed laid down for the sake of the heavenly world. "Let the four quarters proceed; let the fires [proceed]," he says. (5.7.8.3) By this, he comes to know the directions. "May he, knowing, lead this sacrifice of ours," he says, for the purpose of leading toward the heavenly world. "The *brahman* becomes the kindling-stick of the oblations," he says. By means of the *brahman*, the gods went to the heavenly world; in that he lays it down with a verse containing the word *brahman*, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world by means of the *brahman*.

This Agni is indeed Prajāpati; his offspring, cattle, and the meters are his form. He should make the bricks of all colors; by means of their very form, he wins offspring, cattle, and the meters. Moreover, having won him for the sake of offspring, cattle, and the meters, he piles him up.

(5.7.9.1.a) In me I first receive Agni for the increase of wealth, for good progeny, and for heroic vigor. In me I place offspring, in me splendor; may we be unharmed in body and possessed of heroic sons.
(5.7.9.1) O Fathers, that immortal Agni who has entered into us mortals within our hearts—him we enclose within ourselves; may he not abandon us and depart.

(5.7.9.1) If the Adhvaryu were to pile the fire-altar without first taking Agni into himself, he would be piling for the sacrificer even that fire which is his own. (5.7.9.2) Indeed, cattle stand around the fire; thus the cattle might be inclined to depart from him. [Therefore] he says, "I first take Agni into myself"; verily, he establishes his own fire within himself, and the cattle do not depart from him.

(5.7.9.2) The exponents of the Veda say: "Since clay and water are not food for Agni, why then is Agni built with clay and water? When he mixes [the clay] with water—(5.7.9.3) water, indeed, is all the deities; verily, by means of the deities he unites him. When he builds with clay—this earth is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara; verily, by means of Agni he builds Agni.

(5.7.9.3) The exponents of the Veda say: "Since the fire-altar is built with clay, water, and fire, why then is it called *agni* (fire)? Because he builds it with the *chandases* (metres), and the *chandases* are indeed fires; therefore it is called *agni*. Moreover, this earth is indeed *agni vaiśvānara*; because he builds it with clay, therefore it is called *agni*. (5.7.9.4) He places gold bricks upon it. Gold is light; verily he bestows light upon it. Moreover, gold is brilliance; verily he bestows brilliance upon himself.

He who piles the fire-altar facing in all directions eats food among all creatures and conquers all the quarters. He places a *gāyatrī* verse in the east, a *triṣṭubh* in the south, a *jagatī* in the west, an *anuṣṭubh* in the north, and a *paṅkti* in the middle. This indeed is the fire-altar facing in all directions; he who, knowing this, piles it, eats food among all creatures and conquers all the quarters. Moreover, he extends quarter after quarter in every direction; therefore, quarter is woven into quarter.
Prajāpati created Agni. Once created, he rushed away from him toward the east; he threw a horse after him.
He turned toward the south; he threw a ram after him.
He turned westward; they threw a bull at him. He turned northward; they threw a goat at him. He ran upward; they threw a man at him.
In that he places the heads of the animals, he piles [the fire-altar] after having secured it from every side.
These animal heads are indeed the breath-supporting, sight-endowed bricks.
In that he places the heads of the animals, by means of them the sacrificer breathes in the yonder world; moreover, by means of them these worlds shine forth for him.
He places them after smearing them with clay for the sake of purity.
This Agni is indeed an animal, and animals are food;
for these heads of the animals are truly this Agni.

(5.7.10.2) If he should desire of someone, "May his food be less," he should place the animal heads closer together for him; his food will indeed become less. (5.7.10.3) If he should desire of someone...
(5.7.10.3) "May his food be equal," [thinking thus], he should place [the bricks] in the middle for him; thus his food becomes equal.

(5.7.10.3) For whomsoever he should desire, "May his food be more abundant," he should place them having pushed them apart at the ends for him; from the very ends he secures food for him, and his food becomes more abundant.
With his two tusks the tortoises, with his jaws the frogs, and with his palate the water-snakes he shall devour.
(5.7.11.1) [He offers] vigor with *saṃsūda*;
(5.7.11.1) the forest with *jāmbīla*;
(5.7.11.1) clay with the *barsva* reeds.
(5.7.11.1) [He covers] the Avakā plant with pebbles; (5.7.11.1) the pebble with Avakā plants;
[he covers] the tongue with the Utsādana.
(5.7.11.1) One should worship Avakranda with the palate;
(5.7.11.1) one should worship Sarasvatī with the tip of the tongue.
(5.7.12.1) Strength with the jaws,
(5.7.12.1) water with the mouth,
(5.7.12.1) and the Ādityas with the beard.
(5.7.12.1) The *upayāma* with the lower lip, the *sada* with the upper lip;
between them, the *anūkāśa*.
The external [world] with light;
the thundering with the *nirbādha* bricks;
the sun and fire with the two eyes.
(5.7.12.1) He [places] lightning with the two *kanānaka* [bones], (5.7.12.1) the thunderbolt with the brain,
(5.7.12.1) and strength with the marrow.
(5.7.13.1) One should [offer] tortoises with the hooves;
(5.7.13.1) francolins with the bones of the feet;
(5.7.13.1) and the *sāman* with the knuckles.
Speed with the shanks;
freedom from disease with the knees; vigor with the hollows of the thighs.
Fright from the two forefeet;
the cave from the two flanks; the Aśvins from the two shoulders.
Aditi with the head,
Nirṛti with the headless head.
The thong with the vultures;
the yoke with the *ānata* [vessels];
the mind with the *manyā* [vessels].
With the *saṃkrośa* chants he [covers] the vital breaths;
with the *prakāśa* chant, the skin; with the *parākāśa* chant, what is within.
(5.7.14.1) Maśakas with the hair;
(5.7.14.1) Indra with the well-performing vehicle;
(5.7.14.1) Bṛhaspati with the sitting on dung.
(5.7.14.1) The chariot with the *uṣṇih* verses.
Mitra and Varuṇa [are assigned] to the two hips;
Indra and Agni to the two buttocks;
Indra and Bṛhaspati to the two thighs.
(5.7.15.1) Indra and Viṣṇu with the two knee-caps;
(5.7.15.1) Savitṛ with the tail;
(5.7.15.1) the Gandharvas with the penis.
(5.7.15.1) The Apsarases with the testicles;
(5.7.15.1) Pavamāna with the anus;
(5.7.15.1) the filter with the two *potrā* vessels.
Advancing with the two thighs,
retreating with the two knees.
The breast belongs to Indra;
the belly belongs to Aditi;
the collarbones belong to the quarters.
The clouds with the two heart-coverings,
the intermediate space with the pericardium,
and the sky with the belly.
Indrāṇī with the spleen,
the anthills with the lungs, and the mountains with the entrails.
The ocean with his belly,
Vaiśvānara with his ashes.
The rectum belongs to Pūṣan; the thick entrails belong to Andhāhi;
[one offers] to the serpents with the entrails.
The seasons by the ribs;
the sky by the back;
the first rib-bone belongs to the Vasus.
The second [verse] belongs to the Rudras;
the third to the Ādityas;
the fourth to the Aṅgirases.
The fifth [verse] belongs to the Sādhyas;
the sixth belongs to the Viśvedevas.
(5.7.18.1) Might with the neck-bones; (5.7.18.1) Nirṛti with the bones;
(5.7.18.1) Indra with the well-fashioned vehicle.
The unshakable shoulder of Rudra;
the second [shoulder] of day and night;
the third of the half-months.
It is the fourth of the months;
it is the fifth of the seasons;
it is the sixth of the year.
Bliss with the word *nandathu*; desire with the two words beginning with *prati* and *āsā*; fear with the two words beginning with *śiti*.
(5.7.19.1) The two commands with the two commands;
(5.7.19.1) the sun and the moon with the two kidneys;
(5.7.19.1) the dark and the brindled with the two kidneys.
(5.7.19.1) [He wins] the dawning by means of form, (5.7.19.1) and the setting by means of non-form.
Day with flesh,
night with fat,
and the waters with broth.
(5.7.20.1) [He strikes] the ghee with the juice, (5.7.20.1) the dark [part] with the fat,
and the *hrāduni* with the *dūṣīkā*.
With tears [he sprinkles] the earth;
with form, the sky;
with his reflection, the stars.
(5.7.20.1) [I cover] the earth with hide, the skin with skin.
(5.7.20.1) Svāhā to the one brought near!
Hail to the one being immolated!
Hail to the one offered as a sacrifice!
The first rib belongs to Agni; the second rib belongs to Sarasvatī; the third belongs to Soma.
The fourth belongs to the waters;
the fifth belongs to the plants;
the sixth belongs to the year.
The seventh belongs to the Maruts; the eighth belongs to Bṛhaspati; the ninth belongs to Mitra.
The tenth belongs to Varuṇa;
the eleventh to Indra;
the twelfth to the Viśvedevas.
The side of heaven and earth;
the rib of Yama.
The primary wing belongs to Vāyu;
the secondary wing belongs to Sarasvant;
the third belongs to Candramas.
The fourth belongs to the Nakṣatras;
the fifth to Savitṛ; the sixth to Rudra.
The seventh belongs to the serpents;
the eighth to Aryaman; the ninth to Tvaṣṭṛ; the tenth to Dhātṛ.
The eleventh belongs to Indrāṇī;
the twelfth belongs to Aditi;
the side belongs to Heaven and Earth.
(5.7.22.1) A wooden bowl for Yami.
The path with the two *anūvṛc* [muscles],
continuity with the two *snāvanī* [veins],
and the *śuka*s with the bile.
The jaundice with the liver,
the halīkṣṇas with the evil wind,
and the kūśmas with the śakas.
(5.7.23.1) [He should offer] to the Śvartas with the undigested contents of the stomach, to the dogs with the entrails, and to the serpents with the smell of blood.
The birds [are attracted] by the smell of cooked food;
the ants, by the sacrificial remains.
With all strides, the steed has stepped across, in harmony with all the gods worthy of sacrifice.
May he lead us to the world of the well-done; may we rejoice in that [world] of yours through the offering of food.
Heaven is your back, the earth your seat, and the intermediate space your soul.
The ocean is your womb;
the sun is your eye;
the wind is your breath.
The moon is the ear;
the months and half-months are the joints;
the seasons are the limbs.
The year is the greatness.
Agni was the sacrificial animal; with him they sacrificed;
he won this world in which Agni dwells.
(5.7.26.1) That is your world; you shall conquer it.
Now, smell this.
Vāyu was the sacrificial animal; with it they sacrificed;
he won this world in which Vāyu dwells.
(5.7.26.1) That is your world; therefore, I shall enter within you if you do not smell me.
(5.7.26.1) The sun was the sacrificial animal.
With that they sacrificed;
he won this world in which the sun is situated;
that is your world.
You will conquer him if you smell him.
(6.1.1.1) He constructs the hall with the beams facing east.
(6.1.1.1) Gods and men divided the quarters among themselves:
the gods [took] the eastern quarter, the ancestors the southern, men the western, and the Rudras the northern.
In that he makes the hall with the beams facing east, the sacrificer thereby approaches the world of the gods.
He encloses it; for the world of the gods is indeed separated from the world of men.
(6.1.1.1) "One should not, as it were, depart from this world," they say.
(6.1.1.1) "For who knows whether one exists in that world or not?
(6.1.1.1) He makes the openings wide.
(6.1.1.2) For the conquest of both worlds,
he shaves his hair and beard and trims his nails.
(6.1.1.2) For that which is the hair and beard is indeed dead skin, impure.
(6.1.1.2) Having cast off the dead, impure skin, he becomes fit for sacrifice and approaches the sacrificial essence (*medha*).
(6.1.1.2) When the Aṅgirases were going to the heavenly world, they caused consecration (*dīkṣā*) and austerity (*tapas*) to enter into the waters.
(6.1.1.2) He bathes in the waters.
(6.1.1.2) Verily, he directly obtains consecration and austerity;
(6.1.1.2) he bathes at a sacred ford,
for they caused him to enter it at a sacred ford.
(6.1.1.2) He bathes at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*). (6.1.1.3) Thus he becomes a ford for his equals. (6.1.1.3) He drinks water;
thus he becomes pure within.
(6.1.1.3) He initiates him with a garment. (6.1.1.3) Linen indeed belongs to Soma by deity;
he who undergoes initiation approaches Soma as his deity.
"You are the body of Soma; protect my body," he says.
Thus he approaches his own deity;
moreover, he invokes this very blessing.
(6.1.1.3) The binding of the tuṣa-grass belongs to Agni;
(6.1.1.3) the air-holes belong to Vāyu; (6.1.1.3) the girdle belongs to the Pitṛs.
(6.1.1.3) The striking down of the plants; (6.1.1.4) the eastward-stretching of the Ādityas,
the warp of the Viśvedevas,
and the openings of the constellations.
(6.1.1.4) Now, this garment indeed belongs to all the deities.
In that he consecrates him with a garment, he consecrates him with all the deities.
Man, indeed, has his vital breaths outside [the body].
(6.1.1.4) Its eating is the vital breath.
(6.1.1.4) He eats; thus, possessing the vital breath, he undergoes consecration. (6.1.1.4) He becomes one who has eaten.
(6.1.1.4) To whatever extent his vital breath extends, with that he approaches the sacrificial essence.
(6.1.1.4) Clarified butter belongs to the gods; the whey belongs to the ancestors.
(6.1.1.4) It is fully matured for human beings.
(6.1.1.4–5) Indeed, this fresh butter belongs to all the deities;
when one anoints oneself with fresh butter, one gratifies all the deities.

(6.1.1.5) He who is consecrated has indeed departed from this world and has not yet arrived at the world of the gods; fresh butter is, as it were, in between. Therefore, he anoints himself with fresh butter.
(6.1.1.5) In the natural order;
(6.1.1.5) with a sacrificial formula (yajuḥ),
for the sake of distinction.
Indra slew Vṛtra;
his eye-pupil flew away,
and that became collyrium.
When he anoints his eyes, he appropriates the very sight of his rival; he anoints the right eye first.
(6.1.1.6) For men first anoint the left [hand];
(6.1.1.6) he does not rub it down; (6.1.1.6) for men do not run away as it were.
He anoints five times;
the *paṅkti* consists of five syllables; the sacrifice is fivefold.
(6.1.1.6) He indeed wins the sacrifice; (6.1.1.6) he anoints a measured amount,
for men anoint an unmeasured amount.
(6.1.1.6) He anoints with the tuft. (6.1.1.6) For humans anoint with what is without the tuft;
it is for the sake of distinction.
If he were to anoint with a tuftless [grass], it would be like a thunderbolt;
he anoints with a tufted [grass] for the sake of friendship.
Indra slew Vṛtra.
He died upon the waters.
Whatever in them was pure, fit for sacrifice, and possessed of the gods, that went forth from them.

(6.1.1.7) They became *darbha* grass. In that he purifies him with bunches of *darbha* grass, he purifies him with those very waters which are pure, fit for sacrifice, and accompanied by the gods. He purifies him with two [verses].
(6.1.1.7) By means of day and night alone he purifies him; (6.1.1.7) he purifies him with three [verses];
(6.1.1.7) for these worlds are three.
(6.1.1.7) By means of these very worlds he purifies him; (6.1.1.8) with five [verses] he purifies.
The *paṅkti* consists of five syllables.
The sacrifice is fivefold;
he purifies him for the sake of the sacrifice. He purifies him with six [verses].
(6.1.1.8) There are six seasons;
(6.1.1.8) verily by means of the seasons he purifies him; (6.1.1.8) he purifies with seven [verses].
(6.1.1.8) There are seven meters; (6.1.1.8) by means of the meters he purifies him; (6.1.1.8) he purifies him with nine.
There are indeed nine vital breaths in a person; he thus purifies him along with his vital breath. He purifies him with twenty-one [verses].
(6.1.1.8) There are ten fingers on the hand and ten toes on the feet; the self is the twenty-first.
(6.1.1.8–9) As great as man is, him he purifies entirely.
(6.1.1.9) "May the Lord of Thought purify thee," he says.
The mind, indeed, is the Lord of Thought.
By means of the mind itself he purifies him. "May the Lord of Speech purify you," he says.
(6.1.1.9) By means of speech itself he purifies him.
(6.1.1.9) "May the god Savitṛ purify you," he says;
(6.1.1.9) thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he purifies him.
"O Lord of the Purifier, with thy purifier, may I be able to accomplish that for which I purify myself"—thus he says;
verily, he invokes this very blessing.
(6.1.2.1) As many gods as purified themselves for the sacrifice, they indeed became [successful].
He who, knowing thus, purifies himself for the sacrifice, certainly becomes [successful]. Having purified [the Soma] outside, he causes it to enter within.
(6.1.2.1) Having purified him in the world of men, he leads him, thus purified, forward to the world of the gods.
