(6.1.2.1) "One who is not initiated [is purified] by a single oblation," they say;
he offers four with the *sruva* spoon for the sake of initiation, and the fifth with the *sruc* ladle.
The *paṅkti* consists of five syllables; the sacrifice is fivefold.
Verily, he wins the sacrifice itself.
(6.1.2.1) "To intention, to impulse, to Agni, svāhā! he says.
(6.1.2.2) For by means of intention a man impels himself toward sacrifice, thinking, "May I sacrifice."
"To Medhā, to Manas, to Agni, svāhā! he says;
for by means of wisdom and the mind, a person approaches the sacrifice.
"To Sarasvatī, to Pūṣan, to Agni, svāhā! he says.
Sarasvatī is indeed speech, and Pūṣan is the earth.
By means of speech and by means of the earth, he sets the sacrifice in motion.
"O divine waters, vast, bringing welfare to all," he says.

(6.1.2.2) Those waters which belong to the rain—(6.1.2.3) "The divine, vast waters, the source of all well-being. If he were not to recite this sacrificial formula (*yajus*), the unappeased celestial waters might come to this world.
Therefore, he says: "The divine, vast waters, the source of all well-being."
He pacifies them for this very world;
therefore, being pacified, they come to this world. "O Heaven and Earth," he says.
For the sacrifice belongs to heaven and earth;
he says, "The wide atmosphere," for the sacrifice indeed resides in the atmosphere.
"May Bṛhaspati increase us with the oblation," he says. Bṛhaspati is indeed the sacred power (*brahman*) of the gods; by means of that very sacred power, he secures the sacrifice for him.
(6.1.2.4) If he were to say "vidheḥ" (by the injunction), he would strike against the sacrificial post.
(6.1.2.4) He says "vṛdhātu" (let it grow); thus he avoids the sacrificial post.
Prajāpati created the sacrifice. Once created, it went away from him.
It collapsed the *yajus* and collapsed the *sāman*.
The *ṛc* lifted it up. Because the *ṛc* lifted it up, that is the reason for the name "lifting" (*audgrahaṇa*) of the *audgrahaṇa*.
One offers with the *ṛc* for the sake of lifting up the sacrifice.
(6.1.2.5) "The Anuṣṭubh raised up the meters," they say;
therefore one offers with the Anuṣṭubh for the raising of the sacrifice.
(6.1.2.5) "They raised up twelve Vātsabandha verses," so they say;
therefore, those who know the Vātsabandhas dedicate themselves with twelve [verses].
This very *ṛc* is an *anuṣṭubh*.
Speech is the *anuṣṭubh*.
When he consecrates him with this verse, he consecrates him with speech in its entirety.
He says, "Of every god who leads," [which is] the verse addressed to Savitṛ.
(6.1.2.5) "May a mortal choose friendship," he says; this [verse] has the fathers as its deity.
(6.1.2.6) "May you seek all riches," he says; this [verse] has the Viśvedevas as its deity.
(6.1.2.6) "May you choose glory, O nourisher," he says; this [verse] has Pūṣan as its deity.
(6.1.2.6) This ṛc, indeed, belongs to all the deities;
when he consecrates [the sacrificer] with this ṛc, he consecrates him with all the deities.
The first foot has seven syllables; the other three have eight syllables each.
(6.1.2.6) Those which are three, they become eight;
(6.1.2.6) those which are four, they become eight.
(6.1.2.7) Because it consists of eight syllables, it is the Gāyatrī.
In that it has eleven syllables, it is the *triṣṭubh*;
in that it has twelve syllables, it is the *jagatī*. Thus, this very *ṛc* contains all the meters. When he consecrates [the sacrificer] with this *ṛc*, he consecrates him with all the meters.
(6.1.2.7) The first foot has seven syllables;
(6.1.2.7) the *śakvarī* consists of seven feet;
(6.1.2.7) cattle are the *śakvarī*.
Verily, he wins cattle.
The first foot is deficient by one syllable;
therefore, men subsist upon that which is deficient in speech.
(6.1.2.7) He offers with a full [ladle];
for Prajāpati is, as it were, full;
[he does so] for the attainment of Prajāpati.
(6.1.2.7) He offers with a deficient [oblation]; for from the deficient Prajāpati created offspring; it is for the creation of offspring.
(6.1.3.1) The *Ṛk* and the *Sāman*, not remaining with the gods for the sacrifice, departed and stood apart, having assumed the form of a black antelope.
(6.1.3.1) They thought, "Whomever these two shall approach, he will become this [world]. They invited them; having set aside the greatness of day and night, they approached the gods.
(6.1.3.1) This indeed is the color of the *ṛc*, namely that which is white in the black antelope skin;
this is that of the *sāman*, namely that which is black.
"You two are the artistic forms (*śilpa*) of the *ṛc* and the *sāman*," he says.
(6.1.3.1) Verily, he wins the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman*.

(6.1.3.2) That which is white on the black antelope skin is the color of the day; that which is black is the color of the night. Whatever of these two is inherent therein, that very thing he wins by means of the black antelope skin.
He consecrates him with the black antelope skin; for the black antelope skin is the form of the *Brahman*. Verily, by means of the *Brahman*, he consecrates him.
"O God, [teach] this thought to one who is training," he says; this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula (*yajus*).
The consecrated one (*dīkṣita*) is indeed an embryo; he wraps himself in a garment as a caul (*ulba*). Therefore, embryos are born covered.
He should not uncover himself before the purchase of the Soma. If he were to uncover himself before the purchase of the Soma, the embryos of his progeny would be liable to fall away.

(6.1.3.3) When the Soma has been purchased, he uncovers [his head]; for it is as if he is born anew, and it is just as when one uncovers [the head] for a superior person. (6.1.3.3) When the Aṅgirases were going to the heavenly world, they divided their vital strength (*ūrj*); what remained over became reeds (*śara*). Reeds are indeed vital strength; in that the girdle (*mekhalā*) is made of reeds, he wins vital strength for himself.
He ties it on at the middle; verily, he bestows vital strength upon him in the middle; therefore, people enjoy vital strength from the middle.

(6.1.3.4) Indeed, that part of a man which is above the navel is pure (*medhya*), while that which is below is impure (*amedhya*). In that he girds [the sacrificer] at the middle, he separates his pure part from his impure part.

(6.1.3.4–5) Indra hurled the thunderbolt (*vajra*) at Vṛtra; it split into three parts: one third became the wooden sword (*sphya*), one third the chariot, and one third the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Those arrow-shafts (*śara*) which were shattered within became arrows; that is the reason for the name "arrow" (*śara*).

The arrows are indeed a thunderbolt, and hunger is truly the enemy of man. In that the girdle is made of reeds, he strikes away the enemy of hunger from the very middle by means of the thunderbolt itself.
It is threefold; for the breath is threefold. Thus he places the threefold breath in the middle of the sacrificer.
It is broad, for the sake of distinguishing it from ordinary ropes.
(6.1.3.5) He consecrates the sacrificer with a girdle and the wife with a yoke-thong for the sake of forming a couple.
(6.1.3.6) The sacrifice longed for the sacrificial fee. (6.1.3.6) He united with her. (6.1.3.6) Indra perceived that.
He thought, "Whoever shall be born from this shall become this world.
He entered her,
and from her Indra himself was born.
He thought, "Whoever else shall be born from me after this, he shall be this [world]. Having reflected upon her, he tore open her womb.
She became a barren mare;
that was the birth of the barren mare.
(6.1.3.7) He wound it around his hand; (6.1.3.7) he deposited it among the wild animals;
it became the black antelope horn.
(6.1.3.7) "Thou art the womb of Indra; do not harm me," he says as he hands over the black antelope horn.
Thus he makes the sacrifice have its own womb, the sacrificial fee have its own womb, and Indra have his own womb, for the sake of having a common womb.
"For tillage thee, for good crops," he says; therefore plants ripen even without being ploughed.
He says, "For you, from the plants with good fruit"; therefore, the plants bear fruit.
If he were to scratch himself with his hand, his offspring would be prone to scabies; if he were to smile, they would be prone to nakedness.
He scratches himself with a black antelope horn and smiles while covering [his mouth], for the protection of his offspring.

(6.1.3.8) He should not cast down the horn of the black antelope before the sacrificial gifts have been led forth; for if he were to cast down the horn of the black antelope before the sacrificial gifts have been led forth, the womb of creatures would be liable to fall away.

(6.1.3.8) When the sacrificial gifts have been led forth, he throws the horn of the black antelope into the *cātvāla* pit. The *cātvāla* is indeed the womb of the sacrifice, and the horn of the black antelope is the womb; thus he places the womb within the womb, so that the sacrifice may possess its proper womb.

(6.1.4.1) Speech indeed departed from the gods, refusing to remain for the sacrifice; it entered the trees. This is that speech which speaks in the trees—that which is in the drum, that which is in the flute, and that which is in the lute.
When he gives the consecration-staff, he wins speech itself.
It is made of Udumbara wood; the Udumbara is strength, so he wins strength itself.

(6.1.4.1) It is measured by the mouth; verily, he bestows strength upon him from the very mouth. Therefore, they enjoy strength from the mouth. (6.1.4.2) When the Soma has been purchased, he hands the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa. For the Maitrāvaruṇa distributes speech among the priests beforehand; the priests establish that speech in the sacrificer. (6.1.4.2) "Svāhā! To the sacrifice, with the mind! he says, for by means of the mind a man approaches the sacrifice.
(6.1.4.2) "Svāhā! To Heaven and Earth! he says, for the sacrifice belongs to Heaven and Earth.

(6.1.4.2) “Svāhā from the wide atmosphere! he says, for the sacrifice is indeed in the atmosphere. “Svāhā! I take hold of the sacrifice from the wind,” he says; this one who blows is indeed the sacrifice; thus he takes hold of it directly.
(6.1.4.3) He closes his fists and restrains his speech for the support of the sacrifice.
“This Brahmin has been consecrated,” he says three times in a whisper; he thus announces him to the gods. Three times aloud; he thus announces him to both the gods and men.
(6.1.4.3) One should not release speech before the stars appear.
(6.1.4.3) If one were to release speech before the stars appear, one would cut asunder the sacrifice.

When the stars have risen, he releases his speech with the words, “Prepare the vow. For the consecrated one is under the vow of the sacrifice; thus he releases his speech for the sake of the sacrifice itself.
If he should release it [prematurely], he should recite a verse addressed to Viṣṇu; for Viṣṇu is the sacrifice, and by means of the sacrifice he thereby extends the sacrifice.
He says, “We meditate upon the divine thought”; thereby he softens the sacrifice.
"May our will be easy to cross," he says; verily, he wins the dawning.
The exponents of Brahman say:
"Should one offer oblations in the house of the consecrated, or should one not offer?

For the consecrated is indeed the sacrificial food (*havir*); if he were to offer, he would offer having taken a portion from the sacrificer; if he were not to offer, he would exclude a limb of the sacrifice. He says: "O gods born of the mind, yoked by the mind..."
The breaths are indeed the gods born of mind, yoked by mind; it is into them that he offers in secret. That is neither offered nor unoffered.
(6.1.4.5) Indeed, while the consecrated one is sleeping, the Rakṣases seek to slay him; [but] Agni [protects him].
(6.1.4.6) "O Agni, slayer of demons, do thou indeed keep watch well; may we be well refreshed," he says; having thus made Agni his guardian, he sleeps for the sake of driving away the *rakṣases*.

(6.1.4.6) He who, being consecrated, sleeps, acts as it were contrary to his vow. "Thou, O Agni, art the protector of vows," he says; Agni is indeed the lord of vows among the gods; he (Agni) causes him to take hold of the vow once again.
"The god has come among mortals," he says;
for being a god, he is indeed among mortals.
"You are to be praised at the sacrifices," he says; for they indeed praise him at the sacrifices.
(6.1.4.7) Indeed, from the consecrated one who has slept, the vital power (*indriya*) and the deities depart.
(6.1.4.7) "The All-Gods have turned toward me," he says. By means of that very vital power and by means of those deities, he brings him back into harmony.

(6.1.4.7) If he were not to recite this *yajus*, as many cattle as he consecrates himself for would be his cattle. "O Soma, grant me so much! (6.1.4.8) he says; "Grant me more! he says; thus he wins unlimited cattle.
(6.1.4.8) "Be for my enjoyment in the moon," he says;
thus he receives them according to their respective deities.

(6.1.4.8) “For Vāyu thee! For Varuṇa thee!”—if he were not to assign these in this manner, he would cause the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) to go to those who are not the proper deities; he would be cut off from the deities. (6.1.4.8) In that he assigns them in this manner, he causes the sacrificial gifts to go to the respective deities; he is not cut off from the deities.
(6.1.4.9) “O divine waters, O offspring of the waters,” he says.
"Whatever of yours is pure, worthy of sacrifice, and divine—that may I not step upon," with these words he indeed says this.
"May I follow the unbroken thread of the earth," he says; having thus made a bridge, he passes over.
(6.1.5.1) The gods, having settled upon the place of sacrifice, did not know the directions. They ran to one another, saying, "By you let us discern it; by you!
They agreed upon Aditi, saying, "By you let us discern it. She said, "I shall choose a boon: let my departures be your sacrifices, and my arrivals be your sacrifices."
Therefore, the Āditya [offering] is the introductory rite of sacrifices, and the Āditya is the concluding rite.
He sacrifices to five deities; [this is] for the discernment of the five directions.
Moreover, the *paṅkti* consists of five syllables; the sacrifice is fivefold; verily, he wins the sacrifice itself.
They sacrificed to Pathyā Svasti; by her they discerned the eastern direction: by Agni the southern, by Soma the western, by Savitṛ the northern, and by Aditi the upward direction.
He sacrifices to Pathyā Svasti; by her he discerns the eastern direction.
Having sacrificed to Pathyā Svasti, he sacrifices to Agni and Soma; for these two, Agni and Soma, are the eyes of the sacrifice, and through them he beholds [the sacrifice] accordingly.
(6.1.5.3) Having sacrificed to Agni and Soma, he sacrifices to Savitṛ; verily, impelled by Savitṛ, he looks upon [the world] in due order.
(6.1.5.3) Having sacrificed to Savitṛ, he sacrifices to Aditi; Aditi is indeed this earth; verily, on this very foundation he looks upon [the world] in due order.
(6.1.5.3) Having sacrificed to Aditi, he recites a verse addressed to the Maruts for the successful ordering of the people.
(6.1.5.3) The exponents of the Veda say:

"The Prāyaṇīya [offering] should be performed with the Prayājas but without the Anuyājas; the Udayanīya [should be performed] with the Anuyājas but without the Prayājas. (6.1.5.4) These indeed are the Prayājas, and those are the Anuyājas; this is the continuity of the sacrifice.

(6.1.5.4) That should not be done in that way. The *prayāja* offerings are indeed the self, and the *anūyāja* offerings are offspring. If one were to omit the *prayāja* offerings, one would omit the self; if one were to omit the *anūyāja* offerings, one would omit offspring. For whatever part of the extended sacrifice is not performed, the sacrifice perishes accordingly.
(6.1.5.4) Following the perishing sacrifice, the sacrificer himself perishes.

The *prāyaṇīya* [offering] should be performed with the *prayāja*s and the *anūyāja*s; the *udayanīya* should be performed with the *prayāja*s and the *anūyāja*s. He does not exclude himself, nor his offspring, nor the sacrifice; the sacrifice does not perish, nor the sacrificer.
He pours out the scrapings of the *prāyaṇīya* over the *udayanīya*; that indeed is the continuity of the sacrifice.
If he were to use those which are the *yājyā*s of the *prāyaṇīya* as the *yājyā*s of the *udayanīya*, he would ascend to yonder world face-ward and would be liable to die prematurely.

(6.1.5.5) He makes those which are the invitatory verses (*puro'nuvākyā*) of the introductory offering (*prāyaṇīya*) the offering verses (*yājyā*) of the concluding offering (*udayanīya*); thus he establishes himself in this very world.
(6.1.6.1) Kadrū and Suparṇī indeed vied with each other over their own forms. (6.1.6.1) Kadrū defeated Suparṇī.
(6.1.6.1) She said:
"In the third heaven from here is Soma; bring him down, and with him ransom yourself.
This earth, indeed, is Kadrū; yonder sky is Suparṇī; and the meters are the daughters of Suparṇī.
She said:
"Indeed, parents support their sons; Soma is in the third heaven from here—bring him down! With him, ransom yourself! "So Kadrū spoke to me," [she replied].
Thereupon the Jagatī flew up, being composed of fourteen syllables.
(6.1.6.2) Having failed to reach it, she turned back.
(6.1.6.2) Of her, two syllables were lost.
(6.1.6.2) She returned with the sacrificial animals and the consecration.

Therefore, among the meters, the *jagatī* is most conducive to cattle; therefore, the consecration (*dīkṣā*) inclines toward one who possesses cattle. The *triṣṭubh*, being composed of thirteen syllables, flew upward.
(6.1.6.2) Having failed to reach it, she turned back.
(6.1.6.2) Two of her syllables were lost.
(6.1.6.3) She returned with the sacrificial gifts and through austerity.
(6.1.6.3) Therefore, at the midday pressing in the world of the Triṣṭubh, the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) are led forth.
(6.1.6.3) "This indeed is austerity," they say, "that one gives away one's own property.
(6.1.6.3) The Gāyatrī flew up, being four syllables short of its full form, together with the light.
He secured it for her by means of goats;
that is the reason for the goat's name (*aja*).
She brought back the Soma and four syllables.
(6.1.6.3) She became possessed of eight syllables.
(6.1.6.3) The exponents of Brahman say:
(6.1.6.4) "For what reason does the *gāyatrī*, being the smallest of the meters (*chandas*), encompass the mouth of the sacrifice?
(6.1.6.4) "Because it brought that Soma here, therefore it encompassed the mouth of the sacrifice; therefore it is the most brilliant."
(6.1.6.4) With his two feet he gathered two pressings, and with his mouth one.
(6.1.6.4) That which he gathered with his mouth, he sucked;
therefore two pressings contain *śukra* [pure soma], namely the morning pressing and the midday pressing.
Therefore, at the third pressing, they press out the *ṛjīṣa*;
for they regard it as if it were already milked. He pours in the *āśir* mixture for the sake of its brilliance; thus he also gathers it together.
While that Soma was being brought forward, the Gandharva Viśvāvasu stole it away.
(6.1.6.5) He remained for three nights as one whose property had been stolen.
(6.1.6.5) Therefore, the purchased Soma remains for three nights.
Those gods said:
"The Gandharvas are indeed desirous of women; let us ransom [the Soma] with a woman," they said.
They made Speech into a one-year-old female and ransomed it with her.
Having assumed the form of a red deer, she departed from the Gandharvas and stood aside.
(6.1.6.6) That was Rohita’s birth.
(6.1.6.6) Those gods said, "He has stepped away from us; he does not turn back toward us. Let us call him back!"
(6.1.6.6) The Gandharvas spoke the *brahman*, the gods sang.
(6.1.6.6) She turned toward the gods as they were singing.
(6.1.6.6) Therefore, women desire a man who sings.
(6.1.6.6) Women desire him who knows this; moreover, even when he is among those who are to be wooed, they give to him, even when there are many suitors.
(6.1.6.7) He purchases [the Soma] with a one-year-old cow;
verily, he purchases it with speech itself in its entirety.
Therefore, human beings speak speech at the age of one year.
He purchases [the Soma] with a cow that is not crippled, not deaf, not lame, not maimed, and not seven-hoofed;
he purchases it with one that is entirely whole.
(6.1.6.7) If he were to purchase [the cow] with a white one, the sacrificer would suffer from skin disease;
(6.1.6.7) if it were a black one, she would be a cow for immolation, and the sacrificer would be liable to die prematurely.
(6.1.6.7) If the cow used for the purchase were two-colored,
he would either defeat another, or another would defeat him.
(6.1.6.7) He purchases [the Soma] with a ruddy, yellow-eyed cow.
(6.1.6.7) This, indeed, is the form of Soma;
he purchases him with his own deity.
That became gold;
therefore, they purify gold from the waters. Thus say the exponents of the Veda.
(6.1.7.1) "From what truth do offspring, though conceived boneless, come to be born with bones?
(6.1.7.1) Because he offers gold, having placed it in ghee, therefore offspring, though conceived boneless, come to be born with bones.
Ghee is indeed the beloved abode of Agni, and gold is his splendor.
“This is your bright body, this is your luster,” he says;
thus he makes him possessed of splendor and possessed of a body. Moreover, he truly gathers him together.
If he were to set it down unfastened, the embryos of his offspring would be liable to fall away.
He sets it down fastened for the support of the embryos;
he ties it with a *niṣṭarkya* cord.
(6.1.7.2) For the procreation of offspring.
(6.1.7.2) This cow that purchases the Soma is indeed Speech; thus he says, "Thou art swift."
"For what one hastens toward with the mind, that one speaks with speech. "It is held by the mind," he says;
for speech is indeed held by the mind.
"Delightful to Viṣṇu," he says.
“Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice.
Thus he makes her pleasing for the sake of the sacrifice.
“In the impulse of you, whose impulse is true,” he says.
(6.1.7.3) Verily, he wins speech impelled by Savitṛ.

(6.1.7.3) Indeed, as each section of the sacrifice is being performed, the Rakṣases seek to destroy the sacrifice. This path, indeed, is not struck down by the Rakṣases: the path of Agni and of Sūrya.
"I have mounted the eye of the sun, the pupil of the eye of Agni," he says;
he thus ascends that very path which is not struck by the Rakṣases.
This cow for purchasing Soma is indeed Speech.
"You are consciousness, you are mind," he says; he thus instructs her, and therefore instructed offspring are born.
"Thou art consciousness," he says;
for what one perceives with the mind, that one speaks with speech.
"Thou art the mind," he says.
"For what one approaches with the mind, that one performs. He says, "Thou art intelligence," for what one meditates upon with the mind, that one speaks with speech.
"Thou art the sacrificial fee," he says;
for she is indeed the sacrificial fee.
"Thou art worthy of sacrifice," he says.
(6.1.7.5) He thus makes it worthy of sacrifice.
(6.1.7.5) "Thou art a Kṣatriyā," he says; for she is indeed a Kṣatriyā.
"You are Aditi, double-headed," he says.
Since the Āditya [cup] is the introductory rite of sacrifices and the Āditya [cup] is the concluding rite, therefore he speaks thus.
If it were not bound, it would be unextended.
(6.1.7.5) If the Anustaraṇī cow were bound by a foot,
the sacrificer would be liable to die prematurely.
(6.1.7.6) If the verse addressed to Vṛtra-slayer were one held by the ear,
he would either defeat another, or another would defeat him.
(6.1.7.6) "May Mitra bind you by the foot," he says.
Mitra is indeed the auspicious one among the gods;
with him he binds her by the foot.
"May Pūṣan protect the paths," he says.
(6.1.7.6) This earth, indeed, is Pūṣan.
(6.1.7.6) He has made this very [earth] her guardian.
(6.1.7.6) For the sake of complete attainment.
"To Indra, the overseer," he says;
verily, he makes Indra the overseer of this [earth].
"May your mother permit you, may your father permit you," he says;
thus he purchases her with their permission. "Go, O goddess, to the god," he says.
(6.1.7.7) For she is a goddess and Soma is a god.
(6.1.7.7) "Soma for Indra," he says;
(6.1.7.7) for Soma is brought for Indra.
(6.1.7.7) If he were not to recite this *yajus*, the cow for purchasing Soma would simply turn back.
(6.1.7.7) He says, "May Rudra turn you back," for Rudra is indeed the fierce one among the gods. (6.1.7.8) [He is] of the gods.
(6.1.7.8) He places that very [name] for her beyond, for the sake of turning back.
(6.1.7.8) Verily, he does something harsh when he recites [the name] of Rudra;
therefore he says, "On the path of Mitra."
(6.1.7.8) For the sake of pacification:
(6.1.7.8) He who purchases [Soma] with a female goat purchases it by means of speech;
therefore he says, "O Soma, come back again in safety, together with wealth and as a friend."
Having sold speech by means of speech itself, he places speech back within himself;
his speech becomes non-exhausting for one who knows thus.
He steps down six steps;
for six days one does not speak beyond [the prescribed limit]. Moreover, during the course of the year, he secures as much speech as there is.
He offers at the seventh step;
the *śakvarī* consists of seven steps;
cattle are the *śakvarī*.
Verily, he wins cattle;
there are seven domestic animals, seven wild animals, and seven meters—
for the attainment of both.
"You are a Vasu; you are a Rudra," he says. He thus proclaims her form and her majesty.
"May Bṛhaspati cause you to rejoice in happiness," he says.
Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman among the gods.
By means of the Brahman, he wins cattle for him. "May Rudra take heed with the Vasus," he says.
"For the sake of turning back," [he says].
"On the head of the earth, on the place of sacrifice to the gods, I sprinkle thee," he says;
for this place of sacrifice to the gods is indeed the head of the earth.
"In the footprint of Iḍā," he says;
for this is indeed the footprint of Iḍā, namely that of the cow for which the Soma is purchased.
"In the one rich in ghee, Svāhā!"—thus he says.
Because the clarified butter was squeezed from her very foot, he speaks thus:
"If the Adhvaryu were to offer an oblation where there is no fire, the Adhvaryu would become blind; the Rakṣases do not slay the sacrifice.
Indeed, at every stage as it is being performed, the Rakṣases seek to destroy the sacrifice.

"Traced around is the Rakṣas, traced around are the enemies," he says, for the purpose of striking away the Rakṣases. "Here do I cut off the neck of the Rakṣas, whoever hates us and whom we hate," he says;
for there are indeed two persons: him whom one hates and him who hates one. It is the necks of these two alone that he cuts off without interval.
The footprint of the Soma-purchase cow is indeed cattle.
In that he scatters as much [clay] as is kneaded together, he wins cattle for himself.
(6.1.8.4) "May wealth be ours," with these words he pours [the grain] together.
(6.1.8.4–5) Thus the Adhvaryu does not exclude himself from the sacrificial animals.
(6.1.8.5) "In thee may there be wealth," with these words he hands it over to the sacrificer.
The sacrificer himself bestows wealth; he says "to thee, O wealth" for the sake of the wife,
for the wife is indeed half of one's own self.
(6.1.8.5) Just as one deposits [the seed] in the houses, so indeed is that. (6.1.8.5) "May you consort with Tvaṣṭṛ’s mate," he says. Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the fashioner of the forms of paired animals.
(6.1.8.5) He bestows form itself upon the cattle. (6.1.8.5) The Gārhapatya fire is established for this world, and the Āhavanīya for that [world beyond].
(6.1.8.5) If he were to scatter [the grain] on the Gārhapatya, he would be possessed of cattle in this world.
If he were to scatter [the grains] only on the Āhavanīya fire, he would possess cattle only in that world.
He scatters them on both;
thus he makes him possessed of cattle in both worlds.
(6.1.9.1) The exponents of Brahman say: "Should the Soma plants be gathered or not gathered? (6.1.9.1) Soma, indeed, is the king of plants.
(6.1.9.1) Whatever has fallen into that [fire] is indeed swallowed by it.
(6.1.9.1) If he were to sift it, it would be just as if one were to extract what has been swallowed. (6.1.9.1) If he does not sift it, it is just as if what has fallen into the eye runs away.
(6.1.9.1) The Adhvaryu would become hungry, and the sacrificer would become hungry.
(6.1.9.1) He should say to the Soma-seller, "Cleanse the Soma! (6.1.9.2) If he says otherwise—whether [he says] one thing or the other—he causes the Soma-seller to suffer by both means.
(6.1.9.2) Therefore, the seller of Soma is hungry.
Aruṇa Aupaveśi used to say:
"By the very act of purchasing the Soma, I secure for myself the third pressing."
(6.1.9.2) He measures out on the skin of animals; verily he wins cattle for himself, for cattle indeed are the third pressing. (6.1.9.2) Regarding whomsoever he may desire:
"He would be without cattle," so [the sages] measured it out from the side of the *ṛkṣa*.
Indeed, the *ṛkṣa* is unfavorable to cattle;
he truly becomes one who is without cattle.
(6.1.9.2) If he should desire of someone, "May he be rich in cattle," (6.1.9.3) he should measure it for him from the hair;
for this is indeed the form of cattle.
(6.1.9.3) By means of form itself, he wins cattle for him; (6.1.9.3) he indeed becomes possessed of cattle.
(6.1.9.3) He purchases [the Soma] at the edge of the waters.
(6.1.9.3) He purchases him as one who possesses sap. (6.1.9.3) "You are a companion," he says. (6.1.9.3) He thus makes him a companion.
(6.1.9.3) “The *śukra* is your cup,” he says;
for the *śukra* is indeed his cup. (6.1.9.3) And he goes with a cart.
He goes toward his very greatness.
He goes by means of a cart;
therefore, one's livelihood on level ground is to be carried by cart.
Since they indeed carry him away with the head, therefore life on the mountain is "to be carried by the head. He measures [the Soma] with the *aticchandas* verse: "To that god Savitṛ..."
The *atichandas* indeed contains all the meters;
with all the meters he measures it.
The *atichandas* is indeed the summit of the meters.
In that he measures with an *aticchandas* verse, he makes him the preeminent one among his equals.
He measures with one [verse] for each [finger], omitting [one]; verily, he measures him with what is not exhausted, for that reason the fingers have diverse powers.
(6.1.9.5) He presses the thumb down upon all [the fingers];
therefore it possesses equal strength with the other fingers;
therefore it moves along with all of them.
If he were to measure with all [the fingers] together, the fingers would be born joined together;
he measures with each one separately as they are released,
therefore they are born distinct.
He measures five times with a sacrificial formula; the *paṅkti* consists of five syllables, and the sacrifice is fivefold.
Verily, he wins the sacrifice.
Five times silently; they amount to ten.
The *virāj* consists of ten syllables.
Food is the *virāj*; by means of the *virāj* he wins the eating of food.
In that he measures with a *yajus*, he wins what has come into being.
(6.1.9.6) As for that which will be done silently:
(6.1.9.6) if indeed there were only as much Soma as he measures out, it would belong to the sacrificer alone and not to the members of the assembly.
(6.1.9.6) With the words, "For the offspring, thee," he pours it together.
(6.1.9.6) He distributes [the portions] among the members of the assembly (sadasya).
(6.1.9.6) He binds [them] with a garment. (6.1.9.7) For the garment belongs to all the deities.
Verily, he causes him to prosper with all the deities;
Soma is indeed cattle;
"For breath, thee!"—with these words he ties [the fastening].
Verily, he places the out-breath (*prāṇa*) in the cattle;
with "For the through-breath (*vyāna*) thee," he ties it on;
verily, he places the through-breath in the cattle.
Therefore, the vital breaths do not abandon one who is sleeping.

(6.1.10.1) If one should bargain, saying, "I will buy [Soma] from you for a sixteenth part, for a hoof," he would make the Soma worth less than a cow, the sacrificer worth less than a cow, and the *adhvaryu* worth less than a cow.
One should not diminish the greatness of the cow;
rather, one should simply say, "I will buy [Soma] from you for a cow."
(6.1.10.1) He makes the Soma worth a cow, the sacrificer worth a cow, and the Adhvaryu worth a cow;
he does not diminish the greatness of the cow. (6.1.10.1) He purchases it with a goat.
Verily, he purchases him who possesses fervor;
he purchases him with gold;
verily, he purchases him together with brilliance.
He purchases [the Soma] with a cow;
thus he purchases it with [Soma] mixed with milk.
He purchases it with a bull.
(6.1.10.2) He purchases him [Soma] together with Indra.
(6.1.10.2) He purchases him with an ox;
for the ox is indeed a carrier.
(6.1.10.2) He purchases the fire of the sacrifice with fire itself; (6.1.10.2) he purchases it with a pair,
for the attainment of a pair.
He purchases [the Soma] with a garment.
The garment indeed belongs to all the deities; he thus purchases it for all the deities.
They amount to ten.
The Virāj consists of ten syllables; the Virāj is food. By means of the Virāj, he obtains food.
"You are the body of austerity, the form of Prajāpati," he says.
By this, the Adhvaryu indeed makes amends to the cattle for himself so as not to be cut off; he attains prosperity and obtains cattle—he who knows thus.
"I buy your bright [soma] with the bright," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula itself.
(6.1.10.3) "The gods indeed took back by force that gold with which they purchased Soma, [saying], 'For who would sell away his own brilliance?
(6.1.10.4) With whatever gold one should purchase Soma, that he should take back by force; thus he places brilliance within himself. (6.1.10.4) 'Light for us, darkness for the Soma-seller,' he says."
He bestows light upon the sacrificer;
he strikes the soma-seller with darkness.
If he were to kill [the ox] without tying it up, the serpents would become biting snakes for that year.

"I here bind this upon the necks of the biting serpents," he says; thus they become non-biting serpents. With darkness he pierces the Soma-seller. "O Svāna, Bhrāja! he says. These [dogs] indeed guarded the Soma in yonder world; from them they brought the Soma.
If he were not to assign the Soma-purchase items to these [dogs], his Soma would be as if unbought, and these would not guard his Soma in yonder world.
In that he assigns the Soma-purchasers to these [deities], his Soma becomes purchased; they protect his Soma in yonder world.
The Soma, once purchased and bound, belongs to Varuṇa.
"As a friend, come to us, bestowing good friendship," he says for the sake of pacification.
"Enter Indra's right thigh," he says.
For when the gods purchased Soma, they placed it upon Indra's right thigh.
Indeed, he who performs the sacrifice is now that very Indra.
Therefore, he says thus:
"Up with life, with good life," for he stands having taken hold of the deities themselves.
"Go along the wide mid-region," he says, for at this time Soma has the mid-region as his deity.
"Thou art the seat of Aditi; sit on the seat of Aditi," he says.
(6.1.11.2) This is exactly according to the sacrificial formula.
(6.1.11.2) Verily, he deprives it of its full power when he makes that which belongs to Varuṇa belong to Mitra;
(6.1.11.2) he settles it with a verse addressed to Varuṇa, and thus he endows it with its own deity.
He wraps it around with a garment;
for the garment belongs to all the deities. Thus, he causes him to prosper through all the deities together.
(6.1.11.3) Moreover, for the sake of striking away the Rakṣases,
he says, "In the forests he has spread out the intermediate space," for indeed, in the forests he has spread out the intermediate space.
"Victuals in the horses," he says, for there is indeed victual in the horses; "milk in the cows," he says.
"For milk is in the cows;
'in their hearts, the will,' he says— for the will is indeed in their hearts."
"Varuṇa [placed] Agni among the people," he says; for Varuṇa indeed placed Agni among the people.
"Sūrya in heaven," he says.
"For in heaven [is] the sun;
[in] the rock [is] Soma," he says;
for the pressing-stones are indeed the rocks.
In those [fires], he indeed places the Soma for him who sacrifices;
therefore he speaks thus:
"Upwards that Jātavedas," with this verse addressed to Sūrya, he fastens the black antelope skin.
For the sake of driving away the *rakṣases*.
"O two oxen, come hither, you who bear the yoke," he says;
this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula.
"Move forward, O Lord of the world!
he says, for he is indeed the lord of all beings. "Toward all abodes," he says.
"For he indeed moves toward all abodes.
"May no thief find you," he says;
for when that Soma was being brought, the Gandharva Viśvāvasu stole it from around, therefore he speaks thus.
"For the sake of non-deprivation," he says, "you are the means of well-being for the sacrificer.
This is indeed the sacrificer's taking hold of the sacrifice.
(6.1.11.5) For the sake of non-interruption.
(6.1.11.5) Verily, Varuṇa comes against the sacrificer when the purchased Soma is bound [in the cart].
(6.1.11.6) "Homage to the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa," he says.
(6.1.11.6) For the sake of peace;
(6.1.11.6) they carry Soma;
(6.1.11.6) he establishes himself with Agni.
(6.1.11.6) As they come together, they come together toward the sacrificer.
(6.1.11.6) Truly, he who is consecrated moves about having already seized his own self for the sacrifice.
When he immolates the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, that is indeed his ransom.
Therefore, that [debt] of his must be paid off,
for it is like a ransom for a man;
moreover, they say:
"By means of Agni and Soma, Indra indeed slew Vṛtra"—thus it is said.
When one sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, that [offering] of his is truly a slayer of Vṛtra; therefore, it is to be eaten.
He moves around with a verse addressed to Varuṇa;
he thus moves around him by means of his own deity.
(6.2.1.1) If he were to receive the guest-offering while both oxen are unyoked, he would cut the sacrifice asunder.
(6.2.1.1) If he were to do so without unyoking both, it would be just as if the guest-offering were made for one who has not yet arrived.
(6.2.1.1) One ox is unyoked and the other remains unyoked; then he receives the guest-offering for the continuity of the sacrifice.
(6.2.1.1) The wife takes hold [of him]. For the wife has authority over the household goods; it is with the wife’s consent that he offers the oblation.
Whatever the wife performs in the sacrifice, that constitutes a productive union.
(6.2.1.1) Now, this is indeed the wife’s taking hold of the sacrifice so that it may not be interrupted.
(6.2.1.2) With as many attendants as the King [Soma] arrives with, hospitality is offered to them all; for the meters are indeed the attendants of King Soma.
"Thou art the hospitality of Agni; for Viṣṇu thee!"—he says this for the sake of the Gāyatrī.

(6.2.1.2) "Thou art the guest-reception for Soma; for Viṣṇu, thee!"—with this he effects the Triṣṭubh metre. (6.2.1.2) "Thou art the guest-reception for the guest; for Viṣṇu, thee!"—with this he effects the Jagatī metre.
(6.2.1.3) "For Agni, the giver of increase of wealth; for Viṣṇu, thee!"—with this he effects the Anuṣṭubh metre.
(6.2.1.3) "For the eagle, the bearer of Soma; for Viṣṇu, thee!"—with these words he acts for the sake of the Gāyatrī.
(6.2.1.3) He draws [the cup] five times; the Paṅkti has five syllables, and the sacrifice is fivefold; verily, he wins the sacrifice. (6.2.1.3) The exponents of sacred knowledge say:
(6.2.1.3) For what reason is the *gāyatrī* verse used on both sides of the *ātithya* offering?
(6.2.1.3–4) Because he brought that Soma from there, therefore the *gāyatrī* is used on both sides of the *ātithya*, both before and after.
(6.2.1.4) The *ātithya* is indeed the head of the sacrifice; the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is prepared on nine potsherds, and for that reason the head is split into nine parts.

There is a cake on nine potsherds; these are three sets of three potsherds, commensurate with the *trivṛt* stoma. The *trivṛt* is brilliance; verily, he places brilliance at the head of the sacrifice.

There is a cake on nine potsherds; these are three sets of three potsherds, commensurate with the *trivṛt* breath. The breath is indeed *trivṛt*; verily, he places the *trivṛt* breath itself, in due order, at the head of the sacrifice.

(6.2.1.5) These horse-tail grasses (*aśvavāla*) are indeed the eyelashes of Prajāpati; the crosswise blade of sugarcane is [his eye]. When the *prastara* bundle consists of horse-tail grass and the crosswise blade is of sugarcane, he thereby gathers together the very eye of Prajāpati.

(6.2.1.5–6) The gods, indeed, offered certain oblations, and the Asuras snatched them away by means of a hollow reed (*niṣkāva*). Those gods saw the *kārṣmarya* tree; [they thought], "It is fit for ritual action (*karmanya*); with it one may perform the rite. They made the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) out of *kārṣmarya* wood; with them they struck away the Rakṣases.
(6.2.1.6) In that the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) are made of *kārṣmarya* wood, it is for the smiting away of the *rakṣases*.

(6.2.1.6) He makes them touch one another so that the *rakṣases* may have no passage between them. He does not place one in the east, for the rising sun itself smites away the *rakṣases* from the east.
(6.2.1.6) He places two kindling-sticks upright; verily from above he smites away the Rakṣases.
One with a sacrificial formula, the other silently, for the sake of pairing.
He places two, for the sacrificer has two feet, for the sake of stability.
(6.2.1.6) The exponents of Brahman say: (6.2.1.7) "Agni and Soma—how is it that hospitality is offered to Soma but not to Agni?
(6.2.1.7) When one churns fire and throws it into the fire, by that very act hospitality is offered to Agni.
Furthermore, they indeed say, "Agni is all the deities"; when one churns the fire after the oblation has been set down, he generates all the deities for the sake of the oblation already placed there.
(6.2.2.1) The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict.

(6.2.2.1) Those gods were at variance with one another. (6.2.2.1) Not yielding to one another for the sake of preeminence, they divided themselves into five groups: Agni with the Vasus, Soma with the Rudras, Indra with the Maruts, Varuṇa with the Ādityas, and Bṛhaspati with the Viśve Devas.
(6.2.2.1) They reflected:

(6.2.2.1) "We are indeed yielding to our enemies, the Asuras, because we are at variance with one another. Let us share these bodies of ours that are dear to us; he who among us first acts treacherously toward another shall be excluded from them.
(6.2.2.2) Therefore, whoever among those who have performed the *satānūnaptra* rite acts treacherously first, he meets with ruin.
In that he portions out the *tānūnaptra* butter, it serves for the overcoming of his rivals; he prospers by himself and his rival is defeated. He portions it out five times.
For they agreed upon that in five ways;
moreover, the *paṅkti* consists of five syllables, and the sacrifice is fivefold.
(6.2.2.2) Verily, he wins the sacrifice. (6.2.2.2) "I take thee for the one who comes hither," he says.
(6.2.2.3) The breath, indeed, is the one who comes hither.
(6.2.2.3) He gratifies the breath itself. (6.2.2.3) "For the protectors," he says; for the protector is indeed the mind.
(6.2.2.3) "It is the mind alone that gratifies," he says; (6.2.2.3) "At the *tanūnaptra*," he says,
for those [limbs] of his were indeed joined together at the *tanūnaptra*.
‘For the Śākvara chant,’ he says;
for they agreed upon those [verses] for the sake of power. ‘For the most powerful strength,’ he says.
(6.2.2.3) For they agreed upon that most powerful part of his very self. (6.2.2.3) "It is unassailable, it is invincible," he says;
for this is indeed unassailable and invincible.
"The vigor of the gods," he says;
for this is indeed the vigor of the gods.
"Protecting against imprecation, not to be imprecated," he says.
"For this is indeed a protection against imprecation and is itself beyond imprecation.
"May the Lord of Consecration favor my consecration," he says;
this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula.
(6.2.2.4) The gods, having made ghee their thunderbolt, struck Soma.
(6.2.2.4) Indeed, they proceed with the *tānūnaptra* rite as if approaching him closely.
(6.2.2.4) He says, "O divine Soma, may each of your stalks swell."
Whatever of it becomes exhausted or wasted, that very thing he causes to swell by means of this [rite].
He says, "May Indra swell for you; may you swell for Indra.
Thus he causes both Indra and Soma to swell.
"Make thy friends swell with gain and wisdom," he says;
for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are indeed his friends;
it is them he causes to swell.
"May it be well with you, O divine Soma; may I attain the pressing," he says. By this, he invokes this very blessing. Indeed, those who cause the Soma to swell depart from this world.
For Soma, having been made to swell, has the intermediate region as its deity.
"Desired riches, for the impulse, for fortune," he says;
thus, by paying homage to Heaven and Earth, they find firm standing in this world.
(6.2.2.6) The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict.
(6.2.2.6) Those gods, being afraid, entered Agni. Therefore they say:
"Agni is all the deities"—thus [it is said]. Having made Agni their protection, they overcame the Asuras.
Indeed, he who enters upon the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*) enters into Agni himself.
It serves for the overcoming of rivals;
he prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated.
By means of the consecration (*dīkṣā*), he protects himself; by means of the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*), he protects his progeny.
(6.2.2.7) He fastens the girdle more tightly;
for offspring are closer to oneself.
He becomes one who has undertaken the heated vow.
(6.2.2.7) He purifies himself with the *madantī* waters;
for Agni is chilled by the cold, and [this is done] for the sake of kindling him.
(6.2.2.7) "That body of yours, O Agni, which belongs to Rudra," he says; (6.2.2.7) by means of that very deity he causes him to undertake the vow, for the sake of common origin and for peace.
Those Asuras had three fortresses: one of iron was the lowest, then one of silver, and then one of gold.
The gods were unable to conquer them; they sought to win them only through the *upasads*.
Therefore, they say: "Whether one knows this or not."
(6.2.3.1) "By means of the *upasad* rites, one indeed conquers a great city," they said.
They then fashioned an arrow: Agni as the point, Soma as the shaft, and Viṣṇu as the barb.
They spoke:
(6.2.3.1) "Who will pierce this? he asked.
They said, "Rudra! [saying], "Rudra is indeed cruel; let him shoot. He said, "I shall choose a boon: may I alone be the lord of cattle. Therefore, Rudra is the lord of cattle.
Rudra released it; having shattered those three fortresses, he drove the Asuras away from these worlds.
Because the Upasad rites are performed, it is for the purpose of driving away one's rivals.
One should not offer any other oblation before this.
(6.2.3.2) If he were to offer another oblation first, he would make another mouth.
(6.2.3.3) He pours the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* ladle for the sake of the discernment of the sacrifice;
having stepped across away from it, he offers the oblation.
(6.2.3.3) By [the offering] directed away from these worlds, the sacrificer drives his rivals away.
(6.2.3.3) Having stepped across again, he offers the *upasad* oblation.
Having indeed driven them away from these worlds and having conquered them, he ascends to the world of his rivals.

The gods, indeed, by means of those *upasads* which they performed in the morning, drove away the Asuras from the day; by those which they performed in the evening, [they drove them away] from the night.
In that the *upasads* are performed both in the evening and in the morning, the sacrificer thereby drives away his rivals by means of both day and night.
(6.2.3.4) Those which are the *yājyā*s for the morning [service], he should make them the *puro'nuvākyā*s for the evening, so that there may be no loss of vigor.
(6.2.3.4) He enters upon three *upasad* days; these worlds are three; verily he gratifies these worlds.
They amount to six; the seasons are six; verily he gratifies the seasons. In the *ahīna* Soma sacrifice he enters upon twelve [days]; the year has twelve months; verily he gratifies the year.
They amount to twenty-four.
There are twenty-four half-months; verily, he gratifies the half-months.
He who desires [this] should undertake the intermediate consecration that is sharp-pointed.

(6.2.3.5) "May there be prosperity for me in this world," [thinking thus], he should first take one [day], then two, then three, then four. This indeed is the intermediate consecration (avāntaradīkṣā) that is sharp-pointed like an awl; it brings prosperity to him in this very world. (6.2.3.5) He who desires, "May there be prosperity for me in yonder world," should undertake the intermediate consecration that is wider at the top and narrower at the bottom (parovarīyasī). [He should take] four days first, then three, then two, then one. This indeed is the intermediate consecration that is wider at the top and narrower at the bottom; it brings prosperity to him in yonder very world.
(6.2.4.1) Those who undergo the Upasad rites go indeed to the heavenly world.
Of them, he who draws [the Soma] out is surely left behind; "He did not bring it," they say, for it must be well-drawn.
(6.2.4.1) He who, exhausted, falls away from those who strive for their own goal indeed dwells apart from them. Therefore, having drawn [the Soma] once, one should not draw it again;
one should draw it with curds.
(6.2.4.1) This, indeed, is the form of cattle;
by means of this very form, he wins cattle.
(6.2.4.2) The sacrifice fled from the gods, having assumed the form of Viṣṇu.
(6.2.4.2) It entered the earth.
(6.2.4.2) The gods, joining their hands together, searched for it.
Indra stepped over him from above;
he said,
"Who is this that has stepped over me from above?"
"I am he who slays in the fortress. "Then who are you?
"I am he who brings [booty] from the fortress.
He said:
(6.2.4.2) "In the fortress indeed you have spoken as a slayer; this boar is the one who steals away your wealth."

"Beyond the seven mountains lies the wealth of the Asuras that is to be known; slay him if you would slay him in a place difficult to reach. He uprooted a bunch of *darbha* grass, split the seven mountains, and slew him.
He said:
(6.2.4.3) "From the stronghold you have indeed spoken; bring this one here!
(6.2.4.3) He brought that sacrifice to them from the sacrifice itself.
(6.2.4.3) That which they found among the Asuras was the wealth to be found; that is the singular quality of being found (*veditva*) belonging to the *vedi*.
(6.2.4.3) This earth belonged to the Asuras in the beginning.
(6.2.4.4) As far as one can see while sitting, that much belonged to the gods.
Those gods said:
"Let it be so for us even in this [matter]," they said.
"How much shall we give you?
"As much as this female jackal takes three steps around, so much give us."

That Indra, having assumed the form of a female wolf, thrice strode around this [earth] on all sides. Thereby they found her; because they found her (*avindanta*), that is the reason for the *vedi*’s name, *veditva*.
(6.2.4.5) This earth, indeed, is the entire altar.

(6.2.4.5) Having measured it out as far as they think they will be able [to perform the sacrifice], they sacrifice upon it. It is thirty steps wide at the back, thirty-six steps long toward the east, and twenty-four steps wide in front.
They amount to ten by tens;
the *virāj* consists of ten syllables,
and the *virāj* is food.
By means of the *virāj* [verse], he obtains food.
He digs up; whatever in it is impure, that he strikes away.
He digs up;
therefore plants perish;
he spreads the sacrificial grass.
Therefore the plants come into being again.
He spreads the *uttarabarhis* over the *barhis*;
the *barhis* is indeed offspring, and the sacrificer is the *uttarabarhis*.
(6.2.4.5) He thus makes the sacrificer superior to the non-sacrificer;
(6.2.4.5) therefore, the sacrificer is superior to the non-sacrificer.
(6.2.5.1) Or rather, he who takes up a burden without being capable of bearing it surely breaks under it.
If there were twelve *upasads* for the *sāhna* sacrifice and three for the *ahīna* sacrifice, the ritual would be performed in a contrary manner.
There should be three *upasads* for the *sāhna* sacrifice and twelve for the *ahīna* sacrifice; this is for the sake of its possessing strength, and thus the ritual is performed in the proper order.

(6.2.5.1) For the calf has but one teat as its share; thus he approaches the vow with one teat, then two, then three, then four. This indeed is the vow called *kṣurapavi* (the razor-edged), by which one drives away the rivals already born and opposes those yet to be born; moreover, by means of the less, he attains the more. (6.2.5.2) First he approaches the vow with four teats, then three, then two, then one. This indeed is the vow called *sujaghana* (the well-thighed); it is conducive to austerity and leads to heaven; moreover, he is procreated with offspring and cattle.
(6.2.5.2) Barley-gruel is the vow-food for a Rājanya; for barley-gruel is indeed fierce, and the Rājanya is as it were fierce. It is the form of the thunderbolt, for the sake of prosperity.
(6.2.5.3) Curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) is the vow-food for a Vaiśya; it is the form of the domestic sacrifice (*pākayajña*), for the sake of nourishment.
(6.2.5.3) Milk is the vow-food for a Brāhmaṇa. The Brāhmaṇa is indeed splendor, and milk is splendor; by means of splendor he places splendor, milk, within himself.
(6.2.5.3) Moreover, embryos indeed grow by means of milk. He who is consecrated is truly like an embryo; that his milk becomes his vow serves to nourish his very self.
(6.2.5.3) Manu had three vows, the Asuras had two vows, and the gods had one vow.
(6.2.5.4) In the morning, at midday, and in the evening—such was the vow of Manu, the form of the *pākayajña*, for the sake of prosperity.
In the morning and in the evening, the time for the Asuras is when food is not yet churned out; that is the form of hunger, and because of that, they were defeated.
At midday and at midnight, it belongs to the gods; because of that, they prevailed and went to the heavenly world.

When his vow (*vrata*) takes place at midday and at midnight, he eats from the middle [of the meal]; for one eats from the middle with food, and thus he places strength in the middle for the sake of overcoming his rivals.
(6.2.5.4) He prospers in himself; (6.2.5.5) his rival is defeated.

(6.2.5.4) He who is consecrated is indeed an embryo, and the consecrated shed is the womb. If the consecrated one should depart from the consecrated shed, it is just as when an embryo falls from the womb; such is that [act]. One must not depart for the protection of oneself. (6.2.5.4) This Agni is indeed the tiger, the guardian of the clan; therefore, if the consecrated one should depart, he [Agni] is liable to rise up against him and slay him. One must not depart for the sake of self-protection.
(6.2.5.4) He lies on the south; for this is the place of the sacrificer, and thus he lies in his own place.
He lies turned toward the fire; verily, he lies turned toward the deities and the sacrifice.
(6.2.6.1) One should cause him whom one desires to sacrifice on a *purohavis* sacrificial ground to perform the sacrifice, [thinking]:
"May the subsequent sacrifice incline toward him; may he conquer the heavenly world.
(6.2.6.1) This indeed is the *purohavis* sacrificial ground, where the Hotṛ, while reciting the *prātaranuvāka*, gazes toward Agni, the waters, and the sun.
The higher sacrifice inclines toward him; he conquers the world of heaven.
One should cause one who has rivals to sacrifice on a site where the gods have been reached, or he should cause him to touch a path or a dug-out pit.
(6.2.6.1) As long as it is not fit for a cart to go there, nor for a chariot—this indeed is the sacrificial ground of the gods that has been obtained.
(6.2.6.2) He truly obtains his rival; his rival does not obtain him.
On a sacrificial ground elevated on one side, one should cause him who desires cattle to sacrifice.
(6.2.6.2) From a sacrificial ground that is elevated in one place, the Aṅgirases indeed created cattle. (6.2.6.2) It should be elevated between the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna*.
(6.2.6.2) This, indeed, is the sacrificial ground elevated in one place.
(6.2.6.2) He indeed becomes possessed of cattle.

(6.2.6.2) One should cause him who desires heaven to sacrifice on a sacrificial ground that is elevated in three places. From a sacrificial ground elevated in three places, the Aṅgirases went to the heavenly world.

(6.2.6.2) Between the Āhavanīya fire and the Havirdhāna shed, it should be elevated. (6.2.6.3) Between the Havirdhāna shed and the Sadas, and between the Sadas and the Gārhapatya fire, it should likewise be elevated. This, indeed, is the three-elevated sacrificial ground of the gods;
by it, one goes to the heavenly world itself.
One should cause a person desiring stability to sacrifice on a firmly established place of sacrifice for the gods;
for that place of sacrifice for the gods which is level on all sides is indeed firmly established; he truly finds firm standing.
(6.2.6.3) Where various plants are intertwined, there he should cause one who desires cattle to sacrifice.
(6.2.6.3) This, indeed, is the form of cattle.
(6.2.6.4) By means of that very form, he wins cattle for him.
(6.2.6.4) He indeed becomes possessed of cattle.
(6.2.6.4) One should cause him to sacrifice on a sacrificial ground seized by Nirṛti for whom one should desire: "May I cause Nirṛti to seize his sacrifice."
(6.2.6.4) This indeed is a sacrificial ground seized by Nirṛti: that which is rough, even though it be level.
(6.2.6.4) By means of Nirṛti itself, he causes his sacrifice to be seized.
He should cause one who desires distinction to sacrifice on a distinct sacrificial ground—[one] over whom they might have deliberated [as to whether he is fit] regarding either his vessel or his bed.

It should slope toward the east from the Āhavanīya fire and toward the west from the Gārhapatya fire; this indeed is the distinct sacrificial ground. One turns away from evil and from the rival; they do not scrutinize him regarding his vessel or his bed.
(6.2.6.4) One should cause a person desiring prosperity to sacrifice on a prepared sacrificial ground.
(6.2.6.4) For man is indeed something to be prepared; (6.2.6.4) thus he truly prospers.
(6.2.7.1) To them, the high altar, having assumed the form of a lioness, stepped aside between both groups and stood there.
(6.2.7.1) Those gods thought:
"Between whomsoever she shall turn toward, they will become this [world]."
They invited her;
she said, "I shall choose a boon: may you obtain all desires through me, but let my oblation reach Agni first."

Therefore, they sprinkle the eastern part of the fire-altar over the high altar (*uttaravedi*), for that is what she has chosen. He measures it around with a yoke-pin; this is its proper measure, and moreover, by means of what is already yoked, he secures what is to be yoked.
"You are my path to wealth," he says;
for wealth indeed protected them.
"You are my path to refreshment," he says.
"For they have helped these bitter ones," he says;
"help us, O savior, from distress," he says;
for he has helped these who were in distress.
"Unfold me from what is distressed," he says; for he has unfolded these [bricks] from what was distressed. "May Agni find the name Nabhas. "O Agni Aṅgiras," he carries [the firebrand] three times.
(6.2.7.3) Those very fires that are in these worlds—he wins them. He carries the fourth silently;
he wins what is undefined.
"You are a lioness, you are a buffalo," he says;
for she, having assumed the form of a lioness, stood there having stepped away between the two [worlds].
"Be wide, spread out; may the lord of the sacrifice spread out widely for you," he says.
He causes the sacrificer himself to expand with offspring and cattle.

With the words, "Thou art firm," he strikes [the earth] for the sake of stability. With the words, "Be pure for the gods! Be beautiful for the gods! he sprinkles water downward and scatters [grains] for the sake of purification.
He says, "May Indra’s roar protect thee from the east with the Vasus"; thus he sprinkles it from all the quarters.

(6.2.7.4) "If the high altar should turn toward the gods, we shall surely conquer here! Thinking thus, the Asuras raised their thunderbolt and rushed at the gods. Indra’s roar, together with the Vasus, drove them away from the east; Manojava, with the Pitṛs, from the south; Pracetas, with the Rudras, from the west; and Viśvakarman, with the Ādityas, from the north.
(6.2.7.5) In that he sprinkles the high altar in this manner, the sacrificer thereby drives his rivals away from all the quarters.
Indra gave the travelers to the hyenas; they devoured them on the south side of the high altar.
Whatever remains of the sprinkling water, one should pour that down on the south side of the high altar;
by that, he pacifies whatever there is cruel in it.
(6.2.7.5) Whomever he may hate, let him meditate upon that person; verily, he strikes him with affliction.
(6.2.8.1) That high altar said:
"Through me, you shall attain all desires."
(6.2.8.1) Those gods desired: "May we overcome our rivals, the Asuras. (6.2.8.1) They offered oblations.
(6.2.8.1) "Thou art a lioness, overcoming rivals; Svāhā!
(6.2.8.1) They overcame their Asura enemies and kinsmen. Having overcome their Asura enemies and kinsmen, they desired [to attain further success].
"May we obtain offspring," they said;
they offered [the oblation]:
"Thou art a lioness, a winner of good offspring, svāhā!"
(6.2.8.1) They obtained offspring. (6.2.8.1) Having obtained offspring, (6.2.8.2) they desired: "May we obtain cattle."
They offered:
"Thou art a lioness, winning the increase of wealth, svāhā! Thereby they found cattle.
Having obtained cattle, they desired: "May we find a firm foundation. They offered oblations.
(6.2.8.2) "Thou art a lioness, winning the Ādityas; Svāhā! (6.2.8.2) They found this foundation;
having found this foundation, they desired.
(6.2.8.2) "We shall approach the deities with blessings," they said.
(6.2.8.2) They offered the oblation: (6.2.8.3) "Thou art a lioness; bring the gods hither for the one who offers sacrifice to the gods, svāhā!"
Those deities approached with blessings;
he sprinkles five times;
the *paṅkti* consists of five syllables.
The sacrifice is fivefold;
verily he wins the sacrifice itself.
He sprinkles crosswise.
Therefore, animals move their limbs crosswise for the sake of stability;
with the words, "For the beings, thee," he lifts up the offering-spoon.
(6.2.8.3) Those very deities who have come into being—their portion is that.
(6.2.8.3) He gratifies them with that.
(6.2.8.3) He lays around enclosing-sticks made of *pautudrava* wood.
(6.2.8.3) For the support of these worlds.
(6.2.8.4) Agni had three elder brothers;
while carrying the oblation to the gods, they perished.
That Agni was afraid, thinking, "In this very way, he will surely bring me to ruin.
He hid himself.

That [portion] of his which dwelt among the trees remained in the *pūtudru* tree; that which was among the plants remained in the *sugandhitejana*; and that which was among the animals remained between the horns of a ram.
The deities sought him all around;
they found him;
they spoke to him.

"Turn toward us; carry our oblation," he said. He replied, "I shall choose a boon: whatever of the portion already taken but not yet offered should fall outside the enclosing sticks, let that be my brothers' share."
Therefore, whatever of the taken [oblation] that is not offered spills outside the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), that is their share; he gratifies them with that very thing. He thought:
"My former brothers were possessed of bones; let me cause my bones to fall away."
(6.2.8.5) Those bones which he caused to fall apart became *pūtudru* wood.
(6.2.8.6) That flesh which was crushed became *gulgulu*. In that he gathers these materials, he thereby gathers Agni himself.
He says, "Thou art the soil (*purīṣa*) of Agni."
For these materials are indeed the soil-covering of Agni.
Moreover, they say:
"These enclosing-sticks of *pūtudru* wood are truly his brothers who lie around him."
He unties what is bound;
verily he releases them from Varuna’s noose. He sprinkles them with water; verily he makes them pure for sacrifice.
Having offered with the *sāvitrī* verse, he causes the two *havirdhāna* carts to move forward.
Verily, impelled by Savitṛ, he causes them to move forward.
This axle, indeed, is Varuṇa, bound on both sides and difficult to speak around.
If he were to let out [the breath], he would let it out toward the house of the sacrificer. "O God of fair speech, speak in the dwellings," he says;
for the dwellings are indeed the *duryā*s.
(6.2.9.1) For the sake of peace; (6.2.9.1) the wife anoints [the axle]. (6.2.9.2) For the wife is the friend of all.
(6.2.9.2) For the sake of friendship.
(6.2.9.2) Whatever the wife performs in the sacrifice, that constitutes a union.
Furthermore, this is the wife’s taking hold of the sacrifice so that it may not be cut off.
(6.2.9.2) Following along the path, the Rakṣases seek to destroy the sacrifice.
(6.2.9.2) He offers oblations on the two paths with two verses addressed to Viṣṇu;
for Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice.
(6.2.9.2) From the sacrifice itself he strikes away the Rakṣases.
(6.2.9.2) If the Adhvaryu were to offer an oblation where there is no fire, the Adhvaryu would become blind, and the Rakṣases would destroy the sacrifice.
(6.2.9.3) Having placed gold [on the ladle], he offers the oblation.
(6.2.9.3) He offers indeed into that which possesses fire;
(6.2.9.3) the Adhvaryu does not become blind, nor do the Rakṣases destroy the sacrifice.
"Go forward, fashioning the sacrifice," he says;
verily, he causes these two to go to the heavenly world. "Rejoice here on the height of the earth," he says.
For this sacrificial ground is the height of the earth;
the oblation-holder (*havirdhāna*) is indeed the head of the sacrifice.
With the verse containing the word "blessing" (*āśīrpadā*), "O Viṣṇu, from heaven or from the earth," he drives in the central post (*methī*) of the southern oblation-holder.
(6.2.9.4) Thus, from the very head of the sacrifice, the sacrificer obtains his blessings.
(6.2.9.4) The staff of Aupara, at the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ* call, broke the axle of the third *havirdhāna* cart.
When the third roof-covering of the two *havirdhāna* carts is brought forward, it is for the sake of obtaining that third *havirdhāna*.
The oblation-holder (*havirdhāna*) is indeed the head of the sacrifice.
He says, "Thou art the forehead of Viṣṇu; thou art the back of Viṣṇu"; therefore, the head is spread out to this extent.

"Thou art Viṣṇu’s seam; thou art Viṣṇu’s fixed point," he says, for the oblation-holder belongs to Viṣṇu by deity. If the Adhvaryu should tie the first knot and not loosen it, he would die of urinary retention.
Therefore, it is to be loosened.
(6.2.10.1) "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," with these words he takes up the spade, for the sake of impulsion. "With the arms of the Aśvins," he says;
for the Aśvins were the two Adhvaryu priests among the gods.
‘With the two hands of Pūṣan,’ he says for the sake of restraint.
‘Like a thunderbolt indeed is this spade; you are a spade, you are a woman,’ he says for the sake of pacification.
Verily, at every stage when the sacrifice is being performed, the Rakṣases seek to strike it down.
"The Rakṣas is encircled; the enemies are encircled," he says for the purpose of driving away the Rakṣases.

(6.2.10.2) "Here I cut off the necks of the Rakṣas; him who hates us and him whom we hate," he says. There are indeed two persons: him whom one hates and him who hates one. It is for these two that he cuts the necks without interval.

(6.2.10.2) "For heaven thee, for the atmosphere thee, for earth thee," he says; thus he sprinkles it for these very worlds. (6.2.10.2) He sprinkles from above downward; therefore (6.2.10.3) men live upon strength from above downward.

Verily, he does something cruel when he digs; he pours down water for the sake of pacification. He pours down [water] mixed with barley; barley is strength, and the udumbara is strength; verily, by means of strength he causes him to attain strength. The udumbara post is commensurate with the sacrificer; as great as the sacrificer is, so much strength he bestows upon him.

"Thou art the seat of the Fathers," with these words he spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); for that which is dug out belongs to the Fathers. If he were to erect [the post] without having spread the *barhis*, it would belong to the Fathers; by spreading the *barhis* he erects it, so that he erects it upon this very [earth] and makes it firmly rooted.
"Support the sky, fill the mid-region," he says, for the separation of these worlds.

"May Dyutāna Māruta set thee up," he says; for Dyutāna Māruta used indeed to set up the Audumbara post for the gods; by that very means he sets this one up. "Thee, winner of the priesthood, winner of the nobility," he says; this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula.
"With ghee, O Heaven and Earth, fill yourselves," he offers on the Audumbara post; verily, he anoints Heaven and Earth with sap.
He pours it down to the very end; verily, he anoints the sacrificer with brilliance to the very end.
"Thou art for Indra," he says, and places the roof-covering down; for the *sadas* has Indra as its deity.
"The shade of all people," he says; for this *sadas* is indeed the shade of all people.

(6.2.10.5) [One] with nine coverings. (6.2.10.6) One desiring splendor should measure [the hall] with nine coverings; it is commensurate with the *trivṛt* stoma. The *trivṛt* is splendor; he indeed becomes possessed of splendor. (6.2.10.6) One desiring sensory power [should measure it] with eleven coverings; the *triṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables, and the *triṣṭubh* is sensory power. He indeed becomes possessed of sensory power. (6.2.10.6) One who has rivals [should measure it] with fifteen coverings; the thunderbolt (*vajra*) consists of fifteen parts, for the sake of overcoming rivals.

(6.2.10.6) [The shed] with seventeen coverings is for one desiring offspring; Prajāpati is seventeenfold, [and this serves] for the attainment of Prajāpati. (6.2.10.6) [The shed] with twenty-one coverings is for one desiring stability; the twenty-one-fold is the foundation of the *stomas*, [and this serves] for stability.

(6.2.10.6) The *sadas* is indeed the belly, and the *udumbara* is vigor (*ūrj*). He erects the *audumbarī* post in the middle; verily, he bestows vigor upon offspring in their very midst. Therefore, they enjoy vigor from the middle.

The southern roof-planks indeed belong to the world of the sacrificer, while the northern ones belong to the world of his rival. By making the southern ones higher than the northern, he places the sacrificer above the non-sacrificer; therefore, the sacrificer is superior to the non-sacrificer.
He makes internal partitions for the sake of separation; therefore, creatures subsist upon the forest.
"O lover of songs, may our songs encompass thee," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula itself.
"Thou art Indra’s seam; thou art Indra’s firm foundation," he says, for the *sadas* has Indra as its deity.
If the Adhvaryu should not loosen the first knot he ties, he would die of urinary retention; therefore, it must be loosened.
The oblation-holder (havirdhāna) is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the sounding-holes (uparava) are the vital breaths. They are dug out in the oblation-holder;
therefore, the vital breaths are in the head.
They are dug below;
therefore the vital breaths are below the head.
"I dig you, the Rakṣas-slayers, the spell-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu," he says.
For the sounding-holes have Viṣṇu as their deity.
Indeed, when the Asuras were departing, they buried magical spells (*valaga*) in the vital breaths of the gods;
those [spells] they discovered at the height of the arms.
Therefore, they are dug out to the depth of an arm's length:
"Here I dig up that hidden charm."
"Whomsoever, whether a kinsman or a stranger, has buried [a spell] against us," he says.
There are indeed two kinds of persons: the one who is a kinsman and the one who is a stranger.
Whatever spell those two have buried for him, that very thing he now digs up.
He pierces them together; therefore the vital breaths are pierced together within. He does not split them apart.
Therefore, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are undivided.
He pours out water;
therefore, the vital breaths are moist within.
He pours down [the water] so that it reaches the barley.
Barley is indeed strength; the sounding-holes are the vital breaths; verily, he bestows strength upon the vital breaths.
He spreads the sacrificial grass;
therefore the vital breaths are hairy within.
He sprinkles [the offering] with clarified butter.
Clarified butter is indeed brilliance;
the sounding-holes are the vital breaths;
verily, he bestows brilliance upon the vital breaths.
(6.2.11.3) These two pressing-boards are indeed the jaws of the sacrifice; (6.2.11.3) he does not join them together, for the jaws are unjoined.
Moreover, indeed, in a long soma sacrifice they should be joined together for the sake of stability;
for the oblation-holder (havirdhāna) is the head of the sacrifice.

The sounding-holes are the vital breaths; the two pressing-boards are the jaws; the skin is the tongue; the pressing-stones are the teeth; the Āhavanīya fire is the mouth; the Uttaravedi is the nose; the Sadas is the belly.
Indeed, when one chews with the tongue upon the teeth, it then enters the mouth;
when it has entered the mouth, it then enters the belly.
Therefore, having pressed [the Soma] with the stones upon the skin in the *havirdhāna* shed and having offered it in the *āhavanīya* fire, they go back westward and consume [it] in the *sadas*.
He who knows the milking of the *virāj* at the beginning of the sacrifice truly milks her.

This earth is indeed the *virāj*. Its hide is the skin; the two pressing-boards are the udder; the sounding-holes are the teats; the pressing-stones are the calves; the officiating priests milk it; Soma is the milk.
He who knows thus truly milks her.
(6.3.1.1) From the *cātvāla* he scatters [the earth] for the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths. (6.3.1.1) The *cātvāla* is indeed the womb of the sacrifice; it is for the sake of providing a womb for the sacrifice.
(6.3.1.1) The gods, indeed, were defeated in the sacrifice.
(6.3.1.1) They drove him back again from the Āgnīdhra.
(6.3.1.1) For that which is the Āgnīdhra is indeed the unconquered part of the sacrifice.
(6.3.1.1) In that he distributes the hearths from the Āgnīdhra, he extends the sacrifice once more from that very part of it which is unconquered.
(6.3.1.1) Indeed, those who creep out for the *bahiṣpavamāna* go as if they have already been defeated.
(6.3.1.2) When the *bahiṣpavamāna* has been chanted, he says: (6.3.1.2) "O *Āgnīdh*, carry forth the fires; strew the sacrificial grass; prepare the sacrificial cakes!"
(6.3.1.2) Having conquered the sacrifice, they proceed to perform it again.
(6.3.1.2) He distributes the coals for two pressings; for the third, he uses splinters, in order to provide it with brilliance.
(6.3.1.2) Moreover, he indeed collects it together. (6.3.1.2) The *dhiṣṇiya* hearths, indeed, guarded the Soma in yonder world; from them they brought forth the Soma.
They followed him; they entered into him.
He who knows thus finds a server.
They were deprived of the Soma-draught.
They sought the Soma-drinking among the gods.
The gods said to them, "Take two names each; then you shall obtain it, or perhaps not."
Now, the hearths are indeed the fires; therefore, a Brahmin who has two names prospers.
Of those [hearths], those which were situated closest attained the drinking of Soma: the Āhavanīya, the Āgnīdhrīya, the Hotrīya, and the Mārjālīya.
Therefore, they offer oblations into them. He utters the *vaṣaṭ* call after passing over [the cups],
for these [cups] are excluded from the drinking of Soma.
(6.3.1.4) The gods, indeed, by means of those oblations which they offered facing eastward, drove away the Asuras who were in the east;
by means of those [oblations] which were directed westward, they drove away the Asuras who were in the west.
Other oblations are offered facing eastward, but he, sitting facing westward, pours out the libations upon the hearths.
(6.3.1.4) Thus, both from behind and from the front, the sacrificer drives away his rivals. (6.3.1.4–5) Therefore, offspring are born facing backward and are conceived facing forward.
(6.3.1.5) These hearths (dhiṣṇiyas) are indeed the vital breaths.
(6.3.1.5) If the Adhvaryu were to pass beyond the Dhiṣṇiya hearths while facing westward, he would draw together the vital breaths; he would be liable to die.
(6.3.1.5) For the Hotṛ is indeed the navel of the sacrifice.
(6.3.1.5) Indeed, the out-breath (*prāṇa*) is directed upward from the navel, while the in-breath (*apāna*) is directed downward.
If the Adhvaryu were to pass behind the Hotṛ, he would place the out-breath into the in-breath, and he would be liable to die.
Therefore, the Adhvaryu should not sing along.
The Adhvaryu is indeed the strength of speech.
If the Adhvaryu were to join in singing, he would hand over his speech to the Udgātṛ; his speech would be liable to perish.
Thus say the exponents of sacred knowledge.

(6.3.1.6) While the Soma has not yet been concluded, the Adhvaryu should not pass westward across the Sadas; for how then does he go to offer the Dakṣiṇās? For that is their path. [The opponent asks: "Why would the gods acknowledge either his path or his non-path? (6.3.1.6) Having gone around the north of the Āgnīdhra fire, he offers the Dakṣiṇās;
thus he does not draw together his vital breaths.
(6.3.1.6) Some *dhiṣṇiya* hearths are piled, others are not.
Those which he piles, he gratifies by that act; those which he does not pile, he gratifies by dedicating them [in speech].
(6.3.2.1) These Vaisarjana offerings are indeed offered for the sake of the heavenly world.
(6.3.2.1) He offers two with the Gārhapatya fire;
the sacrificer has two feet.
For the sake of stability,
he offers in the Āgnīdhra fire-shed;
thus he strides forth in the intermediate space itself.
(6.3.2.1) He offers in the Āhavanīya fire;
(6.3.2.1) he thus causes him to go to the heavenly world.
(6.3.2.1) When the gods were going to the heavenly world, the Rakṣases sought to strike them.
Having struck away the *rakṣases* with Soma as their king, and having made themselves secure, they went to the heavenly world so that the *rakṣases* would not seize them.
Soma has been taken up; then he offers the *vaisarjana* oblations for the striking away of the *rakṣases*.
“O Soma, [protect us] from those who harm our bodies,” he says;
for he is indeed a harmer of bodies.
“From hatreds wrought by others,” he says.
"For the *rakṣases* are created by others.
