"Thou art a wide-extending protector," he says;
by this he indeed says, "Make wide room for us."
"May the swift one, the winner of waters, enjoy the clarified butter," he says. Having thus made the sacrificer swift, he causes him to go to the heavenly world,
so that the Rākṣasas may not seize him.

(6.3.2.2) They bring forward the Soma; (6.3.2.3) they bring forward the pressing-stones, the Vāyu-cups, and the wooden trough. (6.3.2.3) They lead the wife forward; (6.3.2.3) they cause the carts to move out after her.
(6.3.2.3) By whatever he possesses, with that he goes to the heavenly world.
(6.3.2.3) He offers in the Āgnīdhra fire-pit with a verse containing the word "lead," for the sake of leading [him] to the heavenly world.

(6.3.2.3) The Āgnīdhra sets down the pressing-stones and the *droṇakalaśa* vessel for the Vāyu-cups; for they draw [the Soma] from them. If he were to set them down together, it would be as if he were to cause [the Soma] to flow away.
He causes him to step forward with a verse addressed to Soma;
thus he causes him to step forward by means of his own deity.
"Thou art the seat of Aditi; sit on the seat of Aditi," he says.
(6.3.2.4) This is exactly according to the sacrificial formula.
(6.3.2.4) Previously, the sacrificer was its protector.
(6.3.2.4) "This, O God Savitṛ, is your Soma," he says.
Impelled by Savitṛ, he indeed hands him over to the deities.
"O Soma, as a god you have approached the gods," he says;
for being a god, he indeed approaches the gods.
"I here, a man, [approach] men," he says;
for being a man, he approaches men.
If he were not to recite this sacrificial formula (*yajus*), the sacrificer would be without offspring and without cattle.
"With offspring, with the increase of wealth," he says; thus, together with offspring and cattle, he returns to this world. "Homage to the gods," he says.
(6.3.2.5) For the salutation belongs to the gods.
(6.3.2.5) "Svadhā to the ancestors," he says; (6.3.2.5) for the utterance of "svadhā" belongs to the ancestors. (6.3.2.6)
(6.3.2.6) "Here I release myself from the noose of Varuṇa," he says; (6.3.2.6) thus he is released from the very noose of Varuṇa.
(6.3.2.6) "O Agni, Lord of Vows..."
(6.3.2.6) "One's former body should be taken back," they say.
(6.3.2.6) For who knows whether, once [the Soma] has come under one's own control, one will give it back again or not?
(6.3.2.6) The pressing-stones are indeed King Soma’s army of thieves.
He who, knowing thus, causes the pressing-stones to rest in the Āgnīdhra shed, does not encounter him with the army of thieves.
(6.3.3.1) Having offered with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, he approaches the sacrificial post. For the sacrificial post has Viṣṇu as its deity; thus he approaches it with its own deity.

(6.3.3.2) "I have passed beyond some, I have not approached others," he says; for he indeed passes beyond some and does not approach others. "I have found you on this side by means of those that are further, and by those that are nearer," he says; for he finds it on this side by means of those that are further and those that are nearer. "I delight in you, who belong to Viṣṇu, for the sacrifice to the gods," he says; for he delights in it for the sake of the sacrifice to the gods.

"May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey," he says; verily, he anoints him with splendor. "O plant, protect him! O axe, do not harm him! he says; for the axe is a thunderbolt, [and he says this] for the sake of pacification.

(6.3.3.2) From the tree that fears the *svadhiti* axe, brilliance flies away along with the first chip. That first chip which falls away—one should pick that up as well, so that he brings it back with its brilliance. (6.3.3.3) These worlds indeed fear the sacrificial post as it is being raised. [The priest] says, "Do not scratch the sky with your top; do not injure the intermediate space with your middle," thereby appeasing it for these very worlds. (6.3.3.3) He offers an oblation on the stump with the words, "O Lord of the Forest, grow with a hundred shoots! Therefore, from the stump of trees, many more sprouts arise.
"May we grow with a thousand branches," he says; thus he invokes this very blessing.
He should cut [the branch] so that it does not touch the axle. If he were to cut one that touches the axle, the chariot-pole would be liable to cause the death of the sacrificer.

For whomsoever he desires, "May he be without a firm foundation," for him he should cut one that is inclined upward; for among trees, this is indeed the one without a firm foundation, and he becomes truly without a firm foundation.

(6.3.3.4) If he should desire of someone, "May he be without cattle," he should cut for him [a branch] without leaves and with a dry tip; for this among trees is unpropitious to cattle, and he indeed becomes without cattle.

(6.3.3.5) If he should desire of someone, "May he be rich in cattle," he should cut for him one with many leaves and many branches; for this among trees is propitious to cattle, and he indeed becomes rich in cattle.

One desiring a firm foundation should cut one that is firmly established; for among trees, that which grows on level ground from its own natural place is firmly established, and he indeed finds a firm footing. He should cut one that leans toward the west, for it has leaned toward the sacrifice. For him whom he desires, "May the subsequent sacrifice incline toward him," he should cut one five cubits long; the *paṅkti* meter has five syllables, and the sacrifice is fivefold; thus the subsequent sacrifice inclines toward him.

(6.3.3.6) One of six cubits for one desiring a firm foundation; for there are six seasons, and thus he finds a firm foundation in the seasons. (6.3.3.6) One of seven cubits for one desiring cattle; the *śakvarī* verse consists of seven feet, and cattle are the *śakvarī*; verily, he wins cattle. (6.3.3.6) One of nine cubits for one desiring splendor; it is commensurate with the *trivṛt* stoma, and splendor is threefold; verily, he becomes possessed of splendor.

(6.3.3.6) One eleven-cubit [sacrificial post] is for one who desires sensory power; the *triṣṭubh* meter has eleven syllables, and the *triṣṭubh* is sensory power; he thus becomes possessed of sensory power. (6.3.3.6) One fifteen-cubit [post] is for one who has rivals; the thunderbolt (*vajra*) is fifteenfold, for the purpose of overcoming rivals.
(6.3.3.6) One seventeen-cubit [post] is for one who desires progeny; Prajāpati is seventeenfold, for the attainment of Prajāpati.
(6.3.3.6) It is twenty-one cubits long for one who desires a firm foundation; the Ekaviṃśa is the foundation of the Stomas, [serving] for the sake of stability.

(6.3.3.6) It has eight corners; the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, the Gāyatrī is brilliance, and the Gāyatrī is the mouth of the sacrifice. Thus it is commensurate with brilliance, with the Gāyatrī, and with the mouth of the sacrifice.
"For the earth thee! For the atmosphere thee! For the sky thee! he says; thus he sprinkles it for these very worlds.
He sprinkles it facing away, for the world of heaven is, as it were, turned away.

(6.3.4.1) Indeed, he does something harsh when he digs; he pours down water for the sake of pacification. He pours it down mixed with barley; barley is indeed strength. The sacrificial post is commensurate with the sacrificer; thus, he bestows upon him as much strength as the sacrificer himself possesses. (6.3.4.2) "Thou art the seat of the Fathers," [with these words] he spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). For that which is dug in has the Fathers as its deity; if he were to set up the post without spreading the grass, the dug-in post would belong to the Fathers. By spreading the grass, he sets it up; he thus sets it up upon this very earth.
(6.3.4.2) He inserts a chip of the sacrificial post; verily, he sets it up with its own brilliance.

(6.3.4.2) "May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey," he says; verily, he anoints it with brilliance. (6.3.4.2) "For the plants with good fruit," [he says] as he releases the top-ring onto the post. Therefore, from the top, the plants bear fruit.
Clarified butter is indeed brilliance. The corner facing the fire is commensurate with the sacrificer; when he anoints that corner facing the fire, he anoints the sacrificer himself with brilliance.
He anoints it to the very end; verily, he anoints the sacrificer to the very end with brilliance. He strokes it all around; verily, he bestows brilliance upon him without leaving any part excluded.

"Supporting the sky, fill the mid-region," he says; this is for the separation of these worlds. With a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, he prepares it; for the sacrificial post has Viṣṇu as its deity, so he prepares it with its own deity.
He prepares it with two verses; the sacrificer has two feet, [and this is] for stability.

(6.3.4.4) If he should desire of someone, "May I deprive him of brilliance, of the deities, and of sensory power," he should cause the corner of that [post] facing the Agniṣṭha to lean away from the Āhavanīya fire, either in this manner or that; thus he deprives him of brilliance, of the deities, and of sensory power. (6.3.4.4–5) If he should desire of someone, "May I endow him with brilliance, with the deities, and with sensory power," he should align the corner of that [post] facing the Agniṣṭha with the Āhavanīya fire; thus he endows him with brilliance, with the deities, and with sensory power.

"May you be a winner of Brahman, a winner of Kṣatra," he says; this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula. He winds [the rope] around [the post]; the rope is indeed strength, and the sacrificial post is commensurate with the sacrificer; thus he endows the sacrificer himself with strength. He winds it around at the height of the navel; verily, he bestows strength upon him at the height of the navel. Therefore, they enjoy strength at the height of the navel.
(6.3.4.5) If he should desire of someone, "May I deprive him of strength," he should either pull up its tip or pull it down; thus he deprives him of strength by means of strength itself.

(6.3.4.6) If he should desire, "May Parjanya be rainy," he should pull it down; verily he brings down rain. If he should desire, "May he be without rain," he should pull it up; verily he holds back the rain.

(6.3.4.6) That which is buried belongs to the ancestors; that which is above the buried part up to the girdle belongs to human beings; the girdle belongs to the plants; that which is above the girdle up to the top-ring belongs to the Viśve Devas; (6.3.4.7) that which is above the top-ring up to the *caṣāla* belongs to Indra; the *caṣāla* itself belongs to the Sādhyas. What is left over belongs to the Excess. Indeed, this sacrificial post (*yūpa*) belongs to all the deities; in that he erects the sacrificial post, he gratifies all the deities.

(6.3.4.7) By means of sacrifice, the gods went to the heavenly world. They thought, "Men will follow after us. Having concealed themselves by means of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), they went to the heavenly world. The seers recognized that [world] by means of the sacrificial post alone; that is why the sacrificial post has its name, *yūpa*. (6.3.4.8) In that he erects the sacrificial post, it is for the purpose of discerning the heavenly world.

(6.3.4.8) He measures it in front, for that which is in front of the sacrifice is discerned; for that which has passed by is undiscerned, as they say of it when it is gone: "This was to be done. The Sādhyas, indeed, overthought the sacrifice; the sacrifice did not touch them. What was redundant in the sacrifice, that touched them. This is indeed redundant in the sacrifice, namely, that one churns fire and throws it into the fire. This is redundant. (6.3.4.9) That part of the sacrificial post which is above the *caṣāla* (top-ring)—that is their share; he thereby gratifies them.

(6.3.4.9) When the *soma* sacrifice was completed, the gods indeed lifted up the offering-spoons; they thought of lifting up the sacrificial post, thinking, "We are committing an injury to the sacrifice. They saw the *prastara* grass-bundle as the ransom for the spoons and the *svaru* chip as the ransom for the post. When the *soma* sacrifice is completed, he lifts up the *prastara* and offers it, [and likewise] the *svaru*, so that there shall be no injury to the sacrifice. (6.3.5.1) The Sādhyas, indeed, were the gods in this world; nothing else whatsoever stirred.
(6.3.5.1) They offered Agni himself to Agni for the sake of the sacrifice, for they found nothing else fit to be offered;
from that, indeed, these creatures were produced.
(6.3.5.1) When he churns fire and throws it into the fire, it is for the procreation of offspring.
(6.3.5.1) This fire is indeed Rudra; the sacrificer is the victim.
(6.3.5.1–2) If he were to churn the fire after having immolated the victim, he would deliver the sacrificer over to Rudra.
(6.3.5.2) He would be liable to die prematurely.
(6.3.5.2) Now, however, they say:
(6.3.5.2) "Agni is all the deities; this animal is the oblation."

When, having immolated the victim, he churns the fire, he generates all the deities for the sake of the oblation that has been set forth. One should churn the fire after having brought the victim near; thus it is neither already immolated nor not yet immolated.
"You are the birthplace of Agni," he says;
for this is indeed the birthplace of Agni.
"You two are the testicles," he says.
For these two are testicles;
he says, "Thou art Urvaśī; thou art Āyu," for the sake of pairing.
"Anointed with ghee, bestow virility," he says;
for those who kindle the fire bestow virility. "Be born after the Gāyatrī metre," he says.
(6.3.5.3) By means of the meters he indeed brings him forth.
(6.3.5.3) "Recite for Agni as he is being churned," he says;
he recites a verse addressed to Savitṛ.
(6.3.5.3) Impelled by Savitṛ, he [the Adhvaryu] addresses him with the *mantha* verses. (6.3.5.3–4) "Recite for him as he is born! "Recite for him as he is being hurled forth!"—so he says.
Thus, at every single section (*kāṇḍa*) as it is being performed, he causes him to prosper.
(6.3.5.4) He recites all the Gāyatrī verses; (6.3.5.4) for Agni has the Gāyatrī as his metre; he thus causes him to prosper by means of his own metre.
The fire-altar exists beforehand; having churned the fire, he casts it [upon the altar]. As these two come together, they come together toward the sacrificer.
"Be of one mind for us," he says.
For the sake of pacification, having cast [the fire], he offers an oblation; verily, he bestows food upon him as soon as he is born.
(6.3.5.4) He offers with clarified butter. (6.3.5.4) Clarified butter is indeed the dear abode of Agni; verily, he causes him to prosper through his own dear abode, and also through splendor.
(6.3.6.1) "For food, thee!"—with these words he takes the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), for he who sacrifices is, as it were, one who desires.
(6.3.6.1) "Thou art the invoker," he says, for he indeed brings them near.
(6.3.6.1) "The divine clans have approached the gods," he says, for these clans, being divine, approach the gods.

(6.3.6.1) “The bearers, the eager ones,” he says; for the bearers are indeed the priests and the eager ones are the priests; therefore he speaks thus. (6.3.6.1) “O Bṛhaspati, bestow riches! he says. Bṛhaspati is indeed the sacred power (*brahman*) of the gods; by means of that sacred power, he secures cattle for him.
(6.3.6.2) “May the offerings be sweet to thee! he says; he thereby makes them sweet.

"O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, make the wealth delightful," he says; Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the fashioner of the forms of paired animals; verily, he bestows form upon the cattle. "O wealthy ones, rejoice," he says; the wealthy ones are indeed cattle; verily, he causes cattle to rejoice for him. "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," [he says]; with these words he takes up the cord for the sake of impulsion. "With the arms of the Aśvins," he says, for the Aśvins were the two *adhvaryu* priests among the gods. "With the hands of Pūṣan," he says for the sake of restraint.
(6.3.6.3) “I seize you, O divine oblation, with the noose of *ṛta*,” he says; for *ṛta* is truth; thus he seizes him with truth by means of *ṛta*.
(6.3.6.3) He carries [the victim] around diagonally, for they bind a victim facing backward for the sake of distinction.
(6.3.6.3) “Be bold against men!”—with these words he fastens [it], for the sake of firmness.
(6.3.6.3) "I sprinkle you for the waters, for the plants," he says, for this animal originates from the waters and from the plants.
(6.3.6.4) "You are the drinker of the waters," he says, for he who is undertaken for sacrifice is indeed a drinker of the waters.
(6.3.6.4) "O divine waters, make this well-tasted oblation, which is already tasted by the gods, palatable! he says; thus he indeed makes it palatable.
He sprinkles it from above; verily, he makes it pure from above. He causes it to drink [the water]; verily, he makes it pure within. He sprinkles it from below; verily, he makes it pure on all sides.

(6.3.7.1) By means of Agni, the gods indeed overcame the Asuras through the office of the Hotṛ. "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni as he is being kindled," he says, for the sake of overcoming one's rivals.
He recites seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; Prajāpati is seventeenfold, [and this serves] for the attainment of Prajāpati.
He recites seventeen: twelve months, five seasons—that is the year—and offspring are born after the pattern of the year, for the procreation of offspring.

(6.3.7.1) The gods, having recited the *sāmidhenī* verses, did not perceive the sacrifice. Prajāpati then offered the *āghāra* libation silently; then indeed the gods perceived the sacrifice. In that he offers the *āghāra* libation silently, it is for the illumination of the sacrifice.

(6.3.7.2) The sacrifice was indeed among the Asuras; the gods seized it by means of the silent oblation. In that he offers the *āghāra* libation silently, he thereby seizes the sacrifice of his rival.

(6.3.7.2) He wipes the enclosing-sticks; verily he purifies them. He wipes each three times; for the sacrifice has a threefold course, and also for the smiting away of the Rakṣases. They amount to twelve; twelve are the months of the year; verily he gratifies the year, and also bestows the year upon him for the attainment of the world of heaven. (6.3.7.3) The Āghāra-libation is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and Agni is all the deities. In that he pours the Āghāra-libation, the sacrificer wins all the deities from the very head of the sacrifice.

(6.3.7.3) This libation (*āghāra*) is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the animal is the body. Having poured the libation, he anoints the animal; thus he places the head of the sacrifice back upon its own body.

(6.3.7.4) "May your breath unite with the wind," he says. For the breath has Vāyu as its deity; verily, he offers his breath into Vāyu. "May the limbs unite with the sacrificial objects; may the lord of the sacrifice [unite] with the blessings," he says. Verily, he causes the lord of the sacrifice to attain the blessings.

(6.3.7.4) Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, indeed struck the animal from above; therefore, they do not cut off portions from above the animal. In that he anoints the animal from above, he makes it pure for sacrifice.

(6.3.7.5) He chooses the officiating priests; verily, he chooses the meters. He chooses seven; there are seven domestic animals and seven wild animals, and there are seven meters—for the attainment of both.
He performs eleven fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*); there are ten vital breaths in the animal, and the self is the eleventh. Thus, he sacrifices for the animal in its entirety.
(6.3.7.5) One lies around the omentum; verily, the self lies around the self.

(6.3.7.5) The axe is indeed a thunderbolt, and the splinter of the sacrificial post is a thunderbolt. For the gods, having made ghee into a thunderbolt, struck at Soma. "Anointed with ghee, protect the animal," he says; thus, having brought it under control by means of the thunderbolt, he seizes it.

(6.3.8.1) He carries fire around it; he thus makes it completely offered so that nothing may be spilled, for that which spills from what has been offered is not truly spilled. He carries fire around it three times, for the sacrifice is threefold; moreover, it is for the smiting away of the Rākṣasas. (6.3.8.1) The exponents of the Veda say: "Should one touch the victim or not? Indeed, this victim is led forth unto Death. If he were to touch it, the sacrificer would be liable to die. Yet, on the other hand, they say:

(6.3.8.1) This animal is indeed led forth for the sake of the heavenly world. (6.3.8.2) If he were not to touch it [while leading it], the sacrificer would be excluded from the heavenly world. He touches it with the two omentum-spits; thus it is both touched and untouched. (6.3.8.2) "O Hotṛ, give the command for the oblations to the gods! he says, for a rite is performed only when it has been impelled.
(6.3.8.2) "O wealthy ones, enter the lord of the sacrifice in a friendly manner," he says; this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula.
(6.3.8.2) He goes forward with fire at his head to drive away the Rakṣases.

(6.3.8.2–3) With the words, "Protect [me] from contact with the earth," he throws down the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) so that it does not spill; for that which spills onto the sacrificial grass does not truly spill. Moreover, he thereby establishes it upon the sacrificial grass.
(6.3.8.3) The Adhvaryu turns away from the animal as it is being slaughtered; he thus withdraws from the cattle themselves to avoid injury to himself.

"He who knows thus goes to prosperity and obtains cattle" (6.3.8.3). This wife is led forward from the western world; when he says, "Homage to thy stretchings," it is indeed to the rays of the sun that he pays homage, for the rays are the stretchings. He says, "Go, unhindered! The adversary is indeed the hindrance; [he says this] for the removal of the adversary.

"Along with a stream of ghee, together with offspring, together with the increase of wealth," he says; verily, he invokes this very blessing. "O divine waters, you who seek purity," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula itself.
When an animal has been immolated, pain afflicts its vital breaths.
He says, "May your speech swell; may your breath swell," whereby he pacifies the pain of this [animal] from its very vital breaths.
That pain then enters the earth from the vital breaths.
(6.3.9.1) "Peace with the two days," he says as he brings [the wood] down; verily, by means of day and night, he pacifies the heat from the earth.
(6.3.9.1) "O herb, protect him! O axe, do not harm him! he says; for the axe is indeed the thunderbolt. (6.3.9.2) It is for the sake of pacification.
He cuts from the side, for humans cut from the middle. He cuts across, for humans cut lengthwise; it is for the sake of distinction.

(6.3.9.2) "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases," he says, and having smeared the thick end of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he throws it away; verily, by means of the fleshless part, he expiates the Rakṣases.

(6.3.9.2) "This Rakṣas I lead down to the lowest darkness—him who hates us and whom we hate," he says. There are indeed two kinds of persons: him whom one hates and him who hates one; both of these he leads down to the lowest darkness. (6.3.9.3) "For food thee! he says, and he extracts the omentum (*vapā*); for he who sacrifices is, as it were, in a state of exhaustion.

If he were to pierce [the altar] with one [blade], Rudra would be likely to strike down his cattle; if he were not to pierce it at all, it would be unextended. He pierces with one blade and not with another for the sake of stability.

"With ghee, O Heaven and Earth, cover yourselves," he says; thus he anoints Heaven and Earth with essence. "Unbroken is wealth accompanied by brave sons," he says; this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula.
(6.3.9.4) Verily, he does something cruel when he extracts the omentum; therefore he says, "Go along the wide mid-region," for the sake of pacification.
(6.3.9.4) He who takes hold of the animal as it is being led to death falls away from this world; he takes hold again of the two omentum-spits and thus establishes himself in this very world.
(6.3.9.4) He goes forward with Agni at his head to strike away the Rakṣases, and furthermore, he follows the deities with the oblation. (6.3.9.5) He follows after them.
(6.3.9.5) He should not carry the last ember beyond [the altar]; for if he were to carry the last ember beyond, he would disregard the deity.
(6.3.9.5) "O Vāyu, come to the drops," he says; therefore the drops fall separately.

(6.3.9.5) This, namely the omentum (*vapā*), is the foremost part of animals, and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is the foremost part of plants; thus, by means of the foremost part, he unites it with the foremost part, and furthermore, he establishes the animals in the very plants.

"Recite the offering prayer for the *svāhākṛti*s," he says, for the sake of the sacrifice’s completion. Indeed, the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) is the out-breath and in-breath of the animals, and the omentum (*vapā*) is their body. By sprinkling the speckled butter over the omentum, he places the out-breath and in-breath of the animals into its very body.

"Svāhā! Go to the Maruts of the upward sky! he says; for the Maruts of the upward sky used to carry away the omentum-offering spits of the gods. With that very [formula], he thus carries them away. He carries them away in opposite directions; therefore, the out-breath and in-breath move in opposite directions.

(6.3.10.1) Having immolated the animal, he offers the sacrificial cake; thus he immolates it together with its fuel. (6.3.10.1) Having proceeded with the omentum, he proceeds with the sacrificial cake. The sacrificial cake is indeed strength; verily he places strength in the midst of the cattle. Moreover, he mends the breach of the animal itself. Having taken up the speckled butter, he asks three times:
(6.3.10.1) "The oblation is cooked, O Śamitr," [he says], for the gods are fond of the threefold truth; he who says that what is uncooked is cooked incurs sin.

(6.3.10.1–2) These two, the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), are indeed the out-breath and the in-breath of animals. When an animal has been immolated, its heart comes together with its self (*ātman*). In that he bastes the heart with speckled butter, he places the out-breath and in-breath of the animals in its very self.
By means of the animal, the gods went to the heavenly world; they reflected: [...]

(6.3.10.2) "Men will follow after us," [they thought]. Having cut off his head, they let the sacrificial essence (*medha*) flow away; it became the *plakṣa* tree. That is why the *plakṣa* has its name. In that there is a *plakṣa* branch as the upper layer of the sacrificial grass (*uttarabarhis*), he cuts portions from the animal sacrifice as one possessing that very sacrificial essence.
(6.3.10.3) Indeed, the Rakṣases follow after the animal when it is being carried away. He carries it between the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the Āhavanīya fire in order to strike down the Rakṣases.
When the animal has been seized for sacrifice, its mind departs.

"Recite the invitatory prayer for the *manotā* as the oblation is being cut," he says; thus he secures the mind of this [victim]. He cuts eleven portions; for there are ten vital breaths in the animal, and the self is the eleventh. In its entirety, as great as the animal is, he cuts it. First he cuts from the heart, then from the tongue, then from the breast. For what one perceives with the heart, that one speaks with the tongue; what one speaks with the tongue, that one utters forth from the chest.

(6.3.10.4) This indeed is the proper order for the animal sacrifice: for him who, having thus taken the portions from the preceding parts, takes the portions of the subsequent parts according to his desire, the taking of this animal’s portions becomes truly in the proper order.
(6.3.10.4) He takes a portion of the intestinal fat from the middle, for the vital breath is in the middle; he takes a portion of the last part [the tail] from the top.
(6.3.10.5) For the breath is supreme; whether it be the one or the other, both together are indeed non-violent (*ajāmi*).

(6.3.10.5) When being born, a Brāhmaṇa is born burdened with three debts: he owes the sages his studentship (*brahmacarya*), the gods his sacrifice, and the ancestors his progeny. He is indeed free from debt who has a son, who is a sacrificer, and who has lived as a student. It is by means of these portions that he pays off [the debts]; this is why they are called "portions" (*avadāna*). (6.3.10.5) The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. Those gods said to Agni:

"By you as a hero, may we overcome the Asuras! He said, "I shall choose a boon: let me take out a choice portion (*uddhāra*) from the animal. He took out this choice portion: the fore-arm from the front half, the intestines from the middle, and the hip from the rear half. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. In that he cuts portions from these three limbs, it is for the sake of overcoming his rival; he prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated.
He cuts across the diagonal; therefore animals move their limbs across the diagonal for the sake of stability.

(6.3.11.1) He covers the two offering-spoons with fat; cattle are indeed of the nature of fat; verily, he bestows form upon the cattle. (6.3.11.1) Having placed [the fat] in the broth, he covers it; this broth is indeed the essence of cattle; verily, he bestows essence upon the cattle. (6.3.11.1) He mixes the oblation of the omentum-fat with the rib; the rib is indeed the middle part of cattle, and the omentum-fat is the essence of cattle; in that he mixes the oblation of the omentum-fat with the rib, he bestows essence upon the cattle from their very center.

(6.3.11.1) They indeed kill the victim when they quiet it. The out-breath (*prāṇa*) has Indra as its deity, and the in-breath (*apāna*) has Indra as its deity. "May the out-breath settle limb by limb," he says; thus he places both the out-breath and the in-breath into the victims.

(6.3.11.2) "O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, let your abundance come together," he says, for cattle have Tvaṣṭṛ as their deity. "When you, though of diverse forms, become of one mark," he says, for these, being of diverse forms, now become of one mark at the invocation.

"Going to the gods for help, may your friends, mother, and father rejoice after you"—with these words he says, "He makes him go to the heavenly world with the approval of his mother and father. At the half-verse he offers the *vasā* oblation; for that half-verse is yonder [heaven] and this half-verse is this [earth]; thus he anoints these two very worlds with essence. He offers to the quarters; thus he anoints the quarters with essence, and moreover, he wins strength and essence from the quarters.

The speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) is indeed the out-breath and in-breath (*prāṇāpāna*) of animals; for animals belong to the deity Vanaspati. When he has taken a portion of the speckled butter and says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Vanaspati! Give the command for Vanaspati!", he thereby places the out-breath and in-breath within the animals.
He cuts off portions from each different part; therefore, animals are of various forms.
(6.3.11.4) He sprinkles with broth; for this broth is the essence of cattle, and thus he places essence into the cattle.
(6.3.11.4) He invokes the *iḍā*; for the *iḍā* is cattle, and thus he invokes cattle. He invokes four times, for cattle are four-footed.
Regarding whomsoever he may desire: (6.3.11.5) [he should act accordingly].

(6.3.11.5) "He would be without cattle," [thinking thus], one should give him [the portion] without fat; for cattle are of the nature of fat. Thus, by means of their very form, he excludes him from cattle, and he indeed becomes without cattle.

(6.3.11.5) For whomsoever he may desire, "May he be rich in cattle," one should give him [the portion] with fat; for cattle are of the nature of fat. Thus, by means of their very form, he wins cattle for him, and he indeed becomes rich in cattle.

(6.3.11.5) Prajāpati created the sacrifice; he created the clarified butter (*ājya*) in front, the animal in the middle, and the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) behind. Therefore, the fore-offerings (*prayāja*) are performed with clarified butter, the animal offering in the middle, and the after-offerings (*anūyāja*) with speckled butter. Thus, this [speckled butter] is, as it were, mixed, for it was created last. (6.3.11.6) He performs eleven after-offerings. There are ten vital breaths in an animal, and the self (*ātman*) is the eleventh; he thus sacrifices according to the full extent of the animal.

(6.3.11.6) Indeed, they kill the animal when they quiet it. Now, speckled butter is indeed the out-breath and in-breath of animals; in that he performs the after-offerings with speckled butter, he places the out-breath and in-breath back into the animals.

(6.4.1.1) By means of the sacrifice, Prajāpati indeed created offspring; he created them by means of the *upayaj* offerings. When the sacrificer performs the *upayaj* offerings, he thereby creates offspring.
(6.4.1.1) He cuts from the hind part;
for from the hind part offspring are produced. He cuts from the thick part.
(6.4.1.1) For from that which is solid, offspring are born.
(6.4.1.1) He cuts off [the portions] without piercing through, for the non-piercing of the vital breaths. (6.4.1.1) He does not turn [the flesh] over.
(6.4.1.1) If he were to turn it back, there would be a disorder of the upward breath (*udāvarta*), and offspring would be seized by disease.
(6.4.1.1) "Go to the ocean, svāhā! he says. (6.4.1.1–2) Thus he bestows semen.
"Go to the intermediate space, svāhā! he says.
By means of the intermediate space itself, he causes offspring to be born for him;
for it is after the intermediate space that offspring are born.
"Go to the god Savitṛ, svāhā! he says; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he procreates offspring for him.
"Go to day and night, svāhā! he says.
(6.4.1.2) By means of day and night alone he procreates offspring for him;
for it is in accordance with day and night that offspring are born.
(6.4.1.3) "Go to Mitra and Varuṇa, svāhā!"—thus he says.
(6.4.1.3) He places the out-breath and the in-breath in the offspring that have been born.
(6.4.1.3) "Go to Soma, svāhā! he says, for offspring have Soma as their deity.
"Go to the sacrifice, svāhā! he says;
verily, he makes the offspring worthy of sacrifice.
"Go to the meters, svāhā! he says.
The meters are indeed cattle;
verily he wins cattle.
"Go to heaven and earth, svāhā! he says.
He encloses the offspring already born on both sides by means of heaven and earth.
"Go to the celestial realm, svāhā! he says;
thus, he bestows rain upon the offspring already born.
‘Go to Agni Vaiśvānara, svāhā! he says;
verily, he establishes the offspring already born upon this earth.
Indeed, he who cuts off a portion of the rectum cuts away the vital breaths.
"Grant my mind, grant my heart," he says;
thus he invokes the vital breaths to their respective places. For when an animal has been immolated, its pain reaches the heart.

That [sacrificial post] comes together with the heart-spike. If one were to set down the heart-spike on the earth, he would afflict the earth with pain; if [he were to set it down] in the waters, he would afflict the waters with pain.
He causes it to rise up at the junction of the dry and the moist for the pacification of both.
He should meditate upon whomsoever he hates;
he thus strikes him with impurity.
(6.4.2.1) The gods indeed divided the sacrifice at the Āgnīdhra fire-hall.
(6.4.2.1) Then, that which remained over, they said: "Let this remain for us."
(6.4.2.1) That is why the *vasatīvarī* waters are called *vasatīvarī*.
(6.4.2.1) They were not able to reach it in the morning;
they caused it to enter into the waters.
(6.4.2.1) They became the *vasatīvarī* waters;
(6.4.2.1) he draws the *vasatīvarī* waters;
(6.4.2.1) the *vasatīvarī* waters are indeed the sacrifice.
(6.4.2.1) Having undertaken and taken hold of the sacrifice itself, he performs the *upavasatha* rite.
(6.4.2.1) If the sun were to set upon him while the [Soma] has not yet been drawn, his sacrifice would remain uncommenced; he would cut the sacrifice asunder.

(6.4.2.2) He should either draw [the Soma] when the light is still visible, or having placed gold [in the vessel], he draws it from those [plants] that possess luster. Thus, he indeed draws from those that are radiant.
Or, one may take [the water] from the jars of a Brāhmaṇa who has performed many sacrifices, for he is one who has already taken the *vasatīvarī* waters;
[thereby] one takes the *vasatīvarī* waters.
The Vasatīvarī waters are indeed cattle;
he stays overnight having taken hold of and grasped the cattle themselves.
If he were to take them while standing facing along [the stream], the cattle would tend to stray away from him.
Standing facing the opposite direction, he draws [the cup];
verily, by obstructing them, he secures cattle for him.
Indra slew Vṛtra.
He died within the waters.
That which among them was pure, fit for sacrifice, and possessed of the gods, was released;
they became flowing rivers.
He takes [the water] from flowing waters;
he takes from those very waters which are pure, fit for sacrifice, and accompanied by the gods.
He should not pass over the nearest flowing waters.

(6.4.2.3) If he were to pass over the waters that flow nearest [the altar], he would disregard the sacrifice. (6.4.2.3) He should not take water from stagnant sources; for stagnant waters are indeed seized by Varuṇa.
(6.4.2.3) If he were to take [the water] from stationary things, Varuṇa would cause his sacrifice to be seized.
(6.4.2.4) For when it is day, night enters the waters;
therefore, the waters appear copper-colored by day.
(6.4.2.4) That which becomes night, the waters indeed enter the day;
(6.4.2.4) therefore the waters appear bright at night. He takes [the water] at the junction of shadow and sunlight.
(6.4.2.4) He takes on the color of day and night for him.
(6.4.2.4) "These waters are rich in oblation," he says;
thus he takes them as those already prepared with the oblation.
"May he be possessed of the oblation," he says; "Sūrya," he says; thus he draws [the draught] of those that are bright. He draws with an *anuṣṭubh* verse.
The *anuṣṭubh* is indeed speech;
verily, by means of speech in its entirety, he takes them up.
He takes them up with a four-footed verse.
He sets it down three times;
they amount to seven;
the *śakvarī* consists of seven feet.
The Śakvarī verses are cattle;
verily, he wins cattle for himself.
For this world the Gārhapatya fire is established, and for yonder world the Āhavanīya fire.
If he were to place it near the Gārhapatya fire, he would possess cattle in this world;
if he were to place it near the Āhavanīya fire, he would possess cattle in that world. Therefore, he places it near both.
(6.4.2.6) He thus makes him possessed of cattle in both worlds; (6.4.2.6) he carries it around on all sides for the smiting away of the Rakṣases.
"You are the share of Indra and Agni," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula itself. The Āgnīdhra priest causes them to settle nearby.
(6.4.2.6) This, indeed, is the unconquered part of the sacrifice, namely the Āgnīdhra shed.
By means of that very part of the sacrifice which is unconquered, he causes them to dwell together.
For wherever there is anything left undone in the sacrifice when it has been spread out, along that path the Rakṣases descend upon the sacrifice.
In that he draws from the flowing waters, he thus causes the sacrifice to lie as it is being performed,
so that the *rakṣases* may not enter;
for these [waters] do not falter.
They lie around until the third pressing,
for the continuity of the sacrifice.
(6.4.3.1) The exponents of Brahman say:
"He indeed should be the Adhvaryu who, when bringing down the Soma, brings it down for all the deities. (6.4.3.1) He says, "For the heart, thee!"—by this, he acts for the sake of human beings.

‘To the mind thee! he says; by this he makes it for the fathers. ‘To the sky thee! To Sūrya thee! he says; by this he makes it for the gods. So many indeed are the deities; to all of them he brings it down.
Before the utterance of speech, he introduces the Prātaranuvāka; as much as there is of speech, that he secures.

(6.4.3.2) He utters speech first with the word "water. Water is indeed the sacrifice; thus he releases his speech toward the sacrifice itself. (6.4.3.2) He recites all the meters. The meters are indeed cattle; thus he wins cattle for himself. For one desiring splendor, he should conclude with the *gāyatrī*; for one desiring power, with the *triṣṭubh*; for one desiring cattle, with the *jagatī*; for one desiring stability, with the *anuṣṭubh*; for one desiring the sacrifice, with the *paṅkti*; and for one desiring food, with the *virāj*.
"May Agni hear my call with his kindling-stick," he says. Thus, impelled by Savitṛ and having announced [the sacrifice] to the deities, he approaches the waters.
"O Hotṛ, send forth the waters," he says; for a rite is performed only when it is sent forth.
"O Camasādhvaryu of the Maitrāvaruṇa, come hither! he says; for Mitra and Varuṇa are the leaders of the waters; through them indeed he approaches them.

"O divine waters, O offspring of the waters," he says; thus, having ransomed them by means of an oblation, he draws [the water]. Moreover, he draws [the water] from those that have been prepared as the sacrificial offering and sprinkled with clarified butter.
(6.4.3.4) "Thou art the furrower," he says; verily he causes their impurity to float away.

(6.4.3.4) "Lift them up for the swelling of the ocean," he says; therefore the waters, though being eaten and drunk, are not exhausted. The pit is indeed the womb of the sacrifice; the Vasatīvarī waters are the sacrifice. Having brought the Hotṛ’s cup and the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup into contact, he pours out the Vasatīvarī waters for the sake of providing a common womb for the sacrifice.
(6.4.3.4) Moreover, he thus causes them to be born from their own womb. (6.4.3.4) "O Adhvaryu, do thou protect!"—thus he says. "Apā3!"—thus he says.
"And so they have eaten, and so behold these!"—this is indeed what he says when, if it is an Agniṣṭoma, he offers an oblation;
if it is an Ukthya, he wipes [the ladle] on the enclosing-stick; and if it is an Atirātra, he enters while reciting a Yajus formula, for the sake of distinguishing between the sacrificial rites.
(6.4.4.1) "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," with these words he takes up the pressing-stone for the sake of impulsion.
(6.4.4.1) "With the arms of the Aśvins," he says.
"For the Aśvins were the Adhvaryu priests of the gods. "With the hands of Pūṣan," he says for the sake of restraint.
Soma is indeed cattle; the Upāṃśusavana stone is the out-breath.
In that he measures out [the Soma] toward the *upāṃśusavana* stone, he bestows the diffused breath (*vyāna*) upon the cattle.
He measures it out, saying, "For Indra thee! For Indra thee!
For it is for Indra that the Soma is brought forth.
(6.4.4.1) He measures five times with a sacrificial formula.
The *paṅkti* consists of five syllables; the sacrifice is fivefold.
Verily, he wins the sacrifice itself.
Five times silently;
they amount to ten;
the *virāj* consists of ten syllables.
Food is the *virāj*; by means of the *virāj* he wins the enjoyment of food.
"Ye are invigorating, ye are conquerors of Vṛtra," he says.
(6.4.4.2) This, indeed, is the Soma-draught of the waters. He who knows thus does not meet with misfortune in the waters.
(6.4.4.2) "O Soma, that light of thine which is in heaven," he says.
(6.4.4.2) From these very worlds he gathers him together.
(6.4.4.3) King Soma, indeed, gazed upon the quarters;
he entered into the quarters.
"Eastward, westward, northward, southward," he says;
verily from the quarters he gathers him together, and thus he wins the quarters for himself.
"O mother, come hither! he says.
(6.4.4.3) Women become desirous of him who knows thus.
(6.4.4.3–4) "That which is yours, O Soma, the invincible name, the watchful," he says.
This indeed is the drinking of Soma from Soma.
(6.4.4.4) He who knows thus does not meet with misfortune related to Soma.
(6.4.4.4) For they indeed kill this Soma when they press it;
he takes up the stalks.
(6.4.4.4) He indeed protects him.
(6.4.4.4) The stalks are the vital breaths; Soma is the cattle.
He pours the stalks back again.
Verily, he places the vital breaths in the animals;
he emits them two by two,
and therefore the vital breaths are in pairs.
The Upāṃśu cup is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Since the cups are drawn with the Upāṃśu as the first, they proceed following after the vital breath.
Aruṇa Aupaveśi used to say:
"I establish the sacrifice at the morning pressing itself; with it, once thus established, I proceed.
He presses [the Soma] eight times first;
the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables.
The morning pressing belongs to the *gāyatrī* meter;
by this, he obtains the morning pressing itself.
He recites the second [verse] eleven times.
The *triṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables;
the midday pressing belongs to the *triṣṭubh*. By this, he obtains the midday pressing itself.
The third [libation] is twelve times;
the jagatī has twelve syllables,
and the third pressing belongs to the jagatī.
By this, he indeed attains the third pressing. This, truly, he declared to be the completion of the sacrifice, so that nothing may be spilled.
For that which spills from the sacrifice once it has been completed is indeed imperishable.
Moreover, they say:
"The Gāyatrī at the morning pressing is indeed not subject to censure."
(6.4.5.2) One who knows this becomes such that his rival does not speak him down.
(6.4.5.3) Therefore, it should be pressed eight times each. The exponents of sacred knowledge say: [this is so].
(6.4.5.3) "The other cups are drawn with strainers; what is the strainer for the *upāṃśu*?
(6.4.5.3) "One should say: 'Speech is its strainer.
(6.4.5.3) "'Flow pure for the Lord of Speech, O vigorous one,' he says."
(6.4.5.3) By means of speech itself he purifies him.
(6.4.5.3) "With the two shoots of the bull," he says;
for these two shoots indeed belong to the bull that is Soma.
"Purified by the rays," he says; for indeed, he purifies him with the rays.
"Thou art the god, the purifier of the gods," he says.
"For he is indeed a god" (6.4.5.3). "The purifier of the gods; for those whose portion you are, to them [I take] you," he says (6.4.5.4);
for he takes this [soma] for those whose portion it is.
"Thou art made one's own," he says; verily, he has made his own the vital breath. "Make our offerings honey-sweet," he says.
(6.4.5.4) "He makes all this palatable for him.
(6.4.5.4) "For all thy faculties, celestial and terrestrial," he says;
(6.4.5.4) thus he bestows the vital breaths upon both gods and men.
"May mind consume you," he says; verily, he attains the mind.
"Go along the wide atmosphere," he says.
For breath has the intermediate region as its deity.
"Svāhā! To thee, O well-being-born, for Sūrya! he says;
for the well-being-born gods are indeed the vital breaths.
(6.4.5.5) He offers among them in secret.
(6.4.5.5) "To the gods who drink the rays, thee! he says.
For the rays of the sun are indeed the gods who drink the rays.
That is their share;
he gratifies them with that, if he so desires.
"If Parjanya should be rainy," [he thinks], he should wipe downward with his hand;
thus he brings down the rain itself,
if he so desires.
(6.4.5.6) If he should think, "May it not rain," he should wipe [the fire] with the palm turned upward;
thus he brings forth the rain itself.
(6.4.5.6) If he should practice sorcery, he should say: "Kill so-and-so, and then I shall offer you as an oblation."
(6.4.5.6) He kills him by striking him as if he were a sacrificial oblation.
(6.4.5.6) If he should be at a distance, he should stand until he is exhausted; having followed after his breath, he kills him.
(6.4.5.6) If he should practice sorcery, he should set it down [with the formula]: "I set thee down in the breath of so-and-so.
(6.4.5.7) For the breath is indeed unestablished; verily, he thus establishes his breath.
He purifies him with six rays;
for there are six seasons;
verily, he purifies him by means of the seasons.
He purifies it three times;
these worlds are three;
verily, by means of these very worlds he purifies it.
(6.4.5.7) The exponents of Brahman say:
(6.4.5.7) "By what truth are there three animals that seize with their hands? (It is because) he seizes [the Soma] three times silently with his hand.
Therefore, among animals, there are three that grasp with their hands: man, the elephant, and the monkey.
Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did that as well.
Those gods saw that the sacrifice was to be completed in the *upāṃśu* [whispered] manner;
they completed it in the *upāṃśu* manner.
(6.4.6.1) Those Asuras, having raised the thunderbolt, advanced against the gods.
(6.4.6.1) Terrified, those gods ran to Indra for protection. (6.4.6.1) Indra separated them from [the sacrifice] by means of the Antaryāma cup.
(6.4.6.1) That is the reason for the *antaryāma*’s name as *antaryāma*.
(6.4.6.1) In that the *antaryāma* cup is drawn, the sacrificer thereby places his rivals within himself.
(6.4.6.1–2) “Within thee I place heaven and earth; within the wide mid-air,” he says.
By these very worlds, the sacrificer excludes his rivals.
Those gods reflected:
"Indra has indeed become all this that we once were."
They said,
"O Maghavan, grant us a share.
He replied, "In harmony with the gods, both those below and those above."
"Both those gods who are higher and those who are lower—him he causes to share in both," [the text] says; "In harmony with the gods, both the lower and the higher," he says;
thus he causes both those gods who are higher and those who are lower to share in it.
"In the Antaryāma cup, O Maghavan, rejoice," he says;
thus he does not exclude the sacrificer from the sacrifice.
"Thou art taken with a support," he says.
(6.4.6.3) For the support of the out-breath:
if both [the breaths] were to be taken while unpurified, the out-breath would follow after the in-breath; he would be liable to die prematurely.
(6.4.6.3) The Antaryāma cup is drawn with the purifier.
(6.4.6.4) For the separation of the out-breath and the in-breath.
(6.4.6.4) These two, the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma [cups], are indeed the out-breath and the in-breath; the Upāṃśusavana [stone] is the diffused breath (vyāna).
Regarding whomsoever one might desire—
(6.4.6.4) [Thinking,] "He might die," one should set down those two [cups] without touching them.
(6.4.6.4) By means of the *vyāna* alone, he cuts off his *prāṇa* and *apāna*; (6.4.6.4) he dies instantly.
(6.4.6.4) If he should desire of someone, "May he attain a full lifespan," he should set those two down in contact with each other for him;
by means of the *vyāna* breath, he thus unites his out-breath (*prāṇa*) and in-breath (*apāna*).
He reaches a full lifespan.
This [cup] for Indra and Vāyu is indeed speech.
When the cups are drawn with that for Indra and Vāyu first, they proceed following speech itself.
The gods said to Vāyu:
"Let us slay King Soma," they said. He replied, "I shall choose a boon: let the cups be drawn for you beginning with me."
Therefore, the cups are drawn beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu. They struck him; he became putrid.
The gods could not overpower him;
they said to Vāyu,
"Make this palatable for us."
He said, "I choose a boon: let your vessels be called after me alone. Therefore, although they belong to various deities, they are called *vāyavya* (dedicated to Vāyu).
Vāyu indeed made it palatable for them.
Therefore, whatever becomes putrid, they hang out in a strong wind;
for Vāyu is its purifier and its maker of what is palatable.
(6.4.7.2) They could not find a way to divide it.
Aditi said: "I choose a boon; then you shall divide it through me. Your Soma-pressings shall have me as their deity. (6.4.7.3) "Are they pressed? they asked. "They are," she replied.
He says, "Thou art taken with a support," because they belong to Aditi as their deity. For those vessels which are made of wood have originated from her womb;
those which are made of clay are directly from her.
Therefore, he says this:
"Speech indeed spoke away, unarticulated;
those gods said to Indra:"
"Expound this speech of ours," [they said].
He replied, "I shall choose a boon: let this cup be drawn for both me and Vāyu together."
Therefore, the draught for Indra and Vāyu is drawn together.
Indra, having stepped into its midst, separated it;
therefore, this speech is uttered as something distinct.
Therefore, it is drawn once for Indra from the middle, and twice for Vāyu;
for he chose two boons.
(6.4.8.1) The gods said to Mitra, "Let us slay King Soma.
He replied:
"I am not [the friend] of everyone, nor am I the friend of anyone," he said.
They replied to him, "Let us kill him!"
He said, "I choose a boon: let me mix the Soma with milk.
Therefore, they mix the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk.

(6.4.8.1) Therefore the cattle departed from him, saying, "Being Mitra, he has committed a cruel act. (6.4.8.1) Indeed, he who sacrifices with Soma performs what is truly cruel. (6.4.8.2) He who sacrifices with Soma performs what is indeed cruel.
Therefore, cattle depart [from him].
In that he mixes the oblation for Mitra and Varuṇa with milk, he thereby causes Mitra to prosper through cattle and the sacrificer to prosper through cattle.
Indeed, it was formerly known to Mitra in this way.
(6.4.8.2) "The cattle will step away from me who has committed a cruel act," [thinking thus],
(6.4.8.2) he chose in this manner.
(6.4.8.2) The gods said to Varuṇa:
"Let us slay King Soma with you as our ally," he said. He replied, "I shall choose a boon: let this [cup] be drawn for me and for Mitra together."
Therefore, the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa is drawn together.
Therefore, they strike a king with one who is a king by birth, a Vaiśya with a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra with a Śūdra.
Indeed, this world was neither day nor night; it was undifferentiated.
Those gods said to Mitra and Varuṇa, "Make this manifest for us. They both replied:
(6.4.8.3) "Let us choose a boon: let one cup alone be drawn first.
(6.4.8.3) Therefore, the cup for Indra and Vāyu is drawn before the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa;
for these two, the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups, are indeed out-breath and in-breath.
Mitra generated the day, Varuṇa the night; from that, indeed, this world became manifest. Therefore, when the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa is drawn, it is for the sake of manifestation.
The head of the sacrifice was cut off. The gods said to the Aśvins, "You two are indeed physicians; restore this head of the sacrifice."
The two of them said, "Let us choose a boon: let a cup be drawn for us here as well.
For them, they drew this cup for the Aśvins.
(6.4.9.1) Thereupon, those two indeed restored the head of the sacrifice.
(6.4.9.1) In that the cup for the Aśvins is drawn, it is for the restoration of the sacrifice.
(6.4.9.1) Regarding this, the gods said to them:
(6.4.9.1) "These two who move among men are indeed unpurified," (6.4.9.2) "they are physicians.
(6.4.9.2) Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not practice medicine, for he who is a physician is unpurified and impure.
(6.4.9.2) Having purified those two by means of the *bahispavamāna* chant, they drew this cup for the Aśvins from them.

Therefore, when the *bahiṣpavamāna* has been chanted, the *āśvina* cup is drawn. For this very reason, one who knows thus should approach the *bahiṣpavamāna*; for the *bahiṣpavamāna* is indeed a means of purification (*pavitra*), and he purifies his own self.
They distributed the healing power of those two in three parts.
(6.4.9.2) One third [of the oblation] is in the fire, one third in the waters, and one third in the Brāhmaṇa.
(6.4.9.3) Therefore, having placed a vessel of water nearby and having seated a Brāhmaṇa to the south, one should perform the healing rite.
Whatever healing rite he performs with that [water], it becomes effective for him.
(6.4.9.3) The exponents of Brahman say:
(6.4.9.3) "On what basis is it that the cups for two deities are drawn in one vessel but offered in two vessels?
(6.4.9.3) Because they are drawn in one vessel, therefore there is one vital breath within; because they are offered in two vessels, therefore there are two by two vital breaths on the outside.

(6.4.9.3) These offerings to the dual deities are indeed the vital breaths, and the *iḍā* is the cattle; if one were to invoke the *iḍā* before the offerings to the dual deities, [it would be as if one were to take the cattle away from the vital breaths].
(6.4.9.4) If he were to place the vital breaths within himself by means of the sacrificial animals, he would be liable to die.
(6.4.9.4) Having consumed the portions for the dual deities, he invokes the *iḍā*;
thus, having placed the vital breaths within himself, he invokes the sacrificial animals.
Speech indeed belongs to the cup for Indra and Vāyu, the eye to that for Mitra and Varuṇa, and the ear to that for the Aśvins.

He consumes the cup for Indra and Vāyu first; therefore, one speaks with speech from the front. He consumes the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa next; therefore, one sees with the eye from the front. He consumes the cup for the Aśvins by moving it all around; therefore, one hears with the ear from all sides.
(6.4.9.4) These offerings to the dual deities are indeed the vital breaths.

He sets down the vessels so that they are not empty; therefore the vital breaths within are not empty. For indeed, when a rite of the sacrifice that has been spread out is not performed, the Rakṣases descend upon it.
In that he sets down the vessels so that they are not empty, that part of the sacrifice which is being performed remains intact, so that the Rakṣases do not descend upon it.

(6.4.9.5) He places [the Soma] on the northern track of the southern *havirdhāna* cart; verily, he bestows speech upon speech. (6.4.9.5) They lie around until the third pressing for the continuity of the sacrifice.
(6.4.10.1) Bṛhaspati was the domestic priest of the gods; Śaṇḍa and Marka were those of the Asuras.
The gods were possessed of the *brahman*, and the asuras were possessed of the *brahman*. They were unable to overcome one another.
Those gods then took counsel with Śaṇḍa and Marka.
The two of them said, "Let us choose a boon: let these two cups indeed be drawn for us here as well.
For them, they drew these two, the Śukra and the Manthin.
(6.4.10.1) Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.

(6.4.10.1) For one who knows thus, when the Śukra and Manthin cups are drawn, he prospers in himself and his rival is defeated. (6.4.10.2) His rival is indeed defeated; those two [cups] the gods set aside and offered to Indra for themselves.
"Driven away are Śaṇḍa and Marka together with so-and-so," he should say, naming whomsoever he hates. With him whom he hates, he drives these two away.
"He is the first fashioner, the maker of all"—with these words they offered them as a sacrifice for Indra from their own selves.
(6.4.10.2) For Indra, repeatedly assuming these forms, moved about.
(6.4.10.2) Yonder sun is indeed the *śukra* (the bright cup), and the moon is the *manthin* (the stirred cup).
(6.4.10.2–3) Having closed their eyes, the two step forth toward the east.
Therefore, those going eastward do not see; turning westward, they offer the oblation;
therefore, those going westward see.
The Śukra and Manthin vessels are indeed the two eyes of the sacrifice, and the high altar is the nose. They offer the oblations while walking around on both sides;
therefore, the two eyes are on both sides of the nose.
Therefore, the two eyes are held apart by the nose;
they move all around for the purpose of driving away the *rakṣases*.
Indeed, whatever eastern oblations the gods offered, with those they drove out the Asuras who were in the east.
With those [oblations] which are directed westward, they drove away the Asuras who were behind.
Other oblations are offered facing east, while the *śukra* and *manthin* cups face west;
thus the sacrificer drives his rivals away both from behind and from the front.
"Therefore, offspring are impregnated facing away, but they are born facing toward [the parent].
Indeed, offspring are born after the *śukra* and *manthin* cups—both the eaters and those who are eaten.

"Generating offspring rich in heroes, go around with the bright [cup], O *śukra*, with your bright luster! "Generating offspring rich in progeny, go around with the stirred [cup], O *manthin*, with your stirred luster! so he says.
(6.4.10.5) These indeed are the "good heroes," namely those who eat;
these are the "good offspring," namely those who are eaten.
He who knows thus, his offspring is born as eaters, not as those who are eaten.
The eye of Prajāpati swelled;
it fell away;
it entered the vikaṅkata tree.
It did not find rest in the *vikaṅkata* tree;
it entered the barley;
it found rest in the barley.
That is why barley is called *yava*.
As for the fact that the churning-vessel is made of *vikaṅkata* wood: he mixes it with groats; thereby he restores the eye of Prajāpati.
The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say:
(6.4.10.6) Why does the *manthipātra* not enter the *sadas* while the [other] cups are present?
(6.4.10.6) One should say: "Because it is a cup for one who is afflicted.
(6.4.10.6) If it were to enter, the *adhvaryu* would become blind and would meet with calamity.
Therefore, he does not attain it.
Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did that as well.
The gods perceived the cups to have the Āgrayaṇa as their first; they drew them.
(6.4.11.1) From that, indeed, they attained preeminence.
For one who knows thus, when the cups are drawn with the Āgrayaṇa as the first, he attains preeminence among his peers.
One who has rivals should draw [the cups] with a verse containing the word "broken" (*rugṇavatī*).
Having indeed taken away the splendor of his rival, he moves to the forefront among his equals.
"O gods, you who are eleven in heaven," he says.
(6.4.11.2) There are indeed so many deities; from all of them he draws it for him.
(6.4.11.2) "This is your womb; for the All-gods you," he says, for it belongs to the All-gods by its deity.

(6.4.11.2) Speech indeed departed from the gods, refusing to remain for the sacrifice. When speech had departed, the gods drew the cups in silence. Speech reflected, "They are excluding me," and she returned to the Āgrayaṇa vessel.
That is the reason for the Āgrayaṇa's name.
Therefore, at the Āgrayaṇa, speech is released.
Since the earlier cups are drawn in silence, it is like a hunter who, thinking, "The animal's track extends this far;
I shall not miss it," lets go his arrow. In the very same way, the Adhvaryu, having drawn the Āgrayaṇa and commenced the sacrifice, releases his speech.

He utters the *hiṃ* three times; thus he chooses the Udgātṛs. This Āgrayaṇa cup is indeed Prajāpati; when, having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, he utters the *hiṃ*, it is Prajāpati himself who thereby smells his offspring. Therefore, a cow smells her newborn calf.
The Āgrayaṇa cup is indeed the self of the sacrifice; by drawing it at each pressing, he extends the sacrifice within his own self.
He pours it down from above; thereby he bestows seed. He draws it up from below; thereby he causes procreation.
(6.4.11.4) The exponents of Brahman say: "By what truth does the Gāyatrī, being the smallest of the meters, carry all the pressings?
(6.4.11.4) This Āgrayaṇa cup is indeed the calf of the Gāyatrī; by turning toward it, she carries all the pressings.
Therefore, when the calf has been driven away, the cow turns back toward it.
(6.5.1.1) Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra.
(6.5.1.1) That Vṛtra was afraid of the raised thunderbolt. He said:
"Do not strike me; there is indeed this vigor within me, and I shall give that to you. He offered him the Ukthya cup. He held up a second one for him.
He said, "Do not strike me; there is indeed this vigor within me, and I shall bestow it upon you."
To him he gave the Ukthya itself;
for him he raised up the third [libation];
Viṣṇu stood by him.
"Kill!
he said. He replied, "Do not strike me; there is indeed this vigor within me, and I shall bestow it upon you."
He gave him the Ukthya itself;
he struck it down when it had become devoid of *māyā*,
for the sacrifice was its *māyā*.
(6.5.1.2) When the Ukthya cup is drawn, it is indeed sensory power. (6.5.1.3) By that, the sacrificer wrests away the virility of his rival.
(6.5.1.3) "For Indra, thee, the possessor of the great and the possessor of vigor," he says;
for he gave it to Indra.
"To him for thee, to Viṣṇu for thee," he says; because Viṣṇu stood by [the sacrifice],
saying "Slay!", therefore he shares out a portion to Viṣṇu.
He draws it out three times;
for thrice indeed did he give it to him. "This is thy womb; thou art the oblation again," he says.
Again and again he draws [the Soma] from us;
for the Ukthya is indeed the eye of the sacrifice;
therefore, once the Ukthya has been offered, the other Soma draughts follow it.
Therefore, the self follows after the eye;
therefore, when one goes, many follow after him;
therefore, one among many becomes blessed.
Therefore, one man obtains many wives.
If the Adhvaryu should desire,
"May I endow myself with the glory of the sacrifice," he should pour [the water] down while standing between the Āhavanīya fire and the Havirdhāna shed.
(6.5.1.5) He bestows the glory of the sacrifice upon himself.
(6.5.1.5) If he should desire,
"May I bestow the glory of the sacrifice upon the sacrificer," he should pour [the water] down while standing between the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna*.
(6.5.1.5) He thus endows the sacrificer himself with the glory of the sacrifice.
(6.5.1.5) If he should desire,
"May I endow the members of the assembly (*sadasyas*) with the glory of the sacrifice," he should take hold of the *sadas* and lead [the victim] down.
(6.5.1.5) He thus endows the members of the assembly themselves with the glory of the sacrifice.
The *dhruva* cup is indeed the life-span of the sacrifice.
It is drawn as the last of the cups; therefore, life is the last of the vital breaths.
"The head of heaven, the messenger of earth," he says.
(6.5.2.1) Verily, he makes him the head of his equals.
(6.5.2.1) "Agni Vaiśvānara, born for the sake of Truth," he says;
for Vaiśvānara is indeed life by virtue of his divinity.
The Vaiśvānara cup is drawn on both sides;
therefore, the vital breaths are on both sides—
both below and above.
The other cups are drawn as halves; the *dhruva* cup is a whole.
Therefore, the downward vital breath of others is a half [of the total].
The other cups are set down on a surface that has been strewn with sand; the *dhruva* is set down on a surface not strewn with sand.
Therefore, some creatures find their support in bone, others in flesh.
The Asuras indeed sought to overturn the earth from the north;
the gods made it firm with the Dhruva [pole-star].
(6.5.2.2) That is the fixedness of the *dhruva* cup.
(6.5.2.2) That the *dhruva* is set down to the north is for the sake of support.
(6.5.2.2) The *dhruva* is indeed the life-span of the sacrifice, and the *hotṛ* is its body.
When he pours the *dhruva* into the *hotṛ*'s cup, he bestows life upon himself within the sacrifice. "It should be poured before the *uktha*," they say,
for one enjoys life from the front.
(6.5.2.3) "One should pour it out in the middle," they say;
for one enjoys the middle of life.
(6.5.2.3) "One should pour it out on the northern half," they say.
For he enjoys the very best of his lifespan.
While the verse addressed to the Viśvedevas is being recited, he pours [the water] down;
for offspring indeed belong to the Viśvedevas.
Verily, he bestows life upon the offspring.
(6.5.3.1) By means of sacrifice, the gods went to the heavenly world. (6.5.3.1) They thought, "Mankind will follow after us. (6.5.3.1) [They feared: "Mankind will become like us."
Having exhausted themselves over the course of a year, they went to the heavenly world.
The seers recognized that [world] by means of the seasonal cups (*ṛtugraha*) alone. Therefore, when the seasonal cups are drawn, it is for the sake of recognizing the heavenly world.
Twelve are taken;
twelve months are a year;
it is for the sake of the recognition of the year.
The first two are drawn together, and the last two are drawn together;
therefore there are two seasons each.
The *ṛtupātra* cup has openings on both sides.
(6.5.3.1) For who indeed knows that which is the mouth of the seasons? (6.5.3.2) He says "Prompt by the season" six times; for there are six seasons.
(6.5.3.2) He thus gratifies the seasons.
(6.5.3.2) With the words "by the seasons," [he recites] four times.
(6.5.3.2) He thus gratifies the four-footed animals.
(6.5.3.2) He says "with the season" twice; thus he gratifies bipeds.
(6.5.3.2) He says "Prompt with the season" six times, and "with the seasons" four times.
(6.5.3.2) Therefore, four-footed animals live upon the seasons.
(6.5.3.3) He speaks again with the season twice;
therefore, two-footed beings live upon four-footed animals.
"Prompted by the season," he says six times; "by the seasons," four times; and twice again, "by the season.
This is indeed a stepping-stone; the sacrificer thereby constructs a bridge for the attainment of the heavenly world.
One should not follow after another;
for if one were to follow after another, season would follow upon season, and the seasons would become confounded.
The Adhvaryu enters by the south in the established manner, and the Pratiprasthātṛ enters by the north in the established manner.
Therefore, the sun moves by the south for six months and by the north for six months. "You are taken with a support; you are the gliding one; for Aṃhaspatya, you! he says.
"They say there is a thirteenth month;
by that, he gratifies him."
(6.5.4.1) These seasonal libations (*ṛtugraha*) are indeed drawn for the sake of the heavenly world.
(6.5.4.1) Indra and Agni are light;
when he draws the libation for Indra and Agni with the seasonal cup, he places light above him.
(6.5.4.1) It is for the illumination of the heavenly world.
(6.5.4.1) Indra and Agni are indeed the bearers of vigor among the gods; when the cup for Indra and Agni is drawn, one secures vigor itself.
(6.5.4.1) He draws the Vaiśvadeva cup with the Śukra vessel. (6.5.4.1) Offspring indeed belong to the All-gods;
yonder sun is the Śukra.
Because he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup with the Śukra vessel, therefore that sun rises facing all creatures;
therefore everyone thinks,
"It has risen toward me."
(6.5.4.2) He draws the Vaiśvadeva cup with the Śukra vessel. (6.5.4.2) For offspring are indeed related to the All-gods;
brilliance is the Śukra.
In that he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup with the Śukra vessel, he bestows brilliance upon the offspring.
Indra, together with the Maruts through their shared knowledge, slew Vṛtra at the midday pressing.

Since the Marutvatīya cups are drawn at the midday pressing, they are drawn for the sacrificer as slayers of Vṛtra. When he had slain Vṛtra, the seasons became confused; he drew the Marutvatīya cups using the Ṛtu-vessel.
(6.5.5.1) Thereupon, he indeed discerned the seasons.
(6.5.5.1) In that the Marutvatīya cups are drawn with the Ṛtu-vessel, it is for the discernment of the seasons.

(6.5.5.1) Verily, this thunderbolt the sacrificer hurls at his enemy; in that the Marutvatīya cups are [drawn], he holds it aloft with the first, (6.5.5.2) he hurls it with the second, and he lays him low with the third.
(6.5.5.2) Indeed, the sacrificer prepares this weapon when he performs the Marutvatīya offerings: the first is the bow, the second is the bowstring, and the third is the arrow.
(6.5.5.2) With the first he takes aim, with the second he releases, and with the third he pierces.
(6.5.5.2) Having slain Vṛtra, Indra went to the furthest distance.
Thinking, "I have committed an offense," he became greenish-yellow;
he then perceived these Marutvatīya offerings as means for self-protection.

He drew those [cups]. With the first, he secured the out-breathing (*prāṇa*); with the second, the in-breathing (*apāna*); with the third, the self (*ātman*). For these Marutvatīya cups are drawn for the sacrificer as means of securing the self;
with the first, he secures the out-breathing; with the second, the in-breathing; with the third, the self. Indra slew Vṛtra.
The gods said of him,
"Great indeed has he become, who slew Vṛtra"; that is the reason for Mahendra's name as Mahendra.
Having slain Vṛtra, he drew out this Mahendra as a special portion above the other deities.
In that Mahendra is drawn, the sacrificer likewise draws out that special portion above the other offspring.
He draws it with the Śukra cup.
(6.5.5.3) Mahendra indeed has the sacrificer as his deity; the *śukra* is brilliance. In that he draws the *māhendra* cup with the *śukra* vessel, he bestows brilliance upon the sacrificer himself.
(6.5.6.1) Aditi, desiring sons, cooked a brahmaudana for the Sādhyas, the gods.
(6.5.6.1) They gave her the remnants; she ate it.
She conceived seed;
from it the four Ādityas were born.
She cooked [a second sacrificial cake].
She reflected:
"From the remnants these [beings] have been born; if I were to eat first, those superior to me would be born from me. She then ate first.
She conceived seed;
from her, an undeveloped egg was born. She cooked it for the Ādityas as a third [offering].
"Let this toil of mine be for my enjoyment," he said.
They replied, "We shall choose a boon: whoever is born from this [offspring] shall be our one [lord]; whoever prospers in his progeny shall be for our enjoyment."
(6.5.6.2) From him Vivasvat Āditya was born.
(6.5.6.2) His offspring, indeed, are these human beings;
among them, he alone is successful who performs sacrifice.
He becomes the source of enjoyment for the gods.
Indeed, the gods withdrew from the sacrifice; they entered into Rudra.
He then pursued the Ādityas.
They sought refuge with the deities of the two-fold cups;
he did not surrender them to them.
Therefore, even today, one does not surrender a person who has come for protection, even if he is deserving of death.
Therefore, even when one who is to be executed has surrendered, they do not hand him over again.
Therefore, the Āditya cup is drawn from the offerings for the dual deities. Because they were born from the remnants, it is therefore drawn from the remnants.
He draws [the cup] with three verses.
The mother, the father, and the son—that indeed is a pair. The amnion, the embryo, and the chorion—that indeed is a pair. A pair it is.
These Ādityas are indeed cattle; curds are vigor. By mixing [the oblation] with curds in the middle, he places vigor in the midst of the cattle, using the boiled *ātaṅkya* curds.
For the sake of purity;
therefore, the raw [cow] yields the cooked [milk];
for these Ādityas are indeed cattle.
Having enclosed [the altar], he draws [the cup];
verily, by hemming them in, he secures cattle for him.
These Ādityas are indeed cattle, and this Agni is Rudra.
Having enclosed [the place] with a fence, he draws [the cup]; verily, he shields the cattle from Rudra.
(6.5.6.5) This Upāṃśusavana stone is indeed Vivasvat Āditya. He lies around this very draught of Soma until the third pressing.
"O Vivasvat Āditya, this is your draught of Soma," he says.
(6.5.6.5) He thus causes Vivasvat Āditya to prosper through the drinking of Soma.
(6.5.6.5) "With that which is divine rain, I mix thee"—with this [formula] he should mix [the offering] for one who desires rain;
verily, he secures rain.
(6.5.6.5) If it falls quickly, Parjanya will be rainy; if it takes a long time, he will be dry.
He does not set [the vessel] down.
For from non-existence, indeed, creatures are born.
He does not utter the *anuvaṣaṭ* call;
for if he were to utter the *anuvaṣaṭ* call, he would let Rudra loose upon the creatures.
(6.5.6.5) One should not look at [the oblation] after having offered it.
(6.5.6.5) If one were to look at it, his eye would be liable to perish; therefore, it should not be looked at.
(6.5.7.1) He draws the Sāvitra cup from the Āgrayaṇa vessel using the Antaryāma cup.
(6.5.7.1) This Āgrayaṇa is indeed Prajāpati; [it is drawn] for the procreation of offspring.
(6.5.7.1) He does not set it down;
for from what is not set down, offspring are produced.
(6.5.7.1) He does not utter the *vaṣaṭ* call after it.
(6.5.7.1) If he were to utter the secondary *vaṣaṭ* call, he would let Rudra loose upon his offspring.
(6.5.7.1) Savitṛ is indeed the Gāyatra among the gods;
this Āgrayaṇa cup is drawn in the world of the Gāyatrī.
(6.5.7.1) In that he draws the cup for Savitṛ from the Āgrayaṇa vessel with the Antaryāma cup, he draws him forth from his own womb.
(6.5.7.2) The All-gods could not obtain a share in the third pressing. They led Savitṛ—who had a share in the morning pressing—to the third pressing.
(6.5.7.2) Thereupon, they indeed raised up the third pressing.
(6.5.7.2) Since the cup for Savitṛ is drawn at the third pressing, it serves for the raising of the third pressing.
He draws the cup for the Viśve Devas from the pitcher using the cup of Savitṛ.
Offspring indeed belong to the Viśvedevas;
the pitcher belongs to the Viśvedevas; Savitṛ is the lord of instigations.

In that he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup from the pitcher with the Savitṛ vessel, it is as if, impelled by Savitṛ, he procreates offspring for him. He draws Soma over Soma; verily, he thereby bestows seed.
"You are a good refuge, a firm foundation," he says;
for he draws Soma into Soma for the sake of stability.
(6.5.7.3) Indeed, in this very cup, [the offering] is made for humans, for the gods, and for the ancestors.
(6.5.7.3) "Thou art a good refuge, a firm foundation," he says;
(6.5.7.3) by this, he indeed makes [the offering] for humans.
"Bṛhat," he says;
by this, he acts for the sake of the gods.
"Namaḥ," he says.
By this, he indeed acts for the sake of the ancestors.
So many indeed are the deities;
from all of them he takes it for him.
"This is your womb; for all the gods you," he says, for this [oblation] belongs to the Viśvedevas.
The Upāṃśu cup is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Because the first and the last cups are drawn with the Upāṃśu vessel, they follow after the vital breath and proceed toward the vital breath. The Āgrayaṇa cup is Prajāpati, and the Upāṃśu is the vital breath; [thus] they procreate offspring through the wives.
In that he draws the Pātnīvata cup from the Āgrayaṇa vessel with the Upāṃśu vessel, it is for the procreation of offspring.
Therefore, offspring are born after the vital breath.
The gods, indeed, from here desired to go to the heavenly world together with their wives.
They did not find the world of heaven;
they saw this offering for the wives (pātnīvata); they took it.
(6.5.8.2) From that, indeed, they discerned the world of heaven.
(6.5.8.2) In that the cup for the wives is drawn, it is for the discernment of the world of heaven. That Soma did not remain when it was being drawn for the women.

(6.5.8.2) Having made that clarified butter into a thunderbolt, they struck him; (6.5.8.2) having deprived him of his virility, they seized him. (6.5.8.2) Therefore women are devoid of virility and do not inherit; yet they speak more intimately than even a wicked man. (6.5.8.3) So they say.
