In that he mixes the Pātnīvata cup with clarified butter, he draws it after having brought it under control by means of the thunderbolt itself.
"Thou art taken with a support," he says;
for this earth is indeed the support.
"Therefore, offspring are born after this [earth]. He says, "Of thee, pressed by Bṛhaspati.
Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman among the gods.
By means of the Brahman itself, he causes offspring to be born for him.
He says, "O Indu! For the Indu is indeed seed.
(6.5.8.3) He thus bestows seed.
(6.5.8.4) "Possessing power," he says;
(6.5.8.4) offspring, indeed, is power.
Verily, he procreates offspring for him.
"O Agni! he says;
for Agni is the depositor of seed.
"Like a wife," he says, for the sake of pairing. "In harmony with the god Tvaṣṭṛ, drink the Soma," he says.
Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the fashioner of the forms of animals that exist in pairs; he thus bestows form upon the animals. The gods, indeed, sought to slay Tvaṣṭṛ.
He entered among the wives;
they did not hand him back.
Therefore, even today, they do not hand back one who has sought refuge, even if he is one deserving of death.
Therefore, a portion is taken for Tvaṣṭṛ associated with the Patnīvat cup;
he does not set it down.
For from that which is not set down, offspring are produced.
He does not perform the *anuvaṣaṭ* call.
For if he were to perform the *anuvaṣaṭ* call, he would let Rudra loose after the offspring.
If he were not to perform the *anuvaṣaṭ* call, the *agnīdh* would consume the Soma while it is still unappeased.
He pronounces the *vaṣaṭ* call in a whisper;
he does not release the progeny unto Rudra. The *agnīdh* consumes the Soma in a state of peace.
"O *agnīdh*, sit upon the lap of the *neṣṭṛ*! [The *adhvaryu*] says, "O *neṣṭṛ*, lead the wife forward."
The Āgnīdhra places the seed in the Neṣṭṛ; the Neṣṭṛ [places it] in the wife. He causes her to look together with the Udgātṛ;
for the Udgātṛ is indeed Prajāpati.
For the procreation of offspring;
he pours forth water,
for he thereby pours forth seed.
He causes it to roll forward with the thigh;
for with the thigh semen is emitted. He causes it to roll forward naked upon the thigh.
For when the thigh is naked, then they couple;
then semen is emitted;
then offspring are born.
Indra slew Vṛtra;
he split open his skull-bone,
and it became the *droṇakalaśa* vessel.
(6.5.9.1) From that, Soma flowed forth; (6.5.9.1) it became the Hāriyojana. He reflected upon it.
"Shall I offer? Shall I not offer? He thought: "If I offer, I shall offer what is raw; if I do not offer, I shall cause a disturbance of the sacrifice."
(6.5.9.1) He resolved to offer it. (6.5.9.1) That Agni said: "You shall not offer what is raw in me."
He seasoned it with parched grains.
He offered it once it had become cooked.
In that he mixes the *hāriyojana* cup with parched grains, it is for the sake of cooking; thus he offers it only after it has indeed become cooked.
He mixes it with many [milk-cows].
As many as these there are, so many milch-cows become available for him in yonder world.
Now, moreover, they say:
"These indeed are Indra’s dappled wish-fulfilling cows, namely the *hāriyojanī* verses.
Therefore, one should mix [the soma] with many [verses].
The *ṛc* and *sāman* are indeed Indra’s two bay steeds, the drinkers of soma.
The enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are their support.
If one were to offer the oblation without having cast the enclosing sticks [into the fire], he would be offering fodder to those two while they still have their support.
By casting the enclosing sticks [into the fire] and then offering the oblation, he offers fodder to them precisely when they are without support.
The Unnetṛ offers the oblation,
for at this point the Adhvaryu has already performed his work and uttered the *svagā* call.
If the Adhvaryu were to offer it himself, it would be just as if one were to yoke again what has already been unyoked.
(6.5.9.3) Having placed it upon the head, he offers;
for from the head it came into being.
He offers after taking a stride.
For by stepping forth Indra slew Vṛtra;
it is for prosperity.
The Hāriyojanī verses are indeed cattle.
If he were to break it, few cattle would attend upon him while feeding on him;
if he were not to break it, many cattle would attend upon him while not feeding on him.
He presses it together with his mind.
He performs both.
Many cattle indeed attend upon him, feeding him.
They seek an invitation from the Unnetṛ.
(6.5.9.4) They obtain for themselves that very draught of Soma which is there.
(6.5.9.4) He scatters [the earth] on the high altar (uttaravedi);
for the high altar is indeed cattle.
The verses for the Hāriyojana cup are cattle;
verily, they establish cattle in cattle.
(6.5.10.1) After the cups (grahas), indeed, offspring and cattle are produced: (6.5.10.1) goats and sheep [are born] after the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma; men [are born] after the Śukra and Manthin.
The one-hoofed animals correspond to the seasonal cups (*ṛtugraha*). Cows correspond to the Āditya cup;
the Āditya cup is drawn with the greatest number of verses.
Therefore, among domestic animals, cattle are the most numerous. Because he draws [the Soma] three times silently with his hand,
therefore a goat gives birth to two or three [kids], but birds are more numerous still.
The Āgrayaṇa is indeed the father, and the Kalaśa is the son.
If the Āgrayaṇa should fail, one should draw [the Soma] from the Kalaśa;
just as a father, when exhausted, resorts to his son, so too is that.
(6.5.10.2) If [the Soma] should fail in the *kalaśa*, one should draw from the *āgrayaṇa*.
(6.5.10.2) Just as a son, when exhausted, runs to his father for refuge, even so is that.
(6.5.10.2) For this *āgrayaṇa* is indeed the self of the sacrifice.
(6.5.10.2) If either a cup or the pitcher should be exhausted, one should draw from the Āgrayaṇa vessel.
(6.5.10.2) Thus, he restores the sacrifice from its very self.
(6.5.10.2) For this Āgrayaṇa is drawn as something unmanifest.
He draws [the offering] with a pot and offers it with a *vāyavya* cup; therefore, one who has killed a Brahmin is not recognized by his embryo. They go down to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*);
they cast away the pots and carry up the *vāyavya* cups.

Therefore, they cast away a girl when she is born, but they carry off a boy. When he recites the *puroruḳ*, it is just as if one were bringing something to a superior; that is exactly what it is like.
When he draws the cup (*graha*), it is just as if one, having brought something to a superior, announces it; that is exactly what it is like.
In that he sets it down, it is just as when one moves away after leaving something deposited with a superior.
Whatever part of the sacrifice is performed with the *sāman* or the *yajus*, that is loose; whatever is performed with the *ṛc*, that is firm.
Those with the *upayāma* formula first are taken with a *yajus*; those with the *upayāma* formula last are taken with a *ṛc*, for the support of the sacrifice.
Some vessels are joined [used] and others are not;
those which are used facing away, by means of them he conquers that very world, for that world is, as it were, turned away.
Furthermore, those [vessels] which are employed, by means of them he conquers this very world;
for this world is, as it were, ever recurring.
Some vessels are employed, while others are not.
(6.5.11.1) Those [vessels] which are employed facing away, after those the plants perish;
(6.5.11.2) those which are employed again, after those the plants come back into being. Some vessels are joined together, others are not.
Those [vessels] which are employed once for all, after them the wild animals depart to the forest;
those which are employed again, after them the domestic animals return to the village.
Verily, he who knows the foundation of the cups becomes possessed of a foundation.
(6.5.11.2) "The clarified butter" is the *uktha*; that indeed is the foundation of the cups (*graha*).
(6.5.11.2–3) That which he recites in a whisper belongs to the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups; that which he recites aloud belongs to the other cups.
(6.5.11.3) This, indeed, is the fundamental principle of the cups.
He who knows this becomes possessed of that fundamental principle.
(6.5.11.3) He who knows the pairing of the cups is procreated with offspring, cattle, and pairings.
Some cups are drawn with potsherds, others with Vāyu-vessels;
this indeed is the pairing of the cups.
He who knows thus is procreated with offspring, cattle, and pairings.
Indra forcibly drank Tvaṣṭṛ’s Soma;
he was shattered all over,
and he found no rest within himself.
He saw these sacrificial cakes at each pressing;
he offered them,
and by means of them, he created for himself a place of rest.
Therefore, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are offered at each pressing;
therefore, one should eat of the sacrificial cakes at each pressing. Thus he creates a place of rest for himself, and Soma does not flow past him.
The exponents of the Veda (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say:
(6.5.11.4) "The *pañkti* is not attained by means of the *ṛc* nor by the *yajus*; then what constitutes the fivefold nature (*pāṅktatva*) of the sacrifice?
(6.5.11.4) "The parched grains (*dhānāḥ*), the groats (*karambhaḥ*), the parched rice (*parivāpaḥ*), the cake (*puroḍāśaḥ*), and the curd-mixture (*payasyā*)—by these the *pañkti* is attained."
That is the fivefold nature of the sacrifice.
(6.6.1.1) These offerings of the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) are indeed offered for the sake of the heavenly world.
(6.6.1.1) He offers two [oblations] on the *gārhapatya* fire;
the sacrificer has two feet.
For the sake of stability,
he offers in the Āgnīdhra fire-shed;
thus he takes a step within the intermediate space itself.
He goes toward the Sadas; verily he causes him to go to the world of heaven;
with two verses addressed to Sūrya, he makes an offering on the Gārhapatya fire.

(6.6.1.1) He causes him to ascend to that very world. (6.6.1.1) He offers in the Āgnīdhra fire with a verse containing the word "lead" (*nayavatī*), for the purpose of leading [the sacrificer] to the heavenly world.
"Go to heaven, fly to the light!"—having thus offered, he takes up the gold.
He thereby causes him to go to the heavenly world. "With form I approach your form," he says.
"For by means of their form one approaches their form, when [one approaches] with gold.
"May Tutha, the all-knowing, distribute you," he says;
for Tutha, the all-knowing, used indeed to distribute the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) of the gods.
(6.6.1.2) By that very means he distributes them.
(6.6.1.2–3) "This is your gift, O Agni, which comes flowing with Soma," he says;
for his gift indeed comes flowing with Soma.
"Lead them by the path of Mitra," he says for the sake of peace.
"Go forth by the path of Truth, O you whose sacrificial fee is a moon," he says.
"Truth indeed is the cosmic order (*ṛta*). "By truth itself, by the cosmic order, he distributes them," [the priest] says, "leading them along the path of sacrifice toward prosperity."
"For these sacrificial gifts go by the path of the sacrifice.
'May I today attain a Brāhmaṇa,' he says; 'a seer, a descendant of seers.
For he who has heard [the sacred lore] is indeed a Brāhmaṇa, a seer, and a descendant of seers."
Therefore he says thus:
"Behold the heaven, behold the mid-region," he says;
verily, he causes him to go to the heavenly world.
"Exert yourselves together with the members of the assembly," he says for the sake of friendship.
"Go among the gods as our givers; full of sweetness, enter into the giver," he says.
"We here are the givers; may you, full of sweetness, enter into us there!"—this indeed he says when he gives gold. For gold is indeed immortality.
(6.6.1.5) He places light itself in front, for the purpose of illuminating the world of heaven.
(6.6.1.5) He gives [the gift] to the Agnīdh.
(6.6.1.5) He gratifies the seasons, which have Agni as their mouth;
(6.6.1.5) he gives [the garment] to the Brahman priest;
(6.6.1.5) for the sake of impulsion.
(6.6.1.5) He gives to the Hotṛ.
(6.6.1.5) For the Hotṛ is indeed the self of the sacrifice.
(6.6.1.5) Thus he endows the very self of the sacrifice with the sacrificial gifts.
(6.6.2.1) He offers the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations for the completion of the sacrifice.

Whatever in the sacrifice is cruel, whatever is mangled, whatever it oversteps, whatever it does not overstep, whatever it does in excess, and whatever it does not do at all— that very thing he gratifies with them.
(6.6.2.1) He offers nine oblations;
(6.6.2.1) there are indeed nine vital breaths in a person; the sacrifice is commensurate with the person.
(6.6.2.1) He gratifies the sacrifice in its entirety.
(6.6.2.1) He offers six verses containing the word *ṛc*;
for there are six seasons.
(6.6.2.1) Verily, he pleases the seasons.
(6.6.2.1) There are three sacrificial formulas. (6.6.2.2) These worlds are three;
verily, he pleases these very worlds.
"O sacrifice, go to the sacrifice; go to the lord of the sacrifice," he says;
verily, he causes it to go to the lord of the sacrifice. "Go to your own womb," he says.
(6.6.2.2) He causes him to go to his very own womb.
(6.6.2.2) "This is your sacrifice, O lord of the sacrifice, accompanied by the *sūktavāka* and rich in heroes," he says;
(6.6.2.2) thus he bestows vigor upon the sacrificer himself.
(6.6.2.2) Vāsiṣṭha Sātyahavya asked Devabhāga:

(6.6.2.2) "When you performed the sacrifice for the Sṛñjayas, who were great sacrificers—at the sacrifice, did you establish the sacrifice in the sacrifice, or did you establish it in the lord of the sacrifice?
(6.6.2.3) He replied:
"In the lord of the sacrifice," he says.
"The Sṛñjayas indeed perished because of the truth," he said; "the sacrifice was established in the sacrifice so that there might be no defeat for the sacrificer.
"O gods who know the way, having found the way, go on the way," he says.
He establishes the sacrifice within the sacrifice itself,
for the sake of the sacrificer’s non-defeat.
(6.6.3.1) He offers the *avabhṛtha* oblations.
(6.6.3.1) Whatever sin he has committed prior to one year [of age], that very thing he expiates through them.
He goes down to the waters for the *avabhṛtha*.
(6.6.3.1) Varuṇa is indeed in the waters; (6.6.3.1) thus he directly propitiates Varuṇa. (6.6.3.1) Or else, having followed along the path of the sacrifice, the Rakṣases seek to destroy it.
The Prastotṛ follows along with the Sāman;
for the Sāman is indeed the slayer of Rākṣasas, for the purpose of driving away the Rākṣasas.
He approaches the *nidhana* three times;
these worlds are three.
From these very worlds he strikes away the *rakṣas* demons.
(6.6.3.2) Man after man attains the *nidhana*; for man after man is possessed by *rakṣas* demons;
[this is] for the smiting away of the *rakṣas*.
"For King Varuṇa has made wide space," he says for the sake of stability;
"A hundred physicians are yours, O King, a thousand," he says.
He thereby provides a remedy for him.
"Varuṇa’s noose is trodden underfoot," he says;
thus he truly tramples Varuṇa’s noose underfoot.
He offers upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the stability of the oblations;
moreover, he offers upon that which possesses fire.
He performs the fore-offerings excluding the *barhis*. The *barhis* is indeed offspring; verily, he releases offspring from the noose of Varuṇa.
He offers the two portions of clarified butter;
he does not depart from the very eyes of the sacrifice.
He sacrifices to Varuṇa.
Verily, he releases him from Varuṇa’s noose.
He sacrifices to Agni and Varuṇa;
verily, he directly releases him from Varuṇa’s noose.
(6.6.3.3) He performs the two after-offerings without the *barhis*.
(6.6.3.3) The *barhis* is indeed offspring;
verily, he releases offspring from the noose of Varuṇa.
He performs four fore-offerings and two after-offerings;
they amount to six.
There are indeed six seasons.
Verily, he finds firm support in the seasons.
He says, "O Avabhṛtha, O Nicaṅkuṇa," whereby he propitiates Varuṇa just as has been prescribed.
"In the ocean is your heart, within the waters," he says; for Varuṇa is indeed within the ocean. "May the plants and the waters enter into you," he says.
Verily, by means of the waters and the plants, he makes him harmonious.
"O divine waters, this is your embryo," he says;
this is according to the sacrificial formula itself.
Soma is indeed cattle.
If he were to consume the drops, he would possess cattle, but Varuṇa would seize him. If he were not to consume them, he would be without cattle, yet Varuṇa would not seize him.
(6.6.3.5) One who merely touches [water] becomes possessed of cattle; Varuṇa does not seize him.
(6.6.3.5) "The noose of Varuṇa is cast off," he says; thus he is released from the very noose of Varuṇa.
They approach without looking back, for the sake of concealment from Varuṇa.
"Thou art fuel; may we prosper," he says; thus, with fuel, they approach Agni while paying him homage.
"Thou art splendor; bestow splendor upon me," he says;
verily, he bestows splendor upon himself.

(6.6.4.1) He digs up the altar with the wooden sword, measures out [the space] with the axle of a chariot, and erects the sacrificial post; having thus prepared the threefold thunderbolt, he hurls it at his rival for the sake of striking him down. If he were to erect it inside the altar, he would conquer the world of the gods; if outside the altar, the world of men. He erects it at the junction of the edge of the altar, for the conquest of both worlds.

(6.6.4.1) One should measure [the sacrificial post] level with the bottom-ring for one who desires the world of the fathers; level with the girdle for one who desires the world of men; level with the top-ring for one who desires sensory power; all equal for one who desires stability. Those three which are middle-sized, those he should make equal for one who desires cattle; indeed, cattle attend upon these; thus he becomes possessed of cattle.
(6.6.4.2) He should interlace the others; verily, by means of offspring he interlaces him with cattle.

(6.6.4.2) If he should desire of someone, "May he be liable to die," he should erect for him a *gartamit* [pit-measured] post, making the northern one the tallest and the other shorter. This indeed is the *gartamit*; for whomsoever he erects it thus, he quickly dies.
He should erect the southern one as the tallest for one who desires heaven, and the other as shorter; thereby the sacrificer makes a staircase and a bridge for the attainment of the heavenly world.

(6.6.4.3) Because he winds two girdles around a single sacrificial post, therefore one man finds two wives; because he does not wind a single girdle around two posts, therefore one woman does not find two husbands. (6.6.4.3) If he should desire of someone, "May a female child be born to him," he should interlace the two girdles near the ends; thus a female child is born to him.
If he should desire of someone, "May a male child be born to him," he should wrap them right through to the ends; thus a male child is born to him. (6.6.4.4) Thus a male child is born to him.

(6.6.4.4) The Asuras indeed led the gods from the south; the gods repelled them by means of the *upaśaya* (the leaning post). That is why it is called the *upaśaya*. Because it leans (*upaśaye*) toward the south, it serves for the repelling of the enemy. (6.6.4.4) All other sacrificial posts have animals [dedicated to them], but the *upaśaya* alone is without an animal. The sacrificer is its animal. If he were not to designate it, the sacrificer would meet with ruin. He should designate it, saying, "That one is your animal," referring to whomsoever he hates. Whomever he hates, him he designates as the animal for him.
(6.6.4.5) If he should not hate [anyone], he should say, "The mouse is your animal"; thus he harms neither domestic nor wild animals.

(6.6.4.5) Prajāpati created living beings; he was deprived of food. He saw this set of eleven victims, and by means of it, he indeed obtained food. In that there are ten sacrificial posts—the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is food—he wins food by means of the Virāj itself.
The eleventh [post] is indeed its udder; he milks it by means of that.

This set of eleven is measured out as a thunderbolt; it is capable of crushing the sacrifice from the front toward the back. In that he erects the post for the wives' deity (*pātnīvata*), it is for the support and stabilization of the sacrifice.

Prajāpati created offspring; he felt himself emptied. He perceived this set of eleven [animals], and by means of it, he placed life-span, sensory power, and vigor within himself. Truly, he who sacrifices creates offspring; he is, at this point, as if emptied. In that there is this set of eleven, the sacrificer thereby places life-span, sensory power, and vigor within himself.

(6.6.5.1) With the offering to Agni, he causes [the seed] to be cast; with that to Sarasvatī, he creates a pair; with that to Soma, he places the seed. (6.6.5.2) He causes it to be born by means of the offering to Pūṣan. There is an offering to Bṛhaspati; Bṛhaspati is indeed the sacred power (*brahman*) of the gods; verily, by means of the sacred power, he causes offspring to be born for him. There is an offering to the Viśve Devas; offspring belong to the Viśve Devas; verily, he causes offspring to be born for him. Verily, he wins sensory power (*indriya*) by the offering to Indra; the people (*viś*) by the offering to the Maruts; vigor and strength by the offering to Indra and Agni. There is an offering to Savitṛ for impulsion; there is one to Varuṇa for freedom from Varuṇa’s noose.

(6.6.5.2) He offers the animal to Indra in the middle; verily, he bestows power upon the sacrificer in the very center. (6.6.5.3) Before the offering to Indra, he offers one to the Viśvedevas; for food belongs to the Viśvedevas, and thus he places food at the front. Therefore, food is eaten from the front. Having offered to Indra, he offers to the Maruts; for the Maruts are the common people (viś), and thus he binds the common people to him.

(6.6.5.3) If he should desire, "May he who has attained [power] be excluded, and may he who is excluded attain [power]," he should offer a victim to Varuṇa in the place of the one for Indra, and a victim to Indra in the place of the one for Varuṇa. (6.6.5.4) He who had attained is excluded, and he who was excluded attains.
(6.6.5.4) If he should desire, "May the subjects become bewildered," he should intermingle the animals; thus he bewilders the subjects.
If he were to offer an animal to Varuṇa facing upstream, Varuṇa would seize his offspring; he offers it from the south, facing north, flowing downstream, so that Varuṇa does not seize his offspring.

Indra caused Manu to sacrifice with his wife; he released her after she had been encircled by fire. By means of her, Manu prospered. In that he releases the Pātnīvata offering after it has been encircled by fire, the sacrificer attains that very prosperity which Manu attained.

From the lack of a firm foundation for the sacrifice, the sacrifice perishes; when the sacrifice perishes, the sacrificer perishes along with it. In that he completes the Pātnīvata offering with clarified butter, it is for the sake of the sacrifice’s firm foundation; when the sacrifice is firmly established, the sacrificer is firmly established along with it.

(6.6.6.1) The offering with the omentum is made; (6.6.6.2) the offering with the animal victim is not yet made. Then he proceeds with the Pātnīvata offering; thus he proceeds at the very ford. Moreover, his journey is now [completed].
The Tvaṣṭṛ-offering belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ; for Tvaṣṭṛ indeed fashions the forms of the emitted seed. He releases that bull among the wives; he (Tvaṣṭṛ) fashions forms for him.
(6.6.7.1) Indeed, they kill Soma when they press him. (6.6.7.1) That the offering belongs to Soma is just as if one were to kill a cow to accompany a dead man; such indeed is that.

(6.6.7.1) If he were to offer on the northern half or in the middle, he would cause strife among the deities; he offers on the southern half, for this is the quarter of the Fathers; thus he gratifies the Fathers in their own quarter.
(6.6.7.1) They carry [the Soma] to the Udgātṛs; for the Soma belongs to the Sāman. Whatever they do wrongly regarding the Sāman, this [offering] is the atonement for that.

(6.6.7.2) They look down [into the water]; for the Soma is a means of purification. They purify themselves. He who does not see his own self would be as one whose life has departed. Having made a reflection [of himself], he should look [into it]; for in that he sees his own self, and thus he purifies his very self.

(6.6.7.2) He whose mind has wandered away should look [at the ghee] with the words: "My mind that has gone afar, or that which has not gone afar—by means of King Soma, we establish that within us. Thus he establishes his own mind within himself. (6.6.7.3) His mind does not wander away.

Indeed, at the third pressing, the sacrifice departs from one who has sacrificed toward one who has not sacrificed. With a verse addressed to Agni and Viṣṇu, he offers an oblation of ghee; for Agni is all the deities and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice. Thus he establishes both the deities and the sacrifice. He offers in a low voice for the sake of forming a pair.

(6.6.7.3) The exponents of sacred knowledge say: "Mitra takes charge of the well-offered part of the sacrifice, and Varuṇa the ill-offered part; where then does the sacrifice go, and where does the sacrificer remain? When one offers a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa, he pacifies the well-offered part of the sacrifice by means of Mitra and the ill-offered part by means of Varuṇa; thus the sacrificer does not come to ruin.

(6.6.7.4) Just as they break up the soil with a plough, so do the *ṛc* and the *sāman* break open the sacrifice. When he offers a cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa, he provides nourishment for the sacrifice that has been broken open, for the sake of pacification. The meters of one who has sacrificed become exhausted; the essence of the meters is the cow. When he offers a cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa, he gratifies the meters again so that they are no longer exhausted, and thus he places the essence back into the meters.
The gods, indeed, divided up power and vigor.
What remained over from that became the *atigrāhya* cups; that is why the *atigrāhya* cups are called *atigrāhya*.
(6.6.8.1) In that the *atigrāhya* cups are drawn, the sacrificer thereby places within himself sensory power and vigor.
(6.6.8.1) Splendor is obtained through the cup for Agni, sensory power through the cup for Indra, and spiritual luster through the cup for Sūrya.
(6.6.8.1) These *atigrāhya* cups are indeed the support of the sacrifice, as are the wheels and the *pṛṣṭha* chants.

(6.6.8.1) If one were not to draw [the Atigrāhya cups] during the Pṛṣṭhya [Ṣaḍaha], they would crush the forward-moving sacrifice with the Pṛṣṭha-stotras. (6.6.8.2) If one were to draw them during the Ukthya, they would crush the backward-moving sacrifice with the Atigrāhyas.
They should be drawn in the Viśvajit sacrifice which contains all the Pṛṣṭhas, for the sake of providing the sacrifice with full vigor.
Prajāpati assigned the sacrifices to the gods;
he cast off his beloved bodies,
and they became the *atigrāhya* cups.
(6.6.8.2) "The sacrifice of him whose *atigrāhya* cups are not drawn is, they say, bodiless.
(6.6.8.2) "They should indeed be drawn even at the *agniṣṭoma*, for the sake of the body of the sacrifice.
(6.6.8.2) "All the deities were once alike."
They did not attain distinction.
Those gods saw these cups; they drew them.
Agni [took] the draught for Agni, Indra that for Indra, and Sūrya that for Sūrya.
Thereupon, they indeed attained distinction from other deities.
For him who, knowing thus, these cups are drawn, he attains distinction from his evil rival.
(6.6.8.3) "These worlds are to be made luminous and equal in power," they say.
(6.6.8.3) One places light in this world by means of [the offering] to Agni; in the intermediate space, by means of [the offering] to Indra;
for Indra and Vāyu are yoked together.
(6.6.8.3) By means of the offering to Sūrya, he establishes light in yonder world.
(6.6.8.4) These worlds become luminous for him; he makes them equal in strength.
Bambā and Viśvavayas indeed discovered these cups.
Through these two, these worlds—both those that extend away and those that come toward us—became manifest.
For him who, knowing thus, has these cups drawn, these worlds, both those that extend away and those that come toward him, shine forth.
Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did that too.
Those gods established the meters and the pressings within the Adābhya cup. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
For one who knows this, when the Adābhya cup is drawn, he prospers in himself and his rival is defeated.
Indeed, because the gods overcame the Asuras with the Adābhya, it is called "unassailable" (adābhya).
He who knows this truly overcomes his rival; his rival does not overcome him.
This indeed is the body of Prajāpati called "the deliverer," namely the Adābhya cup.
He draws [the Soma] from [the vessel] while it is still bound for the sake of deliverance.
He who knows thus is delivered beyond evil and his rival.
(6.6.9.2) They indeed kill this Soma when they press it. When the Soma is killed, the sacrifice is killed; when the sacrifice is killed, the sacrificer is killed. Thus say the exponents of the Veda.

"What does the sacrificer perform at the sacrifice by which he goes to the world of heaven while still living? "The Adābhya is indeed a draught of one who is alive; he draws it from [Soma] that has not been pressed."

(6.6.9.2) He causes him to go to the heavenly world while he is still alive. (6.6.9.2) They indeed cut the sacrifice asunder when they conclude it at the Adābhya cup. He pours out the stalks for the continuity of the sacrifice.
The gods indeed drew the cups separately.
Prajāpati saw this *aṃśu* cup; he drew it.
By that indeed he prospered.
For whomsoever, knowing thus, the *aṃśu* cup is drawn, he surely prospers;
he draws it from what has been pressed once.
For once he prospered by means of that;
he takes [the portion] with the mind,
for Prajāpati is, as it were, the mind.
For the attainment of Prajāpati,
he takes [the Soma] with a vessel made of Udumbara wood;
for the Udumbara is indeed strength.
Verily, he wins nourishment.
It has four corners;
thus he finds firm support in the quarters.
Whoever knows the abode of the *aṃśu* cup becomes possessed of an abode.
The *vāmadevya* is the *sāman*; that indeed is its abode. Singing it with the mind, he draws [the cup]; thus he becomes truly possessed of an abode.
(6.6.10.2) If the Adhvaryu, while drawing the *aṃśu* cup, should fail to succeed, he would fail for both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer. (6.6.10.2) If he should succeed, he would succeed for both.
(6.6.10.2) He draws it without pausing; that itself is his success.
He breathes over the gold.
Gold is indeed immortality, and breath is life; thus, by means of life, he bestows immortality upon it.
It is one hundred mānas in weight.
Man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers; he thus establishes himself in life and in power.
Prajāpati assigned the sacrifices to the gods. He felt himself depleted; he drew out from himself the sixteenfold sensory power and vigor that constitutes the sacrifice.
That became the *ṣoḍaśin*.
Indeed, there is no sacrifice named "the *ṣoḍaśin*";
rather, because its chant (*stotra*) consists of sixteen [verses] and its recitation (*śastra*) consists of sixteen [verses], it is therefore called the *ṣoḍaśin*.
That is the reason for the *ṣoḍaśin* being called *ṣoḍaśin*.
In that the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is drawn, the sacrificer thereby places within himself sensory power and vigor.
Indeed, the heavenly world belongs to the gods.
It did not prevail. They saw this *ṣoḍaśin* [cup] and drew it.
(6.6.11.2) From that, indeed, the heavenly world became accessible to them.
(6.6.11.2) In that the *ṣoḍaśī* cup is drawn, it is for the conquest of the heavenly world. (6.6.11.2) Indra, indeed, was the youngest among the gods.
He ran to Prajāpati;
he gave this *ṣoḍaśin* to him,
and he took it.
(6.6.11.2) Thereupon he indeed attained preeminence among the deities;
for him who, knowing thus, takes up the *ṣoḍaśī* cup.
He goes to the very forefront of his equals;
he draws [the cup] at the morning pressing;
for the *ṣoḍaśin* is indeed a thunderbolt.
The morning pressing is the thunderbolt;
he draws him from his own womb;
he draws him at each pressing.
Verily, he causes him to be born from each pressing.
One who desires cattle should draw [the cup] at the third pressing;
for the *ṣoḍaśin* is indeed a thunderbolt, and the third pressing is cattle.
By means of the thunderbolt itself, he wins cattle for him from the third pressing.
One should not draw [the cup] at the Ukthya; for offspring are indeed cattle, and the Ukthas are cattle.
If he were to draw it at the Ukthya, he would burn away his offspring and cattle.
He should draw it at the Atirātra for one who desires cattle;
for the Ṣoḍaśin is indeed a thunderbolt.
(6.6.11.4) Having secured the cattle for him by means of the thunderbolt itself, he pacifies them from above with the night.
(6.6.11.4) One may also draw [the cup] for a Rājanya at the Agniṣṭoma;
for a Rājanya sacrifices desiring distinction.
On the very day of the *sāhna* sacrifice, he takes up the thunderbolt for him;
that thunderbolt either kindles him toward prosperity or consumes him.
There is a twenty-one-fold hymn of praise for the sake of stability.
(6.6.11.4) It is recited with the word "harivat.
(6.6.11.4) One attains the beloved abode of Indra.
(6.6.11.5) Among the gods, the meters were fewer, while among the asuras they were greater.
Those gods, by means of a smaller metre, over-recited a larger metre.
Thereby, indeed, they wrested the world of the Asuras from them.
When one over-recites a larger metre by means of a smaller metre, one wrests the world of one's rival.
They exceed by six syllables;
there are indeed six seasons;
verily, he gratifies the seasons.
(6.6.11.5) They arrange four [verses] first; verily, he wins four-footed cattle. Two [verses] are last; verily, he wins two-footed [cattle].
They bring them together to form an *anuṣṭubh*;
for the *anuṣṭubh* is speech.
Therefore, speech is the highest of the vital breaths.
When the sun has half-risen, he begins the chant of the Ṣoḍaśin.
For it was in this very world that Indra slew Vṛtra.
(6.6.11.6) He hurls the thunderbolt directly at his rival.
(6.6.11.6) A reddish-brown horse is the sacrificial fee.
(6.6.11.6) That, indeed, is the form of the thunderbolt.
For prosperity.
(7.1.1.1) Procreation is light; Agni is the light among the deities, the Virāj is the light among the meters, [and] the light.
(7.1.1.1) The Virāj settles in the fire of speech; he attains the Virāj.
Therefore, that is called light.
Two *stomas* carry the morning pressing, as do inhalation and exhalation;
two [carry] the midday pressing, as do sight and hearing.
Two [are for] the third pressing, namely speech and the foundation;
this sacrifice is commensurate with man and is not one-sided.

(7.1.1.2) Whatever desire one desires, that one attains by means of this; for by means of the *asthūri* [chariot], one attains everything. (7.1.1.2) By means of the *agniṣṭoma*, Prajāpati indeed created offspring.
(7.1.1.2) He enclosed them by means of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice itself. (7.1.1.2) Of those thus enclosed, a mule ran away. (7.1.1.2) Having pursued it, he took its seed.
(7.1.1.2) He wiped it off on a donkey. (7.1.1.2) Of those that were seized, a mule ran away. Having pursued it, he took its semen.
He wiped it on the donkey; therefore the donkey has double seed.
Moreover, they say:
"He struck her in the mare," so it is said;
therefore, the mare has double seed.
Furthermore, they say:
(7.1.1.2) Regarding the plants: (7.1.1.3) "He has rubbed them down," it is said; therefore, the plants, though unanointed, hum.
Moreover, they say:
"He struck them down among the offspring"—
therefore twins are born;
therefore the mule does not procreate, for its seed has been taken away.
Therefore, he is not eligible for the *barhis* [sacrifice];
rather, he is eligible for either the *sarvavedasa* or the *sahasra*.
For he has surpassed the unyielding.
He who, knowing this, sacrifices with the Agniṣṭoma, procreates offspring not yet born and takes hold of those already born. Therefore they say:
"It is the sacrifice of the eldest."
Prajāpati, indeed, is the eldest; for he was the first to sacrifice with this [rite]. Prajāpati desired: [7.1.1.4]
(7.1.1.4) "May I procreate," he thought.
(7.1.1.4) From his mouth he measured out the Trivṛt-stoma;
after it, Agni was emitted as the deity, the Gāyatrī as the metre, the Rathantara as the Sāman, the Brāhmaṇa among men, and the goat among animals.
Therefore they are the principal ones,
for they were created from the mouth.
From the chest and the two arms, he measured out the fifteenfold [Stoma].

Indra was created as the deity corresponding to him; the Triṣṭubh became the metre, the Bṛhat the Sāman, the Rājanya among men, and the sheep among animals. Therefore, they are full of vigor, for they were created from vigor.

(7.1.1.5) He measured out the seventeenfold [stoma] from the middle. After it, the Viśve Devas were created as its deity; the Jagatī was the metre, the Vairūpa the Sāman, the Vaiśya among men, and cattle among animals.
Therefore, they are to be eaten.
For they were created from the vessel of food;
therefore they are more numerous than others,
for the greatest number of deities were created after them.
Pata measured out the twenty-first;
after it, the Anuṣṭubh metre was released, the Vairāja Sāman, and among men, the Śūdra; among animals, the horse.
Therefore, both the horse and the Śūdra are transmitters of the elements; therefore, the Śūdra is not entitled to the sacrifice,
for he was not created after the deities.
Therefore, they subsist upon the feet; for the feet were created [last]. The *trivṛt* is indeed the vital breaths.
The half-months are fifteen;
Prajāpati is seventeen;
these worlds are three.
(7.1.1.6) Yonder sun is the twenty-onefold [stoma].
Indeed, these [worlds] rest upon it; they are established upon it.
He who knows thus rests upon it and is established upon it.
At the morning pressing, indeed, he goes forward bestowing light upon the *trivṛt* stoma by means of the *gāyatrī* metre;

with the *trivṛt*, which is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he goes forward bestowing light upon the *pañcadaśa* stoma; with the *pañcadaśa*, which is vigor and heroism, he goes forward bestowing light upon the *saptadaśa* stoma.
(7.1.2.1) With the seventeenfold Stoma belonging to Prajāpati, which is generative, he goes forward bestowing light upon the twenty-onefold Stoma;
thus, it is the Stoma itself that, bestowing light upon the Stoma, goes forward.
Moreover, it is the Stoma itself that leads the Stoma onward.
As many as are the *stomas*, so many are the desires; so many are the worlds; so many are the lights.
He wins just as many Stomas, just as many desires, just as many worlds, and just as many lights.
(7.1.3.1) The exponents of Brahman say:
"He indeed should sacrifice who, having sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma, then sacrifices with the Sarvastoma.
For him whose threefold [stomas] pass away, his vital breaths pass away.

(7.1.3.1) "May there also be for me in the vital breaths," with this thought indeed the sacrificer performs the sacrifice. If they omit the fifteenfold [stoma], they omit his vigor; "May there also be for me in vigor," with this thought indeed the sacrificer performs the sacrifice.
(7.1.3.1) For whomsoever they omit the seventeenth [stotra], they omit his offspring.
(7.1.3.2) "May there be offspring for me," with this thought indeed the sacrificer performs the sacrifice. For whomsoever they omit the twenty-first [stotra], they omit his foundation.
(7.1.3.2) "May there also be for me a firm foundation," with this thought indeed the sacrificer performs the sacrifice by means of the sacrifice.
For him whose *triṇava* stoma is omitted, both the seasons and the *nakṣatriyā* *virāj* are omitted.
(7.1.3.2–3) "May there be for me [a share] in the seasons and in the *nakṣatriyā* *virāj*," with this thought indeed the sacrificer performs the sacrifice by means of the sacrifice.
(7.1.3.3) He whose thirty-three deities pass within [the *stoma*], his deities pass within.
"May there be a share for me among the deities," with this thought indeed the sacrificer performs the sacrifice by means of the sacrifice.
He who knows the lowest of the *stomas* as reaching the highest state, reaches the highest state itself.
The *trivṛt* is indeed the lowest of the *stomas*, and the *trivṛt* is the highest. He who knows thus attains the very state of being highest.
The Aṅgirases indeed performed a sacrificial session;
they went to the heavenly world.
Of them, both Haviṣmān and Haviṣkṛt were left behind.
(7.1.4.1) They two desired: "May we go to the heavenly world. (7.1.4.1) They two saw this two-night rite.
They brought it; with it they sacrificed. Thereupon, indeed, those two went to the heavenly world.

(7.1.4.1) He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Dvirātra, goes indeed to the world of heaven. (7.1.4.1) These two [days] came together; they reached it by means of the first day and by means of the second. (7.1.4.2) The Abhiplava becomes the first day; the Gati is the second.
(7.1.4.2) The Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma becomes the first day; by that he wins splendor.
(7.1.4.2) An Atirātra with the Sarvastoma is the latter [part], for the attainment of everything and the securing of everything.
(7.1.4.2) On the preceding day, the Sāman is the Gāyatra;
the Gāyatrī is indeed brilliance.
The Gāyatrī is spiritual luster;
he places spiritual luster, which is indeed brilliance, within himself.
The next [verse] is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
The *triṣṭubh* is indeed vigor and strength;
he thus places vigor and strength within himself.
On the first day, the *rathantara* becomes the *sāman*.
(7.1.4.3) This earth, indeed, is the Rathantara;
he finds firm support upon this very [earth].
(7.1.4.3) The Bṛhat is in the higher [world].
(7.1.4.3) That [heaven] indeed is the Bṛhat. (7.1.4.3) He thus finds firm support in that very [heaven]. (7.1.4.3) Regarding this, they say:
(7.1.4.3) "Wherein do the Jagatī and the Anuṣṭubh [reside]? (7.1.4.3) On the first day, the Vaikhānasa is the Sāman; by that, he does not depart from the Jagatī.
On the second day, there is the Ṣoḍaśin; by that, [he does not depart] from the Anuṣṭubh.
(7.1.4.3) Now they say: "If these two [pressings] were to occur on the same half-month, the vigor of one day would fall away.
(7.1.4.3) The first day occurs on the new moon, and the latter on the following day.
The two half-months are indeed distinct;
they possess distinct powers.
The day with the *haviṣmat* finale comes first, and the day with the *haviṣkṛt* finale comes later.
For the sake of firm establishment.
(7.1.5.1) In the beginning, this world was indeed water, a vast expanse. Within it, Prajāpati, having become the wind, moved about. He beheld this [earth].
Having become a boar, he took her;
having become Viśvakarman, he wiped her clean; she expanded.
She became the earth;
that is the earth-nature of the earth. Upon her, Prajāpati exerted himself.
(7.1.5.1) He created the gods: the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas.
(7.1.5.1) Those gods said to Prajāpati, "May we procreate."
He said.
"As I have created you through austerity (*tapas*), so do you seek procreation through austerity," he said. He granted them fire as their abode, saying, "Exert yourselves with this abode."
(7.1.5.2) They toiled with fire as their abode.
(7.1.5.2) In the course of a year, they produced a single cow.
(7.1.5.2) They presented her to the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas.
"Guard her! they said. The Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas guarded her.
She brought forth offspring for the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas: three hundred and thirty-three.
(7.1.5.3) Then she herself became the thousandth.
(7.1.5.3) Those gods said to Prajāpati: "Sacrifice for us with the thousand."
He caused the Vasus to sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma;
they conquered this world and took possession of it.
He caused the Rudras to sacrifice with the Ukthya;
they conquered the intermediate space,
and he gave that to them.
He caused the Ādityas to sacrifice with the Atirātra;
they conquered that world,
and he gave it to them.
That became the intermediate space. It split apart; therefore the Rudras are destroyers, for they were without a dwelling place.
Therefore they say:
"The middle day of the three-night rite is indeed loose, for it was relaxed.
The *ājya* hymn of the middle day is in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
He recites the Saṃyāna hymns;
he recites the Ṣoḍaśin hymn,
for the support of the day and to prevent it from becoming loose.

Therefore, in the three-night sacrifice, the first day should be an Agniṣṭoma, then an Ukthya, and then an Atirātra; this is for the separation of these worlds. He gives three hundred [cows] each day in succession, without interruption.
For the continuity of these worlds,
one should not break off a set of ten; [one should think],
"Lest I cut off the Virāj."
(7.1.5.5) Now, as for that cow which was the thousandth, Indra and Viṣṇu contended over her.
(7.1.5.5) That Indra thought:
(7.1.5.5) "By means of this [cow], Viṣṇu will indeed win this thousand."
In that [sacrifice], they two made their allotment: Indra received two parts, and Viṣṇu the third.
Regarding this, the following verse is recited:
"Both have conquered," with these words the Achāvāka indeed recites this [verse].
Now, that which is the thousandth [cow] is to be given to the Hotṛ.
(7.1.5.6) Or rather, it exceeds the *hotṛ*.
(7.1.5.6) That which exceeds is the *hotṛ*’s means of making good what has not been obtained.
(7.1.5.6) Now they say:
"O Unnetṛ, you have won!
This [cow] is indeed the surplus of the thousand;
she is the surplus among the officiating priests.
(7.1.5.6) Now they say:
"One should give it to all the members of the assembly.
(7.1.5.6) Then they say:
(7.1.5.6) "Having been given away, she should live under his control," they say.
(7.1.5.6) Then they say:
"She should be given to both the Brahman and the Āgnīdhra."
(7.1.5.7) Two parts for the Brahman and a third for the Agnīdh.
(7.1.5.7) For the Brahman belongs to Indra, and the Agnīdh belongs to Viṣṇu. (7.1.5.7) It is so that these two may be properly constituted.
(7.1.5.7) Now they say:
"She who is beautiful and multiformed is the goddess.
(7.1.5.7) Then they say:
(7.1.5.7) That cow which is two-colored and brindled on both sides is the *devī* (the divine one); she is for the securing of the thousand.
(7.1.5.7) This, indeed, is the path of the thousand;
there are a thousand *stotrīyā* verses.
The sacrificial gifts are a thousand;
the heavenly world is measured by a thousand;
[this is] for the conquest of the heavenly world.
Soma indeed found a thousand;
Indra found it after him;
Yama approached them both.
He said to them: "Let there be for me a share here as well. They replied: "So be it! (hī3).

(7.1.6.1) Yama perceived the creative power (*vīrya*) concentrated in one [of the thousand]. He thought, "This earth indeed bears the creative power of this thousand. He said to them, "Let this be mine; let that belong to you two.
They replied: (7.1.6.1) They said:
(7.1.6.1) "All this, indeed, is the virility within her. (7.1.6.2) "Let us look all around; let us bring back a portion!
(7.1.6.2) Having brought back a portion from her, they cast her into the waters.
"O Soma, come forth!
At this, Rohiṇī, the reddish-brown one-year-old cow, assuming her form, came forth together with three hundred and thirty-three [cows].
Therefore, one should purchase the Soma with a reddish-brown one-year-old cow.
He who, knowing thus, purchases Soma with a reddish-brown, one-year-old cow of the Rohiṇī breed, [obtains] for him both thirty-three and three [breaths].
(7.1.6.3) Soma becomes purchased for hundreds; (7.1.6.3) he sacrifices with that well-purchased [Soma];
they caused it to enter into the waters.
"O Indra, come forth!"— saying this, she who was a ruddy,
marked, four-year-old cow, the slayer of Vṛtra, having assumed her form, rose up together with three hundred and thirty-three [gods].
Therefore, one should give a ruddy, marked, four-year-old cow, the slayer of Vṛtra.
(7.1.6.3) When one who knows thus gives a red, marked, four-year-old cow that slays enemies, that gift becomes for him three hundred and thirty-three.
(7.1.6.4) They caused her to enter the waters with the words: "Go forth to Yama!"
She, having assumed the form of an old, foolish, and most wretched woman, went up together with three hundred and thirty-three [gods].
Therefore, one should make an old, foolish, and most wretched cow the *anustaraṇī* (the cow sacrificed over the corpse).
For him who, knowing this, makes an old, foolish, and most wretched cow the *anustaraṇī*, there shall be three hundred and thirty-three [deities] for him in yonder world.
Speech itself is the thousandth;
therefore a boon should be given,
for she is indeed the boon.
(7.1.6.5) A thousand is given for it;
therefore, a bride-price (*vara*) should not be accepted, for that [thousand] is indeed the bride-price.
(7.1.6.5) A thousand have been received by him. (7.1.6.5) He should say, "This is the boon. (7.1.6.5) Then he should speak to another.
"This is mine"—
in this way, those thousand [cows] of his remain unaccepted.
It should be a cow that is variegated on both sides.
Regarding this, they say:
"It should be a piebald cow, with a thousand [cows] beyond it.
She should indeed be a bride, beautiful and endowed with perfect form.
For she is indeed a boon;
it is for prosperity. Having led her around the north of the Āgnīdhra fire, one should cause her to smell the *droṇakalaśa* at the edge of the Āhavanīya fire.
"Smell the jar for me; may you be of wide stream and full of milk. May the drops enter you as rivers enter the ocean.
Grant me a share of a thousandfold, together with offspring and cattle; may wealth come back to me again.
Thus, he causes him to prosper with offspring, cattle, and wealth.
(7.1.6.7) He who knows thus becomes possessed of offspring, cattle, and wealth.
(7.1.6.7) Having gone with her to the Āgnīdhra shed, he should offer the oblation while she stands in front, facing westward:
"Both of you have conquered; you two are not defeated; neither of these two has been defeated."
"O Indra and Viṣṇu, when you two contended, you two distributed a thousand threefold.
In the three-night rite, a thousand is indeed divided threefold;
thus he makes it thousandfold.
He makes her the measure of a thousand;
he offers the forms;
verily by means of the forms he causes her to prosper.
(7.1.6.8) Having approached her, he should whisper into her ear:
(7.1.6.8) "O *iḍā*, *rantī*, *aditi*, *sarasvatī*, *priyā*, *preyasi*, *mahi*, *viśrutī*—these are your names, O inviolable one (*aghnī*).
Declare me as a doer of good deeds among the gods. (7.1.6.8) Thus he says.
(7.1.6.8) He makes him known to the gods;
(7.1.6.8) the gods take notice of him.
(7.1.7.1) By means of the thousandth cow, the sacrificer indeed goes to the heavenly world;
she causes him to go to the heavenly world.
"May she cause me to go to the heavenly world," he says.
He causes him to go to the heavenly world itself.
"Lead me to the luminous world," he says; he thus causes him to go to the luminous world itself.
"May she lead me to all auspicious worlds," he says;
verily, she leads him to all auspicious worlds.
"May she lead me to a firm foundation, together with offspring and cattle; may wealth return to me again"—verily, by means of offspring and cattle, he establishes him in wealth.
He who knows this becomes possessed of offspring, cattle, and wealth.
He should give her to the *agnīdh*, or to the *brahman*, or to the *hotṛ*, or to the *udgātṛ*, or to the *adhvaryu*;
thus, a thousand have been given by him.
A thousandfold is the [sin] received by him who receives it without knowing this. One should receive it [with the knowledge]:
"Thou art one; thou art not a thousand."
"I accept you as one being, not as a thousand; do not enter me as a thousand beings, but as one.
He who knows thus accepts her as one being, not as a thousand.
"Thou art pleasant, easy to sit upon, and very gracious; enter me as one pleasant, enter me as one easy to sit upon, enter me as one very gracious," he says.
Thus, having become pleasant, easy to sit upon, and very gracious, she enters him and does not harm him.
The exponents of the Veda say:
"The thousandth follows after the thousand; the thousand follows after the thousandth.
If he were to let it go toward the east, the thousandth would follow after the thousand;
that [number] of one thousand would be indistinguishable.
He would not know the world of heaven;
he releases [the arrow] toward the west,
and it revolves a thousand times around it.
Knowing it,
she goes to the heavenly world;
she releases the sacrificer upward.
(7.1.7.4) Quickly he is born as a thousandfold progeny;
(7.1.7.4) led as the last, he goes as the first to the gods.
Atri gave his offspring to Aurva, who was desirous of progeny;
he, feeling depleted, thought himself devoid of vigor, relaxed, and exhausted. He beheld this four-night sacrifice.
He fetched it; he sacrificed with it.
From that, indeed, four heroic sons were born to him: a skilled Hotṛ, a skilled Udgātṛ, a skilled Adhvaryu, and one fit for the assembly.
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the four-night rite, to him are born four heroic sons: a skilled Hotṛ, a skilled Udgātṛ, a skilled Adhvaryu, and one successful in the assembly.
Those Pavamāna chants which consist of twenty-four [verses] constitute spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
The *stomas* that rise upward are prosperity (*śrī*).

When Atri, whose deity was faith, was performing sacrifice, four powers did not come to him: brilliance, sensory power, spiritual luster, and the enjoyment of food. He beheld these four *soma* sacrifices consisting of fourfold *stomas*.
He brought them; with them he sacrificed.
By the first, he won splendor; by the second, sensory power; by the third, spiritual luster; by the fourth, the food of the earth.

He who, knowing this, brings these four Soma sacrifices characterized by the fourfold stoma and sacrifices with them, wins splendor by the first, sensory power by the second, spiritual luster by the third, and the food of the earth by the fourth.
Whatever prosperity Atri attained, that very same prosperity the sacrificer attains.
Jamadagni, desiring prosperity, sacrificed with the four-night rite; he thereby attained these prosperities.
Therefore, two descendants of Jamadagni who have turned grey do not recognize one another.
He who, knowing this, sacrifices with the four-night rite, nourishes these very prosperities.
The Upasad days consist of sacrificial cakes;
for the sacrificial cake is indeed cattle.
Verily, he wins cattle.
The sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is indeed food;
verily, he wins food.
One who, knowing thus, performs the four-night sacrifice becomes an eater of food and possesses cattle.
(7.1.10.1) This universe was indeed the Year alone. (7.1.10.1) It desired: (7.1.10.1) "May I create the seasons."
He saw this five-night rite;
he took it up and performed sacrifice with it.
Thereupon, indeed, he created the seasons.
(7.1.10.1) He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Pañcarātra, truly procreates. (7.1.10.1) Those seasons, once created, did not turn away from one another; they beheld this Pañcarātra.
They brought it; they sacrificed with it,
and then indeed they became distinct.
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Pañcarātra, is separated from evil and from his rival.
Sārvaseni Śauceya desired,
"May I be possessed of cattle."
He brought forth this five-night rite; he sacrificed with it,
and thereby he indeed obtained a thousand cattle.
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Pañcarātra, obtains a thousand cattle.
Babara Prāvāhaṇi desired,
"May I be a speaker of speech."
He brought this five-night rite; he sacrificed with it,
and from that, indeed, he became a speaker of speech.
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the five-night rite, becomes indeed a master of speech;
moreover, they call him "the Lord of Speech.
The four-night rite is incomplete, and the six-night rite is excessive; but this five-night rite is the sacrifice that is perfectly proportioned.
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Pañcarātra, truly sacrifices with the sacrifice.
It consists of five nights;
for the year indeed has five seasons.
Verily, he finds firm support in the seasons and in the year;
moreover, the *paṅkti* consists of five syllables, and the sacrifice is fivefold.
Verily, he wins the sacrifice;
it becomes a threefold Agniṣṭoma;
verily, he wins splendor.
It becomes fifteenfold;
verily, he wins power.
It becomes seventeenfold.
For the attainment of food; moreover, by means of it one is indeed propagated. There is a Pañcaviṃśa Agniṣṭoma for the fulfillment of Prajāpati.
(7.1.10.4) One who performs the Mahāvrata [rite] does so for the attainment of food. (7.1.10.4) There is an Atirātra sacrifice with the Viśvajit [stoma] and all the Pṛṣṭha [stotras],
for the conquest of everything.

(7.1.11.1.a) At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I take you up. (7.1.11.1.b) The seers of old grasped this rein of Cosmic Order at the assemblies during their former life; through it the gods attained the pressed juice, making the flowing stream of Cosmic Order resound.
(7.1.11.1.c) Thou art the utterer; thou art the world; thou art the restrainer; thou art the supporter. Go thou to Agni Vaiśvānara, the far-extending, consecrated by *svāhā*.
(7.1.11.1ḍ) On earth, thou art the restrainer, the sovereign; thou art the restrainer, the controller; thou art the supporter, the sustainer.
(7.1.11.1.e) For the sake of agriculture thee; for the sake of security thee; for the sake of wealth thee; for the sake of prosperity thee.
For the earth thee, for the intermediate space thee, for the sky thee;
for what exists thee, for what does not exist thee, for the waters thee, for the plants thee, for all beings thee.

(7.1.12.1.a) Abundant through my mother, powerful through my father; you are a horse, you are a steed, you are a racer, you are a manly one, you are a courser, you are a prize-winner, you are a stallion, you are manly-minded; your name is "the swift"; follow the flight of the Ādityas! (7.1.12.1.b) To Agni, svāhā! Svāhā to Indra and Agni! Svāhā to Prajāpati! Svāhā to the All-gods! Svāhā to all the divine powers!
(7.1.12.1.c) Here is steadfastness, svāhā! Here is separation, svāhā! Here is delight, svāhā! Here is enjoyment, svāhā!
(7.1.12.1ḍ) You are *bhūḥ*; for the past I consecrate you, for the present I consecrate you, for the future I consecrate you; for all beings I consecrate you.
(7.1.12.1.e) O gods, guardians of the quarters, protect this horse, consecrated for the sacrifice, for the gods.
Hail to the coming! Hail to the departure!
Hail to the fleeing away!
To the one who has run out, svāhā!
To the one who snorts, svāhā!
To the one who has snorted, svāhā!
(7.1.13.1) Svāhā to the one who has fled! (7.1.13.1) Svāhā to the one who has not fled! (7.1.13.1) Svāhā to the one who is running toward!
(7.1.13.1) Svāhā to him as he steps forward! (7.1.13.1) Svāhā to him as he comes!
(7.1.13.1) Svāhā to him as he proceeds!
(7.1.13.1) Svāhā to everything!
(7.1.14.1) Svāhā to Agni! (7.1.14.1) Svāhā to Soma!
(7.1.14.1) Svāhā to Vāyu!
(7.1.14.1) To the delight of the waters, svāhā!
(7.1.14.1) To Savitṛ, svāhā!
(7.1.14.1) To Sarasvatī, svāhā!
(7.1.14.1) Svāhā to Indra! (7.1.14.1) Svāhā to Bṛhaspati!
(7.1.14.1) Svāhā to Mitra!
Svāhā to Varuṇa!
Svāhā to the All!
(7.1.15.1) Svāhā to the earth!
(7.1.15.1) Svāhā to the intermediate space! (7.1.15.1) Svāhā to the sky!
(7.1.15.1) Svāhā to Sūrya! (7.1.15.1) Svāhā to Candramas! (7.1.15.1) Svāhā to the Nakṣatras!
Hail to the eastern quarter!
Hail to the southern quarter!
Hail to the western quarter!
Hail to the northern quarter!
Hail to the upward quarter!
Hail to the quarters!
To the intermediate quarters, svāhā!
To the years, svāhā!
To the autumns, svāhā!
(7.1.15.1) Svāhā to the days and nights! (7.1.15.1) Svāhā to the half-months! (7.1.15.1) Svāhā to the months!
(7.1.15.1) Svāhā to the seasons! (7.1.15.1) Svāhā to the year!
(7.1.15.1) Svāhā to the All!
(7.1.16.1) Svāhā to Agni! (7.1.16.1) Svāhā to Soma! (7.1.16.1) Svāhā to Savitṛ!
(7.1.16.1) Svāhā to Sarasvatī! (7.1.16.1) Svāhā to Pūṣan!
(7.1.16.1) Svāhā to Bṛhaspati!
(7.1.16.1) To the joy of the waters, svāhā!
(7.1.16.1) To Vāyu, svāhā! (7.1.16.1) To Mitra, svāhā!
(7.1.16.1) Svāhā to Varuṇa!
(7.1.16.1) Svāhā to the All!
(7.1.17.1) Svāhā to the earth! (7.1.17.1) Svāhā to the intermediate space!
(7.1.17.1) Svāhā to the sky!
(7.1.17.1) Svāhā to Agni! (7.1.17.1) Svāhā to Soma! (7.1.17.1) Svāhā to Sūrya!
(7.1.17.1) Svāhā to the Moon! (7.1.17.1) Svāhā to the Day! (7.1.17.1) Svāhā to the Night!
Hail to the upright!
Hail to the virtuous!
Hail to the good dwelling!
(7.1.17.1) Svāhā to hunger! (7.1.17.1) Svāhā to the act of eating! (7.1.17.1) Svāhā to disease!
(7.1.17.1) To the cold, svāhā!
(7.1.17.1) To the chill, svāhā!
(7.1.17.1) To the heat, svāhā!
(7.1.17.1) Svāhā to the forest! (7.1.17.1) Svāhā to heaven!
(7.1.17.1) Svāhā to the world!
(7.1.17.1) Svāhā to everything!

(7.1.18.1.a) You are the path of the world for the gods through their work; you are the path of the cosmic order. With the Vasus as gods, with the deity [Agni], and with the Gāyatrī metre, I yoke you; with the spring season, with the oblation, I consecrate you.
(7.1.18.1.b) With the Rudras as gods, with the deity [Indra], and with the Triṣṭubh metre, I yoke you; with the summer season, with the oblation, I consecrate you.
(7.1.18.1.c) With the Ādityas as gods, with the deity [Sūrya], and with the Jagatī metre, I yoke you; with the rainy season, with the oblation, I consecrate you.
With all the gods as the deity, with the *anuṣṭubh* metre, I yoke you. With the autumn season as the season, I consecrate you with the oblation.
With the Aṅgiras gods as the deity, with the *paṅkti* metre, I yoke you. With the winter and cool seasons as the seasons, I consecrate you with the oblation.

I have ascended the consecration, the consort of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*), with the *gāyatrī* metre and with the sacred formulation (*brahman*). I have established Cosmic Order in Truth; I have established Truth in Cosmic Order.
(7.1.18.2.g) To the great one indeed;
(7.1.18.2ḥ) to the good protector; (7.1.18.2.i) here is stability, svāhā!
(7.1.18.2.k) Here is support, svāhā!
(7.1.18.2ḷ) Here is delight, svāhā!
(7.1.18.2ṃ) Here is pleasure, svāhā!
(7.1.19.1) Svāhā to the sound *īṃ*!
(7.1.19.1) Svāhā to that which has uttered *īṃ*!
(7.1.19.1) Svāhā to the one who roars!
To him who bellows, svāhā!
To him who snorts, svāhā! To him who snorts repeatedly, svāhā!
(7.1.19.1) Svāhā to smell!
(7.1.19.1) Svāhā to the one who smells! (7.1.19.1) Svāhā to the breath!
(7.1.19.1) Svāhā to the out-breath! (7.1.19.1) Svāhā to the in-breath!
(7.1.19.1) Svāhā to that which is being kindled!
Hail to him when being bound!
Hail to him while being loosened!
Hail to him when loosened!
Hail to him who is about to flee!
Hail to him who has fled!
Hail to him who will desist!
To him who has ceased, svāhā!
To him who is about to enter, svāhā!
To him who is entering, svāhā!
To him who has settled, svāhā!
To him who will settle, svāhā!
To him who is settling, svāhā!
To him who is seated, svāhā!
(7.1.19.2) To him who will sit, svāhā! (7.1.19.2) To him who is sitting, svāhā! (7.1.19.2) To him who has sat, svāhā!
(7.1.19.2) To him who is about to fall, svāhā!
(7.1.19.2) To him who is falling, svāhā!
(7.1.19.2) To him who has fallen, svāhā!
(7.1.19.2) To him who will lie down, svāhā! (7.1.19.2) To him who is lying down, svāhā! (7.1.19.2) To him who has lain down, svāhā!
To him who is about to close his eyes, svāhā!
To him who is closing his eyes, svāhā! To him who has closed his eyes, svāhā!
(7.1.19.2) To one who will sleep, svāhā! (7.1.19.2) To one who is sleeping, svāhā!
(7.1.19.2) To one who has slept, svāhā!
To him who will awaken, svāhā!
To him who is awakening, svāhā!
To him who has awakened, svāhā!
To the one about to wake, svāhā!
To the waking one, svāhā!
To the one who has awakened, svāhā!
Svāhā to him who desires to hear;
svāhā to him who hears;
svāhā to what has been heard.
(7.1.19.2) He shall look upon [it], svāhā!
To him looking about, svāhā!
To him having looked, svāhā!
To him who will yawn, svāhā!
To him as he is rising up, svāhā! To him as he is rising up, svāhā! To him as he is about to turn back, svāhā!
Hail to him who is turning;
hail to him who has turned!
Hail to him who is about to rise!
(7.1.19.3) Svāhā to him as he rises!
(7.1.19.3) Svāhā to him who has risen!
(7.1.19.3) Svāhā to him as he is about to perform the rite!
To him who is shaking off, svāhā!
To him who has shaken off, svāhā!
To him who will ascend, svāhā!
(7.1.19.3) Svāhā to him as he steps out! (7.1.19.3) Svāhā to him who has stepped out!
(7.1.19.3) Svāhā to him as he will walk about!
Hail to him who is walking about!
Hail to him who has walked about!
Hail to him who will scratch himself!
Hail to him who is scratching!
Hail to him who has scratched!
Hail to him who will scratch!
Hail to him as he is being rubbed!
Hail to him when he has been rubbed!
Hail to that which he eats!
To that which he drinks, svāhā!
To that which he urinates, svāhā!
To that which he excretes as dung, svāhā!
Svāhā to semen; svāhā to offspring;
svāhā to procreation.
(7.1.19.3) Svāhā to everything!

(7.1.20.1.a) To Agni, svāhā! To Vāyu, svāhā! To Sūrya, svāhā! (7.1.20.1.b) You are the cosmic order (*ṛta*); you are the *ṛta* of the *ṛta*. You are truth (*satya*); you are the truth of the truth. (7.1.20.1.c) You are the path of the *ṛta*, the shadow of the gods. That which is your name, the *ṛta*, is truth; for you are Prajāpati.

When the beautiful ones vie for him as for a prize-winning steed, he flows as a sage, choosing the waters of heaven along with the sun; like a watchful herdsman guarding his cattle, he, the active one, moves all around.
The Sādhyas, the gods who desired heaven, saw this six-night rite;
they took it up and sacrificed with it.
(7.2.1.1) From there, indeed, they went to the heavenly world.
Those who, knowing thus, perform the six-night rite go to the heavenly world itself.
The six-night rite is indeed a sacrificial session of the gods.
(7.2.1.1) For these *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed directly perceived. Those who, knowing thus, perform the six-night rite, mount the deities face to face.
There is a six-night rite.
There are six seasons;
there are six *pṛṣṭha* chants. By means of the *pṛṣṭhas*, they ascend after the seasons; by means of the seasons, [they ascend] after the year. They find firm support in the year itself.
(7.2.1.2) They proceed with the Bṛhat and the Rathantara.
(7.2.1.2) This [earth] indeed is the Rathantara, and yonder [sky] is the Bṛhat. (7.2.1.2) It is by means of these two that they proceed.
(7.2.1.2) Moreover, they find firm support in these two alone. (7.2.1.2) These indeed are the two direct paths of the sacrifice; by means of them, they go to the heavenly world.
The Agniṣṭoma is threefold; they thus obtain brilliance. It is fifteenfold.
(7.2.1.2) They indeed obtain the sense-faculties.
(7.2.1.2) It consists of seventeen [verses].
(7.2.1.3) This is for the attainment of food.
(7.2.1.3) Moreover, by means of it they are indeed procreated. (7.2.1.3) It consists of twenty-one [verses] for the sake of stability; moreover, they place radiance within themselves.
There is a Triṇava [stoma] for the sake of victory;
there is a Trayastriṃśa [stoma] for the sake of stability.
(7.2.1.3) Those who possess the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds should sacrifice with this six-night rite.
(7.2.1.3) The *havirdhāna* and the *āgnīdhra* sheds are made of *aśvattha* wood; for that leads to heaven.
The two [posts] have rings for the attainment of the heavenly world.
The sacrificial post has a mortar-base.
For the sake of stability;
they go eastward,
for the world of heaven is, as it were, facing the east.
They proceed along the Sarasvatī;
this indeed is the path leading to the gods, and it is that very path they ascend.
They go along reviling;
having fastened misfortune upon another, they attain a firm foundation.
When they make ten into a hundred, that is one rising.
A man has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundred faculties; they are thus established in both life-span and faculty. When they make a hundred into a thousand, that constitutes a single rising.
(7.2.1.4) For that world is measured by a thousand;
(7.2.1.4) they conquer that very world.
(7.2.1.4) Whenever one of them should die, or whenever they should be defeated, then there is one rising.
For that indeed is the sacred ford.
(7.2.2.1) Kusurubinda Auddālaki desired,
"May I possess cattle. (7.2.2.1) He performed this seven-night sacrifice.
With that he sacrificed. With it, indeed, he won as many domestic animals as there are.
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the seven-night rite, wins as many domestic animals as there are.
It lasts for seven nights;
there are seven domestic animals, seven wild animals, and seven meters.
This is for the attainment of both.
The Agniṣṭoma is threefold; verily, he thereby wins brilliance. It is fifteenfold.
Verily, he wins the sense-faculties;
it consists of seventeen parts for the attainment of food.
Moreover, by means of it, one is indeed propagated.
It consists of twenty-one [verses] for the sake of stability.
Moreover, he bestows radiance upon himself;
it consists of twenty-seven verses for the sake of victory.
The Agniṣṭoma consists of twenty-five [stomas] for the attainment of Prajāpati;
it includes the Mahāvrata for the acquisition of food;
and there is an Atirātra with all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras, the Viśvajit.
(7.2.2.2) For the sake of conquering everything.

(7.2.2.2) If they were to employ the *pṛṣṭha* stotras visibly on the preceding days, it would be visible [on the last day as well]. (7.2.2.3) On the *viśvajit*, the final day should be like approaching a cow that has already been milked;
not even a single-night sacrifice (*ekarātra*) should take place.
(7.2.2.3) They proceed with the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] on the preceding days.
This earth is indeed the Rathantara, and yonder sky is the Bṛhat.
It is by means of these two that they do not depart; moreover, it is upon these two that they find firm support.
That they employ the *pṛṣṭha* chants in the Viśvajit sacrifice which are directly perceived is exactly like milking a cow that has already been milked.
(7.2.3.1) Bṛhaspati desired, "May I be possessed of the splendor of sacred knowledge.
(7.2.3.1) He beheld this eight-night rite.
He brought it; he sacrificed with it. Thereupon, indeed, he became endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*).
(7.2.3.1) He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the eight-night rite becomes possessed of spiritual luster.
(7.2.3.1) It is an eight-night rite;
(7.2.3.1) the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables.
The *gāyatrī* is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
By means of the *gāyatrī* itself, he wins spiritual luster.
There is an eight-night rite.
There are four quarters;
there are four intermediate quarters.
Verily, from the quarters he wins spiritual luster for himself.
The Agniṣṭoma is threefold; verily, he wins brilliance. It is fifteenfold.
Verily, he wins the sense-power;
it consists of seventeen parts for the attainment of food-eating;
moreover, by means of it, he is indeed propagated.
It consists of twenty-one [verses] for the sake of stability;
moreover, he bestows radiance upon himself.
There is a Triṇava [stoma] for the sake of victory;
there is a Trayastriṃśa [stoma].
It is for stability; it is a Pañcaviṃśa Agniṣṭoma for the attainment of Prajāpati;
it includes the Mahāvrata for the securing of food.
The Viśvajit sacrifice, an Atirātra with all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras,
takes place for the sake of conquering everything.
Prajāpati created offspring;
once created, they fell into hunger.
He beheld this nine-night rite.
He brought it; he sacrificed with it;
from that, indeed, he became fit for all creatures.
(7.2.4.1) When people fall into hunger, then one should sacrifice with the nine-night rite.
(7.2.4.1) For these worlds of theirs are indeed unsettled when they thus fall into hunger.
(7.2.4.1) He thereby establishes these very worlds for them.
As they are being prepared, he prepares them for the sake of offspring;
they become fit. Through these three nights, he bestows vigor upon these worlds and places it within the offspring.
By means of the three-night rite, he prepares this world; by the three-night rite, the intermediate space; and by the three-night rite, yonder world.
(7.2.4.2) Just as one follows a quality with a quality, even so does that world follow the world for the sake of firmness and non-laxity.
(7.2.4.2) "Light, Cow, Life"—these are the known *stomas*.
This [earth] indeed is light, the intermediate space is the cow, and yonder [sky] is life.
In these very worlds they find firm support;
they attain the leadership of progeny.
There is a nine-night rite.
(7.2.4.3) He bestows brilliance upon him in successive order.
(7.2.4.3) He who has been long ill should sacrifice with the nine-night rite;
for his vital breaths have indeed become unsteady.
(7.2.4.3) Now, if he suffers from a chronic illness, it is because [the priest] has thereby established the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) within him.
(7.2.4.3) Therefore, even if his life-breath has departed, he nevertheless lives.
Prajāpati desired, "May I be propagated. He beheld this Daśahotṛ.
(7.2.5.1) He offered it;
(7.2.5.1) by means of it he created the ten-night rite;
(7.2.5.1) by means of that ten-night rite he was procreated.
One who is about to undergo initiation for the ten-night sacrifice should offer the Daśahotṛ oblation.
By means of the Daśahotṛ itself, he creates the ten-night sacrifice;
through that ten-night sacrifice, he is procreated.
This ten-night sacrifice is indeed the Vairāja;
he who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the ten-night rite, attains the Virāj.
This ten-night sacrifice is also that which belongs to Prajāpati.
(7.2.5.2) He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the ten-night rite is indeed procreated.
(7.2.5.2) Indra, indeed, was equal to the other deities; he did not attain distinction.
He ran to Prajāpati;
he gave this ten-night rite to him,
and he took it.
With that he sacrificed. Thereby, indeed, he attained distinction from the other deities.
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the ten-night rite, attains distinction from his evil rival.
(7.2.5.2) This ten-night sacrifice is indeed three-peaked.
(7.2.5.3) The fifteenfold [stoma] is a peak; the twenty-onefold is a peak; the thirty-threefold is a peak.
He who, knowing this, performs the ten-night sacrifice, becomes three-peaked among his equals.
The sacrificer is the fifteenfold; the sacrificer is the twenty-onefold; the sacrificer is the thirty-threefold; the others are the fortresses.
One who is being practiced against with malevolent magic should sacrifice with the ten-night rite;
thus he encircles the very fortresses of the gods.
For him there is no injury from any quarter;
one practicing sorcery against him does not strike him down.
The gods and the asuras were engaged in conflict.
Those gods saw these divine fortresses, namely the ten-night rite;
they surrounded them,
and for them there was no affliction from any quarter whatsoever.
(7.2.5.4) Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
(7.2.5.4) He who has a rival should sacrifice with the ten-night rite;
he thus encircles the very strongholds of the gods.
For him there is no injury from any quarter;
he prospers in himself, while his rival is defeated;
the *stoma* becomes the underlayer for the *stoma*.
(7.2.5.4) He thus makes his rival a servant.
(7.2.5.5) Indeed, they commit a repetition when, having approached a larger *stoma*, they approach a smaller one.
In that the *agniṣṭomasāmans* occur both below and above, it is for the sake of avoiding repetition.
The Agniṣṭoma is a Trivṛt; it takes place with verses addressed to Agni in the Agniṣṭut rite, whereby one obtains splendor.
The Ukthya is a Pañcadaśa; it takes place with verses addressed to Indra.
Verily, he wins sensory power;
with the *trivṛt* *agniṣṭoma* on verses addressed to the Viśvedevas,
he wins prosperity.
The Agniṣṭoma with seventeen stomas is performed with the Tīvrīsoma cups dedicated to Prajāpati;
it is for the attainment of food.
Moreover, through this, one is indeed born here.
The Ukthya sacrifice is the twenty-one-fold [stoma] with verses addressed to Sūrya for the sake of stability; furthermore, he thereby places radiance within himself.
The Agniṣṭoma is the seventeen-fold [stoma], and the Upahavya is performed with verses addressed to Prajāpati.
(7.2.5.6) He indeed obtains the invitation.
(7.2.5.6) There are two *agniṣṭoma* sacrifices with twenty-seven verses on both sides, performed with verses addressed to Indra,
for the sake of victory.
The Trayastriṃśa Ukthya [is performed] with the Vaiśvadeva verses for the sake of stability; it becomes a Viśvajit Atirātra sacrifice characterized by all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras.
For the conquest of everything.
(7.2.6.1) The seasons, desiring offspring, did not find offspring.
They desired:
"May we create offspring; may we win offspring; may we find offspring; may we be possessed of offspring."
They saw this eleven-night rite;
they brought it forth; with it they sacrificed.
(7.2.6.1) Thereupon they indeed created offspring; they won offspring; they found offspring; they became possessed of offspring.
They became the seasons (ṛtu). That is the reason for the name "seasonal" (ārtava) of the seasonal offerings.
(7.2.6.1) These are indeed the sons of the seasons; (7.2.6.1) therefore they are called "seasonal" (*ārtava*).
(7.2.6.2) Those who, knowing this, perform the eleven-night rite, create progeny, secure progeny, obtain progeny, and become possessed of progeny.
There is a Jyotis Atirātra;
they place the Jyotis in front for the purpose of illuminating the world of heaven.
There is a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period.
There are six seasons and six *pṛṣṭha* chants; by means of the *pṛṣṭhas*, they ascend after the seasons, and by means of the seasons, [they ascend] after the year.
They find firm support in the year itself;
it consists of twenty-four [stomas],
for the Gāyatrī has twenty-four syllables.
The Gāyatra is spiritual luster.
Verily, they find firm support in the Gāyatrī and in spiritual luster.
It consists of forty-four [syllables].
The *triṣṭubh* consists of forty-four syllables;
the *triṣṭubh* is power.
They find firm support in the *triṣṭubh*, which is power.
It consists of forty-eight [verses].
The Jagatī meter has forty-eight syllables;
cattle are of the Jagatī nature.
(7.2.6.3) They find firm support in cattle through the Jagatī metre itself.
(7.2.6.3) There is an eleven-night rite;
for there are five seasons, and five seasonal periods.
Having established themselves in the seasons, in the seasonal periods, and in the year, they win progeny.
There are Atirātra rites on both sides for the sake of securing what has been born.
(7.2.7.1) He who desires, "May offspring be established in due order," should draw the cups beginning with that for Indra and Vāyu.
