Indeed, offspring are established according to the establishment of the sacrifice; they are not established according to the non-establishment of the sacrifice.
(7.2.7.1) He arranges the subjects exactly as before;
(7.2.7.1) the younger does not overstep the elder.
(7.2.7.1) One who is afflicted by disease should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu.
(7.2.7.1) He whose illness afflicts him is indeed deprived of his vital breath (*prāṇa*).
(7.2.7.1) The cup for Indra and Vāyu is the vital breath.
(7.2.7.1) By means of the vital breath itself, he causes him to prosper again.
(7.2.7.1) Those whose consecrated member should die should draw the cups beginning with that for Mitra and Varuṇa.
(7.2.7.2) Those among the consecrated who die are deprived of out-breath and in-breath.
(7.2.7.2) Mitra and Varuṇa are out-breath and in-breath;
thus they restore out-breath and in-breath from the very beginning.
(7.2.7.2) One who is of lower birth should draw the cups beginning with that for the Aśvins.
(7.2.7.2) The Aśvins were indeed the two of lowest birth among the gods; they attained the foremost place as if by means of cattle.
The Aśvins are the deity for him who is of lower birth.
Those two indeed lead him to the forefront.
One who has attained prosperity and desires a firm foundation should draw the cups with the *śukra* first.
Yonder sun is indeed the *śukra*; he is within this [world].
(7.2.7.2) A man [reaches] the end. (7.2.7.3) Having gone for the sake of prosperity, he returns from the end; verily, from the end he seizes the end, and he does not become worse than before.
(7.2.7.3) One practicing exorcism should take the draughts from the *manthin* cup.
(7.2.7.3) For this *manthin* cup is indeed a vessel for the afflicted;
thus, he causes death itself to seize him.
(7.2.7.3) He swiftly meets with ruin. (7.2.7.3) One whose father and grandfather were virtuous, but who has not yet attained that [status], should draw the cups beginning with the Āgrayaṇa.
(7.2.7.3–4) Verily, he whose father and grandfather were virtuous but who does not attain that [status] is deprived of speech and of vital power.
The Āgrayaṇa is like the breast of the sacrifice, like speech.
Verily, by means of speech and power, he causes it to prosper;
he does not become worse than before.
(7.2.7.4) One who is being subjected to malevolent magic should draw the cups beginning with the Ukthya.
(7.2.7.4) For this Ukthya cup is the vital power (*indriya*) of all the vessels.
(7.2.7.4) Thus, by means of every vital power, he impels him forward.
(7.2.7.4) He should use as the *puroruc* [the verse]: "O Sarasvatī, lead us toward what is better.
(7.2.7.5) Sarasvatī is indeed speech; verily, by means of speech he impels him forward.
(7.2.7.5) "May we not go from thee to alien fields," he says.
(7.2.7.5) The fields of Death are indeed desolate.
By that very means, one does not go to the fields of Death.
One should draw full cups for one who is ill.
The pain reaches his vital breaths when he is ill;
the cups are the vital breaths;
verily, he releases the pain from his vital breaths.
(7.2.7.5) Or even if he has departed the life-force, he indeed continues to live.
(7.2.7.5) One should draw the full cups when Parjanya does not rain.
For at that time, pain afflicts the vital breaths of living beings when Parjanya does not rain.
The vital breaths are the cups;
verily, he releases the vital breaths of living beings from affliction,
and it rains immediately.
The cup for Indra and Vāyu is indeed of the Gāyatrī metre;
the opening day is of the Gāyatrī metre;
therefore, on the opening day, the cup for Indra and Vāyu is drawn.
(7.2.8.1) He draws it in its own abode;
(7.2.8.1) for the Śukra cup belongs to the Triṣṭubh,
and the second day belongs to the Triṣṭubh.
Therefore, on the second day, the Śukra cup is drawn;
he draws it in its own proper abode.
For the Āgrayaṇa belongs to the Jagatī metre.
The third day belongs to the Jagatī metre;
therefore, on the third day the Āgrayaṇa draught is drawn.
Thus he draws it in its own proper abode.
(7.2.8.1) This indeed is the attainment of the sacrifice when one attains the meters.
(7.2.8.2) When the Āgrayaṇa is drawn on the following day, he joins that sacrifice again from the very point where they first beheld it.
The second three-night rite has the Jagatī as its opening.
The Āgrayaṇa cup belongs to the Jagatī metre.
In that the Āgrayaṇa is drawn on the fourth day, he draws it in its own proper abode;
moreover, they return to their own respective metres.
The cup for Indra and Vāyu is connected with the *rathaṃtara* chant;
the fifth day is connected with the *rathaṃtara*.
Therefore, on the fifth day, the cup for Indra and Vāyu is drawn.
He takes him up in his own abode;
for the Śukra belongs to the Bṛhatī,
and the sixth day belongs to the Bṛhatī.
Therefore, on the sixth day, the *śukra* cup is drawn;
he draws it in its own proper abode.
Indeed, this is a second sacrifice that one reaches when one obtains the *chandas* meters.
In that the Śukra cup is drawn on the following day, he thereby re-employs the sacrifice from the very point where they first beheld it.
The third three-night period has the Triṣṭubh as its opening; the Śukra belongs to the Triṣṭubh.
In that the Śukra is drawn on the seventh day, he draws it in its own proper abode;
moreover, they turn back according to their own metre.
The Āgrayaṇa, indeed, is speech.
Speech is the eighth day;
therefore, on the eighth day the Āgrayaṇa cup is drawn.
Thus, he draws it in its own proper abode.
The cup for Indra and Vāyu is indeed the vital breath;
the ninth day is the vital breath.
Therefore, on the ninth day, the cup for Indra and Vāyu is drawn.
He takes it in its own very abode.
This, indeed, is the third time they have reached the sacrifice when they reach the meters.
Since the cup for Indra and Vāyu is drawn on the following day, he joins the sacrifice again from the very point where they first beheld it.
(7.2.8.5) Moreover, they return according to their own very metre.
(7.2.8.5) Those who proceed by another [path] than the one following the Aindravāyava cup indeed go from the path onto a non-path.
(7.2.8.5) For this tenth day is truly the interior of the sacrifice.
On the tenth day, the cup for Indra and Vāyu is drawn;
having thus reached the end of the sacrifice, they do not go astray from the path. Moreover, it is just as when they drive with a more powerful vehicle back toward the starting point.
The *chandases* (metres) sought one another's place;
the gods separated them by means of this very [rite].
This fourth day is indeed the resting place of the cup for Indra and Vāyu.
In that [cup] the Āgrayaṇa is drawn.
Therefore, on the ninth day, the Aindravāyava is drawn in the place of the Āgrayaṇa. For the fifth day is indeed the place of the Śukra.
(7.2.8.7) In that [cup] the draught for Indra and Vāyu is drawn.
(7.2.8.7) Therefore, on the seventh day, the *śukra* cup is drawn in the place of the draught for Indra and Vāyu.
(7.2.8.7) For the sixth day is indeed the place of the *āgrayaṇa*.
For him the *śukra* cup is drawn;
therefore, on the eighth day, in the place of the *śukra*, the *āgrayaṇa* cup is drawn; thus he causes the meters themselves to move apart.
He who knows thus obtains a marriage with a more excellent woman;
furthermore, he establishes an agreement among the deities at the sacrifice,
and therefore one person gives this to another.
Prajāpati desired, "May I be propagated. He beheld this twelve-night rite.
He brought it; he sacrificed with it;
from that, indeed, he was procreated.
(7.2.9.1) He who should desire, "May I procreate," he should sacrifice with the twelve-night rite.
(7.2.9.1) He is indeed born. (7.2.9.1) The exponents of the Veda say:
"The sacrifices have the Agniṣṭoma as their starting point; why then is the Atirātra employed first?"
(7.2.9.1) These two Atirātras are indeed the eyes of the sacrifice, and the two Agniṣṭomas are the pupils.
(7.2.9.2) If they were to perform the Agniṣṭoma first, they would place the pupils on the outside;
therefore, the Atirātra is performed first.
Having placed the two eyes upon the sacrifice, they set the two pupils in the middle.
Verily, he who knows the Gāyatrī with wings of light goes to the heavenly world by means of its light and radiance;
those two Agniṣṭomas are its two wings.
The eight Ukthya-stotras that are within constitute the body.
This Gāyatrī indeed has light for its wings;
he who knows thus goes to the heavenly world by means of light and radiance.
(7.2.9.3) This twelve-night rite is indeed Prajāpati divided into twelve parts.
(7.2.9.3) The two *atirātra*s are the two wings;
(7.2.9.3) those eight *ukthya*s in between are the body.
This [sacrificer] is indeed Prajāpati; being real, he truly rescues himself by means of the *sattra*. The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed the real; verily, he rescues the vital breaths.
(7.2.9.3) "Those who sit for a sacrificial session (sattra) sit with the vital breaths (prāṇa) of all creatures; therefore they ask: 'Are these men performers of a sacrificial session?'"
He who knows this becomes beloved by his subjects and rises up.
(7.2.10.1) This Vaiśvānara, indeed, was not able to reach the heavenly world from any other direction.
(7.2.10.1) He was stretched out upwards; those gods then pushed this Vaiśvānara around for the attainment of the heavenly world.
The seasons indeed caused Prajāpati to sacrifice with this;
he prospered among them. He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the twelve-day rite, truly prospers among his officiating priests.
They desired him;
he gave the essence to the spring. He gave barley to the summer, herbs to the rainy season, rice to the autumn, and mung beans and sesame to the winter and the cool season.
With that, Prajāpati caused Indra to sacrifice.
(7.2.10.2) From that indeed Indra became Indra; therefore they say,
"The sacrifice belongs to one who follows behind."
For he indeed sacrificed with this first.
Verily, he who accepts [gifts] at a *sattra* eats a corpse—he eats the corpse of a man, the corpse of a horse. Cattle, indeed, are food.
From whatever vessel they carry food and do not wash it clean, impurity arises from that. Only one person should sacrifice; for Prajāpati alone prospered.
One should remain consecrated for twelve nights.
Twelve months constitute a year;
the year is Prajāpati.
Prajāpati, indeed, is this;
for he alone is truly born who is born from austerity.
These twelve *apasads* consist of four sets of three nights each.
With those which are first, he collects the sacrifice;
with those which are second, he undertakes the sacrifice. With those which are third, he washes the vessels;
with those which are fourth, he purifies himself within.
Whoever eats his animal, he eats its flesh; whoever eats the sacrificial cake, he eats its marrow; whoever eats the parched grain, he eats its dregs.
He who [accepts] the clarified butter accepts the marrow; he who [accepts] the Soma accepts the sweat.
Indeed, he who accepts gifts at the twelve-day sacrifice receives even the secret excretions from his head.
Therefore, one should not perform the sacrifice with the twelve-day rite for the sake of warding off evil.

(7.3.1.1) By means of this tenth day, they indeed proceed with speed;
by means of this tenth day, they indeed become free from evil.
For he who, when traveling swiftly, takes to a wrong path, or strikes against a stump, or falls into error—he is left behind.
(7.3.1.1) Indeed, whoever is struck down on the tenth day, the *avivākya*, is excluded.
He who pronounces the verdict for that one who has been struck down, by taking hold of him, attains [the sacrifice] together with him.
But he who pronounces the verdict is himself excluded. (7.3.1.2) He is excluded.
Therefore, on the tenth day, the *avivākya*, one should not speak out against one who has been struck down.
Now, moreover, they say:
"By the success of the sacrifice, the gods went to the heavenly world; by the failure of the sacrifice, they brought about the defeat of the Asuras."
(7.3.1.2) Whatever indeed is successful in the sacrifice belongs to the sacrificer; whatever is unsuccessful belongs to his rival.
(7.3.1.2) He who is struck down on the tenth day, the *avivākya*, he alone causes [the sacrifice] to overflow.
(7.3.1.2-3) Those who are outsiders, the *dṛśīkas*, they should speak out against him.
(7.3.1.3) If they should not find [the *stotra*] there, it should be recited from within the *sadas*.
(7.3.1.3) That indeed must be recited.
(7.3.1.3) Or rather, they chant this with the verses of the Queen of Serpents (*sarparājñī*).
(7.3.1.3) This earth is indeed the queen of the serpents (*sarparājñī*).
Whatever they praise in her, and whatever they have praised, by that she is the queen of the serpents.
(7.3.1.4) "Whatever we have praised with speech, and whatever those who will praise after us shall praise—having attained and secured both of these, let us rise up. Thus [they thought].
(7.3.1.4) With these [verses] they praise with the mind.
(7.3.1.4) Indeed, neither a horse-chariot nor a mule-chariot is able to traverse this earth instantly;
only the mind is able to traverse it instantly, for the mind is capable of encompassing it.
(7.3.1.4) Then they discourse on Brahman:
"The *ṛc*s are indeed limited, the *sāmans* are limited, and the *yajus* formulas are limited; but of this Brahman there is no end. Therefore, one should explain it to him who responds."
That is the response.
(7.3.2.1) The exponents of Brahman say:
(7.3.2.1) "What does the sacrificer win from the officiating priests by means of the first day of the twelve-day rite?
(7.3.2.1) "Vitality and sensory power."
"What is gained by the second?
"The vital breaths and food. "What is gained by the third?"
"These three worlds"—
with what [does he correspond] by means of the fourth?
"Four-footed cattle."
(7.3.2.1) "What [is gained] by the fifth?
(7.3.2.1) "The *paṅkti* meter, which consists of five syllables.
(7.3.2.1) "What [is gained] by the sixth?"
"Six seasons"—
with what as the seventh?
"With the seven-footed Śakvarī verse."
"What by the eighth?
"The *gāyatrī* of eight syllables. "What by the ninth?"
"The threefold hymn-form"— by what [is it attained]? "By the tenth"— [meaning] "the ten-syllabled *virāj*."
(7.3.2.2) "What is the purpose of the eleventh?
(7.3.2.2) "To obtain the *triṣṭubh* meter, which consists of eleven syllables.
(7.3.2.2) "What is the purpose of the twelfth?"
(7.3.2.2) "The twelve-syllabled Jagatī"— as much as there is, so much indeed is this. Whatever exists, that he seizes from them.
(7.3.3.1) This twelve-day rite is indeed complete when it consists of thirteen nights.
(7.3.3.1) For that day which is the opening day and that which is the concluding day are identical; (7.3.3.1) there are three *atirātra* rites.
(7.3.3.1) These are the three worlds. For the attainment of these worlds,
the first *atirātra* is indeed the *prāṇa*, the second is the *vyāna*, and the third is the *apāna*.

(7.3.3.1) Those who, knowing this, perform the thirteen-night rite, find firm support in the out-breath, the in-breath, and the up-breath, as well as in the eating of food; they reach a full lifespan.
(7.3.3.1) Regarding this, they say: (7.3.3.2) "This twelve-day rite is indeed speech stretched out."
(7.3.3.2) They should break that [sequence] if they were to place the *atirātra* in the middle; the speech of the householder would be liable to fail.

They perform the *mahāvrata* after the *chandomas*; thus he secures speech as a continuous flow, and the speech of the householder does not fail. The *chandomas* are indeed cattle, and the *mahāvrata* is food.
(7.3.3.2) In that they perform the Mahāvrata after the Chandomas, they find firm support in cattle and in food.
(7.3.4.1) The Ādityas desired,
"May we prosper in both worlds. (7.3.4.1) They beheld this fourteen-night rite.
(7.3.4.1) Bringing it, they sacrificed with it. Thereby, indeed, they prospered in both worlds— both in this one and in that one.
Those who, knowing thus, perform the fourteen-night rite, prosper in both worlds—both in this one and in yonder one.
There is a fourteen-night rite;
there are seven cultivated plants and seven wild plants, for the attainment of both kinds.

In that there are *pṛṣṭha* stotras directed forward, they conquer yonder world by means of them; in that there are *pṛṣṭha* stotras directed backward, they conquer this world by means of them. There are two *triṃśat* stomas in the middle; verily, they attain sovereignty.
There are two *adhirāja* [Soma] offerings; thus they become supreme rulers among their equals.
There are *atirātra* [sacrifices] on both sides for the sake of complete enclosure.
Prajāpati went to the heavenly world;
the gods followed him;
the Ādityas and the cattle followed them.
Those gods said,
"Those cattle upon which we have subsisted have followed after these [cattle].
For them, they set aside this fourteen-night rite.

(7.3.5.1) Those Ādityas ascended to the heavenly world by means of the *pṛṣṭha* chants; by means of the two three-day periods (*tryaha*), they drove cattle back to this world. (7.3.5.1–2) By the *pṛṣṭha* chants the Ādityas prospered in yonder world; by the two three-day periods, cattle [prosper] in this world. Those who, knowing thus, perform the fourteen-night rite, prosper in both worlds—both in this one and in yonder one.
(7.3.5.2) By means of the *pṛṣṭha* chants they prosper in yonder world; by means of the two three-day periods (*tryaha*) they prosper in this world.
(7.3.5.2) There is a three-day period consisting of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus.
This [earth] indeed is Jyotis, the intermediate space is Gauḥ, and yonder [sky] is Āyus.
(7.3.5.2) They ascend these very worlds;
for if the *pṛṣṭha* chants were on one side, there would be a lack of connection. The *pṛṣṭhas* are in the middle to ensure continuity.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed vigor and strength;
they place vigor and strength in the very middle.
They proceed with the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara*.
This [earth] indeed is the Rathantara; that [heaven] is the Bṛhat.
By means of these two alone they proceed; moreover, they find firm support in these two alone.
(7.3.5.3) These indeed are the two direct paths of the sacrifice; by means of these very paths they go to the heavenly world.
Those who perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants in succession are indeed ascending to the heavenly world in a forward direction.
The three-day period proceeds in reverse order for the sake of descending again and also for the sake of stability;
having prospered in both worlds, they stand firm.
These [days] are fourteen.
Of those [days], ten are ten-syllabled *virāj* verses; the *virāj* is food, and by means of the *virāj*, they obtain food.
Those which are four are the four quarters; thus they find firm support in the quarters.
There are *atirātra* rites on both sides for the sake of enclosure.
Indra was indeed equal to the other deities; he did not attain distinction. He ran to Prajāpati for refuge.
He gave this fifteen-night rite to him; he took it up and sacrificed with it.
(7.3.6.1) Thereupon, he indeed attained distinction from the other deities.
Those who, knowing thus, perform the fifteen-night rite, attain distinction from evil and from their rival. It consists of a three-day period: Jyotis, Go, and Āyus.
(7.3.6.1) This [earth] is indeed light; the intermediate space is the [second].
(7.3.6.2) "The cow is that life-force.
(7.3.6.2) Thus they find firm support in these very worlds.
(7.3.6.2) That which is without *chandomas* is indeed not a *sattra*.
In that there are Chandomas, it is thereby a *sattra*.
By means of the *pṛṣṭha* stotras they win the deities, and by the Chandomas they win cattle.
They find firm support in strength, in virility, and in cattle.
There is a fifteen-night rite.
The thunderbolt is fifteenfold;
they hurl the thunderbolt at their enemies.
There are Atirātra rites on both sides,
for the sake of securing power.
(7.3.7.1) Indra, indeed, was as if loose and without support; he was afraid of the Asuras. He ran to Prajāpati for refuge.
To him he gave this fifteen-night rite as a thunderbolt.
With it, having overcome and conquered the Asuras, he attained glory.
By means of the Agniṣṭut, he burned away evil; by means of the fifteen-night rite, he placed vigor, strength, sensory power, and heroism within himself.
(7.3.7.1) Those who, knowing thus, perform the fifteen-night rite, having utterly defeated their rivals and conquered, attain prosperity.
(7.3.7.1) By means of the Agniṣṭut they burn away evil; by means of the fifteen-night rite they place vigor, strength, sensory power, and heroism within themselves.
These [rites] are indeed conducive to cattle.
There are fifteen nights in a half-month;
the year is attained by means of half-months;
animals are born following the year.
Therefore, these [days] are favorable for cattle; they are indeed conducive to heaven. There are fifteen nights in a half-month.
The year is attained by means of half-months;
the year is the world of heaven;
therefore, they lead to the world of heaven.
The three-day period consists of the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, and the Āyus.
This [earth] indeed is the Jyotis, the intermediate space is the Gauḥ, and yonder [sky] is the Āyus.
Verily, they ascend these very worlds.
(7.3.7.3) If the *pṛṣṭha* stotras were on one side, there would be a lack of connection. (7.3.7.3) The *pṛṣṭha* stotras are in the middle for the sake of providing connection.
(7.3.7.3) The *pṛṣṭha* stotras are indeed vigor and strength.
(7.3.7.3) They place vigor and strength in the middle;
they proceed with the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans].
This earth is indeed the Rathantara, and yonder sky is the Bṛhat.
(7.3.7.3) They proceed by these very two; thus, they find firm support in these two.
These indeed are the direct paths of the sacrifice.
By means of these two alone, they go to the heavenly world.

Indeed, those who perform the *pṛṣṭha* days in forward succession ascend to the heavenly world in a forward direction. There is a three-day period in reverse order for the sake of descending back [to earth] and for the sake of firm establishment.
Having prospered in both worlds, they stand firm.
These [verses] are fifteen;
of these, those which are ten are the Virāj, for the Virāj has ten syllables. The Virāj is food; verily, by means of the Virāj, they obtain food.
The five [sets of] five directions find firm support in the very quarters. There are Atirātra rites on both sides for the sake of grasping power, vigor, progeny, and cattle.
Prajāpati desired,
"May I be an eater of food.
He beheld this seventeen-night rite.
He brought it; he sacrificed with it. Thereupon, indeed, he became an eater of food.
Those who, knowing thus, perform the seventeen-night rite become eaters of food.
There is a five-day period;
for the year consists of five seasons.
Verily, they find firm support in the seasons and in the year;
moreover, the *paṅkti* consists of five syllables, and the sacrifice is fivefold.
(7.3.8.1) They indeed obtain the sacrifice.
(7.3.8.1) That which lacks the Chandomas is, as it were, not a sacrificial session (asattra).
(7.3.8.2) In that there are Chandomas, by that it becomes a sacrificial session (sattram).
By means of the *pṛṣṭha* stotras they win the deities; by means of the *chandomas* they win cattle. They find firm support in strength, in vigor, and in cattle.
There is a seventeen-night rite.
The seventeenfold [stoma] is Prajāpati;
it is for the attainment of Prajāpati.
There are Atirātra rites on both sides.
For the securing of food.
(7.3.9.1) That Virāj, having stepped forth, stood established among the gods by means of the *brahman* and among the *asuras* by means of food.
(7.3.9.1) Those gods desired: "May we win both—the *brahman* and food. (7.3.9.1) Thus they thought.

(7.3.9.1) They saw these twenty nights. Thereby they indeed gathered both together—both the sacred word (*brahman*) and food—and they became possessed of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*) and eaters of food. Those who, knowing this, perform these [nights], gather both together—the sacred word and food—and they become possessed of spiritual luster and eaters of food. (7.3.9.2) They become possessed of spiritual luster and eaters of food.
(7.3.9.2) These two, indeed, are Virājs;
upon these two they find support separately.
Man consists of twenty parts: ten fingers on the hands and ten on the feet.
Having reached the man in his full extent, they stand up.
There are three-day periods consisting of Jyotis, Go, and Āyus.
This earth is indeed Jyotis, the intermediate space is Go, and yonder sky is Āyus.
They ascend these very worlds. The three-day periods proceed in regular succession;
indeed, they ascend to the heavenly world in regular succession.
In that the *pṛṣṭha* stotras, which are elsewhere [at the ends],
are placed in the middle, it is for the sake of providing a point of support.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed vigor and strength;
they place vigor and strength in the very middle.
They proceed with the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans].
This [earth] indeed is the Rathantara, and yonder [sky] is the Bṛhat.
By means of these two alone they proceed; moreover, they find firm support in these two alone.
(7.3.9.3) These indeed are the two direct paths of the sacrifice; by means of them they go to the heavenly world.
Those who perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants in a forward direction truly ascend to the heavenly world.
The three-day period proceeds backwards for the sake of descending again and for the sake of stability;
having prospered in both worlds, they stand firm.
There are Atirātra rites on both sides.
For the securing of spiritual luster and the eating of food.
Yonder sun was in this world.
The gods, having enclosed it with the *pṛṣṭha* chants, caused it to go to the heavenly world;
they secured it from below with the subsequent [chants] and established it in the heavenly world by means of the *divākīrtya*.
With the *para* [stomas] they enclosed it from beyond; with the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] they descended.
Now, that sun is indeed enclosed on both sides by the *paras* in yonder world.
In that there are *pṛṣṭhas*, the sacrificers go to the heavenly world by means of them.
(7.3.10.1) They enclose it from below with the *par-* verses; by means of the *divākīrtya* hymn, they find firm standing in the heavenly world.
(7.3.10.2) They enclose it from above with the *para-* verses; they descend with the *pṛṣṭha* chants.
If there were no *para-* verses from above, they would fall headlong down from the heavenly worlds.
If there were no lower *paraḥsāman*s, they would burn away the offspring.
The *paraḥsāman*s are on both sides of the *divākīrtya*;
thus, they encompass them on both sides in the world of heaven itself.
The *divākīrtya* chant is indeed the sacrificer; the *paraḥsāman* chants are the year. The *paraḥsāman* chants occur on both sides of the *divākīrtya*.
(7.3.10.2) They find firm support in the year itself on both sides.
(7.3.10.3) The Divākīrtya is indeed the back, and the Paraḥsāmans are the two sides;
the Paraḥsāmans are on both sides of the Divākīrtya.
Therefore, being afraid, they draw the most numerous cups for the back and the flanks;
the most numerous [verses] are recited.
(7.3.10.3) They tie a knot in the middle of the sacrifice itself to prevent it from slipping apart.
(7.3.10.3) Seven [libations] are taken;
for there are indeed seven vital breaths in the head.

Verily, they bestow the vital breaths upon the sacrificers. In that the *pṛṣṭha* chants are performed in successive order, they ascend thereby to yonder world. If they were not to descend again to this world, the sacrificers would either become intoxicated with pride or perish.
In that the *pṛṣṭha* chants are performed facing westward,
they descend toward this very world by means of them;
moreover, they find firm standing in this very world to prevent madness.
Indra, indeed, was without a firm foundation;
he ran to Prajāpati,
who bestowed upon him this twenty-one-night rite.
He brought it; he sacrificed with it;
from that, indeed, he established himself firmly.
(7.3.10.4) Those who are great sacrificers but lack a firm foundation should perform the twenty-one-night sacrifice.
(7.3.10.5) There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun as the twenty-first.
So many indeed are the worlds of the gods.
In those very [worlds] they find support again in their respective order.
That sun did not shine;
it ran to Prajāpati for refuge.
He gave him this twenty-one-night sacrifice; he took it up and sacrificed with it.
(7.3.10.5) Thereupon he indeed shone forth.
(7.3.10.5) Those who, knowing thus, perform the twenty-one-night rite, truly shine forth.
It is a twenty-one-night rite.
The twenty-one-fold [stoma] is indeed splendor;
they attain splendor, and also stability,
for the twenty-one-fold is stability.
There are Atirātra rites on both sides for the sake of encompassing spiritual luster.
(7.3.11.1.a) May the sacrifice come hither toward me from yonder, he who is the domestic priest of the seers.
Having rendered it godless and heroless, let the Viṣkandha disease fall upon him who hates us; let the body, the impurity of sacrifice, and the debt sink into him who hates us.
O Sacrifice, with that splendor which belongs to you, the sacrifice, come over to me; through the austerity of the sacrifice, I invoke for myself the Brahmins, the officiating priests, and the gods.
(7.3.11.1ḍ) With what has been offered, I call upon the cooked [oblation] for you. (7.3.11.2) I gather together for you your well-performed deeds, your offspring, and your cattle.

(7.3.11.2.e) I hear for you the calls, the *sāmidhenī* verses, the two *āghāra* libations, the two *ājyabhāga* portions, the *āśruta*, and the *pratyāśruta*. I choose for myself the *prayāja*s and *anūyāja*s, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the *iḍā*, the blessings, and the light of heaven.
With Agni, Indra, Soma, Sarasvatī, and Viṣṇu—the deities—with the invitatory and offering verses, I invoke you; with the *svāhā* call, I take up the sacrifice for you, the *vaṣaṭ*-uttered.

(7.3.11.2.g) The *stotra*, the *śastra*, the response, the cup, the *iḍā*, and the blessings. (7.3.11.3) I choose the light; I summon the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings for thee; with the cry of *svāhā*, I take the *samiṣṭayajus* from thee.

(7.3.11.3) I invoke for you the cattle, the pressed juice, the sacrificial cakes, the pressings, and also the sacrifice; the gods together with Indra, those who have Agni as their mouth and Soma, and all the others.
(7.3.12.1) The past, the present, and the future—*vaṣaṭ*, *svāhā*, obeisance!
(7.3.12.1) The *Ṛgveda*, the *Sāmaveda*, and the *Yajurveda*—*vaṣaṭ*, *svāhā*, obeisance!
(7.3.12.1) The *Gāyatrī*, the *Triṣṭubh*, and the *Jagatī*—*vaṣaṭ*, *svāhā*, obeisance!
Earth, atmosphere, sky—vaṣaṭ! Svāhā! Homage!
Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya—vaṣaṭ! Svāhā! Homage!
Prāṇa, vyāna, apāna—vaṣaṭ! Svāhā! Homage!
Food, agriculture, rain—*vaṣaṭ*, *svāhā*, obeisance! Father, son, grandson—*vaṣaṭ*, *svāhā*, obeisance!
*Bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, *suvar*—*vaṣaṭ*, *svāhā*, obeisance!
(7.3.13.1.a) May houses be mine, may offspring be mine; may the heroic sacrifice enter me. May the divine, worshipful waters enter me; may the abundance of a thousandfold not forsake me.

(7.3.13.1.b) May my *graha* cup be present; may the *puroruc* be present; may the *stotra* and *śastra*, joined together, enter into me. May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus be my fellow-sitters in the assembly. May the abundance of the thousandfold not depart from me.

May the Agniṣṭoma enter me, and may the Ukthya and the Atirātra enter me; may the Āpiśarvara enter me, and may the well-offered Tiroahniya offerings enter me. May the abundance of a thousandfold wealth not forsake me.
Through Agni he attained heat;
through Speech, the sacred formulation (*brahman*);
through the amulet, forms.
With Indra, [he unites] the gods;
with Vāta, the vital breaths;
with Sūrya, the sky.
The lunar mansions with the moon,
the ancestors with Yama,
and human beings with the king.
With the fruit [he subdues] the water-dwellers; with the python, the snakes; with the tiger, the wild beasts.
With a hawk, [the sacrificer wins] winged birds;
with a stallion, horses;
with a bull, cattle.
(7.3.14.1) From the goat’s skin, goats;
(7.3.14.1) from the ram’s skin, sheep;
(7.3.14.1) from rice, foods.
