(7.4.8.1) They undergo initiation by directly beginning with the year itself.
(7.4.8.1) Those who undergo initiation on the Ekāṣṭakā day indeed undergo initiation against the afflicted part of the year; they fall upon the two seasons named "End.
(7.4.8.1) Those who undergo initiation on the Ekāṣṭakā day indeed undergo initiation against the disintegrated part of the year; they fall upon the two seasons named "End."
(7.4.8.1) They should undergo initiation on the full moon of Phalgunī.
(7.4.8.2) For this full moon of Phalgunī is indeed the mouth of the year;
thus they undertake initiation by grasping the year at its very beginning.
(7.4.8.2) Of that [rite], there is only one exit: it culminates in the Viṣūvant at the conjunction of the moon.
(7.4.8.2) They should undergo initiation on the full-moon day of Citrā;
for the full-moon day of Citrā is indeed the mouth of the year.
(7.4.8.2) They undergo initiation by beginning the year from its very mouth;
for him, there is no exclusion whatsoever.
They should undergo initiation four days before the full moon.
For them, the purchase [of the Soma] coincides with the Ekāṣṭakā;
thus they do not treat the Ekāṣṭakā as a failure. For them, the pressing of the Soma coincides with the bright fortnight.
The months join together with the fortnight of the waxing moon; they rise up during that fortnight of the waxing moon, and as they rise up,
the plants and the trees rise up after them.
Auspicious fame follows after them, saying,
"These sacrificers have succeeded";
and following that, everyone prospers.
(7.4.9.1) Those who enter upon a sacrificial session (sattra) go indeed to the heavenly world.
(7.4.9.1) They kindle themselves with the consecrations (dīkṣās), and they cook themselves with the Upasad rites.
(7.4.9.1) With two [of these rites], they shave the hair.
With two [verses], the skin;
with two, the blood;
with two, the flesh.
With two [verses] he offers the bone,
with two the marrow; indeed,
the sacrificial session has the self as its sacrificial fee.
Having led the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) as their very self, they go to the heavenly world;
they shave their topknots for the sake of prosperity.
(7.4.9.1) "Moreover, being more vigorous, may we go to the heavenly world."
(7.4.10.1) The exponents of sacred knowledge say:
"The Atirātra is the supreme among the sacrificial rites; why then do they perform it first?
(7.4.10.1) They indeed approach the Agniṣṭoma first, then the Ukthya, then the Ṣoḍaśin, and then the Atirātra.
Having approached these sacrificial rites in their proper sequence, having performed them and grasped them, they sit here drinking Soma alone.
They first approach the Jyotiṣṭoma;
for the Jyotiṣṭoma is indeed the mouth of the Stomas.
(7.4.10.1) They yoke the *stomas* at the very beginning. (7.4.10.2) When they have been chanted together, they culminate in the *virāj*, and two verses remain over.
(7.4.10.2) By one [verse] the cow is in excess; by one, life is deficient.
(7.4.10.2) The world of heaven is indeed light, vigor, and the *virāj*; by means of that, they go to the world of heaven.
(7.4.10.2) "The *rathantara* occurs by day, the *rathantara* by night," so say the exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*). "By what means is that not a repetition (*ajāmi*)? they ask.
The *Saubhara* is the *Brahmasāman* at the third pressing; they place it in the middle with the *Bṛhat* [sāman] for the sake of separation.
By this, there is no confusion.
They perform the Jyotiṣṭoma first;
by that, they find firm footing in this very world.
They perform the Goṣṭoma second.
By that, they find firm support in the intermediate space itself.
They proceed to the third [sacrifice], the Āyuṣṭoma;
by that, they find firm support in yonder world itself.
This [earth] indeed is the *jyotis* (light), the intermediate space is the *go* (cow),
and yonder [sky] is the *āyus* (life). When they perform these *stomas*, the performers of the sacrificial session (*sattrins*) proceed while firmly established in these very worlds.
(7.4.11.1) When these are recited together, they amount to a *virāj* verse;
(7.4.11.2) two *ṛc*s remain in excess:
one by which the *go* is in excess, and one by which the *āyus* is deficient.
The heavenly world is indeed light, vigor, and the Virāj; they truly obtain vigor.
They do not suffer from the pain of hunger; they become free from hunger.
For those engaged in a sacrificial session (*sattra*) are, as it were, oppressed by hunger. The two *agniṣṭoma*s on either side are the two fellies;
the *ukthya*s in the middle are the hub.
This very thing is the wheel of the gods.
When they proceed by means of this six-day rite, they mount the very wheel of the gods for safety;
they attain well-being.
They proceed by means of the six-day rite; for there are six seasons;
verily, they find firm support in the seasons.
They proceed with the light on both sides;
indeed, they proceed establishing themselves in the heavenly world from both sides.
There are two six-day periods.
These amount to twelve days.
Man indeed consists of twelve parts: two thighs, two arms, the trunk, and the head—these are four limbs; and the two breasts make twelve.
They revolve around that person;
there are three six-day periods;
these amount to eighteen days.
"New ones, new ones. There are indeed nine vital breaths in a person;
thus they turn back following after the vital breaths.
There are four six-day periods;
these amount to twenty-four days.
There are twenty-four half-months in a year.
They revolve in accordance with the year.
Indeed, they say that the year is unstable, being greater than its foundation.
Truly, O Brāhmaṇa, the sacred teaching regarding the year is as much as that of the month.
Month by month indeed they proceed, finding firm support.

(7.4.12.1.a) May the ram protect you with cooked offerings; the red-necked one with goats; the *śalmali* tree with growth; the *parṇa* tree with sacred knowledge (*brahman*); the *plakṣa* tree with wisdom (*medha*); the *nyagrodha* tree with cups (*camasa*); the *udumbara* tree with strength (*ūrj*); the *gāyatrī* with meters (*chandas*); and the *trivṛt* with hymns (*stoma*).
(7.4.12.1.b) You are the protectors; may the protectors protect you. We invoke you, the beloved among the beloved, the most exalted among kin, the lord of treasures among treasures—O Vasu, mine!
Hail to the wells!
Hail to the rivulets!
Hail to the marshes!
Hail to those dwelling in pits! Hail to those dwelling in excavations!
Hail to those dwelling in the heart!
Hail to the waters of the wells!
Hail to the waters of the lakes!
Hail to the waters of the pools!
Hail to those of the pools!
Hail to those of the rain!
Hail to those that do not rain!
Hail to the hailstones!
Hail to the speckled ones!
Hail to the flowing waters!
Hail to the stationary ones!
Hail to those of the rivers!
Hail to those of the Sindhu!
Hail to those belonging to the ocean!
Hail to all!
Hail to the waters!
Hail to the flowing waters!
Hail to the surrounding waters!
Svāhā to those flowing all around!
Svāhā to those flowing swiftly! Svāhā to those flowing rapidly!
Svāhā to those carrying the fierce; svāhā to those carrying the terrifying;
svāhā to the waters.
To the expanses, svāhā!
To the greatnesses, svāhā!
To the All, svāhā!
(7.4.15.1.a) Varuṇa strikes down him who seeks to kill the courser; far away is the mortal, far away is the dog.
I and you, O slayer of Vṛtra, have come together for the sake of gains; even the hostile, O wielder of the stone, shall acknowledge us both, O Hero—blessed are the gifts of Indra.

(7.4.15.1.c) O Indra, you have indeed surpassed all in wisdom upon the earth; the realms of space cannot encompass your greatness. For by your own power you struck down Vṛtra; no enemy has found the limit of your might in battle.
Homage to the King;
homage to Varuṇa;
homage to the Horse.
(7.4.16.1) Homage to Prajāpati!
(7.4.16.1) Homage to the Overlord! (7.4.16.1) You are the overlord; make me an overlord; may I become the overlord of creatures.
Place me; place me within me.
To the one brought near, svāhā!
Svāhā to the one being sacrificed;
svāhā to the one offered as an oblation.

May the wind blow pleasantly upon the cows; may they graze upon nourishing plants. May they drink from the fat, life-bestowing waters. O Rudra, be gracious to the footed creature that seeks your protection.

Those who are alike, those who are diverse, those who are of one form, whose names Agni knows through sacrifice—those whom the Aṅgirases produced here for the sake of heat—to them, O Parjanya, grant great protection.

(7.4.17.1.c) Those who have extended their bodies among the gods, whose every form Soma knows—grant us those cows, swelling with milk and rich in offspring, O Indra, in our stall! (7.4.17.2) Grant them to us!
Prajāpati, bestowing these upon me, in harmony with all the gods and the ancestors, has brought them—the auspicious ones—into our cow-pen; may we abide together with their offspring.
(7.4.17.2.e) Here is steadfastness, svāhā!
(7.4.17.2.f) Here is separation, svāhā!
(7.4.17.2.g) Here is delight, svāhā!
(7.4.17.2: Here is delight, svāhā!
(7.4.17.2.i) The great earth indeed...
(7.4.17.2.k) Sutrāman.
(7.4.18.1.a) What indeed was the primordial thought? What indeed was the great vital power? What indeed was Piśaṅgilā? What indeed was Pilippilā?
The sky was the first thought; the horse was the great vital power. Night was the blood-drinker; the ewe was the slippery one.
Who indeed wanders alone? Who indeed is born again? What is the remedy for cold? What is the great vessel?
The sun moves alone; the moon is born again; fire is the remedy for cold; the earth is the great vessel for sowing.
I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth; I ask you about the navel of the world. I ask you about the seed of the stallion; I ask about the highest heaven of speech.

They call the altar the furthest limit of the earth; they call the sacrifice the navel of the world. They call Soma the seed of the stallion; the sacred word (*brahman*) alone is the highest heaven of speech.
O Ambā, O Ambālī, O Ambikā!
No one leads me away; the little horse sleeps.
(7.4.19.1.c) O fortunate one, dweller of Kāmpīla, may you both clothe yourselves together in the heavenly world.
(7.4.19.1ḍ) I have conceived a child; may you conceive a child.
(7.4.19.1.e) May we two together cause four feet to extend forth.

(7.4.19.1.f) May the bull, the bestower of seed, bestow seed upon you both. (7.4.19.1.g) Place strength in the two thighs; apply the ointment, drive forth the ointment! That which is the life-consuming [organ] of women, that which among them—(7.4.19.2)—which moves within the secret parts, which is dear to women and hidden, which has struck down the secret strength in their dark mark.
(7.4.19.2) "O Mother! O Ambālī! O Ambikā! No one at all copulates with me; the little horse sleeps."
Raise her upward, like a load of bamboo upon a mountain; then let her middle swell, like one purifying oneself when the cold wind blows.
(7.4.19.2.k) O Ambā, O Ambālī, O Ambikā! No one at all copulates with me; the little horse is sleeping.
When the spotted doe eats barley, she does not consider it nourishment for her offspring; when the Śūdra woman has an Aryan as a lover, she does not desire wealth for the sake of prosperity.
(7.4.19.3ṃ) O Ambā, O Ambālī, O Ambikā! No one at all copulates with me; my little horse is sleeping.
This little bird that crawls along saying "Ahala," the *dhāṇikā*—its feet are struck within the womb and it gurgles.
(7.4.19.3.o) O Ambā, O Ambālī, O Ambikā! No one at all is mating with me; the little horse is sleeping.
Both your mother and your father ascend to the top of the tree. "I loosen it," your father said, as he thrust his fist into the womb.
(7.4.19.4.q) I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan, the victorious, the swift steed. May he make our mouths fragrant; may he prolong our lives.
(7.4.19.4ṛ) O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss; grant us strength for great joy and for the sight [of light].
Whatever most auspicious flavor is yours, grant us a share of it here, like longing mothers.
(7.4.19.4ṭ) Therefore, we come gladly to you, for whose dwelling you quicken us; O Waters, give us life.
(7.4.20.1.a) Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ.

(7.4.20.1.b) May the Vasus anoint you with the Gāyatrī metre; may the Rudras anoint you with the Triṣṭubh metre; may the Ādityas anoint you with the Jagatī metre. (7.4.20.1.c) Since the wind has gone to the waters, the beloved body of Indra—O singer of praise, by this path bring back to us this horse again.
(7.4.20.1ḍ) O you who win parched grain, O you who win wealth—may glory be mine!
(7.4.20.1.e) For the sake of barley-corn and for the sake of cattle, O gods, eat this food; eat this food, O Prajāpati!
(7.4.20.1.f) They harness the ruddy, bright one as he moves around those who stand still; the luminaries shine in the sky.
They yoke his two beloved bay horses to the chariot on its two sides—red, bold, and carrying the hero.
Making a signal for the signal-less, O men, making a form for the formless, you were born together with the dawns.
(7.4.21.1) Svāhā to the out-breath!
(7.4.21.1) Svāhā to the diffused breath! (7.4.21.1) Svāhā to the in-breath!
Hail to the sinews!
Hail to the continuations! Hail to the further continuations!
Hail to the joints!
Hail to the connections!
Hail to the bodies!
Svāhā to the sacrifice!
Svāhā to the sacrificial fees!
Svāhā to heaven!
Hail to the world!
Hail to everything!
To the white one, svāhā!
To the black one, svāhā!
To the addressed one, svāhā!
Svāhā to the unexpressed!
Svāhā to the yoked!
Svāhā to the unyoked!
Hail to the well-yoked!
Hail to the one being yoked!
Hail to the released!
To the one who has escaped, svāhā!
To the one who deceives, svāhā! To the one who deceives completely, svāhā!
To the one who deceives, svāhā! To the one who deceives after, svāhā! To the one who deceives upward, svāhā!
To the one moving, svāhā! To the one running, svāhā! To the one standing, svāhā!
(7.4.22.1) Svāhā to everything!

(7.5.1.1) Once, the cows performed this sacrificial session (*sattra*) with the desire, "Though we are hornless, may horns grow upon us. They remained seated for ten months, and then their horns grew.
They stood up, saying,
"We have succeeded. Then those whose [offspring] had not been born stood up after having reached a year.
"We have succeeded," they said;
both those among whom offspring were born and those among whom they were not rose up together, saying,
"We have succeeded."
The Gosava sacrifice is indeed the year.
Those who, knowing this, undertake the year-long rite, truly prosper. Therefore, the hornless cow grazes during the two months of the rainy season.
For this [sacrifice] has conquered through the sacrificial session (*sattra*);
therefore, whatever is performed in the house of one who sits for a year-long session is performed as something attained, secured, and conquered.
Indeed, those who undertake the year-long session set out upon the ocean.
(7.5.1.2) "He who does not see the far shore of the ocean certainly does not emerge from it. (7.5.1.3) The year, indeed, is the ocean;
its far shore is these two *atirātra* sacrifices.
(7.5.1.3) Those who, knowing thus, undertake the year-long rite, go to the highest world unharmed.
(7.5.1.3) This [earth] is indeed the first Atirātra, and yonder [heaven] is the latter.
(7.5.1.3) Mind is the first, and Speech is the latter.
The out-breath (*prāṇa*) is the former, the in-breath (*apāna*) is the latter;
the former is the entry, the latter is the emergence.
The *jyotiṣṭoma* is indeed the *vaiśvānara* *atirātra*.
(7.5.1.3) They place light in front for the illumination of the heavenly world;
the introductory offering consists of twenty-four [verses].
(7.5.1.3) There are twenty-four half-months. (7.5.1.4) The year is [the goal]; indeed, they find firm support in the year itself. (7.5.1.4) It has three hundred and sixty stotriya verses.
There are as many nights in the year;
they thus attain both forms of the year. Having reached completion and being unharmed, they proceed with the subsequent days.
There are six-day periods;
for there are six seasons in the year.
Verily, they find firm support in the seasons, in the year.
The *gauḥ* and the *āyuḥ* become the two *stomas* in the middle;
that is the pairing of the year itself placed in the middle.
They place it for the sake of procreation;
light surrounds it on all sides.
(7.5.1.5) That is indeed liberation. (7.5.1.5) Thus the meters go to that liberation.
(7.5.1.5) Moreover, by means of the six-day rite which has light on both sides, they go to the world of heaven.
(7.5.1.5) The exponents of Brahman say:
"By what do they go when they sit?
One should reply: "By the path of the gods."
The meters are indeed the path leading to the gods: the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Jagatī.
The Gāyatrī is light, the Triṣṭubh is the cow, and the Jagatī is life. In that these Stomas are employed, [it is for this reason].
(7.5.1.5) By the very path of the gods they go.
(7.5.1.6) The *sāman* is the same;
for the *sāman* is indeed the world of the gods.
They do not go from the world of the gods;
the *ṛc*s become one after another,
for the *ṛc*s are indeed the world of men.
From the world of men alone they go, ascending to one divine world after another.
The *abhivarta* becomes the *brahmasāman*,
for the purpose of ascending to the heavenly world.
There is the Abhijit [sacrifice],
for the conquest of the world of heaven;
there is the Viśvajit, for the conquest of all.
Month by month they perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants;
month by month the *atigrāhya* cups are drawn;
month by month indeed they bestow vigor.
(7.5.1.6) For the stability of the months; (7.5.1.6) they perform the Pṛṣṭha-stotras above the months;
therefore, plants bear fruit at the end.
(7.5.2.1) The cows indeed performed this sacrificial session (*sattra*), being hornless yet desiring to obtain horns.
Ten months passed while they remained seated;
then, their horns grew.
They said, "We have succeeded;
let us rise up. We have attained that desire for which we sat down.
Of them, some said this, while others said as much as they were worth.
(7.5.2.1) "Let us stand up after completing these twelve months as a year," they said.
(7.5.2.1) In the twelfth month, horns grew upon them, either through faith or without faith; they are these cows that are hornless.
(7.5.2.2) Both indeed prospered: those who produced horns and those who secured nourishment.
He prospers when rising after ten months; he prospers after twelve, he who knows thus.
Truly, they go by means of a footprint; truly, one finds by means of a footprint.
This, indeed, is the prosperous path;
therefore, it is a winner of cattle.
In the first month they perform the *pṛṣṭha* days; in the middle [month] they perform them; in the last [month] they perform them.
Regarding this, they say:
"That cow which they milk three times a day yields very little compared to the two other milkings; how then will she yield when they milk her twelve times?"
(7.5.3.1) Having completed the year, they should perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants once in the final month. (7.5.3.1) Thus the sacrificers obtain the sacrifice and cattle.
(7.5.3.2) Indeed, those who undertake the year-long rite float upon an ocean that is shoreless and boundless.
(7.5.3.2) If they were to omit the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans], it would be as if they were to omit a boat in the middle of the ocean; such is that.
(7.5.3.2) By proceeding with the Bṛhat and Rathantara without omission, they attain a firm foundation.
(7.5.3.2) The *sandhi* indeed milks all desires.
(7.5.3.2) Thus, the sacrificers obtain all their desires.
The *ṛc*s are common;
the *ṛc*s are indeed the world of men.
Thus, they do not depart from the world of men.
(7.5.4.1) One *sāman* becomes different from another;
(7.5.4.1) the *sāman* is indeed the world of the gods.
Thus, descending from the world of the gods, they go toward one human world after another.
(7.5.4.1) They approach with the Jagatī first.
(7.5.4.1) Indeed, the meters descend in reverse order to the Jagatī; the Āgrayaṇa cup among the draughts, the Bṛhat among the *pṛṣṭha* chants, and the thirty-three-fold hymn-form among the *stomas*.
(7.5.4.1) Therefore, the younger descends toward the elder.
(7.5.4.1) The cup for Viśvakarman is drawn;
by it the sacrificers obtain all ritual acts.
(7.5.4.2) The cup for Āditya is drawn.
This earth, indeed, is Aditi.
In her they find firm support. They are drawn one after the other for the sake of pairing and procreation.
(7.5.4.2) By means of the ten-night rite, Prajāpati indeed created offspring.

(7.5.4.2) In that there is a ten-night rite, the sacrificers thereby create offspring. (7.5.4.2) Udanka Śaulbāyana declared this to be the prosperity of the sacrificial session (*sattra*), namely the ten-night rite.
In that there is a ten-night rite, it is for the prosperity of the sacrificial session (*sattra*);
moreover, it is the pacification of whatever irregularity (*viloma*) has been committed during the preceding days.

(7.5.5.1) If two Soma sacrifices should coincide, one should commence the Prātaranuvāka during the latter part of the night. (7.5.5.1) By doing so, he first secures the speech, first the deities, and first the meters; he should employ a *pratipad* containing the word "vṛṣan" (bull).
Thus, from the very morning pressing, he secures Indra for them.
Now, moreover, they say:
"It should be performed at each opening of the pressings.
Verily, by doing so at each opening of the pressings, he excludes Indra from them.

(7.5.5.1) For reclining, for sitting, for the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, the Anuṣṭubh, the Paṅkti, for overcoming—svāhā! (7.5.5.1) Reclining and sitting are indeed the meters; by means of the meters he appropriates their meters. (7.5.5.2) He appropriates the meters of those [others].
The *sajanīya* hymn is to be recited;
the *vihavya* hymn is to be recited;
Agastya’s *kayāśubhīya* hymn is to be recited.
(7.5.5.2) There is only as much as this; (7.5.5.2) whatever exists, that he seizes from them.
(7.5.5.2) If the pitcher should break at the morning pressing, they should chant verses addressed to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.
Whatever indeed is redundant in the sacrifice, that is redundant over Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.
Thus Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa places the redundant portion upon the redundant itself. Moreover, by means of the redundant, they obtain and secure the redundant.
(7.5.5.2) If it should break at midday, they should perform the *sāman* with the *vaṣaṭ*-call as its finale (*nidhana*).
(7.5.5.2) The *vaṣaṭ*-call is indeed the foundation of the sacrifice; thus they cause it to reach its very foundation.
(7.5.5.2) If it is at the third pressing, this very same [rite] applies.
(7.5.6.1) Having completed the months by means of six-day periods, they release a day;
for by means of six-day periods they perceive the completion of the months.
Having completed the months by means of half-months, they release a day.
For by means of half-months they perceive the months;
having completed the months with the new moon (amāvāsyā), they release them into the day;
for indeed, by means of the new moon they perceive the months.
(7.5.6.1) Having completed the month with the full-moon sacrifice, they release the day.
(7.5.6.1) For they perceive the end of the month at the full moon.
(7.5.6.1) He who pours out when it is full, he pours away.
(7.5.6.1) He who draws water from the full [jar]—(7.5.6.2) he bestows vital breath (*prāṇa*) upon this [sacrifice].
When they conclude the months with the full-moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) and then release the day for the sake of the year, they thereby bestow vital breath upon the year itself;
accordingly, the performers of the sacrificial session (*sattrin*) breathe.
If they were not to release [the fires] on that day, the year would fall apart just as a bound leather bag falls apart;
they would meet with calamity.
Since they release the fires on the day they have completed the month at the full moon, they thereby provide an outlet for the year.
Thereupon the performers of the sacrificial session drink;
they do not come to ruin,
for on the full moon day the Soma has been pressed for the gods.

When they conclude the month with the full-moon sacrifice and then omit a day, they thereby descend from one sacrifice to another through the sacrifice of the gods. They indeed sever the sacrifice when, after it has been continuous for six days, they omit a day.
They immolate an animal dedicated to Prajāpati.
Prajāpati is all the deities.
By means of the deities themselves, they extend the sacrifice.
Those who omit the day go away from the *savana*. They abandon it.
(7.5.6.4) This *sāṃnāyya* offering is indeed the fourth pressing.
(7.5.6.4) Since there is a *sāṃnāyya*, they do not depart from the pressings; having invited one another, they consume it.
For they indeed partake of the Soma-draught at this time.
Indeed, the deities who share in the pressings go to their respective places for those who omit a day.
At each pressing, they offer sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*).
(7.5.6.4) By means of their respective abodes, they obtain the deities who partake in the pressings:

cakes on eight potsherds at the morning pressing, cakes on eleven potsherds at the midday pressing, and cakes on twelve potsherds at the third pressing. (7.5.6.4) Having thus attained the meters, they obtain them.
At the third pressing, they offer a *caru* oblation for the Viśvedevas;
for the third pressing belongs to the Viśvedevas.
Thus, they do not depart from the third pressing.
(7.5.7.1) "Should one release [the breath] or should one not release it? thus do the exponents of the Veda deliberate. Regarding this, they say: "One must indeed release it."
(7.5.7.1) "One should discontinue [the fire] on the new moon day and on the full moon day," so they say;
for "these two carry the sacrifice. But they say, "These two indeed should not be discontinued," for "they have shared in the intermediate sacrifice."
(7.5.7.1) Regarding the first *vyaṣṭakā*, they say that one should discontinue [the ritual] on that day. (7.5.7.1) "This month is indeed a dissolution (*viśara*)," so they say;
it is not specifically prescribed. (7.5.7.2) They may discontinue [the ritual].

(7.5.7.2) If they should omit what has been prescribed, then at whatever point during the middle of the six-day period the [sixth] day may coincide, having completed the months with six-day periods, they should omit it on that seventh day.

(7.5.7.2) They should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni accompanied by the Vasus; curd to Indra; a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra accompanied by the Maruts; and a cake on twelve potsherds to the Viśvedevas. For the morning pressing belongs to Agni accompanied by the Vasus.

(7.5.7.2) In that he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni accompanied by the Vasus, they thereby make the deity a sharer [in the sacrifice]. (7.5.7.3) They approach the pressing with eight [verses];
in that there is curd for Indra, they do not deprive Indra of his share.
The midday pressing belongs to Indra accompanied by the Maruts.
(7.5.7.3) In that they offer a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra accompanied by the Maruts, they thereby make the deity a sharer; with eleven [potsherds] they approach the pressing.
(7.5.7.3) The third pressing belongs to the All-gods together with the Ṛbhus.
In that they offer a cake on twelve potsherds for the Viśve Devas, they thereby make the deities sharers; with twelve [potsherds] they approach the pressing. (7.5.7.4) They approach it.
(7.5.7.4) They immolate an animal dedicated to Prajāpati;
for Prajāpati is indeed the sacrifice, [this is done] so that the sacrifice may not be abandoned.
(7.5.7.4) For six months from here, the *brahmasāman* is the *abhivarta*.
The *abhivarta* chant is indeed the Brahman.
It is by means of the Brahman that they go forth, ascending toward the heavenly world;
for the heavenly world is, as it were, turned away from here.

"O Indra, bring us wisdom, just as a father provides for his sons. Teach us, O much-invoked one, on this path; living, may we attain the light"—this *Brahmasāman* is performed during the six months when [the sun] moves northward. This world is indeed the light, and progeny is the light.
Beholding this very world, they come forward, addressing it.
When the gods had reached the end, their sensory power and vigor departed.
They recovered it by means of the *krośa* (shout);
that is the reason for the name *krośa*.
In that they chant at the edge of the *catvāla* pit with the *krośa* [chant], having reached the very end of the sacrifice, they win for themselves sensory power and vigor.
They chant at the edge of the *āhavanīya* fire for the prosperity of the sacrificial session (*sattra*). Having made Agni their witness, they attain prosperity.
With the *Prajāpater hṛdaya* they chant within the two *havirdhāna* sheds; thus they attain his very love. They chant with the *Śloka* in front of the *sadas*, and with the *Anuśloka* behind it.
Having reached the very end of the sacrifice, they become partakers of the hymn of praise.
The Adhvaryu chants the *udgītha* with nine [verses].
Indeed, there are nine vital breaths in a person.
Verily, he bestows the vital breaths upon the sacrificers;
all [the cups] belong to Indra;
verily, they bestow sensory power upon the vital breaths.
He chants the *udgītha* with unobstructed [breaths];
therefore, a person draws back all other limbs toward the head,
but not the head itself.
The Rathantara chant becomes fifteenfold; verily they obtain sensory power.
The Bṛhat chant becomes seventeenfold for the acquisition of food;
moreover, by it they are indeed propagated.
The *ekaviṃśa* is auspicious; it is performed in *dvipadā* verses for the sake of stability.
The wives sing along for the sake of pairing and procreation.
Prajāpati created living beings. He desired:
"May I attain sovereignty over these."
(7.5.8.3) By means of the Rājan [Sāman] alone, they attained sovereignty over them;
that is the reason for the name of the Rājan.
When there is a Rājan [Sāman], the sacrificers thereby attain sovereignty over the subjects.

It is the twenty-fivefold [stoma] for Prajāpati, for the sake of attainment. Standing, they chant with five [verses], thereby conquering the world of the gods; sitting, they chant with five [verses], thereby conquering the world of men.
They amount to ten; the *virāj* consists of ten syllables, and the *virāj* is food. By means of the *virāj*, they obtain food.
Having sat down in five ways, they chant;
there are five directions;
verily, they find firm support in the directions.
With each individual chant they come together; from the very quarters they gather food.
With those [chants] the Udgātṛ sings the *udgītha*;
having gathered food from the very quarters, they place splendor within themselves.
Therefore, the single vital breath protects all the limbs.

Moreover, just as a bird about to fly up makes its head the highest part, even so do the sacrificers become the highest among their offspring. The Udgātṛ ascends the throne; they attain true sovereignty.
The Hotṛ [climbs] the *pleṅkha* swing; they indeed ascend to the back of the firmament (*nāka*).
The Adhvaryu [climbs] the two *kūrca* seats; they go to the very summit of the sun (*bradhna*).
So many indeed are the worlds of the gods; in them they find firm standing, each according to his precedence.
Moreover, by this they, the sacrificers, construct a bridge for crossing, for the attainment of the heavenly world.

(7.5.9.1) By means of the *arkya* hymn, Prajāpati indeed created offspring by the thousands. Through the *ilāndas*, he obtained food for them. In that there is an *arkya*, the sacrificers thereby create offspring.
There is an *ilāvat* chant; for the sake of the subjects once they have been created, they thereby obtain nourishment (*irā*) and sustenance.

Therefore, in whatever year a sacrificial session (*sattra*) is successful, the subjects in that year become hungry, for they take away from them their food and strength. In whatever year it is unsuccessful, the subjects in that year do not become hungry, for they do not take away from them their food and strength.

(7.5.9.2) They make a loud shout; just as those being released from bonds make a loud shout, even so do the sacrificers, being released from the bonds of the gods, make a loud shout, placing food and strength within themselves.
(7.5.9.2) The lute has a hundred strings.
A man has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundred powers. They establish themselves in life and power.
They run the race for the sake of winning what has not yet been won.
(7.5.9.2) They beat the drum.
(7.5.9.2) This speech that is in the drum is indeed the supreme speech;
(7.5.9.3) thus they obtain the very supreme speech.
They beat the earth-drum;
verily they win that speech which has entered this [earth],
and moreover, they conquer this very [earth].
They utter all speech;
[this is] for the attainment of all speech.
On a moist hide they engage in the contest.
For the attainment of sensory power.
One cries out, another recites;
he who cries out purifies them indeed.

He who praises [them] places food-eating power (*annādya*) in those very [beings] that have been purified; and it is also made by the *ṛṣis*. By means of the previous months, they obtain what is made by the gods and what is made by the *ṛṣis*; in that the *bhūtechad* chants (*sāman*) are employed, it is for the attainment of both.
Those who undertake the year-long rite indeed depart from the pair.
Two pairs unite within the sacrificial altar;
by that very means, they do not depart from the pair.
They split open the hide;
verily they split open their evil. "Do not fail, do not overreach," he says.
(7.5.10.1) Right now they split asunder the evil of these [men].
Having placed water-jars upon [the mound], female slaves dance around the *mārjālīya* fire, stamping their feet and singing, "This is honey.
Honey, indeed, is the supreme food of the gods.
They obtain the highest food; they stamp down the footprints;
thus they bestow greatness upon them.
To the earth, svāhā! To the intermediate space, svāhā! To the sky, svāhā!
To that which will be submerged, svāhā! To that which is being submerged, svāhā! To that which has been submerged, svāhā!
To that which will become a cloud, svāhā! To that which is becoming a cloud, svāhā! To that which has become a cloud, svāhā! To the cloud, svāhā!
To the mist, svāhā! To the frost, svāhā!
To the flash, svāhā! To the lightning-strike, svāhā!
To that which will flash, svāhā! To that which is flashing, svāhā! To that which is flashing all around, svāhā!
(7.5.11.1) To the one about to thunder, svāhā! To the one thundering, svāhā! To the one thundering fiercely, svāhā!

(7.5.11.1) To the one about to rain, svāhā! To the one raining, svāhā! To the one raining upon, svāhā! To the one raining all around, svāhā! To the one raining together, svāhā! (7.5.11.2) To the one raining after, svāhā! (7.5.11.2) To the one about to sprinkle, svāhā! To the one sprinkling, svāhā! To the one having sprinkled, svāhā!

To him who will sprinkle, svāhā! To him who is sprinkling, svāhā! To him who is sprinkling all around, svāhā! To him who will lift up, svāhā! To him who is lifting up, svāhā! To him who has lifted up, svāhā! To him who will overflow, svāhā! To him who is overflowing, svāhā! To him who has overflowed, svāhā!

(7.5.11.2) To the one who heats himself, svāhā! To the one who heats himself intensely, svāhā! To the fierce one who heats himself, svāhā! (7.5.11.2) To the *ṛc*s, svāhā! To the *yajus* formulas, svāhā! To the *sāman* chants, svāhā! To the Aṅgirases, svāhā! (7.5.11.2) To the Vedas, svāhā! To the *gāthā*s, svāhā! To the *nārāśaṃsī*s, svāhā! To the *raibhī*s, svāhā!
(7.5.11.2) Svāhā to all!
To the toothed, svāhā! To the toothless, svāhā!
To the breathing, svāhā! To the breathless, svāhā!
To the mouthed, svāhā! To the mouthless, svāhā!
To the one with a nose, svāhā! To the noseless one, svāhā! To the one with eyes, svāhā! To the eyeless one, svāhā! To the one with ears, svāhā! To the earless one, svāhā!
Hail to the one with a head, hail to the headless! Hail to the one with feet, hail to the footless! Hail to the one with breath, hail to the breathless!
To him who speaks, svāhā! To him who does not speak, svāhā!
To him who sees, svāhā! To him who does not see, svāhā! To him who hears, svāhā! To him who does not hear, svāhā!
(7.5.12.1) To the mindful one, svāhā! (7.5.12.2) To the mindless one, svāhā!
(7.5.12.2) To the one possessing seed, svāhā! To the seedless one, svāhā! (7.5.12.2) To offspring, svāhā! To procreation, svāhā!
Hail to the hairy one, hail to the hairless one! Hail to the skin, hail to the skinless one! Hail to the one possessing hide, hail to the one without hide!
To the blood-red one, svāhā! To the red one, svāhā!
To the one possessing flesh, svāhā! To the fleshless one, svāhā!
To the sinews, svāhā! To the sinewless one, svāhā!
Svāhā to the boneless, svāhā to the one without bones;
svāhā to the marrowed, svāhā to the marrowless;
svāhā to the limbed, svāhā to the limbless.
Svāhā to the self; svāhā to the non-self;
svāhā to all.
Who yokes you? Let him yoke you. May Viṣṇu yoke you for the success of this sacrifice, for my attainment.
For that desire.
For life, for out-breath, for in-breath, for diffused breath; for the dawning, thee!
For wealth thee, for prosperity thee;
for fame thee, for nourishment thee, for distant fame thee;
for displacement thee.

(7.5.14.1) To Agni, who is connected with the *gāyatrī* metre, the *trivṛt* stoma, the *rathaṃtara* sāman, and the spring season, [an offering] on eight potsherds; (7.5.14.1) to Indra, who is connected with the *triṣṭubh* metre, the *pañcadaśa* stoma, the *bṛhat* sāman, and the summer season, [an offering] on eleven potsherds;
(7.5.14.1) to the All-gods (*viśve devāḥ*), who are connected with the *jagatī* metre, the *saptadaśa* stoma, the *vairūpa* sāman, and the rainy season, [an offering] on twelve potsherds.
To Mitra and Varuṇa, who are associated with the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the twenty-one-fold stoma, the *vairāja* sāman, and the autumn season, there is a dish of curds (*payasyā*).
To Bṛhaspati, who is associated with the *paṅkti* metre, the twenty-seven-fold stoma, the *śākvara* sāman, and the winter season, there is a sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
To Savitṛ, who is associated with the *aticchandas* metre, the thirty-three-fold stoma, the *raivata* sāman, and the cool season (*śaiśira*), there is an offering on twelve potsherds.
(7.5.14.1) A pap offering for Aditi, the wife of Viṣṇu;
(7.5.14.1) a cake on twelve potsherds for Agni Vaiśvānara; (7.5.14.1) a pap offering for Anumati.
The Kāya cake is offered on a single potsherd.
That which is the fire offered into the fire, and that which is King Soma—of these two, this Agniṣomīya [offering] is the guest-offering (*ātithya*).
Now, this Rudra is he who is piled up;
if one were not to offer these oblations when the fire has been piled, [Rudra would consume him].
(7.5.15.1) This very Rudra, if not appeased, might rise up and take ill-will toward the progeny and cattle of the sacrificer.

When he offers these oblations once the fire has been piled, he pacifies him by means of his own portion; thus Rudra, being appeased, does not rise up and take ill-will toward his progeny and cattle. (7.5.15.2) There are ten oblations.
There are indeed nine vital breaths in a person, and the navel is the tenth; verily, he places the vital breaths in the sacrificer.
Moreover, the *virāj* consists of ten syllables.
Food is the *virāj*; verily, he finds firm support in the *virāj* and in the eating of food.
"He is to be piled with the seasons, the meters, the *stomas*, and the *pṛṣṭhas*," they say.
In that he offers these oblations, he piles [the fire-altar] with the seasons, the meters, the *stomas*, and the *pṛṣṭhas*. "By means of the consecrated one, the quarters are conquered," they say;
in that he offers these oblations, it is for the conquest of the quarters.

(7.5.15.3) By means of this very [offering], the gods caused Indra to sacrifice; therefore it is called *indrasava*. (7.5.15.3) By means of this, men caused Manu to sacrifice; therefore it is called *manusava*.
Just as Indra is among the gods and Manu is among men, so does he become who, knowing this, sacrifices with this offering.
The invitatory verses (*puro'nuvākyā*) contain references to the quarters;
this is for the conquest of all the quarters.
(7.5.16.1.a) He who by his greatness became the sole king of all that breathes and blinks, who rules over these bipeds and quadrupeds—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
(7.5.16.1.b) You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Prajāpati. The sky is your greatness, the stars your form, and the sun your splendor. To that greatness, to Prajāpati, svāhā!

(7.5.17.1.a) He who is the giver of self, the giver of strength, whose command all the gods revere—he whose shadow is immortality and whose [other side] is death—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?

(7.5.17.1.b) You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Prajāpati. Earth is your greatness; herbs and trees are your form; Agni is your brilliance. To that greatness, to Prajāpati, svāhā!

(7.5.18.1) May a Brahmin be born in this Brahma-knowledge, endowed with spiritual luster; may a Kshatriya be born in this kingdom, skilled in archery, a hero, and a great chariot-warrior; may there be a cow that yields milk.
The draft-ox is the bearer; the swift steed is the male;
the wise woman is the bride.
May a victorious one, standing upon his chariot, a youth fit for the assembly,
be born as a hero for this sacrificer.
May Parjanya rain for us according to our desire; may our plants ripen with fruit;
may our security and well-being be established.

(7.5.19.1.a) The vigorous steed has stepped upon the earth; the vigorous steed has made Agni his companion. The vigorous steed has stepped into the mid-air; the vigorous steed has made Vāyu his companion. The vigorous steed has ascended to heaven; the vigorous steed has made Sūrya his companion.

(7.5.19.1.b) O steed, Agni is your yoke-fellow; I take hold of you—convey me safely across! O steed, Vāyu is your yoke-fellow; I take hold of you—convey me safely across! O steed, Āditya is your yoke-fellow; I take hold of you—convey me safely across! You are the sustainer of the out-breath; make my out-breath firm. You are the sustainer of the through-breath; make my through-breath firm. You are the sustainer of the in-breath; make my in-breath firm. You are sight; bestow sight upon me. You are hearing; bestow hearing upon me. You are life; bestow life upon me.
The seed is born;
Parjanya is the rain-giver; the grain is ripened.
May the plants bear good fruit; may this earth be easy to traverse;
may Agni be easy to approach.
The atmosphere has a good overseer; the purifying wind is easy to drink from;
the sky is a good place of refuge.
(7.5.20.1) That sun shines auspiciously;
(7.5.20.1) day and night are as before;
(7.5.20.1) the half-months consist of fifteen [days].
The months consist of thirty days;
the seasons are well-ordered;
the year is peaceful.
(7.5.21.1) A cake on eight potsherds for Agni; (7.5.21.1) a pap for Soma;
(7.5.21.1) a cake on eight potsherds for Savitṛ.
(7.5.21.1) An oblation of cooked rice for Pūṣan; (7.5.21.1) an oblation of cooked rice for Rudra;
(7.5.21.1) a cake on twelve potsherds for Agni Vaiśvānara at the den of wild beasts, if [the victim] should not come.
(7.5.21.1) A cake on eight potsherds for Agni, the deliverer from distress;
(7.5.21.1) milk for Sūrya;
(7.5.21.1) a portion of clarified butter for Vāyu.
(7.5.22.1) A cake on eight potsherds for Agni, the deliverer from distress; (7.5.22.1) a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, the deliverer from distress;
(7.5.22.1) a dish of curdled milk for Mitra and Varuṇa, the deliverers from distress.
(7.5.22.1) A pap of cooked rice for Vāyu and Savitṛ, the deliverers from evil; (7.5.22.1) parched grains for the two Aśvins, the deliverers from evil;
(7.5.22.1) a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts, the deliverers from sin.
(7.5.22.1) A cake on twelve potsherds for the Viśve Devas, the deliverers from sin;
(7.5.22.1) a pap for Anumati;
(7.5.22.1) a cake on twelve potsherds for Agni Vaiśvānara.
A cake on two potsherds for Heaven and Earth, the deliverers from distress.
(7.5.23.1) He bowed down to Agni; he bowed down to the Earth.
(7.5.23.1) Just as Agni bowed down to the Earth, so may auspicious inclinations bow down to me. (7.5.23.1) He bowed down to Vāyu; he bowed down to the Atmosphere.
Just as Vāyu has concurred with the intermediate space, so has he concurred with Sūrya;
as Sūrya has concurred with the sky.
He made obeisance to the moon; he made obeisance to the lunar mansions, just as the moon [obeisance] to the lunar mansions. He made obeisance to Varuṇa; he made obeisance to the waters.
(7.5.23.1) Just as (7.5.23.2) Varuṇa conciliated with the waters, he conciliated with the Sāman; he conciliated with the Ṛc.
Just as the Sāman [conciliated] with the Ṛc...
It bowed down to the *brahman*; it bowed down to the *kṣatra*.
Just as the *brahman* bowed down to the *kṣatra*, so did it bow down to the king; it bowed down to the *viś*.
Just as the king prepared himself for the people, he prepared himself for the chariot;
just as the chariot was prepared for the horses.
It has bowed down to Prajāpati; it has bowed down to all beings. Just as Prajāpati bowed down to all beings, so may auspicious submissions bow down to me.
(7.5.24.1.a) O Savitṛ, those paths of yours which are ancient, dustless, and spread out across the mid-air—by those easy-to-traverse paths, protect us today and speak for us, O God!

Homage to Agni, who dwells on earth, who fills the world; grant a world to this sacrificer! Homage to Vāyu, who dwells in the intermediate space, who fills the world; grant a world to this sacrificer! Homage to Sūrya, who dwells in heaven, who fills the world; grant a world to this sacrificer!
(7.5.25.1) Whoever knows the head of the sacrificial horse becomes possessed of a head and fit for sacrifice.
(7.5.25.1) Dawn, indeed, is the head of the sacrificial horse; the sun is its eye.
The wind is the breath;
the moon is the ear;
the quarters are the feet.
The intermediate directions are the ribs;
day and night are the winking of the eyes;
the half-months are the joints.
The months are the joints;
the seasons are the limbs; the year is the body.
The rays are the hair;
the constellations are the form;
the stars are the bones.
The clouds are his flesh;
the herbs are his body hair; the trees are his hair.
Agni is the mouth;
Vaiśvānara is the gaping maw.
The ocean is his belly;
the intermediate space is his anus;
heaven and earth are his testicles.
The pressing-stone is the penis; Soma is the semen.
That which he gnaws is what flashes forth as lightning.
When he shakes himself, that is thunder;
when he urinates, that is rain;
his speech is indeed his voice.
(7.5.25.2) Verily, as the horse is being born, its greatness is born before it; night, as its greatness, is born after it.
These two greatnesses have indeed encompassed the horse on both sides.
As a steed (*haya*), he carried the gods; as a courser (*arvan*), the Asuras; as a racer (*vājī*), the Gandharvas; and as a horse (*aśva*), human beings.
The ocean, indeed, is the womb of the horse; the ocean is its kin.
